This is the first Nancy Drew game I've played, but it quickly became one of my all-time favourites. My only gripe is that it ended too quickly! Just the right amount of challenging puzzles and spookiness and humour. The game has quite a dark, gothic theme to it which I enjoyed, but younger players migth be a little unsettled if they play it late at night.
The puzzles are quite difficult and I got stuck once or twice and even had to take a few days off the game to try to come up with new solutions. There's a lot of material to study in this game if you want to solve it without cheating-- and I do mean study! I had several pages of notes and sketches in my notebook by the time I was done and I'd probably be able to write an essay on the Penvellyns now. That might frustrate some players but if you enjoy being challenged, this is the game for you!

Before I say any of the good things about this game I will say that it does have its fair share of bugs and issues. Also trying to attack bad guys who are in the terrain (a bush or such) can be tedious. Also the first town of this game causes the player to be forced into a good hour (minimum) before they really get back into any combat.
Also, QUICK SAVE OFTEN! And when I say often i mean like every 5 minutes or so cause♥♥♥♥♥♥can go south FAST here ( dig a wrong grave and lava pours out insta killing your party kinda fast).
This all being said I still highly suggest this game for the story driven RPG player. It has such a deep world that you can explore and enough quests to keep you doing something new at every turn. Its a slow starting game but once you learn how the game works it sucks you in. Also i have about 60 hours of play time into this game (i spend a lot of time in game and AFK) and I STILL have yet to beat the game which to me is a HUGE plus. This isnt some RPG that you play and as soon as you really start getting into it with the super strong spells and such its all over.
Next it has to be said that a lot of the downvotes are people complaining that the combat is too hard or not explained enough or unfair. I will admit that i probably spent an hour in the second fight after you get to the first town before i finally beat the zombies but once I did I got the feeling of acomplishment I have not felt since the era of easy♥♥♥♥♥games arrived. Yes its hard as nails at first, it is like that on purpose. It forces you to learn HOW to take advantage of the terrain or the weaknesses of the bad guys or how to combine the abilities of your characters.
Next, the combat in the game is awesome. Using the enviroment to your advantage is the standard not the expection here. Use those oil, water, or poisen barrels to change the terrain or cause massive explosions evening the odds in those hard fights. I loved going into a large open area for a fight and leaving with the entire area scarred from the fight with blood, fire, poisen, ice, water, and corpses. It really is something else to finally finish off the last guy and step back and just look at what you just went through to win that fight.
To sum everything up about this game, its tough to start out get into but worth every second. It is an immersive RPG that brings back those countless fond memories of Baulder's Gate. Give the game a chance and if all else fails use google to help you figure some of the harder puzzles out.

Civilization, along with pretty much other strategy game, is for the thinking man, always looking at the long-run benefits. Civ in particular, though, has always had several options for you to go about achieving your victory, most of them relatively peaceful. It's not hard to see why they pump out sequels.
PROS:
* Models and textures are surprisingly high quality, both on and off the board.
* Soundtrack is varied, pleasant, and changes seamlessly to fit what's happening. Could range from anything to a wartime theme complete with trumpets and drums, to something you'd hear at a classical ball.
* As always, the narration and voice work in general is on point.
* Customizable to the extreme in almost every aspect--gameplay, UI, tutorial hints, graphics, sound--if you can think it, this game can do it. As advertised, it seems to be capable of running on any rig with no trouble.
* Bonus points for upgrading from square tiles to a hex grid.
I struggle to think of any cons for this one. The whole game's mechanically sound, it's tuneable, everything is as-advertised, and it's got polish (pun intended). If you're looking forward to Civ VI and haven't already done so, snag this one, at least when it goes on sale, it's the best game of the series by a long-shot.

I bought this game really wanting to love it. The concept of parkour and run-and-gun gameplay sounds great on paper, but its execution in Mirror's Edge is questionable. The story is boring and the voice acting, while not the most dreadful I've heard, is still pretty bland. The ending was incredibly rushed and there was practically no substance or depth throughout the plot.
The parkour mechanics work and do pump some adrenaline in your gaming veins (I also have a phobia of heights, so it was kinda fun in that sense). There are moments where Faith will unexpectedly not grab ledges (where your margin to grab onto one is pretty reasonable) and you will end up raging quite a bit when Faith will jump to a pipe but not grab it because you're SLIGHTLY off-centered. The game isn't broken per se, but it could've used a lot more work in regards to parkour fluidity and ledge detection.
The enemy AI is incredibly dumb and unfair. All the "blues" do is charge towards you with a constant set of bullets, and snipers have 110% accuracy, even when you're in mid-air. The parry system works half the time since when enemies try to hit you it's always hard to see if the gun turns red (prompt to parry and take the gun). Headshots deal the same amount of damage as a shot to the torso. There is also ZERO variation in enemies. You can argue that they have different weapons and abilities but they all the feel the same; they're all male (except for that one exception), they all have guns, and they all charge towards you.
The story is painfully predictable. Every "twist" I witnessed, I expected early on (the antagonists have the stereotypical "this is how the world works bla bla bla" attitude). Also, the game takes four hours to complete on NORMAL. The other hour I spent playing was me trying to escape the train section, which was absolutely pointless and unrewardingly difficult.
BUT I did have fun with this game. The main parkour sections are well laid out and I did enjoy using different tactics to take down enemies. The visuals are refreshing and the environments feel very open (albeit a little repetitive). The textures are appropriately saturated and detailed.
I can only give this game a maximum of 6 out of 10, and can only recommend Mirror's Edge to people who don't mind trying retracing their steps multiple times. I am looking forward to Mirror's Edge Catalyst, hoping some of my issues with this installment will be fixed for the sequel.

I have so many thoughs about this game, I don't know where to start to write a proper review, so I'll just start off with this: what a game!
You're the omnipresent commander of your own starship, where you have the job of mainting your crew, upgrading your ship, fighting past enemies, and much more, in your journey of survival across space. You come across differerent species of aliens, different types of ships that you can unlock depending on your choices, possible allies, and life or death choices.
Now, despite the graphics and the very easy to learn game mechanics, this game is deceptively difficult! You have to practice the management of fuel, resources, time, and make decisions that can affect your outcome for the rest of the game. What elevates this even more is the game's permadeath mode. If you die, you lose everything have to start over from the beginning. There are no redos, and no way to go back and undo something.  This adds very high level of challenge to the game, as the tactics that may have fared well for you before may get you killed the next time you attempt them, or they may not come around at all. You have to think about every decision you make, because it will affect you later in the game, and you won't get the chance to make such a decision again in the same scenario, because the next game you try will be completely different.
While some may find this a con to the game, and may even discourage some from playing, I find that it's actually what makes the game fun. I've gotten very close to victory several times, and every time I die and have to start over, it's like a second chance at redemption to save my crew, but also to see how much better I can get another time around.
It's for this reason that this game is also highly addicting! Even though you lose everything in death, the fact that you did reminds you of how all of your decisions matter, and that with every time you play, you come that much closer to winning.

I hyped for this game. I was really excited and I couldn't stop thanking my friend for giving me this 'piece of art'.
At least, that's what I would have called it when speaking to me a month ago. Instead, I've tortured myself by playing this game, which is completely my view.
To my disappointment, I think this game lacked parkour. I felt this game was just as focused on parkour as it was on stealth, combat and puzzle.
The puzzle part? Alright, when you're not bound by a time limit, it would be okay. Fortunately, most of the time there was no time limit.
Stealth? Well, trying to hide from snipers sure sounds like fun, but you know? I'd rather not have snipers lethally shoot me down when I'm trying to jump building to building.
Oh, man. How I loved this combat system. When you're carrying a gun, you don't have any aim. No zooming unless you got a sniper. And even when you manage to shoot 'em in the head (without a sniper). Well, no! You're too far away for the game to realise you've landed a correct shot! The game will pretend you hit a wall instead, you wouldn't know how many times I've been screwed over like this.
You'd think that melee would do the job here, right? That just felt underpowered. Confiscating weapons is the most successful, but it takes a mad amount of skill and timing. Not what I hoped for,
I've found some enemies taking me out with two melee hits. All I could do was try steal their gun, but while doing that, I get a bullet rain down on me from another blue. Feels unbalanced to me.
Another point of critique I have, and my main point why I won't really recommend it: It's definitely not for amateurs. I'm not so well at playing games, so I decided to play on easy, yet I still failed over and over again.
I'm at least glad that the story is really well cut out in my eyes. Gave me a sense that this game was at least worth the pain I've gone through.
My thought after finishing this game: I'll never touch it again.
I don't recommend this game for amateurs. If you're not so cut out for gaming, I recommend you watch a playthrough instead.
If you're an experienced gamer, you might enjoy this.
It's a 50/50, but for my own experiences as an amateur gamer, I'll have to give it a pass.

I played this game 4/5 times, so I think that is enough to make a review.
Story:
This game is a first person 3D platformer. You play as Faith, a runner who had her sister framed for a crime and now she has to find the truth about who really committed the crime while running from the government.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very fast paced and forces the player to make sudden choices. The parcore can be very challenging and sometimes there are glitches, but the gameplay is solid and entertaining.
Graphics:
The game itself is very pretty and colourful. It has a certain feel to it which makes you feel like your in a city or a building. The graphics all in all don't matter too much as the game on lowest settings dont look too bad (Although shadows do glitch at times). The reason the graphics dont matter too much is because:
1. There not half bad
2. The game is so fast paced its not too important
3. Its really well made, the first 2 times I played it was on a laptop you can buy at pc world for £300
Sound:
The music is amazing. It doesn't make you want to sing or hum but its really nice to listen to. The sound effects make you feel like your in a city and the voice acting isn't half bad.
Overall I give it and 9/10. The game would be a 10 from me sadly the glitches puts it down one. I still howether strongly recommend this game as its really fun and its got lost of replay ability.

The Walking Dead: Michonne is an episodic miniseries adventure game with only three episodes instead of the five episodes normally seen in a Telltale game and is a filler between The Walking Dead: Season 2 and The Walking Dead: Season Three, developed and published by Telltale Games, the same people behind other such great adventure games as The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones. The game is based on Robert Kirkman's comic book series of the same name
Although the game does not follow the same exact storyline as the comic book series, it follows the same universe as the comic book follows only seeing it in a different point of view. The story does not continue after the events of Season 2 but you play as Michonne, a character from the comic book series in an entirely new story
As mentioned previously, the game is split up into three episodes. The game works as a normal television series. Each length of an episode is roughly one to two hours long
The gameplay is very simple, you move around, selecting stuff and talking to people and using button prompts when told to. The main bulk of gameplay is through the dialogue options. What you say and what you do will effect the game in the long run. Choosing who survives and who dies, choosing who stays and who leaves is all effected by your choices
The game's graphics are nice for the most part however there are some ugly texture work here and there. The sound and music options also vary in quality. Sometimes the sound quality is really good and sometimes the sound quality is bad. I have encountered numerous amounts of glitches which seems as if Telltale Games never got round to fixing them, too many to mention in this review
The game deals with heavy amounts of gory bloody violence which although fine with me can be a bit disturbing for some people
Telltale's The Walking Dead: Michonne is an okay filler for a Telltale Game and the continuation of the story through the recently announced (2016) The Walking Dead: Season Three make for a stellar Telltale series

If, before I got my hands on this game, somebody had shown me a screenshot of The Banner Saga and told me this is a major Hollywood animated film, I would probably have believed them.  That is how gorgeous this game looks.
In The Banner Saga, you are the leader of a caravan forced onto a perilous journey by the onslaught of the creatures known as "dredge".  Besides the relentless advance of the dredge, always just one step behind you, creating an atmosphere of dread and urgency, you will also encounter strangers - villagers, bandits, warriors, etc. - whose intentions are never clear to you and the ways you choose with which to deal with these people would often have unexpeceted, and sometimes even dire, consequences for your caravan.  Such events usually come to affect the 3 major resouces for you and your caravan - renown, manpower and supplies.  Supplies are what keeps your people fed, without them, you would start losing manpower to starvation.  Since a portion of the manpower is warriors and warriors are need to stave off the dredge, you are under constant pressure to keep your people fed.  Renown works both as experience points and as currency.  It can be used to level up your main characters and to buy items and supplies from merchants.
Combats are resolved in the fashion of traditional turn-based battles with full-fledged mechanism.  The whole system is very well thought-out - simple, easy to grasp yet able to present challenges on high difficulty.  With the exception of the final boss fight, combats that are lost don't mean the end of your journey.  Rather, they just make things worse and leave your heroes who have fallen in the battle wounded.  With a few days rest, they'll be able to join you in battle again.
A very original and well fleshed-out fantasy world realized by the breath-taking art design, the choices that you have to make and the outcomes of each hard-fought battle; these pieces come together just right to make you feel like you are experiencing a riveting adventure shaped by your own hands, which is what The Banner Saga all about.
The final boss fight feels like it does not quite deserve the strife your heroes have been put through, and even after it, the major issues of the entire story are still unresolved, and consequantially the ending feels somewhat abrupt.  My guess is there are more to come, and if that's true, I would be very, very happy indeed.

Very important: Nancy will generally mention if you have solved the puzzle correctly.  You don't have to run all the way to the other end of the house to check... again.... and again... and again.
I really wish I'd realized that much earlier in the game.  I would have saved at least 2 hours of gameplay moving around a labrynthine manor of dark, twisty tunnels only to discover that my solution wasn't correct and have to go running back.
Although I love puzzles, this game's puzzle system frustrated me.  At least twice, I solved a puzzle correctly, but hadn't refreshed the puzzle.  Naturally, I thought I had the wrong solution and reached profound levels of frustration before finally resorting to a walk-thru only to discover that I had been correct to begin with.  I struggled with the mini-game about the plants for 3 hours before resorting to a walkthrough only to discover that the plants could be rotated by right-clicking, a fact that is included in the jigsaw puzzle mini-game but omitted in the plant mini-game.  Two of the puzzles were so obscure that even after reading the walkthrough I didn't think I ever would have solved them.
And more than anything, the game's insistence on poorly-lit movement through copious passageways frustrated me into turning toward a walkthrough in the final game instead of running back up to examine the clues in the main manor.
I believe I would have enjoyed this game immensely if the manor tunnels had included a 'hidden dumbwaiter' to transport Nancy around without copious navigation or at least a 'secret lightswitch' to make the navigation easier.  The main puzzles were very enjoyable and the story was interesting.  But with so many other great adventure games out there, it's hard to justify the 14 hours that it took me to finish this one, especially when only half of those hours were spent enjoyably solving puzzles and exploring the mystery.

Talisman has pretty steep learning curve but tutorial/tooltips explain good amount of things to get hang of this game. For those not familiar with Talisman (board game transferred to digital form) first you choose your hero which all have special abilities and six different stats: resolve (hp), fate (rerolls mainly), resources (money), close combat, ranged combat and strategy.
At the beginning of each turn you roll the dice to see where you move and every space has different kind of encounters (and usually need dice roll to determine what happens) and they also are different to each faction. You will travel around battling enemies and other players, buying gear, units etc. Board is divided into three parts: outer, middle and center and to complete the game you must reach the center of the galaxy. When combat happens it is usually done by dice rolls (with added bonuses of equipment and such) but there are some specific special abilities also.
If you do not like Talisman then you do not like this either! But if you are fan of WH40k universe and Talisman then this is your dream come true!

Okay, I want to start by saying if you’re new to Warhammer/Talisman then I wouldn’t recommend you starting here. I wanted to try out the franchise and though I am giving it a positive review I had to invest a decent amount of my own time reading up on things and learning the basics. This is most certainly NOT an intro into the series and in my opinion is not newbie friendly at all but once you’ve learnt what you need to know the gameplay is very, very fun. (This is obviously a personal opinion and others may disagree).
If you’ve played Talisman you’ll be familiar with the gameplay. You can choose a character (or randomly select one) based on your own playstyle. Each character has different stats, Resolve, Fate, Strategy and a few others and these stats determine how you play and essentially if you win or not. Resolve is health, once you lose it all you die. Fate is basically your luck and determines things like die rolls. Resources are your currency and are used to buy services and equipment as you progress. Each of your stats are explained to you when you begin so you’ll quickly grasp those if you're not played before.
You move around the board into different sectors and each sector has different effects/events that’ll trigger when you land on them. Once you’ve rolled your die you’ll be able to move to any sector that is highlighted facing whatever encounter might happen to be there.
The aim of the game is to find the Talisman get to the centre of the board where you’ll face the final battle to determine the fate of the planet. Whilst travelling to toward the centre you’ll face various battles that will (hopefully) make you stronger as you play.
You can play 1v1 or go 2v2 if you want to play with an AI on your side, though the AI isn’t programmed great in my opinion and will make lots of stupid mistakes that’ll end up annoying you.
The gameplay itself is fun, though a little complex to learn but it’s one of those games (like Magic) that once you’ve learn the basics it’s something you’ll never forget and will translate well into other games in the series.

I will start by saying that I own both the physical and digital versions of the original Talisman game and have also been a WH40K fan for close to 20 years.
The game is based on the period in 40k history known, you guessed it,as the Horus Heresy. It began about 10,000 years before the regular timeline when the Emperor of Mankind's greatest Warmaster Horus became corrupted by Chaos which plunged the Imperium of Man into a devastating civil war that saw the rise of the Chaos Space Marines and the near-death of the Emperor along with the fall of almost all the Primarchs(the progenitors of the various Space Marine Legions) and deaths of trillions.
The game mechanics will be familiar to anyone who has played Talisman before:You pick or have a character randomly picked for you, but rather than fantasy archetypes these are heroes and villains of the HH era such as Primarch Vulkan of the Salamanders and Abaddon the Despoiler.Each character has a set of traits: Resolve (HP) Resources(money)Fate (like the original game, this allows you to spend a point to reroll a die) Ranged Combat score, Close Combat score, and Stratagem score:this is like Magic in the original game, stratagems grant your character special abilities.They also have different special abilities, much as regular Talisman characters.One interesting aspect and big change from regular Talisman is that this is a co-op game:You can have up to 4 players with 2 on either side vying for control.
You roll a die to determine where to travel, in this case between planets.The goal is to get to Terra,in the middle of the board, and the battle between the Emperor and Horus to determine victory.  There are Loyalist planets, Traitor planets, and Contested planets.Like in regular Talisman you draw cards (called dataslates here) for encounters which may range from an enemy you have to fight, equipment you can pick up, events that unfold, or locations. In this game, rather than Followers you can attempt to  add an allied unit to your cadre. Even if you fail, the unit stays there for your enemy to fight and adds its own combat scores to your own if you have an encounter there.
Overall I found this to be an enjoyable game, the mechanics make sense and the setting will be pleasing to 40k/Horus Heresy fans as they even use the same aesthetics from the Black Library novel series.I will say that watching your allied AI make illogical choices can be frustrating, but the Random Number Generator mechanic are also at play. You can prepare as well as you like, sometimes the dice just aren't in your favor.
I would heartily recommend this game to anyone who enjoys original Talisman, Warhammer 40,000, or both.

Talisman: The Horus Heresy:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The galaxy is sent into chaos . . . the famous Horus Lupercal, first Imperial Warmaster, has his eyes firmly set on Terra, once the favourite son of the Emperor of Mankind, now the biggest traitor of all. Who are you going to support? Will you help Horus in his quest or will you assist the Emperor to successfully eliminate the greatest Warmaster and traitor of Mankind? The choice is yours!
Talisman: The Horus Heresy is a strategy/fantasy/board game set in the Warhammer 40K universe. At the start of the game, you will have to choose which side you will back up - the loyalist or the traitor?  Then you will have to decide how many warlords (including yourself) will be part of the game - 1 vs 1 or 2 vs 2. After laying out how many players will be part of the game, it will be time to determine which warlord to be. All Warlords have different abilities, but share six statistics, which are – resolve, fate, resources, close combat, range combat and strategy. A number is attached to each statistic to determine which are the strengths and weaknesses of your warlords.
Now you will be presented with a board of forty nine squares. The grid, or galaxy, will be divided into three parts – the outer, the middle and the centre. Your goal is to find first the Talisman and to make your way to the centre of the galaxy; to board the Vengeful Spirits and eliminate either the Emperor or Horus. You will have to roll the dice to move your character (a Hologram) on the board. As you land on a square, you can investigate the sector and possibly find useful resources. Units might join your cause, find spies or assassins, and a lot more.
Eventually you will land on a square with either an enemy unit, or in the worst case scenario, an enemy Warlord. Sometimes it will be a close battle and other times it will be a long range battle. The winner of the battle will be determined with a roll of the dice, in addition to any modifying ability you acquired during the game.
When you lose a battle, one of your resolve points will be deducted. If it was your last resolve point and you are defeated in that battle, your hero will die. However, if you win, it will either increase the close or range combat statistics. If the result of the battle was not kind to you (in other words, you lose), you can re-roll the dice and hope you get a higher number.  For that you must have a point in your fate statistics.
Ultimately, this is a really good board game based, and whether or not you know about the Warhammer 40K universe, I am sure you will enjoy it!

I am writing this under "odd" circumstances. But I thought it was important to get my story out there. And to let you all know I'm ok.
Yesterday evening around 8:30pm I got up from my computer desk in the den for the first time in approx 16 hours to go to the kitchen to see if I had stashed another Redbull in the refrigerator, as my mini frige stockpile in the den had run dry. I opened thr refrigerator and realized my luck had run out. I heard a faint but familiar voice calling out to me from the livingroom, "Honey, can you please come in here and sit down with me". It was my wife, I haden't seen or spoke to her in weeks? As I crept around the corner horror filled my soul! There sat my wife, next to her was a older looking man, with a baulding head and goofy mustashe. He reached his hand out and said "Hi Eli, my names Jeff VanVonderen, would you like to take a seat"?
At that point I realized what was going on! I saw my sister, my aunt, even my dog Nepoleon sitting on the couch. Then to the left of me I saw the cameras, boom operator, gaffer boy, and so on. "There's a place that can help you Eli, in Holand", my sister called out. I made a break for it. Diving back into my den I shoved my chair from my desk under the door handle, grabbed my laptop off the desk, and dove head first out the window! I ran, ran for hours it seemed like. clutching onto my laptop, barefoot, thirsty for my Redbull, eagar to take just one more turn.
My thoughts were racing, my wife had DENOUNCED me. And for this Jeff guy, I'd seen his show, I know the power and money they have, theirs no way there letting a client escape from rolling cameras, they probably have access to Giant Death Robots to track me down. Then I saw it, salvation!
So here I sit writing all my fellow addicts and "soon to be addicts" behind the McDonalds dumpster. It's just close enough to recieve the wifi, I have all the free left over Big Mac's one can eat, and I even replaced that traitor dog of mine with a racoon I named Darius. I figure this is the safest spot in town, even if they decide to launch a nucular missle the dumpster will give me just enough protection to take just one, more, turn.

I have so many thoughs about this game, I don't know where to start to write a proper review, so I'll just start off with this: what a game!
You're the omnipresent commander of your own starship, where you have the job of mainting your crew, upgrading your ship, fighting past enemies, and much more, in your journey of survival across space. You come across differerent species of aliens, different types of ships that you can unlock depending on your choices, possible allies, and life or death choices.
Now, despite the graphics and the very easy to learn game mechanics, this game is deceptively difficult! You have to practice the management of fuel, resources, time, and make decisions that can affect your outcome for the rest of the game. What elevates this even more is the game's permadeath mode. If you die, you lose everything have to start over from the beginning. There are no redos, and no way to go back and undo something.  This adds very high level of challenge to the game, as the tactics that may have fared well for you before may get you killed the next time you attempt them, or they may not come around at all. You have to think about every decision you make, because it will affect you later in the game, and you won't get the chance to make such a decision again in the same scenario, because the next game you try will be completely different.
While some may find this a con to the game, and may even discourage some from playing, I find that it's actually what makes the game fun. I've gotten very close to victory several times, and every time I die and have to start over, it's like a second chance at redemption to save my crew, but also to see how much better I can get another time around.
It's for this reason that this game is also highly addicting! Even though you lose everything in death, the fact that you did reminds you of how all of your decisions matter, and that with every time you play, you come that much closer to winning.

The score is perfect. It adds so much to the game without drowning out the sounds of the city when you would expect to hear it. It was also very captivating at times that you would want it to be. Faith's movements feel very real and fluid. It is extremely satisfying to jump from a high place and hit the ground with a roll. The story in this game is quite good, but not the best. This is because I was overwhelmed by the fantastic score and eye candy building interiors.
Though this game is outstanding in almost every way, it also has its faults. I found it extremely difficult to memorize the controls. Certain actions, such as jumping, are mapped to an odd place on the controller (Left shoulder button). However, I don't see it being mapped any other way that would have made sense. The only other down side that I have noticed would be the rare glitch in the free running mechanics. This is expected because no video game is without a glitch or flaw somewhere.
Overall, Mirror's edge is one of the best gaming experiences I have had in a long time. This is definitely one of my favorite games.  I see myself playing it in the future time, and time again.

No need to feel as just a spectator to the game. Most enemies wont attack you as they are driven to their goal. However, as the levels proceed difficulty increases. With newer enemies comes new threats, and new threats begat new traps to counter. If strategy and defense is your cup of tea. I highly recommend this title as the ability to attack will bring something new that you will enjoy. However, if it is not your cup of tea. I still recommend it for the very same reason.

Now, the bad, which completely ruined this game for me:

Yep, just that.  They were so unbelievably heavy, imprecise, and tank-like that it almost sapped all the fun out of my experience. I really wish the developers had provided an option to play with either "original" or "modern" controls.  As it is, I can't recommend it.

Jumping into Wonder Boy: The Dragon’s Trap by DotEmu will feel familiar. It doesn’t take long to know that the bones of this game are the same as the platform action-adventure games it was based on, specifically Wonder Boy III: The Dragon’s Trap from 1989. This new Wonder Boy (or Wonder Girl if you prefer – one way the game has updated to the 21st century) makes no attempt to hide its roots. The foundation is built on the simplistic left-right-up-down-attack-duck model of platform games from the 80s and 90s, but it manages to give this old gaming style a boost of new blood and energy.
A lot of that new blood comes from the hand drawn graphics. Traveling from the central village hub, you unlock new areas of gameplay, from dry, volcanic wastelands to underwater lagoons. These graphics, combined with a dynamic and interesting score, gives Monster Land a new, beautiful, yet somehow still raw, look and feel. But Wonderboy is all about paying tribute to the old. If the new graphics feel a little too polished for you, the click of a single button with transform your world into 8-bit in the blink of an eye, and with it, the score becomes a nostalgic arcade ditty to accompany your pixelated hero. You can be in the middle of a boss fight, suddenly long for the days of old, and transform your battle into the 90s platform game that you know and love.
Underneath the pretty new graphics, the game is still fundamentally the same. As you journey through Monster Land, you battle new dragons and transform into different creatures (because of course you’ve been cursed by the Meka-Dragon). You begin as a lizard that spits fire, but as you unlock new creatures, you unlock new abilities. The mouse-human can climb walls, the hawk-human can fly, and so on.
Fighting consists of a few basic attacks, which vary slightly depending on which cursed animal-human you happen to be. Starting off with low health and low armor, these fights require a certain level of patience and caution at first. It’s a matter of figuring out the rhythm, getting used to different tools at your disposal, and a bit of luck. It’s that last part that can get frustrating. Especially during the boss fights (when the stakes are at their highest), leaping in for an attack has to be so perfectly timed that it starts to feel a bit like a guessing game. Be prepared for a test of patience, especially since dying sends you, yet again, back to your main village hub.
During your travels, you’ll also come across some helpful tools like arrows, which allow you to shoot up at the sky, or potions, which give you a second life for when you get trampled by a giant red frog. The only way to get these items is stumbling upon them either in treasure chests or after killing an enemy. Die, and these items will disappear again. Though you have the option of buying armor and visiting a flirtatious nurse to restore your health, the endless amount of coins you procure from killing fish and snakes starts to feel pointless if you can’t spend it on useful weapons. It would have been a nice touch to be able to purchase some of these items in stores, rather than relying on luck dropping them into your lap.
For anyone nostalgic for these platform games, while eager to see some of the physics and kinks worked out in a modern setting, Wonder Boy won’t disappoint. It’s boldly simple and boldly new. From me, it gets an 8/10.

An excellent remake of one of my alltime favorite games. Nice handdrawn sprites with lots of new backgrounds in multiple parallax layers, adding more atmosphere due to the feeling of depth. My only complaint is that the remixed soundtrack sometimes diverges too much from the original compositions, I would have preferred a more subtle interpretation. Most tracks are beautiful though and I really appreciate the option to mix and match original content with remake content such that the new graphics can be combined with the original music or vice versa.
For those unfamiliar with the original, it is a platforming action RPG where you travel to different areas, always on the path to the next dungeon in which to beat the next boss. After defeating a boss, you get transformed into some new form, each one having their own unique abilities enabling you to reach previously unreachable areas where you can find new stores in which to by better equipment and reach the next dungeon. The different forms into which you are transformed enable you to run up certain walls (as Mouse-Man), swim under water (Pirahna-Man), hit blocks above you and below you with your sword (Lion-Man) and fly (Hawk-Man). Later in the game you can access certain rooms where you can change back and forth between all forms unlocked so far. It all creates a Zelda-like feeling where you often backtrack to previously visited areas because you realize you can now access parts which were unreachable earlier.
The remake changes almost nothing gameplaywise, the few tweaks feeling like improvements. There are a few additions like difficulty levels, the hardest one making you take damage as time progresses and unlocking an achievement upon completion, and newly created short dungeons to complete for each character granting you access to one final piece of equipment upon completing all of them.
This is who a remake is supposed to be done: cosmetic upgrades to visuals and audio, minor tweaks and some small additional areas and/or features. The end result is the same magical feeling created by the original and whether you feel like enjoying the experience with new high-quality graphics and audio or prefer the originals, the experience is superior to taking out your old Master System and playing the original yet again (not that I don't recommend adding the original game to you collection).

The recipe is getting old, and as Telltale doesn't improve themselves in any way, it's becoming hard to justify playing these games as opposed to watching a let's play of it.
Choices don't make much of a difference, and since Michonne is a well-established character, with her own distinct personality, some choices can just feel character-breaking. The fans know who Michonne is and what to expect from her!
As for the story itself? Nothing you haven't seen before in the previous episodes. Even the characters feel like clones of characters you have seen before, but with a different skin-job. I know that this is the zombie apocalypse, but if you cannot do something fresh with this narrative, why don't you just stop milking this cow?
I mentioned above that Telltale doesn't improve themselves. That's because, to be blunt, this game's gameplay sucks, which is almost scandalous considering that it is not their first rodeo.
As one would expect, the game still relies on QTE, and yet, it somehow manages to do it with the most lazy controls in modern history:
- playing with a gamepad? You can't tune the stick's sensibility. I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not! Either the option does not exist, or it is pretty damn well hidden (if so, congratulation, because tracking down this option is the only real challenge this game will offer you!) What is this? 2005?
- playing with a keyboard and mouse combo? Then, be aware that while it uses wasd for movement, the game controls as if you were using an analog stick in all sequences. No big deal, but wait, there is more...
- if you play with keyboard and mouse and your country doesn't use a qwerty layout, you will be stuck with a non-sensical button layout since the game assumes that your keyboard does have a qwerty layout! Of course, you can use the maj+alt shortcut to fix this temporarily, but then, you will be faced with another issue: the buttons the game tells you to press during QTE and the button you actually have to press won't always match! A freaking disgrace in 2016.
- lastly, if you own a steam controller and wish to use the hybrid controls to get the best of both worlds, forget it since moving your mouse makes some button prompts disappear, and some commands that are mapped on the left click with a mouse are sometimes mapped to A, and sometimes to right trigger and you won't be able to tell which is which.
Of course, those mapping issues are small and hardly deal-breakers, but when your game has barely any gameplay and when your issues are pitfalls developers have been aware of and have known how to avoid for over a decade, it's hard to forgive.
Add to that the fact that there is no real penalty for death, that choices don't have real consequences, and that gameplay still relies on mindless button-mashing, and you are left to wonder why Telltale insists on making games when they clearly have little to no interest in putting the 'game' back in 'video-game'.
This was not a big deal in TWD 1 and 2, but TWD:Michonne is just not good enough to compensate for those pitfalls.
TLDR: I don't recommend buying this game because the 'gameplay' just distracts from the story, and neither gameplay nor storyline bring anything fresh or interesting on the table for those already familiar with the franchise. If you haven't already, you are better off playing the first and second seasons of the franchise. Also, proper controls mapping is still too hard for Telltale.

While I do believe that developers were sincere in their attempt to create something new, i.e. a story-driven adventure with challenging tactical combat, I do have to say that at the end of the day this game is neither a good story, nor a good tb-rpg/tactical combat game. Moreover, YOU ARE NOT EVEN BEING SOLD "THE WHOLE GAME"-THE END OF THIS GAME IS BARELY THE MIDDLE OF THE MAIN STORY. So, it's also a bunch of bad marketing thrown into the mix.
While not a terrible game, THIS SHOULD NOT BE SOLD AT $25. Even if this game delivered a long, developed story akin to a fantasy book (which it does not both in the quality of its predictable plot and in its length), the price would still be too high. Considering that in order to truly finish the game you will have to buy a future expansion, THIS IS A BLATANT MONEYGRAB.
If you are a story-lover, then Banner Saga is NOT for you. It has developmental depth of a comic book and dialogue is not necessarilly great either. This game to reading a good book is what Cheez Its are to a good meal.
If you are looking for role-playing experience and to make impactful choices in a dynamic environment, then, again, this game is NOT for you. This game is a ride on a rail-road track, with events that force you to make decisions half the time without giving you enough feedback on the possible impact of those decisions. You will have to simply guess many times, and then the game would try to anticipate your choices by delivering cheap plot twists. It's quite silly. Moreover, after completing the game, it is easy to see that there is actually an optimal way to run through the story.
If you are expecting a deep, addictive tactical combat game, then just go for the f2p BS: Factions. Vanilla BS only delivers many boring copy-paste fights against highly-generic AI enemies.
Conclusion:
Under the pretense that this game is an interactive story deeply affected by your choices and spiced up by some awesome tactical combat you are being sold an elaborate beautiful Flash game akin to the games from sites like Armorgames and Newgrounds. This product lacks in content, delivering only the first chapter of the story, without a definitive ending. That is a giant no-no and a red flag for any story-based game, considering the whopping price of $25.
While a good buy at a price of, let's say, $10 (considering the de facto NECESSITY of expansion purchase), this is a lackluster buy at $25.

Pretty close to my ideal game. Similar to Temple of Elemental Evil but not burdened by a PnP mechanic system nor the desire to recreate a PnP module. Single player alone would be amazing, but the multiplayer through the campaign is fully supported and essentially plays out like all the good parts of a PnP session (down to internal party conflicts, if minimally) with all the benefits of being a CRPG. The combat system is incredibly deep but follows consistent rules and heavily rewards clever tactics, with huge emphasis on proper positioning and use of environment.
The game is also quite challenging, giving a reason to need good tactics. Crowd control is brutal, you will almost always be outnumbered and your enemies are not afraid to lock your party down if you mess up. A number of special encounters also introduce little gimmicks, ensuring major fights don't get completely repetitive.
On top of that, the game is fairly freeform within the constraints of a linear plot. Most side quests have alternative resolutions that can impact how other missions play out. The quests themselves are handled as journal entries rather than specific tasks and rewards exploration and proactive investigation.
The only real issues are that the very end game feels a bit rushed (that said, this is after 50+ hours of very high production quality campaign) and, arguably, balance issues (due to the emphasis on battlefield control, ranged and caster characters are extremely strong in comparison to melee). However, the balance is debatable and on the whole a lot more enjoyable due to the high differentation in the skillsets compared to a very tightly tuned skillset, and the ability of any character to essentially multiclass freely gives you lots of options if something isn't working out.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is a 4X video game in the Civilization series developed by Firaxis Games. The game was released on Microsoft Windows in September 2010,[3] on OS X on November 23, 2010, and on Linux on June 10, 2014.
In Civilization V, the player leads a civilization from prehistoric times into the future on a procedurally generated map, achieving one of a number of different victory conditions through research, exploration, diplomacy, expansion, economic development, government and military conquest. The game is based on an entirely new game engine with hexagonal tiles instead of the square tiles of earlier games in the series.[5] Many elements from Civilization IV and its expansion packs have been removed or changed, such as religion and espionage (although these were reintroduced in its subsequent expansions). The combat system has been overhauled, removing stacking of military units and enabling cities to defend themselves by firing directly on nearby enemies.[6] In addition, the maps contain computer-controlled city-states as non-player characters that are available for trade, diplomacy and conquest. A civilization's borders also expand one tile at a time, favoring more productive tiles,[7] and roads now have a maintenance cost, making them much less common.[8] The game features community, modding, and multiplayer elements.[5] It is available for download on Steam.
Its first expansion pack, Civilization V: Gods & Kings, was released on June 19, 2012 in North America and June 22 internationally. It includes features such as religion, espionage, enhanced naval combat and combat AI, as well as nine new civilizations.[9]
A second expansion pack, Civilization V: Brave New World, was announced on March 15, 2013. It includes features such as international trade routes, a world congress, tourism, great works, as well as nine new civilizations, eight additional wonders, and three ideologies. It was released on July 9, 2013 in North America and in the rest of the world three days later.

Gameplay[edit]
A player starting location with one city and one warrior unit showing.
Civilization V is a turn-based strategy game, where each player represents the leader of a certain nation or ethnic group ("civilization") and must guide its growth over the course of thousands of years. It starts with the founding of a small settlement and ends after achieving one of the victory conditions—or surviving until the number of game turns end, at which point the highest-scoring civilization, based on several factors, such as population, land, technological advancement, and cultural development, is declared the winner.
During their turn, the player must manage units representing civilian and military forces: directing units to explore the world, found new cities, go into battle to take over other civilizations, control production in their cities to produce new units and buildings, improve land, handle diplomacy with other civilizations in the game, and finally direct the civilization's growth in technology, culture, food supply, and economics. Victory conditions can include taking over the entire world by force, convincing the other civilizations through diplomacy to acknowledge the player as a leader, becoming influential with all civilizations through tourism, or winning the space race to build a colony spaceship to reach a nearby planet, or winning from being the most powerful civilization on the globe after a set number of turns.
The artificial intelligence (AI) in Civilization V is designed to operate on four levels: the tactical AI controls individual units; the operational AI oversees the entire war front; the strategic AI manages the entire empire; and the grand strategic AI sets long-term goals and determines how to win the game. The four levels of AI complement each other to allow for complex and fluid AI behaviours, which will differ from game to game.[6] Each of the AI-controlled leaders has a unique personality, determined by a combination of 'flavors' on a ten-point scale; however, the values may differ slightly in each game.[6] There are 26 flavors, grouped into categories including growth, expansion, wide strategy, military preferences, recon, naval recon, naval growth, and development preferences.[10]
As in previous versions, cities remain the central pillar of Civilization gameplay. A city can be founded on a desired location by a settler unit, produced in the same way as military units, and the city will grow in population, produce units and buildings, and generate research, wealth and culture.[11] The city will also expand its borders one or more tiles at a time, which is critical in claiming territory and resources. The expansion process is automated and directed towards the city's needs, but tiles can be bought with gold.[6][12]
Siege warfare has been revamped. Whereas cities in previous Civ games relied entirely on garrisoned units for defense, cities in Civ V now defend themselves, and can attack invading units with a ranged attack expanding two tiles outward. Cities have hit points that, if taken down to zero, will signal the city's defeat to invading forces; surviving an attack allows a city to recover a fraction (approximately 15%) of its hit points automatically each turn. In addition, any melee unit loses hit points upon attacking a city, dependent upon the strength of the city and unit. Hit points can be increased by garrisoning a unit in the city or building defensive structures (e.g. walls).[12]
Captured cities can be annexed, razed, or transformed into a puppet state, each option having distinct advantages and disadvantages; for example, puppet states will provide resources, have lower unhappiness, and not increase the cost of cultural polices, but has reduced science and culture yields and cannot be directly controlled, being controlled by the A.I. instead.[13]
In this iteration of the series, tactical gameplay in combat is encouraged in place of overwhelming numerical force, with the introduction of new gameplay mechanisms. Most significantly, the square grid of the world map has been replaced with a hexagonal grid, a feature inspired by the 1994 game Panzer General, according to lead designer Jon Shafer.[14] In addition, each hexagonal tile, including city tiles, can accommodate only one military unit and one civilian unit or great person at a time, forcing armies to spread out over large areas rather than being stacked onto a single tile. This has the effect of moving most large battles outside of the cities, and forces increased realism in sieges, which are now most effective when surrounding the city tile because of bonuses from flanking.[6][13]
Increased movement points, simpler transportation over water (embarkment instead of unit transport with water vessels), ranged attacks, and swapping of adjacent units allows for more precise maneuvering of units.[6][13][15] There is also a balance between ranged and melee units. Ranged units can attack melee units without retribution, but melee units will normally destroy ranged units.
In an effort to make individual units more valuable to the player (compared to previous games in the series), they take longer to produce, and gain experience from defeating enemy units. At set levels this experience can be redeemed for promotions, which provide various bonuses for increasing their effectiveness, or to substantially heal themselves. In a further departure from previous games, units are no longer always destroyed if defeated in combat, taking partial damage, which can be healed at various rates depending on their type, location, and promotions earned.

I love this game.  Everything about it has an old-school feel that blends tabletop RPGs with NES graphics.  There is a lot of grinding in this game, but that's what RPGs are about.  You choose your initial characters from an assortment of people who each have their own unique bonuses, then pick a class for them based on those bonuses and what you want in your party.
If you make challenging enough fights, they require a bit of strategy.  My paladin typically casts a shield to reduce damage by 50%, then increases his threat to draw attention, while my rogue stuns people for 3 turns (thanks to items I have that extend the time by 2 turns).  My mage will either AoE the entire group or fireball for a burning DoT.  My cleric has a powerful single heal, decent group heal, an offensive move called smite, and a debuff on 3 enemy's attack strength.  My newest addition, the berserker, goes berserk (I can't choose his targets but he gains extra damage and regen) and has passives/equipment that boost his crit rate above 30% while also allowing him to heal for 63% of his total damage.  And those are just my 5 classes, there's quite a few more to unlock as you play.
The grinding part comes in two forms.  You'll find yourself moving back and forth to caves often to get grindstones to upgrade your blacksmith.  You'll also want to fight a lot, and grind quests to earn gold.  Gold can be spent buying yourself some equipment at the blacksmith, or on a whole bunch of upgrades to the room you play in, the table you play on, etc.  Purchases made will give your party bonuses, such as higher RNG die rolls, more gold/exp, boosted stats, regen, etc.
There's always something to do in this game.  It can be tedious at times, but the humor of the game, including comments from the game master and party members help to ease this.  Overall, I think it would be a worthy addition to anyone's library who is a fan of old school RPGs.

Wonder Boy: TDT is somehow a game that doesn't look or feel out of place with modern releases but is simultaneously really quite faithful to the 1989 original. That the new graphics and music fit in so well with what is basically a 20 year old game is (1) a testament to how much love and effort has gone into the remake, and (2) a clue as to how good the original really was. I find it astonishing how well the game holds up, even as someone who played the original SMS version back in the day.
The game also gets plus points for the 8-bit graphics mode doing a really good job at recreating what the game actually looked like on a CRT TV, whilst still running at 60 FPS. The game also includes an internal frame-limiter, so you don't need to worry about the game running at odd speeds if you use a faster refresh rate.
The 'hard mode' timer also does more to change the strategy you need to use far more than any 'enemies do more damage' type mode would.
If you like that old-school-adventure vibe, I can't recommend this enough.

Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap was my favorite Sega Master System game, hands down.
And now, the remake has been released, let's see why it is worth your attention, instead of, for instance, buying an emulated version on the Wii Virtual Console (is that still a thing?)
- New graphics: they are nothing short of sublime. The game's aesthetics were redrawn in a style halfway between Japanese and Franco-Belgian comic books, they look amazing and 100% fit with the original game's style.
- New music: to be honest, I would have preferred a more energetic soundtrack, because some of the remastered compositions are rather on the mellow side. But never mind my take on the chosen direction, the execution is a thing of beauty. The OST is worth buying, and I'm saying than even without having heard the extra tracks!

- Quality-of-life improvements : If you still struggle to determine which piece of equipment is best for one form or another, or which ones have special capabilities, now you can, even before you buy them. Also, items are now used using a separate button, and not Down+Jump. It does make a difference, believe me. Limitations due to the Master System technology are also gone: you can now actually save the game (passwords in the original only save an approximate state of the game) and you can access the items/equipment menu during boss fights (what, you didn't know you couldn't in the original? try pausing while fighting a dragon and see what happens) .
- Humor : yes, it has it now. Between some of the items' descriptions, and the eternally snarky pigs and nurses, these little things bring more flavor to the adventure.
- Extra content: The Unknown, six hard mini-dungeons for you to find and complete.
- Retro mode: switch between retro and modern graphics and sound. It really helps appreciate the difference between the original and the remake, and to realize how faithful to the original the engine is.
- Difficulty modes: While I didn't need the Easy mode, the Hard mode was rather challenging, and the idea behind it is both a very good fit for the game and a great reference to a previous installment in the series!
- Moddability: Thanks to the format of several files, the dev tools still in the game, and good-willed developers who participate in discussions about modding the game, this game has awesome potential for becoming something more in the future.
Look, I don't pretend I can list all the good parts in this review. However, what is for sure is that, in addition to the original game being really good, this remake should set the standard for retro remakes. This is truly an exemplary case of "by fans, for fans".

I was disappointed with this game. It seemed to promise the fun, thrill and adventure of dangerous sports like Wingsuit flying and base jumping, but failed to deliver.
Even at the installation stage, I ran into issues. I use family sharing on Steam for my games, so my six year son can play some of them. But that's not allowed here, as it uses a Ubisoft launcher which requires another account and log in, and only one Steam account can be associated with it. So no family sharing with this game. I suppose that's what we can expect from Ubisoft. The have always had controversial DRM.
On the first play, I was required to fly and parachute into a specific target area. I missed this by a fair distance on the first attempt, and ended hunreds of metres ahead of the target, stuck in snow not knowing what to do. There was no obvious way to get back or re-start the event. The user interface was missing a simple feature to try again. My son and I were just stuck there, not knowing what to do. I checked the Internet, and even asked on the Steam forum if anyone knew what to do, but found nothing. I restarted the game, and guess what? There I still was, stuck in the snow a few hundred metres off the target. So I gave up for a while. Apparently, it uses some kind of cloud save that it does not give you control over.
So I came back to the game again, a week ot so later, and yes, there I still was stuck in the snow, with no apparent way of resetting the game. As a last resort I decided to try walking back to the target area. It took several long minutes, but it worked. Finally I could do the next activity!
I'm sure there are settings that
that fix some of these issues but they should be easy to find and they are not.  From an end user experience point of view, that is terrible design.
The whole game seems to be like this, forcing you to go through all these hoops to complete stages, and punishing you stupidly if you don't do anything exactly the way they want you to, and not allowing you to restart the game easily. I absolutely hated my few hours on this. There seemed to be no way to save, nor reset the game. The controls were clunky and complicated, and I found the experience dull and constrained, with no freedom to experience these sports in a fun way, as the game seemed to promise. It required too much thought when it should have been simple and fun.
I had far more fun with the free-to-play "Snow", also available on Steam. I'm just glad I got "Steep" in a sale, because it would have hurt very much to have paid the premium AAA price for it.

Grim Dawn is the spiritual successor to the classic hack & slasher: Titan Quest. It uses a revamped version of the engine, the same dual class system and talent trees, and there is a lot of randomly generated loot for you to pry out of the cold dead hands of the (un)dead. The zombie apocalypse has broken out, and for some mysterious reason you did not turn into a zombie when you were supposed to. That makes you special, and thus the hero of the story :-)
The world is pretty grim, with a bit of a Victorian / Western feel to it. There's magic, there are guns, there's guys with hats, there are zombies, there are goblin-like monsters and lots of angry mutated wildlife. And then there is this cult of Ch'Thon mucking things up. Killing monsters feels satifying, and with a lot of different skills to choose from, you have plenty of viable character builds to try out. With the addition of the Devotion system back in beta 29, you have even more options to customize your character as you progress through the game.
The faction system starts to develop once you have finished the first major story arc, and it is nice. Each character and monster in the game belongs to a faction. Factions have relationships with each other. If you kill enough Aetherials, they are going to dislike you more and more, to the point where they might start setting up ambushes and sending champion monsters after you. The reverse also works: if you manage to get a good reputation with a faction, you get access to more special items from their vendors, as well as a Bounty Quest table.
Another addition to the game over Titan Quest is crafting. You can create magical items appropriate for your level, as well as build some pretty cool Epic items, if you find the plans and obtain the neccessary crafting materials.
I started playing in Beta 27, which added the Shaman class. It combines very nicely with the Occultist, because they both offer summonable pets. In previous betas I have tried other class combinations, which had a completely different playstyle. All of them were a lot of fun.
Beta 28 and 29 added Act 4 to the game, so the storyline is now complete. Judging on my progress so far, the storyline is going to take about 30 hours to complete on a first playthrough.
Since the game went from early access to live, the devs have released a number of balance patches and improved performance a bit. Crucible DLC added an optional wave defense mode to the game that gave you an alternative means to play and level your characters.
Ashes of Malmouth is a full-blown expansion that adds two classes, expands the story from four to six acts, gives you some (much needed) additional shared stash space, and adds a bunch of items that modify your skills. An expanded Devotion system gives you even more tools to customise your character. All in all, it is a very nice addition to the whole game and worthwhile to get if you are going to play the game for the first time.
I've played through the game a couple times with different characters, and recorded it all on Youtube. If you are curious about some gameplay, then you might be interested in the series I started with the release of Ashes of Malmouth: a summoner Necromancer.

A true work of passion on the part of the developers. It's very faithful to the original game, the animation is of exquisitely high quality, the music is spot-on, revisiting Meka Dragon's area for example feels really great, there's only a few tracks slightly unsuited for the sort of action we see in the game, but the option to quickly switch from retro to modern makes up for it. The content added to the remake, the puzzle platforming areas that contain a charm stone for every transformation are tastefully done, challenging but not impossibly so, require mastering the controls but also feel like solving a puzzle in how you look for the right spots to jump from, with how much momentum and so on, which block to destroy. Those areas give me confidence in the developer's ability to design a solid platforming experience of their own in the future, should they decide to make a brand new game.
As for reviewing the parts that belong to the original game : it's a fantastic platformer/metroidvania-ish game with touches of inspiration from the arcades. The game length is thus on the short side if all you care about is completing it once, but there is more fun to be had if you are the sort of player who have an interest in getting better at the game, such as playing hard mode and setting new challenges for yourself such as how fast you complete it, or with how many resources. The base mechanics of the game are solid enough to support that sort of playstyle, it is not unlike the enjoyment found in replaying shmups whose absolute game length are 30 minutes, but whose goals of endless higher scores or perfect no-death 1 credit continues leave players with the desire to play more. The game can get easier if you use all the resources at your disposition, but you can also have fun doing runs with no magic or powerful items. The only negative bit, where the game hasn't aged well, is the boss fights, which can feel tricky in your first attempt, but become rather trivial once you've noticed the way the single pattern works. With that said, it does not overly detract from the game, which at the core is a platforming experience about dealing with various enemy spawns on multiple sides of the screen.
A last thing to note, on the technical side : it runs perfectly well on Linux, with not a single bug spotted during my runs. I am grateful for the level of quality provided by this new indie developer studio.

As someone who has never played a Talisman game before I was unsure what to expect.
Being a big Warhammer Horus Heresy & 40K fan I decided to buy all of the DLC including the soundtrack.
It took me about an hour or so to fumble my way through learning the basics. I confess that I am impatient with most tutorials and largely ignored them.
They have certainly captured the feel of the Horus Heresy with most of the lead characters/Primarchs having abilities that make sense. Graphically the game looks really good and I especially like the background details when zooming into different sectors. For a board game come video game the graphics are really good when you consider most images used in the game are still rather than animated.
Overall I would recommend this game especially to Heresy fans even though I do have a few gripes that let the game down.
Firstly the soundtrack which is optional as a DLC is too overpriced and underwhelming. I can't say I actually notice the music very much, only really noticing the in game sound effects.
Secondly the achievements for completing character goals to 100% requires far too much repetition and far too much luck. For example you can complete most character goals in a few games with the same character but some goals require you to play the game over and over in order to get enough points to complete. I would rather have spent this time completing other characters and enjoying the game with some feeling of freshness rather than playing the same character endlessley to get an achievement.
Third, it can take quite a while to get players to join online games which is a real shame as I only see this game having longevity by playing against human opponents.
I do recommend this game but would caution against buying the DLC until you try the game. If you can get a few mates to play with you then the DLC is definitley worth it.

A Fun Game with a unique gameplay model that destroys  the hemogony of the last decade of RTS only battle strategies.  The Turn based style is built around percentage shooting where the soldgier's chance of hitting an enemy scales up based on cover, distance, and the angle of attack.  The random unforgiving gods of probability can ruin your mission by having your snipers miss a round of 90% shots or saving you with a lucky pistol shot from across the map.
Buy this game if you can enjoy round after round of brutal uncertainty everytime you enter a battle againt a hostile alien force that is determined to terrorize the major cities of our world and crush the resistance of our technologically inferior people.
In the game, you manage an international team of elite warrior, scientists, and engineers trying to defeate the alien menace where you can, recover their artifacts and reverse engineer their technology before the steadaly growing threat overwhealmes humanity.  You manage what projects your scientist reasurch, what equipment your engineers built, and when and where you pick your fights.  Most importantly you also manage the tactics of your squads in their incounters with the small teams of extraterresterals who aassult our world.

I am writing this under "odd" circumstances. But I thought it was important to get my story out there. And to let you all know I'm ok.
Yesterday evening around 8:30pm I got up from my computer desk in the den for the first time in approx 16 hours to go to the kitchen to see if I had stashed another Redbull in the refrigerator, as my mini frige stockpile in the den had run dry. I opened thr refrigerator and realized my luck had run out. I heard a faint but familiar voice calling out to me from the livingroom, "Honey, can you please come in here and sit down with me". It was my wife, I haden't seen or spoke to her in weeks? As I crept around the corner horror filled my soul! There sat my wife, next to her was a older looking man, with a baulding head and goofy mustashe. He reached his hand out and said "Hi Eli, my names Jeff VanVonderen, would you like to take a seat"?
At that point I realized what was going on! I saw my sister, my aunt, even my dog Nepoleon sitting on the couch. Then to the left of me I saw the cameras, boom operator, gaffer boy, and so on. "There's a place that can help you Eli, in Holand", my sister called out. I made a break for it. Diving back into my den I shoved my chair from my desk under the door handle, grabbed my laptop off the desk, and dove head first out the window! I ran, ran for hours it seemed like. clutching onto my laptop, barefoot, thirsty for my Redbull, eagar to take just one more turn.
My thoughts were racing, my wife had DENOUNCED me. And for this Jeff guy, I'd seen his show, I know the power and money they have, theirs no way there letting a client escape from rolling cameras, they probably have access to Giant Death Robots to track me down. Then I saw it, salvation!
So here I sit writing all my fellow addicts and "soon to be addicts" behind the McDonalds dumpster. It's just close enough to recieve the wifi, I have all the free left over Big Mac's one can eat, and I even replaced that traitor dog of mine with a racoon I named Darius. I figure this is the safest spot in town, even if they decide to launch a nucular missle the dumpster will give me just enough protection to take just one, more, turn.

'Wonder Boy: the Dragon's Trap' is the remake of an late 80's Platformer/Action-Adventure for the Sega Master System. And to say it right from the start: it is a wonderful game! Every aspect of it is extremely well done... but let's take a closer look:
The art for this game is simply stunning, at least for my taste. The characters and backgrounds look very beautiful and make use of a wide and colorful palette. The animations are smooth and suit the game very well. I'm really impressed by the overall graphical appearance which is way above of what I usually would expect from a platformer. In this sense I put it next to gems like 'Ori and the Blind Forest' or 'Rayman: Origins'.
Some of the 8bit classics are pure masterworks gameplay-wise, but they were graphically limited. The developers of the remake decided not to change the original controls, level-design, enemies and puzzles, but rather left everything as intended and just gave it a modern look. This concept works incredibly well! Thanks to the graphical overhaul the original gameplay can really shine and can be enjoyed by a modern audience. IMHO this is how remakes should be done and I would love to see other classics like Super Mario Bros. 3, Metroid, Contra or Mega Man 2 remade this way.
Regarding the gameplay: Wonder Boy is a solid Platformer with minor Adventure-elements. It's a light-hearted game, not too easy but never frustrating at any point. It's not very long and you could probably beat it on a sunday afternoon. I'd say it has high replayability since those games where made the be played again and again. And like most of the classics: No grinding, no unnecessary elements that stretch the game. Pure fun!
A nice gimmick is the option to switch between the modern appearance and the classic 8bit graphics (and music).

Overview
Wonderboy: The Dragon’s Trap is a remake made by Dotemu and Lizardcube for the 1989 Sega Master System Game: Wonderboy III: The Dragon’s Trap. This remake has the same feel as you are playing the original one: It’s mixes the difficulty + exploration across the places very well. You will need to be prepared to pass across some really difficulty levels if you don’t have the necessary character or weapon/shield/armor equipped. And this version has the addition of the Wonder girl for you to play.
Story
It remains the same as the original. The game starts on the last battle versus the Meka Dragon from the previous game: Wonderboy in the Monster Land. After you defeat the Dragon,you’ll be cursed and transformed in different monsters with unique abilities after defeating the Dragon Bosses. You will return to your original form only when you defeat the last boss. Your goals are to defeat the dragons and remove the curse.
Gameplay
One of the many charms of this game. The game has easy controls and smooth gameplay. You have a inventory that shows you every item that you got,and it’s divided into four categories:Special Powers,Swords,Shields and Armors. You also can quickly swap the magic items with the mapped keys. In the start you will find that the enemies can kill you very quick and the game is hard,but after find the hearts and the right weapons across the levels the things gets better and you will enjoy each and every moment that this game can offer without getting killed almost all time.You’ll have a chance of getting a potion on the game over screen,if you don’t get it and die across the level,you will have to restart the whole level again.
To defeat the bosses you need to find the pattern of attack of each one,after getting on it,it’s pretty easy to find what you have to do to not lose hearts and defeat them.
You’ll find a lot of secrets hiding new weapons,powers,shops and money.Some are easy to find but most of all are well hide and will require a exploration across the whole level to find it.
And the game also reserves secrets for who bravely searches it: Each character of the game has a charm stone hidden somewhere. To find it,you will need to search even more,after you find the correct door,it leads you to a level that you can only use the right character without changing it’s form. These levels requires more attention since they are harder compared to the normal levels,After getting the 6 stones you’ll have the ability to buy the last sword of the game: The Gallic Sword.
Graphics
Well,the graphics of this game can attend to two kinds of people: The Nostalgic ones who want to play the classic game without enhancements and the ones that want to relive their memories with new and updated graphics. The art and design of this game was really done with love,making the game beautiful and delicious to play. And in the other side you can activate the retro mode that will lead you back to the 1989 original game without losing the feeling that this remake brought.
Soundtrack
The same attends to the soundtrack: You can listen the original one or the new one. The new soundtrack maintains the nostalgic feeling but with renewed songs and instruments. The music can go from the calm village song to the intense boss fight song music. The sounds are very good and can help you find hidden enemies sometimes.
Summary
Wonderboy: The Dragon’s Trap is the definitive remake that everyone asked for. It’s blends the nostalgic feeling of playing the original game plus the feeling that the game evolved with the remake too. The game difficulty is fine,but if you do not have patience for dying constantly it can be a trouble. It’s a game that suits for anyone,even the ones that have knowed the game only on this remake.
