Sometime ago I promised a review to the dev, so now I'm going to correct that mistake.
Grim Dawn is a great action RPG title from the ex-Titan Quest dev (also a great ARPG), with a lot of offering in terms of very good graphics, multi-class characters and a lot of depth in gameplay.
Even though Grim Dawn looks like a classic Diablo clone, it is actually a lot more than that, because of the several reasons: the world is much larger; you have an ability to create a balance in the world between the factions (if one faction likes what you're doing, you can buy cheaper stuff from the merchants etc.); and dynamic weather - which is an awesome visual feature.
There are areas that could be somewhat improved, like combat animations and an ability to move the inventory around the screen, or at least to choose a position of the inventory in the GUI.
To sum it up, a very good ARPG offering.

Super Hexagon is a super simplistic indie game created by Terry Cavanagh - known for games such as "Don't Look Back", "Naya's Quest", and "VVVVVV (two aforementioned games are free to play in website, go search and try them if you haven't) - that is based on this free Flash game which then got upgraded into this game I'm about to review:
(Before buying this, to prevent the feeling of regret on not being able to beat one of these insane levels, I recommend to play the link first to get the gist of the concept. Also yes, embrace the difficulty.)
I just got a chance to play this today (despite nominating this for "Simplest Addiction" yesterday) and I LOVE it. The premise is simple, you play as a tiny triangle and you have to avoid obstacles in an insanely trippy environment with left & right arrow button (I think mouse buttons work too), then survive in 60 seconds to beat the level. Compared to "Hexagon", the levels presented in this game are hecka "hardestest" with the screen being panned in some occassion, and quick rotations once you unlock more levels. Personally the music kept me engaged to repeat, repeat, and repeat the level until you managed to beat your old record (only 1/6 so far though, still need more time for sure lol). So mad props to Chipzel for the 8-bit musics - I listened it a lot last year from his Bandcamp page  and this game made me re-embraced its goodness.
There are only 6 Steam Achievements in this game, in which each of them requires you to beat one level, that will progressively get harder and harder. No silly achievements like "you have to die x times to get this achievement", something like that, and I'm totally fine with it. Sorta helps to focus yourself to finish each of them, because once you get one, praise yourself to finish it. Congrats. Now go to the final level and see how much you suffer further for one, last achievement for 100% completion. Good luck.
All in all, I recommend this game for those who love high difficulty in a simple vector graphics, and because Mr. Cavanagh. I'm a fan of his simplistic, yet phenomenal works. It's cheap as well, so extra plus for that.

Although still in development Grim Dawn has become one of the more interestng and deeper action RPG's available.  The skill system and item enhancement are very similar to those of Titan Quest.  Skills advance by spending points earned three at a time when the character levels up and can be spent on specific skills to acquire and upgrade them or on the class specialization to increase stats and gain access to new skills.  There are a wide variety of skills in each class and you can even add a second class should you want to diversify even further giving each character a high degree of customization and unique-ness.  Use of items is restricted by stat and character level, have a wide variety of more or less generic effects (stat bonus, reistance bonus, etc) and occaisonal skill bonuses.
The game so far has proven to be fairly expansive and enjoyable.  I look forward to further development.

Overall a fantastic remake.

A Fun Game with a unique gameplay model that destroys  the hemogony of the last decade of RTS only battle strategies.  The Turn based style is built around percentage shooting where the soldgier's chance of hitting an enemy scales up based on cover, distance, and the angle of attack.  The random unforgiving gods of probability can ruin your mission by having your snipers miss a round of 90% shots or saving you with a lucky pistol shot from across the map.
Buy this game if you can enjoy round after round of brutal uncertainty everytime you enter a battle againt a hostile alien force that is determined to terrorize the major cities of our world and crush the resistance of our technologically inferior people.
In the game, you manage an international team of elite warrior, scientists, and engineers trying to defeate the alien menace where you can, recover their artifacts and reverse engineer their technology before the steadaly growing threat overwhealmes humanity.  You manage what projects your scientist reasurch, what equipment your engineers built, and when and where you pick your fights.  Most importantly you also manage the tactics of your squads in their incounters with the small teams of extraterresterals who aassult our world.

However! From what I have experienced so far - definitely worth a pick-up if you enjoy the genre. The graphics are nothing to write home about - in fact, there is something about the art style in general I personally found ever so slightly 'off'. It is nonetheless quite serviceable and the animation quality is great.
The skills appear to have quite a weight to them for the most part, both for physical melee and ranged - spells are a bit more hit and miss, but by and large also look quite great.
What I think I enjoy the most though, is that even in Act 1 there are signs of non-linearity and some randomisation elements (despite the zones themselves actually being static layouts) - e.g., there are 'secret' dungeons which may or may not spawn entrances in a particular play through and will not show on your map. These and certain other side quests might also contain creatures well over the level you'd expect to be even by end of act.
Some of them you can defeat regardless with good play - others, perhaps not so much. (Because frankly, my play is impeccable*. <cough>
If you remember the early (and for some, not so early!) days of TQ, and wanted to try MP in that game - you may recall the awful issues it had with lag and connectivity in general.
Grim Dawn even in its beta form does not appear to exhibit any such issues. I've had a few sessions with my brother via the net and it was flawless - easily some of the best times I've had with the game so far. :)

I nominated this game for the "Defies Description Award" because it is quite literally that... a game that must be played to be understood.  However I will give it a try...
Antichamber is at its core a puzzle game, however they are not simple logic or physics puzzles as many puzzle games would employ, but rather Antichamber is akin to a labrynth of the mind.  There is no logic in the world of Antichamber, but through the course of the game you must learn to navigate the labrynth using your brain and a special tool to unlock passageways and maniuplate the environment.  Over the course of the game you will find upgrades to your tool 3 times, the final upgrade allos you to access the final area of the game or the "exit" of the labrynth if you will.
Overall I think this game was executed amazingly well  and the combination of atmospheric music/sound and mind-bending puzzles was a lot of fun to explore and solve.  If you are a fan of conventional puzzle games, give this one a try... it may surprise you!

The Banner Saga is something special. The music, writing, and art all come together to make an experience that feels genuine, beautiful, and engaging. The story is very interesting, and it had me baying for more even after the end. This alone was enough to make me enjoy the experience.
In terms of gameplay, a lot of the game comes down to managing supplies and making decisions on your journey, punctuated by turn-based tactical combat. There are a lot of interesting decisions to be made, and the travel aspect feels like a much prettier, much more interesting version of The Oregon Trail. Worry about who's been stealing supplies, keeping morale up, whether you should save the people of a village considering it means more mouths to feed, decide if the fighters on the road are actually who they say they are... all with a looming threat trailing too close behind and no guarantee of safety. I found myself getting stressed about how far we had to go to get to the next town, as my supplies were running low and people started to die of starvation.
The Banner Saga, as an overall experience, is very much worthwhile. It is a story worth telling, paired with the music and art necessary to tell it effectively, and gameplay to make you feel like a part of that story. It is not a game you want to miss out on.

Sid Meier's Civilization V is a 4X video game in the Civilization series developed by Firaxis Games. The game was released on Microsoft Windows in September 2010,[3] on OS X on November 23, 2010, and on Linux on June 10, 2014.
In Civilization V, the player leads a civilization from prehistoric times into the future on a procedurally generated map, achieving one of a number of different victory conditions through research, exploration, diplomacy, expansion, economic development, government and military conquest. The game is based on an entirely new game engine with hexagonal tiles instead of the square tiles of earlier games in the series.[5] Many elements from Civilization IV and its expansion packs have been removed or changed, such as religion and espionage (although these were reintroduced in its subsequent expansions). The combat system has been overhauled, removing stacking of military units and enabling cities to defend themselves by firing directly on nearby enemies.[6] In addition, the maps contain computer-controlled city-states as non-player characters that are available for trade, diplomacy and conquest. A civilization's borders also expand one tile at a time, favoring more productive tiles,[7] and roads now have a maintenance cost, making them much less common.[8] The game features community, modding, and multiplayer elements.[5] It is available for download on Steam.
Its first expansion pack, Civilization V: Gods & Kings, was released on June 19, 2012 in North America and June 22 internationally. It includes features such as religion, espionage, enhanced naval combat and combat AI, as well as nine new civilizations.[9]
A second expansion pack, Civilization V: Brave New World, was announced on March 15, 2013. It includes features such as international trade routes, a world congress, tourism, great works, as well as nine new civilizations, eight additional wonders, and three ideologies. It was released on July 9, 2013 in North America and in the rest of the world three days later.

Gameplay[edit]
A player starting location with one city and one warrior unit showing.
Civilization V is a turn-based strategy game, where each player represents the leader of a certain nation or ethnic group ("civilization") and must guide its growth over the course of thousands of years. It starts with the founding of a small settlement and ends after achieving one of the victory conditions—or surviving until the number of game turns end, at which point the highest-scoring civilization, based on several factors, such as population, land, technological advancement, and cultural development, is declared the winner.
During their turn, the player must manage units representing civilian and military forces: directing units to explore the world, found new cities, go into battle to take over other civilizations, control production in their cities to produce new units and buildings, improve land, handle diplomacy with other civilizations in the game, and finally direct the civilization's growth in technology, culture, food supply, and economics. Victory conditions can include taking over the entire world by force, convincing the other civilizations through diplomacy to acknowledge the player as a leader, becoming influential with all civilizations through tourism, or winning the space race to build a colony spaceship to reach a nearby planet, or winning from being the most powerful civilization on the globe after a set number of turns.
The artificial intelligence (AI) in Civilization V is designed to operate on four levels: the tactical AI controls individual units; the operational AI oversees the entire war front; the strategic AI manages the entire empire; and the grand strategic AI sets long-term goals and determines how to win the game. The four levels of AI complement each other to allow for complex and fluid AI behaviours, which will differ from game to game.[6] Each of the AI-controlled leaders has a unique personality, determined by a combination of 'flavors' on a ten-point scale; however, the values may differ slightly in each game.[6] There are 26 flavors, grouped into categories including growth, expansion, wide strategy, military preferences, recon, naval recon, naval growth, and development preferences.[10]
As in previous versions, cities remain the central pillar of Civilization gameplay. A city can be founded on a desired location by a settler unit, produced in the same way as military units, and the city will grow in population, produce units and buildings, and generate research, wealth and culture.[11] The city will also expand its borders one or more tiles at a time, which is critical in claiming territory and resources. The expansion process is automated and directed towards the city's needs, but tiles can be bought with gold.[6][12]
Siege warfare has been revamped. Whereas cities in previous Civ games relied entirely on garrisoned units for defense, cities in Civ V now defend themselves, and can attack invading units with a ranged attack expanding two tiles outward. Cities have hit points that, if taken down to zero, will signal the city's defeat to invading forces; surviving an attack allows a city to recover a fraction (approximately 15%) of its hit points automatically each turn. In addition, any melee unit loses hit points upon attacking a city, dependent upon the strength of the city and unit. Hit points can be increased by garrisoning a unit in the city or building defensive structures (e.g. walls).[12]
Captured cities can be annexed, razed, or transformed into a puppet state, each option having distinct advantages and disadvantages; for example, puppet states will provide resources, have lower unhappiness, and not increase the cost of cultural polices, but has reduced science and culture yields and cannot be directly controlled, being controlled by the A.I. instead.[13]
In this iteration of the series, tactical gameplay in combat is encouraged in place of overwhelming numerical force, with the introduction of new gameplay mechanisms. Most significantly, the square grid of the world map has been replaced with a hexagonal grid, a feature inspired by the 1994 game Panzer General, according to lead designer Jon Shafer.[14] In addition, each hexagonal tile, including city tiles, can accommodate only one military unit and one civilian unit or great person at a time, forcing armies to spread out over large areas rather than being stacked onto a single tile. This has the effect of moving most large battles outside of the cities, and forces increased realism in sieges, which are now most effective when surrounding the city tile because of bonuses from flanking.[6][13]
Increased movement points, simpler transportation over water (embarkment instead of unit transport with water vessels), ranged attacks, and swapping of adjacent units allows for more precise maneuvering of units.[6][13][15] There is also a balance between ranged and melee units. Ranged units can attack melee units without retribution, but melee units will normally destroy ranged units.
In an effort to make individual units more valuable to the player (compared to previous games in the series), they take longer to produce, and gain experience from defeating enemy units. At set levels this experience can be redeemed for promotions, which provide various bonuses for increasing their effectiveness, or to substantially heal themselves. In a further departure from previous games, units are no longer always destroyed if defeated in combat, taking partial damage, which can be healed at various rates depending on their type, location, and promotions earned.

Adventure games are not for me...
But, this one has got some good qualities. Most noticeably, at least to me, this particular Nancy Drew game features a lot of traditional occult symbolism and you have to familiarize yourself with it to pass some of these puzzles. You get to learn runic, alchemical symbols and astrology symbols as well. So that's cool. The puzzles are also quite satisfying to solve, once you get it. Admittedly, I did have to consult a FAQ on a few occasions.
The interface of the game is pretty traditional for first-person adventure games. You have to click left or right or up or down in order to get anywhere, otherwise there's a scrolling screen where you get a 360 view. The thing is that navigating through the manor can get really tiresome. You sometimes have to solve a puzzle over again in order to get where you've already been. At that point, it's just annoying.
And speaking of annoying, there was one particular puzzle where you had to get an answer from a character, navigate to the point of the puzzle, plug in your answer and then run back... four times. And did I mention that you have to do one of those puzzles to open a passageway to get to the place where the puzzle is?
Well, I give this one a passing grade, but you feel more like a puzzler than a detective. THOUGH, there is a plot point that was never resolved that is driving me crazy.
TL;DR - It's a puzzle game, not a mystery solving game.

From all the Nancy Drew games I have played (about 10), this is by far the hardest, and by a big margin. Many of the puzzles are extremely obscure and hard to figure out without a guide. If you like easy casual games and do not like hard puzzles that you have to figure out via vague hints given in the game, then you will get stuck and you will not like this game. Getting through this game without reading an online guide even once is a real challenge, and probably unsurmountable for most casual players.
That being said, you might notice that I'm actually giving this a positive review. That's because personally I just loved this game. When I started to play this game and noticed how amazingly hard and obscure the puzzles are, I decided that come hell or high water, I will complete this game without looking at an online guide even once. And I did.
And the thing is: When I finally succeeded, it was amazingly rewarding. I don't mean that the game rewards you with something special; I just mean that being able to figure out all the puzzles without any external help feels really rewarding all in itself.
All puzzles are solvable with logic, either using what the puzzle itself presents, or information gotten elsewhere (and most often both.) No puzzle requires blind guessing or trying all possible combinations. You will most probably require making notes or take screenshots to remember some of the info, but that's just part of the charm.
If you like hard logic puzzles and want to challenge yourself, I recommend this game. It's technically speaking very old (even for the year it was published), but that's not a big deal. However, if you don't have the patience, you will most probably not like this game.

I want to recommend this game because it really is a lot of fun and it's one of my favorite games to just chill with but like so many Ubisoft games, it has some glaring issues. I would recommend it if you have friends to play with and/or really just want a chill and pretty snowsports game, otherwise you can pass this up.
Pros
-Beautiful game, like soooooooo visually stimulating if you like winter and cold. If you're an avid snowboarder you'll really enjoy the visuals, this game really gets down the different lightings of being on a mountain, like its awesome.
-This doesn't really deserve to be a pro because not locking content behind microtransactions shouldn't be something we have to be thankful for but in this age of sleazy locking content behind microtransactions, I kind-of sort-of appreciate that there is a good amount of aesthetic stuff that can be earned in-game, however that doesn't mean there isn't locked content in this game bc there is a bunch.
Cons
-Mechanics can get veryyyyy tiresome.
-Some of the sports are just not a lot of fun or well designed.
-Next to no trick variery.
-Took me 40hrs of playing to find a single spot where I could grind for like a grand total of 5 seconds,
-The world is SO empty, like utterly barren of things to find which is such a shame because it's so beautiful but there's just noooooothing there. No items, no cool or hidden stuff to find, just vast emptiness which sucks because it takes out alot of the fun of exploring. Like it's so big and beautiful that if you're like me you want to explore every nook and cranny just to be sure but like after a whileyou just realize there isn't anything there and so the thrill of like getting to some super inconvenient/high up place or rock or something just becomes negligible.
-Whoever decided that there needed to be challenges going through dense forest that's essentially a crapshoot because the only way to make the time limit is by barreling through as fast as you can, again a complete and total gamble, needs to get fired lol and honestly is just poor level design. I can think of a thousand more interesting runs than just putting stuff behind trees because they one-shot you out of a race, forcing you to start over lol
-My number one beef with this game lol this game is about 10%victory and 90%retries if you always go for gold/silver. You're gonna be restarting your runs alotttttttttttttttttttt later game, whether it be because you can't make a single mistake to make the time/score or because crashing once is a KO in that sport aka any of the flying/falling ones.
-The longessttttttt falls. Like goddddd falling is so tedius and time consuming it's almost never practical to continue after falling.
-There's next-to no reason to group up with people and all the reasons to do it are hidden behind the unnavigable UI so don't expect much socializing, the only time you'll be with other players is at the start of runs pretty much. You barely see eachother on the run after bc everyone is just constantly restarting races so if youre boarding next to someone chances are they're just gonna randomly disappear in the next couple seconds to restart the run, breaking any and all feeling of it being an mmo or social game lol. Feels more like you're viewing peoples ghosts/bloodstains in Dark Souls lol.
TLDR
All in all I want to recommned it because it's a really good time if you're an avid snowboarder/appreciate beautiful winter visuals but it really is only worth it for the reasons I mentioned. It can be an immensely calming game if you just cruise and enjoy and board which is why I bought it but there's just no content if that's how you want to play, the only way to unlock new gear and stuff is through score and time challenges, which is so lame bc it's like why even make this to be open world in the first place if there's like no content/reward for exploring/finding cool stuff with your friends outside of unlocking some new challneges/runs that look and feel exactly the same as the last ones.  Theyre just more of the same challenges and desolate winter, which is imo a lot of wasted space and potential because I DIG the idea of a social/open world snowboarding game like seriously Ubi hide some cool sh*t in the mountain man, its so vast and big add some depth and mystery, literally anything to give it some more life.

Sometime ago I promised a review to the dev, so now I'm going to correct that mistake.
Grim Dawn is a great action RPG title from the ex-Titan Quest dev (also a great ARPG), with a lot of offering in terms of very good graphics, multi-class characters and a lot of depth in gameplay.
Even though Grim Dawn looks like a classic Diablo clone, it is actually a lot more than that, because of the several reasons: the world is much larger; you have an ability to create a balance in the world between the factions (if one faction likes what you're doing, you can buy cheaper stuff from the merchants etc.); and dynamic weather - which is an awesome visual feature.
There are areas that could be somewhat improved, like combat animations and an ability to move the inventory around the screen, or at least to choose a position of the inventory in the GUI.
To sum it up, a very good ARPG offering.

Very well made. The new art and music re-create a lovely game world. Being able to switch between the original and new presentation is great. New aspects such as the menus are all very easy to use. You can see a lot of careful effort has gone into this. Recommended to anybody who enjoyed the original game. Having said that, the animation and music are so good I suspect many who didn't play the riginal would also like this.

Although still in development Grim Dawn has become one of the more interestng and deeper action RPG's available.  The skill system and item enhancement are very similar to those of Titan Quest.  Skills advance by spending points earned three at a time when the character levels up and can be spent on specific skills to acquire and upgrade them or on the class specialization to increase stats and gain access to new skills.  There are a wide variety of skills in each class and you can even add a second class should you want to diversify even further giving each character a high degree of customization and unique-ness.  Use of items is restricted by stat and character level, have a wide variety of more or less generic effects (stat bonus, reistance bonus, etc) and occaisonal skill bonuses.
The game so far has proven to be fairly expansive and enjoyable.  I look forward to further development.

I know now the rage and disappointment that the Emperor must have felt when he was betrayed by Horus for I feel betrayed by another shoddy GW game that has once again taken my time and money and delivered nothing but the laughter of the dark gods in return...
I am a fan of the 31K Horus Heresy lore and a fan of Talisman so I made an incorrect assumption that this may be actually a game that delivers on both the lore and an interesting new version of Talisman.
I could feel the nurgle rot setting in when I find DLC packs released alongside the ACTUAL game. I knew straight away that this was not looking good.
But I thought dont worry lets play the game, lucky I have a friend who also likes Talisman so we both got stuck in with a 4 player game. I couldnt wait to have an assortment of characters to choose from after  reading many horus heresy books. Such a rich tapestry of lore awaited me.
It seemed the lore was getting massacred worse than the loyalists at Istvaan III. Not being able to choose most of the Primarchs or characters for both sides showed that they plan to milk this for all they can.  They should have had dozens of characters for each of the legions not just a few characters in total. For a game as bare as this that could have made it alot more fun. Do I want to be Fulgrium or a random World Eater Warlord which strangely enough generated for the loyalist.......so disappointing.
After a couple of hrs I knew that Tzeentch had tricked me into purchasing a shoddy game. It was nothing more than a  mod of the original Talisman that was just a grind to play. So many game play faults like not being able to scroll around the map while other players are having their turn make me wonder if anyone actually play tested this.
Computer characters just floated around the outer regions and didnt even challenge for the inner regions and to win the game. I couldnt believe how bad that was as it shouldnt be hard to get that right at least. Maybe they borrowed a few programmers from Total War to program the AI or something.
By the time we got to the end sequence fighting either Horus or the Emperor we had just about had enough, we were hoping to end the first game with a bang but all we got was just each of us trading turns to annihilate  a resolve point of the emperor. A flat finish to a flat game. It only got flatter with the terrible end credits.
To charge $22 USD for a game like this and release DLC is a disgrace and nothing less. Forget the bloodthirster demon this is another GW moneythirster demon that spawns across steam and tried to take my money and sanity. The only redeeming feature was that I got a refund.

Single handedly the worst 40K (30K?) game I've played, and there are some very shonky 40K products out there. I simply do not possess the vocabulary to describe how utterly tedious this was even while playing with a good friend. Also, I have played Talisman (board game) so I was aware going into this that there are good game mechanics and not so great ones.
Here are a few things I didn't like:
- Horrendous UI. It is both aesthetically♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and also functionally broke. In-game descriptions of game mechanics are vague with some guesswork required. You are also locked into watching each player's turn and can't explore the board or your own items while you wait. No helpful labels, if you're looking for a particular planet you better know them by memory or you're clicking each one to find a name. Colour palette is very ordinary. Yes 40K is meant to be dark and gloomy but this is just so boring compared to other 40K franchise interfaces.
- The AI. Couldn't find a quest on the questingest day of the year if they had an electrified quest finding machine. Also, I know Talisman can get a little 'grindy' but comeon AI, your stats are ridiculous, head towards the middle now or maybe start that quest? AI, do you really have to play ever possible strategem you have during the end game when turns are already tedious enough? Really?
- The ending. I cannot even begin to explain how utterly mundane it was. An image shows, some random in-game 'achievements' count up the stats in a vain effort to encourage you to do more playthroughs on different characters (even the day one DLC ones, see below) and then you're dumped at the main menu. There's no explanation of the monumental feat you've just achieved, no lore to read through. Nothing. Hey I'd feel good if I didn't just want the game to be finished at that point.
- Day one DLC. Why let your♥♥♥♥♥♥game get in the way of charging more money for characters? Maybe the funds raised could be pumped back into the game to make it... better? Nah.
- The fact I cannot get a refund because my one complete playthrough took me over 2 hours. Yep. Pretty sure that's an intended feature.
Also Apologies to my mate Rick Havoc who I shared this experience with. We were making the best of a bad game but towards the end we both just wanted out.

A turn-based tacticle strategy with a deep story.  You will experience the story through the eyes of different characters who journey through an infested land after the Gods destroyed each other.. and if that wasn't bad enough, the sun just went out and no one knows why.
You command a caravan of soldiers and travel throughout the land.  Each decision you make will factor into the story and even  those that join your party can cause you nightmares.  You may have to dicipline your troops or find ways to improve morale, manage your supplies and of course, level your heroes.
Combat begins with troop placement after you decide who will be in the team for that fight.  Kind of reminds me of FFTactics.  Troops can move/attack as usual in this type of combat system.  You have archers, fighters, giants, etc to battle with.  Each troop has special attacks that you can use as well.
A special turn on this combat system is that your strength is also your health.  So after chopping through armor, you begin to weaken your opponent as you are killing them.  Battles are a challenge.
No pixles here.  This game looks great.  It reminds me of many cartoon movies I saw growing up.  It all looks hand drawn, even the still shots have some movement in them (like snow blowing hair).
The story is not all voice acted, so you will read some.  But the story is solid, with heavy Viking overtones.  If you are looking for a grid based, turn based battle system similar to the style of FFTactics or Baldur's gate with a good story this is it.

Understand that this game is its own world. It has its own rules and logic and not all of them are recognizable right away. At first, the game seems hard, and it almost is. This game is not a guided tour. You’ll need to reload quick saves here and there, and might even lose progress up to 30min of play or more because of a surprise encounter or trap.
But! This game is outstanding. All of the above points only help to realize and flesh out the world. The sense of achievement you get when figuring out a difficult puzzle or beating a tough encounter is huge. This game is great, and if you aren't playing it and have a tiny shred of interest, i'd reccomend it without hesitation. In short this is a fantastic game and I cant recommend it enough.

Half-Life, what is it, is it a video game, could it be a tale that no other game could do without getting it wrong, yes...
For me, Half-Life was the first ever game I bought and owned, I remember that day. August 2nd, 2007, my father got me my very own steam account, and my first game on that steam account, MY VERY OWN GAME! It was amazing to me, I remember fearing for my life, crying as the civil protection was "clearing" the apartments, I never would have imagined the police would ever be my foe, back at the age of 7, I remember questioning why the CP's were doing this, and why they acted so, un humane (until I later learned about American Police problems). Or when I first encounter Alyx Vance, Barney, Doctor Kliner, and his pet head crab, Lamar. But what about when I first saw the Air Boat, and yeah, an air boat is cool on its own, BUT WHAT ABOUT A UPGRADE THAT WOULD MAKE ME AND THE HUNTER CHOPER EQUALS, AND ABLE TO FIGHT IT ON! I fought with the metallic flying beast, and we both knew only one of us would survive to tell the tale. I remember when I first met D0G, a robotic canine, well, similar, but more then just a yaye-high pet. Then I grew of anger as the combine destroyed everything that was of Black Mesa East. I had to go to Ravenholm, a place that even my most cherished companion, Alyx, feared and avoided to look towards that direction, I wondered why this was the case. But I had to put my friends fears of that pace aside, and march in, and continue my journey towards the end goal. As I slowly put my foot on the old, and ruined grass, I see death, despair, and danger. But sadly, my 7 year old self feared Ravenholm a lot, I guess you could say, it was too much for me. Ever since, I never escaped Ravenholm...
BUT! In the summer of 2012, I returned to Half-Life 2, played through it again, and looked towards that dreaded place as Alyx was explaining about it, before the combine attack. I knew I had to finish Half-Life 2! And so, I got a ♥♥♥♥ing huge 2 L bottle of Coca Cola, and journeyed through that place, I remember my hart beating as those Fast Zombies were clawing at me, and waiting for that small platform to carry me away from danger. Then me, and a creepy religious man with a double barrel shotgun walked through the graveyard, and at that last moment, he sacrificed himself for ME! I remember my shocked mind as he ran through fire, laughing and killing the zombies. I turned towards the exit, and ran without looking back. I remember seeing the sun again, and never felt the same ever again. I remember seeing the Jeep and was shocked, first an Air boat, now a Jeep with, a, umm, laser gun, oohhh boy, the looks were deceiving, I then killed my first gunship, and crossed the large, shaking bridge, and avoiding the train as it did its routine...
Oh yeah, then the sand traps, I ran right through that, then the prison, oh boy, I remember laughing as I saw the antlions take down combine and/or the turrets, and seeing how loyal they were to me, this was just the beginning, then me and Alyx teleport in the FUTURE, well more like a week, but then all of humanity decided to start an uprising due to the signal after teleporting from the citadel. Then I fought lots of striders, soldiers, CP's, gunships, till I got to the citadel. That first moment where intense music started right as I exit a sewage pipe, to see the citadel slowly mining into the planet, I had to stop them, and so I did, with the help of the combine and their ♥♥♥♥ed up anti-weapon device, they modified my anti-gravity gun, to grab soldiers, and also, have an higher carnage. And I fought with Breen, destroyed the citadel, and saw the Gman again, this all felt amazing ,the carnage, the intense finally, and the perfect cliff hanger for the next 2 episodes, that I got later...
If you made it this far in reading, I thank you for reading an gamers story, of Half-Life 2 and a young gamer...

Star Wars Battlefront® II is a first/third-person shooter that brings together a solid combination of infantry and vehicular combat; to create the feel of large-scale and epic battles, and to allow the player to relive the conflicts that have taken place within the Star Wars movie saga.
The game includes four factions - with each one containing their own unique infantry, weaponry and vehicles. The character classes are fairly balanced, and can make use of different play styles.This puts more emphasis on teamwork as opposed to just firepower; although in certain scenarios sheer manpower is required to best the enemy, and can cause the experience to feel more like that of a team-based deathmatch from a classic FPS game e.g.: Unreal Tournament.
Unlike its predecessor - Star Wars Battlefront® II has replaced air vehicles with whole new space-based levels; which make use of capital ships to spawn the teams and their pilotable spacecraft. These maps can either be played with the Capture the Flag game mode or the Assault game mode; with the latter requiring the destruction of certain enemy objects. To get the full space battle experience it is recommended to play space levels with the Assault game mode.
Overall it is a very enjoyable game, both for its single-player and multiplayer aspects, and is one which is worthy of being named as part of the Star Wars franchise.

What could possibly make the Star Wars universe even better? Hundreds of troops running around with rockets, snipers, bowcasters, and practically anything you can think of from a galaxy far, far away blowing one another up under the impending destruction of AT-ATs and Snowspeeders. This game, despite it's obviously out-dated engine and its many glitches discovered by the faithful players of its community after years of play, still holds strong as the high point of LucasArts' game-creating career. If you want a solid 1st/3rd person shooter or just love Star Wars and it's many epic battles, you want this game. And if you want a much more modern version after that, well we've finally got our wish thanks to DICE and EA. Star Wars Battlefront II itself, though, was well worth my time and money for the many years I spent on this game, and I would recommend it to anyone with a love for shooters or the Star Wars universe.

You can probably tell at a glance whether you will like this game. If you are a fan of the Pixel Art style and enjoy RPGs, then you will love Knights of Pen and Paper. Otherwise, move along. This game is quirky, entertaining, and more robust than a lot of people give it credit for.
The last game I bought on Steam before Knights of Pen and Paper was Final Fantasy III, and I have to say, I actually think KoPaP has a better class system than FFIII. I certainly enjoyed it a lot more. There are six classes available at first, with another six that you can unlock for future playthroughs by completing side quests throughout the game. Each class has four abilities which you can upgrade over time as the character levels up. These abilities can either be passive (increasing attack power, critical chance, physical resistance, etc.) or active (dealing extra damage, buffing friendly units, etc.), and the variety of different classes and different abilities means that you can come up with different strategies and play styles on each and every playthrough.
This game has a ton of replay value. Setting up a unique and balanced party is half the fun--the other half is learning how to make the most out of the combinations you choose. And since each of the twelve (or seventeen) playable characters has unique traits as well (such as extra experience, extra luck, or skill bonuses), this game provides way more variety between one playthrough and the next than you might think from the "casual" label the game has earned from a lot of people.
Furthermore, KoPaP's gameplay successfully solves some of the problems inherent in turn-based RPGs--including Final Fantasy III. Turn order is determined at random at the start of every battle (bases on each character and enemy's Initiative stat), but it stays the same throughout the entire battle. Thus, the game allows you to strategize, knowing exactly which characters get to move when, but still introduces an element of randomness that makes every battle feel unique. Consecutive fights against the exact same enemies will play out differently and require slightly different strategies.
Visually, KoPaP makes clever and effective use of the faux-8-bit style that's currently so popular in indie games. When characters from other Behold Studios games appear as part of certain quests, the humorously obvious contrast between the blocky KoPaP characters and the much higher-resolution guest characters serves to remind you that this game looks the way it does as a matter of choice--not of hardware or software limitations.
The backgrounds in nearly every area you visit are loaded with minimalistically rendered pop culture references, from Lord of the Rings to Captain America. But these references get annoying quickly once they start working their way into the game's main plotlines. What is amusing as a background easter egg comes across as cheesy, clunky, and unfitting as a major foreground element. The game tries to spin these pop culture interpositions as an inside joke about how real-world RPG dungeon masters come up with their material, but the joke, in my opinion, falls flat.
Therein lies one potential pitfall of the game: KoPaP derives most of its humor from stereotypes and inside jokes about real-world RPG players. Sometimes, the game strikes on some genuinely amusing and accessible ideas. All of the original twelve playable characters are pretty funny--from Hynx (the hardcore guy who came up with his own lame fantasy name) to Mr. John (the totally normal business man who plays in his scanty spare time) to Grandma (who doesn't know what's going on and wants everyone else to speak up). But after a few hours, you'll probably be pretty bored with characters complaining about stupid quests. Or asking for the hundredth time whether someone can order a pizza. Or worse, laughing at the game's own jokes. Self-congratulation is never funny or desirable in a video game.
The game has other flaws as well. KoPaP was made by a Brazilian company, which is really cool. But the localization is really spotty, and--especially as you get closer to the end of the game--a lot of the dialogue is totally garbled and difficult to make out. Given how much of the humor and plot of this game depends on dialogue for delivery, that's a pretty serious problem. Also, outside of a single box of flavor text when you first create a character, none of the playable characters has any unique dialogue. Each character simply gets assigned different lines of text that are the exact same on every playthrough. And while it can be amusing to hear Grandma complain about why there aren't more hot girls in the game's quests, the canned dialogue gets old once you've already seen it once or twice.
For the most part, the game does a good job "scaling" enemies so that you are always at an appropriate level to tackle  the main storyline quests. But towards the end of the game, more enemies gain powerful abilities that can make them much harder than their level suggests. You will face some frustrations from enemies that are pushovers in one battle and obliterate you in the next. The game also helpfully tells you approximately what level of enemies you will face in any specific quest. But there are a lot of mistakes--particularly on quests that have you going to multiple locations or that show up as a set--which can lead to you stumbling into difficult areas before you're ready (or abandoning a quest halfway through).
Really, I can only see two truly "casual" elements to this game. First, you can save and quit at any point when you aren't fighting enemies. It's a nice touch, since it means you can play this game for five minutes or two hours. But, second, this game shows its "casual" nature in that you will probably start to get bored if you play for much more than an hour or an hour-and-a-half at once. For one thing, the game's story is pretty goofy and trivial--more entertaining than engrossing. And there are only so many variations on the "go to X, battle Y" formula that the game can throw you before it gets a little tiresome. Seriously. The gameplay in this game consists entirely of traveling to different areas and fighting different enemies. Of course, combat is fun and engaging, but the game is still better in small doses.

I admit, I miss tabletop gaming. I miss the DM trying to kill off my characters. I miss creating ridiculously out-of-the-box characters. Heck, I miss the days of popcorn, Mountain Dew, and just hanging out and rolling some dice. Those days have been gone for me quite some time, and yet playing a little game called Knights of Pen and Paper reminded me of those good old days.
Knights of Pen and Paper attempts to mimic tabletop gaming for an accessible audience. Players start by selecting three noobs to join the adventuring party, along with their class and starting skill. Like any tabletop RPG, as the adventuring party explores, kills baddies, and completes quests, they earn experience to level up and gain more skills. Each party member gets one skill point every time they level up and can only put points into one of four skills. While this creates simplicity for those unfamiliar with RPGs, it doesn't provide a lot of variety.
In fact, variety is what Knights of Pen and Paper struggles with throughout its twenty hour campaign. Although the backgrounds mimic an 8-bit style, there isn't much in terms of detail or design. The soundtrack loops, but it feels like there's only three tracks in the entire game. Although there's plenty of classes in the game, many of them are locked and the requirements for unlocking them appear random. The base classes — paladin, mage, cleric, etc. — while classic, are trapped with only four skills, which wouldn't be the case in tabletop gaming.
While variety isn't the game's strong suit, accessibility is. It provides a simple turn-based battle system wherein players can select between attack, skill, defend, item, and flee. This makes for an easy learning experience, but it lacks any real depth that a tabletop game has. The game is also surprisingly grindy, and while it does a great job of teaching players what to expect in encounters (usually enemies three to five levels higher than the adventuring party), it's a bit crazy how much players will have to stop and grind because it's not entirely on par with the party's level. It feels like the developers set out to make a simple RPG to give players the feel of tabletop gaming, but the combat could have benefited from actual dice rolls on screen to indicate whether or not the player's characters succeeded or fail in their actions. However, with the grindy combat, perhaps adding dice rolls would have just made everything take longer than provide more accessibility. Still, the combat lacks depth and it needs something else to make it a more engaging process.
Dice rolling does exist within Knights of Pen and Paper, it's just not as frequent as it should be. Dice rolls occur when players travel between areas, failures leading to battles, successes leading to safety. Dice rolls occur when players are mining for grindstones or moving through dungeons. These elements are done well and are fairly straightforward, but this game would really benefit if it was implemented into all actions, especially if its goal is to mimic tabletop games. What's further disappointing is the campaign itself. While the writing is charming and hilarious, the majority of the quests are either escort missions, collecting items, slaying some bad dudes, or traveling from place to place for plot purposes. The amount of backtracking in this game is brutal and inexcusable, and even the adventuring party complains about it. It goes back to that problem of accessibility versus variety — on one hand, the campaign should be easy to learn and follow along, on the other hand there should be more to do than then the standard affair. The charm in the writing, and even its awkward translation errors, can only go so far and will likely leave veteran RPG gamers wanting something more substantial.
However, Knights of Pen and Paper does succeed in its overall atmosphere. Players get the sense of gamers hanging out, bantering, and asking to pass the Mountain Dew. There is an overall sense that the Dungeon Master is out to kill the adventuring party, and the back and forth within the writing really does work well. The graphics and music, though overly simplistic, are vibrant and give the feeling that players are on an adventure and there is loot to be had. The game is also a fantastic time waster because in its lack of depth it success at being the type of mindless game where players find themselves going, "just one more quest." Considering all of the game's flaws, it admittedly succeeds in the one area that for some people matters most: it's actually fun.
There are some perks in Knights of Pen and Paper's PC release that differ from the original mobile version. For starters, it allows players to leave party members at the tavern, and bring a new adventurers into the party. They can roll for a new character and not feel like they have to start their entire campaign from scratch. There's also an extended campaign for those who want to explore more of what the game has to offer, and there's tons of new dungeons and loot to acquire. The main campaign can be completed in around twenty hours, with the extended campaign offering quite a bit of replay value. There's also tons of items that can be purchased in shops that can give added bonuses to various stats, which is a nice cosmetic feature.
Knights of Pen and Paper is a sweet little throwback to the days of pen and paper gaming, but its simple approach may not be enough to entice every RPG gamer. Yes, the combat is simplistic, but it's fast and easy to roll with. Sure, the story is simple, but it's cute in its presentation. Knights of Pen and Paper's imperfections are many, and yet it's completely easy to sink time into. It's straightforward in its approach and yet, despite its flaws and frustration, I kept playing. Knights of Pen and Paper will never offer gamers a deep experience, but it offers mindless gameplay that admittedly can keep you coming back for more.

I seriously wanted to like it. It has an iconic art style and there's nothing wrong with running and jumping and an occasional kick in a baddie's face.
But for some reason the devs thought that rubbing a jump fail or weapon grab fail (and you'll have 100s of those) in our noses would be a good idea. When you fail you'll have to endure a fall to death with horrible bone break and squishy wet noises in the end. Thats kinda ok once or twice but believe me it gets tedious. And that's the best outcome.
In some cases you can't even fall to your death and yet you know that you've failed (because you haven't escaped the guards). In that case you'll have to let the guards kill you. You might ask "but can't I just go back to the previous save point?" No you can't. You have to let yourself fall to death. When that doesn't work you have to let the guards shoot you down. And even for that, sometimes you have to climb a long ladder because the guards are too stupid to reach you otherwise.
Seriously, dear devs, this kind of game design stopped being good around 1989.
Additionally one might mention that putting puzzles (finding a non-trivial way in a building) and pressure (guards rushing in) together results in frustration. It breaks immersion when you solve the puzzle by just dying and respawning and trying again. This alone wouldn't break the game but it is a point.
Difficulty is ok if the player has control. XCOM can be very difficult but there the player has control. Here too many things (wall runs come to mind) are far too random. There difficulty turns to frustration.
As I said, I wanted to like it but it's impossible. I also thought about recommending it only for its art style but I think it's necessary to discourage this kind of game system design.
If you are looking for something where immersion isn't broken all the time, that also has a very good art style and actually likable characters and a likeable story, try Remember Me.

Orcs must die! That one sentence is actually all you have to know about the game with the same title. It's a mixture between tower defense and an kind of action-rpg, where you have to prevent orcs and all their fellow companions like ogres, flying wyvern, and all that good stuff to enter the portals to the outer world. To do this, you have to... kill them. Of course.
Story:
If you actually want to play this game because of the story, you're considering buying the wrong game. There is basically no story, except if you call that little bit of dialoges between the hero and the villain a story. They're fun to listen to, as mentioned below aswell, but nothing special. Just the regular "evil person wants to destroy the world, hero has to stop her"-story.
2/10, but f*ck that, that's not what makes the game the great game it is, so read on.
Gameplay:
Before starting a game, you have to decide which items you want to use. There are about 25 different defense elements and 5 weapons for the player, such as a lightning ring, an ice ring or a blade, and of course the crossbow, which is your standard weapon.
Then, after having built your line of defence, you enter "G" and the actual fun begins. Orcs and other creatures come and run to the portal (or portals, as you have multiple ones to protect on higher maps). Depending on your build you'll have to do more or less yourself, while your defence units are killing the mobs.
There are three difficulties, one for beginners, "Warmage-Difficulty" (which is the standard one) and "Nightmare-Difficulty", which you unlock after beating the game on Warmage-Difficulty. On nightmare, you have only 3 seconds before the game begins, then you can't stop it anymore, so you have to think fast and play fast. There's actually skill required.
9.5/10
Graphics:
The game is not the newest. It hasn't got high-end graphics, but I like the comic-style of the art design. It's playful, fun, and excentrical. It fits perfectly to the game and to the main character, who's a little bit narcisstic, sarcastic and feels over-the-top, which makes him super fun.
7/10
Sound/Music:
The entire sound is great. While fighting, there's a mixture of rock/metal music with old, somehow medieval music playing. It's fast, it's hard, it rocks, it's just excellent if you like this kind of music.
If you headshot enemies, there sometimes might be special e-guitar riffs played, which makes them quite satisfying.
The monsters sometimes may comment your actions or say stupid things like "why does his crossbow shoot 1000 times a second?" with ultra-stupid voices, which makes them REALLY fun to listen to. Also, they make somehow fun of themselfes, which fits into the concept of Orcs Must Die! pretty well aswell.
The hero - the Warmage - is nice voice acted and sometimes also comments the action going on on the screen in his sarcastic way. Pretty fun aswell.
The villain is nice voice acted aswell, and the dialoges between her and the Warmage are in most of the cases really fun to listen to.
10/10, definitely.
Overall:
Orcs Must Die! is a great tower defense game. It's fun, challenging, entertaining, humorous, and hours fly by like a few seconds when playing it. I love it.
36.5/40 (as story isn't important, if you want to consider it, you get a 38.5/50; but trust me, it's a 50/50 for me personally.)

I've put 100s of hours into Talisman between the Steam and tablet versions, and I love it. That said, I bought Horus Heresy not expecting too much but have been floored at just how little it really is.
Make no mistake, Horus Heresy is nothing more than a re-skinned Talisman. The engine is blatently identical. While the animated backgrounds and board graphics are definitely a step up, I can't help but feel like I'm playing a Talisman *mod* rather than another game entirely. If anything, playing Horus Heresy simply makes me want to go back and play more Talisman.
Another thing bothering me is the potential for expansions. Whereas Talisman has plenty of Board-n-Box expansions to digitally recreate, Horus Heresy is an in-house creation from Nomad, so there is no canon to really go off of when adding content. This is only made worse when you realize...
... The content they create is going to milked even worse to players, since there are no physical expanions to recreate as in the original Talisman. Without something physically to copy, there is no real place to begin and end. No "finish line" for the DLC product. It's all up to them, and the example is already set with the two garbage DLCs they have released already on Day 1. It's a few extra cards and classes that could have been easily included in the base game.
Not doing so is a gesture of bad faith.
I will never, ever forgive a company for releasing Day #1 DLC. It only shows they they were willing to hold back content that could have been (and arguably, should have been) packaged in base game. They are deliberately short-selling the main product to nickle and dime you about it, on the same shelf. If they had waited at least a few months or so that would be one thing, but *same day* DLC is inexcusable. I don't understand how a company can do this and not feel completely covered in shame.

Brilliant. A refreshing dose of 'choices matter' in an age of gaming that offers everything but, even if it says so on the box.
You're not a legend or a hero. You the sun has been stuck in the sky for days on end, without explanation. You lead your small village away on a quest for safety, chased by an inhuman foe that can not or will not be reasoned with. You wonder whether what few resources you have should go towards: Equipment, upgrades, food, all seem equally important and each more scarce with each passing day. Who do you trust? Safety in numbers is well and good, until one of those numbers decides your skull would look better with an axe through the back. And even those you can trust will always squabble amongst themselves, complaints and greivances becomming more common than sand on the beach. Then the ambush happens. All the while you try to keep your caravan together, hoping that behind each turn will be salvation, answers, or at least a brief respite from the harshness of the end of the world.
This game is as much about the story as it is the gameplay, and it does deliver on that with the help of a beautiful art style and soundtrack. Though the gameplay is still there, and every bit as unforgiving as the tale it's tied to. Taking fairly simple isometric turn-based strategy and adding a system of armor/armor damaging, and willpower which units can spend in combat on more damage/movement/abilities. The turn system is a little odd and might take some adjusting, but by the 3rd chapter I managed to settle in to it. I believe there is a free game called Banner Saga Factions that one can check out to get a feel for the combat.
The only real disappointment I had was how abruptly the game ended. There were also two points in the game where I was shoe-horned into making a certain decision in order to progress, but in truth there is only one point in the game where you are presented with the illusion of choice. The final fight is also insanely difficult if you aren't prepared or don't have characters with certain capabilities ready to kick♥♥♥♥♥ The final boss is a right♥♥♥♥♥♥ but considering what he is he should be anyway. Be prepared to fight him about ten times before reluctantly turning the difficulty down to easy and kick him in the nuts.
In closing I will say that this is the only game that has presented me with a choice and forced me to get up and do something else while thinking it through. If you're the type that likes to get attached to characters and immerse yourself in the story of a game and love(or at least can put up with) a somewhat difficult bunch of battles this is definitely for you.

Before this Remake / Remaster I had never heard of this series. The look got me really interested though, so much that I had to buy the game.
For me, the style totally carries the game. It just looks awesome. I love the look of the characters and the animations. Being able to change the graphics and music to the original style at will is also pretty neat, not much more though.
Sadly, the controls are not as crisp as you would like in a game like this. I heard some people say that it plays exactly like the original, which is probably the reason why. Since I do not have any nostalgic feelings for the game / series that does not really do anything for me. It just makes the game a bit worse.
Also the "stun locks" are not really fun (when they happen to you). When you get hit you get knocked backwards a bit and are invincible for a short time. The same happens with enemies, just without the invincibility. Pretty typical platformer stuff. While you are invincible, you can still get hit and knocked back though, and sometimes you get hit 2-4 times back-to-back and are basically just getting "tossed" around. This was extremely bad during the last boss fight, where I got carried from one side of the room to the other regularly, because I missed a hit on the boss. Luckily you do not take extra damage during this, the invincibility is apparently renewed every time you get hit. Still, you basically do not get to play for a few seconds and it just feels bad.
The character switching is nice and adds a bit of variety to the game. I probably could have done without the bird or fish though. They are pretty same-y, just that one can fly through the air the other through the water.
I'm not a fan of the weird secret doors. A few doors are in spots where it makes sense, others are just completely random.
I can not decide if it's good or bad that it is possible to (accidentally) skip bosses / transformations. I happend to completely miss the Shipwreck level, and subsequently did not fight the Captain Dragon and got transformed into the lion but I still managed to get to the Daimyo Temple (ninja / samurai level) as the mouse. This made things way harder for me than they were supposed to and only after getting the Tasmainian Sword (to change characters at will), was I able to beat the level. Luckily I unlocked the lion at the same time as the bird, otherwise I would have been screwed.
All in all, the wonky controls and my "inability" to find the correct level entrances are not enough for me to not recommend the game, because it just looks soooo good.

I can say without fear of being wrong that this is, by far and large, not only the best remaster of a classic game. It's also perhaps the best of the whole nostalgia gaming wave to date.
If your age range is around the 40s and you grew up with a Sega Master System then all I have to say is: YES, it IS as good as you remember, it is just as sweet, and the remaster will bring a tear to your eye. The downside, if you have been a gamer this long, however, is this: The game is going to be too short and too easy. While gaming today has gotten a lot more forgiving in several areas, it has grown also more complex and provides richer experiences, so unless you pace yourself and play in hard mode, then you'll probably finish the game in two days tops (even if now you're a busy person).
Still, short as it may be, and easy as it may be, BUY IT. It's worth every penny, and you won't have a sweeter trip down the nostalgia lane.

For gamers that grew up on the Infinity Engine games from Black Isle Studios and BioWare, this game is a breath of fresh air in a landscape of ever more action oriented RPGs.  It blends the old and the new with incredible sensitivity for what made the golden age of isometric western RPGs great and what needed improvement.  Top notch writing, incredibly deep and engaging combat mechanics, excellent world building, and a campaign of staggering scope work together to make one of the best games I've played in recent memory, and one that really brings meaning back to the Role-Playing label.
Everything about this game is deliciously old school, without the clunky interfaces, horrible pathfinding, and opaque game mechanics that our rose-tinted nostalgia glasses regularly filter from older games.  The quests require actual reading and investigation, without giving you quest icons or other blatant guide markers that can be followed blindly to their resolution.  The world is deeply interactive with a plethora of items to find or steal, NPCs to aid or slaughter, and an interesting item movement mechanic that allows you to relocate or reposition most items or furniture you see sitting around.  Combat and puzzle difficulty is punishing but not unfairly so, and character progression is similarly challenging as sloppy choices can come back to bite you later on.
If I had to nitpick, I'd say that the crafting system is a little too inaccessible and takes too much effort to be useful, but the fact that it was implemented with as much depth as it has is impressive.  There could stand to be a few more tooltips in combat to help you navigate your character around dangerous ground effects.  The AI is pretty basic, and can be taken advantage of in some of the harder fights.  Regardless, I don't hesitate to recommend this game and can't wait to see what campaigns and additional content come out of the mod community.

The atmosphere of this game is absolutely amazing...the world it builds, the level of detail in the lore, the characters and their struggles, the plot and the overwhelming sense of despair. It paints an amazing picture that sucks you into the story.
Unfortunately, the end of the game, particularly the final "boss" fight, ruins the game for me. The boss fight is a lesson in tedium and gives an artifical difficulty in cheap tactics and requiring exactly one tactic, despite however you've played the game prior to this.
And after that boss fight? Nothing. The game ends, tying up absolutely nothing in the story. Supposedly it's meant to be a trilogy, but it ends at such an underwhelming spot in the story. It's like if Star Wars ended when the Millennium Falcon escaped the Death Star, and you had to wait for the next movie any sort of resolution whatsoever. What kind of climax is that?
Worse, the "boss" at the final battle is ultimately meaningless for the story, which combined with the stupidly frustrating fight leaves a sour taste in my mouth.
I really, really, really liked this game until the end.
So I cannot recommend it. The world it built is amazing and I want to see so much of it, but the story is very slow and methodical, and ends abruptly and without much progress. My mind may change when the sequel (or sequels) is done, but at this rate I would recommend waiting until the creators have finished weaving this so-called saga.

This is a game about little space dudes trying to save their space empire from the evil space rebels, only to find that they run out of missiles on some dumb automated scout who's shields are too tough for their burst laser II to get through. So then they're sitting there waiting for their FTL drive to charge so they can jump away, hoping that their own shields hold, when the automated scout gets a missile through and hits their cockpit. So now their FTL is delayed, and the cockpit is on fire, and the mantis that was piloting the ship is trying his darnedest to put out the fire that's slowly killing him (but you know that giant space mantis has a hard time holding a fire extinguisher, so he'll die before the fire goes out). So the guy at weapons control heads to the cockpit to help, but since he's a rock dude he takes 15 years to get there. And while he's on his way, the mantis has had to leave before being cooked, heading to the med bay.
So now the fire is spreading, entirely engulfing the cockpit and the hallway outside of it. The mantis, upon reaching the med bay, is surprised to find that it's not working because power has been routed from it to supply the weapons systems. So they reroute power to the med bay, taking it from the O2 supply. But don't worry, they'll bring that back up before everyone suffocates, hopefully.
The rock dude has finally made it to the cockpit and is stomping out the fire, when another missile hits the shield generator and the shields go offline. Right as the shields go down, a halberd beam rips across the ship, hitting mostly empty rooms, but causing the automated warning sirens to alert the crew that hull integrity is down to 50%. Immediately, the remaining crew abandon their posts and rush to the shield room to get them back online. All of a sudden, the internal view screens go dark as the sensors are knocked offline by another missile.
The crew is panicking now. The rock dude, having finally put out the fire, is starting repairs on the navigational systems (though the crew still wonders how a large humanoid rock man can fix a computer terminal by simply hitting it, but hey, whatever works). Repairs to the shields are around 50%, so they come partially online, stopping the halberd beam. The automated drone, knowing no sympathy (or any emotion for that fact), continues it's relentless assault. Missiles continue to hit the ship, some tearing holes in the hull, others starting more fires. The rock dude makes his final repairs and brings navigation back online. It's only got another minute or so before it resolves the jump trajectory, but the crew isn't sure if they have that long.
Another explosion and siren sounds, this time signaling hull integrity at 25%. The shields are now fully online, and the mantis is back at the helm. There seems to be a shred of hope after all. The rock dude heads off to the sensor room to figure that mess out. Explosions continue to rock the ship; another missile strike to the shields (bringing them back down), and another halberd beam across the weapons systems. No shields, no weapons, and the only human on the crew is pretty sure that if she sneezes the whole ship will break apart.
This is when the crew realizes that they never brought the O2 back online. They try to route power to it, but the O2 control was hit by a missile and is offline. And the room is on fire, along with a good portion of the rest of the ship. The crew will never know this though, because the sensors are still offline (the rock dude is sill on his way). No oxygen, an unrelenting missile barrage, and the heat from the out of control fire sap the rest of the hope from the crew. Will they make it?
Probably not. But one thing is certain; they'll try again. And again. And again. Each journey a new adventure, a new story to be told. And maybe they'll get through to the end, to warn their friends in the space empire about the impending doom they all face.
Or maybe they'll have all their doors open when the door control is hit by a missile and all the oxygen rushed into space. That'll happen at least once too.

Let me start off by saying that I have been a part of the Killing Floor community since its inception.
I have witnessed the game take shape and form, becoming a standalone title (Killing Floor "1") and onwards it went. I have contributed to the original KF community via Mapping as well as providing many servers to this day.
I loved the original game and still do.
The sum of my thoughts in regards to KF2 is pretty much this: I would have liked nothing more than Tripwire releasing Killing Floor 2 under a completely different title that shares nothing with its "PREQUEL" and i ♥♥♥♥ing loathe having to use that term now, as it does a terrible ♥♥♥♥ing job at carrying on what made the "original" (and as far as I am concerned, ONLY) Killing Floor great.
If ALL you are looking for is fastfood gaming, no emphasis on actual teamwork or skill, in other words the ultra casual variant of its daddy, that all it has going for it is a prettier packaging, then KF2 is just the game for you.
I wanted to love it, I really did and now all I would wish for would be for the game to be renamed, because it does not deserve to piggyback off the original.
Other negative reviewers pointed out specifics quite well, no need for me to write an eyecancer inducing wall of text with all the countless things wrong with it and how it didnt manage to capture anything that made the real Killing Floor great.
Aside from the superifical, namely the gore and resulting carnage. If thats all you require, if thats the extent of your expectations, you are good to go and throw your money at this clown company (that it has become).
