Robot Entertainment mixes elements of different game types to conjure up a brilliant rendition of the tower defense genre. Taking action packed battles and mixing them with strategy you get a game that pushes both hack ‘n slash as well as base management.
The order has fallen, the last War Mage is dead, and protecting the realm is now left up to you his apprentice. You must fight your way through the unlimited hordes of orcs as you defend the rifts from falling into the wrong hands. As you press through your adventure you come to learn the evil forces are being led by a corrupted War Mage who plans to destroy humanity. Will you be able to save the world from falling into darkness?
The campaign is broken down into three acts. The first act has ten levels, the second act has 8, and the third act has 6. Despite each act having fewer levels than the last they are all about the same length as the number of waves increases throughout the campaign. Each level unlocks a new element to the game and once you’ve completed the level you gain the new item for any preceding or future level. Each time you beat a level you get a rating of one to five skulls, unlike most games these skulls actually are given to you as a currency which you can use to upgrade items. You can only get five skulls per level, meaning you cannot beat a level scoring five skulls then play it again to get another five skulls. Each level you can choose from a mastery tree that allows you to kit yourself out for that level, based on your strategies this can vary greatly throughout the campaign. You will progressively unlock more tower/item slots, which start as you only being able to equip three towers/items but later on you’ll find yourself with 10+ slots. You play the entire game in third person, and similar to other games of the genre you are able to join in the battle and help your towers out. This means you are not just sitting there waiting between waves, but rather taking an active part into the gameplay. Some levels you may find yourself not needing to join in, while others you will be right in the fray.
Each level allows you to equip an inventory which allows you to choose from a combination of spells, weapons, and towers. There are two weapons (crossbow and bladestaff), four spells (flame bracers, ice amulet, lightning ring, and wind belt), two guardians (paladins and archers), and 17 towers. I found myself typically sticking to the same set throughout the entire campaign, but there are many different strategies you can go for. By placing player activated traps you can take a large part of the game, you can sit back and use guardians to do most of the work, or even mix and match. The gameplay is fast paced and really pulls you into the mix by getting you to experience new elements each level.
Artifacts of Power is a DLC that includes new items and towers. The DLC includes two traps (Shock Zapper and Floor Scorcher) and two spells (Vampiric Gauntlets and Alchemist Satchel). I used the Floor Scorcher and Vampiric Gauntlets a few times, found the Shock Zapper completely useless (as you need a roof for it to function), and used the Alchemist Satchel to get a +50 kill streak for the achievement. All and all this DLC isn’t exactly necessary, but if you can get it on sale and included in the pack it’s worth grabbing.
Lost Adventures is a DLC that includes new level, enemies, and even a new tower. There are five new levels, which offer more skulls allowing for even more upgrades. There are two new enemies the Frost Bat, and Cyclops Mage. It also includes one new trap the mana well which allows you to refill your mana gauge. This DLC is completely worth it as it adds additional content, new enemies, towers, and refined leaderboards. If you can get this on sale or in the bundle you will not regret it.
Orcs Must Die is an epic tower defense hack ‘n slash game that keeps you pressed and wanting more. With rating systems that actually give you rewards, fun and interesting enemies, a long and arduous campaign, and an amusing little story Orcs Must Die is a Must Buy (too easy). If you are looking for something similar to Sang-Froid or Sanctum this is pretty much in that line. Once you beat Orcs Must Die you’ll feel like you need to buy the second one as it makes you just want to play more.
Pros:
+Leaderboard system that allows you to rank yourself amongst friends.
+Level rating out of five skulls which can then be used to buy upgrades.
+Loads of spells, weapons, and towers to choose from.
+Skill trees which can be customized each level to allow you to change how you play (more player intensive, tower support, or mixture of both).
+Smooth graphics which look good and don’t push it too far.
+Funny and amusing dialogue which gives you a laugh without being offensive.
+Intense amount of action, keeps you pressed and fighting between each wave.
+Built in level traps (such as rolling locks, acid pots, lava pots, and ballista).
Cons:
-I had a few levels glitch where an enemy wouldn’t leave the spawn point and thus I couldn’t kill it requiring me to restart (this was annoying if it was at the end of the level).
-If Gnoll Hunters fall into acid pits they do not die (as I learned when I set up a level that used nearby acid pits to kill enemies).
-One of the DLC levels (Reverse Tower) is just The Tower in Reverse. I know this is obvious from the title, but if you purchase the DLC before playing the game its disappointing to find out one of the levels is the same thing just backwards.

People who like board games are going to like this. People who like Warhammer are really going to like this. People who like board games and Warhammer are going to ♥♥♥♥ing love this. Allow me to take the time to explain this to you with my awful grammar and dry sense of humor.
TL:DR/Gameplay Version - Scroll to Bottom
Talisman is a board game by Games Workshop that was originally transferred to a digital version a few years ago by the same guys who made this game. Talisman is a game where you defeat monsters, gather equipment, gain followers and eventually try to become the strongest hero in the land. Now take that concept, replace equipment with Space Marine companies and vehicles, monsters with chaos and Titan Legions and the replace the final battle with the massive encounter between Horus and The Emperor himself. It's also worth noting that there are two factions in the game for those unfamiliar with Warhammer 40,000 lore; the Loyalists and the Traitors. The loyalists fight to protect the Emperor of Mankind and the Traitors fight for Horus against the Emperor. I'm sure it's obvious which side you should choose. (The Emperor Protects).
Now here comes the part where I give you a rather poor tutorial of how the game works. You start out with by choosing a character, if you want to be a Loyalist Commander (good) or a Traitor Commander (bad). Each Primarch/Praetor/Captain has special abilities and varying stats to choose from so it's beneficial to take your time and read each one's specials. For you loyalists, Roboute Guilliman is a good place to start... and Traitors can start with Mortarion or Angron. Every commander has 6 basic stats aside from their special ability. These are Resolve (health), Fate (rerolls), Resources (used for buying junk or paying "tolls"), Melee Combat, Ranged Combat and Strategy (used for various combat rolls, only used when stated). You can increase your Combat skills (Melee/Ranged) by fighting enemies of the same type and leveling up based on it's combat skill. For example, to increase your melee, you have to use melee fighting. You need 7 exp to level up so if you fight a Combat skill of 6, you'll need to fight one more opponent of at least 1 to lvl up. If your opponent has 7 or more, you pretty much level up on kill. It should be noted that equipment, fleets, companies and legions (followers) will also increase your melee and ranged combat skills. It'll tell you which. Your stats can also be increased/decreased by various events that occur when you move spaces.
These events are generally "dataslates" (encounters). Encounters can be equipment, fleets, bad guys etc etc. Most of the time you'll run into bad guys and you'll have to kill them (combat works like Munchkin, units on the same tile that are allowed with you can support you in combat).
There are 3 zones (regions) in the game and as mentioned previously, your goal is to reach the inner region and save/kill the Emperor. The outer region is the largest and is the safest for newbs. The mid region is smaller and a bit more threatening, expect to be fighting the other players a lot in this zone. The Inner Region is the final region and has the hardest encounters by far... do not even try to go here unless your combat skill is at least 10 in either category. Also, bring a Talisman... if you don't bring a Talisman you won't be able to fight either Horus or the Emperor in the Final Battle. You'll just have to turn back around and go complete a quest to get one (did I not mention that? You have to complete an errant quest on your corresponding factions planet in the mid region (Davin for Traitors, Titan for Loyalists)). I could go on but I think I've explained enough for someone to get started.
What does this game do right? Well a lot actually. Aesthetically, it's freaking awesome! This is some of the best 40k artwork I've ever seen and realy brings the game alive. There isn't much in the way of animations or graphics which is a shame but the game's presentation is absoultely stellar with a painstakingly ridiculous amount of detail placed into each unit card, each event card and all the game's assets. The game itself is also a lot of fun, although it does take about 2-3 hours just to complete one game at the fastest setting and I don't think the tutorial does an adequate job explaining the game. It might be because it was just too wordy (I'm just being nitpicky). This is also one of the most lore heavy 40k games I've ever seen, with short descriptions on every single in game item/unit/commander that helps explain the lore to those who are unintiated.
Is there anything that is blatantly bad? Not from the time I've played so far. The dice-rolls can be frustrating sometimes but that's any game involving an RNG (I feel like I roll waaaaay too many ones). Aside from that, this game is a great purchase for any board game enthusiast or Warhammer fan.
Verdict:
Approved by the God-Emperor of Mankind.

This game both looks gorgeous and has a rather nice feel to it. I've always been a bit reserved when it comes to the original Talismans playstyle remedied a couple of my concerns with the original. Even though it heavily borrows from Talisman it feels as it tries to do its own thing with it and those efforts are, at least in my opinion, successful.
That said, the game feels rather bare-bones sadly, even though the store page says that you can play all 18 Space Marine legions in their struggle to stop/help Horus from dethroning ol' emps this isn't exactly true. Out of the 18 Legions only 9 are actually given any sort of flavour at all. The Ultramarines, The Raven Guard, The Salamanders, The Sons of Horus (although with both loyalist and traitor versions), The Imperial Fists, The World Eaters, The Death Guard, The Night Lords and the Word Bearers, the rest are DLC or coming as DLC.
Normally this wouldn't be this much of an issue for me, but coming as this is a social game that I'd prefer to play with friends, and playing board games on a PC hot-seat isn't as popular as it used to be, this means that the game instantly becomes much less attractive as people don't only have to get the core game but also the DLC that they want to play their favourite characters etc.
Speaking of favourite characters! This game adheres rather strictly to the book series it seems and many of the primarchs are replaced with champion stand-ins, neither Rogal Dorn or Lorgar Aurelian are playable at this time which is a bit of a dissapointment but not a major concern. The Luna wolves/Sons of Horus are naturally represented by Garviel Loken and Ezekyle Abaddon since Horus is one of the the bosses of the game.
There are a few more complaints that I have, for example you're unable to switch sides, heretics can't redeem themselves and loyal space marines can't go traitor, characters can very easily get ridiculous amounts of resolve so they become impossible to kill (there doesn't seem to be any realistic upper cap), the UI is a bit convoluted so reading about different effects and bonuses is something that, at least I, usually just skip and let the game determine the outcome.
In closing I'd like to say that the game is probably pretty enjoyable as a fan of the setting and even though I'll probably play it some more, the incredibly greedy business model with a majority of the cast cut out to sell the 4€ DLC for 2 characters each makes the game earn a negative review.

Whether you're a fan of Talisman or Warhammer 30,000, you'll find lots to enjoy here. Gameplay is very similar to Talisman digital. The setting is different (obviously), with the board being replaced by the star systems surrounding Holy Terra in the time leading up to the penultimate battle of the Horus Heresy. The graphics are truly stunning, with planets and stellar constructs replacing the geography of the original board.
Your player characters are Warlords of either the Loyalist or Heretical chapters of the Space Marines and the forces of Chaos. The extensive library of artwork from Games Workshop has been put to excellent use here representing the characters. Equipment and followers are now 'dataslates' fulfilling their expected functions within the Talisman engine.
Combat graphics are attractive with sparks and energy discharges crossing the screen between combatants. Combat mechanics remain functionally the same.
I've been playing Talisman since its initial release as a board game in the 1980s. I've been purchasing Fantasy Flight Games' revised fourth edition and more recently 'Relic' which, like this game, is set in the 'grim darkness of the far future, where there is only war', while utilising the Talisman gameplay engine. The Horus Heresy takes place 10 Millenia prior to the current setting of Warhammer 40,000, hence the change in nomenclature. Nomad games have taken the new setting and graphic style from Relic and translated it deftly into the digital realm.
For the extremely reasonable price, this is definitely worth the purchase. My only criticism is releasing two hero and villain DLC packs on the day of release. These add two new Warlords in each pack. The game soundtrack, which is usually included for free in a core game purchase, is pay-for DLC as well. At this stage I feel there is plenty of variety in the core game so I will be holding off purchasing the packs. While I enjoy soundtracks, I feel the price tag is a little too steep to warrant a purchase.

Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a remake of the 1989 classic Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap from the Wonder Boy series also known as Monster World. I did not know of this game in the past nor played the original version but I did do some research. There are many ways to look at this game and list out the reasons on why it's great solid game, why it's an example to be followed by any developer trying to remaster a game, and why It has some minor issues.
Pros:
-Amazing Soundtrack.
-Short but well designed areas.
-Diverse gameplay mechanics throughout all of the character's transformations.
-Areas are challenging but mostly up to how the player wants to approach it (equipment).
-Marvelous 2D art and animations.
-Fair and balanced difficulty curve.
-The option to swap graphics and sound from remastered to retro on the click of a button.
-For those looking for a faithful Remaster of the old game. It delivers exactly that.
-You can be a Wonder Girl too.
Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap was an enjoyable experience from start to end. It's hard to say what is most captivating, the amazing music or the gorgerous art that sorround the game as a whole. Having the power to see how the game used to look like back in the day makes everything even more impressive. The gameplay it's classic from the original's gaming era, a solid 2D action plataformer. Now while some old games would resort to sometimes exceeded difficulty in order to make the game feel longer, Wonder Boy takes a different step allowing players to take on the challenge head on or slowing down and getting some gold to buy equipment to overcome difficult obstacles. Skillful gameplay is rewarded but the game will not pose as a hassle for those who just want to play through a more relaxing experience.
It's important not to forget though that this is a pretty faithful Remaster of its predecessor and the game does present the player with challenges that cannot be 'worked around', some of these challenges can get quite frustrating due to some old game quirks that the game has.
Cons:
-Player character got some heavy physics applied to movement, which does not go well with some areas that require precision plataforming.
-Some secrets require a guide or a lot of trial and error to be found.
-Hard mode can sometimes be a bit too RNG dependant.
-Simplistic story.
Note that most of the criticism made here related to the gameplay apply mostly to optional areas and content, some of those might be frustrating for the reasons that were listed but they can be seen by nothing more than another challenge to be overcome with practice and dedication. As I mentioned previously, this is a very faithful Remaster of it's predecessor, In terms of Story it is just a reflection of the original game, back in Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap from 1989 you were the Wonder Boy (or Girl) who journeys across the land defeating dragons in order to remove his or her curse, in this game it's no different.
When it comes to Hard Mode the very beggining can feel sometimes unfair, but just like the normal difficulty, skillful gameplay is rewarded even though RNG can be against you sometimes in terms of health drops. It's important to say that the RNG can be somewhat countered by just knowing the areas well and by planning your actions carefully.
Overall Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a marvelous game that brought a classic back to life with beautiful graphics and animations, a great soundtrack and solid gameplay. For fans of the original game this is definitely a must without a doubt. For those who never played the original one before it's an amazing experience especially if you like the retro gameplay vibe or just plataformers in general. Definitely one of the best retro remakes I've ever seen and lucky are those who find this gem and become the Wonder Boy or Girl to defeat the dragons and free themselves from their (not so horrible) curse!

Divinity delivered, just what I was looking for: a solid RPG experience with a fresh twist and a lots of fun. I wouldn’t call it very polished diamond, but it’s a diamond after
During the first hours of play the game reminded me of Baldur’s Gate or maybe Icewind Dale. As I played further I tossed away these comparisons, as clearly these games are clearly from different periods of time.
Here are features that made the Divinity fun game for me:
• Ability to be your own boss, decide how you handle things, even thought there might be still some higher forces to in play, at least you are not micromanaged to kill 20 rabbits
• Turn based combat
• Reactive environment, just wow & lots of fun!
• Character development system (especially talents) and the freedom to develop character the way you like it
• Challenging Puzzles
• Unique battles that seemed to have meaning – there is no “grind” in this game
Divinity has it’s shortcomings too. My three biggest disappointments were:
• Crafting system complex, and too bothersome for my taste
• Dialogs that do not get closure they deserve
• Turn switching system in combat didn’t always work that well, sometimes ending to double skip when the first turn didn’t seem to skip at all. When it worked as intended it was okay, but not great.
I understand that this is a kickstarter game. I do not actually know the budget, but I am really amazed HOW MUCH CONTENT this game had. I really had expected to end in first map, but there was more, and a lot more. I really felt that I got more than I paid for this game, so even though it’s a rough diamond, it’s really a diamond!
In the end I can recommend this game to anyone, who is able and willing to immerse themselves in the RPG. This is not mindless grindfest, it’s more like dialogue, exploration, puzzles and meaningful combat, when the words alone are not enough.

It's another wonderful Divinity game from Larian complete with the freedom to shoot yourself in the foot.
You will not be held by the hand while questing (you have to put 2 and 2 together yourself). But this just makes you pay attention to the characters around you and all the tidbits of information you need in order to progress. Don't want to listen to the npcs? Blow them all up and just progress by finding the quest items they carry. You will certainly blow up a few quest rewards along the way, but the main quest will be just fine.
The interface is good but not great (a junk tab would be nice, since you get a lot of vendor trash and targeting mobs can sometimes be a bit finicky since a few of the mobs have moving idle-animations that don't go well with having to click their body to attack). Other than that it does it's job well -- the information is presented well and being able to send your stuff between characters instantly (no matter the distance) is a lovely feature.
Hints for new players (no spoilers):
At character creation, I would suggest not making hybrids. You will get quite a few skill points; stat points; and abilities during the game and until you have played for a bit, you don't really know what is a fun build. You will most likely go hybrid during the game, but some combinations just work better than others (most good combinations are a mix of magic + melee/archer/backstabber).
Talking to pets is fun, so consider taking that ability from the start.
TL;DR: best rpg in years and even 100 hours into the game I still feel the same.

This is a game about little space dudes trying to save their space empire from the evil space rebels, only to find that they run out of missiles on some dumb automated scout who's shields are too tough for their burst laser II to get through. So then they're sitting there waiting for their FTL drive to charge so they can jump away, hoping that their own shields hold, when the automated scout gets a missile through and hits their cockpit. So now their FTL is delayed, and the cockpit is on fire, and the mantis that was piloting the ship is trying his darnedest to put out the fire that's slowly killing him (but you know that giant space mantis has a hard time holding a fire extinguisher, so he'll die before the fire goes out). So the guy at weapons control heads to the cockpit to help, but since he's a rock dude he takes 15 years to get there. And while he's on his way, the mantis has had to leave before being cooked, heading to the med bay.
So now the fire is spreading, entirely engulfing the cockpit and the hallway outside of it. The mantis, upon reaching the med bay, is surprised to find that it's not working because power has been routed from it to supply the weapons systems. So they reroute power to the med bay, taking it from the O2 supply. But don't worry, they'll bring that back up before everyone suffocates, hopefully.
The rock dude has finally made it to the cockpit and is stomping out the fire, when another missile hits the shield generator and the shields go offline. Right as the shields go down, a halberd beam rips across the ship, hitting mostly empty rooms, but causing the automated warning sirens to alert the crew that hull integrity is down to 50%. Immediately, the remaining crew abandon their posts and rush to the shield room to get them back online. All of a sudden, the internal view screens go dark as the sensors are knocked offline by another missile.
The crew is panicking now. The rock dude, having finally put out the fire, is starting repairs on the navigational systems (though the crew still wonders how a large humanoid rock man can fix a computer terminal by simply hitting it, but hey, whatever works). Repairs to the shields are around 50%, so they come partially online, stopping the halberd beam. The automated drone, knowing no sympathy (or any emotion for that fact), continues it's relentless assault. Missiles continue to hit the ship, some tearing holes in the hull, others starting more fires. The rock dude makes his final repairs and brings navigation back online. It's only got another minute or so before it resolves the jump trajectory, but the crew isn't sure if they have that long.
Another explosion and siren sounds, this time signaling hull integrity at 25%. The shields are now fully online, and the mantis is back at the helm. There seems to be a shred of hope after all. The rock dude heads off to the sensor room to figure that mess out. Explosions continue to rock the ship; another missile strike to the shields (bringing them back down), and another halberd beam across the weapons systems. No shields, no weapons, and the only human on the crew is pretty sure that if she sneezes the whole ship will break apart.
This is when the crew realizes that they never brought the O2 back online. They try to route power to it, but the O2 control was hit by a missile and is offline. And the room is on fire, along with a good portion of the rest of the ship. The crew will never know this though, because the sensors are still offline (the rock dude is sill on his way). No oxygen, an unrelenting missile barrage, and the heat from the out of control fire sap the rest of the hope from the crew. Will they make it?
Probably not. But one thing is certain; they'll try again. And again. And again. Each journey a new adventure, a new story to be told. And maybe they'll get through to the end, to warn their friends in the space empire about the impending doom they all face.
Or maybe they'll have all their doors open when the door control is hit by a missile and all the oxygen rushed into space. That'll happen at least once too.

When completing the game, it said I had played for 40 hours; that is missing one side mission, missing some collectibles, needing to meet a few odd characters, and probably needing to complete most of the challenges (testing weapons, running courses).
I recommend working towards the grappling hook upgrade, this increases the fun factor.

WARNING!!! This game is a MINISERIES - three episodes only. Please don't be a dumbass and don't go crying on forums You were cheated of Your hard earned money, because even the game price states it's not the same kind of product as both previous TWD Telltale games.
Common misconception - game is NOT based on The Walking Dead Tv series. It is based on comic book series and tells us what was happening with Michonne during her absence in those comic books.
Another fact - all TWD games are based off the comic books AND also take place in comic book universe. Tv series is based on comic books BUT tells the story differently, and thus creates its own universe. Michonne story is placed in the former.
All in all game is not that good as both previous Telltalle games about TWD, but it holds its ground where needed. It shows us a little about Michonne past, her current state of mind and her struggle with her inner demons.
Gameplaywise it's the same as earlier TWD games from Telltale, with some minor changes in QTE. Also - do Yourself a favor and play with controller, keyboard and mouse aren't nearly that comfortable here.
I would recommend buiyng it with some discount - even 50% is enough if You like comic book Michonne like me.
P. S. Game has a tendency to erase Your savefiles, so try to keep a backup on Your own.

Star Wars Battlefront II is one of my favorite games of all time.  It's a cryin' shame that LucasArts never produced a successor to one of their strongest franchises for the seventh generation of gaming; one can only hope in the hands of EA, fans will see a resurgence of quality Star Wars shooters.
I admire the basic gameplay mechanics of Battlefront II a lot.  In the standard Conquest (Deathmatch) mode, each team gets the same amount of starting reinforcements and must take over neutral and enemy bases to increase your team's deployment opportunities and decrease enemy reinforcement count.  This has to be one of the most realistic respawn mechanics I have ever had the pleasure of playing.
Galactic Conquest is long but FUN.  It's a combination of standard FPS battles for planets combined with Risk of moving fleets to guard some planets and invade others.
Space Combat is the HYPEST♥♥♥♥♥♥  It's equal amounts of fun to drive a troop transport into the enemy hangar, shoot up pilots before they reach their ships, and sabotage the cruiser's systems from the inside as it is to take a starfighter and dogfight it out in the vacuum of space.  Playing a 1 vs 1 space mission, especially a Galactic Civil War 1-Flag, is probably among the most FEROCIOUS cat and mouse-style hunting experiences you're ever going to find in gaming.
Playing as a Hero (Jedi, Sith, or gunslinging warrior like Han Solo or Jango Fett) is pretty nifty, especially since almost every hero does behave uniquely in combat.  For example, Darth Maul's sprint attack is SAVAGE against clone troopers, while Leia Organa's pistol does pretty insane damage.  Being able to throw all Heroes together in Mos Eisley for a Hero Assault is pretty amazing; you can observe noncanon showdowns like Luke Skywalker vs General Grievous or Darth Vader vs Mace Windu, or relive epic duels from the series such as Yoda vs Palpatine or Anakin vs Obi-Wan.
So why the hell are you still reading this?  BUY.  PLAY.  LOVE.

Orcs Must Die is a third person tower defence game. You play as the magicians apprentice and you must stop the Orcs from reaching the Rift, which is a portal to your universe.
Each level the Orcs break through the doors (or fly through holes in the ceiling) and make their way to the Rift coming in waves. You lay traps in their path, from spiked floors to swinging blades the Orcs blunder through your traps becoming so much meat and with each death you get more money to place more traps. Of course should you get bored of watching them die you can enter the fray yourself firing either a rapid fire crossbow or engaging in melee. Once you complete the level you get skulls based on how well you did which you use to purchase and upgrade traps.
This game is pretty good, if a little repetitive and the difficulty really ramps up in the later levels, especially if you haven't got the right traps or upgraded them enough. It's very satisfying to see a horde of Orcs be decimated as they wander through your traps, all the while never firing a single shot yourself.
For £6.99 it's a great game, well worth the price.

Let me start off by saying that I have been a part of the Killing Floor community since its inception.
I have witnessed the game take shape and form, becoming a standalone title (Killing Floor "1") and onwards it went. I have contributed to the original KF community via Mapping as well as providing many servers to this day.
I loved the original game and still do.
The sum of my thoughts in regards to KF2 is pretty much this: I would have liked nothing more than Tripwire releasing Killing Floor 2 under a completely different title that shares nothing with its "PREQUEL" and i ♥♥♥♥ing loathe having to use that term now, as it does a terrible ♥♥♥♥ing job at carrying on what made the "original" (and as far as I am concerned, ONLY) Killing Floor great.
If ALL you are looking for is fastfood gaming, no emphasis on actual teamwork or skill, in other words the ultra casual variant of its daddy, that all it has going for it is a prettier packaging, then KF2 is just the game for you.
I wanted to love it, I really did and now all I would wish for would be for the game to be renamed, because it does not deserve to piggyback off the original.
Other negative reviewers pointed out specifics quite well, no need for me to write an eyecancer inducing wall of text with all the countless things wrong with it and how it didnt manage to capture anything that made the real Killing Floor great.
Aside from the superifical, namely the gore and resulting carnage. If thats all you require, if thats the extent of your expectations, you are good to go and throw your money at this clown company (that it has become).
Although, to be fair, they never were that much different, really.
Killing Floor 1 success was entirely on the back of its community that created all its content and shaped it into the great game it then became. From total rebalancing and the addition of countless custom perks, weapons and even zeds to whole game modes.
Point being, if you are looking for a game in this "niche" genre and you like the basic appeal, the original is where its at.
Unless you are a console gamer, then KF2 is perfect for you. Watered down casual ♥♥♥♥♥how. But thats the price you pay when a game is developed with consoles in mind. The gameplay from a to z as well as its pacing. Sad really. Wish I could refund.
And im not even mentioning all the things that others pointed out already, broken promises and so forth.

This game sucked up hours of my life. It is AMAZING. I'd never played the original X-Com but this was a great way to get someone interested in the universe. Essentially, I had a group of virtual GI JOEs and I was sending them out on missions against the Alien Menace. Now THAT's something I wanted to do since I was five.
X-Com has two primary parts, base building and "away team" missions, and it's amazing how the two complement each other. Want to have plasma cannons for your next away mission? You're going to have to research them in your base, but that'll require you to go on this other mission to gather the resources to do it. It's addictive and the "just one more turn" syndrome is clearly in full force here. Both types of missions are filled with razor edge decisions. Do I launch a satellite to quell the panic in Nigeria? I could, but I've got no interceptors to protect it... Can I build this power plant? Yes, but then I'd not be able to research my upgraded armour... Should I risk sending my sniper up to this elevated location, because she'll be totally alone up there for the next turn? I've got a group of civilians surrounded by Chrysallids, do I pick them off with weapons fire (risking misses) or say "to Hell with this" and break out the rocket launchers (guaranteeing civilian deaths)? For a game with surprisingly few character interactions, it manages to make you actually care about your guys and girls.
The Enemy Within expansion adds whole different levels of awesomeness. You can enhance your troops with gene mods a la Space Marines or go for broke and turn a guy into a heavily armed cybernetic battlesuit wearing juggernaut. Ever wanted to rocket punch someone in the face like in Pacific Rim? Now you can! New missions and side storylines add to the depth and make for a great way to develop the story. Chief of these is EXALT, your darker and edgier counterparts who have their own ideas on how to deal with the alien menace. The aliens aren't slouching with the reinforcements either a mission to St. John's, Newfoundland up in Canada hit me rather close and had me jumping at shadows.
Just a couple of quibbles, all extremely minor in my mind. First, the Interceptor missions could have been a bit more fleshed out. In the game you launch the fighter to take out the UFO and that's pretty much it, except for having some limited control by activating a couple of abilities to boost the fighter's speed, evasion and firepower. I would have preferred to have a kind of rail shooter section or even a full on dogfight filled with Macross Missile Massacres. That's the opinion of an irredeemable joystic jockey though. One other feature I'd have liked to have seen was the ability to walk about your base. Yes I'm digging out this underground lair and have this big overall view, but it'd been nice to actually go hang out with the guys at the bar, or visit them in the medbay while they're laid up.
All in all X-Com Enemy Unknown is probably the best damn game to have showed up in the last couple of years. I'll be playing it for a good while longer!

This is Talisman WH40K edition.
General gameplay mechanics are similar to the fantasy Talisman, but mostly it's a very different game.
For example instead of being every man for himself it's a struggle of two teams, making sure it's your guys who will put an end to the Emperor or Horus. Encounters are different too - like when encountering warriors of your faction they will either try to join you, help you out with some resources or even fight together with you in that sector. Meaning that alignment nets more consequences than just sector penalties like in a fantasy Talisman.
It's also very stylish.
Overall it's one of a very few modern WH40K PC games worth playing and is a fun addition to your game's library even if you already own the original Talisman. There are some downsides however - there's less content and DLCs seem to offer less too. Granted - some expacks may come in the future.

Just a summary:
+ Graphics, it's a gorgeous game.
+ Sound effects are good and add a lot of atmosphere.
+ Mountains are good, huge both of them with almost infinite possibilities for great trails. A lot to explore even after many hours into the game.
+ Several sports to choose from, wingsuit is a highlight for me. The extreme pack adds 3 more but the new ones are kinda situational and there aren't many challenges for them yet.
+ Challenges are well designed for the most part, some of them are kinda hilarious.
+ Community challenges add replayability since they're constantly adding them.
+ Customization is alright. Several characters to play and a lot of costumes, clothes and gear skins.
+ Replays and director mode are great, you can make very very nice videos of your rides.
+- Leaderboards are good to have and being able to spectate the best times and such is nice but they are too small and should allow for easier browsing and let you choose any trail from the top 10 at least, etc.
+- Trick system. While there's more depth to it than it appears at first I find it a bit clunky sometimes and the G-system can get in the way and become bothersome forcing you to slow down too much or fall. IMHO there should be a freeride mode that does away with this or tone it down a lot, but I get that they're going for more of a sim game than arcade.
+- Multiplayer stuff could be better but what's there is ok. I haven't played much with people but trying to beat friend's scores was fun.
+- Stories. Although most of them were fun to complete, some had terrible voice acting and were very cheesy or silly in a bad way.
- No character progression beyond cosmetics and no stats even for the gear. Apparently every snowboard is identical.
- Music isn't very good and the way it's implemented annoyed me a lot. The constant slow down on fall clashes with the way the challenges are designed (hard ones are repeat after repeat until you get it right). After a while I completely turned it off and began playing my own things while in the game. They should allow players to play custom music anyway like other games do. Pretty meh feature.
- Mountain navigation is pretty terrible and imprecise, clunky UI. I ended exploring as much as possible and then just playing the challenges from the start menu instead most of the time. Also, you can't input coordinates manually and sometimes you do need to go to a specific location, very bothersome having to move the pointer around until you more or less find the area.
Tl;dr: A good game not without its flaws. Don't expect SSX at all. Probably worth playing for the wingsuit gameplay alone :).

If you like Titan Quest, you'll probably like this too.
Grim Dawn is one of the best ARPGs I have played. It is the spiritual successor of Titan Quest and featured many of the mechanics and gameplay that make TQ great. While I prefer the mythological setting of TQ to Grim Dawn's post-apocalyptic one, it's hard to deny that the mechanics that were good in TQ have been refined and improved to great effect here. The inventory and item transfering system is easy to use and the loot feels to me to hit the right balance, offering satisfying rewards without flooding the game with rares. And the class system...that's so good that it deserve another paragraph.
In Grim Dawn, your characters begin the game without a class. You are allowed to chose one class mastery (out of six masteries) at level two and another one once you hit level 10. This system allows you nign limitless customisation. Expecially since each mastery in Grim Dawn often offer quiet versatile abilities, allowing two characters with the same classes to have quiet a different playstyle.
Overall, it's quiet an amazing game. If you like ARPGs, this one is a no brainer. If you've never tried or is indifferent on the genre, I still think that you should at least consider playing this.

The Banner Saga is a post-apocalyptic Viking Age Oregon Trail with fights. If you're still reading instead of buying this game on that description alone, fine - let's get serious: The Banner Saga is a story-driven, turn-based strategy-RPG with incredible art and music that oozes atmosphere and sucks you right into its bleak yet beautiful world.

Basically the game tells the story of caravans of Nordic humans and horned giants called Varl struggling to survive after Ragnarok. The gods are dead. The sun has stopped moving in the sky. A great darkness is descending from the North, bringing with it an unstoppable host of mysterious stone creatures called Dredge. The game looks like a Disney animated feature (one of the good ones), but the story has more in common with Game of Thrones than Pocahontas, filled with old blood feuds, betrayal, and grey morality. The point of view switches back and forth a few times at first, getting the player acquainted with the many different characters. Players who aren't paying close attention may find themselves confused, especially in the dialogue scenes where it's not always made abundantly clear who is speaking.

The art in this game is gorgeous - just look at the screenshots. Unfortunately the only fully animated and voiced sequence comes at the very beginning, and all of the following dialogue scenes are silent and only minimally animated (blinking eyes, blowing hair, etc.). A bit more animation in the conversations - changing facial expressions to fit what is being said, for instance - would not have been amiss. But even so, everything looks fantastic, including the character animations in combat.
The sound is great too. One of the requisite Kickstarter "stretch goals" was to hire a live orchestra for composer Austin Wintory, and it shows. Some of the vocal elements weirded me out at times, but on the whole the soundtrack is outstanding, and perfectly complements the mood and setting of the game. There is very little voice work - mostly limited to narration - but all of it is good, if heavily accented.

There are two sides to the gameplay. Let's call them Oregon Trail and Gladius.
In the Oregon Trail parts, you will see your caravan trudging slowly over the picturesque landscape. As you travel, you will lose Supplies. Supplies can be purchased in towns using Renown, the other currency in the game, which is also used for leveling up characters and buying magic items (each character only has 1 inventory slot for 1 magic item). If you run out of supplies, then each day some of the people in your caravan will die. You can rest for 1 day's worth of supplies to improve your caravan's Morale. High morale will grant you bonus Willpower in combat. Random encounters pop up on the way, offering a series of choices. Choose carefully. I will talk more about the Choices & Consequences aspect of the game later.
Unfortunately, aside from a those event choices, the Oregon Trail gameplay has little actual effect on the combat or the story. There are Steam achievements for managing your caravan well, but otherwise you can let everyone die and still finish the game, since apparently your main characters are able to live without eating (?), and a bit of rest will still improve morale. It seems like that needs fixing to me.

Now for the Gladius part of gameplay: the turn-based combat. It's an interesting system. Each unit has both Armor (blue) and Strength (red). You can attack a unit's Armor to make it more vulnerable to Strength attacks. Reducing a unit's Strength not only lowers its health but also its damage. Here's where things get interesting... As long as you both have at least 2 units alive, you and your opponent will always alternate turns. This means that, if you reduce an enemy unit's strength to 1, it's often better to leave it alive but crippled than to finish it off, because your enemy's turns will be wasted on these weak units. But even crippled units can still take you by surprise, and killing them grants you bonus Willpower points, so it's a strategy you have to learn to play just right.
What I'm saying here is that I found the combat fun and challenging. Though it could benefit from added variety (each character only has one special ability), it's a solid and engaging system that makes you think. You can switch the difficulty mode at any time if combat feels too easy or hard. I found the standard difficulty perfect on my first playthrough, though that final boss battle was... we'll just say adequately frustrating.

The final boss is also the only fight of the game (I think) that you need to win. All other fights can be lost, and the story will continue without a game over screen. Though characters who fall in combat do not die if you win (they only become injured for a few days), losing combat too often can have an impact on the story that could possibly get characters killed.
In fact, let's talk Choices & Consequences, which to me is the most important aspect of any RPG or semi-RPG. Unfortunately, most of the choices in the Banner Saga story have a clear good option and several bad options. And I don't mean "good vs. evil" - the game does an excellent job of maintaining a grey morality. I mean "ideal choice" vs. "less ideal choices", instead of equally viable options with a mix of good and bad consequences. This is bad, because it encourages metagaming and savescumming in order to find the "right" choice.
Despite this, the consequences of your choices aren't to be underestimated. While they won't change the overall path of the story (which, like your path of travel, is pre-determined and linear), some choices can have immediate, disastrous consequences like the loss of many supplies or the sudden permanent deaths of characters in your group. Others (especially one in particular) can have delayed consequences that you might not see coming much later in the story. Which is a good thing!
Speaking of savescumming, I should mention that this game has no manual save system - just a checkpoint system that creates separate saves at the start of each chapter. I'm tempted to call this a good thing, because it curbs the temptation to load frequently. And if there's one thing I can say for certain, it's that The Banner Saga is best played by going in blind and never loading your game, even if you lose a fight, especially since there are very few ways to get a true "game over" screen. You will get the most out of the story and the experience this way.

And yes, it's an experience. The story builds up slowly, so stick it out through the first few parts and you'll be rewarded. You will fight and struggle to survive as resources dwindle, you will make tough choices and watch beloved companions die, as you lead your ragged fellowship to the bitter end. Only... it's not quite an ending, because this is only the first chapter of a planned three-chapter game. Sorry! Don't get me wrong; the story definitely reaches a satisfying climax. But it's fairly short, and you're left wondering what happens next. Guess we'll have to wait and see!
The Banner Saga is a relatively short and simple game, but it's a good one. Sure, it could be improved by things like non-linear map roaming, a branching story, and more unit abilities and terrain variety in combat. But I applaud the small team at Stoic for not being overly ambitious with their size and budget. They seem to have a clear vision of exactly the game they want to make, and they made it with passion. Nearly everything the Banner Saga tries to do, it does very well: outstanding art and music complement a unique and interesting epic story with solid writing, backed up by fun and challenging gameplay. What more can one ask for? Basically just more of it, but that should be on the way! Perhaps the next two chapters will bring added features and complexity too.

I had little expectations about this game, but it I was Really impressed after the first 10 minutes. Tho I recommend Co-Op for this, it is playable solo too.
First off you start with two characters you can customize all from class to looks. Tho the character customization isn't the strongest point, but it isn't lackluster. While the class customization is where this game first shine for me!
You can start with choosing 1 of 11 different bases, all from your standard Fighter to even a hybrid ranger/wizard. Then if you like to tweak it even further, you can go into the attribute tree and change your weapon bonus, your defense, what element of magic you would like to master and even handy skills such as if you would like to pickpocket or steal things from other, even crafting and bribing is here!
Then you have the last tweaking. Bonus traits, This is one small but powerful thing, it can change how you character plays, all from like you stink so people tends to hate don't like you in their first impression, but melee attackers also avoids you in combat, to Zombie that makes poison heal you, at the price of normal heals will hurt you instead.
The story is quite interesting, you really need to listen to people when accepting their tasks, because even if you have a journal with a notes about what to do, it doesn't mean you don't miss out of any clue about it.
The interaction with environment is absolutely stunning for me. You can literally take about anything you see, even steal, if you succeed with a sneak and no one looks at your way(best way to describe this is like Skyrim)
The combat is also Really nice, as some one who's not the biggest fan of turn base, This was the biggest surprise of'em all. You can interact with the environment to change the battle flow even before the fight(with some sneaky moves) and if you fail can can try fix the last preparation in combat(or with another character if the enemies haven't seen you yet). While in combat you use take turns,  who that starts is based on Constitution(a stat).
The Difficulty in this game is just about right for me. Easy is casual hard, normal is some head on fighting but still CC is required(a whole lot), and hard is a mind game, where CCs and position makes A-Z.
Worth mentioning is that you can take cover behind almost everything in this game, and i will recommend to use it too, the NPCs use tons(and i mean tons) of CCs...
To add, the game has tons of old features and some new, well mixed in together that makes this game quite refreshing. Even tho I myself think the personal choices would affect the game flow a little more, it isn't something that bothers me at all. and I would recommend it to about any RPG fan that like a open world to explore and interact with. Also to try it with a friend(makes the game a little more fun((Friendly fire exists)).
Oh and to save you from traumatizing agony and despair. Save a lot...

Had a great time playing through this last weekend! Definitely want to do another playthrough,
Games like this should definitely be supported, and I think that one should play this game, period.
Some may find it too short for $25, but it would be a certain must buy at 50% off or lower.
If you're on the fence, I say pick it up when it's on sale. Personally, I'm getting my money's worth out of it.
It's definitely not easy, but in a game about vikings dealing with the end of the world, that seems appropriate. With A LOT of effort, I managed to get a caravan of over 500 people to Boersgard without losing them to low morale and starvation, and it actually felt like an achievement. It's the vibrant characters that got me invested and made me try and save the ones I care about, forcing myself into harder situations involving having mostly level 1 characters until the last chapter of the game.
The world and art are beautiful and unique in a genre saturated with elves and dwarves, and Austin Wintory's soundtrack gives me chills. The elements of Icelandic culture and storytelling tropes have been woven into the setting and narrative excellently and make the game feel like a saga, an incomplete one though.
My one gripe would be that the ending is that it's tone felt much more like the second act than the first, however that tone, while strange was unarguably new and fresh to me. With so much left unresolved in anticipation of a sequel, I feel like Stoic has a lot of responsibility to consumers to ensure the trilogy is concluded, and I hope to see them overcome their legal battle with King over the use of "saga" in their title. As long as this is ensured, I think any problems fans might have with the ending will be forgotten in context of the entire trilogy as a whole, and it is a good thing that the ending made me want more in that sense.
This hopefully will also resolve what I feel is not enough variation on what is a unique ad interesting combat system, with a lot of depth and potential to develop in the single player campaign. In the sequel I would hope to see scenarios that add more of a twist to the mechanics than placement, as well as more boss battle scenarios. It would be interesting to see battles where you're defending a specific position, or have to escape an immortal Sundr by confining its movement. A good example of this variation would be half life, which introduced mechanics to players early on, and spent the rest of the game putting players in scenarios where the player's current strategies were challenged. Does the player always use a shotgun to kill this enemy type? Put them in a room with explosive barrels. Half life did have the benefit over Banner Saga of a longer campaign
Ultimately I feel like games that do what Banner Saga does right are too few and far between, especially because I feel that larger studios are unwilling to take risks anymore. So while the game has areas that it needs to improve on, I want the studio to get the support and opportunities it needs to meet those needs and be a better game, because I thoroughly enjoyed it and want to see it succeed

Link to my Let's Play of The Banner Saga:
Between The Banner Saga and The Banner Saga: Factions, I've probably put WAY too much time into this game... and I've loved every minute of it. They have taken your classic turn based strategy tactical game and wraped it in a layer of Oregon Trail and topped with a brilliantly told epic saga based around classic viking-esque lore.
Total length: Roughly 10 hour or so storyline.
The combat differs from a game like XCOM wherein you'd get your turn where you move all of your units and then let the enemy take a turn moving all of their units. In The Banner Saga you trade off on each unit movement. The Order they're moved in is based on how you organize your units prior to batter. This very miniscule difference makes for a pretty spectacular change in how combat is paced. Look at it this way, if you're getting slaughtered and the enemy has 5 units to your 2. You get to move your units 2-3 times before one of their units gets a second turn. It can really help turn the tide IF you're very smart about it but it isnt enough that it feels too powerful. The enemy also gets this advantage while outnumbered and can make setting up traps and cornering/surrounds units a solid strategy to make quick work of them.
The Banner Saga is single player only... If you want Multiplayer go download The Banner Saga: Factions here on steam. It's free to play and has miniscule micro transactions for basic stuff like unit color variations or small boosts to the amount of renown (experience) you get in battle. The game does solid work of balancing your opponents as well. So if you're curious about this game but not quite convinced... go download Factions and give the combat a shot at least. Cheers!

I started playing this game with a bit of doubt. Normally I try to avoid games that take a long time to play and have lots and lots of text in them that doubles, if not triples the playtime.
This game has all of that but in a way I never seen it possible. It actually dragged me in and after playing only a few minutes I was already convinced this would be the best RPG experience I’ve had in years.
Building your character is very far going as you can start out with a warrior on paper but end up with a tank that can fling spells like there is no tomorrow! This goes for all classes as they are not locked in their roles and can easily become some hybrid beast or even the full opposite of what they started out to be.
Now I am not much of a reader as stated above but the dialogues between characters and NPC’s are fairly interesting. This is something major coming from me since I’ve had games (Diablo 3) where I just click on and start smashing everything I see. The stories have a nice depth and an occasional joke is hidden in them as well which makes it really rewarding for reading it all eventually. Just a side note is that there are a few spelling mistakes in the dialogues and books but since I’m not a literal wonder myself I can look past those.
The combat… oh boy where do I begin. At the start you are limited to some attacks which look very nice and simple but once you start to learn how it all should be played it is extremely cool to fight! The combat is turn based and goes further on action points. At the start this was my biggest doubt since this requires a lot of patience in some games that I previously played . In DOS it just makes the fights more tactical and beautiful. Prepping the zone around you in fight and lighting those enemies up once they reached you is just something you can’t get enough of!  Also other combination of using the elements create a depth in battle I have never seen in my previous RPG’s and knowing you got 4 elements to use that give various combinations make every fight require another approach.

IMHO Civ 5 is a big disappointment, still kind of addicting, but a big disappointment.  I played Civ 2 and Civ 4 a lot and I still play Civ 4 every so often, but Civ 5 is a mess.  There's so many bugs and it crashes so frequently.

Multiplayer is hit and miss.  I play only LAN with my friends and it's nowhere near as stable as Civ 4's and even Civ 4's had desync's pretty often with events enabled.  Now you need to have events and barbarians disabled and play with 8 or less total AI/players. Have yet to get anywhere near to finishing a game in MP.
The graphics bug out fairly easily, even with a good graphics card and cp. Idk how many times it's crashed due to graphic errors.

There are thankfully a lot of modders out there making mods to try to improve the game, but Civ 5 has ZERO reliability with these mods and will still crash very often.  I have yet to finish a game with mods enabled.  Not to mention modding was made a lot more complicated and difficult compared to Civ 4.
The AI is ridiculous.  Usually once the AI has met you, they usually make some outragous demand or get angry at you for placing a city in their general direction, and then declare war on you, they proceed to have half their cities taken, they demand peace, after the peace treaty ends after 10ish turns, the AI re-declares war and the process starts over.  The AI doesn't know how to effectively use most of it's units, like air units or ships, and either just stockpiles them (air units) or throws them away and doesn't try to rebuild them (ships).
In order to get most of the options provided in Civ 4, you need to buy $120 worth of DLC (which I do have thanks to a friend who received it in a giveaway).  There's no technology trading, no map trading, no vassalage, in base Civ 5 there are no religions or corporations.  Why add these in as DLC in Civ 4 and then do it again with Civ 5?  (other than to make $$$).
A good thing about Civ 5 though is the cultural expansion of your cities.  It's easily controlled and manipulated compared to Civ 4's.
It is nice how war isn't just a massive unit stack fight since units cannot stand on the same tiles.  Plus combat is kind of neat, but it does take forever, especially late game.
Basically, imo Civ 5 feels like a beta or alpha release game, kind of like Stronghold 3.  There were a few improvements but overall has as many bugs and problems as Fallout 4 and Skyrim combined.  Probably the last Civilizations game I, or my friends, will buy.

Star Wars Battlefront® II is a first/third-person shooter that brings together a solid combination of infantry and vehicular combat; to create the feel of large-scale and epic battles, and to allow the player to relive the conflicts that have taken place within the Star Wars movie saga.
The game includes four factions - with each one containing their own unique infantry, weaponry and vehicles. The character classes are fairly balanced, and can make use of different play styles.This puts more emphasis on teamwork as opposed to just firepower; although in certain scenarios sheer manpower is required to best the enemy, and can cause the experience to feel more like that of a team-based deathmatch from a classic FPS game e.g.: Unreal Tournament.
Unlike its predecessor - Star Wars Battlefront® II has replaced air vehicles with whole new space-based levels; which make use of capital ships to spawn the teams and their pilotable spacecraft. These maps can either be played with the Capture the Flag game mode or the Assault game mode; with the latter requiring the destruction of certain enemy objects. To get the full space battle experience it is recommended to play space levels with the Assault game mode.
Overall it is a very enjoyable game, both for its single-player and multiplayer aspects, and is one which is worthy of being named as part of the Star Wars franchise.

This game is everything that the original game is not.  Indeed, Half-Life 2 is the franchise grown up, and proving that it still has legitimacy in todays gaming world.
The story of Half-Life 2 is a bit of a roller coaster in that there are great moments of narrative flow and others where you are left scratching your head a bit thinking "why did they put that in there?".  But saying that, there are plenty of ups to the few downs.  The story is overall strong and immersive with a few deviations that help create a vibrant lore.
The game mechanics are obviously much smoother, and well structured.  By todays standards, they stand up.  There are some nice features with the engine that work well.  The feel of the game when using certain weapons and the ability to manipulate some aspects of the environment help the gameplay support the story.  There are still a few things that don't seem right, such as no hands on steering wheels, being able to climb a ladder whilst simulatenously reloading or firing a heavy weapon, getting caught on obstacles, and the clumsy and altogether painful squads that do 2 things - 1) Die over and over, and 2) Get in your way when you need to do a run and gun (or often a grenade lob and duck).  The squad could definitely have used some more commands other than point and press C to have them run uselessly a couple feet before returning to interfere.
The weapons pretty much were a joy to use, especially the Pulse Rifle and the SMG.  No alien weapons to use in this game, other than the Antlion Pheropods, and this was the clumsiest weapon.  A few odd decisions were made with some of the weapons though, especially the .357 Magnum revolver.  Having a total ammo store of 18 rounds resulted in this being an often unused weapon.  Surely, Gordon could carry more than 18 bullets for this gun, considering the number he could carry for some of the others like the 9mm with a total ammo store of 168.  I'm sure it was for a balance purpose, but only being able to carry 18 rounds felt silly and frivolous.  The magnum went from being a mainstay weapon of the original series to a bit of a joke weapon in my mind.
Of the gameplay, I'm so happy that they decided to move away from the platform styled approach.  Moving across impossible terrain features and engineering in the original games made it feel like a caricature of a game.  Those titles didn't know if they were a shooter, narrative or platformer, often falling more towards the latter.  This game for the most part does away with that completely.  There are still a few gameplay components that aren't well thought out, mainly by being overly long and taking something novel and at first fun, and making it tedius - namely riding the airboat, and crossing the sand without touching it.  Both were fun at first, but quickly devolved into just hoping that it would soon be over, but nope - there was more and more of it.  Still, those didn't detract too much from the game as a whole.
The passage of time in the game, like in the first one though, still seems odd.  The immersion of that point is lost easily with the change from night to day as you are constantly on the move, never seeming to rest.... Jack Bauer, eat your heart out.
Overall, Half-Life 2 was and still is a great game, and my concerns with the game are more exagerated nitpicks than hangups.

Arrivando da diverse settimane di gioco su un RPG tripla A, mi sono approcciato a Stories: The Path of Destinies in maniera curiosa, ma leggera. Non avrei mai pensato che un gioco così anonimo mi avrebbe assorto al punto da dedicarci tutto il mio tempo libero, fino al suo completamento.
La caratteristica di punta di Stories è il suo sistema di trame in cui le scelte del giocatore vanno a cambiare drasticamente l'esperienza: i luoghi visitati sono diversi, i poteri a disposizione, le persone...molto più di qualunque altro RPG. Ogni volta la storia cambia. Ma qui arriva la parte interessante: alla fine di ogni storia il protagonista (non solo il giocatore) viene riportato indietro all'inizio, consapevole del suo passato, dei suoi errori e di ciò che ha scoperto. E la storia ricomincia, finchè egli non riuscirà a trovare il sentiero che lo porterà a vincere la guerra. Il tutto narrato in terza persona, con uno stile romanzesco che immerge il giocatore come se stesse "leggendo" il gioco.
Tutto questo  viene corredato da un gameplay che contiente tutti gli elementi di un RPG classico, limitati ma piacevoli nella loro essenzialità. Il sistema di combattimento ricorda un Arkham basato sulla scherma, bilanciato e piacevole, e rende scorrevoli i livelli basati altrimenti solo su esplorazione e progresso.
E' un titolo che consiglio a tutti i miei amici patiti di RPG e fantasy, non perchè rappresenti l'esperienza videoludica definitiva, ma per riscoprire la bellezza nell'essenziale
Coming from several weeks of gameplay on a triple A RPGs, I approached "Stories: The Path of Destinies in a curious but light way. I never thought that an anonymous game like this one would take me to the point where I would spend all my spare time to complete it.
The main perk of Stories point is its plot system, in which the player's choices change drastically the experience: the places visited, the powers available, the people ...all is variable, much more than any other RPG. Every time the story changes. But here comes the interesting part: at the end of each story the protagonist (not just the player) is brought back to the beginning, aware of his past,  of his mistakes and of what he discovered. And the story begins anew, until he can find the path that will lead to the victory of the war. Everything is narrated in a third person,  romance styled voice that makes the player feel as if he was "reading" the game.
All this is attachedby a gameplay geared with  all the elements of a classic RPG, limited but tuneful in their simplicity. The combat system remembers an Arkham based on fencing, balanced and enjoyable, and makes sliding layers based otherwise just on exploration and progress.
It is a title that I recommend to all my friends who are in love with RPGs and fantasy, not because it represents the ultimate videogaming experience, but to rediscover beauty in the essential.

Just a summary:
+ Graphics, it's a gorgeous game.
+ Sound effects are good and add a lot of atmosphere.
+ Mountains are good, huge both of them with almost infinite possibilities for great trails. A lot to explore even after many hours into the game.
+ Several sports to choose from, wingsuit is a highlight for me. The extreme pack adds 3 more but the new ones are kinda situational and there aren't many challenges for them yet.
+ Challenges are well designed for the most part, some of them are kinda hilarious.
+ Community challenges add replayability since they're constantly adding them.
+ Customization is alright. Several characters to play and a lot of costumes, clothes and gear skins.
+ Replays and director mode are great, you can make very very nice videos of your rides.
+- Leaderboards are good to have and being able to spectate the best times and such is nice but they are too small and should allow for easier browsing and let you choose any trail from the top 10 at least, etc.
+- Trick system. While there's more depth to it than it appears at first I find it a bit clunky sometimes and the G-system can get in the way and become bothersome forcing you to slow down too much or fall. IMHO there should be a freeride mode that does away with this or tone it down a lot, but I get that they're going for more of a sim game than arcade.
+- Multiplayer stuff could be better but what's there is ok. I haven't played much with people but trying to beat friend's scores was fun.
+- Stories. Although most of them were fun to complete, some had terrible voice acting and were very cheesy or silly in a bad way.
- No character progression beyond cosmetics and no stats even for the gear. Apparently every snowboard is identical.
- Music isn't very good and the way it's implemented annoyed me a lot. The constant slow down on fall clashes with the way the challenges are designed (hard ones are repeat after repeat until you get it right). After a while I completely turned it off and began playing my own things while in the game. They should allow players to play custom music anyway like other games do. Pretty meh feature.
- Mountain navigation is pretty terrible and imprecise, clunky UI. I ended exploring as much as possible and then just playing the challenges from the start menu instead most of the time. Also, you can't input coordinates manually and sometimes you do need to go to a specific location, very bothersome having to move the pointer around until you more or less find the area.
Tl;dr: A good game not without its flaws. Don't expect SSX at all. Probably worth playing for the wingsuit gameplay alone :).

Funny, clever and mostly enjoyable hack'n'slash type adventure but with a couple of *really* annoying flaws (imo):
• "right-click to move" control method does not always direct reynardo where you want him to go, causing him to run around walls straight into enemies you were trying to avoid if you click too close to them - especially annoying in the beholder maze bits
• controls do not seem super-responsive during combat with multiple (4+) foes meaning you can quickly get overwhelmed despite desperately trying to dash or right-click to move to a free area
• restarting at a checkpoint only gives half health and a bit of sword energy, so having to wait to recharge energy to replenish to full health to re-try a failed combat section quickly gets tedious and frustrating when you just want to charge straight back in to give it another shot
• final gripe is loading times; the game takes longer than some recent AAA games to fire up in the first place, but then each level takes an age as well! Yes, it does look very pretty, but it doesn't feel like there's enough going on to justify the wait imposed...
Overall, I'd rate the game as 7/10 as I bought it during the summer sale, but it would definitely drop a few points if I'd paid full price for it.

This game does everything Titan Quest did, but better and more. It's practically a complete game and at time of writing I have 95 hours in-game (minus 10 for approximate game time) and only just recently completed act III with a level 49 Trickster. Granted, I do have roughly 8 characters most are around level 20.
This game sucked me in from the word go, and didn't disappoint. I keep finding new reasons to love this game, or going back to reasons I'd discovered before and finding new things. The crafting system is amazing for an ARPG, I was blown away when I saw how in-depth it actually can be. The fact that one can craft Epic items if you find a blueprint? Brilliant.
The amount you can tweak your character also doesn't disappoint. One skill tree can have various play styles and with the current max of two choices from 6 classes means play styles are endless. I've not been bored once, and this isn't on full content yet.
The game is atmospheric. More so than Titan Quest. The music is outstanding and each map never feels repeated. A couple of times I think, "Haven't I seen this corner somewhere before?" but then the rest is completely different or the fact that over 2-3 weeks I put in 96 hours makes me see things. The fact that there are few communities in this game make's it feel like you have a home base, that you need to protect and build upon and that's why you explore and fight. It doesn't feel like you're being led down a single path from village to village as Titan Quest did (granted paying attention to lore and other does help). I love every aspect of this game.
One thing I love is how they brought in consequence. (Spoilers) Kill the men harassing New Harbour, come back later New Harbour has been pillaged by the rest of the gang. Save the little girl from the cave in, demon tears a Rover camp apart. Side with Kymon's Chosen or Order of Death's Vigil and the other becomes your enemy.
All I can say is this game will only get better and I'm definitely behind Crate Entertainment all the way. They made my dream game a reality, and now they just need to release B28 plx.
Edit: This game has simply gotten better throughout development and I can't wait to see future plans for the game. I would love additional content in storyline.

I played this because it's XCOM, and the original XCOM might be my favorite game ever. After going through this twice, once with the vanilla Enemy Unknown and once with the add-on, it has the basic elements of XCOM, but it's not as deep as the original.
For example, in the original XCOM, I used to keep around some of the earlier weapons like the auto-cannon and the laser rifle, because they had advantages in some situations - some enemies were vulnerable to fire or explosives or laser. In this one, plasma is just better than anything else. Also, in the original, base missions really felt like a big deal and required preparation. The one base mission in this game went by before I knew it.
The AI for the aliens is much, much worse than in the previous XCOM games. They seem to slightly wander around in their assigned groups of usually three aliens until you find them, when they then go for a good firing position and make you come at them. The primary tactic you learn is how to avoid coming at them.
In the end, it's a big disappointment, and the DLC just makes it worse.

A loving remake handled by the guy that practically established the Master System fandom online. Every element of the original game is recreated, but feels entirely accurate.
Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap was easily one of the top games on the Master System and Game Gear, but it's age shows at parts, particularly with the hit detection, level layouts and bosses. Newcomers may be very offput by these, but failure is not punished too hard and the game itself is rather short (should take 5 to 7 hours for a first playthrough). The game has no leveling system but does have increasingly better gear that can be purchased or found. Enemy designs and their colors clue how strong they are and are used as a hint of sorts to the player to travel elsewhere; Harder monsters naturally give better money and loot too, so although prices for swords and armor increases it never feels as if there is a need to 'grind', but players could choose to do so anyways.
A crazy amount of effort was applied to make this remake look like a cartoon in motion, and they absolutely succeeded. It is one of the best looking hand drawn games out there and in no way feels cheap like most other modern 2D games do. Personally, I was initially extremely negative of the new aesthetics in terms of art and musical direction upon it's reveal, but it has all grown on me. The new animations add a lot of personality to the world but also help the player better understand the character momentum and where to go to next, It is more than well designed, it is clever!
The original visuals, sound and music are still included in this game though and can be swapped between without even having to pause. Better yet is that there are a great deal of customization options to mix and match between these. There are also options for different types of older television screen effects and the Japanese-exclusive FM sound add-on!
Lizardcube have gone above and beyond in recreating this SEGA / Westone classic. I absolutely cannot wait to see what they are working on next, whether it is another remake or a completely original title.
