This is a game about little space dudes trying to save their space empire from the evil space rebels, only to find that they run out of missiles on some dumb automated scout who's shields are too tough for their burst laser II to get through. So then they're sitting there waiting for their FTL drive to charge so they can jump away, hoping that their own shields hold, when the automated scout gets a missile through and hits their cockpit. So now their FTL is delayed, and the cockpit is on fire, and the mantis that was piloting the ship is trying his darnedest to put out the fire that's slowly killing him (but you know that giant space mantis has a hard time holding a fire extinguisher, so he'll die before the fire goes out). So the guy at weapons control heads to the cockpit to help, but since he's a rock dude he takes 15 years to get there. And while he's on his way, the mantis has had to leave before being cooked, heading to the med bay.
So now the fire is spreading, entirely engulfing the cockpit and the hallway outside of it. The mantis, upon reaching the med bay, is surprised to find that it's not working because power has been routed from it to supply the weapons systems. So they reroute power to the med bay, taking it from the O2 supply. But don't worry, they'll bring that back up before everyone suffocates, hopefully.
The rock dude has finally made it to the cockpit and is stomping out the fire, when another missile hits the shield generator and the shields go offline. Right as the shields go down, a halberd beam rips across the ship, hitting mostly empty rooms, but causing the automated warning sirens to alert the crew that hull integrity is down to 50%. Immediately, the remaining crew abandon their posts and rush to the shield room to get them back online. All of a sudden, the internal view screens go dark as the sensors are knocked offline by another missile.
The crew is panicking now. The rock dude, having finally put out the fire, is starting repairs on the navigational systems (though the crew still wonders how a large humanoid rock man can fix a computer terminal by simply hitting it, but hey, whatever works). Repairs to the shields are around 50%, so they come partially online, stopping the halberd beam. The automated drone, knowing no sympathy (or any emotion for that fact), continues it's relentless assault. Missiles continue to hit the ship, some tearing holes in the hull, others starting more fires. The rock dude makes his final repairs and brings navigation back online. It's only got another minute or so before it resolves the jump trajectory, but the crew isn't sure if they have that long.
Another explosion and siren sounds, this time signaling hull integrity at 25%. The shields are now fully online, and the mantis is back at the helm. There seems to be a shred of hope after all. The rock dude heads off to the sensor room to figure that mess out. Explosions continue to rock the ship; another missile strike to the shields (bringing them back down), and another halberd beam across the weapons systems. No shields, no weapons, and the only human on the crew is pretty sure that if she sneezes the whole ship will break apart.
This is when the crew realizes that they never brought the O2 back online. They try to route power to it, but the O2 control was hit by a missile and is offline. And the room is on fire, along with a good portion of the rest of the ship. The crew will never know this though, because the sensors are still offline (the rock dude is sill on his way). No oxygen, an unrelenting missile barrage, and the heat from the out of control fire sap the rest of the hope from the crew. Will they make it?
Probably not. But one thing is certain; they'll try again. And again. And again. Each journey a new adventure, a new story to be told. And maybe they'll get through to the end, to warn their friends in the space empire about the impending doom they all face.
Or maybe they'll have all their doors open when the door control is hit by a missile and all the oxygen rushed into space. That'll happen at least once too.

While people across the web compare D:OS to games like Baldur's Gate and older TES series, there is a series that does a much better comparison job imo - Ultima!
It is common for all old RPGs not to lead a player through with objective markers and scalable content, but Ultima games were unique because of the interactivity.
Original Sin does a great job expanding this concept; all the ways player can interact with the world around: move things, break things, create things - affects gaming experience, from immersion to actual combat tactics. The overall game design perfectly complements those interactive mechanics, creating a dense and rich gameplay.
An absolute must see for every RPG fan, new or old alike, even if only to understand how far the genre deviated for the last decades and what RPGs used to be about.

This is the first episodic Telltale game that I just cant recommend in good conscience.
TL;DR:
Now Telltale Games have always been more Interactive Movies than actual games, that for the most part merely gave you the Illusion of choice. So is and does this one.
That's not my problem with it, I can dig that. At least the choices at the end of an episode somewhat matter and they usually present the Story very well so that I can forgive choices not having an actual impact.
But in this particular one Michonne has hallucinations that last throughout the entire game.
They are annoying, they are pointless and they completely break the flow of the game.
When I am fighting for my life and suddenly everything is quiet and i see my daughters running around, that to me does not evoke any emotional response except for anger and thinking "aww not this crap again!"
I guess it was supposed to add to the story....somehow?! In my opinion, it completely fails to do so. It does not make me care about her daughters.
It actually makes me hate them. Dumb things happen due to Michonne not moving because of her hallucinations.
This lead to me being more angry than enjoying the story unfold before me.
Furthermore, I know this is a mini series, and that's okay. But if you're gonna make it that short you should probably adjust the price you're asking for it. This game will last you about 4 hours. So if you want me to pay almost 4€ per hour of enjoyment it better be pretty damn good.
This isn't, it's okay at best. Although i will admit that it has 2 or 3 instances where it is very satisfying!
It is also worth noting that the cloud save does not seem to be working correctly. I had to replay most of Episode 1 because I quit inbetween and apparently it was never saved. Considering you cant even skip forward in conversations that was rather tedious.
Lastly I actually got some major framedrops at parts, which is weird. Never had that in a Telltale game before and I'd think if my PC can handle DA: Inquisition, Witcher 3 and the likes it shouldnt have a problem with something like this.
Overall, if you can look past the cons, you might want to pick it up on a sale. Otherwise I recommend skipping this one.

Yes ladies and gentleman, this is Saints Row IV, the sequel to that other crazy game we know and love, a game that at the time of its release quite deviated from what the second game was all about and succeeded at it, but now, how does this one hold up?
Well, to get you started, just like many other games in this day and age, Saints Row IV introduces you to the storyline in an painfully scripted, slow and linear way (although admittedly, the first minutes are pretty humorous).
Thankfully after about 30 minutes of hand holding, the game finally provides us with the ability to explore this massive open world packed with story missions, side missions and diverse stores that'll sell you all kinds of goods (ranging from cosmetic items to a variety of normal and/or alien weapons) but my favorite of them all has got to be the garage that provides us with the ability to costumize our vehicles to our liking! Think of this as a throwback to the old days of the yearly 2000's and all of the Tunning and customizable options you could find in many racing games.
Unfortunately all of this glorious indepth vehicle customization put at our disposal is all but thrown out of the window once we get our "Super Powers", and the reason for such is, once you get'em, you wont feel the need to use another vehicle throughout the entire game ever again, and believe me when I tell you that you will get those very, very early in the game.
Tunning aside, let me tell you something, the "Super Powers" in this game are insane... Insanely fun that is! And man, there are tons of them, including Super Speed, Super Jump, telekinesis, freezing/burning abilities, gliding and far, far more that I won't spoil... On top of that each and every ability cam be costumized and evolved, think of it as a nice rpg element.
The game also packs a punch when it comes to your arsenal, there are well over 30 weapons to choose from, alien and regulars, and each of them feel different from one another on top of that, every single weapon is fully customizable, some are absolutely exceptional to goof around such as the Gravity Gun, specially in Co-Op with a friend.
And now that we're talking about the Co-Op, oh man, this is a game that'll offer you a pretty decent solo experience, but if you have a friend who plays Saints Row IV, make sure you play it in Co-Op, it takes the fun to a whole different level!
Though some of the level design in a few of the story missions that might not take place in the city, do feel a little bit to linear for their own good, specially when you're striped of off your super powers and are put to wonder around shooting hordes of enemies in claustrophobic corridors.
Now the most important thing, be aware, while the game definitely packs a punch in the fun department, to be totally honest with you, it is also a buggy pile of programing! After spending over 20 hours in the game, I must say that I don't have enough fingers in my hands to keep track of every single bug/glitch I have gone trough, and while some of them made me genuinely laugh, other made me want to throw something out of the window, it is clear that the game's very unstable for its own good and that let's say, a few more months in development could have done Saints Row IV nothing but wonders.
All in all, this is definitely a good game on it's own, even though it has a few problems here and there, winning a final score of 6/10

A fantastic little FPS puzzle game that immediately throws you into a room and expects you to find your way into the next room(s). There's no distracting story to interrupt your puzzle-solving spree. It has branching paths, but you can -- and often must -- come back and solve any puzzle that you skipped, discover a path you've overlooked the first time around. You're given a map that shows all the paths that you've missed so you can teleport to the nearest solved room and find them again.
The puzzles in the first part of the game are the most fun: to solve them means to challenge your own preconceptions of how the game's going to work. Later, the game intriduces new mechanics, and all of the puzzles start to be based on those mechanics instead, which is less fun, but still enjoyable.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is a good game, although it has many things that needed to be polished it at least kept me interested long enough.
When I started playing this game I delved into a great world. The combat was nice and simple yet filled with enough action to keep me interested and I was accompanied by a sly narrator along the travels of Reynardo, the main character. Each decision I had made along the way was hard and it made me just sit back and think about it for at least 2 minutes before I had come to some conclusions.
However, as I played along the game there were flaws that revealed themselves which sort of ruined the experience. I came across frequent bugs like invisible terrain which, after I had searched it up, was apparantly not an uncommon problem among people among other bugs which showed that the game itself was not polished. The game saw you collecting items and whatnot which was to be expected but they very quickly became useless after easily getting all items. The game became repetitive quicker than I thought it would and having to repeat the story over and over, it annoyed me when I found I couldn't skip cutscenes which I noticed played through at an obscenely slow rate after a while.
Overall, the game fills you with fun from the beginning as you're accompanied by continuous jokes keeping you entertained as you play through. This game is far from perfect but finding out all the storylines kept me hooked even when times were tough. Even though I recommend this game, I think its purchase needs to be thought through more thoroughly than when buying other games as its pros and cons almost come to an equilibrium based upon what type of player you are.

This game is a damn classic. If you're at least a bit into strategy games, you HAVE to at least heard about the Civilization series. And well, here we have Civ V. Is it good? As usual I'm going to start with the stuff the game doesn't do quite right:
First and foremost, barbarians. I don't think too many people here actually loves them. They do serve a prupose, they make sure players don't completely ignore the military side of the game until Mid-game, however their camps seem to always spawn right at your borders instead of a few spaces away, and they'll do nothing but f#ck around♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥everyone off. If the game had an option for, for example, pay them money so they'll go♥♥♥♥♥♥off other players, I would actually like them much more. However as they are, I usually end up just disabling them before a match starts.
Second, the AI. They do play nicely, but have their moments of serious brain damage when they commit some of the most stupid mistakes you can ever see, even on high difficulties. Specially Civs that are focused in the early-game such as Montezuma will do things like attacking well-defended cities with extremely early game troops against soldiers WAAAAY above their league.
The last problem I have with this game is the amount of DLC's it has. People who know me will probably know I'm not a big fan of any sort of cash-grab DLC and selling maps when the game has both a map editor and Steam Workshop is just f#cking stupid. To their defence though, the game has two big DLC's that work more like expansions, those two are actually worth buying but they're just SO DAMN EXPENSIVE! SERIOUSLY, EACH ONE IS PRICED JUST AS MUCH AS THE GAME ITSELF! That's an issue XCOM Enemy Unknown also had, and would you look at that, they're made from the same developers.
However, looking away from those problems, is the game good? Hell yeah! From all Civ games, this one has to be the best one so far (until the VI one comes, probably). It offers so much gameplay options that makes any other game in the series look obsolete.
The amount of Civs the game has by default is actually quite good, and they're all well balanced. Most of them follow a way to be played (being more based on building, trading or conquering other people), have their own music, their own unique troops, their own buildings, and it's seriously hard to just pick one favorite. The DLC's add a f#ckton of more Civilizations, and I haven't even played them all yet, that's how many there are.
Something you also gotta love about the game is the trade system. Future games kinda ignored and over-looked this, but I think it's a key feature. You can trade tons of things you own, from special resources to even cities themselves. In the same dialogue you can also ask other civs what they think of other rivals, ask them if they're interested on starting wars together, join forces as allies... Or be a bully to them, if you feel like it. You're also able to always see what each Civ things of you from the same menu, which is great.
The maps themselves, mostly randomized, always seem to be interesting. Even though at times the game places too many of the same resource in the same place or even glitch out and put two of the same natural wonders in the same map, right next to each other, they're always fun. Only times I found them lame was the one or two times I spawned on artic areas and was too far away from proper lands to colonize.
The game also has neutral sort of cities if they're allowed to spawn and the map is big enough. They're actually really fun and add quite to the gameplay, as everyone will always try to ally the best ones and fight over their trust.
Lastly, the game also offers an Experience system to troops. If they fight and kill enemy units, they level up and then you can choose from different bonuses to gain, from dealing more damage to cities or healing nearby ally units to just instantly heal the unit instead. It's a great system that for some dumb reason was pretty much ignored on the sequel the game got a year ago.
This game is just fun to play. To I recommend it? Yes, if you like strategy games this is a must own. However, there's the DLC's. I'd say, just wait for a sale, and pick the game with the two big DLC's, ignore the rest as they don't bring too much to the game. It's also a great game to play with people, though expect the matches to take a long time to finish.
TL;DR Edition: A "must have" strategy game. Extremely fun, tons of difficulty modes and tons of variety with the maps and Civs, no two games will ever be the same. It also has way too many DLC'S, I only recommend getting the two expensive ones, the rest barely add anything that great.

Probably the most rewarding is the ability to play a large variety of skill/build combinations thanks to the variety of gear and classes. The skill tree is reminiscent somewhat of TQ and TL2, with a very bloated set of 'character sheet' details. Game mechanics are fairly basic - perhaps even moreso than D3, and graphics are just ... OK. Story line is decent, group play is sort of meh, mob/pet AI is mediocre. The faction system is quite interesting - but sadly not account wide.
All in all, worth the money for a 'yet another' D3/TL2/POE/TQ clone.

Dying Light doesn't stray far from the typical open-world zombie apocalypse game, you take side quests where you fetch things, kill things, blow up some stuff and then you have the main quest, which can be completed at your own pace. The game does not hold you to a schedule, so you can easily do whatever side quests you want and then do the main quests after leveling-up. I’m not sure if monsters level with you, the game did seem much easier when I was leveled-up.
Dying Light is by the same people that made Dead Island so there will be some similarities, but Dying Light actually feels much more polished than the Dead Island games; it runs good, the graphics are nice, and the audio is very good. I played on an i7-950 with a GTX 970, I cranked all details except I ran shadows at one notch below max to keep the game above 60FPS.
When completing the game, it said I had played for 40 hours; that is missing one side mission, missing some collectibles, needing to meet a few odd characters, and probably needing to complete most of the challenges (testing weapons, running courses).
I recommend working towards the grappling hook upgrade, this increases the fun factor.

This game does everything Titan Quest did, but better and more. It's practically a complete game and at time of writing I have 95 hours in-game (minus 10 for approximate game time) and only just recently completed act III with a level 49 Trickster. Granted, I do have roughly 8 characters most are around level 20.
This game sucked me in from the word go, and didn't disappoint. I keep finding new reasons to love this game, or going back to reasons I'd discovered before and finding new things. The crafting system is amazing for an ARPG, I was blown away when I saw how in-depth it actually can be. The fact that one can craft Epic items if you find a blueprint? Brilliant.
The amount you can tweak your character also doesn't disappoint. One skill tree can have various play styles and with the current max of two choices from 6 classes means play styles are endless. I've not been bored once, and this isn't on full content yet.
The game is atmospheric. More so than Titan Quest. The music is outstanding and each map never feels repeated. A couple of times I think, "Haven't I seen this corner somewhere before?" but then the rest is completely different or the fact that over 2-3 weeks I put in 96 hours makes me see things. The fact that there are few communities in this game make's it feel like you have a home base, that you need to protect and build upon and that's why you explore and fight. It doesn't feel like you're being led down a single path from village to village as Titan Quest did (granted paying attention to lore and other does help). I love every aspect of this game.
One thing I love is how they brought in consequence. (Spoilers) Kill the men harassing New Harbour, come back later New Harbour has been pillaged by the rest of the gang. Save the little girl from the cave in, demon tears a Rover camp apart. Side with Kymon's Chosen or Order of Death's Vigil and the other becomes your enemy.
All I can say is this game will only get better and I'm definitely behind Crate Entertainment all the way. They made my dream game a reality, and now they just need to release B28 plx.
Edit: This game has simply gotten better throughout development and I can't wait to see future plans for the game. I would love additional content in storyline.

If you like the original game you'll love this one! In all honesty I'd almost forgotten about the game ever existing until it popped up on Steam. This modern remake brings back so many memories and feelings. Wonderboy is up there with the likes of Sonic, Mario, Tetris, Bomberman, Zelda and other classics. This game is a must play for boys n girls who grew up playing games in the late 80s and 90s. The Wonderboy Series is a series of games that all gamers should experience from that era. I hope they remake the other games from the series in the same style. This isn't a diverse RPG in the Final Fantasy sense nor is it a complete platformer like Mario it takes bits and pieces from both types of game genres... be warned it only has very minor roleplay elements this is not like Phantasy Star or Zelda.
This is essentially a platforming adventure where by you the hero who is cursed by a Dragon, you must quest through platform style levels and beat various bosses using your skills and occasionally visiting the village to buy upgrades to find a way to turn you back into a human. Sure you have a shield, a sword and some abilities but the mechanics are all about timing, jumping and dodging rather than stats and spells.

I played Wonder Boy The Dragons Trap in the 90s on my Sega Gamegear as a kid. I remember it being a very hard game and I remember it being unique as not many games are both an rpg and a platformer. That said the rpg elements are the story and shops there's no character building or skill trees the mechanics are jump, dodge and attack as I mentioned before. Just think Legend of Zelda from the SNES but in a 2D platform style rather than overhead birds eye view and you have Wonderboy.
I'm not sure if I ever completed it back in the day but I remembered the Lionman and the Birdman forms when I watched the Steam trailer and was sold on the brand new graphics and art style.
The developer has made this game look and run fantastically whilst keeping the retro feel, it feels like a 90s game not a game from 2017. Many remakes or retro remakes suffer from trying to incorporate modern gaming too much but bar a few fixes and tweaks this is the original Dragons Trap with new age sprites and great graphical design. The original game had very hard difficulty and relied on password generated saves meaning you often had to complete certain areas of the game over and over upon loading up a save. Luckily this modern version has had the difficulty balanced out and the password system is replaced with modern save data. For some reason which is cool I guess you can use your 90s passcode if you want to load up an old character.
There aren't many retro remakes that stay true to the original game but this one does very well. It runs on my work PC just as well as my gaming PC so onboard graphics users will be able to run it.
You still jump around platforms, explore rooms, slash enemies and feel like your playing a 90s games even with the new artist style and design. The boss mechanics are the same as they were back in the day so most of the difficulty comes from the levels themselves once you determine the boss movement patterns. Finding the secret rooms, heart pieces and collecting gold for weapon and armour upgrades and finishing hidden areas are the main challenges... do you want to just complete the game or are you the type of gamer that has to get every item and unlock as Dragons Trap offers that.
If you wish you can even flip between modern day/old skool sounds and graphics with the press of a key which is a cool feature but to be honest you'll bore of that pretty quickly it's just a quirk.
To sum this game up it is a tweak/reskin of the old game 100% with nothing new in terms of gameplay features and content just subtle improvements.
The Dragon's Trap plays like the original, feels like the original and the difficulty and annoying bugs of the time have been fixed or updated to improve the experience. This is a retro kids wet dream!
Overall I would say there is about 4 or 5 hours max game time involved to complete from start to finish if you really go at it in one session. If like me you do it in 20 minute sessions you might get a lot more satisfaction out of it and for some players they may wish to find every secret room.
The price is a little a bit expensive... once you've completed the game I can imagine you may not play through it again for a long time and I don't expect the developer to add DLC or new levels... but who knows!

Star Wars: Battlefront II is a great nostalgic first-person shooter. With the new ability to play as your favourite heroes from the original trilogy, (And sadly, the prequels. Excluding Obi-Wan) this game is unique but still similar to the first one. Even with saying that though, you should get this instead of the first one due to the fact it's simply improved with great new features. The only disappointment was the fact that you could not use the spaceships while you are on land, unlike the first game but they made up for that with the addition of outer space combat.
The campaign of this game follows you, a soldier in the 501st Legion, renamed Vader's Fist later on. You play in some of the key events in the movie such as The Purge of The Jedi in the Jedi Temple and the battle of Hoth. You first begin as clone troopers but after Order 66, the Galactic Civil War begins and you change into Stormtroopers. Nothing else to add here, that is pretty much the whole storyline in this game.
The gameplay is much more polished in this game, it is smoother and the guns feel better to shoot but they could be improved. Then again, this game is pretty outdated and I shouldn't judge it for that.

There was never a better use of the word "Saga" in videogames.
Because that's what this game is about, the journey that is made, made by the characters through the land, and made by us, players who get personaly engaged with them, with the setting, with the storytelling, with the music and the stunning and amazing art.
You never know what will happen in that saga, you never know the outcomes of your decisions, what perils waits in the journey,  how people will react with your actions, and yet that journey must be made for there is no where else to go.
The combat was simple yet deep, every single turn is meaningfull, your heroes have very few stats yet all of them matter a lot, every square on the grid matter, even thou its not without flaws, every battle was meaningfull, as do every step in your journey.
The saga is filled with beatfully drawn landscapes, people and animations, the music is also fantastic and really make you get into the world.
If you want a good story, excelent visuals and music and a satisfying, deep and hard combat, this is a excelent game.

While much shorter than seasons 1 & 2, the yarn that Telltale spins in this title is no less riveting. It can be completed in around 4 hours. I was trepidatious about this short length but now that I have finished the final chapter, I feel as though I have just experienced an exciting, dramatic and action packed 4 hour interactive movie. I highly recommend this title to any Walking Dead fans and Michonne fans who want to take lead with the legendary lady herself.

This game is everything that the original game is not.  Indeed, Half-Life 2 is the franchise grown up, and proving that it still has legitimacy in todays gaming world.
The story of Half-Life 2 is a bit of a roller coaster in that there are great moments of narrative flow and others where you are left scratching your head a bit thinking "why did they put that in there?".  But saying that, there are plenty of ups to the few downs.  The story is overall strong and immersive with a few deviations that help create a vibrant lore.
The game mechanics are obviously much smoother, and well structured.  By todays standards, they stand up.  There are some nice features with the engine that work well.  The feel of the game when using certain weapons and the ability to manipulate some aspects of the environment help the gameplay support the story.  There are still a few things that don't seem right, such as no hands on steering wheels, being able to climb a ladder whilst simulatenously reloading or firing a heavy weapon, getting caught on obstacles, and the clumsy and altogether painful squads that do 2 things - 1) Die over and over, and 2) Get in your way when you need to do a run and gun (or often a grenade lob and duck).  The squad could definitely have used some more commands other than point and press C to have them run uselessly a couple feet before returning to interfere.
The weapons pretty much were a joy to use, especially the Pulse Rifle and the SMG.  No alien weapons to use in this game, other than the Antlion Pheropods, and this was the clumsiest weapon.  A few odd decisions were made with some of the weapons though, especially the .357 Magnum revolver.  Having a total ammo store of 18 rounds resulted in this being an often unused weapon.  Surely, Gordon could carry more than 18 bullets for this gun, considering the number he could carry for some of the others like the 9mm with a total ammo store of 168.  I'm sure it was for a balance purpose, but only being able to carry 18 rounds felt silly and frivolous.  The magnum went from being a mainstay weapon of the original series to a bit of a joke weapon in my mind.
Of the gameplay, I'm so happy that they decided to move away from the platform styled approach.  Moving across impossible terrain features and engineering in the original games made it feel like a caricature of a game.  Those titles didn't know if they were a shooter, narrative or platformer, often falling more towards the latter.  This game for the most part does away with that completely.  There are still a few gameplay components that aren't well thought out, mainly by being overly long and taking something novel and at first fun, and making it tedius - namely riding the airboat, and crossing the sand without touching it.  Both were fun at first, but quickly devolved into just hoping that it would soon be over, but nope - there was more and more of it.  Still, those didn't detract too much from the game as a whole.
The passage of time in the game, like in the first one though, still seems odd.  The immersion of that point is lost easily with the change from night to day as you are constantly on the move, never seeming to rest.... Jack Bauer, eat your heart out.
Overall, Half-Life 2 was and still is a great game, and my concerns with the game are more exagerated nitpicks than hangups.

So far, this app has worked wonders for me! I have a few questions, but that is for after this review (Tim, if you are reading this firstly thank you, secondly the questions are at the bottom!)
Review: This piece of software is amazing. My relevant specs are as follows: AMD FX 6300 (3c6t), nVidia GTX 1060 6gb, 8gb ddr3, and for sake of comparison a 120gb kingston SSD paired with an old WD Black 2tb HDD. I've had this app for about 2 days now and it has worked wonders, despite its relatively simplistic nature. I on average have a single chrome tab open and maybe a few steam chat windows concurrently alongside my games, one of which (notably PUBG) ran at a low enough framerate that I could count it on both hands, before investing in CPUCores. After running aforementioned game through CPUCores, I legitametly found myself sitting at 60fps consistantly, with my lowest dips in framerate hitting around 45fps at the worst. Overall, the user interface is quite straightforward: Start the software, launch the game through said software (Side note, the default settings worked perfectly fine for me), and enjoy the miracle of more frames!
With that said however, there are a few things I would warn a new buyer to be aware of. Firstly, from my experience, CPUCores opens the game of your choosing but Steam Overlay does no longer work if opening the game in this manner. Secondly, this software (as great as it is) is not a magic bullet. It will not make a CPU perform greater than it physically can. I.e, you will not be able to stream, game, and consume content on low end hardware at the same time, where you normally would be able to on stronger platforms. Finally, this piece of software I imagine (I cannot validate due to lack of resources available to me) will give diminishing returns on higher end gear. This app is designed and functions as a background Windows Cleaner and Sorter of sorts. Essentially it tells the system to allocate and budget as much as it can to a game (or whatever you point it at) and the rest of the running processes take the backseat.
Final Verdict:
Worth it? Absolutely! - If you are suffering below what your considered "standard" framerate should be. I would recommend it to other similarly spec'd PC users, however I would not recommend it for High-End users (people who meet or exceed their "standard" of what is considered acceptable.
QUESTIONS FOR TIM:

I see the option for Twitch under the advanced settings but on this current revision, it feels a little un-intuitive for me to figure out. My second question, what happens if I "CPUCores It" under the current process tab, and have nothing selected? And what about multiple items selected? My final question, the Disable HyperThreading and Game on dedicated cores only options; are they available to AMD FX users? Thanks so much for the amazing software!

Do you like first-person-puzzles and Escher-esque mazes? Then this is for you!
At the start of the game, it's mostly just walking around the labyrinthine world, finding new areas you can teleport directly to from the starting room after you find them. Then you find your way to the magic...gun...thing. You gain the ability to pick up and place down colored blocks. This allows you to reach more areas with new puzzles, which grants access to an upgrade to gun. Wash, rinse, repeat. Some of the puzzles are optional branches, and there are quite a few easter eggs. While some of the time the game uses puzzles encouraging logic, other times it uses puzzles that DEFY logic. Some of the puzzles are hard to figure out because the only help you get is in the form of explanations for controls and proverbs that relate to the area. Some of the puzzles are kind of fun/satisfying, such as platforms that act like trampolines and using chain reactions to your advantage. Overall, I give the gameplay 5/5.
(Btw, try not to 'mine' into a large cube immediately as you form it. I accidentally crashed the game doing that.)
The music is synthetic ambience, sometimes with nature sounds mixed in; it varies based on your location. The visuals are quite simplistic (and sometimes trippy), with the majority of the world white and right-angled. The gun has a detailed-yet-abstract appearance that fits everything else. Also, the proverbs on walls have occasionally-humorous illustrations. Overall, I'd say tone is 4/5.
I'm not sure if the game has a story? The world is more abstract than realistic. The proverbs you find around the place give the sense that this is all a metaphor of life, which is acceptable. This isn't the sort of game that involves lore.
Story is a 3 or 4 out of 5.

PROS:
+ Great graphics.
+ Open world gameplay (to a degree, as you can't leave the mountain).
+ Lots of different winter sports.
+ Competitive multiplayer that isn't ridiculous or juvenile.
+ Lots of items to "buy" with in-game money (or earn through completing events), but none of it gives any unfair benefits. The most it does is give you new clothing options, which while neat, is entirely unnecessary to enjoy the game.
CONS:
- You must have an online connection to play.
- You have to use both Steam and UPlay.
- User interface is very confusing and poorly constructed.
- Gameplay controls are terrible. For the record, I used a controller and the steering is so loose and difficult to control that you spend more time wrestling with the controls to keep your character from constantly slamming into things than actually playing.
Bottom Line: Steep should be an awesome game, especially if you like winter sports. For the most part, it's still fun despite the always-need-to-be-online DRM and requiring UPlay.
The two biggest problems (in my opinion) are trying to figure out the ridiculoulsy unintuitive user interface and the extremely loose steering that has you flapping all over the place as if your character was drunk.
Seeing as how I want to actually play the game and not spend my free time fighting the controls (just to keep my character from flying off the damn mountain), I'm forced to give Steep a negative review.

Each time you play is like a "Choose Your Own Adventure" book, making a "Story". So that gives it
replay value because there are multiple ways to go through the story giving it multiple endings. As you play for the first time you have a Skill set, which are accessed at an Altar. There are several advanced skills as well, but they do not unlock until you play through several times, and discover "Truths", which are facts about the characters you meet. Kind of confuses me though, since I've yet to find out what these "Truths" have to do with your skills.
You also eventually have 4 swords, each with special abilities to use in combat. These swords also act as "Keys" to the many doors around the world, so one would say it's a very minor Metroidvania type, since there will be times when you can't go in the door because you don't have the sword to unlock it yet, so you have to wait until you do have it, and come back to it. Swords are created by collecting various materials from the chests found around the areas. Once you have the requirements, you go to a Workbench cart and create it. Here is also where you use the gems you find in the chests. Your character wears a Gauntlet glove with 3 gem slots in it and each gem you find has a specific property that gives your combat abilities a boost when you place it in a slot. One cool bonus to this is that they are all hot-swappable, and can be removed and replaced at any time. In most Action RPGs that have equipment with slots in them, once you put a gem or whatever in the slot, that's it. Slot's occupied and equipment is permanently buffed by it.  I've only seen a few games that give you the ability to undo this sort of thing somehow.
- The game is beautiful, art and sound wise.
- The combat system is pretty smooth. It's Action-RPG style, and takes a bit of practice to pull off combos, but after a while it's simple once you figure it out.
- As mentioned before, it's an Action-RPG style game, but it's very light in that sense:
- it's just enough to satisfy that itch, but it's not complicated,
- there's not a ton of items or an inventory,
- the game has no gold or any sort of currency, so there's no shops to buy or sell any items,
- there are not very many types of items to collect,
and all of that makes it easy for just about anyone to pick it up and play.
- The "Choose your own adventure" style gives it replay value, but only if played in short bursts.
- One of the biggest cons for this game is the loading times between areas - they are WAY too long - almost feels like the 90's as if the game was on CD-ROM or some other slow reading media.
- Another big con is it seems to bee poorly optimized.  I had a hard time getting it started and once I did it ran really slow, unless I put the Graphics all the way down. I have a pretty decent computer, and I play way more graphically advanced games than this one at full speed, but I couldn't get even a halfway decent framerate out of this game without going to the lowest graaphics setting, and even then I only got 25-30 fps.
- Extended play can cause the game to get old fast, because:
- the game only has 8 or so unique areas, and literally
the stories go through them - pretty much in the same order, too. There are only 1 or 2 variations in the order of each story, so which area you go to can be predictable depending on what choice you make. The only plus to this, is that almost every area is REALLY BIG, and the only way to get everywhere in each area is by playing through multiple times, and making different choices, to get to different parts of the map.
All in all, if you can get over the cons, the game is wonderful. The graphics and music are beautiful. I'd still reccomend it for anyone who likes Action RPGs or even anyone that likes "Choose Your Own Adventure" type things.

It's difficult to decide whether I recommend this game or not, but seeing how I sunk 50+ hours into it and enjoyed most of it, I'd say it's worth your time despite the flaws, and, oh boy, there's a lot of them.
- the game is too random. This is alright on normal, but playing on ironman and higher difficulties is incredibly frustrating, because it gets very luck based, you can execute 5 missions perfectly and then get massacred in one turn despite playing very carefully, which is understandable every now and them when dealing with RNG, but it really doesn't seem like they tried to balancer the game for higher difficulty levels at all (see next point). You WILL get missions you can't beat when playing on higher difficulties (like escorting a 3hp scientist against 6+ thin men and a bunch of sectoids early in the first month, good luck with that), you WILL have your entire squad wiped out after they all miss on overwatch and get critically hit despite being in heavy cover, you WILL have 4 support and 1 assault soldier when your only heavy is wounded.
- the difficulty is highest in the beginning of the game. And I'm not just talking about the learning of mechanics, the game actually gets easier as it goes along, and I only really realized this when after I started a second play through. At the start you only have 4 soldiers who mostly die in one hit, can't hit anything and don't have any useful skills or gear. As the game progresses you get more powerful much more quickly than the aliens do. As you get better armor and more squadmates you get much, much more room for error and mitigating bad luck. Near the end all tension is gone because your sniper just floats around the map and headshots everything, while the MEC stand in the open takes fire and laughs.
- the shooting and cover mechanics are very iffy. I've had enemies in full cover because they kinda leaned against a trash can to one side and my soldiers "flanked" when they were clearly not. On classic and impossible the AI knows how to exploit this and will shoot you at impossible angles. On the other hand your grenades never miss and can often be tosses through building floors and walls killing multiple enemies with splash damage, which is just baffling. Rockets work the same way, but will occasionally steer to one side a little.
- the choice of gear and skills is almost nonexistent. Most classes have access only to 1 (ONE) gun that goes normal - laser - plasma as the game progresses, which, not counting MECs, makes for a grand total of 4 weapons + the mostly useless pistols. There is a lot of equipment, but you'll never use most of it because you can only have one (two with an upgrade) on each soldier, which is another thing that blows my mind, you can either take a grenade (A grenade) or a scope for your gun. Not both. Seriously now.
As for skills, when a soldier levels-up you get a choice of two skills (sometimes there's just one), but usually one of them is much more useful than the other, so generally soldiers of the same class end up as clones. There are options to randomize soldier stats but for some reason they always end up on the lower end of the roll (see also: game is too random). Did I mention the soldier classes are random? It's a horrible mechanic and should be a second wave option at most.
- some plots just go nowhere or kinda end unceremoniously. Without getting into spoilers: EXALT missions left me very disappointed. The DLC is fine, but if I didn't get it as a part of XCOM complete I don't think I would bother with it.
After reading that you might think I hated the game, but I actually really liked it. While in game you don't notice most of this and the game is very fun for what it is, the really bad stuff doesn't become apparent if you don't play on higher difficulties than normal and realize how the game really works. If you want more praise read the other positive reviews, they're mostly right. I just wish the game was more polished and thought out, it might have been great instead of just good.

It's a fun old school crpg, but more than just a nostalgia romp.
You can tell they spent a lot of time polishing the game, because so many little things are right. Automatically rotated quicksaves, roleplaying traits that have a mechanical effect - much more interesting than any karma or alignment system I've seen in a crpg, a pretty good crafting system, unused action points carrying to the next round, fun perks that let you chat with animals, easy and consistent equipment trading amongst party members, a very usable inventory screen, and a sense of humor that pervades the game.
The game doesn't pull punches or provide safety rails, so expect to die a lot. And expect to throw away your first playthrough away once you realize you screwed up your build completely.
There are a few things I'd change in the interface: change gold amounts in bartering to default to balance the current transaction rather than all gold, make single-file the default formation, and make party members more cautious when they auto-follow.

As someone who grew up with the original game and kept playing it over the years since then, this is like a dream come true. The amount of love that went into this, just the fact that it exists make me happy to pay for it.
That makes it kind of impossible to review this from the point of view of someone who never played it before. For me its a big hit of nostalgia wrapped up in beautiful new graphics and music, but I can't really say how the gameplay holds up to modern standards. But something about it kept me coming back every now and then over the years, its just simple fun I guess. An action rpg stripped down to its basic elements.
If you are a fan of the old 8 bit version and were hoping to get something more than the original adventure, well, there is a hard-mode and some extra little challenges to find. I would have liked more than that if i'm honest. As a kid I used to imagine all the places that might be hidden out of reach, up in the sky or behind secret doors and suspicious walls. Thats just me being greedy I guess. Games like this train you to always expect more from them.
So anyway, I'd definitely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the original, or is interested in the history of metroidvania style games. And I'd also like to thank the artists and developers for doing such an amazing job updating the sights and sounds.

Wonderboy: The Dragon's Trap is literally the template to which all other remaster/remakes should aspire to.  You have the option to play it in its original 8-bit Sega Master System 1989 audio & visual glory, or opt for hand drawn, cartoon style graphics and full orchestral audio. Alternatively, you can mix and match.  On the fly.  ON THE FLY!!
Anyway, for those of you who have never played the Wonderboy series (this was the third installment), the game puts you at the end of Wonderboy 2 (Wonderboy in Monster Land) where you are about to enter the dragon's castle.  BE WARNED, there are spoilers regarding the end of Wonderboy in Monster Land ahead! lol
Charging into the castle to take on the dragon, you must navigate a certain way to be able to reach the dragon's lair.  The maze from Wonderboy in Monster Land has been simplified to essentially the first and last section, meaning you don't have to scale the annoying chimney section with moving platforms - hurrah! Additionally, you don't have to fight the dragon to uncover the truth - you're straight into a fight with the Mecha Dragon! Defeating the dragon obviously doesn't end the game or teleport you back to Monster Land, either. It unleaches the dragon's spirit, which on contact turns you into Lizard-Man.  You have to escape the now crumbling castle!
Lizardcube have totally aced this remaster/remake. The new graphics are simply gorgeous, the animation is smooth, and the fully orchestrated soundtrack brings the original 8-bit version into the 21st century in spectacular fashion, while staying true to the original tunes.  The re-vamped audio and visuals add layers of additional atmosphere to the game, while keeping it instantly recognisable to the original.
There are several wonderful touches to this game, from the simply sublime ability to change the audio and visuals from 8-bit to modern with the press of a button - you don't even need to pause the game to do it! - to the fact that if you still have a notepad of the original master system game save codes, you can use these to continue where you left of 22 years ago!
This game first released on Xbox One, and I bought it on day one, as I'm a MASSIVE fan of the Wonderboy series.  When I learned it was coming to Steam, I wishlisted it, and bought it for PC on the day it was released too.  If they released it for Nintendo DS and Wii, I'd buy it for those too.  That's how good it is.
The addition of hard mode, and additional things once you complete the game (no spoilers here!), are welcome additions for new players and old alike, and the price point is, I think, spot on for this title.  Sure you can complete it on easy in an hour, but then you can play on normal, then hard and so on.  My general rule is that if I can pay around £5/hour of game play, I'm happy that I've got value for money.  I know I'm going to get WAY more that that amount of value in this game, without a doubt.
Now I'm hoping on a remake of Wonderboy, Wonderboy In Monster Land, Wonderboy III: Monster Lair, Wonderboy in Monster World and and Monster World IV.  *Sigh* I can only hope.

TL;DR edition:
SP:SoT is a brilliant piece of fan-service and finally a South Park (SP) game actually worth playing. It is a surprisingly solid RPG that hooked me enough to play through twice.
PRESENTATION
The story is as ludicrous as you would expect and the town of South Park itself is littered with easter-eggs that refer to many of the more famous episodes. My only gripe with the presentation is that the game hinges heavily on the more childish humour of SP, and has little of the more intelligent satirical humour that some SP fans prefer (myself included).
VISUALS
The game also looks fantastic. In fact, I would say it looks perfect. It is presented so loyally as the TV show that you could easily mistake it for an episode. The movement in game uses 2D models on a horizontal movement plane with a little depth for 3D movement. The game allows you to create your own character, but your "new-kid" can be heavily customised throughout the game anyway. Each individual weapon and armour also has their own model skin which is shown in-game.
GAMEPLAY
The game plays very smoothly, both in & out of combat. Outside combat you move around and interact with the environment using several abilities. Combat itself is turn-based and others a selection of attacks, abilities, "magic", buffs/debuffs, and a quite large variety of enemies too. The weapons and armour you use can be modded a little too. I enjoyed the fighting in SP but it could be quite easy at times. As long as you show no sentimentality to individual weapons and instead upgrade whenever you can, you can breeze through the game's combat quite easily. The game also has quite a lot of environmental traps the new-kid can spring on enemies to KO them outside of combat which is a very nice addition.
SOUND
My favourite part of SP:SoT though was the audio. The characters are all voiced exactly as they are from the show, and the scripting is very loyal to the TV show style too. The scripting also pulls no punches. It would have been easy for this game to shy away from being controversial, but instead they just went all-in and stayed true to the show. There is also a variety of background tracks that you can stumble across too. There are a lot of sound effects in combat and also little one-off comments your companions will mumble every now & again.
DRAWBACKS
Despite all the good I have detailed above there are some downsides to this game.
1) Censorship: the EU console versions are censored, as are the Germany, Austrian, and Australian PC versions. This game is outrageously offensive and is not ashamed of it, unfortunately this means that some countries do not have the full SP:SoT experience available. Check which version you can get before purchasing!
2) Bugs: the game does have some bugs. I encountered two large ones.
a -- The first was my sound would not play properly as I have 5.1 speakers (the game prefers stereo). In cutscenes I could not hear characters speaking at all. I had to set Windows to stereo mode and then start the game again.
b -- The second was that a previous save kept replicating itself and overwriting all of my other saves. I almost lost all progress due to this and had to manually back up my savegame.
3) Narrative: the story will only appeal to fans of SP. I honestly cannot see anyone who does not like the show enjoying this game.
SUMMARY
If you love South Park, then you must play this game through to the end. It is worth every second you spend with it and is the game SP fans have been waiting so long for. If you dont enjoy South Park though, then just steer well clear of this as there is nothing here for you.
Intresting and experimental, worth buying on a sale, especially if you enjoy puzzles.

I didn't find out about this game until the day of it's release. The original was a classic that stood out in my childhood.
I have played this game twice, in full retro and full remix mode. 100% achievements etc etc.
Classic/Retro graphic/audio Mode Specific Notes:
I've played through this game in the "Classic" Retro graphics/Audio, and am astounded how it was virtually identical to my experience on the Master System so many years ago. With exception to changes to how some of the deeper unlocks of "Charms Stones" work, and some added secrets to the game. The only issue i had, was that the item screens and menus were not retro (like the inventory/pause screens. All stores in the game looked original). It was pretty well streamlined. Though, the ending was probably the most altered. The classic WB had one of my favorite credit sequences ever, and this one was not as good in my opinion. Missed lots of the retro fancy effects. But was still the same music and decent overall. switching both music and graphics to retro independantly at the push of a button was pretty seamless and had great effect. very impressed. There were various options for adding scanlines and altering audio for the different 8 bit experiences the old school players would have experienced.
Remix/Original "New" mode specific Notes:
The art style was a lot of fun. Very animated and a great homage to the original series. Lot's of artistic license with the look and sound of everything. Entirely respectful to the core material in my opinion though. Lot's of added dialogue with store keepers, excellent animations etc. The only issues I had were:
- Occasionallly, things got too dark. Not enough to heavily impact gameplay, but noticeable. There are parts of the game where all rooms are entirely dark, and the interactable objects also became dark and hard to see at times. This includes projectiles (Shurikens and fireballs mostly), this actually affected gameplay and made it a bit more difficult, though overall it was a nice asthetic that didn't really impact negatively too much at all.
- The audio overall was not quite as iconic. It was great to hear direct remixes, and a lot of it was great. However, at many times rather than feeling the beat and impact, things sounded heavy on reverb or an overall sense of echo or muted. Again, not terrible and worth a listen, but not as iconic. It loses some of the action momentum as a result. When tension rises in gameplay, the music does not always follow in kind like the original score did. Though i heavily appreciate how deep and wonderful the music was. Fully composed with real instruments, it is an experience to be hold even with those caveats.
The game itself, regardless of Retro/Remix visuals/audio:
- Just wow. The gameplay is identical in both modes, yet feels different given the insane amount of animation in the remix. Actually had to adjust how i played, purely on asthetic, as i had to learn the new animations and recognize the new timing based on animations.
- You can switch between Wonderboy and Wondergirl modes. including changes to the openings/endings and character specific mentions in the story. Very impressive, and totally welcome.
- There has been an added "Hard" mode, that adds a timer to gameplay. Take too long, and you take damage. I normally hate timers in games, as i love to explore, but this was entirely manageable, and i didn't feel too rushed. You could still farm out hearts, and if you were too worried, you could go hunt down potions to ensure you wouldn't die too quickly. In particular, some boss battles can be extra long with the extra survivability of bosses, and a lack of being able to pick up hearts, so those ended up being more difficult, but in a good way i think. required more prep and being "ready", but not at all terribly difficult.
- Fantastic action/RPG gameplay. most RPG aspects come in the form of aquiring weapons/armor and equiping them specific for the level or type of character you can have. You basically have access to various "Animal" forms, that function differently in the world, and react differently to all the items. That and the open world almost Metroidvania aspect to the world, gives it the RPG feel. There is no leveling system or growth, beyond the aquisition of permanent heart upgrades and equipment aquisition/equipping.
- Overall, there are a lot of actual changes. The gameplay itself, is nearly perfect carbon copy to the original. But additions to the remix, and actual items of the game are welcome. All items/equipment have updated descriptions, many indicating a lot of the "Hidden" effects, or outright adding hidden effects that the original game never had. There are added challenge rooms to aquire Charmstones which are added challenges, that can affect some new item aquisitions and achievement unlocks.
Conclusion:
I love what Lizardcube has done with this game. They clearly have love for the original, and have treated the content with respect. Yet they have entirely embraced the remix and been willing to take artistic license and give their own feel to the visual/audio. I admit to having Nostalgia tinted glasses in my review and playing of the game. But I really do think this game captures the original feel, while making this also feel like a modern game that stands the test of time against many modern games of similar type. If you like Platformers and Metroid/Vania type games, there is a lot of meat in this game to devour. If your not into the retro platforming type games, then this is not probably for you. Though even then, this game was always ahead of its time. I reccomend highly. I very much look forward to more games from Lizardcube.

This game is one of my all-time favorites, and without a doubt the best Star Wars game ever made. Between the old Xbox version and now Steam, I've poured hundreds and hundreds of hours into this game, continue to pour more in to this day, and I don't regret a second of it. This game will provide you endless entertainment, and I wholeheartedly recommend giving it a go because whether you're a Star Wars fan or not, there's one heck of a game to be found here.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a classic-style 2D platformer based on the classic Wonderboy games from decades past, released by new Steam developers, Lizardcube.
The game is most like Wonder Boy in Monsterland, and seems to be attempting to update that title for 2017. You play Wonder Boy (or Wonder Girl -- we have gender equality in gaming now, you know!?), sans skateboard, but equipped with sword and shield, intent on beating the dragon in his castle. I didn't even know dragon's had castles!
I played Wonder Boy and Wonder Boy in Monsterland longer ago than I care to remember. They were good fun, but I remember the parts I liked best were from the first game, with Wonder Boy on his skateboard. I was thus a bit disappointed to see that he's no longer interested in that particular mode of transport. Still, I was interested to see what Lizardcube had done to try to resurrect and modernise this particular classic.
Graphics - The graphics are big and colourful, with a setting reminiscent of Wonder Boy in Monsterland. Levels take the classic approach of scrolling painted backgrounds with a layer of floating platforms in front, and the backgrounds look quite lovely in some cases, with a weird colour texture to them similar to a bande dessinée. Many of the backgrounds include animated components, such as moving clouds, birds, and the like. These are well done and make a nice addition.
The protagonist character looks rather personable after the first level and is very well drawn, but it's a shame that the graphics don't change to reflect equipped items. Animations are good: typical of modern 2D platformers, but somewhat limited in number.
The game has cut scenes to move the story along, with small sections animated on mostly stationary comic-style screens. The art in these is very good, too. There's also a 'retro' graphics mode available from the options menu, which puts the game into a mode reminiscent of the first Wonder Boy on a 16-colour system (I think). It's very well done and really does look 'right'.
Graphics options are limited to windowed/full screen, and various options to do with frame rate, vsync, and resolution. There are no detail or similar settings.
Sound - The music is instrumental with a renaissance-style feel to it, and fits the game perfectly. Some of the tracks may be from the original games; I can't remember. In any case, the style is a great choice.
Sound effects are appropriate for a 2D platformer. They're well balanced, but not especially good or bad.
As with the graphics, there are 'retro' sound effect and music options, which are good for a laugh, or for real fans of chiptunes I suppose. I turned them on for a couple of minutes, but then I'd had enough and disabled the options again.
There are no voices.
Gameplay - No one should be surprised to learn that Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap plays like a traditional 2D platformer. It supports keyboard or controller. I didn't bother with the keyboard as the default controller support is fine.
The game includes controls and actions typical of the genre. You can jump, duck, move left and right, enter doors, fire or attack, and, if your character has a shield, block an incoming attack. You can also pick up a number of single-use weapons, such as boomerangs and fireballs, and throw these at your foes. You can equip one sword, one shield, and one suit of armour, all of which you can buy at shops that you discover on your adventure with coins that you pick up from defeated enemies, or find in chests. And you have a certain number of hearts, which are reduced with hits from enemies (at a rate I haven't quite worked out yet), and can be restored by picking up little hearts that occasionally drop from defeated enemies as well. If you're lucky, too, you'll find a potion, which restores you to full health (minus one hit) when you die.
The first level is essentially an introduction to the story, and I shouldn't be ruining too much of the plot by saying that after this level, your chosen character -- Wonder Boy or Wonder Girl -- is largely irrelevant. The game is divided into areas, with a dragon of a certain type guarding the end of each. Kill the dragon and you are transformed into a different character, sometimes with a special ability that allows you to reach previously unreachable areas. This gradual progression through a number of different bodies is an interesting twist on the old formula.
Another diversion from the classic formula is the use of a sort of 'home' area -- the village -- to which you keep returning, time, after time, after time. This leads to a game that becomes hugely repetitive very quickly, as taking the wrong exit from a screen can end up with you back at the village again, spending ages backtracking to continue from where you were. And you have no idea until you take an exit just where you'll end up, leading to considerable frustration on occasion.
Level design is mostly unremarkable and sometimes even lazy. Most screens include enemies that respawn if you leave and re-enter, which is not a design feature I enjoy. This is made worse still by the need to cover so much ground multiple times, due to being unceremoniously deposited back at the village over and over again. This seems like an attempt to increase play time artificially by forcing the player to redo sections multiple times.
Other disappointments include the one-use inventory items, which are a bit rubbish, and some poor grammar, which seems to be the norm in most games these days. Probably the biggest issue is that the game just isn't as much fun to play as I expected it to be. Controls are quite slow and unresponsive, with some characters more than others. However, with all characters I found inertia too strong and friction too low, making negotiating jumps or attacking groups of creatures harder than it should be.
Pros:
+ It's Wonder Boy, risen from the grave!
+ Graphics are nice, with a convincing retro mode (if you like that sort of thing)
+ Multiple character 'forms' to play with (but you can't choose)
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Controls feel slippery and a bit unresponsive
- Often poor and very repetitive level design
Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is a reasonable two-dimensional platformer in the traditional style that does some justice to one of the genre's classic retro series. It has some problems, but if you don't mind retracing your steps more than you should need to, and aren't prone to fits of controller abuse, it should suffice to scratch a platforming itch.
This game is 100% authentic to its source material. It felt like I was controlling the action in a really long South Park movie. This is a must buy if you are a South Park fan.

Do you like first-person-puzzles and Escher-esque mazes? Then this is for you!
At the start of the game, it's mostly just walking around the labyrinthine world, finding new areas you can teleport directly to from the starting room after you find them. Then you find your way to the magic...gun...thing. You gain the ability to pick up and place down colored blocks. This allows you to reach more areas with new puzzles, which grants access to an upgrade to gun. Wash, rinse, repeat. Some of the puzzles are optional branches, and there are quite a few easter eggs. While some of the time the game uses puzzles encouraging logic, other times it uses puzzles that DEFY logic. Some of the puzzles are hard to figure out because the only help you get is in the form of explanations for controls and proverbs that relate to the area. Some of the puzzles are kind of fun/satisfying, such as platforms that act like trampolines and using chain reactions to your advantage. Overall, I give the gameplay 5/5.
(Btw, try not to 'mine' into a large cube immediately as you form it. I accidentally crashed the game doing that.)
The music is synthetic ambience, sometimes with nature sounds mixed in; it varies based on your location. The visuals are quite simplistic (and sometimes trippy), with the majority of the world white and right-angled. The gun has a detailed-yet-abstract appearance that fits everything else. Also, the proverbs on walls have occasionally-humorous illustrations. Overall, I'd say tone is 4/5.
I'm not sure if the game has a story? The world is more abstract than realistic. The proverbs you find around the place give the sense that this is all a metaphor of life, which is acceptable. This isn't the sort of game that involves lore.

If there's anything that we've learned to expect from developer/publisher TellTale Games over the years, it's a high quality product. Their story-centric, semi-point-and-click series for The Walking Dead catapulted them into fame with the 2012's first installment, and the company has been gaining huge momentum ever since. In the last two entries the playable characters were derived from the brain of TellTale's crew, but The Walking Dead: Michonne puts you directly in charge of a protagonist straight from the comic books and TV show.
It's undeniable that Michonne is a strong female character, not only in physique but in mentality; she's a deadly force to be reckoned with either way. This mini-series explores the events that were previously untold when she disappeared from the comics from issues 126-139, or in TV terms after the group was separated at Hershal's farm and before finding Woodbury. However, none of the other cast is mentioned in the game and Michonne finds herself aboard a ship called the Companion, with a small gathering of new comrades that include a couple of guys named Pete and Oaken. Pete picks up a distress signal on the boat's radio, and he and Michonne set out to help the senders. What they don't expect is the hot water that they land themselves in, and they pay dearly throughout three episodes for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
If you've played any of the other TellTale games, then you'll already be familiar with all of the mechanics here; nothing new has been introduced. When interacting with other characters, you're given three dialogue options plus the ability to not say anything at all; what's really cool though is that all of the verbal replies are something Michonne would definitely say. TellTale has done an outstanding job keeping the in-game persona meshed with that of the comic. Characters will remember your decisions and some of your dialogue choices, and your actions will carry over to the next episode. The title sticks with the same cell shaded, comic style graphics from the prior two releases, though the color is more vivid and there is quite a bit more gore.
Ultimately, your enjoyment of The Walking Dead: Michonne will depend on your view of the character; if you don't like her, you won't find any love here, but if you do enjoy her then this will be right up your ally. It's a great title that pieces together the threads of Michonne's past, and where she disappeared to for so long. Although I must mention that there are still some minor technical problems with the game, such as load times that shouldn't be as long as they are, being able to walk through some obstacles, a small freeze during the third episode (it corrected itself for me), and for some reason when you enter an action sequence the game puts up black bars at the top and bottom of the screen; though if you die, they go away for the remainder of your current session. Also, it's a short ride of about 4 hours, so I recommend grabbing it for 50-75% off. Other than that, for any fans of Michonne this game is a must play.

At the surface level, Antichamber is an interesting and challenging FPP (first person puzzler). Below the surface, Antichamber is an artistic expression of what the video game environment is.
It challenges notions of the regular three-dimensional space that we are naturally accustomed too. It uses unique environment interactions and sharply contrasted designs to put the player outside their comfort zone, invoking what every great FPP should invoke, mental gymnastics. Not the kind that relies on timing or random trial-and-error, but the type that gives you a problem which you know can be solved with the few tools you have, you just have to think about it carefully.
I highly recommend this game. Whether you spend hours inside it, finding every new room and sequence, or whether you just explore for a few hours and give up. You will inevitably come back and find something or somewhere you have never been before, and this will help you with other parts where you are stuck.
The only downside of Antichamber is that it is not exactly linear, and there are ways to find yourself advanced within a puzzle-path without first learning vital environment information that is needed to advance further. Some would argue that this just adds to the challenge, but I argue that there needs to be clear information given about how the world interacts in FPP’s. No puzzle game should hide behind obscure information as part of the challenge, everything should be upfront and taught to the player at the appropriate time.
Antichamber does have mechanisms to do this, and most work well, but inquisitive players can and often do walk off the beaten track which causes them to become confused and disorientated on exactly what is going on, missing out on learning something vital (such as exactly how matter (cubes) operates at various stages of the game).
This is part of the appeal and uniqueness to the game however. I highly recommend that everyone, not just FPP players, experience this game. Yes, there are more refined puzzlers out there (The Talos Principle is the only one I would rate above Antichamber), but none capture the unique and slightly uncomfortable feeling that Antichamber manages to craft so well.

Historical summary of my Civ game: I settle on the South Eastern coast of the oval pangea. It is abundant with silk and rich in stone and marble. Although my location is suitable, it is tight and I cannot settle more than 3 cities. To the north of me is Arabia, to the west Greece, and to the south and east is the sea. Being Portugal, trade is a primary goal. I rush Collosus to use the sea as my advantage for commerce. This gave me an early title for the most wealthy civilization. For 2 to 3 eras, my civilization is ignorant of other civilizations as I focus becoming the best and science. To do this, I use my wealth to focus on infastructure while my focus is on science buildings, wonders, and technologies. I invest my early turns into Hanging Gardens (for fast capital population) and Oracle (for scientist points). My science points win me a great scientist; but, rather than use it for technology boost, I build the science tiles improvements. By the next era I have 4 science tile improvements. This decision pushed me up as 1st place in literacy; however, I lost 1st in GNP. Finally, i reach navigation and I can build my special unit, which replaces the caravel, - the Nau. It's exploration ability is so good, I discover all the possible sea tiles less than 10 turns. Suddenly, I become aware of all my surroundings. Politics and advanced diplomacy rises as I become the first to discover Printing Press. As first Continental Congress leader, I make a proposal in which all adore me. After the first meeting, I retire. I do not participate in politics and I stay neutral to all proposals- never voting to anything. This way, none of the civilizations have anything to hate me; and, I become the most adored. However, my closest ally become Brazil. As I set my sail to a science victory, the other civilizations quarrel. Germany falls to 6th place in literacy; and, thus becomes bullied by all except I - who does not interfere. Germany diminishes into city states when its capital falls. Meanwhile, China becomes my competitor in science - trying to catch up but never exceeding my speed. However, due to it's successful conquest, China becomes the largest empire for a  short while. Arabia plots many times to take my bordering capital but never builds enough courage to face my impenatrable defense composed of the Red Fort wonder and many airborn units. As time passes, Brazil obliverates China and sends them to a few city states. Karma is a ♥♥♥♥♥. Greece never does anything special except try to steal my city state allies. However, my wealth is superior and the city states fall to my influence. By the late 1900s, I have completed all but 1 part of the Science Victory. When all the civilizations spot my near state of triumph, they betray me for little reason. Arabia steals my land with a great general. China, Brazil, and Greece denounce me. Germany jacks off in the background. However, none if this is able to make me trip; and, I sail the winds of the science victory.

Knights of Pen. And Paper! I tried to be witty there.
Now, I'm not one to do really large reviews, but I can tell you this: Buy this game.
A ton of people will go on and on about how it sucks, how it's stupid, but it's a really fun RPG game for those that are into the genre. And a lot of people have gone on to say that it's just a time waster, but no, it's more than that. Like an RPG game, it'll take you into the story the best it can. It's up to you, if you let it do it's job or not.
And as such, this took me to believe that not many people gave it that starting chance. The chance to change their lives forever.
Now, you might be thinking I'm biased, and yeah, I am. I never got the chance to grow up with great games that were released on older gen consoles. Like the NES, the SNES, and even the Sega Mega Drive. I got to miss the truly astonishing ups and lows of gaming history. All because I'm a kid. So, when a game like this comes along, a game that does so well at giving the player a feel of the old world, I take it like it's a van full of candy.
But, TL;DR: Buy this game if you're into the genre, you won't regret it.
