Enjoyable turn based strategy, where overcoming the odds from being kicked into the dirt is a real challenge.
The gameplay is well paced, with decent graphics for the majority of the time (every now and then it'll not want to shift away from cinematic mode, soldiers can point their guns the wrong way and still fire accurately, or hitting the enemy graphically despite the dreaded "Missed!" popping up.. all rare occourances, but can be face-palm worthy with the latter.), a not paticularly deep storyline, if engaging, and a tech tree that will take time to get through.
The A.I. seems smart even on normal, utilising explosives and coverless positions in order to remove you from cover or flank/get a serious injury. As you are in control of your whole squad, you don't have to fear any co-operative AI messing things up for you.
Thoroughly enjoyed burning time with this one, but I highly recommend getting at least the first DLC - the length of the game isn't huge without it, and it adds serveral layers to the story/progressing.

At the time of writing this I have about 60 hours played, over the course of a few years.
Using the old Golie Locks story, If we compare Diablo 3, Path of Exile and Grim dawn:
I would say Diablo 3 is too simple, and too easy. Little depth or freedom
Path of Exile is perhaps too complex, and a bit too hard. With punishing EXP Loss. TONS of depth, and the freedom to completly ruin a character and make it unplayable.
And then theres Grim Dawn which is just right. With Veteran difficulty enabled its a good challenge. Even in death you're allowed to retrieve your exp which prevents total stagnation. The depth and customization is modarate. Not crazy but with many fun possibilities. If you ruin your character, simply refund the points you've spent in your tree.
Cons: (May be fixed as development goes on)
Clunky AI
Areas can be hard to navigate
Poor Map
Mediocre animations
No Voice Overs
Low Loot Variety
With approx 400 hours in D3 and well over 1000 in PoE I must say so far Grim Dawn is a great middle ground between the two.  And I look forward to playing more and seeing what else they update the game with.

Dying Light Review:
Things I do like about Dying Light:
1.) Open World
2.) Slow motion if you do a critical on the zombie your killing.
3.) Double XP at night for agility/strength (But at the risk of night hunters looking for you) also zombies are stronger at night.
4.) Great graphics and world design. ( Add-on coming out called "The Following" bringing buggies into the game and a whole new open world area to drive the zombies over with friends)
5.) Buggies will be upgradeable.
6.) You can repair items and upgrade them if you find an upgrade somewhere in the world!
What I don't like about Dying Light:
1.) If someone joins your world they COULD loot everything good in your world for that day ingame then when its day again everything respawns.
2.) If a low level or new player joins your game they can get annoying and ask you for higher level items for it to be easier to level up with.
3.) If I think of more or when the game updates I will add good or bad to the list on my review.
Thanks for reading my review of what I think of the game! Happy killing zombies! ( If you decide on buying Dying Light!)

Background info
XCOM enemy unknown was released on the 9th of October 2012 in America then in the rest of the world 2 days later (11/10/12 ) It's a reimaged version of 1994's UFO Enemy unknown/XCOM UFO Defense. It's a turn based strategy game with blends of strategic base management to break up the battles. when the player first starts playing XCOM it's not a fight to win its a fight to survive as you quickly learn not only has the game not made the enemy your fighting clear (hence the name enemy unknown) but it's given them better weapons, better resources, better tech and the element of surprise to greatly out way the odds in their favor for example the aliens tend to attack 3 places at one time but you can only respond to 1 meaning even if you beat them they've won on two other attacks.
Feel of the game
The experience of XCOM is very refreshing to a lot of players unlike most games where you know you play through the story and win with XCOM you can play for hours and still lose, it's a real channel to complete on just the normal difficulty but despite this it's very enjoyable because you just want to keep fighting to turn the odds in your favor and the game play can become somewhat addictive.
Immersion and presentation
When XCOM starts you are introduced as the commander overseeing the operations of the XCOM project you never actually see yourself which helps immerse the player in being the commander as you don't just see some character your playing as, as the commander it's your job to oversee the base management as well as the battles themselves which include things like, making sure the hanger is always ready with interceptors to defend your satellites and shoot down enemy UFO's, to instruct the research team on what to research, to make sure new rooms and structures are being built below the base, to monitor the panic level of the 16 funding countries and to make sure the barracks is filled with soldiers which act as the planets first and last line of defense. While at first this can be a bit overwhelming that only helps you immerse yourself as the commander as it wouldn't be easy if it was real and at first you will make mistakes will may become costly later down the line but that only makes your want to go back and improve upon your mistakes. Now one of the funniest things in the game is your soldiers as not only do you control them in battle but you can customize them to make them look like the bas♥♥♥♥♥team you want or like most people your friends which helps you immerse yourself in the game as you start to care for theses soldiers that represent your friends, as time goes on your start to make stories for them like when Joe lead his team into a blood bath and only just managed to get out after losing half his team and retreating back to the ship and how Jon sacrificed himself by taking a bullet so his friend could get out of a bad spot and survive or how one of them won the battle without a single scratch but like in real life when they die they die forever they never come back and the only thing you have of them is a name on the wall which adds an element of consequence unlike most over games where you just do it again if your best guy dies that it's just like that and much like in real life sometimes it isn't fair not even close but that's the nature of XCOM a harsh refreshing approach to gaming which makes each choice a difficult one as every decision has its own real consequences . the customization includes changing the name, voice, hair, face, facial hair and a few other things but it should be noted that you can't change the gender, nationality or class for reason.
Story
The story to XCOM is as follows you are the commander of the XCOM project, 16 country's have united to fund the project as the earth first and last line of defense, as the aliens attack you strike back and start to research them you discover more and more about them and mange to capture one leading you to their base while where you discover there commanders which have some form of power allowing them to control your soldiers minds after this you discover more and more while improving your tech and eventually find and kill their commander to make it brief the point here is XCOM's story isn't its strongest point it's a bit simple but it doesn't need to be anything more and it's just enough to be considered good, with added occasional cut scenes  to help inform you of what's happening.
Combat
The combat itself in the game is very addictive in the form of turn based strategy which adds a certain suspense as you have to wait to see what the aliens/ your opponent will do, while in these battles it's up to you to control your soldiers if you mess up it can lead to your soldiers being killed and possibly losing the battle which will cause the 16 countries funding you to panic if they panic to much they drop out of the project if too many lose you lose the game.
Multiplayer
XCOM enemy unknown dose have a multiplayer where to people can play against eachother but this is clearly not where the develops spent most of their time there focus was in the single and they just kind of added a multiplayer which seems kind of half asked but your be enjoying the single player so much that won't even matter.
Conclusion
In conclusion XCOM enemy unknown is a fantastic game that has been present brilliantly with something for everyone even though it is a hard game you can just lower the difficulty to just play the story or practice, the multiplayer is there for anyone just wanting to play their friends, and the fresh approach of real consequence is there as well over all this is a fantastic game and i shall be awarding it a 9 out of 10.

I can not tell you properly with words how good this game is.
I will try however and I should start, as everyone, comparing it to old school RPG titles. Unlike recent RPG-called titles from this century —mostly made for the new generations of players, with little or no brains needed at all to solve quests—, Divinity: Original Sin looks like a true role playing game reminiscent of the old ages but with very cool new ideas —some of them unique— and fresh graphics.
The main characteristic, typical of Larian games, is the freedom to do almost everything you want: the game is classless, so you can choose a warrior in the beginning and later on you can change your mind and provide him with some spells or range skills, if you like it, when he level up; this way you will end up with four characters, two of them from the start and two more later on, with a combination of skills, traits and talents that fits you. You can interact with almost every item in the game: doors, chests, barrels, pictures, chairs, etc, and you can open them to look inside or destroy them if you prefer, or even take them and move them from one place to another. You can also choose if you prefer to talk to every NPC and solve quests, trade with them, or killing them if you like it, or even steal their items and loot their houses. Every action will make the villagers approach you in different ways, turning hostile to you or being polite instead. And if you don't like to trade with NPCs a lot you are able to craft your own gear and even spells if you choose to do it with the immense amount of ingredients and tools you will find everywhere.
What makes this game unique, and a gem, is a combination of the role playing part with the interaction between characters —even yours!— and its combat system. Divinity is not a combat focused game, it is more a conversational and exploration RPG title; however, combat is also very important and this is not a real time one, it is a turn-based combat system with action points mechanics that forces you to think about your resources, the enemies, and the environment; so each turn you can use your points to move, drink potions, attack or cast spells if you got enough points for them, or if you prefer you can reserve some of your remaining action points for your next turn, for example if you want to wait when the enemy is far away from you and later on you want to hit him two or three times in the same turn. The best part of the system is, no doubt, the chance —and mostly the need— of using the elements on your favour. It means you can cast a rain spell on your characters to stop them from burning; you can also cast rain on enemies, make them wet and then cast electricity spells for extra damage and stuns. You can also use ice spells if enemies are wet —state than come from your spells or from real rain itself!— to freeze them. You can shoot (after throwing it for example) an oil barrel with a fire spell to make it explode and damage the area, or just hit it with your arrows to make it pour the oil and later on cast fire on it if you wish. You can make an ice barrier to protect, wait until enemies are near it and then fire it, making it water and causing enemies to stumble, and then electrify them. You can combine elements to create clouds to avoid being a target. You can stealth and stab enemies too if you have the right character to do such a thing. You can use barrels and things of the environment to take cover, to protect you and to avoid damage. You can also try to flee if you find the situation too chaotic for your taste. You can... well, you can —and you should— do all these things if you want to survive, because combat is not always an easy task on this game.
For all these things I must say this is a heck of a game; I have not THAT fun with a videogame probably since some decades (I'm absolutely for real here). It's also true that there are some things that are not optimal and need improvement. Among the negatives, there is the camera movement, the slow pace of the game sometimes when you need to go from A to B, and the bad interfaz mechanics when you need to equip gear, change items from character to character, sell something or look at the items you got, or pick them. This is not a noob-friendly game; aside from the little dungeon tutorial at the start, you will find little or no help at all and you will find lost yourself if you are not used to RPGs games. However, asking in the forums will help you; there will be trolls, true, but overall the community will end up answering your questions and solving some of your starting problems, I'm pretty sure.
But if I take all these things together and put them all in a balance, I have to recommend this game to every player in the world. If you are an oldschool gamer you just can't pass on this. And if you are a new player and you didn't play or didn't even know any of the games other guys are mention, you have to give this one a chance and compare it yourself with the new RPGs. I promise you won't be disappointed.

At the surface level, Antichamber is an interesting and challenging FPP (first person puzzler). Below the surface, Antichamber is an artistic expression of what the video game environment is.
It challenges notions of the regular three-dimensional space that we are naturally accustomed too. It uses unique environment interactions and sharply contrasted designs to put the player outside their comfort zone, invoking what every great FPP should invoke, mental gymnastics. Not the kind that relies on timing or random trial-and-error, but the type that gives you a problem which you know can be solved with the few tools you have, you just have to think about it carefully.
I highly recommend this game. Whether you spend hours inside it, finding every new room and sequence, or whether you just explore for a few hours and give up. You will inevitably come back and find something or somewhere you have never been before, and this will help you with other parts where you are stuck.
The only downside of Antichamber is that it is not exactly linear, and there are ways to find yourself advanced within a puzzle-path without first learning vital environment information that is needed to advance further. Some would argue that this just adds to the challenge, but I argue that there needs to be clear information given about how the world interacts in FPP’s. No puzzle game should hide behind obscure information as part of the challenge, everything should be upfront and taught to the player at the appropriate time.
Antichamber does have mechanisms to do this, and most work well, but inquisitive players can and often do walk off the beaten track which causes them to become confused and disorientated on exactly what is going on, missing out on learning something vital (such as exactly how matter (cubes) operates at various stages of the game).
This is part of the appeal and uniqueness to the game however. I highly recommend that everyone, not just FPP players, experience this game. Yes, there are more refined puzzlers out there (The Talos Principle is the only one I would rate above Antichamber), but none capture the unique and slightly uncomfortable feeling that Antichamber manages to craft so well.

I bought this after playing the demo, and am currently requesting a refund. The demo felt misleading after playing the full game.
I'll actually start this off by saying what I liked or loved about the game, and then I'll move on to why you shouldn't buy it.
Things I liked:
I like that this game doesn't take itself too seriously. It's a "Survival" game, but you don't have to worry about finding food, or much else, rather than just surviving the zombies.
The combat system is very good, most games make it more difficult by giving enemies a ton of health rather than making them harder to fight. This usually just leads to repetitive, long battles, rather than challenging fast paced fights. The zombies are relatively easy to take out in small numbers, especially after reaching a decent level on your skills. Where you hit a zombie actually matters, a hit to the head may kill it instantly depending on your weapon, or a hit to the arm could dismember the arm. A hit to the abdomen will take a chunk out of the zombie, and after a few successive hits to the same region you could chop a zombie in half. The combat is GREAT, unless you're fighting humans (who are all Jedi, apparently. They tend to block almost all attacks, kicks hardly break their guard, various other inhuman reactions..)
The movement system is also very good. They actually took a bunch of input from David Belle (the man credited with creating parkour), and it certainly payed off. I've been doing parkour for several years, and I have to say, it's implemented rather well (compared to assassins creed, per say.) It takes timing, precision, and learning so that you can better understand the best way to go. When you start the game, you're practically at the level of an experienced rock climber. You have the strength and climbing ability, but you aren't very good at the other aspects of parkour. Scaling a flat wall or climbing up onto a ledge is slow. As you level up your agility, you can learn more techniques, like the roll, or the tic tac (jumping off of the face of a wall, to the side or in front of you, while in motion. This includes climbing higher flat walls by taking a step or two on them before grabbing the top). The movement system makes it easier to defend against groups of zombies, because any more than just a few zombies in a group will overwhelm you. Unfortunately, the movement system isn't perfect, and I'll further explain in the "things I didn't like" section.
The crafting system is silly, but practical, and I love it. Many different and efficient ways of offing zombies.
Going out at night entirely changes the game, it's much more difficult and stealth based, and I love it.
There are a multitude of types of zombies.
Things I didn't like:
The story is terrible (really, it is, just youtube "Dying Light Review" and they'll all say it)
However, I wasn't even interested in the story, as a traceur, I just wanted good parkour, exploration, and combat. Unfortunately, while the movement system is good, it's not as perfectly implemented as it was in Mirrors Edge. What you can and can't grab is inconsistent, identical looking ledges may be grabbable in one place and not the next.
Motion blur can't be entirely disabled, and solar flares are blinding (as if you are actually looking through a camera, which would explain the Film Grain setting that was only recently updated so you have the option to remove it) and it really takes a lot from being able to focus on enjoying everything. You can't enjoy what you can't see when it comes to games.
I read that the full game is moddable (prior to purchase, it's why I made the purchase), so I found a mod that would disable motion blur, sun flares, and chromatic aberration, but I later discovered that the developers totally eliminated the possibility of using any mods that adjust game files, and now they're limited to custom maps and things of that nature. Modifying game files in any way will result in a ban, and you won't be able to play it any more.
The "tutorial" takes forever.
Quests are pretty tedious.
Human enemies are practically Jedi.
Very few graphics settings.
"remove motion blur" setting doesn't affect sprinting motion blur.
My thoughts:
Don't purchase this game. It's not worth the $60, and the season pass for DLC (which, if including in the full game, might make it worth the $60) certainly does not make up for the game's poor development enough to warrant a total of $79.99.  Combat is fun and blends well with movement. Can't really adjust visual settings to what you might like due to limited options. This game was quite obviously developed for console, and is a port to PC. Can't use mods, only custom maps, but the developer says it is moddable. This game could have been so much better had it been designed with the PC in mind, rather than the PC being a second thought. I'd been looking forward to this game since long before it's release, but never had the chance to buy it, and I am thoroughly disappointed now that I have bought it. I would really REALLY not recommend this game.

I only played this because it was free for the weekend, since Roguelikes aren't really my thing, but I was pleasantly surprised by Grim Dawn.  I have to say, it looks and plays like a full retail release already, which spells only good things for the game moving forward, as far as I'm concerned.  The controls are responsive, the different specializations seem relatively well thought out (although I'd hope for a bit more variety in the final release), and the environment looks nice, if a bit generic.
There are hints of a story that hopefully become more fleshed out later in the game, or at least later on in the development cycle, but there's enough there to keep you motivated and to keep you interested, which is something I find a lot of Roguelikes struggle with.
Surprisingly, any problems I had with the game itself were extremely minor, and I expect them to be tweaked very quickly.
I would easily recommend Grim Dawn to people who like the genre, and I would probably even recommend it to people that are unfamiliar with it, or on the fence.  It's shaping up to be a great way to spend time, and the development team seems to know what they're doing.  Personally, I'm seriously considering buying it myself, if the price is right.

Background info
XCOM enemy unknown was released on the 9th of October 2012 in America then in the rest of the world 2 days later (11/10/12 ) It's a reimaged version of 1994's UFO Enemy unknown/XCOM UFO Defense. It's a turn based strategy game with blends of strategic base management to break up the battles. when the player first starts playing XCOM it's not a fight to win its a fight to survive as you quickly learn not only has the game not made the enemy your fighting clear (hence the name enemy unknown) but it's given them better weapons, better resources, better tech and the element of surprise to greatly out way the odds in their favor for example the aliens tend to attack 3 places at one time but you can only respond to 1 meaning even if you beat them they've won on two other attacks.
Feel of the game
The experience of XCOM is very refreshing to a lot of players unlike most games where you know you play through the story and win with XCOM you can play for hours and still lose, it's a real channel to complete on just the normal difficulty but despite this it's very enjoyable because you just want to keep fighting to turn the odds in your favor and the game play can become somewhat addictive.
Immersion and presentation
When XCOM starts you are introduced as the commander overseeing the operations of the XCOM project you never actually see yourself which helps immerse the player in being the commander as you don't just see some character your playing as, as the commander it's your job to oversee the base management as well as the battles themselves which include things like, making sure the hanger is always ready with interceptors to defend your satellites and shoot down enemy UFO's, to instruct the research team on what to research, to make sure new rooms and structures are being built below the base, to monitor the panic level of the 16 funding countries and to make sure the barracks is filled with soldiers which act as the planets first and last line of defense. While at first this can be a bit overwhelming that only helps you immerse yourself as the commander as it wouldn't be easy if it was real and at first you will make mistakes will may become costly later down the line but that only makes your want to go back and improve upon your mistakes. Now one of the funniest things in the game is your soldiers as not only do you control them in battle but you can customize them to make them look like the bas♥♥♥♥♥team you want or like most people your friends which helps you immerse yourself in the game as you start to care for theses soldiers that represent your friends, as time goes on your start to make stories for them like when Joe lead his team into a blood bath and only just managed to get out after losing half his team and retreating back to the ship and how Jon sacrificed himself by taking a bullet so his friend could get out of a bad spot and survive or how one of them won the battle without a single scratch but like in real life when they die they die forever they never come back and the only thing you have of them is a name on the wall which adds an element of consequence unlike most over games where you just do it again if your best guy dies that it's just like that and much like in real life sometimes it isn't fair not even close but that's the nature of XCOM a harsh refreshing approach to gaming which makes each choice a difficult one as every decision has its own real consequences . the customization includes changing the name, voice, hair, face, facial hair and a few other things but it should be noted that you can't change the gender, nationality or class for reason.
Story
The story to XCOM is as follows you are the commander of the XCOM project, 16 country's have united to fund the project as the earth first and last line of defense, as the aliens attack you strike back and start to research them you discover more and more about them and mange to capture one leading you to their base while where you discover there commanders which have some form of power allowing them to control your soldiers minds after this you discover more and more while improving your tech and eventually find and kill their commander to make it brief the point here is XCOM's story isn't its strongest point it's a bit simple but it doesn't need to be anything more and it's just enough to be considered good, with added occasional cut scenes  to help inform you of what's happening.
Combat
The combat itself in the game is very addictive in the form of turn based strategy which adds a certain suspense as you have to wait to see what the aliens/ your opponent will do, while in these battles it's up to you to control your soldiers if you mess up it can lead to your soldiers being killed and possibly losing the battle which will cause the 16 countries funding you to panic if they panic to much they drop out of the project if too many lose you lose the game.
Multiplayer
XCOM enemy unknown dose have a multiplayer where to people can play against eachother but this is clearly not where the develops spent most of their time there focus was in the single and they just kind of added a multiplayer which seems kind of half asked but your be enjoying the single player so much that won't even matter.
Conclusion
In conclusion XCOM enemy unknown is a fantastic game that has been present brilliantly with something for everyone even though it is a hard game you can just lower the difficulty to just play the story or practice, the multiplayer is there for anyone just wanting to play their friends, and the fresh approach of real consequence is there as well over all this is a fantastic game and i shall be awarding it a 9 out of 10.

It has been long road, but after few years I can finally say this game is worth its cost. I mean I liked it ever since it was released as early access, but it had almost no content. I still would like to see more maps, certainly more weapons, and maybe even more enemies and game modes and I'm sure all that will happen in time. Original KF was supported throughout its life cycle until very end and I'm sure the sequel receives similar treatment. But now with recent updates we are at the point when I can finally recommend this.
So what can be said about the game itself? It's a first person shooter and zombie survival and enemies come in increasingly difficult waves . If you liked Left 4 Dead, you will most likely enjoy this, too. Zeds (not zombies mind you) come in many forms like regular cannon fodder, invisible one, screamer, mandatory chainsaw killer and the old good Fleshpound with his two giant♥♥♥♥♥♥gaping fists of steel. At the end of each match you face one of the two bosses, other with minigun and rocket launcher and other with two rifles and grenades. Each enemy having their own abilities and AI (both getting upgrades with higher difficulties) makes things hazardous for even well-organized and especially in higher difficulties total chaos cannot be avoided. Just the way I like it.
KF-2 has character progression just like original KF, this time in form of 10 different perks. They all give bonuses for their own weapon types and some stuff like faster running, more ammo or more powerful healing syringes. This time they are not as grindy as before, but getting maximum level in just one of them takes still loads of time, somewhere between 25-35 hours. Maximum level isn't required for 3 first difficulties, though and even hardest difficulty can be realistically beaten by level 20/25. This time you also start with your weakest perk weapon, unlike in original KF where you had to have almost maximum level for that. This addition makes the game way more accessible for new players. Even so, GRINDING IS STILL ESSENTIAL PART OF THIS AND IF YOU DON'T HAVE TIME TO SPARE, I DON'T RECOMMEND THIS. For me it was worth, though as improvements like faster reloading make the experience much more satisfying.
Shooting feels great in this game. I'm not expert in that area because I don't play much first person shooters. But if it feels awesome for even someone who dislikes shooters, that says a thing. Feedback from each shot feels very nice as zeds scream in pain, stumble and lose their limbs or alternatively become even more aggressive if you fail to put them down fast enough. You really know when you're dealing serious damage and when to run in panic.
As a small side note this game also features PvP mode with other party controlling random zeds and other doing what they've done so far as humans. This is easily the most broken part of the game and so far it has never felt even slightly enjoyable. Weaker zeds are useless, even with increased healt and new abilities, but on the other hand stronger Zeds are borderline unstoppable. Humans on the other hand feel quite underpowered and some perks like sharpshooter are plain useless when some player-controlled zeds move fast and jump high. Even the boss round is screwed as control of the boss is given randomly. Nothing about this mode is fun and if you are thinking about purchasing this game based on it, DON'T.
All in all this very good game in its own right and especially in its genre, especially if you got few friends willing to join you and you got too much spare time like I do. You will get exactly what you are buying, nothing less but also not much more. If you haven't touched similar games before, this is one of the best games to get into the genre and if you are fan of zombie shooters, you should defintily try this one out.

So I played through 3 or 4 "loops" before finishing the game, and after 4 hours i've come away with the results. Would I recommended this game? No is the answer i've come away with.
Graphics:

Gameplay:

STORY:

Voice Acting:

Overall:

With this review, I'm going to gloss over the details about what this game is and go straight to the pros and cons.
Pros:
* The turn-based combat is interesting; it's completely necessary to use the environment to your advantage or you will not have a good time. If you're facing a boss creature, there will often be acid or oil barrels near by to use for spells. Different chains can also be had, such as causing an exploding enemy to detonate near acid barrels and other enemies, quickly wiping the field to your advantage. This is probably one of the greatest strengths of the game in my opinion.
* Divinity has an appealing graphical aesthetic. The graphics, while bright and a little pastel, work well for the theme of the game, and shift depending on the environment that you're in. The magic's effects are stunning, and just look great with the rest of the game. The environments were probably the most attractive in appearance, and Larian really nailed it down there. Armors also have different appearances, and I enjoyed watching my character change as her equipment changed.
* Character Customization, while not deep to my standards, is deeper than many other games' customization. Talents are varied and straight out of chargen, you can change your talents, attributes, and starting skills. On my second attempt, I was able to create a rogue with Man of Arms healing abilities, which greatly helped my party. Talents offer pretty significant advantages outweighed by the fact that you only get them every few levels. Pet Pal, for instance, opened up a lot of dialogue that would have otherwise been inaccessible.
* Coop. Very fun multiplayer once you get past its initial issues. I'll go into that later. For pros, the game was practically made for multiplayer in mind. After the first ten minutes, I grabbed a friend and we went off on our journey together. There were moments of frustration as we both learned the game, but it made it fun. Especially when our characters disagreed. I loved the in-character dialogue between us.
* Aesthetic. I'm going to group sound, atmosphere, and music together here into just one category. The music in the background was never obtrusive or annoying. In fact, I actually quite enjoyed some of the music out of the backtrack. Ambient sounds were plentiful, and I did feel immersed in the game world.
Cons:
* User Interface. In none of the reviews I have seen, no one quite nailed down one of the issues I felt was core to disrupting the game. Overall, the User Interface of this game -sucks-. Pressing enter to chat only works about half the time, then you begin typing to your friend only to have combat skip your turn and open a bunch of windows. After entering a message, and sending it, focus remains on the chatbox. The maps lack indicators for points of interest, such as vendors, or what buildings are which. You cannot click on the map and have your character begin walking there (So in essence, you just have to keep watching your character walking places and guide them every step of the way.) The camera is glitchy, the hotbar is not adjustable, the journal is of no help (but they do have a dialogue log), only one character (in multiplayer) can use a vendor at a time, and it always feels like a competition to see who can talk to an NPC first (so they get the dialogue window.) Dialogue doesn't engage both players at the same time. (Also not including misclicks, accidental turn skips, scrolling jankyness, and more that I just can't think of right now.) This really burned the game for me. 2/10
* Lack of Instruction: Normally not a complaint of mine. I love complex games where you have to figure stuff out. Unfortunately, in this case it's one of the bad examples of a game without instruction. Hirelings aren't immediately visible as something you can have. So if you were like me and my friend, we rushed right into post-cyseal-town-zombie combat and were murdered immediately. You -need- a full party, or it just doesn't work. After looking up online, we found our two story NPCs, Madora and Jahan. In addition to a number of other tips the game won't tell you. Such as sleeping in a bed (any bed) will heal you. Or hirelings. Or where you need to go for your first boss (The lighthouse). Or where to find the healer who will sell you res scrolls. (Ahru, Barracks).
* Pacing Issues. When you're playing with other people, the patience for scrolling through walls of text seems to be limited. This is true here, where my friend would often scroll through walls of text and I would try to read it. While I appreciate the varied responses from NPCs, it just felt like there was way too much fluff that I honestly didn't even care about. It had nothing to do with the quest, and just obfuscated where or what I needed to do next. Especially because we just wanted to jump right back into combat to continue the story (so we both could participate). Not to mention, at times, the story feels a bit ADHD. Upon going to the murder scene, I think many people will know what I mean.
* Coop: It's extremely hard to navigate on how to operate the multiplayer aspects of the game. Like the UI con, everything is obfuscated. I'm not sure how my friend managed to invite me into his game during character creation, but he did, and so I was able to at least make my own character. How he did this is likely some black magic of a variety that I cannot fathom. Unfortunately, my progress with him is not saved on my own machine.  This was likely a design choice made by the developers because of a limitation in the engine, but I really just felt that it was incredibly subpar. Including issues with only one player being able to be in a dialogue at once, as well as vendors.
The cons really drag down the pros for me, making this borderline unplayable due to the frustrations wrought by janky bugs and inconsistency. I feel a little sorry for my friend (who kept wandering off in random directions) due to the horrible pacing and one-player-at-a-time focus of the story. If you're looking for the polished game reviews make this title out to be as if it were sliced bread, I would look elsewhere. If you're willing to look past its flaws and give it a try, this game might do you well. If you know nothing about this game, and are just looking for an RPG title to play, I would not recommend Divinity: Original Sin.

Wonderboy III: The Dragon's Trap was a childhood game I grew up on. As a result, I have a TON of nostalgia for this game, and I loved it back then. As a remake, it's expected to meet the standards of the original game, while also offering a bit more to give you more bank for your buck, as most solid remakes give. So does The Dragon's Trap live up to the original?
Story
====
This game is a direct Sequel to Wonderboy in Monster Land. After the journey, Shion confronts the dreaded Meka Dragon and defeats him; however upon striking down the Meka Dragon, he is inflicted with a curse, transforming him into a dragon. Shion must now travel and journey through Monster Land, striking down more dragons to eventually cure himself of this curse to return himself to being human.
Graphics
======
This is a case where the devs went above and beyond. The game features HD, beautiful designed graphics that are amazing to look at and view. They designed so many awesome animations and truly fleshed out how they thought things looked (details like Hawk Man leaping like a bird for his movement is an amazing touch). But, if you feel homesick for the original Sega Master System graphics, don't fear; hitting Right Back Trigger allows you to switch between Retro Graphics and Modern Graphics.
Gameplay
=======
Gameplay is truly perfectly matched with the original. You get 6 different forms (Dragon, Mouse, Piranha, Lion, Hawk, Human), each with their own different gameplay abilities and functions. Each character has strengths and weaknesses, as well as gain benefits from Swords, Armors and Shields found differently, encouraging you to mix and match to find the best combinations. The gameplay is kept simply, with A jumping, X swinging your sword, Y bringing up your weapon inventory, and B casting magic. Left and Right Shoulder buttons cycle through your magic, and the back shoulder buttons shuffle between Retro Sound and Graphics. It's a nice balance of gameplay. There's also 3 difficulty levels, with Normal being the original game, and easy being a toned back version. However, Hard mode offers in a timer, similar to Wonderboy in Monster Land, adding a new layer of challenge to the original adventure, forcing one to have to rush.
Sound
=====
Music is remixed and wonderfully done, all the areas have a distinct remix of the tracks, but once again if you get homesick for the retro sound, you can switch it on. Sound effects are in a similar boat, they all sounds awesome. Downloadable DLC soundtrack is apparently on it's way.
Bonus Content
===========
So of course, being a remake, bonus content is a must have, however to keep the guide spoiler free, I will not be telling you what, where or how this stuff is used. There are 6 bonus dungeons to complete; hidden decently well, and an all powerful super sword for clearing at least 5 of them. There is also a gallery containing a ton of concept art, recording of the music and developers, and additional unlocks. It's truly a wealth of content.
Overall, I can Strongly recommend this game. If you're a fan of 2D Platformers, Wonderboy III: The Dragon's Trap is a must play. It's a Sega Master System Classic given new life.

Antichamber is a complicated puzzler with a strikingly simple facade.
There is none.  Antichamber wears its puzzle game nature on its four dimensional sleeve.  Puzzles exist and the player's own drive to solve them carries the game forward.  Almost every puzzle is preceded by a little moral quip meant to serve as a hint about how you should look at the problem ahead and often every puzzle is succeeded by another little moral as a treat for solving it.
Set in the first person, Antichamber challenges players to pay attentiont to detail, memorize gameplay and puzzle loops, and work on their timing and lateral thinking skills.  Players can both jump and slow their speed to a walk to assist with or overcome certain puzzles.  Players start off in a hub room with a map of the areas they've accessed so far and which they can return to at any time if they become stuck or wish to press their noggin in a different direction.  The puzzle areas themselves are a tangled mass of interconnected corridors, invisible portals, and rooms that exist on a whim.  Many areas branch off from the center and act as a progression of certain puzzle ideas buliding on one another but some will stone wall you until you have the proper tools to proceed.  Those tools come in the form a matter manipulating gun.  Certain cubes in the game can be sucked up and stored within the gun, fired off, led on a trail, and more.  Cubes have different properties depending on how they're used which can allow players to brute force some puzzles while forcing them to be perfect and precise with others.  Personal experience will probably vary, but when mixed with the other environmental puzzle elements and the game's unwillingness to give you anything more than mysical hints; I found the learning curve steep at first, but things smooth at a quicker rate the further into the game I progressed.  Most of the puzzles are highly gratifying to complete and it feels very sneaky to brute force your way through others but you may need to occasionally push yourself through the sense that there is something incredibly illogical the game won't tell you how to do.  The morals act as collectibles, and a massive wall in the hub room collects each one you've found.
Antichamber is absolutely striking in its usage of color and shape.  The grand majority of the game world is constructed with hard ninety degree angles of pure white nothingness with occasional splashes of single tone color.  Color usage gets creative in some areas but the harshness of the constant, never ending pure white can really be a sore spot for your eyes.  Turn down those brightness settings.  Sound design is an anomaly.  Music itself is very, very ambiet, but calming and smooth.  As you traverse the stark white corridors, you'll hear all manner of noises that sound like anything but.  The blowing winds of a sky scraper's roof top.  The dripping confines of a flooded cave.  The grass and birds and bugs of a gentle spring valley.  It all comes together to help keep you in a thinking mood and engages you that extra little bit when you're not currently solving a puzzle.

"The Walking Dead: Michonne" puts you in control of Michonne during her absence within the comic. As we only have experience the Walking dead mostly through Lee and Clementine, it's interesting to see how they show Michonne dealing with her own issues. You're in for a ride for all 3 episodes in this miniseries.
This installment was originally going to be dlc for The Walking Dead: Season 2 (like how 400 Days was), but the story branched enough to have 3 episodes. They handle Michonne's character pretty well and conveys her struggles throughout the miniseries very uniquely that I didn't expect. The first scene brings the character's attention to how Michonne is, transitioning between her visions to what is really happening smoothly (though it somewhat gets confusing in other situations). Each piece of what happened in the beginning on the apocalypse that caused her to have visions gets revealed as you continue. The beginning cinematic is great and a nice touch. The voice acting also does not disappoint.
The mechanics Telltale has is confusing why it has changed, and I can't help but wonder if this would be the same in Season 3. The prompts doesn't seem as responsive anymore, causing you to press or move the stick (not sure how it is on keyboard) multiple times before it registers in quick time events. This is often frusturating as situations requiring fast reflexes can easily be failed if you can't do the action multiple times. The menus had the character changing positions, which is questionable in the decision as you have to wait for the transition to get to the menu you want, but you won't have to go in it as much.
Each time you start, you are met with an option to sign in or create a Telltale Games account so hopefully this does not transfer to Season 3 as you can not tell the game to not ask you again. I'm not sure if logging into a Telltale account causes the problems with holding saves, as others say it's something to do with TTG's cloud and that I didn't encounter this problem.
The story starts out strong, but seems rushed at the end. This could of benefited having more chapters to delve deeper into the story and have more character bonding for the player.
If you like The Walking Dead comics, the character Michonne, or TellTale games, this is a nice edition.

What makes Antichamber so cool is how it actually is 100% logically consistent: the main puzzle is to figure out how the world works, and it feels incredibly rewarding to connect the pieces and figure out how to get past some obstacle you saw several hours ago. There's often several ways to solve a puzzle, with harder puzzles rewarding you with faster progression (the game can be beat in less than 10 minutes using some advanced tricks), and on top of that there's tons of secret puzzles that aren't shown on the map, rewarding you with interesting behind-the-scenes knowledge if you can solve them... which is a big if.
Also, having played both, I've had more fun playing Antichamber than The Witness, and would recommend Antichamber as the superior game.

- Great gameplay : fast-paced combat with many visual effects, freeze/stun/knockdown, furnitures to demolish
- optional rotatable camera : always fight from the most optimal angle

- Additional rogue-like dungeons :  special challenge dungeons (require rare crafted key) where enemy levels increase as you progress and player can't teleport. Win or die.
- Dynamic weather : - The world is brought to life with region-specific climates and a variety of weather effects. A sunny day can cloud over with mild rain showers that builds into a booming thunderstorm. Variable wind gusts blow grass and affect objects like windmills.
- Crafting system  : with 250 recipes to learn (weapons/armors/jewels/potions), combining/salvaging components, augments
- Respec system : cancel your skills allocation points to create new build based on same mastery.
This is one best game ever. You can buy it, closed eyes, even in beta or at full price. You'll don't regret it.

I only played this because it was free for the weekend, since Roguelikes aren't really my thing, but I was pleasantly surprised by Grim Dawn.  I have to say, it looks and plays like a full retail release already, which spells only good things for the game moving forward, as far as I'm concerned.  The controls are responsive, the different specializations seem relatively well thought out (although I'd hope for a bit more variety in the final release), and the environment looks nice, if a bit generic.
There are hints of a story that hopefully become more fleshed out later in the game, or at least later on in the development cycle, but there's enough there to keep you motivated and to keep you interested, which is something I find a lot of Roguelikes struggle with.
Surprisingly, any problems I had with the game itself were extremely minor, and I expect them to be tweaked very quickly.
I would easily recommend Grim Dawn to people who like the genre, and I would probably even recommend it to people that are unfamiliar with it, or on the fence.  It's shaping up to be a great way to spend time, and the development team seems to know what they're doing.  Personally, I'm seriously considering buying it myself, if the price is right.

The game is really awesome. It's really in line with stuff like Fallout and Baldur's Gate. Starts out feeling a bit overwhelming, especially if you're playing single player. You will be controlling both main characters, and it drops you in a fairly large city with lots of quests to do, npcs to talk to,♥♥♥♥♥♥to figure out, and deadly monsters outside  4 of the 6 town gates. But stick it through the first few hours of figuring everything out, pretty much like any game like this, and you'll realize how  well done and fun to play it is. I'm not even very far, from what I understand it gets kind of easy towards the end, and there are 4 very detailed areas which yield around 80 hours of playtime for most people. But it really leaves people wanting more. Fortunately the modding support may be promising and we could end up getting whole mini campaigns created for it or maybe some other cool stuff.
Co-op feels more satisfying but at the same time it's not without it's small problems. Companions can only be controlled by the host currently, that should be fixed soon I hope. Dialogue is hard to follow when the other player is engaging in it, hopefully they fix that too. Companions seem pretty cool but apparently much of the companion content was cut and they will be releasing new, more detailed companions in a future update in a few months.
Either way though, single or 2 player, now or later, with or without launch day flaws, the game is definitely an instant classic and I would definitely recommend getting it. It will only get better with time but this is one game that I can say with full confidence is worth the full price, and many people would probably play through a few times with different styles of characters. I'll probably play through once now, once when the devs makes all their updates, and then when mods come out I'll play again with some cool mods.

Stories the Path of Destinies is everything a CYOA (Chose your own adventure) fan could ever want.  It's what Telltale games "claim" to be.  A game where your ever choice DOES matter and leads you to a different ending.  And unlike Telltale games the creators of this game actually bothered to put in a freaking combat system, level design, and level up system.  Now granted the combat, level design and level up system is just ok, and if you're like me and trying to get all 24 endings it will start to feel old/repetivite to you by the end.  Made worse by the fact the game only has roughly 6 different levels in it.  However if you're only looking for the true ending you should be fine.
Still I appericate the fact the creators went to the effort of including these things unlike some other lazy organizations *Cough*  Telltale *Cough*.  But obviously the true selling point of this game to you is going to be it's writing.  This is through and through a CYOA game.  If you go into this looking for darksouls you're going to be disappointed.  But if you're going in looking for a TRUE CYOA game where more than just the last 2 choices you make in the game matter, where the story itself changes upon every choice (from the first, middle and third) you're going to have a great time!  The writing and dialgoue is great and 90 percent of the 24 endings are all completely different from each other.  It really does make me wonder what this studio could do if they had the funding of someone like Telltale.
Lastly I do have to point out that this game does suffer from several bugs in it.  While nothing ground breaking or that you have to work around, they happen enough that it does need to be mention.

WHAT KIND OF GAME IS IT?
Civ 5 is a turn-based strategy game, often referred to as in the "4X" genre (eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate). You play a ruler of a birthing nation. From inception, you decide where to explore, what technologies to research, and what kinds of things to add to your cities and armies. Military units can explore the map, uncovering areas previously hidden by the fog of war. Other nations are doing the same and will meet you in the game and either strike up friendships or be aggressive towards you. There is a diplomatic element to the game as well.
Winning can come about five different ways: Domination (wipe out all other players), Science (launching a space ship), Cultural (filling out five trees of social policies and completing the Utopia Project), Diplomatic (winning a vote in the UN), and Time (highest score by end of time period).
IS THE STORY GOOD?
There is no story, per se. This is the story of a nation that you control. Outside of the historical lore at the game loading screen, there isn't much in the way of any narrative.
HOW DOES IT LOOK/SOUND?
The main graphics are nice, blending in stylized maps and tokens with pleasant animations. The ambient noises and narration are some of the best parts of the audio aspects of the game.
BIG QUESTION, IS IT FUN?
This game series is famous for the saying "just one more click". I have burnt the midnight oil trying to end my game only to say those exact things. Once I get my troops set up and hit the 'turn over' button, the computer starts playing all of the enemy moves and as the drums signify that it's your turn once more, it is extremely hard to not make any moves and simply go to bed.
SO WHAT'S MY RATING?
Solid 10/10

Every single developer out there considering remaking an old classic game, take note:
This is how you do it. This is how you freaking remake an awesome game like this.
It is literally a 1:1 remake, with modern graphics, and music, and some enhanced menu interfaces. Thats it, nothing else changed. The feeling, the gameplay, the handling, everything else is 100% the same as the original.
Frequently, us older gamers remember classics from when were younger with what can be termed, rose-tinted glasses. I loved this game as a kid. However, I once tried to go back and play an emulated version of it, and found myself thinking "Were the graphics always like this? I remember them being better..." Of course, they were always like that, and, at the time of release, they were top notch. However, these days, we expect a lot more, and old classics like WBIII just don't hold up, graphics wise. Which is a shame, because the gameplay is what made these games great, but the dated graphics are what prevent new players from even trying them. No more.
This remake literally makes the rose-tinted glasses real. The graphics are amazing, the updated sound, amazing, but the gameplay, the classic gameplay that made this game great. Did. Not. Change. A. Bit.
Good on you Lizardcube, you've done this older gamer right. If you decide to just keep remaking old, classic games like this from here on out, and if you keep to this level of quality, I will buy every single one.

I have a lot of love and nostalgia for the original, even having played it on an emulator only a couple of years ago, so it would have been hard, in my opinion, to really do the game justice if anyone ever remade it... but remake it they did and oh boy, did they do it justice. In fact, I think they even improved on the game a lot.
The graphics are wonderful with the hand-drawn animations by Ben Fiquet really adding so much value and enjoyment as you play. Your animal forms, the dragon bosses, and all the enemy creatures are all a joy to behold. The backgrounds and even foregrounds provide you with a sense of a world that is populated and rich with lore. It's probably one of the biggest improvements on the original game that I can point to.
The musical score of the old melodies composed by Shinichi Sakamoto and newly arranged by Michael Geyre are SO good. I loved the old tunes, they're some of my favorite 8-bit pieces, but the new music is, again, so rich, so lovingly made, that it just adds to the experience and tenfolds your enjoyment.
As an aside, it's always fun to be able to see the old graphics and hear the old music with the press of a button. It really makes for a wonderful trip down memory lane.
Mechanically they didn't much touch the game. Combat still requires skill, patience, zeal, and practice. The different animal forms all have their abilities, special skills, and optimal weapon, shield, and armor load-outs. The enemies all have patterns that you need to remember and anticipate. The world is littered with secret doors and events for you to explore. Frankly, the game was already pretty tight so there wasn't much to improve there (though they did, here and there, with new challenges, smoother mechanics, and a slightly more easy going attitude).
All in all, it's both a blast from the past and a really great new game. I give it a 13 outta 10 and no mistake.

This was the first game i played and finished since i've upgraded my pc. Zombies, towers, palm trees... ugh.
I have to say that despite finishing everything single side quest and finding most of the statues and flags (can't be bothered to watch videos and find all of them) i can't say that i was all that impressed or that i had a lot of fun. It was mostly OCD that kept me going from mission to mission to a pitiful QTE finale.
The simple fact is - this game is exactly like Far Cry 3 and Assassins Creed combined. You climb up the towers, you jump down using either trash piles (say hi to hay) or zip lines (no puns here, too boring). You clear "safe zones", you run fast, you crawl up, you swim, you kill people and zombies, you die, you respawn, rinse and repeat.
At some point i was actually almost convinced i was playing some advanced mod to Far Cry 3 - same palm trees, same slums, same water, same everything sans animals and plus zombies. Honestly - im just tired of this♥♥♥♥♥♥ I think i've climbed enough towers in these sort of games back in Assassins Creed 2 and Far Cry 3 just cemented the feeling of hating to do that over and over and over and yet over again.
I disliked same models for quest npc's. I disliked having to do Bozak's stadium several times to get insanely overpowered bow with explosive arrows (which are lacking sounds by the way). I disliked "survivor sense" (At this point it's easier just to show everything on minimap rather than create some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t vision mode for Batman/Desmond/Jason Brody/Kyle Crane). I disliked obligatory second rate characters dying (why would i care about some teen and his sister if i don't know anything about them besides them being stubborn and stupid?). I disliked mandatory and annoying lockpicking minigame every other minute. I very much enjoyed music and some of the side quests but thats about it.
Overall - i was not impressed. I've chewed through this game and spit it out and i have no desire to come back or play as a hunter. Its just a mediocre mishmash of an ideas from different games which are in turn mediocre mishmash copies of each other.

Let me start out by saying I am a newcomer to games like this. I haven't played the old cRPG games, I haven't explored the roots of this game, and I am generally speaking, a newcomer to this type of game unless you count Torchlight but nobody does.
Knowing that, my opinion is based solely on the merits of this game and not because I hold some sort of affection for its genre. Also, I have only scratched the surface of this game with a mere 10 hours played. This is my initial reaction.
Lets start with pros and cons shall we?
Cons:
-No hand holding at all (can be good or bad)
-Crafting isn't explained at first making it obtruse as to how to go about making stuff
-This game is difficult
-Story isn't spectacular
-Modding support and custom campaigns is currently broken. Should be fixed soon
Pros:
-Fantastic graphics. Zooming in is reminicest of looking at SimCity (The new one) making everything feel like a toy box
-Combat is tight, fun, and hard. Like I said, no hand holding. You gotta figure stuff out for yourself and that includes tactics. That said, enemy AI is good as they avoid dangers, use spells, elements, potions, rely on allies, etc making for every enemy encounter to be tense.
-No hand holding at all. I put this in pros as well because this game treats you like a problem solving individual not a baby who needs to be told how to do 1+1
-Easy to Role-Play. From the start, you control two characters including their interaction with each other. Your characters can disagree over a key decision.
-You can kill everybody in the game and still find a way to complete the main quest
-Freedom. As statedd, you can kill anyone, steal whatever isn't nailed down, find clever ways around obstacles, or do whatever you feel like doing. Tired of playing by the rules? This game encourages you to break them.
-Decent writing for the most part with several times it truly shines.
Overall a polished testament to a successful kickstarter and early access period.
Verdict - 9/10
Still some kinks to work out, I wish there was a way to have items show up on screen at all times instead of holding alt to find that mysterious key that is hiding. The hand holding thing is usually for the better but can make quests frustrating when you don't know where to go or who to talk to. Patience is a must if you want to play this game.
But it offers a ton of content, fun, tense combat, hilarious encounters, and lots of replayabillity. I would reccomend this game to any RPG lover or Turn-Based Tactical Combat lover.
Oh and you can talk to animals.

While I have only played 13 hours of Divinity: Original Sin, I have played enough to tell you that you need to play it. Why, you ask?
Because games are not made like this anymore.  Divinity: Original Sin harkens back to the great CRPGs of the 1990s in style, writing, and gameplay mechanics. The game plays like Baldur's Gate had a sultry affair with Ultima VII and produced a glorious hammer wielding child.
Here's a checklist:
- Very well written dialogue with laugh out loud humor and wit? Check!
- Turn based, tactical combat with real depth and strategy? Check!
- No god damned hand-holding every step of the way, treating you like a baby? Check!
- INTERESTING quests that make you actually use your brain to figure out how to progress? Check!
- Lovingly crafted artwork and graphics that work very well with the setting? Check!
- Up to 4 characters in your party? Check!
- Ability to role play diaglogue between people in your party, which includes having arguments that affect stats on your character? (Think paragon/renegade stuff from Mass Effect, except in this game it actually increases/decreases an array of stats) Check!
- Crafting that is incredibly practical; need a spear? Grab a stick and a dagger or knife and voila! Check!
The game is as close to a pen and paper RPG as I've ever played. I could go on for days about this game, but you have to try it. Give Larian $40, they surely deserve it. Again, I've only played 13 hours, but they have been incredily engrossing and enjoyable. I cannot wait to continue delving deeper into this game!

Me and my buddy were roleplaying some coop. We were investigating a murder which led us to the graveyard. After spontaneously digging up some graves looking for loot, we stumbled upon a secret cavern. We entered the cavern with big round eyes searching for hidden treasure. The cavern was a large hallway which led to an open cavern with a flowing stream. Standing between us and the winding stream was a hunchback. I approached boldy and shouted my salutations. Within a few feet of the figure, he burst into flames. He then looked up at me, his skeletal grin and empty sockets mocking me. Surprised i stumbled backwards. My partner shouted something incoherent and cast teleportation on the skeleton freak. The freak appeared several yards away near the top of the cavern before falling unceremoniously back to the ground. By the time he hit the ground i was already invisible. I creeped over to him as he stood back up. I then noticed a large flaming mechanism in his hand. I ignored this and slipped behind him. I then slid my daggers into his fiery back with a shout of fury. The skeletons head twisted completely around and grinned at me. I let out a shriek as my daggers melted and fire spread up my arms. The fire spread to my torso before i felt the heat. I couldn't help myelf, i screamed bloody murder as i ran in the opposite direction of the stream. I made it nearly a dozen feet before i crumpled to the ground and groaned as i felt my penultimate sigh leave my body as a small puff of steam. My partner screamed in agony as she saw me die. In a manner of rage she charged forward and cast spells at the fiery figure. She took a step out into the clearing and her eyes widened as several skeleton hands forced themselves out of the earth. Soon followed by the bodies of the undead. She stood surrounded by these grinning figures as the fiery figure slowly stalked closer to her. In a rage unrivaled by heroes of old she swung daggers and slung spells untill all were bonepiles except for the fiery abomination. Still grinning, it lifted the mechanism and pointed it at her. A fiery stream protruded from it and she was momentarily engulfed, using her quick wit she throws herself to the ground and rolls. As she stands back up with scraps of burnt clothing remaining, she notices she dropped her pack. From it protrudes a scroll. "The resurection scroll we knicked from the wizard!" She leaps forward and grabs it, still lying on the ground as she recites the incantation. She is already on her feet by the time I am lifted off the ground by some invisible force. My burns diseappear and i land on my feet running toward the flaming skeleton. He aims his mechanism and i slide across the ground underneath him as the flames shoot above me. At the same time my partner is knocking a water arrow and shoots it. It strikes the skeleton in the face, water engulfing it. Steam rises as i do, and i plunge what is left of my daggers into its back. I twist the handles and pull out rapidly, the skeleton lets out a cry and explodes in an inferno. I am disintegrated instantly and my partner's skin melts from the extreme heat. As she slumps to her knees, she hears a faint sound from the stream. The water is gurgling, but it almost sounds like a laugh. She lands on her side and wonders if things would have been different if she had only married the fishmonger her mother was so keen on. Oh, why did she have to live a life of adventure? 11/10

Overall, I think this is a wonderful game.
+ The visuals are beautiful.
+ The storytelling is excellent.
+ The characters are fun.

Now, that being said, I think there are some bugs/glitches and other things that make a playthrough a little annoying.

+ After a certain amount of playtime the Nexus (Chapter 3) will have a section where the platforms are invisible.

+ But my biggest complaint came from having to play the game 25 times and not being able to skip all the cutscenes. You can skip up until the narrator has to explain the choices, and by the 5th time, you have an idea what the choices are. Final rating - 8.5/10

Again, I would like to have more than two options to review a game. TWD:M is neither a recommendation nor should you avoid it at all costs. It's basically TWD with new characters (or old ones, depending on your point of view) and supposedly it's tied into TWD Season 3 from Telltale. At least that's what I heard.
The only sad thing is that this "mini series" only consists of 3 episodes. Each one takes about 1 to 1.5 hours. Apart from following the rather thin story line there isn't really anything else to do. There's no conversations you can have or avoid, there are no "puzzles", no real exploration, there are barely any decisions to make and all of those don't have an impact on the story, since you will only get to the same result anyway. This is the classic Telltale formula...and issue. It's getting a bit stale. If you're just looking for a short little story, TWD:M delivers, but not much else.
The story is ok, but not exceptional. The characters apart from Michonne are bland. There's an optimist guy, a sadist, more shallow bad guys and a family as well as your "crew" you don't really care about. With more time maybe they could have fleshed these guys out a bit more. As it stands, it's not remotely worth the asking price in my opinion. At least not compared to Season 1 and 2, which cost just a few bucks more, but even they offer more gameplay. The graphics engine is still the same one and looks just as bad and clunky. It's getting tiring.
Skip this one or wait for a sale. There's no reason to even play through it again and make different choices.

To put it bluntly: YES, you should buy this game.
Wonder Boy III: The Dragon's Trap was one of those cult classics for the Sega Master System (as well as Game Gear and some other systems) that far, FAR too few people have had the privilege of playing; and those that did consider it an absolute masterpiece. So, when it was announced that it was getting a full-on remake, I was both excited and INCREDIBLY nervous. It's so hard to capture the spirit of the classic while making it accessable to a brand new generation decades later. But the crew behind this really knew exactly what they were doing and made this port live up to and even exceed the original in many ways.
For those of you that don't know anything about this title, I'll do my best to offer a quick primer. In the story of the game, you are Wonder Boy (or Wonder Girl if you prefer in this version), who is confronting a powerful dragon in its lair. Little do you know that the dragon has the ability to curse people, and upon defeating him, you find yourself transformed into a fire-breathing lizard person and fleeing for your life as the castle crumbles around you. What takes place after is a series of misadventures involving battling new dragons and using their "curses" to your advantage as you take new forms to solve puzzles in what could only be described as one of the early "proto" Metroidvania titles.
While the visual appearance of the original was absolutely astonishing and genuinely could be mistaken for 16-bit instead of 8, the hand-drawn and delicately crafted animation cells of the original bring the visual presentation not only to the modern age, but in some ways, further. Not since Dust: An Elysian Tale have I seen to much love and effort put into the highly crisp and fluid frame-by-frame animations. The backgrounds are gorgeous and incredibly deep, the style of the characters and enemies is incredibly anarchic and has a sort of light-hearted humor about it, while still feeling powerfully dynamic and all those other words from the thesaurus. In a nutshell, it really, REALLY is good.
But what if you haven't played the original and want to see what it looked like (for the most part)? Not a problem! With literally the push of a single button you can alternate between the updated animation and the original 8-bit graphics on the fly! No menuing or any of that nonsense; one click, you're there. The appearance is not EXACTLY the same (as there were slight GUI changes), but the tileset is pretty much identical.
I feel as though the graphical upgrade of the new version does more than simply give the game an aesthetic facelift; it improves the gameplay itself by giving monsters better "tells" for all of their attacks. Even though I'm a fan of old-school difficulty, there are aspects of the original did not age well; and monster attacks having no warning is one of them. With the newer graphics you're given a more reasonable chance to react to new challenges than in the original. Definitely a huge improvement. And even if you'd prefer not to, you still have the OPTION of playing old style if you prefer. And more options are almost ALWAYS a good thing.
The same applies to the soundtrack. With the push of the button, you can switch between the energetic chiptunes of the SMS original and the updated, remastered versions of the songs and sound effects; independently of the graphical settings. I find that I appreciated the two options being independent of one another because while the new graphics are a slam dunk in my opinion, I feel that the original soundtrack had a little more energy to it and was more enjoyable for me overall. This isn't to say that the new soundtrack is poor by ANY means! Rather, it just felt a little more plodding and lax than an exciting adventure really should have.
That being said, the fact that you have the option between the two for graphics AND sound, mean that this game does that much more to cater to more people's individual tastes. And the ease in which you can switch means you can fine-tune things just how much you want!
I have one very minor complaint about the graphics, though. Or rather, simply just the addition in general. If you choose to play as Wonder Girl rather than Wonder Boy, only the human forms look different. Since you're almost never going to BE human in the game apart from the beginning, I feel this aspect was kind of a pointless addition. I think it would have been neat to have just a few slight visual differences between the animal genders, like a different color or eyelashes or something. Nothing major; just something to make the different character feel more unique.
The graphical presentation and GUI weren't the only gameplay improvements this game saw. As I said, not every aspect of the original title was perfect. And to me the absolute WORST thing in the old game was the arbitrary and stupid charisma system; where you could only buy certain items if you had enough charisma. And worse, different forms had different base charisma. You would think that would have been the case to keep you from buying the items too early, but no! The second animal form you receive also has the second-highest charisma. And you can grind for charisma anyway, so there was ultimately no point to it other than to give the middle finger to the lizard-man form.
Well, I'm pleased to say that ALL of that nonsense has been done away with (for the most part). Now, shopkeepers will sell indescriminately and you don't have to grind for what is essentially two different forms of currency at once. Charisma IS still technically in the game, but it's only for a single thing, as far as I can tell. I can easily accept that.
Other improvements include quick-switch between subweapons, slightly better clues for proceeding, and a save feature over the old password system. (Don't fret! If you still want to USE your old passwords; they thought of that, too!)
But ultimately it comes down to this: LOVE was put into this remake. It was a masterpiece then and it's even more of one now. They did exactly what it took to dust off the (admittedly few) cobwebs and poorly-aged aspects of the original while keeping 100% true to that title's vision. While the game isn't particularly long, it also doesn't overstay its welcome and it's got enough material packed in to give a memorable adventure to old and new gamers alike!
