Knights of Pen and Paper +1 is a “roleplaying game”, but in truth it has very little roleplaying in it; while this is common to many “RPGs,” this game takes it to an all-new level. The conceit behind the game is that you are sitting at a table with your game master with a group of friends, and that you are going through a campaign. The players are indeed all seated around a table, with the game master on the far side of the table dictating what is going on. It is a very clever idea, but unfortunately the game fails to execute on it at all; instead, the game is a pure hack-and-slash fest which tries to spice things up with humor and gaming references but falls flat because, quite frankly, everyone sitting around a table has already not only made all of these references, but done it better. The plot is every bad game of D&D you've ever played, every unoriginal campaign rolled into one, and it is played straight - sure, one could argue that it is almost comically bad, but it is painfully bad, like Batman and Robin, rather than camp.
As the gameplay itself is thoroughly hack and slash, purely about cutting your way through an extremely large number of monsters using extremely simplistic turn-based combat reminiscent of many JRPGs, with no real coherent or interesting story to speak of, there is little to recommend this game as anything but a time waster, and even there, you can do far better. There's nothing that this game doesn't show you in the first hour, and there's nothing in that first hour worth taking. While the basic underlying idea of having a bunch of players playing a roleplaying game is an interesting one, this game is a total failure at it. Maybe someday, someone will take this idea and do something good with it, but this is not that game.

So, first of all, I love this game. It's got some BS to it, mostly on the higher difficulties, and there are some irritating bugs you're going to have to deal with (especially if you get the expansion, Enemy Within, which I highly recommend in spite of it's flaws). Almost everything depends on the RNG (with options to have even more things influenced by the RNG), so you have to plan for things to go horribly wrong pretty much all the time. I normally despise randomness in gaming, since it seems to often mean that your run depends entirely on the computer, rather than on your skill. But XCOM allows for careful planning, both on and off the battlefield, to allow you to take the advantage back even if the RNG turns against you.
And it's a turn-based strategy game. I love turn-based strategy games, and this is pretty much top-tier as far as those are concerned. If you don't like turn-based games, you'll probably hate XCOM. If you like turn-based strategy, then I highly recommend XCOM.
Seriously, just buy it and give it a try, because my biggest problem with this game is that they haven't made a sequel yet.

A tactical masterpiece, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a challenging, turned-based, and tiled strategy game.
It's 2015 and the aliens has invaded Earth. It's your job as the commander of the XCOM forces to stop the aliens, and figure out their motives. Research alien technology and improve your own equipment to gain an edge in battle. This is no easy task, especially on harder difficulties.
While the base game is great by itself, its DLCs (mainly XCOM: Enemy Within), adds much more content to the game. With options to change each play-through (ex. Soldiers start with differing stats and different base locations), XCOM has great replay value.
BE WARNED. XCOM will drain your life away and cause extremely depressing moments. The addictive nature of XCOM will cause you to do mission after mission, even when you know you should stop. When your troops die, especially when you take the time to customize them, you will be overcome with grief (unless you're alienfied to the point where your emotions are dead, then GTFO my planet or I'm going to eradicate you, fool).
I beg you, no, I demand you, PLAY THIS GAME. If you're a strategy freak, welcome, you're at heaven. If strategy isn't your thing, the thrill of real-time combat is still present. There's no excuse to not play XCOM, unless you're poor, then RIP In Peace.

An absolute masterpiece released by Valve. Half-Lfie 2, along with its episodes, goes down as my #1 favourite game released.
Despite being many years old, Half-Life 2 still manages to accomplish what many modern titles lack; an interesting story told from a unique perspective and a variety of different mechanics being introduced to you. I mean, those are just two of the many things this game accomplishes. The sound, characters, architecture... There's a lot this game does well.
Each chapter in the game always brings something new to the table which keeps gameplay fresh and engaging. While the first chapter plays out a lot like a "normal" shooter, the next chapter brings in an airboat, allowing you to drive through the areas while avoiding enemies or taking them out in unique ways. Then while in the same chapter, your airboat is given an awesome machine gun which allows you to mow down enemies with ease. The third chapter then introduces a weapon unique to the Half-Life series and throws you into a playground to test it out. The trend of seamlessly introducing unique mechanics to the player works fantastically, keeping the game fresh at every turn.
The graphics still hold up today despite being an old game. Your stroll through Ravenholm isn't going to look like trash, it's going to look good and terrifying. Actually, atmosphere is something this game does very well. My first time in Ravenholm generated a genuine fear of the place. It took me pretty long just to get out of there because I was frightened of the place. This is all because Valve managed to create a great atmosphere for Ravenholm, as well as every other location in the game.
Overall, the game is absolutely amazing. The amount of time Valve put into this game paid off in every way. Still, some of the scrapped ideas they had for the game sounded really cool. I'd love to see a game using those ideas. Half-Life 2 was pretty much a completely different game during development, which is pretty cool!

I played this game years after it released because I heard it was fantastic.  Well, the reviewers weren't lying.  It's an excellent sequel to the original Half Life.
It's difficult to know where to begin because there are so many great things I could write about this game. I love how it combines gameplay and storytelling in a seamless way.  It has perhaps the most perfect pacing I've ever seen in a game and I became so engrossed with it that I refused to sleep until I had seen the end.
I love the dystopian atmosphere and the menacing presence of the Combine Citadel and how it literally eats away human civilization.  I love the various enemies you fight and how they are inspired by classic sci-fi monsters such as the Alien Facehugger, the bugs from Starship Troopers, and the Tripods from War of the Worlds.  My favorite part has to be Ravenholm because it managed to disturb me more than most horror games that I've played.  If only the creators of the Dead Space series had studied this level!
The gameplay is also tremendously fun.  Vehicle combat can be hit or miss in some games but in this one they are very easy to use and help your character a great deal. Each level offers an interesting challenge that distiniguishes it from others.  For example, one level teaches you how to use creatures to attack enemies while you run from cover to cover avoiding heavy fire, while another forces you to use objects in the environment as weapons because ammo is scarce.  Usually there is at least one level that's a boring slog in FPS games but I enjoyed all of the ones in Half-Life 2.
Weapon variety and utility can make or break an FPS, but this game does not disappoint. While I enjoyed all of the weapons, the Gravity Gun is one of my all-time favorites for an FPS, ranking up there with the Wraithverge from Hexen (an awesome-looking cross that shoots four wraiths that can traverse through walls to tear apart your enemies).

Half-Life 2 improves upon the original in every way except for level design.  Older FPS games like the original Half-Life have complex levels that offer multiple paths to explore.  Quake is especially known for its amazing level design, which is why its deathmatch community remained strong for many years.  Half-Life 2 is very linear by comparison, and though that assists with story pacing, it reduces the game's replay value.  Even so, I loved this game so much that I played it twice and still had a blast during my second run.
If you have never played this game I highly recommend it.  Yes, the graphics are dated compared to today's games, but Half-Life 2 is so well-crafted that you will enjoy it regardless.

Absolutely amazing. From the creators of the Dead Island franchise, Techland parts ways with Deep Silver and team up with Warner Bros. The end result is truly the best zombie survivor game I have ever played. Fans of the original Dead Island and Riptide will notice similarities with some of the crafting, weapons and looting, but this is by no means a remaster of the original title.
The game boasts the best movement I have experienced in any modern day FPS. (I use the term FPS very loosely, firing weapons in the game draws unwanted attention). The parkour element brings an exilarating angle on exploration and evasion, and is incorporated into the game seamlessly. For me this was a huge selling point, the fact that it also contains multitudes of psycotic zombies is just a bonus!
The game itself is stunningly beautiful, the city just begs to be explored extensively. City design and layout is done well, so you can take full advantage of a fun playground to test your parkour skills on. You are also rewarded for creative thinking, in terms of combat and movement.
Okay, now a quick word on the zombies! With a plethora of titles on a very tired and clichéd genre, zombie games can find it hard to stand out from the mundane and mediocre. This title stands shoulders above the rest. In most zombie games, I am never really scared of dying, and just go about business as usual...hacking, slashing and shooting. Not so with Dying Light.
This was the only zombie game that was terrifying for me. Yes, you still get the slow, mindless shamblers in large numbers, plus a variety of other undead denizens. But the game transforms like some horrid nightmare, showing you it's true form, as soon as that sun sinks below the horizon. That is when the zombies show their unabated strength, speed and cunning as they run, jump and climb whilst alerting others to your presence. I advise doing as much as you can during the day when they are weakened by the sun. Going out at night does have its rewards, but at great risk.
It is also best to play this game solo for the first play-through for a solid horror experience.
Then team up with friends, as the terror level significatly drops when you have a buddy or two watching your back. The great thing is you not only get the blood racing from zombie encounters, you also have numerous heart-in-throat moments with the climbs and jumps you perform.
I highly recommend this game for any zombie or parkour lover. So let the heads and limbs fly, may your hands always find that precarious ledge...and venture forth into the night if you dare!

Dying Light is everything that the Dead Island games should have been in the first place.  Just goes to show that the developers are only doing what they're told really.  Dead Island was published under Deep Silver and Dying Light was published under Warner Bros.
Dying Light is a very open-world zombie game.  The size and scope of the city they drop you in is enormous, especially considering there is no fast-travel or vehicles, you're on foot for this game friends.  I really liked that they kept fast travel and vehicles out of this game, it really would have ruined it, and you can certainly tell they catered the game to people who were going to explore and spend a lot of time roaming around the city, going through the houses and finding all the crafting items they can.
The crafting system in this game is nearly exactly the same as Dead Island, which isn't bad, there are few complaints there from me.
The combat system is nice, but has a few flaws.  The only major one is that when a zombie is rushing you to grab and bite you, you are forced into a button-mashing sequence to get the zombie off, regardless of what you were doing when it lunged at you (you can be crouched, sliding, etc...).  Which gets quite frustrating.  Otherwise, the combat of the game was nicely done really.
The movement mechanics are exactly what they need to be for a parkour game such as this.  You are easily able to run around the rooftops and slide under obstacles, kicking zombies along the way.  You have realistic jumping and running capabilities, and there isn't anything in the game that is too outlandish regarding the way you run, jump and generally get around Harran.
The story of this game is really good.  It gets you invested in the characters and gets you to actually want to play the missions and learn how it all ends.  But this is where I'll add that the ending is bittersweet (as the achievement is titled).  It doesn't go back and revisit some of the characters, or have much closure, and really leaves a nice open gap for DLC or a sequel to fill, which is fine, as long as they fill it eventually.
The graphics are great, but even modern hardware in the mid-end desktop spectrum may have a little trouble with this on high quality, or even medium.  The particle effects (smoke, fire, toxic gas effects, flies and so on) cause some very noticeable frame drops, even on a i5-4690K and a GTX 960 4GB.
The variety in the types of zombies is really nice and very well thought out.  There is the cliched types though.  The normal zombies, the running/fast zombies, the big, hefty zombies, the ones that spit nasty crap at you, the ones that are elusive and mutated, the crazy scary ones that only come out at night and the giant big one that runs you over and throws cars.
I will say though, there are challenges in this game, and most of them were poorly planned and executed and provide for a very annoying time trying to complete.  There is no way to restart the challenge once in it except for dying, and you have to hear the dialog before the challenge every time you restart.  Not to mention some of them are ridiculously difficult for some reason.
There are also a TON of easter eggs to experience, though, from all sorts of references, which I found to be a lot of fun to find.
Overall though, this is a very well developed game, and I thoroughly enjoyed every minute of playing it to completion, and look forward to any kind of continuation of the story.  I feel no regret in giving this game a 9/10.

This is an interesting example of a game made with very limited resources, and still, through clever management of them, give the player a reason to play it over and over again, not running out of things to discover.
At its core, it's a pretty action-RPG with cartoonish graphics, vivid colors and a narrator commenting your action, kind of a poor person's Bastion. The content is very limited: there are 10 levels (you visit half of them in every playthrough), 5 types of enemies to fight (no bosses!), 3 types of traps to avoid. Upgrades include 4 swords, each with one magic spell attached to it (and one type of door it could open), 7 gems and lots of skills most of which give you just a numerical bonus: more damage, more health, more dashes. You can unlock every enemy, sword and gem in 3 hours of gameplay, after which every battle becomes the same (and almost impossible to lose). You can beat the whole game in 6 hours. So why did I spend 20 hours with it?
I'm a sucker for storytelling and stories about storytelling. And I loved how this game's plot was crafted. It starts by giving you a premise: there's a mad emperor, trying to summon the evil gods, a rebellion, and you - a fox swashbuckler who's going to stop him. There's also an unreliable friend, a beloved adversary, and two forbidden weapons. So what are you going to do with them, how do you win the war?
You can try every possible combination of these plot elements. Each playthrough takes about 45 minutes, which makes the game good for short-session playing, and you always find yourself at the square one. Capture one, both or none of the artifacts. Try to kill the girl or to win her heart. Trust your friend or send him away. It always goes horribly wrong. There are 24 endings, each one a different kind of failure: sometimes you are just killed, sometimes you win, but at a price too terrible, sometimes the emperor dies, only for someone else to finish his work - sometimes it's you who takes his place. You try new and new ways until you find the four Truths and combine them to finally realize how to play your cards right and find the true ending where the ones you care for stay alivem and the world is not destroyed.
The game also has tons of narrator speech. Each story has its own narration, and there are a lot of casual commentaries for battles, doors, chests, platforms and like. Even as you have completed it over 20 times, you'll sometimes hear some new pun as you open a chest or board a moving platform, giving you the feeling of something new and fresh.
So, even though the gameplay is nothing to write home about, I recommend this game to everyone who loves storytelling: this storry, with all of its branching paths, is worth hearing.

Knights of Pen and Paper +1 is a “roleplaying game”, but in truth it has very little roleplaying in it; while this is common to many “RPGs,” this game takes it to an all-new level. The conceit behind the game is that you are sitting at a table with your game master with a group of friends, and that you are going through a campaign. The players are indeed all seated around a table, with the game master on the far side of the table dictating what is going on. It is a very clever idea, but unfortunately the game fails to execute on it at all; instead, the game is a pure hack-and-slash fest which tries to spice things up with humor and gaming references but falls flat because, quite frankly, everyone sitting around a table has already not only made all of these references, but done it better. The plot is every bad game of D&D you've ever played, every unoriginal campaign rolled into one, and it is played straight - sure, one could argue that it is almost comically bad, but it is painfully bad, like Batman and Robin, rather than camp.
As the gameplay itself is thoroughly hack and slash, purely about cutting your way through an extremely large number of monsters using extremely simplistic turn-based combat reminiscent of many JRPGs, with no real coherent or interesting story to speak of, there is little to recommend this game as anything but a time waster, and even there, you can do far better. There's nothing that this game doesn't show you in the first hour, and there's nothing in that first hour worth taking. While the basic underlying idea of having a bunch of players playing a roleplaying game is an interesting one, this game is a total failure at it. Maybe someday, someone will take this idea and do something good with it, but this is not that game.

Also, the game attempts to provide puzzles... Apparently, attempting to figure out how to enter a building with no foreseeable entrance is "fun" or considered a mystery. Now some will argue "Why just give everything the easy way". In real life.. there is rational soltutions to entering a building. But we have to realize this is a game, therefore those several solutions are dwindled down to only a few choices that are implemented by the game designers. Movement mechanics already mentioned before,  such as climbing/climbing down seem like more work then an actual game. Comes to the point where the game is no longer a game and it becomes labor.

Detailed review to follow:
I've never reviewed a game on Steam before, but this one compelled me to be more vocal.
BOTTOM LINE: An honest homage to isometric RPGs of yore. The adventure of Baldur's Gate 2, the combat of Fallout Tactics (or other tactical RPGs) with modern fusings such as freedom of environment and NPC interaction ala The Elder Scrolls series. Divinity: Original Sin, while poorly titled, is Larian's best foot forward and will set the tone for roleplaying games going forward.
DETAILS
I coordinated with my ally a strategy, that I thought at the time, would help us overcome a challenge three levels tougher than our state. We positioned ourselves, sneaking behind the orcs as inconspicuous boulders with legs (comical on par with the Metal Gear Solid box). He loosed an arrow on a barrel of ooze, and it burst onto the terrain. With our cover blown, I stood ready to be the good knight I am and take the brunt of the orcs' ire. I was unaware however that the shaman would launch a fireball my way, igniting the ooze into a flaming cloud that would literally disintigrate myself and turn the whole plan sour.
Divinity: Original Sin is full of these dynamic scenarios. As a Source Hunter, an intrepid adventurer that, you guessed it, hunts source energy throughout the land. It's a dramatic undertaking, and during your adventures you too will be faced with environmental hazards and a sprawling story that will test your instincts both on and off the field of battle. Luckily, this is not a solitary adventure. You get a companion that will follow you to the ends of the earth in the form of a loyal NPC or a buddy (or a random online partner).
As a game, D:OS does a lot right without reinventing the wheel. If anything, it takes a few steps back from how esoteric modern roleplaying games have become. Instead, D:OS falls back on old fantasy tropes of swords and sorcery, questing and other broad genre-related themes. Those who remember Dungeons and Dragons, rolling lots of dice and sifting through stats and skills will feel right at home with this digital incarnation, although those seeking the more gimmicky bonuses woven into many modern roleplaying franchises may be missing for others.
The game is a point-and-click, isometric adventure. It's much in the vein of Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Fallout (1 and 2, not your new fangled 3!) with how the game is presented. The graphics are however three dimensional with a moderate capacity to control the camera angle that can be cumbersome at times. Combat in D;OS feels much like it was taken out of any other tactical roleplaying game, such as Fallout Tactics, or more recently XCOM: Enemy Unknown. The seamless integration of this method of combat versus clicking madly is actually seamless. There is no change in scenery, no difference in position, instead if you are spotted by enemies in the wild, you become locked in battle until you win, lose, or run.
That being said, while the game feels fluid and easy, the game's difficulty makes no excuses. It is not for the faint of heart, or patience. You will die. A lot. You will also get lost a lot. With a paucity of quest markers, and enemy mobs can kill you at any level with the help of clever environmental interactions, or your own poor tactical assessment. More on that later. D:OS truly relives the glory days where there are no respawn points, and to be resurrected you better have an ally with a ressurection scroll or spell, or be prepared to load the game. It has notes of a roguelike within its world, and it should not be shied from but embraced, for it only adds to the sense of danger and urgency of every quest you undertake.
As far as imminent and frequent death go, D:OS has no shortage of environmental hazards, penalties and bonuses. As mentioned before, a pen-and-paper roleplayer will feel right at home, but much of what you may need to know is explained in the brief and plain tutorial. Water conducts electricity so don't stand in it if you cast a lightning spell, ooze ignites with fire, fire is put out with water. Someone who is wet takes more damage from air spells and bombs don't ignite. Being flanked leaves you at a disadvantage, and vice versa if you've succeeded at it yourself. Any number of bonuses and penalties can be stacked in a battle which will swing the tide in your favor, or against you, making no fight to be taken for granted, even if it seems like a 'gimme'.
Outside of the conventional RPG elements, D:OS also borrows from some of the things more modern successors have done well. The ability to interact with almost every NPC or object, whether with aggression or kindness, is borrowed directly from The Elder Scrolls. Be prepared for a fight if you attack a guard though. You can pickpocket, sneak, pick locks, steal from stores, and most other free roaming activities with reckless abandon. Your actions will impact those around you, and your personality profile, so be aware of what you plan to do with your character, whether you intend to be honorable, or a real scoundrel
One clever addition Larian has made is that nearly every NPC has a storefront of sorts. Most people have something to buy or barter for, making it exciting to see what some average villager may have. You can never know when someone may have that rare sword you really want.
All good aside, D:OS does come with its faults. Character customization is decidedly limited, with very few aesthetic touches you can change leading to a very homogeneous partnership. Men will be beefcakes and women femme fatales, and would have been something I would have liked to see changed. The camera can be finicky at times leading to a lot of cutting into taller terrain, and sometimes unable to quite get around posts or pillars when you'd really like to see what you're clicking on. Zooming in and out is also nice at times, but the field of view is very centralized on your character and feels claustrophobic and uncomfortable, which is unfortunate because the macro details are quite nice, and not readily seen from the more common aerial angle. Another issue, while it is a rich game in single player, controlling both characters can create an awkward stuccato style of play where you have to position each like chess pieces, and lose the immersion while you get your positions just right.
The user interface also leaves a lot to be desired. Clunky pages of skills and poor inventory management options leave an organized inventory wishful thinking. While a more patient player may be fine with this, there's little reason for games to have such an archaic, manual mode of organization. Spending so much time flipping through text, and pop-up windows and pages of stats is a sure way to be taken out of the immersive story.
The multiplayer is also unique, in the way that a player has to join your game. For all intents and purposes, it's a single player game with another person whom you assign a character. That person cannot independently design their character, or import their character for their game. It is completely dependent on the host.
Larian, all things considered, has struck a home run. Their goal to make a game worthy of a 90 Metacritic score has succeeded fusing old with new. While the game plays well in single or multiplayer, it's clear they favored the latter. The smoothness of two independent people exploring and strategizing together is seamless, and I would say is the best coop experience I've ever had. While the game is good alone, it's incredible with a friend. If you can see past the convoluted pop-up interface, and enjoy team based, Baldur's Gate exploration, you'll enjoy this game. So do yourself, and Larian a favor (so they keep making games of this quality, or continue to update this), and pick up Divinity: Original Sin.

Stories: The Path of Destinies the kind of game where gameplay plays a secondary role to its somewhat gimicky expanding narrative. There are more than 15 endings unlockable, so there is a lot of replay value to this even after you achieved the True Ending. It is still a shame that the game lacks any boss fights since all the cool showdowns are occuring, sadly enough, during cutscenes -- so gameplay is essentially treasure hunting & weapon crafting while slashing through waves and waves of soldiers. The game does ramp up the difficulty when you reach the True Ending, so I'll give it that.
All in all, this is a game especially for those that love to see the branching paths and outcomes of their choices accompanied by approachable gameplay and a quirky yet loveable narrator. It's fun -- also a perfect game to go achievement hunting considering the amount of effort I've put into it is moderate yet I'm almost at 100%. Though I suppose the last few achievements require some extra dedication.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is a fantastic pick up and play game with great visual presentation and an extremely satisfying combat system, I picked this game up on a whim and immediately fell in love with it. Stories follows Reynardo, a mercenery fox who is loosely working alongside a rebellion against a corrupt empire, he's a fun character with a witty personality portrayed brilliantly by the games narrator, the game's only voice actor as it plays out like a story book. Reynardo is also extremely satisfying to control, he's a spellsword of sorts, able to wield both blade and magic effortlessly, Stories combat system is very rewarding, requiring you to time attacks to parry enemies and position yourself strategically. Now while this is nothing new Stories manages to do this in a way that keeps the game challenging, Reynardo feels powerful, but his survival is entirely dependent on expedient responses, the closest comparison regarding this could perhaps be drawn to the Batman: Arkham series, but Stories feels more strategic, victory here feels earned and it keeps the combat from feeling stale.
While Stories looks like an RPG on the surface I'd definitely say it's more of an action game, you can upgrade Reynardo and his sword with varying skills and abilities, but there isn't a great deal of depth to it and to be honest the game doesn't really require said depth. Stories also has a unique choice system in that it encourages you to learn from your choices. Whereas more in depth RPGs cause your choices to carry over the course of the game, eventually affecting how your personal character plays out, Stories instead gauges what kind of hero you are through "truths" which are revealed as you play through the game. Once a truth is revealed time resets, Reynardo finds himself back at the start of the rebellion but with prior knowledge of what is to unfold should he take certain actions, such as trusting an ally or travelling to a certain destination. This system is great because it encourages you to play through the game multiple times, uncovering new truths and improving Reynardo's abilities as you go. While this leads the game to feel fairly short it does mean it's a game you may find yourself coming back to and playing through in it's entirety without requiring a heavy investment of time, which is great if you fancy some light RPG shenanigans but have somewhere to be in an hour.
Stories: The Path of Destinies comes highly recommended, if you enjoy both RPGs and action games you're bound to find something you like here. Definitely give it a look.

The locations, levels, and storytelling to this game have a lot of charm, but ultimately, the gameplay does not deliver enough for me to recommend this game. Some critical bugs currently impact its playability, which I discuss at the end of this review.
I do enjoy the way the Stories frames the concept of restarting and replaying the game, however, this premise necessarily introduces redundancies to the gameplay. The vast majority of the enemies are the same raven grunt for the entire game, with maybe 4 "special" ravens that do little to make the combat feel less repetitive. The levels themselves are diverse enough that running through them multiple times and discovering new paths does not feel like a chore, I cannot say the same for the encounters. It doesn't help that you can pretty much just hit things until they die most of the time, and dash around to avoid being hit.
When the combat is difficult, which is uncommon, it is entirely due to poor performance rather than by design. The areas are large in 3 dimensions, and the enemies are numerous. Occasionally the frame rate would slow to a crawl, making it difficult to react to the influx of enemies.
The biggest problem Stories has is its mechanism of saving. It soft autosaves each time you reach a checkpoint, and hard autosaves when you complete a chapter. This would be fine, if it weren't for the game-breaking bugs that can only be fixed by restarting the game, and therefore having to replay an entire chapter. Reynardo can get stuck on the scenery in several places, and there is no obvious way to dislodge him without forcing a reload. He can also get stuck on poles, but the dash action usually gets him out. On four occasions during my playthrough, all characters in combat froze, and Reynardo was unresponsive, forcing a restart of the chapter.
Overall, Stories offers fun, creative storytelling, colorful and interesting environments, and a combat system that is actually quite enjoyable, but the gameplay issues were a dealbreaker for me.

I was looking for a great action RPG. Grim dawn has stopped me from searching. I have had this game since very early access as the theme of the game caught my attention. I've gotten about 5 friends to purchase this game and multiplayer is very fun ( although a little buggy at times still much fun ). The developers usually keep you updated every couple of weeks so you know that more content will be coming as it goes and they have been very on the ball with this.
As far as gameplay goes it feels very fluid based on the class you create. Spells and abilities are well tuned and all work well together ( I mean if you multiclass you feel you can mix and match yourself well ).
They introduced a faction system which means you can be liked and hated by NPC parties in the game which can cause boss enemies to spawn or harder monsters. On the good side it allows you to purchase nice items from NPC vendors in towns based on the faction.
The story is also very well done and ive heard mixed reviews on the fact no NPC reads their text to you - but personally I kind of like that. As you play through youll find notes and scripts about the lore of the game which I also like it is almost like you add a journal of story as you play the game which in itself is a reward.
All in all I highly recommend grim dawn - theres at least 20 hours of gameplay and with all the muilticlassing you can do theres plenty more. Hidden areas and bosses are also out there.. happy hunting.

The Banner Saga excels more so at being a demonstration at the power and potential of crowd funding more so than it does as a successful tactical RPG. A story driven, episodic, tactical game like this would have had no chance of making it into the public's eye just a few short years ago, and because of this, gamers should be thrilled. Standing on its own, The Banner Saga is a very decent game that just narrowly gets a recommendation from me. The art style is simply stunning, and will undoubtedly land The Banner Saga on many "Best Looking Games of 2014" lists. The story itself is also fascinating with its "Choose Your Own Adventure" style of narrative, although your mileage may vary when it comes to becoming emotionally involved with the plights of the game's multiple protagonists.
The Banner Saga's biggest missed opportunity, in my opinion, is with the combat system. It's a very bare-bones system that adds nothing significant to the genre, and begins to feel quite repititive as you progress through the game and often repeat battles due to the game's high difficulty. It's functional and all, but overall just feels competent at best, and ultimately disappoints, as a stronger combat system could really have propelled The Banner Saga into the realms of the greats. But overall, it's a solid debut effort from Stoic, and if you're a fan of this genre, is worth checking out once the price drops a bit.

This game is a must get game for those who like this genre of game. I personally think that their isn't much wrong with this game at all and it is an absolutely amazing experiance first time around.
I just love how you start with just a squad of rookies and slowly you have to rank them up and upgrade them with the new gear you have aquired from researching the alien technology espicially when you own the DLC which makes it so you can get geneticly enhanced soilders and mech suits, which I think is awesome!
The campaign is really great and I love how it's all laid out, just how you have to build up your base and research new tech, then you have to go to the emergancy room and you have to pick out what you think will be the most beneficial mission not only for your advancement but also to try and keep the other countries happy and to continue giving you thier finacial support. I also love how after you get a few missions like that you get should I say "main story missions" which develope the games story and advances you in the game and bringing you closer to winning, which first time around the "story missions" can really take you by surprise and you can be put up against a encounter which you totally were not expecting which can ultimately lead in your defeat, which is what I liked caused even if you fail the mission the first time around it isn't like "game over press restart" it's well now your squad are all dead and you have to redo it later on with your new rookies, so it makes it quite intense cause you want to do it first time around with hopefully no casulties.
The combat plus death system to the game was great I like it how even though anoying there were a chance to hit and miss cause sometimes you would get a completely surprising result which would either be the turning in point for victory or total defeat. Also how their were ways to increase you chances to hit the enemy for example flanking them behind their cover or by charging in which a shotgun, which I liked cause it forces you to use tactics and sometimes think outside the box and make risky plays.
What I got to say was one thing which I wish was in alot more games in general is this idea of when your soldier dies it over, I really like this concept cause it can sometimes completely change the way you thought the game was going to go, for example one mission which I send all my highest ranked soldier in, I made some bad moves and all but one died, but because I didn't ever really rank up any of my other soldiers in my next couple of missions which my new recruits it made an usual easy going mission into one which I really had to be careful just in case the same happened again. The reason mainly why I love it in games when they are like this is cause sometimes some games become slightly boring once you hit the max level or get the max gear and you never have to worry about anything because if you die and you become an absolute monster killing everything in your path, which even though it can be fun in some games I think they made a really good decision not having that in this game because it takes so much out of a game like this, for example tactics and always worrying about your favourite soldier.
The multiplayer even though I didn't really play it, I thought was good cause it was not much different than the campaign in terms of combat which I like, but it was brillaint how on multiplayer you could be the alien units and put them to some good use, it's just ashame they never made a DLC for a Alien campaign trying to get world domination or something like that. The only thing which I wish they would have made different about the multiplayer was the amount of units and players, I just think it would have been alot more awesome if the battles where alot more bigger scale which more players and units on the field.
Customization was amazing on this game even though you couldn't have individual armour types for example differnt glove and boots, it was more of a set instead which personally I prefered, but I really liked how you could slowly evolve you equipment and customize you soldiers with the newest equipment you had. Then there was the abilities which was done really well cause even though once you soldier got given a class there was only one of two paths he could take it was really done well I think cause personally I don't really think there was ever a bad decision in what abilities you picked cause they always ended up being useful in different ways depending on you tactics and situation.
I also liked how you could customize the campaign and add new features which would alter how the game would be for example you soldier could get random abilities from any of the classes so you could be an assult class with what would normally be a support ability which was fun cause if you did eventually get bored of the "same old thing" you could change it up a bit with these settings.
Overall I think this is a must get game, even if this game isn't usually your type of game I would highly recommend trying it out cause hopefully it will change you opinion on these genre of games. Though I think if you are going to buy the game then definitely but the DLC cause it adds so much more gameplay and just makes the experiance ten times more enjoyable in my opinion. 10/10 must buy! :D

The Walking Dead – Michonne was a short and sweet Telltale Games adventure that tides fans over until the next instalment of The Walking Dead game comes out.
It’s a shorter than usual, 3 episode affair, and each episode takes around 1.5 hours to complete. The game follows Michonne dealing with the grief of losing her two daughters in the apocalypse, and they haunt her through the game, often at the worst times.
The game is more action heavy than the other Walking Dead games since Michonne is far more capable than the characters in the other games. Cons

Telltale's The Walking Dead series, for the most part, has been excellent. In terms of storytelling, voice-acting, writing, dialogue & being very cinematic - each game has delivered without fail. Telltale has even experimented with the format of the series, with Season 1's 400 Days (with 5 different very short stories) and now Michonne in a mini-series format. The Walking Dead: Michonne is the latest experiment, as it's a spin-off from Telltale's main TWD series & that this one is actually based on TWD character Michonne. Telltale has, once again, delivered another great TWD series - this time, in the form of a mini-series.
Michonne is the player's character in this story, as her & a small crew on their boat wind up getting a distress signal & find a ship out in the middle of (practically) nowhere. They search the ship to see if anyone's alive, basically. That is just the beginning, to say the least - and I don't want to run into "spoiler turf" for anyone that wants to actually play this game.
The story + character development is excellent here, as one would expect from a Telltale game. And honestly, it better be - since most of the focus on this game is the story + character development. The writing, dialogue, and voice-acting is nothing short of great here, as it's rich as can be.
Most of the game focuses on the player actually using the controller - or keyboard + mouse, I suppose, if you feel inclined to go that route - and literally being in the moment, as the player will get shoved down their throat an experience of emulating & immitating the motions of horrible things + situations first-hand. The experience is often emotional, moving, draining, brutal, disgusting & gut-wrentching. Not many games do this as well as TWD series, to be honest.
As usual, the very gray decision-making elements are + play an important part in this series - and you will often have to make tough decisions in a very limited amount of time, in which the results will likely (still) be very dark + bleak, no matter what you decide. The game will shape its journey (of often who lives, dies, and where the story pieces can go next), based on your decisions throughout the mini-series - which is excellent.
As great as a lot of this stuff is, there are a few things worth noting: some players might not like certain things about TWD: Michonne. One thing that might turn (some) players off is the fact that it feels even less of an adventure game than ever before. While TWD: Season 1 had a few puzzles, it still wasn't a lot & they often weren't difficult by any means for many players. This was even more so true with Season 2, as that felt more action-like than Season 1 and had even less puzzles to solve - but TWD: Michonne has took it a few steps further. Also, if you weren't a fan of the format of S1 and/or S2, I don't think even its it more compact format that TWD: Michonne will speak to you.
TWD: Michonne has taken the route of going further in the direction with even more action + less of the (old-school) pure-adventure puzzle-solving mechanics. If you weren't happy with TWD: Season 2 going further in this direction, you're certainly not going to like it in Michonne. Michonne has even more action sequences + quick-time events in this series than ever before.
After 4.7 hours (according to Steam), The Walking Dead: Michonne has reached its conclusion for me....and what a conclusion it was! The smaller + more compact format might give the game less "bang for the buck", especially if the player doesn't plan to do multiple playthroughs - so some might want to wait for a sale to buy this game b/c it honestly doesn't last long per each playthrough.
Though, still even in its smaller & more compact format, TWD: Michonne still delivers exactly what fans of the Telltale TWD series want: great storytelling, character, dialogue, voice-acting & tough decisions to make. From start-to-finish, TWD: Michonne has the same kind of gripping, intense, & brutal nature that made the previous Telltale TWD Seasons so great - albeit, in a smaller & more compact format. Fans of the TWD series, this one is a no-brainer: you're going to want to get your hands on this gripping title.

~~RANT, NOT REALLY A COHERENT REVIEW~~
Dying Light starts off as an interesting take on actually being afraid of zombies but having the advantage of mobility over them. For the first third of the game, it uses this idea really well and makes you feel like you're playing something really special. The slow parkour, the weak weapons, the constant scavenging, this makes the game very good. If somehow this element of uniqueness stayed prevalent throughout the whole game, I feel the overall scores would be higher. As such, it does not.
The main problem with Dying Light's gameplay is that the crafting, parkour, and combat elements become way too easy by the 2nd half of the game, a.k.a Old Town. By that point, you are one hitting most enemies, dropkicking undead off countless rooftops, and destroying mini-bosses. While this is fun in its own way, it is brain dead fun. It isn't fun for the specialty or for even playing Dying Light, it is fun because you are playing something else.
Dying Light's combat was, again, very interesting at first because there wasn't very much of it. You were running and climbing ledges like that fat kid in gym class. Narrowly avoiding quick infected and diving and weaving past obstacles while being chased by Nightcrawlers is very fun. Once any of these enemies can be quickly dealt with, it loses that sort of fun. Sure, using parkour and mobility in fights can lead to a bigger advantage and potentially more fun factor, you soon realize that this weapon you got earlier before this fight can deal with your problems just like that.
Dying Light's components are not original. Almost everything in the game was made by someone else, or in Techland's case, even brought in from a different franchise, *cough* Dead Island *cough*. What makes it fun is the way Techland decided to combine them and use them to make a fun game. The only sort of original feature is the hunter to prey mechanic that is advertised quite heavily.
Every now and again I boot up a really underdeveloped save to relive that shock and intrigue and hype I felt when I first played this. If it sounds like I hate on Dying Light, I don't. I really liked Dying Light, even the 2nd half mostly. Like with most games, I guess after playing 144 hours I can say that I feel it could've went in a different direction. A different direction that would've, for me, made for a better game.
Dying Light could've been a totally different game, one more focused on actual survival and scavenging, that sense that you cannot take on an entire zombie horde, that at most times, whether day or night, you are being hunted, yet you do not know it.
~~END RANT~~

This is one of the best remastered games I've played.  The graphics, soundtrack, sound effects have all been drastically improved without changing any of the properties of the game. This isn’t a 1:1 recreation but I felt the very few changes are for the better.  I doubt anyone will ever say they enjoyed grinding for charm stones just to buy new equipment or equip a certain sword to break stones. The added “Unknown Location” levels adds a new challenge for those who’ve already played every nook and cranny of this game whether 20+ years or just a few months ago.

Not only is this an awesome game to remaster(and very well done), it’s also a retro game that can be enjoyed by anyone and I believe the gameplay aged pretty well with its tight controls and simple pacing.

Diablo 3 is too simplified and baby-tier.
Path of Exile requires six spreadsheets and a bible to pray with.
Titan Quest has a weird Greek theme to it and needs mods to run as intended.
So why not play Grim Dawn? For starters its offline so you're not waiting on anyone else's servers or connections (unless you want to play multiplayer) and while it isn't free like PoE its much cheaper than D3 and you don't have to run it through a redundant client. Everything you need to play Grim Dawn gets downloaded through Steam which shouldn't be a selling point but in today's time not coming saddled with DRM or always-online requirements is quite the bow on the box.
As for the game itself its typical ARPG fair. Find monsters, bludgeon them until they die, pick up loot, rinse and repeat. Grim Dawn manages to make that pretty satisfying though, on par with D3 actually (although the gritty aesthetic does appeal more to me than D3s aesthetic) and much more so than PoE where a lot of attacks seem to not even connect. It uses a tri-stat system and is very similar to a finished, polished, and reskinned Titan Quest with more stuff in it. Making a return is the two-class system which is pretty good fun and encourages lots of replay to see what each combination feels like in play (even if you can see, on paper, how they appear if you go looking.)
The mechanics encourage a wider variety of things than D3s 'Add more to your primary stat' equipment. A lot of the time you have to think about things and make sure that the extra +5% Physical damage bonus is worth the loss of 3% of your armor value and all of your Cold resistance because you don't know the next time some random frost-covered skeletor is going to show up and hand you your♥♥♥♥♥on a plate. There are hardly ever any 'pure upgrades' if you keep upgrading your equipment consistently and the crafting system helps this out a lot.
The real shocker is that making equipment is actually worth your time instead of the usual 'I can just pick it up off the ground, why bother?' mentality that plagues most ARP games. A lot of the time you can make better items than what you find so you're going to be almost always short on supplies and currencies which is really pretty unique considering the mountain of gold I'm sitting on in D3 and the bank stashes full of PoE currency items. There just seems to be a lot of attention to detail to make the game better than its competition.
I can't make a sales pitch to people who don't know the genre, you're going to just look deep inside yourself and find out how much grind and loot hunting you're ready to commit to, but for everyone else? You're looking for the buzzwords of 'Its better than Diablo 2' but I'm not here to give you that judgement - I'm here to tell you that its better than everything else in the modern market.
If you want to know if it beats out the classic D2? Try it out.

A fun, if unpolished and simplistic game.
The game suffers a lot of issues from the get go: Minimal Settings options, No control customisation, prone to crashing and very simplistic combat that's somehow the meat of the game.
However, there's real charm behind the game that makes it hard to not recommend. The game does a good job of world-building through the story elements and has a cast of engaging, if a little 2-dimensional, characters.
The constant narration in the background adds to the charm, although it's a little flawed. The juxtaposition between the serious story narration and the silly humorous happenstance narration can be really jarring (Going from talking about the stench of death, to making a joke about breaking barrels). Similarly, there's a lot of one-liner pop-culture references which come out of nowhere.
In spite of all the flaws I enjoyed the game enough to complete the 'main' story. There's a lot of branching paths to still explore, but I don't think I'll find the interest to explore them all.
Worth a look, but don't expect perfection.

If Titan Quest and Diablo 2 had a baby, you would have this game.
Great combination of both games with a few new ideas like hidden quests, hidden books, secret caves, a bit of choice and consequence, bounties, and a ton of other stuff that I probably haven't found yet. Maps are quite large, but they are not randomized yet.
Character classes are pretty much the same like any other ARPG, but with a fresh twist. There's also a few new classes, like the Demolionist. Playing that class now, so much fun  obliterating monsters with a Canister Bomb and dual wielded pistols.
Graphics are Titan Quest quality, maybe a little better. Runs very smooth on my old dinosaur of a computer completely maxed.  The soundtrack is superb, SFX is good but the gunshots can get annoying fast.
Physics will make you laugh out loud. Nothing like seeing a skeleton fly 100 feet into the air, parts flying everywhere haha.
There are a few bugs, but none that are too annoying so far. MP runs well, there is some lag occcasionally. Sometimes the server will drop, but it's still not as bad as Diablo 2 was with that.
If you have played Titan Quest before, it's easy to pick up as it uses that engine. I think a new person to this genre could get into it  easily though.
Game is 100% playable in it's current state, which is great as it's still Early Access. This is my second Early Access purchase and I'm very pleased.

This game was a huge letdown.
The combat is bizarre because a single enemy and a single member of your team will alternate. This means that when the enemy has lower numbers, they get more turns. It lets them get in and beat on your weaker people several times and you may not even have a chance to react. Since losing a character in combat means that you have to rest and that he or she will be weaker in additional fights, it is sort of annoying when there are two enemies left and they both get to move over and over again to take out your weakened guys.
The maps are all flat. There is no terrain at all.
Between battles, there are story portions that play out like a really well illustrated choose your own adventure book. A situation will arise, you choose between two or three options, and then you get a result. There is no indication whatsoever of how the choice might play out, so you might as well just pick the choices at random.
There is one currency in the game and you have to spend it to level guys up. Of course, you never know when one of these random story instances is going to kill someone that you spent that currency on.
It's really not a good game. If you buy it, buy it for the art, which is quite good.

Banner Saga is an awesome and inspiring tactical game. The story telling was superb, and I loved its tactical elements, art style, and the mechanics. I found Banner Saga very hard to put down, and was compelled to finish it before moving onto anything else.
The Story is immediately gripping. You play as a few select groups, each with their own agenda, and destination. However the destination is not what really counts. It’s what happens to you along the way. Hearts will be broken, people will die, and darkness will descend. Seriously, I felt very much caught in a desperate struggle to escape the tides of unfurling events, not always emerging unscathed.
The art style is beautiful, yet minimal. It lends itself to the setting, and describes Banner Saga's setting well. Whilst the screen is never void of interesting landmarks and details, the world doesn’t feel tiny or cluttered and every destination does feel like an achievement. The bleak, often frozen, alpine wastes don’t feel empty but are instead transformed into the beautiful and often surreal.
I didn't mind the permadeath style scenarios or the early choices that affected you much further on. These decisions meant that I had to live with my choices and move on, not reload. It did make things rather difficult however when my most powerful units were permadead, and i my remaining heroes were weaka**. Also, spend your renown wisely. I’m pretty sure i starved most of my people to death.
The only downfall i felt noteworthy is the lack of character customisation, and party options. Most of the story you're forced to use all your heroes, and more often than not, the character you've invested a whole lotta time into, buggers off one way or another. Perhaps I just lucked out. Often.
Banner Saga is definitely worth the purchase if you're into any tactical style games, like 'Heroes of might and magic', or the 'Disciples' series. Think a mash-up of those, mixed with like, organ trails.

This game is a must get game for those who like this genre of game. I personally think that their isn't much wrong with this game at all and it is an absolutely amazing experiance first time around.
I just love how you start with just a squad of rookies and slowly you have to rank them up and upgrade them with the new gear you have aquired from researching the alien technology espicially when you own the DLC which makes it so you can get geneticly enhanced soilders and mech suits, which I think is awesome!
The campaign is really great and I love how it's all laid out, just how you have to build up your base and research new tech, then you have to go to the emergancy room and you have to pick out what you think will be the most beneficial mission not only for your advancement but also to try and keep the other countries happy and to continue giving you thier finacial support. I also love how after you get a few missions like that you get should I say "main story missions" which develope the games story and advances you in the game and bringing you closer to winning, which first time around the "story missions" can really take you by surprise and you can be put up against a encounter which you totally were not expecting which can ultimately lead in your defeat, which is what I liked caused even if you fail the mission the first time around it isn't like "game over press restart" it's well now your squad are all dead and you have to redo it later on with your new rookies, so it makes it quite intense cause you want to do it first time around with hopefully no casulties.
The combat plus death system to the game was great I like it how even though anoying there were a chance to hit and miss cause sometimes you would get a completely surprising result which would either be the turning in point for victory or total defeat. Also how their were ways to increase you chances to hit the enemy for example flanking them behind their cover or by charging in which a shotgun, which I liked cause it forces you to use tactics and sometimes think outside the box and make risky plays.
What I got to say was one thing which I wish was in alot more games in general is this idea of when your soldier dies it over, I really like this concept cause it can sometimes completely change the way you thought the game was going to go, for example one mission which I send all my highest ranked soldier in, I made some bad moves and all but one died, but because I didn't ever really rank up any of my other soldiers in my next couple of missions which my new recruits it made an usual easy going mission into one which I really had to be careful just in case the same happened again. The reason mainly why I love it in games when they are like this is cause sometimes some games become slightly boring once you hit the max level or get the max gear and you never have to worry about anything because if you die and you become an absolute monster killing everything in your path, which even though it can be fun in some games I think they made a really good decision not having that in this game because it takes so much out of a game like this, for example tactics and always worrying about your favourite soldier.
The multiplayer even though I didn't really play it, I thought was good cause it was not much different than the campaign in terms of combat which I like, but it was brillaint how on multiplayer you could be the alien units and put them to some good use, it's just ashame they never made a DLC for a Alien campaign trying to get world domination or something like that. The only thing which I wish they would have made different about the multiplayer was the amount of units and players, I just think it would have been alot more awesome if the battles where alot more bigger scale which more players and units on the field.
Customization was amazing on this game even though you couldn't have individual armour types for example differnt glove and boots, it was more of a set instead which personally I prefered, but I really liked how you could slowly evolve you equipment and customize you soldiers with the newest equipment you had. Then there was the abilities which was done really well cause even though once you soldier got given a class there was only one of two paths he could take it was really done well I think cause personally I don't really think there was ever a bad decision in what abilities you picked cause they always ended up being useful in different ways depending on you tactics and situation.
I also liked how you could customize the campaign and add new features which would alter how the game would be for example you soldier could get random abilities from any of the classes so you could be an assult class with what would normally be a support ability which was fun cause if you did eventually get bored of the "same old thing" you could change it up a bit with these settings.
Overall I think this is a must get game, even if this game isn't usually your type of game I would highly recommend trying it out cause hopefully it will change you opinion on these genre of games. Though I think if you are going to buy the game then definitely but the DLC cause it adds so much more gameplay and just makes the experiance ten times more enjoyable in my opinion. 10/10 must buy! :D

I played this game years after it released because I heard it was fantastic.  Well, the reviewers weren't lying.  It's an excellent sequel to the original Half Life.
It's difficult to know where to begin because there are so many great things I could write about this game. I love how it combines gameplay and storytelling in a seamless way.  It has perhaps the most perfect pacing I've ever seen in a game and I became so engrossed with it that I refused to sleep until I had seen the end.
I love the dystopian atmosphere and the menacing presence of the Combine Citadel and how it literally eats away human civilization.  I love the various enemies you fight and how they are inspired by classic sci-fi monsters such as the Alien Facehugger, the bugs from Starship Troopers, and the Tripods from War of the Worlds.  My favorite part has to be Ravenholm because it managed to disturb me more than most horror games that I've played.  If only the creators of the Dead Space series had studied this level!
The gameplay is also tremendously fun.  Vehicle combat can be hit or miss in some games but in this one they are very easy to use and help your character a great deal. Each level offers an interesting challenge that distiniguishes it from others.  For example, one level teaches you how to use creatures to attack enemies while you run from cover to cover avoiding heavy fire, while another forces you to use objects in the environment as weapons because ammo is scarce.  Usually there is at least one level that's a boring slog in FPS games but I enjoyed all of the ones in Half-Life 2.
Weapon variety and utility can make or break an FPS, but this game does not disappoint. While I enjoyed all of the weapons, the Gravity Gun is one of my all-time favorites for an FPS, ranking up there with the Wraithverge from Hexen (an awesome-looking cross that shoots four wraiths that can traverse through walls to tear apart your enemies).

Half-Life 2 improves upon the original in every way except for level design.  Older FPS games like the original Half-Life have complex levels that offer multiple paths to explore.  Quake is especially known for its amazing level design, which is why its deathmatch community remained strong for many years.  Half-Life 2 is very linear by comparison, and though that assists with story pacing, it reduces the game's replay value.  Even so, I loved this game so much that I played it twice and still had a blast during my second run.
If you have never played this game I highly recommend it.  Yes, the graphics are dated compared to today's games, but Half-Life 2 is so well-crafted that you will enjoy it regardless.

I strongly recommend this game to anybody, espeically to gamers who have their own little stories as they play. Happy Civing everyone :)

Although seemingly simple in design, FTL: Faster than Light has continued to blow my mind with its overwhelming amount of content in such a simple form. From battling Space Slugs, and saving pirates from ship wrecks, to unlocking new ships and races as you play, to being stranded without fuel in the middle of the cosmos, this game will not disappoint you!
FTL: Faster Than Light is a top-down insterstellar space sim, featuring combat much like the old DnD computer games. You can pause and make decisions step by step, and watch your decisions play out moments after. Managing everything aboard your ship while aiming lasers and fighting enemy cruisers can be a lot to handle!
When I first watched the trailer, there was a lot of things going on, and many of which I didn't understand. Even still, I decided to jump right in to this space sim gone horribly right, and it was one of the best purchases on steam I've ever made. The big turning point when most players seem to realize just how complex this game is, is when you first learn to open your own airlocks, to put out fires, suffocate enemies, or even save the equipment in a room from enemies smashing them! New physics not considered anywhere else, that are so simple, that they astound you when you first learn about them.
While not every run will allow you the opportunity to play any way you want, that is also a part of the genius behind its design. You want to become a boarding ship, to take otu your enemies hand to hand? You better hope you run into a teleporter then, they won't always be available to you at every shop. Sometimes you don't run into weapons for a while, when you were saving up for a good weapon. You passed by some mid tier weapons only to realize all your money doesn't mean anything if you do not run into more along the way!
Overall FTL: Faster Than Light will keep you on your toes as you explore alien homeworlds, untraveled Nebulas, surprise bandits and environmental effects that will make each run of the game Unique in its own way. Evolving to meet the demands of each run is the way to success, as not everything always goes your way.
With the patch releasing the new Lanaris Race, the races 3 new ships, new weapons, and an extra ship layout for all previous races, this game will only become better.  So jump on the space train and ride your way into the next adventure awaiting you!

Pros:
-The game looks and sounds great, and runs pretty well.
-Gunplay feels absolutely fantastic, the majority of guns kick realistically and are a blast to use.
-When playing with a coordinated team, it's often a great balance between relaxing moments of headshotting trash enemies while chilling with your friends and coordinating takedowns on larger enemies. Playing with people you know on higher difficulties turns the game into a challenging but satisfying experience where everyone does their role and helps each other.
-Often several different viable loadouts/perk setups to play with.
-Fairly active playerbase, lots of cool custom maps.
Cons:
-There are a ton of different ways for teammates to screw you and the team over (firebug lighting big enemies on fire, for example). Often, bad teammates get good teammates killed, and the game doesn't do much to reprimand them.
-No way to restrict high difficulty games to high-level players. Low level players lack certain perks needed to function properly at a high level, and are thus a burden.
-Some poorly explained ingame mechanics. Did you know that railgun loses 50% of its damage with autoaim enabled? Or that a Commando can extend Zed Time (ingame slowmo) significantly if he scores kills during it? Don't feel bad if you didn't, the game sure doesn't tell you.
-Questionable balance choices (spawnrage fleshpounds, crawlers that explode into gas clouds, etc.) Not gamebreaking, but often extremely annoying.
-Highly repetitive, though this may or may not be an issue for some.
Overall a fantastic wave-based PvE co-op game, but if you want to play on higher difficulties you NEED to have a group of friends you can rely on. Too much can go wrong with randoms.

And gameplay-wise it's a really solid combo-oriented hack and slash. It can get a bit repetetive and given the potential length of the game if you want to unlock every storyline, some elements feel like afterthoughts (the sword upgrades seem crucial at first but are so limited that you've 100%'d them in no time), but it keeps being consistently fun. Definitely recommended - not going to blow your mind, but has a chance to become a memorable personal cult classic experience.

Probably the most interesting game I've played, with the most enjoyable way to experience a story. It's some sort of choose your own adventure, but with only one real ending in which you win. The only way to succeed is trial and error, experimenting with different choices, and learning "True things" to help you find out the best path. After that it's a cake walk to an ending I haven't seen yet. (If you care to know why, read the stuff below, otherwise just skip to the last bit where I mention combat.)
---
The only problem is that even with the lowest settings, my computer seems to turn into a toaster. It's usually not to bad. if I just spam the attack button and hold down the healing swords ability, I can tank any fight, and continue onwards to another ending.
Sometimes, I even get a wonderful moment, where there is no background to load! Just me, the enemies, and a smooth running game. When that happens, it's probably the most enjoyable game I could play! I really enjoy fighting, especially when it's as smooth as those blue-moon moments. But usually it's not like that.
I've played this for a bit now, and gotten past some laggy moments, long load screens (Probably due to toaster electronics) and made it to the TRUE ENDING! which I shall not spoil, that would be rude. That, and I can't get past the last fight scene. It's too laggy, and the enemy horde too big to tank through like every other lag fight.
Sometimes, the land won't even load in, and I'm "Floating" in mid air as I stand on invisible ground.
It's worth it if you don't use potatoes to run pretty games. I'll have to live with the cliff-hanger I've ended up with, but if you have anything better than what I have, and you want this game, go for it. You probably won't regret it.
---
Oh and on a side note, others say the combats a bit repetitive, but IMO it's alright by me. I could see the repetitive argument and why some would say it, but I enjoy the way it goes.
On an XBOX controller, you press X to attack, A to Dash (If unlocked) and Y to hook things (It's a mandatory unlock, but it's not there at start.) You get 4 swords and their abilities that you can use with Right Trigger. You can cycle weapons with the Dpad. Combat is usually pressing X between multiple enemies to beat them to a pulp via a chain of attacks, or to preform a counter attack if an enemy attempts to attack you. You can use abilities in combat, but I'll let you find them out yourself.
You can also get 3 Gems in your glove (There are more than 3, and you can swap what you have at a bench.) which do minor things to affect your game such as attack speed, and damage resist etc.
Thats it, really. I've probably missed something. Anyway It's a pretty fun game, try it out.
EDIT: I almost forgot! BUGS! I don't think this is due to my lag, it seems more like bugs, but Dashes don't always work to the full length of a dash. I seem to get caught on small bumps in the terrain, and can't dash up/down ramps at all. It's caused a few many deaths when Dashes don't work
Dashes also get me through the invisible walls that line the maps playable areas, and I can get stuck in those said walls, or stuck behind them. I bet I could use this to speed-run this game somehow, but it just gets me stuck.
Dashes and attacking props on the map can also make me sink into or even THROUGH the floor itself.
I've also gotten stuck on-top of an enemy, somehow. It happens mid-combat in the more laggy areas, so this might actually be lag. Enemies also get stuck on me, or hang mid-air sometimes aswell.
And to top it all off, Chest's loot doesn't always launch out properly, and can get stuck in the box! I'd like my apples and blue tomatoes please! Atleast gems and sword ore/essence pops out properly!

Everything good about retro RPG video games as well as classic pen and paper like Dungeons & Dragons is mixed into one wonderful experience in the form of Knights of Pen and Paper. In the game, you play as a group of friends, getting together to play Dungeons & Dragons. You're not just picking classes, but picking which "real life" person is playing the characters in game. Want grandma to be the paladin on your team? No problem! Think your little brother would be best suited as a stealthy rogue? You can do that too. Although the character creation is as simple as matching an archetype to a class (like Hipster Mage or Pizza Guy Druid), it's pretty fun and gives the game replayability as you want to experiment with different combinations.
The storyline is light, but definitely will bring back memories to anyone who has played Dungeons & Dragons in their lives. You travel through towns like "Journey Village" and battle monsters to save missing kings in a world full of pop culture references. It might be a bit silly if you're looking for a serious RPG, but if you love the classic turn-based battle style of the early Final Fantasy games, you'll at least appreciate the simple awesomeness of the gameplay. It's also hugely accessible and easy to learn for those who've never played that kinda game before.
You'll get the most out of this if you're just a huge RPG fan, because Knights of Pen and Paper relies a lot on nostalgia. Still, it's a really fun RPG that can eat up many hours of your life in a very satisfying way. It's a really good example of what indie game companies are capable of. Oh, and if you complain about the graphics, I have a fist to shake at you.

Antichamber is fantastically weird puzzle game that sees you exploring the halls of a trippy labyrinth trying to find your way out.
There is no story, no real motivation aside from get out, but the sheer weirdness and creativity the game initially hits you with is enough to get you hooked.  The first thrity minutes, or so, of Antichamber was an absolute blast.  By having no set up, you have no idea what to expect, and the game follows its own logic and mechanics which makes it very foreign for a decent bit of time.
Combined with a simplicstic art style that really extenuates the game design with bright use of color in contrast to the creepily white labyrinth, Antichamber is a truely unique experience that I absolutely loved.
Unfortunatly there is some bad.  For all the good, once the player begins to understand the rules the game really begins to lose its appeal and become a more generic puzzle game.  It's still good, but that initial wonderment and alienation really worked well.  Once you get really far, it becomes painful trial and error trying to find where to go next and how to advance.
For fans of puzzle games, Antichamber is a really cool games that ends up being a mix between Portal and the Stanley Parable.  For people who aren't in to puzzle games so much, there is still a solid hour of gameplay before you begin to understand what's going on.  If you can get it for low enough, it's still a good buy in that case.
