Okay, so: do you A.) Like Dungeons and Dragons-style adventuring games?
B.) Like playing actual D&D style games, on pen and paper?
C.) Would like to try a simulator of the two?
This is that game.
Will you like it? That's debatable.
I bought this game when it was a daily deal because I like pen and paper D&D-style games. Note that I had received all of the boosts from the digital deluxe version.
The retro-style graphics are a nice aesthetic, and there is quite a bit of variety with the creatures you will encounter in the game.
So the game plays with you as the DM (dungeon master) overseeing a game of D20 Knights of Pen and Paper. You have seats that can sit how ever many characters you would like to use, but the last few seats require you to pay the in-game currency. You can keep grinding to afford the seats in the future.
For each seat, you can sit a type of character (ex: hipster, grandma) and assign them a specific class (ex: barbarian, bard). This offers a seemingly wide range of party configurations.
The difficulty is completely self-driven, as you are both the DM and the players. That being said, you may have an "objective" to kill 5 orcs - you can choose to fight them 1-at-a-time, or all at once, or whatever configuration you prefer. The entirety of the game involves A LOT of grinding, and this is even considering the boosts you may have gotten from the deluxe edition.
I love D20 games, but this game can become repetitive extremely quickly. If there was a multiplayer cooperative functionality, it might have saved it a bit, however, there isn't one.
There is A LOT of variety for you to upgrade - you can change everything from the type of table you're playing on (each type provides different bonuses) to the type of door in the room to the DM. All of this can help shape your overall party into a specfic area, like tanky high HP characters, or high MP, magic-relying casters.
I paid ~$5 US for the deluxe edition, and I think even then you may want to hold off and wait for it to be cheaper, if you are interested in trying the game.

Civ V made a couple interesting changes to the gameplay, and IMO the devs did a good job overall with things, but they also also stumbled in ways that seem quite avoidable. V ostensibly makes the game more accessible to novice players, but some of the changes--such as significantly less specific information in diplomacy--end up hurting all players in the long run. The game tries to address some of the balance issues of Civ IV, and does so successfully on a number of fronts; However, in doing so it ends up creating new ones, such as how the changes to trading maps/techs ended up causing player exploration of the map to hit the wall of greatly diminishing returns much more quickly in most games. These are minor points, though, and 1) probably have more to do with the type of player I am than the game itself, and 2) are most likely only brought up because I had gotten used to them in earlier games. In the end this is still one of the best Civ games, and also one of the most balanced strategy experiences in the series, I think.

This game simply sets the new standards for what a remake should be. Somptuous graphics, amazing soundtrack, keeping the simple but powerful gameplay of the original game. Extremely faithful to the original game.
For those who don't know the original, this mostly a platformer, with some rpg elements (gold/equipment), and an unusual character progression, where each boss fight will transform you in a different character, with totally different skills and characteristics (one is smaller, one can fly, one can break some blocks, etc). Those skills almost always allow you to access new zones in places you already visited, making the world feel really big. It's also full of hidden secrets with really clever level design.
Only disappointment might be the new hard difficulty, that doesn't really add much to the game. All it does is make you lose a bit of health regularly, which doesn't impact much the game as much as it sounds (as long as you max potions before leaving for a long trip, or know where to farm them on the way).
Game is also very accessible, I'd recommend it at any age. Do not expect a lot of guidance though, even if there's a bit more information than on the original game, you still have to pretty much figure out everything by yourself.
Edit after a bit longer in game: some new zones have been added, and modify one mechanic of the original game (the charm stone one, that was quite obscure originally). While the idea is interesting, the design of those new zones feels one big step below the original ones.

Unlike a number of people reviewing this game, this is my first sojourn into the Dragon's Trap.  I never had a Sega Master System so this review will be done with the viewpoint of someone coming into the game for the first time.
Wonder Boy: The Dragon's Trap is one the of first Metroidvanias, even preceding that of the famous Castlevania: Symphony of the Night.  It is the second of the Monster World series (and the third Wonder Boy game) and a direct sequel of the first game, Wonder Boy in Monster Land.  It shares a lot of elements with Symphony and like it, begins right off at the end of another game, in this case: Wonder Boy in Monster Land.  You will also be locked out of certain areas until you cleared a previous one first and gaining an item or ability that enable access.
While Monster Boy in Monster Land was originally an arcade game (and ported to various systems), The Dragon's Trap was a console-only exclusive of the Sega Master System, the Nintendo Entertainment System's direct rival.
Fast forward, decades later.  Now we have this, Wonderboy: the Dragon's Trap developed and remade by Lizardcube.
The first thing to remember is at it's essence, it still is the same game as the original, meaning it has the typical length of a title of this kind for an 8-bit system.  Thus for anyone unfettered by nostalgic memories of playing the original, even with all its bells and whistles, any expectations of enjoying the length of a typical Metroidvania made in 1997 and beyond will be sorely disappointed.  It took me a few hours to win and only because of the few instances of getting stuck and wandering around before I could figure out what to do next.
I knew all this beforehand, that I was buying an 8-bit SMS title essentially and it was going to be pretty short.  So why did I buy this in the first place?  The wonderful art and the music, that's why!  The aestethics was just that good.  From the minute I saw the trailer, I knew I had to get it.
If you've been weaned on French style comic books like Asterix, Iznogoud and Ompa-Pa, you'll notice a resemblance in it's rugged detailed style.  The art is wonderful and the game animates like a dream (even on my old outdated laptop), like one of those aformentioned comics coming to life.
The music still uses the same score created by Shinichi Sakamoto in the SMS version but Lizardcube re-presents these same old tunes to be performed by professional musicians.  No midi tunes or techno, you will hear saxophones, pianos, flutes and more as you traipse all over Monster Land and it sounds glorious.  Like Akumajyou Densetsu (Castlevania 3 Japanese version) which I played for so many hours, it's a joy to re-play this game again and again just to listen to the wonderful music.
I played the first game, Wonder Boy in Monster Land in an Amiga 500 and always wanted to play the sequel.  Now I do and I've never been happier that I waited for so long and end up playing this marvelous remake.

Dying Light is definitely one of the better open world zombie apocalypse FPS games out of the bunch.
To me its reminicent of Dead Island, but... better (in a nutshell).
I certainly reccomend this game so I'll just get the bad points i've found out of the way first.
There are obviously a few kinks as there are with all games. Some personal little annoyances and let downs.
1. Loot variance... feels like im picking up the same stuff over and over again. Maybe if the scrap metal had been split up into different types of scrap metal. And tools had to be found in order to craft upgrades... subtle things like that expanded out to be more of a challenge to find specific items to make specific weapons and upgrade. Maybe i've just been playing too much DayZ-type zombie open world games... Its not bad, and it doesnt take the fun from the overall game. But it is a little gear grinder for me I had to point out.
2. Skills... If you found the skills upgrade styles in dead island (or farcry 3) a bit "meh", you'll probably find the same within dying light. Some skills were just pointless to me, while others just changed the game pace too much or exploded the game difficulty out of the water instantly. I found myself skipping on certain upgrades to keep both the pace of play and the challenge during my 2nd playthrough.
3. Storyline... Isnt the game's strong point, bit touch and go, and as everyone's saying, predictable, but i liked the characters and the one you play as. The sidequesting and other seperate interactions were what saved it for me. Some of them made me chuckle "if moma aint happy aint no one happy", while others just seemed more generally "legit" and fitting.
PROS
1. Gameplay - Fluent, addictive... just, bloomin' addictive! The parkour system is ace. And i was actually one of the guys who was verging away from buying this game at first because of it. That was a mistake! If you like parkour, buy this game. If you don't like parkour.... buy this game fool.
2. Scavenging - If you like the whole searching loot boxes for stuff, and grinding for stuff, and getting more STUFF so that you can get more STUFF and then get some more of that stuff? Do you like stuff? Good. Then buy this game.
3. Zombies - Yep, most convincing shuffling zombies i've seen in a game yet. Most convincing recently turned zombies still showing signs of human emotion before flipping back into their rampant zombie state. I'm no fan of over the top mutated monster zombies or BLADE 2 movie inspired vampire style zombies that only come out at night, but it was all actually an acceptable addition in this game tbh. They implemented it well. If you like zombies?... buy this game.
4 - Atmosphere - Yep, nailed it. Just like they did in Dead Island and Farcry games. The lighting and graphics are superb and makes you actually find a nice spot to stand and appreciate your surroundings and the views once in a while. The weather and day system doesn't just create a great atmosphere but changes the game entirely right down to it making you have to completely change up your tactics to get around town. If you like atmosphere and feels.... do it.... buy this game.
Will possibly edit 'n add to this review in time. In the meantime, you buy this game. You do it, you do it now.

Pros:
-The game looks and sounds great, and runs pretty well.
-Gunplay feels absolutely fantastic, the majority of guns kick realistically and are a blast to use.
-When playing with a coordinated team, it's often a great balance between relaxing moments of headshotting trash enemies while chilling with your friends and coordinating takedowns on larger enemies. Playing with people you know on higher difficulties turns the game into a challenging but satisfying experience where everyone does their role and helps each other.
-Often several different viable loadouts/perk setups to play with.
-Fairly active playerbase, lots of cool custom maps.
Cons:
-There are a ton of different ways for teammates to screw you and the team over (firebug lighting big enemies on fire, for example). Often, bad teammates get good teammates killed, and the game doesn't do much to reprimand them.
-No way to restrict high difficulty games to high-level players. Low level players lack certain perks needed to function properly at a high level, and are thus a burden.
-Some poorly explained ingame mechanics. Did you know that railgun loses 50% of its damage with autoaim enabled? Or that a Commando can extend Zed Time (ingame slowmo) significantly if he scores kills during it? Don't feel bad if you didn't, the game sure doesn't tell you.
-Questionable balance choices (spawnrage fleshpounds, crawlers that explode into gas clouds, etc.) Not gamebreaking, but often extremely annoying.
-Highly repetitive, though this may or may not be an issue for some.
Overall a fantastic wave-based PvE co-op game, but if you want to play on higher difficulties you NEED to have a group of friends you can rely on. Too much can go wrong with randoms.

Although seemingly simple in design, FTL: Faster than Light has continued to blow my mind with its overwhelming amount of content in such a simple form. From battling Space Slugs, and saving pirates from ship wrecks, to unlocking new ships and races as you play, to being stranded without fuel in the middle of the cosmos, this game will not disappoint you!
FTL: Faster Than Light is a top-down insterstellar space sim, featuring combat much like the old DnD computer games. You can pause and make decisions step by step, and watch your decisions play out moments after. Managing everything aboard your ship while aiming lasers and fighting enemy cruisers can be a lot to handle!
When I first watched the trailer, there was a lot of things going on, and many of which I didn't understand. Even still, I decided to jump right in to this space sim gone horribly right, and it was one of the best purchases on steam I've ever made. The big turning point when most players seem to realize just how complex this game is, is when you first learn to open your own airlocks, to put out fires, suffocate enemies, or even save the equipment in a room from enemies smashing them! New physics not considered anywhere else, that are so simple, that they astound you when you first learn about them.
While not every run will allow you the opportunity to play any way you want, that is also a part of the genius behind its design. You want to become a boarding ship, to take otu your enemies hand to hand? You better hope you run into a teleporter then, they won't always be available to you at every shop. Sometimes you don't run into weapons for a while, when you were saving up for a good weapon. You passed by some mid tier weapons only to realize all your money doesn't mean anything if you do not run into more along the way!
Overall FTL: Faster Than Light will keep you on your toes as you explore alien homeworlds, untraveled Nebulas, surprise bandits and environmental effects that will make each run of the game Unique in its own way. Evolving to meet the demands of each run is the way to success, as not everything always goes your way.
With the patch releasing the new Lanaris Race, the races 3 new ships, new weapons, and an extra ship layout for all previous races, this game will only become better.  So jump on the space train and ride your way into the next adventure awaiting you!

This is a great game if you can keep your completionist tendencies in check.
It's a novel game with cute mechanics and adorable cats and bunnies and foxes with swords. The game mostly focuses on three things: combat (which was okay), exploration (which was also okay), and choosing your own adventure by making choices between or, rarely, during stages. That last part is where the game shines. It's fun to go through and see what happens if you recklessly use the ancient artifact or listen to the evil gem that surely can't lead you to doom, right?
The problem is that combat and exploration get stale. No new enemies are introduced after the third playthrough. You'll get all the equipment and items after a similar amount of playthroughs, depending on how much you sidetrack and explore. So once it gets to about the fifth time going through the game there's no more character progression.
Combat becomes too easy and there's no incentive to make it less easy because you get more XP for not getting hit and you just want the thing to be over with so you use an OP combo (ice sword + energy on kill) to make combat short but boring. You no longer care about exploring once you found all the hidden lore and items, because all chests give you at that point at HP and energy which you don't need due to you just rushing through combat.
The game does do a good job of making stage traversal easier as you get more powerful (protip: unlock run speed as soon as you can) and unlock more shortcuts with new items. But still, once you get to the 8th-ish playthrough it becomes more of a chore than fun, as the reward of more plot / lore may not be enough to keep you grinding.
But it's okay! You only need to do 5 playthroughs in order to finish the game! You'll probably end up doing a couple more, but unless you are going for the 2 achievements that require you to level up to max level or unlock all the stories you don't need to grind to the point where the game is boring. But if you're one of those people who do want to 100% a game, beware that this game is a massive grind for 100%.

Orcs Must Die! is a nice twist on the traditional tower defence genre. Instead of building towers to defeat creeps (orcs), you set traps along their path. The game is played in third person view, so you can also kill orcs with your own spells and weapons too (similarly to Sanctum). OMD is exactly what it says on the box. You kill orcs in hundreds of different ways as they make their way to the end of the level. The premise is simple and it's fun to work out various strategies to kill orcs. Items, weapons, spells and weavers (special abilities) can all be used. Some levels are frustrating, though a bit of logical thinking goes a long way. The visuals are very smooth and fit into the laid back, humourous style of the game. The storyline and voice acting are a bit cheesy, but OMD doesn't take itself too seriously, which adds to the charm. Great game to play casually.

If you fell in love with Lee and Clementine during their hard-fought journey of survival in the Walking Dead universe, don't expect a full experience with Michonne's TellTale Episodes.
I made the mistake of expecting another deep and engaging narrative like that of Clementine and Lee, but instead I ended up with 3 episodes that felt way too short and also felt that it's plot was way too rushed. You barely have time to invest into any of the characters other than feel irritated with the bad guys who do a-hole things just to make the player hate them.
There are characters where you're probably supposed to care about and feel bad for when they get killed, but in reality, there's barely enough time to learn more about them or get emotionally invested in them other than to have them unceremoniously plopped right in front of you at that very moment just to unceremoniously die and establish how hateable the antagonist is.
I was expecting a 5-episode emotional roller coaster with one of the most bad♥♥♥♥♥characters in the Walking Dead Universe, and instead I only got 3 half-baked episodes that took a lot of shortcuts. It felt more like a quick cash-grab than a full-blown telltale Walking Dead game. 5 hours and I completed it, and greatly regretted spending cash on it.
I loved TWD Season 1 (Lee's story) and TWD Season 2 (Clementine's Story), but feel so DISAPPOINTED with TWD: Michonne. I applied for a refund because I can't believe Telltale would make such a "rushed" game for such great material.
TL:DR
If I had to rate the Telltale TWD games on a scale of 1-10, here are the scores:
The Walking Dead Season 1 (Lee) : 8/10
The Walking Dead Season 2 (Clementine) : 10/10
The Walking Dead : Michonne (Michonne) : 3/10
If you love the series and the previous games from Telltale, don't make the mistake I did in getting this half-baked addition to an otherwise stellar game series.

While I would recommend this game, and I will list the reasons why, I need to start off with the negatives.
The save system is probably the worst I've ever seen in a big budget RPG. You can save anywhere anytime into any file you want - except you can't. You can create a new copy of your last autosave from the last checkpoint you passed, but that's it. In a later part of the game I went through a cave, killed some monsters, got some loot, saved a guy and made him and the Canadian Princess my friends, and I went back into Ottawa. Saved. Quit. Reloaded and was put back in the cave. Sure I only lost a couple of minutes worth of progress, but how stupid is this? For a game that I beat in 13 hours, I should be able to save the minutiae of my equipment changes.
Also, I beat the game in 13 hours on normal difficulty, no guides used. This is a fair length as there's no downtime in the story, there's a whole bunch of sidequests I didn't do, and there's replay value in playing as other classes. Is that enough to buy the game off sale? Your mileage may vary.
While the story had no downtime, it didn't set up the final dungeon and bosses very well. I expected the story would be the first week of New Kid's stay in South Park, maybe 5 days. As day 3 drew to a close and the game was over, it caught me off guard. I'd been thinking of other things they could've added into the game, and what the logical progression of the main story would be. So while it wrapped up nicely, there wasn't a good buildup to it.
I had some issues with the controls. I used the 360 controller setup, and I never got fully accustomed to all the uses of the triggers and right analog stick, but that's on me. More importantly, I blame the game for the problems I had with tutorials and combat. The tutorials did a bad job of informing me why what I just did wasn't what it asked me to do. Combat is worse. Sometimes the terminology is iffy - a character's melee attack comes with the instruction of "Tap A when you see the blink", and I read tap as a repeated action, not as a single press.
But melee attacks are learned quickly; they have the same blink that comes with a sound prompt that gets you to press A or X at the right moment. All abilities aren't as forgiving; they'll tell you what to do, but not give any great visual or auditory clue of when to do it. They'll tell you "too soon" or "too late", but without an on-screen prompt it's still hard to learn the timing. Still, sometimes you'll get prompts for an ability or to dodge a boss's special move - even that can suck when it expects you to mash a random button and the strict countdown begins before you acn react to which button you're supposed to press.
That being said, moving on to the positives;
I really enjoyed the combat. There are some comparisons to be made to the classic pre-Wii Paper Mario games in that you have two choices of physical attacks (normal or ranged), enemies stand in lines so you can only use your normal attack on the guy in the front, and the timed button prompts of your actions significantly impact the effects of attacks.
I also enjoyed non-combat victory conditions that give me EXP. Gotta look around for not-quite-Rube Goldberg contraptions and set them up with a shot or fart to take out enemies before they can act. It almost felt a shame to pass on the opportunity to take part in the great battle system, but sometimes I just wanna save my speed potions for the boss, you know?
The graphics and voice acting are all 100% South Park, it's clear they had the people on board. Wandering around town, you can hear all sorts of music from the TV series being played over radios or whatnot.
I haven't watched South Park in years, and I didn't feel lost in any sense. I think they did a great job of retaining the identity of the show without alienating casual fans.
The amount of customization you can do with your appearance, your equipment, your abilities and perks is staggering.
The amount of sidequests that were made available to me exploring the town on day 1 were overwhelming.
Canada. Videogame jokes in a videogame that could only work in a videogame and yet be totally in line with South Park's portrayal of Canada.

This game is one of those games that is hella fun until you realize that the first couple hours which were so awesome are what you're going to be doing for the next X hours until you're done. I wanted to love this game, I really did. I've been fascinated with it ever since I first heard about the idea of playing an RPG about an RPG and I did manage to avoid paying full price (Steam sale or Humble Bundle, can't remember which anymore), but after about 6 hours with this game, I just gave up. The story was bad, the writing was bad, the gameplay was cool at first but devolved into being bad by way of mindlessly repetitive (as soon as I had 4 worthwhile party members [balance is another issue with the game, honestly] I found myself unconsciously falling into a pattern of using the same attacks every time because it was pretty much a guaranteed win), the humour (read: pop-culture references) is outdated and forced... The graphics are very nice, though. There's something to be said for well-done 8-bit pixel art. I'd say something about the soundtrack here, but after a while I just turned it off and played my own music. I felt that it added more to the "game about a game" experience than generic chiptunes, honestly. I mean, if I were running a game of D&D, I'd probably be playing power metal, not NES soundtracks.
Bottom Line: If you're midly curious, skip it. If you absolutely HAVE to play this game, at least wait until a sale or something. The game deserves some attention for its unique premise, but it's just not worth the full price. At all.

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter that combines frantic action with a dystopian story told seamlessly through the eyes of Gordon Freeman.
Half-Life 2. Where the heck do I begin? Firstly, I will tell you my only gripe. It is related with Valve and not the game. They continue to have Half-Life and all of the expansions at retail price even when it is a decade old. It is not marketable and the price should be lowered or be free for those who want to see the heart of classic games. Same with Half-Life 2.
The story in Half-Life 1, don't get me wrong, was great. The foreshadowing at the beginning leading up to the resonance cascade, the vivid and conflicted world and the characters interacting with you. The story was simple at its core. Get out of Black Mesa 'cause the creepy crawly aliens are coming. The story ended with a chat with G-Man, leaving you with a lot of questions. But there were many pieces that were not filled in.
Half-Life 2 takes that simple story of the resonance cascade and Black Mesa and runs with it. All the way. Valve made a rich environment in number 1, but this was an entire world they created in HL2. There are connections with the first story and you see some old friends from HL1 but this is really, really new stuff. The story is more complex, rich and filled with unanswered questions the deeper you look. Half-Life 2 is not your ordinary big-budget Micheal Bay explosion-filled "romp" action game. It deals with many philosophical and social issues, just in a hypothetical situation. The Combine and Dr. Breen may be fake, but we can gleam some knowledge in the real world. The story is not ultra-super-mega fast paced. It takes a while to build up parts of the story and leaves you with many thoughts. But we'll talk about that later. Half-Life 2 more often than not is a multi-genre game. It follows some fps conventions, but many times is transcends those lines. In parts, it feels like Horror game-ish as you anticipate for the next attack of zombies or other monsters. You create the horror for yourself. Other times it feels like a straight up action game as you run and gun through the streets of City 17.
Beyond defying specific genres, it defies a lot of game logic. Instead of providing exposition dumps through character interaction, it provides it in tidbits and leaves you to make it what you want. There are no cutscenes and you see everything through Gordon's eyes. Many games have loading screens that bridge levels or sections and almost always drop you in a different place. HL2, however, has minimal loading time and maps flow with each other and cohesively connect, making feel less like a game and more like a journey.
But it doesn't stop there. Half-Life 2 decides to defy storytelling as a whole. The Hero's Journey is a monomyth, a common platform or template to tell stories and myths. In Joseph Campbell's The Hero With A Thousand Faces, Campbell says that "A hero ventures forth from the world of common day into a region of supernatural wonder: fabulous forces are there encountered and a decisive victory is won: the hero comes back from this mysterious adventure with the power to bestow boons on his fellow man." The Hero's Journey is a circle, starting with the normal world at the characters status quo, and finishes back where he started, but fundamentally changed. Others say that The Hero's Journey is only a part of the modern hero monomyth and that there are different forms.
Half-Life 2 goes an entirely different direction. The status quo is non-existent. The story continues from HL1. There is no call to adventure or departure to a region of supernatural wonder, rather a trail of questions and questionable ethics following the Black Mesa incident. There is no specific time of trials or tribulations or a mentor that helps the hero along as seen in many a hero monomyth. Gordon is living the trials of others and is a leader without peer, trying to answer the very questions that led him to that moment in time. The most insignificant factor but the most important is that Cambell notes "Refusal of the summons converts the adventure into its negative. Walled in boredom, hard work, or 'culture,' the subject loses the power of significant affirmative action and becomes a victim to be saved. His flowering world becomes a wasteland of dry stones and his life feels meaningless—even though, like King Minos, he may through titanic effort succeed in building an empire or renown. Whatever house he builds, it will be a house of death: a labyrinth of cyclopean walls to hide from him his minotaur. All he can do is create new problems for himself and await the gradual approach of his disintegration." Gordon is not able to hide from "his minotaur". The actions have already been set in motion and are premeditated by the G-Man. The rise and fall of HL2's story, its peaks, and troths, at some point, begin to meld together. Not as constructive interference but as destructive interference. The different aspects of the geopolitical conflict between the humans and the Combine meld and are unrecognizable but visible if you look through the thin sheen of action game it presents its self to be. When these peaks and troths are light waves, destructive interference produces darkness. Similar to Gordon's predicament, he is thrown into a time of darkness. Not only for the value of human life and the situation that the inhabitants of Earth find themselves in but also a time of darkness socially. The world is collapsing at the fundamental seams and Gordon cannot reverse the effects.
Half-Life 2 is a complex game. It is rich and complex as I said at the beginning. Ever since its inception, Half-Life has held up. Through age, the evolution of the market and even changes at Valve, it is still here. It, Stuart Brown said, is "heralded as a shining star in the first person shooter genre that rubs shoulders with the greats..."
Whichever way you see the story or the gameplay is your choice. Just please try and appreciate it.
And buy the darn game.

XCOM is a great tactical game that is tough but fair on your bad decisions. If you leave a unit exposed and you have no units left to perform actions with that turn, that unit will either take a huge beating or die. But, if you just think a little about your actions, some really cool and satisfying things can happen: I once flanked a veritable batallion of aliens by blowing a hole in the back of their ship with a rocket launcher and had my assault charge in guns blazing with a shotgun. They were all dead by the end of next turn.
I also cannot recommend enough the great gameplay extending and expanding content of the expansion, Enemy Within, which adds such things as big effing robots, supersoldiers and an entirely new enemy to contend with.
If you complete the campaign on at least classic difficulty, I can also heartily recommend the Long War mod, which makes your campaign of alien eradication much longer and makes defeat a much more distinct possibility, in addition to adding larger squad sizes, completely retooled class skill trees that bring the number of soldier/MEC classes to 16, increased depth to the game's aerial combat and an overall more tooth-grinding tense experience to the alien invasion. And if my word isn't good enough, one of the developers for XCOM: Enemy Unknown has praised the mod highly, likening it to an entirely free expansion for the game.

My Position: Currently have 66 hours in game and have max level and all achievements.
Summary: Steep is the first AAA title to return to the Extreme Winter sports game scene after the genre ran dry for several years. Developed by Ubisoft, it has many of the drawbacks and advantages that come with being the firs tto return to the genre as well as being devolped by a majopr company.
Buy or no buy? Depends. Here are some pros and cons that I have run into in Steep.
+Pros:
Unrivaled polish for the genre
Graphics are stunnign on max
Great Environment that can be explored pratcially forever
Partial Multiplayer Experience (more later)
Party System (More later)
Decent update rate with more maps and gamemodes coming
Comprehensive Player Customization
-Cons:
THE PRICE
THE OPTIONAL (however surprisingly unobtrusive) MICROTRANSACTIONS
OK party system that caps at 4
Physics that can seem slidy at times
Multiplayer system that often leaves the game feeling empty
Stange Stamina meter physics that makes any good trick feel like complete luck
Incomplete Dare system that won't let you even name your own challenges or share them publicly
graphics that run ok at lower settings but scale very poorly. (i.e. Higher settings become harder to run exponetially)
Points of Interest are almost to compeltely find without a guide (Could be a plus for some, though I doubt it)
2-3 challenges are near impossible to beat (Though many are fixed now)
Conclusion: I am a little harsh on this game, mostly out of love, but also because there are problems with the game that I feel make the game forgetable. Part of the appeal of the extreme sports genre is how timeless they can become and how warmly the people who play them look back on them.
So do I think players will look back on Steep with warm hearts 5-10 from now? NO. While other titles like SNOW (A free to play on Steam) come nowhere close to Steep in terms of quality, I have no doubt that other large game companies are looking at what Steep here and taking note.
Expect to see EA Winter Sports coming soon, as well as other large names entering the field after Steep. Perhaps when gamers go to open their history books, they'll see Steep as the first quirky little seed of a larger green forest.
Thanks for reading. :D

A lot like Spleunky, except with preset levels (not that you can really tell - most of them look about as chaotic and nondescript as the average Spleunky level), more focused on "winning" than merely "surviving", and with a lot more digging.
The platforming isn't so great - the jumping is very laggy, and you dig (well, "drill", to be precise) by holding a movement key when you're against a block. Problem being that if you're digging left or right, your character will start moving in that direction the INSTANT the block is dug out, which can result in some really cheesy bulls­hit deaths. Either having a "hold position" toggle, allowing one to dig but not move, or simply freezing the character in place when digging until the movement key is pressed a second time would help a lot.
It's not beyond all redemption and if you can get past the poor play control, there's a fair smidgen of fun to be had. If I could vote "neutral" this would be a neutral, but all in all this is more frustrating than fun, especially at $7.99. The in-game text and store description are very personable and it gives me the impression that the dev is out there and cares, so who knows, it may well get patched into a more playable, fluid state!

If you like any of The Walking Dead games made by Telltale - and chances are that you do, you will like this game.
It's a bit short, the moral choices are slightly easier and it isn't quite as heartwrenching, but in its core The Walking Dead: Michonne is a true Telltale adventure game, with all the good that comes of it.
The visuals are stellar, as are the voice acting and the soundtrack. The story is compelling and interesting, exploring the character of Michonne while telling a new story about different characters.
Note this game has a bit more 'action' than most of the other Walking Dead games made by Telltale.
The game shines in the choices you make during the game, which alter what happens and make the whole story feel much more personal. Knowing somebody is either dead or alive because of you, makes the interactions with them all the more gripping.
In short - if you like good stories, The Walking Dead (Any version of it), Telltale or adventure games with moral choices, you will love this game - even if it is a little short.
If you don't like wonky combat, and games with a lot of talking, perhaps this isn't for you.

As a veteran player of RPG games, I first purchased Divinity: Original Sin with a 'Ho-Hum' attitude.
Looked like the sort of game where I had been there, done that, got a closet full of those tee-shirts.
Wow, was I wrong.
First mistake I made was customizing my characters via character creation without understanding the game. Wasted a few hours playing them to finally realize that I had nerfed myself badly with characters that had no synergy, duplicate skills, or spells. This game will not hold your hand and will gleefully let you make all the assinine mistakes you wish.
I have not been stuck in an rpg game for years. Most of the time you go in knowing what to expect; Divinity: Original Sin throws all of those ideals out the window. You can fry, electrocute, burn, poison, and otherwise main and kill your own party members, pick all the wrong skills, spells and talents, and etc.
The combat at first was brutal and advancement was difficult. In each fight, one or more members of my party died and had to be ressurected, with each battle barely won by the skin of my teeth.
Now for the good news. After you go to school, take your lumps and learn your lessons. You can start over again with a new party that is better and more thoughtfully created.
Then you will find that those hard battles before are actually very winnable, using a synergy oriented party, better tactics, taking into account the terrain, the surronding elements and objects that you can use to your advantage.
You learn to ask, "Will blowing up that barrel of flammable liquid, be a better use of my spell that targeting that Orc?", or "Will moving this crate, or teleporting that object (or the enemy) change the dynamics of the battle?"
Speaking of combat, you will do yourself no favors assuming the A.I. is going to act in a predictable manner. Even restarting a save after having your behind handed to you, and going back to try again doesn't mean the battle will act out like the previous battle did. The A.I. does a great job of using the enviroment as well, targetting the right people at the right time, acting in harmony, and otherwise being a down right pain in the unmentionable.
Divinity: Original Sin also has some great moments that makes the game world feel real and connected. You may read a sign in one town, and then met someone in the wilderness who's story or actions connect to that obscure sign back in town. You may overhear a conversation in a tavern, and then find something in a dungeon or some remote spot, that makes you remember what you overheard.
Additionally, Divinity: Original Sin supports Multi-Player. However that is a mixed bag and I have mixed feelings on it. For example, its a minor gripe that I can't make my own character, that is multi-player only and level it up through joining other peoples games.
Also, not Larian's fault, but I have seldom joined a game that 'worked'. What I mean by worked is, they are either AFK, kick you as soon as you join (??), or I have had a time or two, where just because you didn't play as they would play the character, they would kick you (and I consider myself to be a decent player that uses forethought and tactics).
In other words, if your doing Multi-player, stick with doing it with friends or otherwise don't expect much, because it's just not going to happen from 90% of the experiences I have had.
Pros:
Lots of humorous moments both in the game and in dialogue.
Character banter and interaction that makes for great roleplaying.
Challenging difficulty in battles that is actually refreshing and forces you to think.
Character Creation that lets you customize to your hearts content.
Sufficent Classes you can choose from, or custom create a hybrid of your own.
Great and interesting Talents to choose from.
Lots of content.
Many Elements and Spells, to satisfy even the most demanding Casters.
Reputation System that lets you be as good or as bad as you want to be.
Be a hero, be an Assassin, or be a Harbinger of Doom to foe and citizen alike. Nothing is off limits or unkillable.
Fast response on bug fixes, updates and patches
Mod support (Nothing out there yet, but the game is very new)
Multi-Player Support.
Cons:
Doesn't hold your hand anywhere at anytime
You have to learn some of Divinity's obscure game mechanics on your own (odd but I consider that a plus also).
Difficulty can be challenging and a player can waste hours building a party that just will not work.
Occassional bug has been stumbled upon, so far nothing game stopping.
The inventory management could be a tad better (such as limited sorting, stacking, etc).
Multi-Player support (joining works, but no character of your own, so no feeling of investement, and no real motivation)
Conclussion:
I recommend Divinity: Original Sin whole-heartedly. If someone is new to RPGs, it may be a baptism by fire, but this could be the game that is one of the rare cross-overs, people will play even if they are not typically RPG inclined.
If anyone is into RPGs, it will be in your gaming libary eventually, if it's not already.
Your computer chair will have a big mark in it by the time you get up.
All-in-all, the game is fine as long as you have a good PC. Mine isn't the best, but I'm willing I would be hooked if I could get past the Medieval era.

Well, this is my third Walking Dead game to review, and I'm sad to say it's the one I least liked (Walking Dead and Season 2 before it). Telltale once again did an excellent job of storytelling, and provided a way for players to be engaged in the action as well as the story without compromising it, but the game felt rushed and was far too short. This review will contain spoilers, so if you wish to avoid them, STOP READING.
SPOILERS FOLLOW:
I completed it in 3 hours without rushing anything; taking my time with each choice, and the ending felt unsatisfying (You should go back with your group. I will, when I'm ready). The majority of the game was one big, neverending PTSD attack about her leaving her daughters since she and her husband were getting divorced, and while I can respect that option of storytelling, it took up far too much of it for it to be a Walking Dead game. The antagonists were predictable; reciting how much of the good guys they are when they have a path of executed people behind them. Characters, like every Telltale game judging you harshly if you so much as pick up a spoon off the floor, but unlike the first two games, the main character doesn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥and will kill if necessary, and not feel bad about it. The first game and Season 2 at least had 5 episodes each that took around an hour and a half - two hours depending, but this one felt rushed compared to those two having only 3 short episodes that took an hour at best to complete. I am glad the game was made though because that unexplained gap in the comics ticked me off so much; "Where is Michonne going? Why is she leaving? Why didn't they explain anything when she came back? Did she just need some alone time?" Seriously, good on you, Telltale Games for making the game. Was worth every penny for me, but it's earned 3rd place among the other two games.
If you love The Walking Dead, and if you love Telltale games, you'll enjoy The Walking Dead: Michonne. At this point, if you'd played the other two games, it's no question that this one deserves a go too.

I absolutely love this game. This really follows the play styles of Baldur's Gate 1 & 2 with modern graphics and modern gameplay. The game world is highly interactive, the ground is on fire? Cast a rain spell to put it out. Enemies standing in a pool of water or a pool of blood? Lightning bolt it and electrocute them all!
Another great thing about D:OS is how awesome it is to be a mage in this game. This game does not have any type of mana system. All skills are controlled by action points and cool downs. So you can always cast your favorite spells when you want to, no micromanaging MP and conserving spells.
This game is challenging, even on normal. It feels like it has been balanced properly since the Early Access where it was even more difficult. It's also possible i knew the progression after playing D:OS the second time. I recommend digging in the graveyard and going out the Western gate of the town before you attempt to go north or east. Level gaps between enemies are a huge deal. if you're level 4 and you fight a level 8 enemy you can win. If you're level 4 and you fight 4 level 8 enemies, you're likely going to wipe.
The other thing about this game it constantly seems to get bigger. When I initially played D:OS, it felt like the map was small. Then i realized there are many more maps outside of the first one. North goes to Silverglen the next town, from there you can go east to Hunter's Edge the 3rd town. There are warps to other areas such as the winter world Hiberheim. There are many dungeons involved with quests.
One of the awesome things about this game is how much freedom you're given. Just like all games there is a mostly linear story line, but like Baldur's Gate 2, you're given a wide range into how you go about it. Want to ignore the current quest and just go fight really tough enemies pushing yourself to the edge? You can do that. Want to go back and mop up easy enemies and roll through quests for the XP rewards? You can do that.
The skill system in the game is about as perfect as you can ask for. The one slightly confusing thing about it, is leveling skills up to higher levels than 1. It takes 1 SP for 1, it takes 2 SP for 2, it takes 3 SP for level 3 and so on. It seems most level ups only come with 1 skill point, so in my original time playing I had tons of skills at level 1 from spending my points immediately. The game rewards you for conserving your skill points. You also have talent points that are rarer ala Fallout type talents like "scientist" that gives +1 to crafting and black smith, "all skilled up" that gives you 2 bonus talent points. And 2 of the ultimate talents "Glass Cannon" (used to be named Raistlin, sad they changed it, i assume copyright risks) which halves you HP and doubles your action points in combat. The reference to Raistlin Majere is the bad♥♥♥♥♥but frail mage from Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman's Dragonlance series. The other skill is "Lone Wolf", which as the name suggests is for your solo play throughs. It basically doubles your hero's power by making it impossible to have companions. You can combine Glass Cannon with Lone Wolf if desired.
Some other random tips, your tank does not need a shield. If anything it seems far better off to use a 2H weapon with your main tank. They do so much more damage. Just grab talents that increase armor and HP for your main tank. Another great early skill for your tank is "Attack of Opportunity". Enemies that try to disengage get attacked by the player for free (think overwatch for melee characters that is always active), it also seems to rob the enemy of action points/movement distance.
There's not many player characters in the game, you build 2 at the start and there's 2 in Cyseal town Madora a 2H warrior in the Inn and a Mage in the Library. The way you get your team up to 4 players without them, after you unlock the End of Time (Go Go Chronotrigger reference!), and unlock the Hall of Heroes, a little bit after that a NPC shows up in the South end of the Hall of Heroes that lets you recruit companions. You get many options, they're level bound too. So if you're high level and decide you need an Off Tank or a Dedicated Healer, you can pick up already leveled companions. WIthout this feature, you could be screwed by your party choice. There is no respawn in this game. When enemies are dead, they are gone forever. So there is only so much you can kill in the game. If you needed to roll new companions you'd  run out of stuff to grind. This is the most anti-grinding game ever. The enemies do not scale with you like Skyrim, the loot scales with you. Aside from several uniques, there is no sneaking into a high level dungeon and running off the with Ragnarok and owning the game. It also makes it interesting that when you get item quest rewards from early quests completed late, you get items that might be relevant. Same for NPCs, when they restock items, or if you never engage in trading with them, even town members in Cyseal can end up with Legendaries for sale, or other item level 10 and so forth items. The NPCs are your friend, many sell usable items, always be on the look out for items sold by NPCs. Also this game is great for stealers. You can take everything that's not nailed down and you can sell anything to anyone. There is no magic knowledge this item was stolen and only special fencing NPCs will accept them. I love to steal the items on the shops' walls and counters and then sell them to the very same NPC.
tl;dr: Do you like Baldu'r's Gate 2? INSTALL THIS NOW.

Stories: The Path of Destines is a really nice little gem of a game. It was worth the money and the time.
There are bits of humor that make you smile throughout and some bad dad puns as well. The mechanics are simple and well put together. You can beat the game once but you'll want to continue trying until you get the "true ending." This might occur after your fifth attempt or so. If you are going to beat the game in less than five tries you won't see all of the endings (20+).
Is it worth it to see all of the endings? For the narration and story elements -absolutely. However the mechanics and combat are something you are racing through just to see how the story ends after the 10th+ attempt. Sadly, you can not skip past some of the dialogue (some you can). Regardless of that you'll still keep moving through because you want to see the endings. They are varied and interesting.
Even if you only beat it a few times it's still fun powering up your character. It's unfortunate that when you move to your 10th try and onward there is no real improvements to make. There are minor adjustments to make with each level increase but by this point you've gathered all of the cool items and played around with your desired load-out of items. Beautiful but Flawed.
Greatness lurks beneath the skin of The Banner Saga. It is a beautiful, emotionally involving and utterly unique experience, but sadly I found this first installment to be marred by a host of frustrating design problems.
The artistic vision of The Banner Saga is without peer. Its world, characters and story are depicted with rare clarity and conviction, without compromise. The visual style is bleak yet gorgeous and can be mistaken for no other game. The music (by the talented Austin Wintory of 'Journey' fame) powerfully evokes a forlorn, dying world. The writing too is excellent throughout, defining tragic characters with sombre nuance.
The combat in the game is also novel and interesting, with great tactical depth. Battles are tense and strategic, and the developers succeeded admirably at weaving it into the storyline - battles affect choices and choices affect battles, each adding meaning to the other. That a turn-based combat game kept me so enthralled with its story (an unremittingly bleak one, at that) is a testament to the talent and passion of the studio.
That said, at the same time everything feels somehow underproduced; voice acting and animation are conspicuously absent in all but a few scattered scenes, and each character has one fixed expression - which can sometimes be incredibly inappropriate to the dialogue. While it is true that the art design of the game is deliberately spare, my impression was that some things had been over-simplified, as if the game had been rushed to completion.
Minor cosmetic issues aside, the game felt unfinished in other more problematic ways. It crashed several times for me, and on each occasion I suffered from poorly placed autosaves. The combat interface also frequently proved vague or incomplete, in many cases failing to explain critical rules. One consistent frustration was the inability to undo or preview character movement, in cases where the (often severe) consequences of a particular move could not be determined beforehand - this did not seem like a deliberate choice, but as with the incomplete UI more likely due to a lack of playtesting.
The most frustrating aspect of the game, for me, was the handling of player narrative choices. This story is one of loss and hopelessness, so as such I accept that there are no happy endings to be found, but rather a series of tragedies to be survived. And as in combat, the player is asked to make difficult decisions, with no clear right answer - but unlike in combat, the consequences are utterly random. In combat, the player is asked to make careful choices and is rewarded with various bonuses on success. These bonuses usually relate to specific characters, as do the combat choices, so this feedback cycle works well, strengthening engagement with the characters and story in a satisfyingly consistent way.
Narrative choices on the other hand, often reward the player with an unforeseeable slap in the face, throwing away much of their prior hard work - for example by stealing away a character in whom the player had already invested a lot of time and emotional energy. I question why player choice is involved at all, if it does not involve skill. If the intended purpose was to make the player identify with the hopelessness of the characters' situation, then this would have worked better if the choices embodied clear tradeoffs: in a bad situation, allow the player to pick which sacrifice to make, based on what is more important to them or to the character. But by consistently leaving me feeling cheated and powerless, by the end of the game it merely served to reduce my engagement with the characters and plot.
Years from now I feel sure that I will remember The Banner Saga more for its strengths than for its weaknesses. The beauty of the experience implies a great deal of talent, and the various flaws are all fixable - as such I still highly recommend the game, and have high hopes for its sequels!

While I would recommend this game, and I will list the reasons why, I need to start off with the negatives.
The save system is probably the worst I've ever seen in a big budget RPG. You can save anywhere anytime into any file you want - except you can't. You can create a new copy of your last autosave from the last checkpoint you passed, but that's it. In a later part of the game I went through a cave, killed some monsters, got some loot, saved a guy and made him and the Canadian Princess my friends, and I went back into Ottawa. Saved. Quit. Reloaded and was put back in the cave. Sure I only lost a couple of minutes worth of progress, but how stupid is this? For a game that I beat in 13 hours, I should be able to save the minutiae of my equipment changes.
Also, I beat the game in 13 hours on normal difficulty, no guides used. This is a fair length as there's no downtime in the story, there's a whole bunch of sidequests I didn't do, and there's replay value in playing as other classes. Is that enough to buy the game off sale? Your mileage may vary.
While the story had no downtime, it didn't set up the final dungeon and bosses very well. I expected the story would be the first week of New Kid's stay in South Park, maybe 5 days. As day 3 drew to a close and the game was over, it caught me off guard. I'd been thinking of other things they could've added into the game, and what the logical progression of the main story would be. So while it wrapped up nicely, there wasn't a good buildup to it.
I had some issues with the controls. I used the 360 controller setup, and I never got fully accustomed to all the uses of the triggers and right analog stick, but that's on me. More importantly, I blame the game for the problems I had with tutorials and combat. The tutorials did a bad job of informing me why what I just did wasn't what it asked me to do. Combat is worse. Sometimes the terminology is iffy - a character's melee attack comes with the instruction of "Tap A when you see the blink", and I read tap as a repeated action, not as a single press.
But melee attacks are learned quickly; they have the same blink that comes with a sound prompt that gets you to press A or X at the right moment. All abilities aren't as forgiving; they'll tell you what to do, but not give any great visual or auditory clue of when to do it. They'll tell you "too soon" or "too late", but without an on-screen prompt it's still hard to learn the timing. Still, sometimes you'll get prompts for an ability or to dodge a boss's special move - even that can suck when it expects you to mash a random button and the strict countdown begins before you acn react to which button you're supposed to press.
That being said, moving on to the positives;
I really enjoyed the combat. There are some comparisons to be made to the classic pre-Wii Paper Mario games in that you have two choices of physical attacks (normal or ranged), enemies stand in lines so you can only use your normal attack on the guy in the front, and the timed button prompts of your actions significantly impact the effects of attacks.
I also enjoyed non-combat victory conditions that give me EXP. Gotta look around for not-quite-Rube Goldberg contraptions and set them up with a shot or fart to take out enemies before they can act. It almost felt a shame to pass on the opportunity to take part in the great battle system, but sometimes I just wanna save my speed potions for the boss, you know?
The graphics and voice acting are all 100% South Park, it's clear they had the people on board. Wandering around town, you can hear all sorts of music from the TV series being played over radios or whatnot.
I haven't watched South Park in years, and I didn't feel lost in any sense. I think they did a great job of retaining the identity of the show without alienating casual fans.
The amount of customization you can do with your appearance, your equipment, your abilities and perks is staggering.
The amount of sidequests that were made available to me exploring the town on day 1 were overwhelming.
Canada. Videogame jokes in a videogame that could only work in a videogame and yet be totally in line with South Park's portrayal of Canada.

XCOM is a great tactical game that is tough but fair on your bad decisions. If you leave a unit exposed and you have no units left to perform actions with that turn, that unit will either take a huge beating or die. They were all dead by the end of next turn.
I also cannot recommend enough the great gameplay extending and expanding content of the expansion, Enemy Within, which adds such things as big effing robots, supersoldiers and an entirely new enemy to contend with.
If you complete the campaign on at least classic difficulty, I can also heartily recommend the Long War mod, which makes your campaign of alien eradication much longer and makes defeat a much more distinct possibility, in addition to adding larger squad sizes, completely retooled class skill trees that bring the number of soldier/MEC classes to 16, increased depth to the game's aerial combat and an overall more tooth-grinding tense experience to the alien invasion. And if my word isn't good enough, one of the developers for XCOM: Enemy Unknown has praised the mod highly, likening it to an entirely free expansion for the game.

I had my eye on this game for a very long time before I bought it, and when i finally rounded up the money, i bought it straight away, and lemme tell ya -worth every penny spent- after only 4-5 days i had around 10 hours in the game. The limitless exploration, the thrilling challenges, the nerd gasm worthy graphics, the fluent movement, perfect atmosphere and absolutely amazing sound track makes this game possibly one of the best games i have ever played. Which says a lot from me, a hack n slash kinda player.
I'll go through each of the things i listed above, just to convince you to get this game even more:
1. Exploration
The game gives you plenty chance to explore, and the game even constantly urges you to do so with the dialogue of the game (which is actually pretty darn good too). I've gone on several runs alone, just to see what i havent seen (which there is still a lot). There's just so much to see, whilst also feeling like a total badass as you shred jump after jump.
2. Challenges
The game's medium and hard difficulty runs are actually crazy difficult and pull you in to complete the challenge very well. Ive spent up to 20 minutes sometimes just to get that gold medal, and its such a relieving feeling.
3. Graphics
The graphics make the game breath taking almost every moment. That's all you need to know.
4. Animations
The animations are so fluent and realistic sometimes you almost feel as if you're inside of the game, especially when looking at replay in first person and listening to the freakishly realistic audio from your gopro. The way the snow carves with every movement is so satisfying. The life in the character you play is real and nearly perfect. Your clothing moves in the wind, just thought you might need to know that, cus i find it awesome.
5. Atmosphere
Your surroundings make it always feel as if you're the best skiier/boarder tackling the hardest slopes.
6. Music/Sounds
The music can either make you feel like the coolest guy on the mountain, or quite relaxed and feeling you're just there for a good time, without putting out your attention or bringing boredom, which few relaxed games can do. The ambient sounds feel so natural and great, as with the crumpling or sliced snow beneath you as you carve down the mountain or take a trek up the mountain to reach the best spots.
In conclusion, buy the bloody game!

Grim Dawn is a really amazing ARPG (Action Roleplaying Game, a.k.a. Diablo-style game).
The world takes place in an apocalyptic world with old-timey shotguns, zombies, and magic. Lots of magic. The world is gritty and interesting, flowing with atmosphere that reeks of Dark Souls inspiration. This is a good smell to have.
The combat is very fun. Each hit on an enemy feels heavy - like there's some weight to it. There's standard health/energy(mana) potions, yet I've never had to use them until I started fighting more hero enemies. The constitution (health regen) system works really well to keep downtime to a minimum. When your health goes down, after combat is done, you regenerate health from your smaller constitution bar, which then goes down. You refill constitution by finding food in the world, which is pretty frequent if you explore the map.
It seems complicated, but it's not.
The skill/class system is refreshing. Basically, you invest points into your class to unlock new skill nodes, and skills can be leveled/extended with passive abilities, which alter or extend their capabilities. Once you hit level 10, you can invest points in a second class, which then results in a new class name altogether (Demolitionist + Occultist becomes Pyromancer).
Loot drops (important in ARPGs) feel pretty damn good in this game. There's no magic find stat (which is counter-intuitive anyway), so they've balanced things in such a way that you feel like you get just enough awesome loot to keep wanting to look for more.
Chests/bosses pretty much have a guarantee of
good dropping, and merchants occasionally carry green-rarity equipment (yellow -> green -> blue is the progression here).
Each merchant's stock refreshes every time you teleport somewhere. Green equipment cost a lot of currency, so being able to refresh their inventories feels like a fair trade for having an easier time finding a rare item.
There's no waypoint scrolls (Thank you, Crate!). You can open a rift (portal) whenever you want, so the game feels very mobile. Yet, you'll usually want to explore every inch of every area, thanks to secret areas hidden behind breakable walls, quests you can find, hero minibosses, and so on.
The game is still in Early Access, yet the foundation is strong and there's plenty of content to sink hours upon hours into. I recommend getting it when you can, and enjoying the game as it continues to evolve. The future's looking bright.
If you enjoy games where your actions have consequences and you have the freedom to do almost anything you want, this game is perfect for you.  It sets a new standard for turn based RPGs.

Update:
After finally mustering up the attention span to finish the game, I'd have to say that the last half of the game is extremely underwhelming. There's no satisfying loot. The story ends up becoming a masturbatory tosser by the end. The tactical feel looses its edge as the developers get lazy with balancing and combat scenarios, with the game distilling down to "tried and true" by character level 10 since the game's enemies never really get more varied or intelligent.
I think the most disappointing part of the game was the last stretch through the Phantom Forest. The story basically is grasping at what uninteresting and forced story elements it's shoved in your face for the last 40 hours of slowly from objective to objective. The "nature" of the two main characters isn't some sort of revelation at the end, they flaunt it particularly often and it's extremely bothersome at this last third or so of the game. On top of it: the last boss fight is a ♥♥♥♥ing escort mission.
The first half of the game is definitely more enjoyable- there was more of a carrot on a stick to how things were paced. It wasn't spectacular or anything, but it was somewhat enjoyable despite all the bugs we were running in to. For whatever reason, that carried on less and less with each additional area. The in-party dialog choices began with so many choices and end up with rail-roaded single responses at the end, even squandering the climax as both characters interact with the antagonist.
Speaking of the antagonist, it's mostly a case of "bait and switch". Aside from being "super evil" and "bad", there's little this antagonist has done to you. Likewise, the antagonist before was basically the main suspect of your initial reason for being in the area. While she was doing dark and sinister things, really what she was guilty of was ♥♥♥♥ing with the local populace and sacrificing tributes to the void god. It was all phoned-in, so to speak. Typical portrayals of morality, all around. Black and white differences with all characters. The closest moral ambiguity comes from Arhu, whom is a side character at best and still not very interesting.
Why this game has earned so much praise, I'll never know. The plot is basically porno level; it exists just to give the characters something to do to showcase the promising but ultimately routine combat. I'm chalking it up to the lack of computer RPGs, but even the aged Fallout and Fallout 2 are more satisfying and much more superior experiences. Mods will be the saving grace of this game.
Original review:
Divinity: Original Sin is a decent RPG. Combat is a turn-based blender of Fallout (1/2) with a helping of cRPG D&D rules and some Dragon Age flair. There's a lot of player agency and the game, for the most part, open for the player to explore and do as they please. All positive notes, as far as I'm concerned.
The game actually offers cooperative play, where each player controls one of the two main characters, and can even split off from each other within the same map. Players can even “interact” with dialog choices between the two players, which colors the character’s “personality” by giving traits that affect their skills and abilities, but the player characters don’t really grow or change with time as they’re always presented two binary choices and the occasional third choice and fourth situational choice. There's a lot to do, but even if it's a decent RPG, I don't think I could say it's a "must play". Here’s why:
The game has some problems. In its quest to not baby the player, which is commendable, it may have gone to extremes by making some systems obtuse. Crafting and the inventory system in general is a mess. While the player is able to "craft" by dragging items on to one another or on to specific blacksmithing fixtures, its a very bare and unintuitive system. Even when the player is presented with similar items or base materials, the methods used are very strict. For example: arrow shafts can only be crafted out of branches, and not logs. Logs can be turned into a branch-like item (a stake) and a few others, but nothing that can result in arrow shafts. Iron is the only material that can be made in to swords, silver can only be made in to arrowheads. See what I'm getting at? Another problem is that learned recipes for crafting are gathered from tomes. These tomes are recorded in the journal, which tell the player how to make a particular item. The problem is that there’s no assistance in the matter when in the actual inventory- even adding a highlight when dragging an item to show what items your character has learned will combine would be enough. It’s a slow and tedious process.
The inventory itself is a weight based one with seemingly unlimited slots, not that I've ever reached an end. Quickly, the inventory becomes a mass of crafting materials, unused scrolls and reading materials, with limited ways to sort these pocket-clogging items. Sorting can be done by weight, worth, and what order they were picked up in. Backpacks can be used to group similar items, but they are share identical icons and (most) have the same name. It quickly becomes a game of either dumping materials, hoarding and selling materials, or jamming them all into storage.
Another terrible design choice is the charm/intimidate/reason system. Picking one of the options will prompt, I♥♥♥♥♥♥you not, a “rock paper scissors” battle. Each time a side wins, they get a few points depending on how skilled they are at that type of persuasion. A side wins the dialog when they reach ten points. It is, without a doubt, the most unsatisfying dialog system ever. Keep in mind: in coop, when one player is doing a persuasion check the other can’t see what’s going on. Failing persuasion checks ends up in combat 80 or 90 percent of the time. Also, the persuasion system is present when two players in coop disagree. The player that wins ends up being the leader for the decision in game.
The game has a lot of bugs, which are slowly being ironed out. T-poses from resurrections, player characters having one-sided conversations or having inappropriate responses to dialog (egomaniac choice prompting a monolog lamenting how “nice” they’ve become), music and sound effects not playing and the occasional "stuck" AI enemy that is unwilling to take a turn. There's also the occasional crash, so the rule of the game is: save, save, save.
You'll probably want to save the game a lot, anyway, as dice rolls have a huge effect on battle. Parties can be knocked down, frozen or stunned for a huge portion or entirety of a battle, forcing the player to reload and start again. Even small things, like characters not moving a short distance, but still using the action point when moving and attacking can change the outcome of a battle. Dexterity characters are outshined and outgunned by strength based warriors and spell-flinging wizards. A warrior with leech is an undying murder machine.
I think a lot of the problems can be fixed in patches, and some of the problems are being solved. However, there’s still a multitude of them, and even when they’re “finished” there will still be some. This isn’t some shining example of a perfect RPG, it’s just a pretty decent one. Thankfully, it’s on track to being pretty good one, some day.

Warning - I'm a fan of Civilization games from the beginning; consider this review may have some positive bias.  ;-) And, this review assumes you can read the basic description of the game in the Store; not going to repeat that.
Likes:
Social Policy System --   A better way to achieve a Cultural victory while helping with other victory conditions.  A needed replacement for the "Civics" feature of the prior Civ game.  The new system offers a great variety of paths to get to Cultural victory.  And, it can be integral in developing strategic advantages and it directly supports other victory conditions.
Tactical Game Play -- Hex tiles; what a concept.  Finally!  Partial damage to units is also an improvement, although a 100% healthy unit can be destroyed if up against a much stronger unit.  Lack of stacking combat units may bother some, but in context of the changes in tactical play, it works very well.  The aspect of tactical game play has improved.
City Defense -- Cities can now defend themselves without a garrison, which improves upon the siege concept.  With a garrison, some strength is added to the city.  Requiring a garrison didn't add much to the game; other than the concern for a stupid, instant death by having no garrison.
City-States -- A useful addition to the game.  As an Ally, you may get two or three types of benefits: food, strategic resources, luxuries, culture, and military units.  Their allegiance can be bought for much gold, but it is best when they offer opportunities to win their favor.  After getting their favor, you get some influence so moving to Ally with money is cheaper.  As an Ally, they will go to war with you, automatically.  Although, they are not very effective except possibly as a distraction to your enemy.
Dislikes:
A bug or two or three --
1. I prefer multiplayer, either competitive or coop.  Unfortunately, when resuming a saved game with AI, the AI gets an extra turn.  We have tried using the Auto-Save versions or the directly saved versions, but it seems to always happen to us.  I try not to save when we are at war; that can be really bad giving the AI a free turn.
2. Workers sometimes stop what they are working on.  This is with no enemy action nearby, (not at war).  It is necessary to click on them and re-order the action.  This applies to building single-tile improvements, or directing a range of action like laying a railroad upon an existing road.
Some things I'm glad are gone from some prior versions, but that's just me:
Religion -- In Vanilla there is no religion aspect.  I actually liked it in some prior versions, but I see now with it gone, it really doesn't matter to me.  It would be more managing and strategizing, but I'm happy with all that I must do in this current version.
Corporations -- Same as with Religion.  It was nice, but I can easily live without it.
Stacking combat units -- Stacking was nice in that you could use combined arms effects by putting a defensive unit stacked with an offensive unit.  I liked the flexibility that gave the player.  Civ 5 doesn't have stacking, but it has made other changes to the tactical game that are an improvement.  Also, I like now that a front line is generally bigger in hex coverage.  That makes for a better feel of a real battle.  Stacking units was, in the end, rather boring.
Conclusion:
The game of Civilization has gone through many changes for a game.  The trend was adding more and more characteristics of the real world.  It was becoming more and more involved and complex.  Although, as with every Civ I've played, it's not strictly necessary to play in a very complex style to achieve victory.  Indeed, some versions took that to a fault resulting in easy quick kills to win the game.
By reducing some of the complexity, (adding Social Policy and City-States some would say they haven't), they have come up with an extremely playable version of Civilization.  And for those that want back some of the removed complexity, the Expansion Packs will fill that need.  In Civ 5, they have not sacrificed any of the key strategic concepts and they have improved upon some.  And, they have most definately improved upon the tactical level.  I will be playing this game for a long time.
