Grim Dawn is one of the most addicting ARPGs you'll play on Steam.
There is much offered here: atmosphere, lore, phat loot, a simple-yet-robust skill tree/stat system, and plenty of Action Role Playing Gaming to go around.
>>
The world of Cairn is painted as a desolate place pushed past the brink of a destructive extinction. Lands are varied in their construction: from dry fields, to swampy meadows, to dank dungeons and haunted ruins (and more), every act offers a multitude of wellcrafted areas to explore, farm and quest in. Not only is there variation, but every level is relatively large in size. There's -lots- of content here. There's also really good music.
Sounding somewhat gothic, most of the instrumentals used set the mood of Cairn appropriately. Everything feels dark and helpless, yet at the same time there's enough tempo/rock to reinforce that you're a badass battling hordes of zombies..and WINNING. So while the ambience may be grim, there's also a twinge of hope. I thought the music was really effective.
>>
If you appreciate a good story, you'll really enjoy the writing in Grim Dawn.
If you're a mid-20s gamer like me, you probably played many RPGs on the PSX and the SNES/N64. One thing I miss alot about those games is that they never really had voice acting. You had to read what they said--so effectively you were playing an animated book.
Grim Dawn doesn't really use any voiceovers except for combat sounds and phrases. I actually think this adds to the charm of the game. I always feel that with any kind of visual art, a percentage of what is produced for the viewer should be left to be made within the viewer's own mind. Being able to read through quests and journal entries and not hear someone read it for me allows for a much more immersive experience in regards to the backdrop of Cairn. The stories are dark and ominous, filled with political intrigue, blood, torture, lust and murder. If you've read The Sword of Truth or Game of Thrones series, you'll find the lore in Grim Dawn addicting. Sometime at the beginning of Act 3, I began wishing that they would release a Grim Dawn novel. I'd buy it.
I read a comment that said this game didn't have much lore to offer; I couldn't disagree more. The Survivors of Burrwitch,  The Survivors of Homestead, The Amalgamation and The Herald, The Investigations of Inquisitor Creed, An Arkovian History, The Torture of Uroboruuk,
The Prison of Warden Krieg, the battle between The Order of Death's Vigil and Kymon's Follower--these are just some of the journal entries you'll collect throughout the world; you get the idea! LOTS of stuff here to read and enjoy.
>>
You can't not fill up your inventory in 20 minutes in this game. It's impossible to go broke/not have gear/not have materials to craft. Everything is vendorable and almost everything except rare components is purchasable.
The gear, depending on rarity, will also have various stats and spells attached to it. Some items will give you the ability to cast a fireball or summon a pillar of lightning from the sky, others will allow you to repulse enemies or lay pools of poison at their feet should they attack you. The gear is buff and it definitely feels rewarding whenever you finally pull a nice upgrade from a tough mob that you've been dying to.
You may also craft gear at the Blacksmith starting in Act 3, but be ready to spend lots of iron bits and scrap metal. The Blacksmith is the brother of RNGesus, so you may either get a semi-decent item or an AMAZING item when one clicks the "combine" button on the Blacksmithing menu. With the availability of scrap and iron bits in the game though, you can go out and farm for an hour or two and have a considerable amount of resources to play with in order to get something exceptional.
>>
There are 3 basic stats in the game: Physique, Cunning, Spirit--upon getting enough XP to complete a level, you earn 1 point that is allocatable to one of these. Physique offers HP, HP Regen, Higher Armor Class, and Critical Hit Avoidance; Cunning increases your specialized melee/ranged damage types (Bleeding, Piercing, Internal Trauma), Accuracy, and Critical Hit Chance; Spirit increases your Energy(MP), Energy Regen, Bonus Magic Damage, Duration Modifier, and affinity with Enchanted Items. Apart from the 3 primary stats are numerous stats and modifiers related to gear. These are too varied to list here, but these are only affected by gear and skill selection and are not innate to your character but only to the class you choose.
There are 6 classes to choose from: Arcanist, Shaman, Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Nightblade. Each specializes in a weapon type or element type (all can use -any- weapon they desire, classes just have skills that give them proficiencies in certain weapon types over others). From summing massive beasts made of bramble and thorns, to drowning your opponents in pools of flame, piercing them with shards of aetherial energy, or cleaving crowds of manticores in two with a massive two-handed sword.. Grim Dawn fills any niche you desire.
Your class isn't chosen at Character selection. Instead, you're allowed to select your class from the skill tree by pressing C and allocating points into any skill tree you want. You can select a second class after level 10 (if you wish). Every class has about 5-6 skill paths, sometimes more, each path with 3-6 skills each. You can mix and match from any skill path, so long as a skill that you want doesn't require another skill in its path that you don't have any points in.
I prefer to do minimalistic builds when I play ARPGs, so most of my emphasis on my character is in Passive stats/aurus with only 2 real skills that I use consistently. However, you can craft your character just like an MMO if you wish and have all 10 keys on your hotbar occupied.
>>
This game is an ARPG at its very core. Isometric camera, a dark world, plenty of dungeon crawling/roguelike (although if you have a rift open, you don't need to start dungeons over from the very beginning upon death), rich story, tons of atmosphere. If you enjoyed Baldur's Gate, Sacrifice, Divinity, Diablo, Ultima Online, Elder Scrolls, etc. You will enjoy Grim Dawn.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is a worthy game unfortunately marred by a title that, while suitable once the branching storyline mechanics manifest, sounds unimaginative and forgetable.
You play as Reynardo, a snarky fox rogue and master of sword-fu with competent, 3D, beat-'em-up gameplay.  I was still hearing new quips from him and the narrator fifteen hours into the game with a decent variety of pop cultural references thrown in.  There are five chapters to play, which means you can get through one run or even more in a single sitting.  Victory in combat will earn you experience to unlock perks, Reynardo remembering his old techniques, and further advancement will offer more enemy types and a larger number of enemies.  I played with a controller, and I recommend that.  More of the story and setting, which involves a rebellion and dark magic overtaking a world of floating islands, airships, and dead gods, is revealed across mutliple playthroughs blended about evenly between showing and telling.  Should your first story end tragically, and there are many intriguing and horrifying ways it can, then you find a way back to the start.  You and your narrator remember an important lesson, and piecing together all these important truths can complete your story.
The levels are pretty and varied and will be mixed differently depending on which storyline you're on, but with just five chapters and two or three options per chapter the number is limited.  If you experience all branches of the main story, it will be because of the strong narrative and in spite of the repetitive combat mechanics and levels.
The game is very fairly priced for its length and quality.  As such, Stories: The Path of Destinies earns a strong recommendation.  This was my 2016 "I'm not crying, there's something in my eye" Steam award nomination, which prompted this review.  Achievement completionists will probably find "Sword Fu Master," unlocking all the perks, to be the final achievement, as after completing every branching storyline and reaching the good ending it still took about ten playthroughs to reach maximum level.

Mirror's Edge meets Dead Island. We've all heard it described like this before, but it's definitely a fitting description of the game. You play as a govenrment agent sent into the city of Harran to investigate the cause of a deadly disease spreading through the city like wildfire, turning everyone into zombies. Or infected, if you want to call them that. Either way, they're essentialy cannon fodder for you as you parkour your way through the Middle Eastern city, looking for things to improve your weapons.
This game manages to do what a lot of other games like it could not: make zombies scary. There was a time when zombies were scary, back when Resident Evil first came out, and even when the first Left 4 Dead was released. But since then, the zombie genre has been so over used that they're beginning to lose their scariness. Dying Light manages to tweak the average zombie in a fun, yet scary way. There's other games where zombies become more powerful in the dark and at night, such as 7 Days to Die, but Dying Light combines that with the ability to free run, and that's a sure win in any book. Day time is spent slowly and meticulously sorting your way through zombie hordes, using your speed and agility to your advantage. During the night, or in the sewers, it becomes a much different story. At night, you are the hunted, hiding and sneaking your way past Volatiles and dashing from safe zone to safe zone. In the sewers, you are having to duck and weave your way through crowds of zombies and volatiles, making the most of the limited space you have to work with.
Over all, the combat is smooth, challenging, and addicting, the parkour and free running is even better, and the game manages to be scary and really exciting. If it has any flaws, it would be in the story, which is fairly predictable and consists of a lot of missions of go here, do this, and then come back and i'll send you to do something else. It gets fairly repetative, but what makes this game awesome are the side quests and the free roaming. The city is fun to explore and there's enough stuff for you to do that you won't be bored for a while.

Even though  Grim Dawn is early access, it's a very polished, and even well balanced game. This game literally IS Titan Quest under the hood functionally, with improved graphics and rotational view perspectives... but the leveling system, the dual class capabilties, even the Spirit Guide to reset your skill points when you'd like, are all taken from what I felt was one of the best ARPG's I'd ever played (Titan Quest - many, many hours logged in that game!)
But it's different in more than just the tilesets and texturing. Grim Dawn feels grittier than TQ ever was. The Story (Yes, I said Story in an ARPG) is very good, and your actions carry weight - sometimes for good... sometimes for not so good, depending on who you're aligning with in terms of Factions. Point is, your acts, the things you chose to do or not do, will impact who you can interact with and at what level you're allowed to interact with them. Want better goods from a Vendor? Get a better reputation with the town he lives in. Want to actually talk to one of the NPC's who for now, won't? Learn, and do, what you need in order to make the world of Grim Dawn react to your presence. While this may sound subtle, it's actual impacts across the game can be felt even in early stages.
This is of course, an Early Access game, so things aren't 100% complete in terms of all the 'Acts' (2/3 of the way complete as of this writing) but the gameplay feels very polished... Don't be surprised to find that updates will blow away your save or change items, etc... It's still in development so these things will happen as the Dev's work to improve the experience. But don't let those things discourage you. This is a GREAT game for its genere and for the price. Show it a little love... I did. No regrets.

I bought this game as a suggestion from my brother-in-law as a must-buy during the 4th of July sale (half price). I have put in about 10-12 hours so far into the game and will speak on three things. Graphics: I have a fairly aged laptop that I game on and this game is easily playable at 70-90FPS on medium across the board without any sluggishness. Gameplay: This is where this game, in my opinion, trumps similiar titles such as Left 4 Dead. This game is incredible, it has multiple classes with multiple perks to allow for a decent amount of customization. However, I have two issues with the gameplay so far... the lack of a crosshair (aside from iron/scope sight guns) and the inability to prime a grenade, I held the grenade button down to prime like I would in CS:GO and threw 5...Whoops killed 20 enemies, GO ME! The third thing I would like to talk about is the pure enjoyment of the soundtrack. I normally don't get into soundtracks that come with videogames because, they are usually... well crap. I learned from Rocket League that, some developers do indeed put together some spectacular tracklists. KF2 has joined RL with having great music, sound effects, and overall ambient tranquility. It could use a little polishing here and there but overall, worth the full price of the game and am told that this is a major upgrade from KF1. I recommend this game!

What Half-Life 2 has done to the video-game industry is unforgettable. It has not only changed the fps genre of gaming, but it has changed the way we make, and experience video-games of all genres today. Half-Life 2 truly introduced video-games as a complex form of narrative, and blew everyone's expectations out of the park.
Although Half-Life 2 was released in 2004 it still exceeds today's standards in 2016 12 years later! This is really impressive especially considering the fact that the video game industry is rapidly changing, and progressing. Something that really stands out to me is the incredible art design, and how it helps to tell the story, as well as the level design. It's dialogue is superb, and realistic, and the facial and body animations make you sympathize with the characters.
You won't find any cut-scenes that clutter up the game, and make it feel hardly intractable, or objectives that seem completely irrelevant to the story placed to add on extra hours of gameplay. In fact Half-Life 2 doesn't have a single cut scenes in the game. It doesn't rely on cut-scenes to tell the story, but instead relies on animations that take place around you. This adds on to the experience, and makes you feel as if you are in the game yourself.
Half-Life 2 is nothing short of a revolution in the video game industry, and it is easily one of the best games that I have ever played.
I would definitley reccomend Half Life 2.

I've owned and played this game for a while. Only now have I come around to writing a review for it.
In a nutshell, I would say:
- If you are a hardcore tactical gamer, I would give this game a 6.5/10.
You'll have definitely played more in-depth tactics games. While this game has good graphics and a relatively streamlined interface and gameplay, you may find it lacking. You may find more tactical satisfaction in a game like Xenonauts. Don't get me wrong, this game still has the potential to be very fun for you.
- If you are a person who enjoys turn-based tactics games, and not too hardcore, I would give this game an 8/10.
You are probably going to enjoy this game. I didn't give it a perfect score for this group because if you play long enough, you will eventually wish that they had done more to make the game feel a little more complete. Until then, you'll probably enjoy dozens and dozens of hours of it, especially if you purchase the expansion, ENEMY WITHIN.
- If you are a casual gamer who does not enjoy tactics games, I would give this a 6/10.
It's a slow turn-based tactics game. You might not like it. But, it's streamlined enough that you MIGHT enjoy it a little.

I have a question. When I tick the function called "Run game with higher priority" and open CSGO, I thought it would have the game run at the highest priority. But I checked it in task manager, the priority is "above average". While when I open CSGO directly, priority is "high"(And I don't think I manually changed it before). I'm wondering is that kinda like a malfunction or it's simply designed to set the priority to above average? My computer hardware is i7 6700k+GTX1060 6g. With high priority I can run CSGO at a consistent 300fps quite smoothly, but with above average priority, the FPS can be around 200+. We all know that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t optimization of source engine. You can still tell the difference between 200fps and 300fps even if you are using 144hz monitor. That can be a little bit annoying tbh.
I will test the function of disabling Hyperthreading in this software to see whether it has a positive effect on FPS in CSGO.
Overall it's an awesome software, keep working bruh xD
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
HT effect tested under 1920*1080 resolution(graphic settings all low, expect multi core rendering on).
1.Without opening the software (which means enabling HT), average FPS on the workshop benchmark map in CSGO is 212.9.
2.Open CSGO through CPUcores(compared at the same priority in task manager). Tick "disable hyper-threading" and "Isolate and constrain the operating sys". The average FPS in benchmark map is 206.35.
3.Open CSGO through CPUcores(compared at the same priority in task manager). Untick "disable hyper-threading" with only "isolate and constrain the operating sys" checked. The average FPS in benchmark map is 215.92.
Well, seems that only the 4th function is useful for CSGO then.

This is quite possibly the most enjoyable game I've run into in the last 3 years. It hits on all the right levels, particularly for those who played games like Baldur's Gate and Icewind Dale back in the day. It plays much like those games, but it is true turn-based combat, not the pause-and-queue-action approach of the Baldur's Gate/Icewind Dale games. For those who enjoy a classic tabletop RPG style feel, you'd be right at home.
The game has a bit of a steeper learning curve than most modern games, and while it does give you some tips on basic mechanics, it doesn't hold your hand much past those basics. You have to see what works and what doesn't, and once you get the hang of things, you'll likely start over a time or two to tune you characters just how you want them.
One of the most interesting elements of the game that lends a great deal of strategy to combat is the interaction between the environment and your (and your enemies') spells, weapons, and items.  You can change almost any environment to suit your strategy with the right spells, using Rain to weak Fire enemies, creating and igniting patches of oil under the feet of your enemies, or toss a bolt of lightning at that pool of water your opponent seems to have ended his turn in, turning the water into an impromptu tazer. You have to be careful because you can hit yourself with these things as easily as your enemies, and they'll happily turn the tables on you if given a chance. It seems like the designers used a bit of common sense and likely played Magicka to get a feel for how different elements combine to amazing effects in combat and in some of the puzzles.
This game doesn't quite have the polish and charm of something like a Baldur's Gate 2 in terms of dialogue, characters and voice acting, but it isn't too far off either. I really look forward to a sequel.
If you like old school RPGS, this is practically a must have.

That's a nice little game we have here, mainly based on replayability : make a choice, go on, make another choice, keep going on, make a third choice, die badly somewhere along the path, tries another path, repeat.
The most interesting part of this mechanism - which strongly reminds me the Way of the Samurai series ♥ - is that you actually *know* what you discovered on your previous paths. Secrets are discovered as you try various choices, each secret unlocking new options you hadn't before, which may lead you to another path, which will allow you to learn more about the events and how they interfere with eachothers.
In short : the only way to win is to go meta and shamelessly use what you, the player, knows of the game to make the character choose wisely. I find the idea rather refreshing :)
As for the rest of the game, it's a classic beat'em all with quite a good amount of abilities to upgrade depending on your playstyle. The gameplay is fast and the character responds well to your commands, to my opinion. Simply charging through ennemies works at first, but as you increase in level, so do the monsters by gaining armors and abilities of their own, and you end up having to make good use of your abilities to get out of some sticky skirmishes. The weapon upgrades are surprisingly skimpy though, and I'd appreciate to have at least more upgrades available.
Graphically speaking, I can only say that the game is cheerful and colorful, with good-looking 3D environments. Obviously it's not an open-world with high quality textures, but it feels nice to wander on the different maps. Each of them contain various paths to avoid boreness, as you end up doing them again and again.
The story itself is kept simple : you're a sea pirate, you flee a bombed town leaving behind you corpses of the few peoples you liked, and ends up roaming the sky trying to match the Bad Empire's influence as hard as you can by every mean you have. Most of these means, of course, lead to a rather unpleasing end.
As for the characters, I like their style. There's not a lot of main and secondary chars, but they sometimes spit out a good punchline or two. Like the story, they are quite classic but enjoyable. The main char is still the funnier of them, as he can either act as a jerk with his friends, end up destroying the world without mercy (or rather without thinking) or decide to not lower himself to this Gandhi-style (the real Gandhi, not the Civ one :3 ).
All in all, it's not a great, big game, but it'll easily keep your attention for a few hours (more if you want to unlock every endings, each more funny or silly than the other). It's pleasant to play, well designed, and *not* bug-ridden (which nowadays is a good point). If you like furries, piracy and multi-ending, you may like it :)

Civilization V is a turn-based strategy game where you build your own empire. You start simple, researching pottery, animal husbandry and the wheel. You can also trade luxury and strategic resources with others. You need to carefully choose your allies. Some will be loyal to you. Others will backstab you if you are weak. Of course, you could also backstab them first, to get the upper hand. But other civilizations will not like that...

Even though  Grim Dawn is early access, it's a very polished, and even well balanced game. This game literally IS Titan Quest under the hood functionally, with improved graphics and rotational view perspectives... but the leveling system, the dual class capabilties, even the Spirit Guide to reset your skill points when you'd like, are all taken from what I felt was one of the best ARPG's I'd ever played (Titan Quest - many, many hours logged in that game!)
But it's different in more than just the tilesets and texturing. Grim Dawn feels grittier than TQ ever was. The Story (Yes, I said Story in an ARPG) is very good, and your actions carry weight - sometimes for good... sometimes for not so good, depending on who you're aligning with in terms of Factions. Point is, your acts, the things you chose to do or not do, will impact who you can interact with and at what level you're allowed to interact with them. Want better goods from a Vendor? Get a better reputation with the town he lives in. Want to actually talk to one of the NPC's who for now, won't? Learn, and do, what you need in order to make the world of Grim Dawn react to your presence. While this may sound subtle, it's actual impacts across the game can be felt even in early stages.
This is of course, an Early Access game, so things aren't 100% complete in terms of all the 'Acts' (2/3 of the way complete as of this writing) but the gameplay feels very polished... Don't be surprised to find that updates will blow away your save or change items, etc... It's still in development so these things will happen as the Dev's work to improve the experience. But don't let those things discourage you. This is a GREAT game for its genere and for the price. Show it a little love... I did. No regrets.

This game is, at least initially, thoroughly engaging, and I must confess that during this initial period I very much enjoyed playing it. However, after beating the easier modes and spending a couple of hours on the harder ones my enjoyment of this game took a nosedive. For one thing, there isn't much variety or content, in any sense. The same patterns appear over and over, and it feels more like memorization than skill after a certain point. Moreover, the repetitive chiptune music is okay to listen to for a few minutes but does begin to grate on you quickly. I did like how the game puts to the test a wide range of your cognitive functions including reflexes, timing, and ability to tune out distractions.
The biggest obstacle to my appreciation of this game is how it feels to control the player. The controls are far too sensitive and it is often frustrating to die because you held the key a split second too long or too short. It reminded me of his other game, the one with a lot of Vs in its title, which I quickly got refunded because I just didn't enjoy the style of playing where you make pixel-perfect movements with such a sensitive, touchy control scheme. And while some may erroneously call me a bad player in response, I daresay that some more thought being put into this aspect would have made the game much better, and I wouldn't be wishing I had stopped before the 2-hour mark.

So like this game is kind of the greatest thing ever. It's sorta like co-op Diablo 3 mixed with Baldurs Gate (which I have yet to play, but I understand the jist of the gameplay and such). You control a party of "Source Hunters" and travel throughout the land fighting monsters in turn-based combat sequences and stuff. Its about as close to the freedom and fun of a good game of Dungeons & Dragons that you can get in a computer experience. One thing in particular that I find interesting is that even thought this game has tons of lore and story to go with the fantasy aspects, I don't really find this game to be a super serious game. For example, the first main story driven quest in the game is to investigate the murder of a councilman in a nearby town. In the middle of this quest you find a stone that teleports you into space with a french space goblin named Zixzax who is a little too giddy about everything that's happening around him. Also you can wear a bucket on your head as a helmet, so that's also pretty funny I guess. I personally don't really enjoy playing single player because I'm not really that good at managing many characters at once and they all have their own gold, inventory, stats, feats, abilities, talents, etc, but that's just me. I highly recommend this game to pretty much any audience of gamers. Sure the beginning starts slowly and doesn't really tell you how to play very well, but you get used to it.It's so splendidly stupid and crazy, but also very relaxing since the game is turn-based, so there's no real need to rush anything and you can lay out a strategy more efficiently. All the "classes" are just templates that you can mold into whatever you want. Take my co-op character I made with my friend for example. I made a Shadowblade which is basically the equivalent of an assassin type character, and yet one of my spells is the ability to teleport an item or enemy to deal damage. So I then use that in combat to send an enemy to my friends character, a Knight, where he then proceeds to royally kick some butt. Also I can turn invisible. And OH MAN THE CO-OP. Its so silly and all you do is joke around the whole time. My friend based his characters appearance on Ronald McDonald, and I loosely based my characters appearance on Elena from Street Fighter. As I mentioned before, I have the power of teleportation, so whenever there's something out of reach, I just teleport my friend to it, which then hurts him and he gets mad at me. And a lot of the story has choices to further develop your characters personality and in co-op this is played out as a minigame of sorts. Say if my friend want to kill a person, but I think they should live, you LITERALLY PLAY AN IN-GAME GAME OF BEST 2 OUT OF 3 ROCK PAPER SCISSORS TO DETERMINE WHAT SHOULD BE DONE. All in all it's a great game 10/10.
EDIT: Also, there's tons of crafting elements and craziness like that, but I haven't delved into all of THAT yet because 1. I've only played like, 2% of the game, sue me, and 2. There is a lot of it. I've heard its relatively simple, but still I'm gonna wait on that. And lastly the game is $40 which is cheapish for today's standards, but you can also get the collectors edition which is $80 and comes with the game and the two previous Divinity games, two dlc's, artwork, soundtrack, and design doc. An improvement over its Dead Island predecessor, but still flawed in many of the same ways.
Gameplay is very similar to Dead Island in terms of being largely quest driven and running around between various points of interest, dodging or murdering zombies along the way.  The new parkour mechanics add some interesting verticality to movement and planning and do help to make the act of traveling between places more engaging.  The game also introduces some tower climb puzzles to further utilize the parkour, which I enjoyed.
The other major change (Day/Night cycle) initially feels exciting but given that running and jumping are the primary means of dealing with zombies during either day or night, eventually loses its luster.
Some of the problems from Dead Island, such as weak characters, skill trees with oddly tiered skills, and samey gameplay have returned with Dying Light.  Eventually, the whole experience starts to feel like a grind.
I eventually put the game down and haven't yet desired to come back to it.  I wouldn't endorse it at $60.00, but could justify a $30.00 price point.  The game is best if you're still into the zombie thing and want a triple A title with a smattering of RPG and platforming elements.  If you want a game that's Dead Island 2.0, this will satisfy you until Dead Island 2.0 is released.

Okay let's be short but meaningful, this game improves upon the already good shoot em up nature of the first Killing Floor and improves it with:
+More destructive weaponry to play with
+Additional perks, the tanky but low offense SWAT that forced to use SMG in tradeoff for more armor-based perks, and the "master of none" Survivalist able to level up with any weapon.
+Able to parry for melee users.
+Sleeker presentation, though for some it feels quite less gritty...
It has however few cons, such as
-Standard 9mm pistols are now useless.
-Smaller, more "choked" maps compared to the first game although custom maps do alleviate this issue
-Still not be able to play with friendly bots (there was in the first game but it's not whitelisted so it will prevent leveling)
-Boss fights can be frustrating for first time players because of "hide and heal" mechanism of one of the boss.
-Zed-Conomy still pretty jarring following the CSGO model of "buy key to unlock drops" i've seen more generous free to play games.
Overall pretty recommended. 9/10.

Now this game is interesting. Its core gameplay is unique and that is the entire game, no story, no characters, just simply the drive of you the player to explore and solve puzzles. Its like if Portal had no story, and was just puzzle rooms built like a maze (so you'd have to return to different places). Could it have benifited from having a story? I think so, but I feel the developer didn't want to ruin his solid game play with something that could miss and that is something I can respect (either that or he is lazy but I can respect that too). And the whole world is built to accomidate the fact its story-lite. The whole is clean, there are little to no textures instead everything is simply solid colors, and its not a bad thing. It allows you to draw in the right amount of information so you can solve puzzles, contrast this with the times in Portal where you need to find the one piece of portal-able tile in the room.
If you want story or action, this is not the game you are looking for, but if you are looking to do something fun and want some challenging puzzles, then look no further.

The Gods are dead. It is this bleak message which welcomes you to the world of The Banner Saga. This one simple phrase intentionally and effectively sets the tone for the adventure to follow. It truly shines in its ability to intertwine story and gameplay mechanics to provide a memorable tale of survival and consequence. True to what an RPG is, or at least used to be,  choice is the central aspect of this title in both combat and story. Between its breathtaking hand-drawn art and unique melding of classics, this title is worth every bit of your time but may lack in wide appeal due to many unorthodox mechanics.
Let’s go ahead and get it out of the way – The Banner Saga is a gorgeous game. So much so that it’s almost a moot point to even discuss. Water is wet and The Banner Saga looks magnificent. The art alone is sure to raise the standard of what a small team with ambition can achieve. Its vintage Disney and Eyvind Earle art style is brimming with detail and polish which is sure to prompt an emotional response from the player, be it nostalgia or awe. In our case it was both.
The story will continually batter on your very soul ‘till the end of its multi-perspective narrative. The Banner Saga puts you in charge of survivors in a sunless, dying world filling with murderous creatures known only as the Dredge. As you and your followers seek asylum along the road you will be met with choices which can and will cost the lives of others, furthering the sense of despair the story conveys...
Simple yet surprisingly addictive game. Great cheap purchase for any RPG or tabletop fan.

Antichamber is a puzzle game in the same vein as Portal: you move around in first person, and you solve puzzles to progress from room to room. What makes Antichamber special is its ability to screw with your preconceived notions about games. The world in which you navigate follows bizarre rules that subverts one's expectations when playing a typical first person puzzle game, and requires that you take a second to try and look at each situation in an entirely different perspective.
If you're looking for a puzzle game that will test the limits of your thinking ability, look no further.

I dashed towards the edge of a building, body glowing. As I kicked off the ground, I shot sixty feet up into the air, clearing the next two streets with ease. I glided the rest of the way towards my target, hitting the street with little fanfare. I was there. . . where was the target I was supposed to kill?
I turned around, just in time to see a truck twisting through the air at me. It struck me and sent me flying down the road, coming to a stop when a civilian panicked and offered my head a cushion on the hood of their car. Once back on my feet, I dusted myself off and pulled out my pistol, hard aiming. . . only to see a floating, gun-toting toilet hovering towards me.
It hunched over-- or, did something, it was a toilet and it's not quite easy to make out what it was doing-- and a giant fist appeared in the air behind it, formed out of green lines similar to that of the scrawling green lines on the monitors in The Matrix. Another car was lifted into the air and thrown at me, but this time I was ready.
As I jumped out of the way, my hand accidentally hit the 'change radio stations' key and Haddaways "What Is Love?" began to blare out of nowhere.
The fight of my life had just begun.

Although I generally love most Telltale games, or rather interactive stories, I tend to get bored somewhere in the middle with most of them… only real exception was „Tales from Borderlands". Now I know many people moan about the shortening length of Telltale games, but I got to say, the pacing of Michonne was perfect. I could not lay the game down.
Another great aspect is that by playing Michonne and not Clem, I felt liberated to indulge in revenge and non-moral behavior, while still being honest and well-wishing. With Lee I felt I need to do the right thing, with Clem I felt I need to do the pragmatic thing, but with Michonne I needed to do the righteous and cruel thing.
Technically I saw lots of upgrades… better textures, much better facial animation, the camera was much more dynamic and that intro song was just pure perfect.
This is yet another great entry for Telltale and franchise itself and even though it is just below 4 hours in length it is worth its asking price!

This is not a product for someone running a top of the line rig, this is for us plebs who managed to scrape enough money together to make a decent computer half a decade ago and are looking to milk what perfomance we can out of it for newer games. People who claim that it did "nothing" for them more than likely haven't seen sub-60fps outside of a frame locked game.
CPUCores interface is pretty easy to navigate and the options are explained well, the ability to launch a game via steam or select the process from a list to use it on is very handy. It has some theme customisation stuff if that's important to you too.
Personally, I went from frame skips and general muddy framerate in Dark Souls III to a much smoother 55-60+fps with only the occasional small hiccup that is easily tolerable. I've tried it with a few other games and got reasonable results, to the point I've been turning up graphics options and still getting a better experience than before. Don't expect miracles though; there are still things like your background processes and other hardware limitations like RAM that it can't help with.
All in all, CPUCores is a great stop-gap if you
to upgrade your PC but don't really have the cash on hand at the moment and still want a bit more performance out of it.

Civ V made a couple interesting changes to the gameplay, and IMO the devs did a good job overall with things, but they also also stumbled in ways that seem quite avoidable. V ostensibly makes the game more accessible to novice players, but some of the changes--such as significantly less specific information in diplomacy--end up hurting all players in the long run. The game tries to address some of the balance issues of Civ IV, and does so successfully on a number of fronts; However, in doing so it ends up creating new ones, such as how the changes to trading maps/techs ended up causing player exploration of the map to hit the wall of greatly diminishing returns much more quickly in most games. These are minor points, though, and 1) probably have more to do with the type of player I am than the game itself, and 2) are most likely only brought up because I had gotten used to them in earlier games. In the end this is still one of the best Civ games, and also one of the most balanced strategy experiences in the series, I think.

I have to confess that the 'Yes' is more hesitant than I'd like.
First off, I like what they did and what they were going for. Repeating and changing things is.. or at least can be.. entertaining and curious. The problem comes in how some of the twists or navigations of things already done happen.
In this case, some of them were, frankly, stupid and frustrating. They weren't fun. "hey this guy totally is a traitor. Killed you, literally, like four times! Trust him? WELL DUH, of course we should!" Stuff like that totally throws off the *point* of learning from your mistakes and re-traveling parts of the story. Or going into a situation, knowing a surprise waits, and not being able to anticipate it the second time around, instead being stupidly caught off guard.. again.
None the less, for the *most* part, it was decently solid. As I repeated and stumbled into more dumb endings, the game fell from a 7-8/10 to the 6 or so realm. Still recommendable and mostly enjoyable, but you could easily be caught in a bunch of dumb endings by merit of not being able to figure out what sort of choice you are presented with - and often doing things you don't intend at all.
Additionally, some of the voice-over was way too obnoxiously pop-culture for me, way too anachronistic for my tastes.. it just pulled me out of the story and world, rather than put me in it or give me a chuckle. They could have done themselves far more justice here, but it wasn't a total ruiner.
The combat is decent fun but, honestly, kinda awkward and ultimately ends up to be just a slog. You can upgrade things pretty early on and get to the point where treasure chests are pointless and enemies are a chore.. Using a controller I often found myself being auto-aimed at exploding enemies I'd dash into, therefore dying, or throwing foes at the wrong enemy, or being attacked by three foes simultaneously just by luck, unable to block them all, etc. It was generally fun, but not always. The upgrades at least changed things up a bit and gave some different approaches, but only so much. The controls for swapping weapons were, in my opinion, unusable in combat. I only really ever used the healing sword, as the othres were so awkward to swap to and use during the thick of combat. A better control scheme for swapping weapons is all they needed here.
I like what they tried to do with the fourth-wall and toying with timelines and changing and branching paths, and if not for this, the game would be a definite thumbs down, if just barely. I think it was done well enough, even if just barely, to warrant a positive nod, but it was a lot closer than I would have liked to a 'meh' instead of a 'yeah, why not.'
Edit: Okay.. I'm sorry, but.. yeah. Some of these endings are just so insanely hamfisted and stupid, I have to change this to a thumbs down. The game even pops up remarks about things you learn, "hey, this sure is this thing you foudn out.. OH WELL you died anyway, despite having a half dozen chances to act on this." It just.. it feels really, really poorly written and, frankly, is killing the fun of trying to hammer out the "right" path.. it just seems random, contrived, and arbitrary than intriguing and fun.
Fewer endings that made more sense, were less ham-fisted, and better written would have done this game better.. I just can't get over having an option where it literally says "You have 0 reason to do this thing, knowing what you know.. BUT YOU DO IT ANYWAY, HAH, you fail." It's also something you can't un-choose, forcing you to play it out, start over, and then try to figure out what else to do instead. There was simply no reason to do that. I guess I can't just.. lie? :|
But MOST OF ALL, I learned a "truth" alongside another, and I guess you can't get two at once? Thus forcing me to take wild stabs at various choices, somewhat blindly, assuming it must not be what I thought.. and then it was. I really like what they were going for here, the idea is great, but the execution is just beyond frustration. I'm finsihing it just to finish it, not because this is fun or satisfying. I'm stymied and frustrated by poor writing and a bad sense of choice and consequence.

TL;DR: Only buy this game on discount.
I am... torn about this game.
On one hand, I like the concept. You try something, you fail and learn something, which can now lead to new paths. It is a good concept and offers some interesting challenges.
Issue is the execution. There is no option to skip to certain points, so you forced to replay the same parts again and again, and watch the same cutscenes again and again, listening to the same dialog again and again. It gets very boring very fast.
In addition to these, it is way too easy to exhaust alternative paths on levels. Since the levels always reuse the same basic  set, you very quickly start to just breeze through the level without any deviation, just to get to the next bit of the story.
This really hurts the replayability. The game has multiple endings, the entire points of the game is to experience them, but finding them becomes a chore, rather than enjoyable experience.
Combat takes cues from Batman series, which is not really suprise, it's a working combat system, It adds several tricks to to it to keep it fresh, but unfortunately, once you reach the certain treshold the battles become either too easy, or those advantages you got are now hinderances. For example, you can get a skill that lets you one-hit-kill any enemy after a certain treshold. Combined with another skill that lets you attack any enemy aywhere, this creates a situation where you can't rack up a good combo, because you can't "forget" skills and you are killing enemies too fast to generate a combo. Equally, some enemies explode on death, so hitting them causes your combo to end, where as if you lacked the skill you would hit them and then be able to zoom out.
Camera is decent, moving on set positions or following the character, but zooms far too close in combat, leaving you guessing what certain enemies are doing or where they even are.
However, biggest issue that I have, is how easy it is to "beat", to get the supposed best ending. You need to uncover 4 truths, and it's all too easy to figure them out. The game will then flat out tell you how to beat it. This means you basically play the game through 5 times. After that, you are trying to see the other bad ends, but as I noted earlier, it becomes a chore.
So this review is very negative. Then why is my review marked as recommend? Because the game is not bad. Graphics is good, story is OK, concept is great and narrator is good. It has issue with execution, perhaps developers should ahve focused on smaller set of path with more widely divergent routes, or given player to option to skip the initial steps until he can choose something he had never tried yet.
It is not worth the full price, low as it is, but at discount, it is nice quick game to play through and return occasionally to see some other end.

One of the best games ever made in the star wars franchise. Its only short coming is that they never made a sequel to it. That's almost not a problem, though because there is a huge amount of content in the modding community to make up for the lack of BFIII. If you like star wars just play this game. What this game does really well is putting you in command of the biggest battles in the star wars series. You can hop in an X-Wing and blow up a star destroyer during a space battle or take control of a super battle droid and eradicate clones at Geonosis. Also, you can play against bots so you don't need friends to play and you don't need to deal with playing against MLG 10th prestige no-lifers with 2000 hours into the multiplayer.
However, it is not without its flaws. First and foremost, the class system is very unbalanced. The basic "soldier" class (i.e. superbattle droids) stands above the rest. The guys with the shot guns and the "heavies" with the rockets especially suck, because shot guns and rockets really suck. With both of those weapons you need really direct hits and sometimes that won't even kill. Its especially frustrating when you nail someone point blank with a rocket, to the face, and it barely takes away 1/3 of their health. Aside from some of the classes being unbalanced, some of the maps are too. An example is Kashyyyk. The CIS nearly always wins because they just have a better spawn than the Republic. There are several other maps like this, too. Finally some of the vehicles and turrets are not to great, because they don't do any splash damage. So, you need a direct hit to do damage.
Overall, as an FPS, this game is a 7/10. It has a really great feel because of the Star Wars universe, but it is really hindered by some of the balancing and game mechanics issues. Definitely pick this game up if you are a fan of the Star Wars series. If you are not, its still and OK FPS but there are better ones out there.

It's not my kind of game. I didn't find it enjoyable to play and found the 2-button control scheme incredibly unintuitive to the point of ruining the game for me. It would be a much better experience if it would be mouse controlled or took advantage of WASD or analog controls.
The aesthetic style of the game is fun and cartoony which I liked, but the execution leaves much to be desired in some areas. Notably, there is little cohesion in terms of image quality in the 2 worlds I forced myself to play through.
Special effects are often repeated ad nauseam and many seem like the normalization was skipped. I didn't notice any spatial convolution or similar effects to adapt sounds to the stage.
The music is ok.
The control system is for me, the greatest problem in the game. I don't know if there's an easy fix, but this 2 button momentum system makes flying unnecessarily hard and is obviously an artifact of it's mobile game roots.
Basically the two buttons make you move and turn clockwise or counter-clockwise, one button when tapped makes you move up slightly and fly forward, while when held makes you turn until you let it go while falling. If you have momentum forward, holding the right button will make you make loops in place.  Note that while changing direction you don't stay in place, you fall and everything moves around you, making steering unnecessarily complex.
Too often you'll die from contact with a border because you missed the "correct" approach 5 seconds before.
The game involves traversing 2D levels where contact with anything kills you and forces you back to the latest checkpoint bought with the coins you collect flying around. There are coins and letters for you to collect and deliver, reaching a purchased checkpoint saves your coins, but not the letters, those you have to deliver without crashing to a floating mailbox which at times is hidden.
The menu UI is basic and reminiscent of the quality of some free mobile games, the images don't seen to be properly scaled or sourced.
And often mouse clicks would not register correctly while on the Overworld.
You start from the first world, but you can go to the left to play tutorial levels. I don't know why it doesn't start from those, but overall the game feels like an incomplete beta version. The difficulty in the tutorial levels is higher than that of what I completed of world 1.
There are a few things added to mix up the flying such as portals to "challenge"/higher difficulty areas, water, moving platforms, enemies, and collectibles.
There is a story there, and some optional mail delivery challenges to go with it, but neither was interesting enough to make me power through the gameplay.
Overall the game's control system ruins the experience. I could get past the lackluster UI and mute the awful sound effects but since the difficulty comes from the control system working against you, not the level design, I can't recommend this experience. The quality of the game is not bad, but overall it is a mediocre game with an awful control scheme which inflates the difficulty and left me disappointed at this wasted opportunity.
Notwithstanding, if you think you would enjoy the control scheme, then you could give it a shot as there is a very low barrier to entry ($1) and there is enough content for at least 6 hours. The arcade nature of the title might be fun if you can tolerate the gameplay and low production values, but it's not for me.
I appreciate the Devs providing a copy for me to try and review, but, sadly, I can't recommend the game mostly due to the control scheme.

Steep is an extreme winter sports simulator developed by everyone’s favourite company, Ubisoft. (Don’t let that put you off). It predominantly features the Alps but Ubisoft recently introduced some Alaskan slopes too as part of a free update. In Steep you take to the slopes with a snowboard or skis or you take to the skies with a wingsuit or a paraglider. You can complete challenges and events already in the game or you can simply explore the mountain, finding new points of interest, challenges and the best lines you can come up with.
When you first get to the Alps, you’ll be struck by the game’s beauty (even if you’re running it on Medium/Low like I am). The dev team did a great job at creating the Alps in-game and you’ll get some truly stunning vistas fairly regularly in the game. Hurtling through a lush forest or gliding your way to a different peak, it’s going to look good. There are some muddier textures which look a bit rough when you get up close (particularly rock textures) but I didn’t see those too often.
The ‘main way’ to play the game is through the challenges and events. Of course, you don’t have to these but they are the best way to unlock Steep credits (used to purchase customization options) and earn EXP (some events have level requirements). There are a few different kinds of events. You have Freestyle events (snowboard or skis) in which you have to score a certain amount of points, you also have Extreme Rider events where you score points by narrowly dodging objects. Bonebreaker challenges can be wingsuit or ground events, they feature doing ridiculous things that inevitably lead to you knocking the ever-living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of your rider several times before success (they’re a lot of fun). You also get race events for the wingsuit and paragliding disciplines. There are also some story-ish ‘challenges’ called Mountain Stories which attempt to tell you a story while you complete objectives such as destroying snowmen or following another rider. Personally, I didn’t see the point in trying to tell a story with the game but the challenges themselves are pretty fun.
So, as I mentioned, some challenges require scoring a certain number of points to be successful. Unfortunately, the game’s trick controls suck and there are no tutorials to help you. The only tutorials are for how you can ollie and then flip or spin, which is good to know but will net you hardly any points. For snowboarding or skiing it’s all about the grabs you do and the game doesn’t teach you how to do anything other than the most basic grab. I had to look up a separate tutorial to figure out how to do and start getting decent scores on jumps. Getting combos is also very important for racking up high scores, the only way to end a combo is to fall over which happens if you take a few hits (bad landings or riding into an object) or if you just go head first into the ground, that’ll mess you up pretty good surprisingly enough.
Now, as much as I enjoy Steep and I think Ubisoft Annecy did a good job with it, there is one part of this game which is simply unforgiveable. It’s always online (and Ubi servers can’t be connected to if you have University WiFi without a VPN connection). It’s one of the most ridiculous design decisions I’ve ever seen in a game. The multiplayer aspect of Steep isn’t even slightly interesting, you can see other riders around the mountain (since you’re always online) and you can group together with them but that just means that the game lets you know what you’re doing and lets you compete with their scores on challenges you’re both doing. Sure, it’s an okay implementation of multiplayer and it can be kind of cool but it most certainly isn’t worth having the game always online. I really hope they add offline functionality before they inevitably shut down the servers. As much as I like the game and want to like Ubisoft for making it, you can’t argue anything other than this is a super ♥♥♥♥♥♥ move on their behalf.
As I mentioned earlier, there are a few different rewards for completing challenges. Levelling up your rider is done by earing EXP from challenges which then unlocks new event challenges (like a Red Bull Extreme Rider event) and new Mountain Story events. Some challenges reward you with items such as new helmets, boards, wingsuits etc. that can only be unlocked by completing said challenges. Lastly, you earn Steep credits (the in-game currency) which can be used to buy more items from the in-game store such as ridiculous unicorn costumes, an imp wingsuit as well Helicopter tickets. Helicopter tickets are used to drop you anywhere on the mountain, very handy if you don’t fancy a trek up a steep incline to find a new dropzone. The customization options can be pretty fun to mess around with but they’re definitely not the main focus of the game and it’s really easy to earn Steep credits so there’s no need to pay for microtransactions.
One of Steep’s strongest points is how quickly the game changes pace. If you want to find your own line from a dropzone it can be an incredibly relaxing experience that’ll take your mind off of the real world for a while. It can also be a controller smashingly infuriating game when you’re playing the hardest challenges, failing time and time again before you finally get the sweet satisfaction of beating the challenge.
Last but not least, this is not a $60 game. I paid $30 for the base game which I’m happy with but I think I’d probably feel different about the game if I had dropped $60 on it. There’s a lot of content here, I still have plenty more to do, and you can create your own content too (finding your own lines etc.) if that’s your kind of thing but this is one to pick up on a sale of at least 50% off.
Steep is a niche game and it doesn’t come without issues but it’s an incredibly enjoyable game that takes you from exhilarating wingsuit challenges, dipping and diving down cliff-sides, to relaxing snowboard rides through a snow-covered forest. It’s well worth picking up on sale whether it’s the kind of game you’d usually play or if you’re looking for something a tad different.

As with the previous entries to the series by Telltale, you advance through the story mostly by making dialogue choices and beating quick time events. It's a tried and true formula,
you don't mind the lack of actual puzzles to solve.
On the plus side you get to play Michonne! As far as I can tell (and I don't know the comics), the game tries hard and pretty much succeeds to do the character justice. The writing in general is superb - as you'd expect from a Telltale game. There is the occasional light-hearted moment and - of course - a lot of drama, tension and violence. The other characters are strong, too, with mostly believable motivation.
Unfortunately, the game gives you very little reason to care about them! The story simply moves too fast, constantly pushing you forward. There is basically no breathing-space, no time to rest and get to know the other characters. Even if you tried to go slow, you'd probably still finish the games in under 4 hrs.
Then there's Michonne's guilt-trip: Much of the game revolves around her coming to terms with the past. But what starts out rather compelling, becomes a bit contrived and annoying by the end, her flashbacks turning up too frequently (and of course at the most inconvenient of times).
"The Walking Dead: Michonne" is a decent game, but too rushed for it's own good. I'd still recommend playing it, but only if you're a fan of the series and able to get it at a discount.

This is a great game. While less intensive than the original verson, which may be a plus for some, but not for me, it still managed to maitain the overall feeling of Xcom. The easier difficulty modes allow people to get into it more, but on classic and impossible difficulties the game feels about as hard as the original on normal or difficult.
--------Features I, personally, like that they added over the original--------
-Different classes with skill trees to match that give each soldier their own identity
-The continent bonuses add another layer of decisions to make when covering a council member
-More variety in the mission types (espicially if you have enemy within)
-More clear explainations of your equipment effects (the UFOpedia in the original was a bit confusing to figure out without the manual)
-The situation room's display of each council member's panic state. In the original, you couldn't really check on how a nation was feeling about the project until the monthly review, and by then it was often too late to stop them from pulling out. In this there is a clear indicator of where each member stands which is something that you need in a game that is like this.
-The aesthetic customization is really nice and allows you to give even more personality to each member of your squad. It's a small touch that I truly appriciate.
-The "Second Wave" settings that can add a bit of change to your game once you've mastered the first version. Randomization aspects are, in my opinion, always nice to have access to.
--------Features that I'm split on--------
-The simplified country coverage system. It makes the game easier to keep track of, for sure, and it always bothered me that you didin't get any form of notation on the map in the original that showed your ring of what you could detect. However, this also means you only get 1 base to work with and you don't have as much room for experimentation with your bases.
-The streamlined combat. On the one hand, it is much more simple to grasp the basics of and allows you to get into more complex idesas for strategies fairly quickly. On the other hand, the original's system was more varied and had a greater variety of strategies one could use because of it.
--------Features I disliked or were removed from the original that should have stayed--------
-The new research system is too simplified for my taste. After completing the game a few times, I noticed that the games I did best in I had taken roughly the same tech progression in each one. Also, being limited to one base means you get to work on one tech at a time, unlike the original. While these aren't HUGE problems with the game, I feel that it is something worth noting.
-Less loadout customization is available from the original. If you've played the original, you'll remember that you had POCKETS. Not just pockets. POCKETS. Backpack pockets, shoulder pockets, pants pockets, belt pockets, every kind of pocket you could imagine. In this one, you get armor, primary weapon, secondary weapon, and one or two equipment slots that are used for anything that doesn't fall under the first two categories. It's not as interesting to work with.
-Less resource management. There is still an aspect of this, but around the early-midgame the only one you continue to care about is money, which is a shame. Some people may see the reduced emphasis on your limited resources as a plus, and I can see where they are coming from, but it was one of my favorite aspects of the original because it added to the feeling of this being a desperate struggle against a seemingly superior foe.
Overall judegement: I'd recommend this game, yes. It's very good. However, it's not quite as good as the original. The two are close enough in quality that I can understand people disagreeing with me there. If you like strategy games and want a challenge, try both of them and see how you like them.

My experience with this game can be summed as thus: every update I found myself testing the changes, nodding in satisfaction, then quitting the game to await the next update.
Arkane knows how to make a good game. No question. But if you film an Oscar-worthy movie and the lens is smudged while filming, you can't judge what's underneath without acknowledging what's been marring your experience the entire time.
=============================
PERFORMANCE
Everyone is aware of the performance issues, and these still persist to this day. It runs much better than at launch, where it was literally unplayable, but that's because the game looks worse than before - the most noticeable change being the extremely aggressive LOD scaling. Out of the corner of your eye you notice the shapes of window frames and posters on distant buildings morphing in shape, or the furniture at the opposite end of a long hallway suddenly blinking into existence. FPS dropped to 15 when stabbing a gravehound, so they simply removed the inky visual effect that was causing the problem instead of optimizing it.
Also, Denuvo authentication is one of the longest "loading screens" of the game. Around half a minute to a full minute or more every startup.
=============================
GAMEPLAY
For the most part, gameplay is excellent and is Dishonored's strongest suit.
Dark Vision was changed to a blurry short range sonar so unlike Dishonored 1 you aren't constantly seeing blue and yellow because you had no reason not to
AI is much smarter
Nonlethal combat options are a blast
Bonecharm crafting system allows for player flexibility and "builds"
Each level feels lived-in while maintaining the duality of directive flow and open options that made the first game so good.
Emily and Corvo have distinct animations and final weapon upgrades. The animations are supremely cool.
Each level is fairly distinct, some with extremely interesting central "gimmicks." I do, however, wish the game relied less on them and had more "regular" areas.
However, under the hood lie other problems. Most of them are quality-of-life issues:
Gone are the hotkeys for journal, inventory, bonecharms, powers. Only one "journal" exists now, despite still having separate subsections.
It took months for the power wheel to be fixed. It took almost a full second after activating to pop up and be usable, breaking flow so badly I almost never used it in the first place. It's finally fixed now, but this issue was glaring and it took so long to be addressed most of us played through without it fixed.
Thrown objects don't always go exactly where your crosshair is. While this adds a layer of difficulty, it feels noticeably more clunky than in the first game.
Mana regen is pitifully slow. From using a power to fully regenerating, Dishonored 1's time is 4.7 seconds -> 3.1 seconds with Spiritual Pool. Dishonored 2's time with 4x Spiritual Pool is 6.3s -> 5.5s. The devs said they fixed this effect, but it was only made worse.
Bugs. Street speakers not playing. Dying after possessing gravehounds. An arc pylon never shutting down after pulling out its power, leaving it to either be dangerous to you to dangerous to your nonlethal playthrough. Some of these still aren't fixed.
=============================
STORY AND ATMOSPHERE
Reactivity
Great. My favorite part of Dishonored. You need to hide from a gang member to access a certain black market shop, and there are different scenarios and dialogue for if you hide, if you run into him outside, kill him outside, or kill him inside.
Emily and Corvo
Emily and Corvo are voiced. And... they don't talk enough. It's good that they're silent for most of the game, but there are times when you come across a portrait or photograph with an "Inspect" prompt. I'd love to hear Emily's thoughts on the High Overseer as see how that compares to Corvo's, or if it changes based on whether or not you accept the Outsider's Mark. Instead, all I get is the protagonist muttering the name of the person pictured. What's the point? Might as well keep them silent.
It made sense to me to play Emily first, but her story felt lackluster, like people at every turn were saying "check your royal privilege" despite my efforts to resolve everyone's problems without drawing blood. Corvo's is MUCH more interesting as a veteran of Dishonored 1.
The Outsider and The Void
I hate the new Outsider and his new voice. He felt threatening and malicious in the first game due to how calm and composed he was, and the Void felt like a strange and otherworldly place. The vignettes of Dunwall made it feel both unnatural and unnerving yet fundamentally woven into the universe. In Dishonored 2, it's just smoky blackness and sharp rocks. The Outsider is much jollier and moves around erratically, making grandiose hand gestures. They actually had a plot plot that could explain this change, but it was never addressed, so it just seems like a pointless retcon to me.
Main Plot
Dishonored's worldbuilding was always one of its appeals, and that remains true in Dishonored 2. However, the villains felt lackluster. Only the main villain has a real presence throughout the game, whereas everyone else feels introduced abruptly only to fall by your hand, all within the same mission. In Dishonored 1 everything felt personal and real. Perhaps it was because of the long intro where you interacted with most of them, or the Hound Pits's cast of characters all having different connections to your targets.
=============================
As you can see, I've played this game a LOT and have put a lot of thought into it. It was definitely worth all those hours and all that money, but the condition it was at launch and the sluggish drip-feed of support we barely get now is unacceptable. To set a precedent for future games, I can't recommend buying this unless they manage to fix all the performance issues and bugs, which doesn't seem to be happening anytime soon.

There are over a hundred paths to the end, and almost all of them end up with you getting executed by guards or blown up by the artifact you were trying to save or other unpleasant fates. Highly recommended!

Warning - I'm a fan of Civilization games from the beginning; consider this review may have some positive bias.  ;-) And, this review assumes you can read the basic description of the game in the Store; not going to repeat that.
Likes:
Social Policy System --   A better way to achieve a Cultural victory while helping with other victory conditions.  A needed replacement for the "Civics" feature of the prior Civ game.  The new system offers a great variety of paths to get to Cultural victory.  And, it can be integral in developing strategic advantages and it directly supports other victory conditions.
Tactical Game Play -- Hex tiles; what a concept.  Finally!  Partial damage to units is also an improvement, although a 100% healthy unit can be destroyed if up against a much stronger unit.  Lack of stacking combat units may bother some, but in context of the changes in tactical play, it works very well.  The aspect of tactical game play has improved.
City Defense -- Cities can now defend themselves without a garrison, which improves upon the siege concept.  With a garrison, some strength is added to the city.  Requiring a garrison didn't add much to the game; other than the concern for a stupid, instant death by having no garrison.
City-States -- A useful addition to the game.  As an Ally, you may get two or three types of benefits: food, strategic resources, luxuries, culture, and military units.  Their allegiance can be bought for much gold, but it is best when they offer opportunities to win their favor.  After getting their favor, you get some influence so moving to Ally with money is cheaper.  As an Ally, they will go to war with you, automatically.  Although, they are not very effective except possibly as a distraction to your enemy.
Dislikes:
A bug or two or three --
1. I prefer multiplayer, either competitive or coop.  Unfortunately, when resuming a saved game with AI, the AI gets an extra turn.  We have tried using the Auto-Save versions or the directly saved versions, but it seems to always happen to us.  I try not to save when we are at war; that can be really bad giving the AI a free turn.
2. Workers sometimes stop what they are working on.  This is with no enemy action nearby, (not at war).  It is necessary to click on them and re-order the action.  This applies to building single-tile improvements, or directing a range of action like laying a railroad upon an existing road.
Some things I'm glad are gone from some prior versions, but that's just me:
Religion -- In Vanilla there is no religion aspect.  I actually liked it in some prior versions, but I see now with it gone, it really doesn't matter to me.  It would be more managing and strategizing, but I'm happy with all that I must do in this current version.
Corporations -- Same as with Religion.  It was nice, but I can easily live without it.
Stacking combat units -- Stacking was nice in that you could use combined arms effects by putting a defensive unit stacked with an offensive unit.  I liked the flexibility that gave the player.  Civ 5 doesn't have stacking, but it has made other changes to the tactical game that are an improvement.  Also, I like now that a front line is generally bigger in hex coverage.  That makes for a better feel of a real battle.  Stacking units was, in the end, rather boring.
Conclusion:
The game of Civilization has gone through many changes for a game.  The trend was adding more and more characteristics of the real world.  It was becoming more and more involved and complex.  Although, as with every Civ I've played, it's not strictly necessary to play in a very complex style to achieve victory.  Indeed, some versions took that to a fault resulting in easy quick kills to win the game.
By reducing some of the complexity, (adding Social Policy and City-States some would say they haven't), they have come up with an extremely playable version of Civilization.  And for those that want back some of the removed complexity, the Expansion Packs will fill that need.  In Civ 5, they have not sacrificed any of the key strategic concepts and they have improved upon some.  And, they have most definately improved upon the tactical level.  I will be playing this game for a long time.

I absolutely recommend this game to people who love detail and RPGs. It's not a Diablo sort of affair, as the turn based combat makes things quite different.
I will say, however, that I really enjoy the turn based fighting of this game, while I haven't really enjoyed turn based for other games. There's just something so right about the way they've implemented it in this game.
Your characters will pick up quests by talking to people, but there's not much in the way of indicators as to who you need to talk to. Reading the journal, scraps of paper, diaries, and talking to everyone, that's how quests are done in this game.
What this means is that you'll probably need to adjust to actually having to think about how to do quests. It also means that completing quests is really something to feel proud of, especially if you don't consult the internet for clues and hints.
I think this is the perfect game for people who have been waiting to experience a game that asks one to think to play. It's smartly done, and you can feel that the developers made this game from the heart.
Multiplayer is limited to you and a single friend, by default, though you can use a hex editor (after creating your first save game) to increase the limit to you and three friends.
I've played my entire time with two of my close friends, and we are waiting to welcome a fourth friend to the mix. Some very funny things have happened, for example, my friends got the town guards after them, though I wasn't part of that mishap. To deal with that group of aggressive guards, I went out of the north gate, aggroed the zombies, and led them to the guards in the town.
The guards all died to the zombies, and (just to see how far things would go) we proceeded to make the zombies chase us into the center of the town.
In the end, everyone in town got involved, all of them also got killed, and my friends and I were laughing our heads off as this all happened turn by turn, with us adding to the carnage by killing any townie that attacked us.
In the end, we were the only survivors, and there was a lake of items dropped by all of the NPCs.
I don't think this game is suitable for someone who wants a quick rush of frantic action, as the mechanics and design of the game reward players who think about what they're doing.
The plus side of this is that you can dream up some pretty cool ways to do stuff in the game, and the game will allow it to happen the way you imagined.
I hesitate to say the game is a 10/10, as people will have their feelings of disagreement, for their own reasons, as though 10/10 is something that is set in stone, and we all judge based on that universally (mis)understood truth.
I will say that I have had the most fun with this game that I've had in a long time. For me, it gets a perfect score.
Sure there are bugs here and there, for example, the text in the game often doesn't show the first letter in some of the words or whatever, but I don't rate a game on its bugs or weaknesses unless those negatives measurably tarnish the play experience.
What I rate the game on is how much I am able to enjoy it, how often I find myself smiling at the "little things" of a game, or pleased by the mechanics.
This game is, without a doubt, a masterpiece of RPG development.
If it sounds like the kind of game you might enjoy, you probably will enjoy it.

I have played Diablo 1 plus expansion, 2 plus expansion, and 3 plus expansion, Titan Quest: Immortal Throne, and last but not least Dungeon Siege 1 plus expansion, and 2 plus expansion. Now having said all of that, I can add Grim Dawn to this list of excellent ARPGs, even at this as yet unfinished stage of development.
What makes Grim Dawn a game that can stand proudly alongside such genre greats? Well, in my opinion Grim Dawn takes a little of each of the aforementioned predecessor's formula and combines it together. From Diablo? The dark, grim atmosphere and story. From Titan Quest: Immortal Throne? The dual-class mastery system and the itemization scheme. From Dungeon Siege? The psuedo-open world exploration of the game world.
I have no doubts that the game, when finished, will definitely be a worthy addition to any ARPG fan's library. Heck, given how fun and stable this early version of the game is, the more adventurous may be tempted to add it to their library now! But, just remember that it is still a product in live development. Expect changes as we approach the release later this year.
