tl;dr: interesting/unique core game mechanic that is fun until it gets a bit repetitive.  Definitely worth checking out, but it can fade after the first few play throughs.
Stories features a very solid core mechanic built around the game basically being self looping - when you "beat" the game, the ending transitions straight into the beginning to start over.  Why?  Because the game is basically a choice-your-own-adventure book, in game form.  Between every level (and occassionally within a level) you will be presented with multiple options on how to proceed.  The game is both satisfying that the choices meaningful change the story, and you have no FOMO because you will eventually be back at that decision point again, only to go down the other story path.  A play through only takes 15-30 minutes, as it is only 5 levels or so per play through, and at the end, you will (hopefully) reveal one of the 4 'truths' about the story line.  Each one unlocks another tier of skill unlocks, and each truth has 4-6 endings (of the 25 or so endings), so you will get the same truth more than once (unless you use a guide or just luck out on your first 4 play throughs).  The levels also have a number of unlockable areas that you can access in later play throughs, after you have upgraded your sword to open the doors.  Additionally, the levels change a bit depending on the story choices you make: you might play the same level on 8 or 9 different story paths, but the context will be different each time, so the level will adjust to reflect that.  The game also features extensive narration/voice acting which does a great job with the story telling.
Everything is groovy as you play the first few playthroughs, but it starts to really drop off there.  There's just not enough levels, path through the levels, and variations for the levels to sustain so many playthroughs.  The combat is solid, but really has a short evolution, so it becomes incredibly repetitive.  This is excerbated by the limited number of enemy types, and their lack of meaningful scaling.  More than once, you will be disappointed when it seems to be building to a boss fight, only for you discover there isn't one, and that's because there isn't ANY bosses, period.  The end result is a real fun first few hours that quickly levels off to repetition.  In the end, the mechanics are solid, but there just isn't enough content.  The developer may have accidentally painted themselves into a corner in that regard, as the game is almost 100% dependent on high quality story content, and it is hard to produce that in large quantities.  Hopefully the game sells well enough to warrant a sequel, as the game features a fantastic 'choose your own adventure' mechanic, but just needs a lot more content in the form of enemies, bosses, levels and paths through the levels, to maintain the experience through the 10-25 play throughs the game tries to deliver.

This is not the first time I have played a Telltale game. I have played every single one since Jurrassic Park and Back to the Future, as well as a few of the earlier ones. I know that the engine has problems. It always has, it always will. However, I have never experienced as many problems as I have in this game. The loading screens are abysmal. They take upwards of a minute to transisition from scene to scene. When there is heavy action on the screen then you are asking for framerates as low as 11fps. The rest of the time it will hover at 60fps with no problems. I have never had this with any other game. Even the most recent games, Game of Thrones and Tales from the Borderlands never had slowdowns for me. It is a buggy mess.
Now, let's move onto the mini-series part. I understand that there are only three episodes here. Normal telltale games have five to six episodes. This is brilliant and all. I mean, this game is half price which makes up for the 'three episode' thing, right? Well, sort of. You get three episodes. However, each of these episodes is half the length of a 'normal' Telltale episode. You get an hour out of it. That is right. There is three hours total gameplay for your money here. With a normal Telltale game, you are getting 9 to 12. You are getting a quarter of the gameplay for half of the price. It is an embarrassment and a pure cashgrab on the part of Telltale.
The main problem with the half-length episodes is that there isn't any real character development. You can't bond with anybody in the game because there is just not enough time. It is shambolic.
That being said, the story is alright. I purchased this game on a sale so I am not 100% disappointed. However, if you purchase at full price then you shall cry yourself to sleep at the wasted cash.

I showed this game to my father the neuroscientist.  For over 40 years, he's been working on decoding the brain circuitry behind visuospatial integration and attention.  Very esoteric stuff.  To make a long story short, there's a point in the game about 10 seconds in, when the entire field starts to spin as a single frame of reference - i.e., your pure beleaguered triangle starts moving rapidly, but so do the walls.  My dad pointed out that if certain parts of your brain are working properly and you've played the game enough, those parts of the brain can learn to ignore the spinning and treat the field as stationary.  But that only works so far, and for the really hard levels, you might not get there anytime soon unless you have superb natural reflexes.
In other words, this game is batshit crazy hard at first but there are verified and well-studied neurological reasons why it starts out hard and gets easier.  Somewhat.  For some people.

Its a hybrid third person action game with tower defense. this means all your descisions and actions play out all in real time so when your defending against those nasty orcs, timing and well thought out traps are crucial. Yor goal is to keep the orcs from reaching a certain point on the map called, the Rift.The Rift was built in a forsakened fortress to keep everyone safe but now the orcs want to get to it and destroy you if you get in their way. Your teacher fell in battle so now it's up to you, The apprentice to defend the rift! The story is not really what this game is about but you are greeted whith the occasional cut scene. The game starts off with only a few waves and the basic set of orcs which are fairly easy to kill, as long as you don't sit there and let them attack you....but who would do that right? Each level in the game has a set number waves, each increasingly more difficult. The good thing is you always know what you're up against and just how many Orcs your going to slaughter in that particular level. The Orcs also range from ground units to archers to flyers and big tanks that take alot of damage. Also, each orc has a weakness so exploiting it in your traps and strategy will help alot. While the onslaught of orcs never stops, you have plenty of weapons and traps at your disposal, which brings me to my next topic, The traps! Each trap has a set fuction and there are a number of them which can only be placed on walls, floors, ceilings etc.
They range from your simple barricades to huge swinging ceiling axes, to decoys and meat grinders, to archers and guardians. You also have weapons to choose from to kill the orcs yourself, thats what i love about the game. Youre not just looking down and watching the fight, youre in it. So it is up to you to work with your traps and stop the orcs from reaching the Rift. Although, in later levels you must defend more than one rift at a time which means the game can get pretty tough.  The rift will heal you when your close enough so if your ever in a pinch, you can go back and refill your hp which is nice. The game also scores you on your accuracy and headshots and the amount of kills in a row. Depending on how well you do, your awarded with up to 5 skulls, these are your currency. However, you cannot move on to the next level(s) unless you have earned enough skulls in previuous levels. So doing well, is essential. Yes the game can get challenging fast and you can lower the dificulty, but that reduces the amout of skulls to be earned, so its sort of a trade off. With the skulls you can purchase new upgrades and traps as well as bonuses that effect you and your traps, later on in the game. Now again i will say have not played this on pc yet but on xbox, there were no problems as far as framrate and lag. So I would check the system specs before you go ahead and make the purchase, as with all games. The visuals are quite nice and really stand out compared to most other tower defenses. The art style is a little silly and cartoony but dont let that fool you. When your killing orcs or watching your traps bruttally tear them apart..the gore and sense of pain does make the game feel less childish. Controls felt great on my xbox game pad although I would imagine mouse and keyboard is slightly better, accuracy and speed do play a big role here. Now i will say the game may have some flaws but I personally think Its close to perfect. And Im sure OMD2 fixes any issues this one may have.
Theres more to the game than I've mentioned but I wont spoil it all. Lets just say if you like tower defense games and third person shooters/action, you should deffinitely give this a go. Robot Entertainment's Orcs Must Die! gets a 5 out 5
edit: I mainly bought this to replay levels in OMD2, and yes i will be reviewing the sequal when I finish it!

I'm enjoying the hell out of this game, and I'm not even too far into the campaign. This is essentially Crackdown mixed with Saints Row. This game could have easily been a stand-alone expansion to Saints row 3, similar to how Undead Nightmare was for Red Dead Redemption. However, it stands as it's own entry to the series just fine.
The side missions are rather weak, consisting of go here, do this activity, then go over here and do this one, rinse wash repeat, then boom; new upgrade. It's not exactly a bad thing though. I found myself at the end of SR3 with almost all the activities still unplayed, but I'm doing activities more in SR4 because of the side missions.
The weapon customization is a nice feature, adding about 3 new skins to most guns and 3 recolors for each skin, but it is entirely aesthetic. The upgrade system has also been revamped, instead of 4 upgrade levels for most weapons, now they've split the upgrades into several categories(damage, accuracy, rate of fire, etc), with 4 levels to each, except for the special upgrade.
The vehicles also got a slight revamp of their upgrades, but it's not as significant. The new thing with vehicles, though, is that you can hit a key while you're driving, and it will automatically save it to your garage. Also, when you call for a vehicle, it automatically appears instead of someone driving it up to you.
The big new draw in this game are the superpowers. Between ice/fire/mind control blasts, throwing cars/people/tanks with your mind, leaping over buildings in a single bound, and running around like the flash on steroids, there's a lot to be done. And that's barely half of the powers in this game.
Instead of safehouses, SR4 only has one safehouse that you can return to at several locations around the map. Crew that you unlock are added to the safehouse, and you can get missions from them, as well as a romance option for some. Romancing your crew in this game seems like a satire of Mass Effect's romance system, instead of branching conversations and choices, you hit the romance button and your character asks them if they "want to ♥♥♥♥", leading to a brief cutscene of them getting intimate. One crew member punches your character in the face, right before jumping on them.
Overall, this game is absolutely worth the price, but I'd recommend waiting until it's on sale to get it, unless you're a die-hard fan of the series. As of the time of writing this review, it's on sale half-off, so get to it!

Half Life 2 is solid first-person shooter, with excellent controls, physics, environment design, and storytelling. While by today's standards, the graphics may seem somewhat dated, there is beauty in this game, particularly in its environments (notably the rural, out of the city areas).
Face animation and voice acting is very strong, which combined with the game's excellent physics simulation, level design, and controls give the game a very intuitive and natural feel, making it very enjoyable.
There is good variety in weapons and combat scenarios which, preventing the game from becoming too repetitive, although certain areas last longer than others, causing them to become slightly boring towards their end. Vehicle sections and physics puzzles help to break up the ground-war type combat and provide some of the game's best moments.
The difficulty level of the game is best described as fair; it's not the most difficult game, but it definitely requires focus and tactics - you cannot spray and pray, even on the default 'Normal' difficulty level.
Overall, Half Life 2 is a fantastic video game, and a worthy continuation of the Half life series. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the original Half Life or its expansions (Opposing Force and Blue Shift) and/or who enjoy science fiction themed first-person shooter type video games.

Extremely fun action-roguelike with good (but not infinite) replay value. Each character plays very differently, and there's tons of unlockables. The game's difficulty is quite high though, it takes a lot of skill and some luck to beat it.
The main unique mechanic is that difficulty scales up as the timer ticks up, which adds a lot to the game. Early levels are a race to find+activate the portal as fast as possible, even if it means getting less money/items, and then race to mow down the incoming waves of enemies and grab all the items you can afford before exiting. Random portal placement and random boss selection means there is some luck, and certain acheivements certainly rely on RNG. Sadly the difficulty scaling mechanic falls away near the end of the game; you're almost guaranteed to "max out" the difficulty meter before you reach level 5 (or even earlier).
The main downside is that enemies tend do become damage sponges later in the game, while still coming in swarms, and you have to kill every enemy to finish a level. This can make levels drag on way too long, in a game that wants to have a frantic pace. Also some of the classes are more biased towards multiplayer than singleplayer, and some have no effective way to fight the final boss solo (*cough*Acrid*cough*).
A successful playthrough should last a little over an hour. A failure could last as little as two minutes. Expect lots of both before this game begins to turn stale.

X-Com Enemy Unknown is the remake of the classic MDOS game which places you as the head of an international task force commisisoned in suppressing a mounting alien threat. You will deal with resource management for facilities, research, and defenses, responding to alien attacks via turn based combat, and overall keeping the council of countries happy and safe in order to keep your resources flowing.
If you played the original game, you will find some game elements to have been removed, such as the necessity to expand your base to other countries and placement of defenses. However, despite the original game's mechanics not faithfully carried over to the remake, what we have is a solid and enjoyable game. The story is solid, with an engaging lore that was not supplemented much from the original, and the graphics are what you would expect from the advencement of the years . The core of the game has been preserved, with some things removed, with the rest polished up to give you the reason why X-COM became a gamng classic.

Stories is a fun, if basic, action-RPG that hangs the bare bones of an enjoyable, but slender, gameplay experience on a truly intriguing story system (hence the name). You play as the fox action hero Reynardo as he battles ravens with the (in-cutscene-only) rabbit bandit Lapino and cat sorcerer Zenobia. The cel-shaded, heavy-bloom art style has a lot of charm to it.
Gameplay is your basic timed-strategy mash-X-to-sword action game, novel seven years ago in Arkham Asylum but done to death since then. While this one doesn't reinvent the wheel in that respect, it uses its basic building blocks well. Beating the crap out of ravens does get old by the time the credits roll, but some new skills and perks that regularly pop up are fun.
The game would be simple fun, but tiresome, if it weren't for the story system. You can complete a storyline in an hour at most, but the hook is that there are 24 stories. Each one differs depending on the branches you decide to take at different points, and you need to keep going through more branches to unlock the full story and help Reynardo win the war of the ravens and toads. You need to play through five stories in total, minimum, to beat the game. If not for the overarching plotline I almost wanted to give up before the finish line, but occasionally the swordplay sings (especially when you're racking up 100+ combos) and the story plays out strong enough to keep you invested to the credits. Most people will want to look up which storylines get you through quickest - you need to find four "truths" in-game, each one of which is accessed from six endings. But it's easy to make mistakes depending on your choices. If you get stuck doing two or three plotlines that unlock the same story piece, you'll lose interest well before the climax, and only completionists will play the 25 hours or so necessary to do so.
Those who churn through games like butter may not be enthused about this one. It's a 7/10 competent brawler raised up by top-notch story innovations. But there's enough fun in there to warrant a recommendation, especially if/when it's on sale.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is a game with a unique and cool idea at its core but which isn't always surrounded in the best execution. The story is relatively short and simple in its concept but is driven by a number of different player choices, both large scale, obvious ones in between chapters and also more subtle ones within the levels themselves. It has a number of different endings and the idea is that you play through it a number of times, altering your choices as you go with the eventual goal of getting the ideal ending. It's a very neat idea but making all these choices can feel like a chore.
Every level revolves around exploration and light combat. The levels are the same but as you progress, you earn resources that allow you to get new weapons, power them up with buffs and get permanent skill upgrades. These eventually unlock alternative paths within the same levels that were previously unavailable to you. Unfortunately, most levels just involve you walking between places, looking for extra loot along the way and playing a rudimentary combat sequence whose core mechanics are essentially less refined and precise versions of the Batman Arkham series combat. Though the enemies do get harder in later playthroughs, it never feels particularly challenging or engaging.
The game also doesn't really indicate when you've made the same choices you have before so if you can't keep track of it all in your head, you may end up doing 30-40 minute exactly the same way you did before and won't know until afterward when it's pointed out to you. This feels like a bit of wasted time.
Despite this, I really enjoy the game and its storytelling innovations still make it compelling and enjoyable, even if some of its other mechanics are a bit of a weak point. Your experience is narrated Bastion style and while some of the writing itself is a bit cringey, the narrator's voice actor does a fantastic job. It also has a nice, brightly coloured art style that is a contrast to the dark story being told but also a nice place to be.
In the end, Stories: The Path of Destinies is a relatively basic brawler game wrapped in a cool and different storytelling method. The base mechanics could have been better implemented but it does player choice in an interesting way and if you pay attention, can be rewarding, even with the many playthroughs it requires. There's nothing quite like it.

I have yet to come even close to completing Stories: The Path of Destinies, but I can already tell you it is one of the most fascinating games on the market.
GAMEPLAY
Many video games these days feature some sort of multi-part ending, with the ending changing based on the choices you make in game. Stories is a game built around that mechanic.
On the surface it is a simple isometric hack and slash akin to Bastion, complete with a narrator. Different swords (also used as keys) can be crafted with picked up items. There's parrying and various powers to aid in combat, nothing too unusual. The real meat is how the game works with the whole multiple endings thing.
Each of the titular Stories is a 30-45 minute segment of gameplay, wherein you will need to make 4 choices, each of which significantly changes the way that particular Story will play out. Each choice you make in turn leads to another set of choices and so on, with a grand total of 24 different endings.
Thankfully your weapons and other upgrades carry over between Stories. Enemy variety is manageable and well paced.
STORY
It's in the title of the game, so one would expect it to be quite good and it's alright. It's pretty cool seeing a story that changes itself so radically depending on the player's choices.
That being said I do wish there was a little more depth to the stories. Maybe I just haven't played enough yet, but from what I've seen so far neither each individual story nor the overarching story are terribly nuanced, just the usual help Rebellion beat Empire thing. A little more uniqueness in that regard would've been nice.
Dialogue is quite well written, not amazing, but still pretty funny. Characters aren't all that well represented in each playthrough, but are fleshed out across multiple Stories.
VISUALS:
Very bright and cartoony. Enviroments are colorful and different levels stand clearly out from each other. It couples nicely with the hand drawn portraits of the characters and the overall tone of the game.
SOUND:
The game employs a narrator, like Rucks from Bastion. This game differs in that characters have distinct voices and lines of dialogue, which can lead to some confusion as the narrator and main character have very similar voices to the point where I think they're the same character. There's also how the narrator narrates as if he were reading a book, which can lead to instances of a character saying a line followed by the narrator saying "said <insert character here>" which I didn't take too much of a liking to. Minor annoyance at best, though.
LIKES:
Again, very unique in it's focus on repeating a story and learning more from it each time. The visuals and bright and pleasing and the dialogue got a few chuckles out of me.
GRIPES:
It does feel a bit like quantity was favored over quality. While the 24 different Stories are certainly impressive and must have taken a huge amount of work to accomplish, I wouldn't have said no to, say, 8 different Stories, each one deeper and better paced.
Combat can feel a bit stiff at times as well and personally I feel that health drops are a bit too rare. None of this is a real deal breaker, though.
VERDICT

A modern choose your own adventure book. I would readily recommend this to anyone who enjoys fairy tales and fables or who loves the idea of choosing different paths to see new outcomes. Some paths are heroic and satisfying while others are tragic (a few of these can even be hilarious, if you have a dark sense of humor). The combat based gameplay is fun, but nothing deep or really that special. I would recommend coming into Stories understanding that the narrative is the meat and the combat is the means to an end. I would certainly love to play a sequel as the fantastic ending sent my heart back to the days before I needed dark low fantasy in my life and could subsist purely on "happily ever after".
Also, the music is great. There are a few tracks that really remind me of the score of Conan the Barbarian, a personal favorite. The lighter tracks, mostly.

I'm a huge snowboard fan, and at first glance, Steep has all it takes for an excellent game.
Casually exploring endless gorgeous slopes while pulling off sick stunts is sublime joy of this game.
Which gets interrupted as soon as the game tries to force you into narrow-scoped parts of gameplay. Which alone are not that bad if not for:
-Speed and three star courses challenge controls which are not set for precision - which leads to endless attemts to beat these courses. In fact, you cannot enjoy this game fully without a decent gamepad.
-Lack of well-designed progression. Yes, you have level and earn currency for outfits. But it doesn't change what you do and how you do it. It's too sandboxy and doesn't engage for lenghts. The career should be more peculiar and directional, with championships to qualify, sponsorships to chase and things to spend dough on.
-Fast-travel becomes too common. New slopes get unlocked instead of being discovered - you loose track of surroundings.
-In-game store lacks of major brands.
-No social activities. Yeah, you can bump into couple of people here and there but there's nothing to do together to stay in touch. Ideally, you would chat with people about cool slopes while in the chairlift - to then get there and explore.
-Annoying region lock. Why should Ubisoft deprive customers of choice of language? Not to say that it came with the chinese pack when installed.
-Offputting price. Regardless of your region, the game costs premium. On top of that, there's microtransactions.
Oh, and remember how much you paid yesterday? IT'S ON 50% SALE A DAY LATER.
-Other sports are kinda... meh.
Note it's just a perfectionist criticism.
I rate the game 7.7/10, and will come back over and over. Just maybe not that often.

General impression:
Mirror's Edge is a homage to parkour practice. The action takes place in an urban setting and wonderfully captures the atmosphere. It's a perfect game for speedrun and encourages players to push forward instead of taking out each and every enemy.
Gameplay:
The controls let you take full advantage of the environment and the feeling that you're doing parkour is ever present. However, once you've learned all the tricks, then that's all you'll have for the rest of the game. The moves became worn out after a while.
It's a very simple game, you can do the wallrun and some other stuff and that's it: no character improvement, no inventory, no new skills.
Fighting was introduced briefly but if felt cluncky. I always left it as the final option.
Shooting felt like a really good idea but the game discouraged you to explore it.
Using a controller is preferred over mouse and keyboard.
Design:
It looked and felt like Portal at times because of the design and also because of the environmental puzzles. I enjoyed the approach, it felt smart and beautiful. However, the lack of variety started to show itself by the time I was almost finished. Good thing that it was a short game.
Characters:
The protagonist Faith is a memorable and interesting character AND you'll see her a lot in cutscenes which help in building an emotional bond with her.
The other characters were a letdown as were their agendas. I found myself wondering why some of them were necessary to build the story.
Story:
Most of the time it was hard to follow why some things were happening as they were. Then I re-read the plot after completing the game and understood that there was no story to follow. The motivating force that set the things in motion was a fuzzy mess. It were the loopholes in the story that made it hard to follow, not it's complexity.
Verdict:
I enjoyed playing this game but also got tired of it by the time I was through. There's a lot of room for improvement, the idea that it was too green for release spins in the back of my mind. If all those good ideas were polished and put into a sequel, I'd definitely show interest.

I'm enjoying the hell out of this game, and I'm not even too far into the campaign. This is essentially Crackdown mixed with Saints Row. This game could have easily been a stand-alone expansion to Saints row 3, similar to how Undead Nightmare was for Red Dead Redemption. However, it stands as it's own entry to the series just fine.
The side missions are rather weak, consisting of go here, do this activity, then go over here and do this one, rinse wash repeat, then boom; new upgrade. It's not exactly a bad thing though. I found myself at the end of SR3 with almost all the activities still unplayed, but I'm doing activities more in SR4 because of the side missions.
The weapon customization is a nice feature, adding about 3 new skins to most guns and 3 recolors for each skin, but it is entirely aesthetic. The upgrade system has also been revamped, instead of 4 upgrade levels for most weapons, now they've split the upgrades into several categories(damage, accuracy, rate of fire, etc), with 4 levels to each, except for the special upgrade.
The vehicles also got a slight revamp of their upgrades, but it's not as significant. The new thing with vehicles, though, is that you can hit a key while you're driving, and it will automatically save it to your garage. Also, when you call for a vehicle, it automatically appears instead of someone driving it up to you.
The big new draw in this game are the superpowers. Between ice/fire/mind control blasts, throwing cars/people/tanks with your mind, leaping over buildings in a single bound, and running around like the flash on steroids, there's a lot to be done. And that's barely half of the powers in this game.
Instead of safehouses, SR4 only has one safehouse that you can return to at several locations around the map. Crew that you unlock are added to the safehouse, and you can get missions from them, as well as a romance option for some. Romancing your crew in this game seems like a satire of Mass Effect's romance system, instead of branching conversations and choices, you hit the romance button and your character asks them if they "want to ♥♥♥♥", leading to a brief cutscene of them getting intimate. One crew member punches your character in the face, right before jumping on them.
Overall, this game is absolutely worth the price, but I'd recommend waiting until it's on sale to get it, unless you're a die-hard fan of the series. As of the time of writing this review, it's on sale half-off, so get to it!

Half Life 2 is solid first-person shooter, with excellent controls, physics, environment design, and storytelling. While by today's standards, the graphics may seem somewhat dated, there is beauty in this game, particularly in its environments (notably the rural, out of the city areas).
Face animation and voice acting is very strong, which combined with the game's excellent physics simulation, level design, and controls give the game a very intuitive and natural feel, making it very enjoyable.
There is good variety in weapons and combat scenarios which, preventing the game from becoming too repetitive, although certain areas last longer than others, causing them to become slightly boring towards their end. Vehicle sections and physics puzzles help to break up the ground-war type combat and provide some of the game's best moments.
The difficulty level of the game is best described as fair; it's not the most difficult game, but it definitely requires focus and tactics - you cannot spray and pray, even on the default 'Normal' difficulty level.
Overall, Half Life 2 is a fantastic video game, and a worthy continuation of the Half life series. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoyed the original Half Life or its expansions (Opposing Force and Blue Shift) and/or who enjoy science fiction themed first-person shooter type video games.

This game has simple game mechanics, small tech tree, but provides a nice skill curve, once you figure out what each thing does, its a matter of how to use them effectively. no instructions (no tutorial) which is kind of expected from old games like this, but they have a tutorial video on the store page so that does help, the game isn't complicated. Though since the game was put on steam it would of been nice if they added window mode or resolution options or make it so the steam overlay worked ingame so thats disappointing. However the game works on new computers and I haven't ran into any color issues that seem to be present in old games on newer systems.
Gameplay:
Players take turns launching units, structures or projectiles around the map. Players must secure resources around the map to gain more energy, the more energy you have the more things you can do per turn. The challenge comes from base planning and launching, every building palced is connected to the hub (the building that creates the other buildings) they are connected by a line, and no line can overlap each other so you must place your buildings carefully.
The hub can only launch the structure so far, when you press the "launch" button you have a charge meter to see how far it goes.
There is plenty of strategy and planning involved, the game has single player and multiplayer, single player offers skrimish mode and challenge mode. Skrimish is multiplayer but with AI. Challenge mode is bunch of scenerios with different objectives to complete. It's a nice way to learn the game and experiment with all the stuff.
Graphics and Audio
The game is old and only supports low resolution but the sprites look really good, everything is pretty easy to identify and there are 4 teams each with different looks of the units so it has a nice mix up of the same units.
The music is catchy and fits the game, totally kickass and really enjoyable, the sound effects are great and the voices that speak to you help create character for the teams and fit really well together.
Options
As expected from an old game there isn't many options specially video options however it does contain the hotkeys and audio options including the ability to turn off the commentary if you so desire.

This game will probably go by unnoticed. Shame, since Moonbase Commander is one of the most original and most entertaining games lately! It might not have stunning graphics and sound, but if it’s fun that matters then this is one great game!
So, what’s the story of this game? It’s quite simple – four companies are fighting for domination of the Moon. That’s all! There are no more details of the story, you will not be briefed about the current situation on the field, nothing! As the single player “campaign” starts, you will play as Niceco Company, then move on to Dewolf, then to System 7 and finally complete the game as Alpha team. Each company offers 4 missions and if you play for about 2 hours per day you should be done in less than 4 days. And I was just beginning to completely enjoy my superior strategy…
The game plays as follows: you construct various structures such as air defense missiles, energy collectors and radar towers as well as fire missiles, bombs or crawlers. Each component can be constructed only in the hub. Hubs are the cores of each “base”. When you want to build a component, you need to select it, pay the price for construction, then aim and fire the component in the wanted direction. New component will be connected to the hub and will be destroyed if hub is destroyed. Hubs can also construct other hubs, but note if the main hub is destroyed so are all others and you have lost. Each component has its price of 1, 3 or 7 energy points. When you start the game you will be getting 7 energy points per turn, but finding energy sources and placing energy collectors gives you extra 3 energy points. Your goal is simple – destroy enemy main hub(s) or place an energy collector on a specific energy source and hold it for a set number of turns (you will be told about your goal).
There is total of 18 components and weapons that can be “fired”. Aside from previously mentioned hubs and energy collectors, you can also build air defense (protects you from various air attacks), towers (provide larger viewable area when fog of war is turned on), shield (protects an area from everything) and so on. On the other hand, guided missiles are great if you are not aiming well, EMP disables shields, hubs and other structures, bombs are dumb and you need to aim well and finally, crawlers are ultimate weapon of destruction… but the move real slow. There are other weapons and components but you need to find something on your own!
Once you complete the single player campaign, you can still play skirmishes versus up to three opponents or in team with a computer against other computers. There is a multiplayer game option but you can only play it online via GameSpy.
The graphics and sound are much below today’s standard but such game doesn't need them anyway. Although the game can only be played in 640x480, everything looks real sharp and nice. Sounds are limited to the usual set of beeping, booming, crashing and whistling, with a voice commentary from your superior’s computers.
Overall, the game is quite fun but it doesn't last long enough. After I was done with the campaign, I lost interest, as I never enjoy playing skirmishes (they just seem pointless to me).

1st person, zombie outbreak, Steven Seagal snapping necks simulator (SSSNS lol), survival game with RPG, parkour, stealth elements. I wont spoil story at all, you have to try it yourselves, only thing I will say is it's very well put together for a zombie masher. That said, this is what original Dead Island games should have been, this being made by the "same" developers. Compared to their former project that felt sluggish in every way, in Dying Light you have all the freedom you wanted. Basically they made game similar to Dead Island only better in every way, plus added bunch of cool mechanics on top.
The most time in this game you will be spending on (killing zombehs!? - no) looting, it's insane how much more loot they added (loot respawns!), and you will even have your own detect loot ability, similar to Witcher 2. My favorite place to loot was the yellow "toolbox" container, it's so cute and when you punch it you get stuffs. xD You will find loot anywhere in the big city, compared to the map size of Dead Island and this game it's insane how much more there is to explore. Here's where "parkour" will help you a lot. The ability of free running and jumping over obstacles without loosing momentum. There's no other way of transportation in the game, not even a fast travel option, only running and occasional zipline and it's great. Game has day and night cycle, by day infected are slower, there's good visibility and it's usually safe to explore. But when it's night time you either chicken out and go to sleep at safehouse, or you man up and roam the darkness, slay the beasts of the night and try not to crap your pants. You can kill any infected in the game, by day or by night, the important thing is how you do it and with what / where you hit them.
There are many different kinds of infected, similarly to Dead Island ones. You have regular infected, those are majority in game, then you have regular "special" ones, like infected in hazmat / firemen suits, policemen or random "goons" type that can't be stealthy executed from behind (yeah game has stealth elements), also infected in special resistant clothing can't be lit on fire, like hazmat / firemen. Then you have runners, they are the fastest ones by day, and can climb surfaces. Next on the list you have big and angry ones with huge hammers, that act similarly to those "arm swinging" infected in Dead Island, which punch you across the map. The few last ones are spitters, that spit blobs of exploding goo at you. Then really giant infected that smash and charge, throw rocks at you. Regular exploding infected, that just explode you (they so annoying). And... I'm not done yet... there are actual children infected, and they are creepy, and they scream, and they are the ones that give you those nightmares. The last ones are night infected that are active only at night, and they are by far the fastest and agile ones in game. That out of the way, you can kill any of them from one hit for regular ones, to two hits on big ones (with melee weapon). The only ones that need more than 2 hits to kill are the night infected. You can silently execute majority of infected from behind ;) if you are under the Camouflage effect. Once again, you have to develop tactics and learn what works on what infected.
Game is filled with sidequests and activities apart from random mini events that randomly "pop up" while you roam around or explore. Completing those will earn you different rewards. You earn experience by doing almost anything, from killing infected, helping survivors, doing missions or even from simple running, jumping and climbing. Depending on what you do, you level up in three skill trees: Survival, Agility, Combat. Every level up in each tree will grant you skill points that you can use to unlock some cool abilities and skills. My advice is to get the ability to Camouflage, it will make your life fighting infected so much easier, trust me and thank me later.
Crafting system is similar to Dead Island, you get mats, you make/upgrade/repair weapons, only difference you don't need the bench now, which is great. So loot and create stuff on the fly. You can find blueprints all the same, that add elemental effect to melee weapons. Repair system was done bit differently, you spend repair charges to repair your weapon, if weapon has no repair charges, it's useless. Firearms don't need repairs, only ammo, which is not good idea to use, because sounds attract infected. Tip about the melee weapons, use the best one you have, keep one for spare, but don't haul 10 of them, because you can find weapons anywhere. You have many types of explosives, noise makers, shurikens, throwing knives / axes (apart from throwing regular weapons), etc. There are also many types of survival gadgets that help you lure, distract, kill the enemy. You can also create "tonics and potions" that give different effects, but didn't find those too useful. Apart from all that, you have environmental traps scattered throughout the city that will aid you in dispersing the wicked.
You can kill infected using your arms and legs as deadly tools, be it simple boot stomp, neck break execution or jump from height for that brutal drop kick / stab. Combine free running and melee for more exotic effect, like sprinting on rooftops and jump kicking the infected off of it. Or using the momentum of zombie running at you and pushing it face forward into the spike covered wall, you are the one man (unless in co-op) army against the army of infected after all.
Game has some optimization issues here and there, but personally I didn't have any gameplay or technical issues with it even on my old rig (Phenom ll X4 965, 8GB Ram, GTX 750ti). Once again game has great story IMHO, awesome voice acting (dam you Chris), great visuals and textures, fluid combat and movement, big open map, tons of infected, incredible amounts of loot and shortest damn loading screens ever. I really enjoyed the game and spent over 50 hours in single player. Did some co-op action too, and it's on the level with everything the game throws at you. So go on, try it out, it's Dead Island 2.0, and it's better than ever. Enjoy.
P.S. The Following was a blast to play through as well. A lot of content, new story arc and big map to explore.

That was a fun romp!
Let's just get the negative points out of the way:
CONS
* The gameplay is repetitive by nature. You'll be visiting the same environments over and over again, and facing the same ~5 enemies nonstop. Very few things change in the actual gameplay from one story path to the next. I didn't have a problem with that, but I understand if some people did.
* There were a few very annoying bugs. I've had problems with the Void Blade where my movement speed was permanently doubled - which, I admit, was a welcome bug - ....and also times where it was permanently halved, which sucked. Most egregious was the fact that, in the last choice of the Hero Path (the 'true ending' so to speak), I deliberately picked the wrong choice to see what would happen. Then, instead of getting booted to the last checkpoint or even the beginning of the level - the game kept on as if I had chosen the right choice, whilst skipping the entire story sequence to give me the context for the final level. A friend of mine also said he had enemies being trapped on unreachable terrain, though I didn't experience that myself.
* The starting story sequence is unskippable. That doesn't sound like a huge issue, especially when the narration is so good, but by the 5th time you just want to get on to the gameplay, especially if you're going for all 20+ endings. While I agree that more swords might not be reasonable to ask for, I feel that adding more tiers to existing swords and gems can't be all that hard, even if they're just flat effectiveness upgrades.
* The progression system is very short, with swords and (useful) skills capping out very early. It was clearly made for a playthrough no larger than ~5 runs. There should be actual gameplay rewards for going for full story completion, other than slowly grinding away at the level bar to pick from the skills you're not interested in in the first place. After you've maxed out your swords, chests give off only a few scraps of health. At the very least they should also offer sword energy.
* Combat checkpoints are excellent, but story checkpoints are seriously lacking. There are a few choices which result in instant Game Overs. This is fine. What isn't fine is that you're booted back to the start of the level, while dying in combat respawns you right before where you died.
* The True Ending is fairly straightforward, and isn't any more involved than any one of the story paths. This isn't a problem for me, but many people expect big twists at the end nowadays.
PROS
* The narration, just - the narration. I'm talking Bastion-level narration here. The narrator goes to lengths to properly voice every single character, and it works beautifully.
* A game where your choices ACTUALLY MATTER! Every single one of them, taking you through a completely different path, every permutation resulting in an unique ending tailored to your choices.
* Charming cartoony artstyle, contrasting with a surprisingly grimdark setting and story. Not something you see every day, and very much a welcome change of pace.
* Lots and lots of story, interspersed in bite-sized chunks throughout the in-game narration, cutscenes and choices. It never feels like too much, and always makes you interested in more.
* Surprisingly good combat. It's fast-paced and fluid, and once you get in the groove of it, you're dashing and slashing, pirouetting, grabbing and throwing and hooking and casting a couple spells for good measure. The only thing that breaks the flow of the combat are the explosive ravens, which are annoying, but understantable as a mechanism to force you to pay attention to your surroundings.
* Beautiful environments and clever level design. The 'floating island' nature of the game's setting makes so levels can have a high amount of verticality, and through shortcut doors, hook-points, floating platforms and teleporters, they can twist around themselves, making them fun to traverse, whilst never making you feel like you're lost, always funneling you where you need to go when you least expect it.
* Music is top-notch. Not much to say beyond that.

An adventure game where the emphasis is on story immersion. Our inventory can hold one or two items (sometimes it is completely absent) and we never really have a complex puzzle-solving sequence. However, we interact with other characters a lot, make decisions (that can later have consequences) and we fight a lot. The latter is especially typical of the Walking Dead series - we fight hordes of zombies and these sequences are all QTE events. If you don't press the desired button in time you'll die and have to start over.
Not very well. This comes just before the 3rd Walking Dead episodic title (Season 3) is released and is meant to tell the story of Michonne - I understand she was absent somewhere in the comic books but since I do not follow that one (just the TV series) it does not make the game more interesting. Bringing over a signature character from the TV show does, but since they managed to do without such a thing for 2 seasons, why make this decision now?
A Walking Dead title usually has 5 episodes which gives enough time for character development, an interesting story and also to see how our decisions affect the story along the way. Michonne's story is only told in 3 episodes - the story-telling is marred by the constant QTE sequences; the battle with the zombie drags on and on and on. Also, it isn't just a story of Michonne and the people she meets along the way; we also have flashbacks that elaborate on her family and how she was affected by the onset of the zombie catastrophe.
Michonne's story is not bad. It's just very far from being as good as the rest of the Telltale games in this franchise. As I found the story interesting I'm not going to downvote this title, however, if you are a newcomer make sure you start with Season 1 instead and then move to Season 2. In fact, since Season 3 will continue Clementine's story I'm not sure who to recommend this game beside Telltale / Walking Dead fans. If it is on sale this may be a good purchase but you should note that Telltale usually makes much better adventures than this.

The title being a reference to a song that was both terrible and awesome at the same time. Much like Saints Row IV.
This game plays with large amounts of both pop-culture references and the antithesis of pop-culture; nerdom.
From the Dubstep menu music with sound effects an emulation of Dubstep FX to the "There is No Pancakes" achievement there's a little something for everyone within the game as a whole.
The gameplay itself is a little lack-luster in difficulty (I recommend you play on hard if you want to be challenged) but incredibly beautiful in design and layout. The physics are a little cheesier than I prefer but the game is geared towards some what of a super-hero character progression.
The opening sequences are admittedly exciting, playing through like a movie with occaisional prompts for your input. Once you've entered the, ahem, "simulation" the game is still very pretty to look at and fluid. The leveling system is simple but expansive. Car upgrades/modifications are an almost sandbox-style car designer. Weapon upgrades are bought in the way that technology is researched in a turn-based strategy without the waiting. Very linear.
I attempt to write this review without giving away too much of the game but at least let you know what you're getting into.
When I first played it (on a 2-day free weekend) I was unsure if it was any good. It grew on me. I wound up purchasing the game because it was on sale during the trial weekend for 50% off. I would never pay full price for this thing, but it is something I decided I wanted to continue playing. I'm unsure of the re-playability. I purchsed the second and third (previous to the current) versions of the game because they were only a couple dollars each. I'll probably play those a little bit if the re-playability of SR:IV isn't what I hope it will be.
IN SUMMARY:
This is GTA IV with crappier physics and the cheats turned on.
You can play almost the whole game without letting go of the "W" key, occaisionally tapping the mouse or "A-S-D."
Wait for it to go on sale before you buy it. It's not worth the asking price.

Highly recommend this game for fans of tactical RPGs, or turn-based RPG combat in general. It makes some questionable design decisions at various points, but is well worth every cent of the asking price. (If you pick it up later on during a Steam sale, congratulations, you're winning.)
Selling points: this is possibly amongst the most beautiful games I have ever played. Not in terms of "graphical fidelity," of course, but the cel-shaded art style is extremely well-done all the way through and quite captivating. I would happily take games in this style over mainstream AAA titles living in the uncanny valley over and over again. My only complaint in this area is the extremely limited character animation during "cutscene" conversations; what is there simply serves to highlight how little there is. I probably wouldn't even have noticed if not for the few efforts they made on this front. (A very, VERY minor complaint, since the game is not relying on FMV-style, and even in still shots, the artwork is simply gorgeous)
The tactical combat is engaging, and the mechanic which links a character's health to his damage output makes an otherwise simplistic system compelling (do I do limited damage against this enemy to lower the danger they bring, or reduce his armor to make my next turn that much more effective while risking him bringing the hurt in the interim?) and makes level-up decisions on characters agonizing. I went the route of "specializing" each character I used frequently, resulting in characters of similar class and starting stat reaching the end-game with vastly different skill sets (i.e. of the two archers I used every opportunity, one was the absolute best at knocking enemy armor out of the picture, while the other was a damage-and-willpower fiend who had my highest kill count by the last fight). Also, while I'm not huge on harping for realism in games, it has always somewhat annoyed me that characters with 1HP out of their 1,000 maximum were just as potent as at full health, and this is a nice way of remedying that.
The story arc is compelling and kept me interested the whole way through without relying on many overdone tropes and archetypes, taking place in a very interesting setting I would happily p[ay to see more of. There is also quite a bit of background lore and information made easily accessible without forcing it to the forefront through excessive exposition, leaving its perusal to those willing to spend the time to enjoy it and letting those less interested mostly ignore it without detracting from the direct experience.
The Renown system, which irritated me a great deal, but in a good way (as odd as that sounds). EVERYTHING in this game - level-ups, food for your tribe, items to supplement your heroes - is purchased with renown, which you gain from victory in battle as well as certain C&C moments in between. While it can be frustrating at times, after beating the game, I view it in a wholly positive light - rather than making something like EXP and Gold to be used for two separate purposes, incorporating both resource pools into one base stat increases the strategic element, and makes every expenditure that much more risky and demanding. I entered the final battle with three fully-leveled characters, and two weaker ones, simply because I had spent the renown necessary to do so along the way to ensure nobody in my caravan starved to death along the way. (Which can also say a lot about you as a person, I suppose, in terms of how you choose to spend it) At times, I would have preferred separate pools for the various resources, but only because it would have made my inherent min-maxing tendencies easier to oblige, and I cannot legitimately call out a design decision that increases complexity and the importance of a player's strategic choice.
Detriments: the touted choice & consequence mechanic, while always nice to see, seems to mostly amount to extremely random and jarring consequences; each major decision seems to have one "correct" option which yields a positive outcome, and the negative consequences of "incorrect" decisions are never forewarned adequately, resulting in major impact up to and including losing substantial characters with absolutely no warning (on courses of action they themself recommend, even). Think the Witcher in terms of its unforseeability, but without the time delay or overall neutral tone which was par for the course in that game. (To be fair, there were a couple consequences - one VERY major one - which took half the game to  conclude and did have ample but not flagrant warning, so the game did this quite well in some instances, but failed in others)
The combat never changes or develops in a significant way after the first battle outside of levelled-up abilities and new character classes with different special skills opening up different strategic options. What you see in the first battle is largely what you're going to get.
In the combat mechanics, again, the game seems to settle in the middle; the endgame battles (especially the final boss) had me biting nails and languishing over every turn, and the beginning was not far removed, but I had comfortably established a routine throughout the middle half of the game which pretty much ensured I'd win any given battle ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥d-drunk with minimal unit injury in the process. A more level experience would be nice.
A mechanic I rather like (linking health and damage output to the same attribute) has its flaw; in many situations, it is often tactically better to leave an enemy unit on the battlefield at very low HP rather than killing them outright. Due to the mechanic Il ike, their damage potential is next to nothing, but this goes against general gaming instinct and raises concerns in compliance with the point below...
MIXED FEELINGS: the way the turn-based system is executed. Instead of some stat which addresses/influences initiative, the game will always go YOUR SIDE-ENEMY SIDE-YOUR SIDE-ENEMY SIDE until only one unit remains on either, at which point one side will execute all of its turns and then the other proceeds. On one hand, I like this to an extent, because it makes battles lopsided in terms of numbers not unwinnable; on the other hand, I think it's fairly backward in terms of a good mechanic; if it were kept the same throuh the last round, it would give that moment of despair when you haver one unit left against four an air of possibility, thinking if you execute well enough you can pull this situation out of the fire (or, conversely, keep you thinking your moves over in the last moments of a fight, as an enemy acting that quickly could turn your 4-1 advantage into a one-on-one exchange if you ♥♥♥♥ it up badly enough). While I do like the mechanic as a whole as opposed to the general turn-based style, it loses its punch with that particular element making the last few turns of any given fight a foregone conclusion when it could have served to bring each and every one down to the wire.
ALL IN ALL: a very, very good game. I didn't catch this game's Kickstarter in time to contribute, but most likely would have, and do not at all regret spending full price for the experience once it released. I'm hoping it does well enough that multiple follow-ups/sequels are developed, so long as they equal or improve on the quality of the original. If you enjoy slower-paced games with combat more tactical and mindful than visceral and egoistic, this is a no-brain purchase that I wholeheartedly recommend. If Call of Duty is your favorite game series... 1. this is probably not for you; 2. please die as painfully as possible in a fire as soon as possible so as to possibly rectify the damage you have already done to the industry as a whole.

Man, I remember this game... Back when I was in middle/high school, picked this up at a Big Lots' bargain bin sale. Thing looked old, but I figured "why the hell not?".
It's a fun little game with an interesting feature: You fight with your buildings, not soldiers.
You become more powerful by expanding your base, setting Energy Collectors to boost the amount of energy you have to spend each turn, which allows you to perform more actions, such as launching more buildings and attacks.
The base is expanded by launching structures from a "Hub", which is the primary building for attacking and expanding the base. The hub can launch other hubs for further expansion, or set defensive buildings like forcefield generators and anti-air missile bases. And, of course, they can launch energy collectors for collecting energy. The Hub can also launch attacks against other buildings by launching a variety of ranged attacks, such as regular bombs, scatterbombs, missiles, and even a virus! The Hub can also launch a special "offensive" building which can only launch attacks, but at a far greater distance than the regular Hub.
This game also has a unique feature where all the bases are connected to each other by Power Cords. The power cord shows not only which bases are connected, but which hubs are supplying them power (aka which hubs they were launched from). If you destroy a hub that is supplying power to other buildings, those other buildings are also destroyed.
All in all, this game is fun. My favorite attack is the Energy Spike. You can hit cords and attack the two buildings on both ends of it!

The Banner Saga Review
by DaniAngione
----------------------------
Art - 9 / 10
Sound - 9 / 10
Gameplay - 8 / 10
Emotional - 10 / 10
Community - 9 / 10
----------------------------
Overall - 9
----------------------------
The Banner Saga; I've never heard of this game until the multiplayer spin-off, Factions, came to Steam. Only after that I've googled it and realized that Stoic's kickstarter campaign passed under my radar. And that was most unfortunate for me, because we're talking about a game that breathes norse mythology, is beautifully crafted with hand-drawn artwork inspired by '1950-60s Disney genious' Eyvind Earle and has an amazing soundtrack by Austin Wintory, the guy behind the musical score from Playstation's big indie hit 'Journey': the only game that makes me cry like a baby after EVERY god damn playthrough.
So, yeah. How did I miss that Kickstarter? I don't know. What I know is that since discovering about Banner Saga I've hyped it so much inside my head that I dare say that, in a way, it was a little disappointing. But not in a way that compromises the game - just in a way that doesn't satisfy the 'almost-fetichist' personal desire I built up for this.
You start playing as Ubin, a varl (horned giants) that leads a tax caravan through the frontier cities between the varl lands and the human cities. After some time, however, you get to meet and play as Rook, a small village huntsman, and Alette - his daughter. They're being chased by Dredge, these humanoid stone creatures that seem to be quite strong and suddenly start pouring from everywhere. From there on the game is a long and arduous road for survival - as simple as that.
Putting it that way, however, doesn't make justice for the beautiful landscapes, the amazing characters and the incredible tale you'll weave along the way. And more importantly: death is around every corner. Choices are tough, choices are insecure and you'll find yourself questioning your own morals for the sake of the people that follows you. Sometimes you'll have to be harsh, sometimes you'll be kind... And might even regret it later. Or be rewarded, even. There's nothing sure in The Banner Saga. Nothing is guaranteed, so it's advised to be careful about who you're going to care about.
I'd certainly give Art and sound a 10 - I'm giving a 9 for two reasons: for art, I must admit that the initial cutscene is so beautiful that the game left me wanting more. There is, however, no more fully animated cutscenes. Not even the ending. So I was a little disappointed there. And for 'sound', the reason is very similar: sometimes I miss some voices or a better use of 'human sounds'. For a game that clutches you so deeply on emotions and attachment, it feels a little out of place that all dialogue is only written.
Gameplay works well. It's not great but it's enjoyable. The fighting mechanics are good and I really liked the balancing and tactics around armor and strength. I wish there was a little more variety, but that's not a big deal.
Emotionally... Well, just play it. I recommend you don't, ever, load your game when something bad happens. Seriously. It's a game about a journey - a true viking saga - and about the pain and the loss and the sadness in said journeys. It's a game about decisions, a game about caring for those you love and losing them because YOU thought that this was the best thing to do... And it wasn't. This is very, very functional as a player-driven narrative. And if you take the plunge into the fantastic and beautiful world of The Banner Saga, it will reward you intensively. I assure you.
Community, well... I didn't play the multiplayer part much, but a few rounds have shown me that people are nice and fun, so I suppose it's ok.
Overall, The Banner Saga is a beautiful yet silent game. And by silent I mean that it has a lot to offer but you have to go there, you have to take it's hand and walk into the forest. If you do - you'll be so immersed that when you're done you'll realize that we are just guests upon the land...
PS.: Just a warning - this game is the first part of a TRILOGY. Don't expect much closure, all will be explained in time...

Amazing... I am planning on getting the seasons pass for this game so I can get The Bozak Horde DLC as well as the new recently announced one and OMG... This game is fun. I actually played it singleplayer first, and then multiplayer. However during the co-op gameplay I did a lot more side missions. This game has amazing ways of keeping you entertained while you fight off the hordes of zombies, or one or two really scary ones (that you should probably run from). This game doesn't have horror as one of its main tags but holy s*** can this game get scary at night. The parkour is great, very few problems, in fact so few that I haven't found one. The skills are mostly worth getting and reward you nicely for just playing the game. This game also has looting which is where you will probably get 99% of your weapons. Some of them need to be lockpicked but the lockpicking system is identical to Skyrim's lockpicking system, so if you have played that, you have a headstart in the learning process. If you played 758 hours on Skyrim on Xbox like I did, this will be much easier on a controller. I used my Xbox One controller for this because the game's PC controls are not the greatest, however, I am in no way saying they are bad. It is still completely playable without a controller, but for the best experience I would have to recommend one. You can pick up an Xbox One or PS4 controller for $60 and use it with a micro USB, and it works on a lot of games, so it is worth trying. Anyways the game also has weapon customisation which makes your weapon feel more like... well YOUR weapon. With the basic Toxic, Freezing, Bleeding, Fire, and Electricity, as well as a combination of all of those, plus weapon mods to make your weapon swing faster, hit harder, or just plain last longer in a fight. You can create the ultimate reliable weapon for the way that you play the game. There are also some stealth elements for you stealth lovers out there like the "Camouflage" skill, that allows you to blend into a group of zombies by rubbing their guts on yourself. I really REALLY wanted to like this game. And honestly, I DO. But can I "recommend" it? No, not at all.
Now you may ask why? Well here is where the fun starts... Or stops I guess I should say.
First, let me start off by saying the story itself is great, the idea and concept, the characters, narrator, ect ect. It's all great. And it saddens me the only way to really experience it is through the interactive medium of video games. Because THIS is where Stories comes SOOOO close and falls just short.
If I were to sum up the entire game in one word, it would be "C-L-U-N-K-Y". Seriously, it is SO clunky. I could sit here and tell you about how the levels and combat is repetitive (which they are after the third or fourth, hour long play through) but I think what really kills this title is just how non consistant the gameplay is. To those of you who've played Assassin's Creed or the Arkham games, you'll be familier with the combat, enemies circle you and have big obvious tells for attacks, and you must dash, block, parry, counter, ect your way through every fight, which is fine... If the controls worked more than half the time.
I can't count how many deaths I've had due to pressing dash and my character on screen simply dashing to nowhere and standing in the exact spot he was already in, or clicking on enemies to block and just sitting there unresponsive, or even attempting to ATTACK them instead and being hit first instead of blocking, because oh yeah, ALL your combat options are done through ONE button, making combat entirely context sensitive. Which means the game sometimes has no idea what you actually want to do when you press this singular button.
Movement is governed by your 2nd mouse button and suffers a similar fate. If your curser is JUST over the invisible walls that line EVERY path, the game has no idea where you want to go and you'll just run in seemingly random directions or just stop dead in his tracks until you correct it. (Oh yeah, sometimes the movement sticks OR the floor randomly turns into an ice level and I don't know why and you can't stop until you hit a wall.)
Speaking of walls, this is a game with no jump or otherwise, acknowledgement of a 3rd dimension, still HAS one. Meaning if you're not careful, you can fall off your horizontal layer and get stuck under the floor. (It would have been better to just make the game borderless and the fall killed you rather then keeping you stuck in 3D purgatory IMO.)
And speaking of design, I have no idea what they were doing with the optimization. Don't let the late PS2-esque graphics fool you, anything above 'VERY LOW' in the settings will probably make your computer feel like a toaster. It did for me.
Okay, enough bashing the game for now... SO WHAT GOOD CAN YOU SAY ABOUT THIS GAME??? you might ask.
Well, apart from the chug-enducing graphics, they are quite appealing to look at. The art-design and overall aesthetic is beautiful, I'd say the game itself is well-written enough, there's a response to pretty much EVERYTHING you do from the narrator, which is fun. It's short but replayable with interesting characters, it's funny and good-humored. Overall, I'd say this game is quite charming and actually pretty fun when it works. Just a shame about there being so much wrong with the 'game' portion of it...
Vinal verdict?

what can I say? Its practically Shaun Whites surf boating with updated textures and levels. Besides the awkward jump button and laggy input response its a pretty okay game. The reasons I would not recommend this game include the sad G Force mechanic, the input lag, the overall buggy terrain, the slight luck factor and its lame music.
The G Force mechanic is your biggest enemy in this game. It adds an unnecessary realism to the game that sometimes gets too real when you are going for the quad front off a cliff side with 4 seconds hang time. The best part is when you are carving at a reasonable speed and hit a hidden lip causing you to catch slight air, do a 90 degree spin resulting in a topped out meter.
Lets talk about the input lag. This mainly concerns the jump button. When approaching the lip of a jump you may hit another one of those tiny hidden jumps which causes your preloaded jump to cancel out. This leaves you riding of the main lip without any hang time and can really grind you gears. This occurs quite often. Another input lag issue regards flips and spins. I believe a month into the games release they apparently fixed flips and spins. On its first month of release you flipped or spun by flicking the stick right after you released jump. Once you figured that out things got fairly consistent. After the update they changed the flip and spin controls so that you could flick yo stick almost any time around jump release. The problem now is that its somehow less consistent as it was before. Now when you go for that quad frontflip off a big ole cliff you may end doing a single flip at an extremely slow rate. Very steezy looking, but not really good for racking up points.
The terrain is A+ in this game. Gorgeous and realistic as all hell. The main issue with it is that it can get rather buggy sometimes. It mostly has to do with structural terrain. You will be mobbin at a jump, preload jump button, hit the bottom of transistion and all of a sudden half your speed disapears, you release jump and do 1.5 flips and land right on your face. If you have ever hit steep transistion in real life wether on a skateboard, bike or skiboard, you know you have to do a little hop  while transistioning in order to retain most of your speed. Unfortunately the game nor you (with jump) can accomplish this resulting in a lousy jump. When flying down a mountain it can sometimes be hard to spot small relief. If you are turning at high speed and manage to catch air off of it you will spin and you will goof up your clean g force meter if you manage to ride it out. Its like in real life. Almost as real as doing a quad fronty off a large cliff side.
The luck factor is strong with this game. Expect to retry some challanges hundreds of times. This is mainly due to reasons listed above. Your multiplier is not easy to earn and will go away with any wipeout. wiping out due to reasons listed above  is common even with your taller than dad "vidya game skill level".
The music is pretty lame. Feels like you are in a modern Disney movie. Where is DIO? Why no Jay zed? No Bhi Bhiman? They have included an option to turn off copyright music. This option is gauranteed to play some tunes you have never heard before but the selection seems microscopic.
If you purchase this game and manage to hit Play, expect to become a slave to it. My "Y" button on my wired Xbox controller has been squished thousands of times from constantly retrying challenges.
Thanks for reading. Add me if you want to master debate about this game.

Not a "modern classic" - a true classic. This is the new benchmark for this kind of RPG. Details below.
This is an old-school-style RPG with modern graphics sound and UI. It is
good. It's a shame hyperbolic terms like "awesome," "incredible," and "phenomenal" are so overused in modern communication, because they apply.
The tone reminds me more of the original two Fallout games than any fantasy series I can point to. The main story is fairly dark and gets more so as the story progresses, but there is still plenty of humor and lightheartedness to be found in the world. Both of these aspects are handled well; I recall my pair of very heroic protagonists being unnerved and dismayed more than once by stuff going on around them, which made them feel like actual good people in a hard situation rather than just wooden protagonist bots that are above things like emotion.
Gameplay in combat feels like the best parts of Jagged Alliance 2, The Banner Saga, and Baldur's Gate with a hefty helping of things I haven't seen before. There are a lot of very satisfying synergies, and the designers clearly know how to design good encounters, because almost every fight in the game is an interesting tactical situation. Attacks feel so weighty that I actually winced a few times.
Social interactions and storytelling are also very good. The game includes a social conflict system, and it's the first time I've seen one that actually managed to create some tension in a video game.
I would also be remiss if I didn't mention how good the soundtrack and sound design are. I wound up purchasing the deluxe DLC because I wanted to be able to listen to the soundtrack, and the sound effects and environment noises are also great.
The art design is similarly spectacular. This isn't the most graphically-intensive game you'll ever play, but it is
to look at, and everything feels like it fits in the world.
If I have one criticism, it's that some times the puzzles are a little bit too obtuse, but I'd rather have to scratch my head and/or look for help in a forum or wiki than have my hand held through the whole game. It respects your intelligence and persistence.
I'm not even done with the main campaign and I already want a sequel. I cannot recommend this highly enough.
