The Metacritic for this game is 75/100 and I'd completely agree with that rating because I'd give it around the same score myself.
Stories: The Path of Destinies is a Narrative Story Hack N Slash that's about creating your own destiny and by completing certain paths you unlock destiny cards or basically different cards with different outcomes.
Now though this game allows you to create your own story, there is a destined story that you'll want to hit in order to unlock the true ending of the game. Without spoiling the game I'd recommend not going down the same patht oo many times if you want to complete the main story in an optimal time.
Pros:
- Talent Tree - allows you to upgrade your guy progressively as you level up your character (the more you play the higher you level), you can increase damage, health, etc.. with this tree.
- Gem/Sword system - each sword you unlock (with a max of two levels for each sword) gives you a special ability that you trigger with the shift button. These swords are also keys which allow you to access different portions of the map that gives you access to gems. Gems are another way for increasing your damange and sustainability within the game. Though you don't necessarily need gems to complete the game, they make you feel extremely awesome.
- The Narrator may have been the whole story with it's witty remarks and references to other games. They did an amazing job with the narration of the game.
Cons:
- Not a true ARPG, it's a Hack N Slash with passive abilities to make your character strong, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but once you've maxed out of sword upgrades you just get health and energy from normal chests.
- There's essentially sound 3 maps, I haven't completed every destiny ending, so there could be more portions to each map, but if you aren't used to replaying maps like in say a diablo you might not like this game because you're basically replaying the same maps and trying to get a different story/create a new destiny basically.
- Menu could get some QoL work. When you open the crafting menu and press escape instead of it closing the upgrade crafting menu it opens the settings menu which is annoying when you want to exit very fast from the upgrade crafting table.
- The grab mechanic sucks, it's very hard to grab when you have your hook ability.
- Oh when you hit a narration portion you've already heard, you can't skip through the dialog with space. Some things you can, but a lot of it you can't which can be very frustrating for some people especially if you die.
Overall the game is great, the main story was fun to figure out and despite the repetitiveness of the combat it did make you feel awesome as you faught enemies.  I'd give this game an easy 7-7.5/10.

Call me a stickler, but this game lacked the punch to really make it something special. The combat is well done (though I'm certain a toddler could fair as well as I did), the levels are interesting, and I can't imagine how long it took to play test each different way though the game. That's where the positives end.
No matter what you choose, the narration has a way of weaving in whatever details need to happen for you to fail, making early playthroughs an exercise in futility.
You play the same 5 (or so) levels over and over again with different choices at the end until you discover the correct combination that gets you a happy ending (though it's success feels just as arbitrary as any other plausible path you could've taken). What this effectively means is that if you make a poor decision (or the narration throws in decisions you don't approve of) you have to spend an hour playing the same levels or again, just to pick a different option on some menu.
After 4 or 5 playthroughs, the combat loses it's magic, you've memorized the levels, the enemies become meaningless, and I was left wondering why I had to navigate all these levels and sit through nearly an hour narration, just to pick a different fork in the road at some point.
Worst of all, there is no reward for picking the correct path. No great and final boss fight, no extra difficult or intriguing extra level, nothing. Just different narration between the same levels.
It's a fine game, built well, well executed, but it lacks that special pop it could've had to be something truly special. And after just a few hours, I'm left feeling like I've explored and learned everything there is for me to know in the game, only to be punished by sitting through more narration to satisfy my curiosity about the other paths.
So, for what effectively amounts to just a few hours of content, even a sale price of $10 feels a little too high.
PROS:
Visuals
Characters
Story detail
CONS:
Repeating levels
Overly-Simple Combat
Length
No back-tracking allowed, hour-long punishment to explore single fork on the road.

South Park: The Stick of Truth is a fantasy-RPG game developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Ubisoft. It was released in March 2014. This review will cover the campaign, the gameplay, and the open-world aspect.
South Park features a good campaign. The campaign is open-world and this involves main missions that advance the story and optional side-missions that do not overly amount to anything useful. I completed the game in roughly 14 hours, which most of this time was dedicated to the main missions. The overall campaign was beautifully constructed. It easily followed the atmosphere of the television show in which Cartman, Kyle, Stan, and Kenny are the protagonists. I also noticed that like any adaptation, the game tries to incorporate those memorable skits from the show into the game, such as the aliens invading South Park and Mr. Poo. Furthermore, the game uses comedy and humour to lighten the environment because the developers expertly created a serious-tone with the battle of the Stick of Truth. The comedy does not feel forced so it hits a nice medium for comedy and seriousness. For instance, during character selection you can choose between four classes that have different abilities. I ultimately went ''thief'' but when I would click Jew, Cartman would tell me ''I guess we can't be friends then'', which personally was hilarious.
The missions individually are not repetitive and are not overly long because within a main mission there are smaller missions within, giving you constantly new objectives and new experiences with the game. South Park also features occasional choice-making that changes the narrative of the game in missions. I personally enjoyed the campaign and found barely any faults. As a moderate fan of South Park I expected wittiness and comedy and that delivered and I loved all of the characters. I did experience some negatives, particularly at the lack of explanation for useful abilities throughout the game, which made me have to google it or guess it a few times. I did feel as if the campaign dragged throughout the middle-portion, particularly when visiting Canada within the game.
The game features unique turn-based gameplay. I don't experience much turn-based gameplay in these sort of RPG games so I found it to be refreshing. The turn-based gameplay also incorporates effects. For instance, in one fight I had a burning boomerang and when I used it, it hurt the opponent but set them on fire so when they would attack me, they would lose a portion of their health. South Park has a variety of weapon abilities to improve your damage or versatility. Fights incorporate fourth grade humour. For instance, to restore a large amount of your health you would eat a box of cookies. If you wanted to get a speed boost, you would drink Tweek's coffee. These little things add to the overall South Park tone which I think improves the experience of the game. I also like the aspect of as you get stronger and gain levels, your enemies get stronger. This progressive system allows the game to become more difficult as it goes on and to better utilise more strategy to win fights, because it's better than a static system where enemies will always have the same health and abilities.
South Park is an open-world game. So, the game beautifully showcases a South Park that includes Starks Pond, City Hall, Token's rich house, and Kenny's poor house. The map is very large and uses Timmy as fast-travel to help reduce the annoyingness of constant travel between one end of town and the other. There are very few locked houses but the majority of buildings can be entered, allowing you to search and find useful things and also grasp the geographical area of South Park. Therefore, I feel the use of open-world benefits the game because it allows the developers to incorporate more stuff from the show into the game.
South Park is a strong game. My review is not as in-depth as I would have preferred due to Steam's word limit but what I covered is the basis of it. You're playing an open-world South Park game that incorporates television show elements and character development into a fantasy setting. It features turn-based gameplay that incorporate 4th-grade humour to provide a better South Park feel to the game. It features geographical locations that resemble the show, which you can explore most areas. I personally felt it dragged in the middle-portion as all Ubisoft games do and provide a lack of tutorial throughout the game. I purchased this game for $7.49 on sale and if you're a moderate South Park fan, buy it on sale. But, if you really like South Park I totally recommend this at $33 because you get value out of it and have fun while playing it.
7.75/10
- The atmosphere of South Park.
- Storyline development.
- Comedy and humour.
- Unique fighting system.
- Tends to drag at various portions throughout the game.
- Very forgettable side-missions.
- Rushed ending.

Ys is a series that I have only recently gotten into, with Ys I & II Chronicles being my first ever experience with the series.
If you are familiar with the later games in the series, you know that they are fast paced action games with amazing boss battles and soundtracks. While Ys 1 & 2 do have a lot of those things (namely the soundtrack and boss battles being awesome) there are a few key differences that can make or break the experience for you.
First off, the localization is a lot of fun in Chronicles. The standout for me is Ys 2 in this collection especially. There is a gift giving system that, despite there being few real rewards from it, is a treat if you appreciate witty dialogue. Rather this means apologizing to someone becaused you "Lit their♥♥♥♥♥on fire" by giving them a few more gifts than normal, or wooing a woman right in front of her husband, there is a lot of fun to be had with that.
As far as the soundtrack goes, Chronicles+ gives you a lot of customization. You can choose from 3 different versions of the soundtrack from the Turbo Grafx, the PSP Complete collection, or the more modern Chronicles mix. Personally I prefer either the Complete or Chronicles soundtracks, but thanks to being able to switch the soundtrack on the fly you can listen to each BGM all 3 ways and see which one you prefer.
The largest barrier to being able to enjoy the Chronicles+ collection is the combat system. Unlike later Ys which use a much more traditional Zelda style battle system, Ys 1 & 2 use the Bump System. Essentially, you just ram your character into enemies to hurt them. The key is to bump into them slightly off center to avoid being damaged yourself, but the hit detection isn't always what you would think it should be.
Personally, the system didn't detract from my experience. However, these were my first Ys games. If you are a a fan of the newer Ys games hoping to play the original games that started it all, you might not be able to look past the strange battle system.
The bosses in the Ys series continue to impress me as I make my way further down the rabbit hole, and 1 & 2 have some great ones. Ys 1 has a clear disadvatage here, with some bosses that can be outright frustrating for all the wrong reasons. There are two bosses that I can recall that felt cheap and relied far too much on luck than skill. One of these was the final boss, which doesn't make for a very convincing showdown (I should mention that I only played through Ys 1 and 2 on the Nightmare difficulty setting, so these problems may go away on lower difficulties). Even with some stumbles, for the most part BOTH games have incredibly well designed bosses, both graphically and mechanically.
When you get right down to it, I do recommend Chronicles+. It's not perfect, but it's a memorable experience with some truly astounding sound direction and epic boss battles. If you are a newcomer to the series, I recommend starting here. If you start with something like Ys: Oath in Felghanna, you might not be able to enjoy these as much thanks to the difference in gameplay. Veterans of the series should only come back if they think they can handle gameplay that feels like a decided step down. Even so, there are a lot of great moments to be had here as long as you don't expect the best in the series.

This review is being written purely for Ys I. If I go through Ys II I'll amend it as needed.
This game isn't necessarily a bad game. I feel like it has a lot of merits to it for a short (6-7 hours) RPG, but it just doesn't come together very well.
*The combat is quirky and I can see people not liking it, but I felt it was refreshingly fast and unique when compared to your average turn-based slog.  I would have liked a bit more variance though, such as combat related items, magic, or similar secondary attacks.
*The game is cleanly made. While the cutscenes are dated, the graphics overall are quite nice, if simple.
*The items collecting. While it's not everyone's cup of tea, I'm a huge sucker for games with lots of items to collect. I'm reminded of things such as La Mulana and The Legend of Zelda: LTTP.
*The soundtrack is honestly kickass. Not much needs to be said about it beyond that.
While these things are nice, there are a lot of problems I have with the game that these just can't redeem.
*The story is not exactly thrilling. It's incredibly basic and generic, and while there's a few interesting bits here and there, they're too sparsely scattered across what is ultimately a painfully boring plot of a generic hero collecting every ancient artifact the world over in a single evening and wooing the girl(s). Oh, and saving the world from a generic fantasy apocalypse. Woo.
*The art, while high quality, is just dull. I'm instantly reminded of decades of unmodified RPGmaker graphics, and as a result, immersing myself in the world is difficult. Between this and the plot, the game comes off as so standard that I'm not sure what to really get excited for.
*The experience mechanics. The levels cap out at 10 halfway through the game, and are practically hard-caps on your progression. The standard enemies either kill you in a few hits, or go down pathetically easy. I feel like the game would be better without the levels entirely, instead substituting in something like slightly more granular equipment.
*The bosses. While they're a good challenge and I don't think they're unfairly difficult, they are boring. I'm pretty sure every boss (except the final boss) has a single attack. Some bosses lack actual attacks entirely, and just rely on bumping into you to deal damage. I feel like a little more variance would've gone a huge way in making the bosses feel more exciting and enjoyable.
Overall, while it's certainly not bad, I can't recommend it. If you don't mind generic games or it goes on sale for cheap, it might be worth it. Otherwise, there's definitely better out there for cheaper.

Personially I highly enjoy and recomend this game. Its a beautiful and well crafted experance that takes in the wonder of the Swiss Alps, or recently Alaska. It also allows for diffrent players and playstyles to thrive in the same environment, with 3 diffrent modes of transportation: ski/snowbord, wingsuit, and paragliding. If that's all you need to hear, then click "Buy". However, this is deffenitly not a geme for everyone. Here's why:
The controlls are purposfully somewhat loose. You might hear people relate this game to SSX, and rightfully so, but you wont be able to do SSX things. In order to jump, you dont just press a button, but release it. To prime a jump you need to hold down the right or left trigger of your controller, and then release it slightly before you wish to jump. For someone who participates in skiing/snowbording this quickly became second nature, but for those who dont, it might take some getting used to. Tricks are some what complicated as well. Directly after initiating a jump, NOT AT THE SAME TIME press a direction on the left joystick to initate rotation, and release to stop rotation. Your rider will right himself durring a jump, but you need to give him time to do so. In order to land well, and not waste g-force meter, you will need to release the direction almost a full second before you reach the ground. When in the air, you can use the left or right trigger to grab with the left or right hand of your rider, and use the left thumbstick to tweak your trick in the air. This all seems very complex, and for some, the inputs to do a simple trick, might be too complex
Steep can be repetitive, some chalenges can start to feel the same after a while, and it can be confusing how the maps and chalengs work, as well as finding them in the maps. After all chalenges are complete, you can retry them for a higher score, or just roam the map and find your own lines. The late-game gameplay is very explorative and open ended, and can be offputting for some.
Everything is not for everyone. I say that I highly recomend this game and that I love the way it controlls. At the time of writing this review, I have almost 40 hours in the game, and I would guess that about 30 min of that is spent paragliding. Some people might really enjoy paragliding, but it's not for me, and I would say as a general rule, to not go in expecting to love everything about this insainly varried game. it trys to do allot well, and might not hit perfect notes on everything. but what you do find and enjoy, is what makes this game really amazing.
With the FREE Alaska dlc, I would recomend steep more than ever now. But buyer be warned, if you like your games to always be fresh every time, and are not one for reppitition, steep might not be for you. If you dont mind that, however, i think you'll really enjoy this game.

Failing in order to succeed. That's the general premise of this game. Play a few levels, make a few choices, inevitably fail. But your character "learns something" each time you fail.
Even though the combat felt kind of awkward at first, after a few levels I got the hang of it. And the graphics are gorgeous. I personally, love the artstyle with both the gameplay, and the hand-drawn aspect of the "cutscenes." It gives the game it's own unique feel.
I don't know if I'd say the game has good replayability or not, considering that you kind of *have to* replay it several times in order to get the "good" ending. The narration style akin to that of Bastion keeps the game flowing well, even when things aren't actually happening on screen. The actual story aspects of the game are kind of cliche from what I've seen, although not terrible. And there are plenty of story choices each playthrough, leading to several different endings.
The only real issue I had was that the levels have nearly no variation on continued play. Aside from the occasional door you couldn't open before, the levels are identical. Sure, there are a couple of different enemies that weren't there before, but the fights all happen in the same places. It makes the game feel really grindy.
Overall, I enjoy this game. It has a fair amount of content, and I do intend to at least get the "good" ending at least once. I would recommend picking it up while it's on sale.

It’s twenty dollars, so damn cheap for what you get. Unless you are broke, BUY IT.
Let's start out with what I expected after watching the trailers and pictures:
I got my parkour, pretty maps, and hand to hand combat. I also got a short story and very simple but annoying and unforgiving controls.
Oh the controls... Given that one of the very important parts of this game is parkour, you would think it would be the most fleshed out and well done part of the game right? Wrong, unless you are on point with your movement every time, the game will punish you with the same old falling animation. Fighting or running away from enemies is a whole other deal. The game has a very simple movement base which can be fun when you fight enemies. Sometimes enemies get weird advantages and knock you down/do a lot of damage that nearly kills you; Some enemies are not meant to be fought so when you do fight them, you know why they are able to nearly instantly kill you. Even though one of the core elements of the game was designed poorly it won’t dock it points for this. Mirror's Edge came out in 2008 and I am willing to bet that not much was done to study how good its combat/movement system was since back then not many games could be used to compare it and see what it lacked/boasted.
The art and modeling is so good. Without a doubt in my mind this game has absolutely beautiful looking maps, just visually at least, and even better looking models for props in the game. The maps however don’t feel like they were meant to be used for parkour. With all the clutter everywhere(yes clutter, even though it looks very clean), it is hard to really enjoy the game. I think the mappers did a lazy job of planning the maps which ended up making most maps feel slow, unintuitive, and clunky. A little bit more effort in the development of player movement through the maps would have gone a long way. On Top of all this the maps are relatively small making it very apparent they are linear. But like I said in my previous paragraph this game was made without much to go off of so this feels more like it was an experiment that went pretty well rather than a real game franchise.
The sounds/music are just ounces of amazing. This game had extremely good and worked out tracks for different times during each map. The attention in detail to the sound as well as the physical location of the player made this special and memorable. I really is a shame that thanks to its initial unpopularity more people didn’t try this out and get to hear the games music. The sounds for the player and VA for the characters are on point and very good. You can tell what you are doing pretty easily by the sound and it doesn’t get in the way or rip out of the immersion. Certainly no argument here at all.
The story in this game was interesting and relevant, but that doesn't really matter as those two descriptions are assigned subjectively. The story is short and lacks implementation. Yes implementation, I don’t mind cut scenes but you could literally play the entire game without ever knowing about the story. It is that loosely attached! Not like it matters since the story itself leaves a few things unanswered but not on purpose. It becomes extremely forced once you get into the later levels. Overall the story is a good idea and concept but it was poorly created and implemented making it feel cheap or unappreciated. This does to me count as a tick against them because it isn’t much effort for a game studio to make a decent story, and Mirror’s Edge story is not even close to being passable.
Overall the game is 7.9/10 Not really mediocre just small and unpolished. The ideas behind it are great and a lot of what carries this game is actually the visuals, music, and maybe sometimes the movement. It’s certainly not a triple-a game, at least it wasn’t on its release, expecting a triple-a game is silly. If someone asked me if Mirror’s Edge is a good game for them to buy, I would ask them if what they were looking for was something quick to pick up or a new thing they can invest a few hours in. If you seek a quick game you don’t really want to get into then don’t bother getting this. But if you want something new and interesting you can really sink your teeth into then Mirror's Edge is the game for you.
Extra:
One of the things I liked the most about this game besides the art, music and gameplay is the fact that this was never even a triple-a game yet it felt like the game had been given access to the kind of resources a triple-a game gets when being developed. It wasn’t pandering and it had its own style instead of a bland mundane repetitive feeling you get from modern triple-a’s but with the quality of one. That’s what made is special to me. I LOVE THIS GAME!!! (hopefully its newfound popularity and hype won’t bog it's prequal(Mirror's Edge: Catalyst) down into another triple-a let down).

This game is definitly a must have. This is something I would strongly recommend to teachers because unlike other games, not one of them more accuratly displays true history than Civilization V. For example, the four thousand year old eternal leader Ghandi, of India, decides that in the year 1958 that he is going to nuke Russia due to the lack of trading cooperation from the communist state. Well as it was, Russia's most powerful ally, the Aztecs, weren't too happy about that and decided that it was time for action, and as a result, entered a full fledged war with the Indians to aid their crippled Russian comrades. Having a hard time fighting a war on two fronts, Ghandi decided to call for aid from his most trusted and closest ally; the Celts. Of course the Celts responded with lightning reflexes, send their most advanced and highly trained troops. After ariving from the 200 year journey to India, the Celtic spearman came to learn that their ally was no more, and in shame walked for another 200 years back to Dublin, to then learn that their own civilization had fallen into ruin. With no home to crawl back to, they decided to walk. Walk as far as their legs could take them. Well as history tells it, Celtic spearman can walk for a really ♥♥♥♥ing long time. Infact, some of you might even be lucky enough to see these legendary spearman still walking the earth to this day.
Of course this is only a small taste of what this game has to offer in terms of historical accuracy. I find this game very educational, so educational in fact that I have decided to throw away my history textbook and just study by playing this game. I mean you could pull any old random history fact out of the air and it would be in Civilization in some, way, shape or form.
So in conclusion, I plead with you to buy this game. It will be worth every cent of it.

Banner Saga is a turn-based tactical combat game that is guaranteed to enthrall you with all its Viking seriousness. Combat mechanics are simple. You take turns and you attack either STRENGTH or ARMOR.
You start off as a small band of Varls, powerful horned giants mowing down puny humans that stand in your way, with the entire story becoming more and more epic as your band of follower grows and new characters are added to the cast. Use your kills (translated into renown) to upgrade your team members. The trick here is always to have an even mix of bleeders (strength damagers) and breakers (those that specialize in attacking armor so your bleeders can have an easier time). You'll make hard choices... choices that will kill off your characters or alter how the ending goes. The art is classic, a refreshing crisp clear feel that stand in its own way against the super-realistic graphics espoused by most third or first person shooters and platformers we see nowadays. I don't know about most people, but I FELL IN LOVE when I reached my first Godstone.
The only sin that this game has done is its way too short, and there are too little items, I suppose... but the Kickstarter somehow mentioned that this is just the first part of this Saga, and I know Viking Sagas have to be much longer than this. STOIC deserve a good pat on the shoulder for this game that redefines the turn-based genre and storytelling. Just make the second part so we can continue dealing with the Jormungand lookalike.

If you haven't played this game, do so. It might have Saints Row in the title, but it's anything but. It's less a game about a street gang struggling to fight for dominance of the city and more about being one of the best superhero simulators on the market. Seriously, the superpowers themselves are so friggin' enjoyable that it overshadows the fact that Volition practically reused the same city and that all the side quests revolve around doing activities instead of, well, y'know, being actual side quests.
Up until the very end, the city of Steelport will be covered in an eternal darkness, which may help with performance on lower-end systems as shadows will be limited to street lights. The city itself has only received a minor facelift, with the addition of a few alien saucers and towers throughout the skyline, as well as the destruction of some of the skyscrapers.
Combat is extremely enjoyable due to the aforementioned superpowers. It almost feels like a pseudo-ARPG in a ways, with you switching between different powers, juggling the cooldowns, and using the active and passive abilities to your advantage. As a result, each combat encounter is unique and challenging. Should you stick to using a Fire Blast to cause explosive damage against enemies, or use a Freeze Blast to freeze a group of enemies and then use a Rock Stomp to shatter your opponents? Or perhaps use Telekinesis to grab that saucer out of the air and use it to smash ground troops against the side of a building, thus killing two birds with one stone? Combat is wild and visceral, and feels just like every superhero battle should be. Plenty of enemy types appear, especially concerning the Zin troops, which feature everything from standard grunts to riot troops and rolling balls with laser eyes of destruction.
Overall, I'd say get it if you don't mind the reusing of certain assets, as well as a relatively uninspiring campaign (main story gets padded out with filler "side quests" and could be finished in a couple hours without said padding) because this game will give you a load of fun. Definitely love the direction Volition has taken with the Saints Row franchise, as the over-the-top, goofy humor and action work well in this context, and voice acting remains top notch. Can't wait to see what they've got in store for Saint5 Row.

Hard to recommend, but recommending nonetheless. Why? It's just full of charm, funny little cultural references and has a pretty good amount of content. However combat gets very boring as each class has 4 abilities, one of which is just a passive for 80-90% of the classes. So you largely spam the same 1-2 abilities, with the rare use (sometimes once a fight later on) of a 3rd ability, and sometimes a basic attack.
Other gripe is upgrading items at the blacksmith. Farming grindstones takes forever after the 1st or 2nd upgrade for him. However if you want upgrades without spending ALL of your gold, you need to gather dozens of these at a time for a 5-10% increase in chance of succesfully forging an item. Don't even bother trying unless you're at about 60% success, because you can waste almost all your gold upgrading one or two items. It's a shame because this could have been a really fun and important mechanic, but feels really forced. The only way to get grindstones is travel to caves, and hopefully roll a high enough number for each ore vein present, or spend 25 G a piece. As I said though this can take ALOT of grindstones and buying that amount can really add up in early-midgame as gold generally isnt earned fast. Battles (depending on bonuses of items you have and what you are fighting) generally drop 1-20 gold.
The blacksmith, repetive fighting and slow accumlation of gold are painfully dull or even annoying. However, the concept, dialogue, references, simplicity and music keep it entertaining enough to play for 20 or so minutes at a time.

Shadowgrounds is a top-down shooter with vague horror elements, and one I wish could have been done better.
This is a game that's very gameplay focused, and the gameplay did not have the polish to justify it. The aiming reticle (the mouse) is always at a fixed distance from the player, so aiming is frustrating. The hitboxes of the character, enemies, and environment are wonky, which resulted in me getting stuck in the environment multiple times. The weapons upgrade system is by far the strongest game element, but is marred by the clunkiness of the gameplay. Movement and dodging are feel unpolished.
Difficulty is also a problem. After fully upgrading the default pistol, there were only a couple times I really had difficulty: during boss fights with bosses that were straight up faster than me, and spawned minions ad nauseum, or 'this area is difficult because the exit seals and enemies spawn in'.
If this was more polished, I'd definitely enjoy it more, but as is, there's no reason to ever play this.

So growing up, one of my favorite games was the infamous Ys clone, Lagoon. Years later, here I am playing the game that influced a part of my childhood and now I'm mad because I feel like I missed out by not playing Ys sooner.
These games are absolutely amazing and have amazing replayability because of their short length (It was short to me, but it's average length for a 80-90s ARPG). The music (I listened to the 'Complete 2001' soundtrack, because synthesizers) is absolutely spot on. And the bump attack mechanic made the whole f'ing game really fast. The story, is okay- but no one cares to be honest, it's all about the action.
Know some people complain about the bump attack, but if you want to know what happens when you remove it with more 'zelda-like' gameplay, I highly suggest you go enjoy the butter knife action that is Lagoon (SNES).
If I had to pick which game I enjoyed more (I or II), I'd have to say Ys I was better. This was only because you got to use your weapon on bosses (in Ys 2 - it is all fireball all of the time, every time) and some of the bosses were harder IMHO. However, both were excellent and I'll definitely be playing them again on nightmare difficulty.

What I thought of "Ys I"
This game does feel outdated. I sort of like the original idea behind the bump style of combat it's not without it's issues. Still I feel like every YS fan should play this game followed by Ys II and I am very happy I started with the original. I learned some very important elements that have stuck with all of the YS titles to come so far. You will also pickup on some story and charachters that will be present going forward in other Ys titles. The combat is straight forward. As many older games this game is challening in different way then more modern Ys titles. For example without a guide it's difficult to sometimes know what to do next! But I suggest trying without a guide as much as possible because it feels good to find the solution to the puzzle yourself. This game feels like an advanture game were your consistantly trying every item you find on every object you can to see what works. The bosses can be tricky. This game is one of the shortest Ys games in general that I have played. There is moments were you need to grind a fair bit. The only main issues I have with the game is that I got lost quite a bit. And some bosses and even the final dungeon areas are very hard at times. But you can save anywhere! The game does feel old but at the same time you will get an original experience out of it. I highly suggest you play this game before Ys II and I think Ys II is one of the best Ys games I have played. Which makes this game important to play.
What I thought of "Ys II"
This game is very simular to Ys I, and does feel a tad bit outdated. It also uses the bump combat system which seems original and uncommon. I suggest every Ys fan to play Ys II but please play Ys I first! It feels very simular to Ys I but improved in every way. The combat is not as straight forward. You get to use magic now. As many older games this game is challening in different ways then more modern Ys titles. For example without a guide it's difficult to sometimes know what to do next just like in Ys I. But I suggest trying without a guide as much as possible. Because it feels good to find the solution to the puzzle yourself. This game feels like an advanture game were your consistantly trying every item you find on every object you can to see what works. The bosses are a tiny bit easier then Ys I in my opinion except for certain moments. This game is longer then Ys I but still not to long of a game. There is moments were you need to grind a lot about the same as Ys I. The game is bigger and has a lot more effort and amazing levels of detail put into exploration. In this way it greatly exceeds YS I. The overall challenge level is simular to Ys I but maybe has more balance. You can still save everywhere. The game does feel old but at the same time you will get an original experience out of it just like Ys I. I highly suggest you play this game before Ys II and I think this game is one of the best Ys games I have played.

The game is pretty damned good, but the co-op is LOCAL only -_- kinda ruins it when i wanted to play with my friends who live on the other side of this god forsaken world. Good game, just no good for multiplayer if your friends aren't local.

THE GOOD
-Combat
You attack enemies by walking into them. Sounds dumb doesn’t it. Why don’t you try watching some gameplay footage of it? Still looks pretty stupid huh? You’re probably thinking how can such a combat system be fun? Well, it is. Ys I and II’s combat system is simple yet fun. It’s one of those things which sounds dumb on paper but is really good in practice. All you need to think of in combat (outside of boss battles) is walk into enemies but don’t collide with them in the centre. For anybody who studies game design, often you would want to aim for the lowest amount of complexity but a high amount of depth, which is what Ys I and II has done with their combat system. It lacks complexity but has a large amount of depth, in other words it is easy to learn yet hard to master, which is great. Such a combat system may sound really boring and easy, but adding in the speed at which Adol, the main character, moves, this creates a very fast pace combat system that is thrilling no matter how many times I experience it.
P.s. If u think the enemy movements in Ys I is too easy, Ys II improves on them by allowing the enemies to move diagonally make the combat tougher
-Boss Battles
All boss battles are unique, no two are the same. Some of these boss fights are really tough and that’s just how I like it. Of course, you could just grind to the point where your level is so high that the boss isn’t even a threat, but where’s the fun in that? I often find myself trying and failing time and time again to beat the same boss. However, each time I get more familiar with the boss’s attack patterns and then eventually I win and that sense of satisfaction I get is just exhilarating.
P.s. I do see some people complaining about how unfair the Vagullion (the bat) boss fight was but I didn’t have too much trouble dealing him so I guess to each his own.
-Story
It’s a typical boy saves the world anime fantasy story with a small amount of romance sprinkled in. It’s simple, nothing really special about it. However, simple is often best when it comes to stories in video games. Video games aren’t a very good storytelling medium. The story often just serves as a motivation for the player to push on or give the player some context and meaning as to what they are doing in the game. Thus, a simple story in a video game not only serves it’s purpose, it also makes it easy for the player to follow along and not get lost in a convoluted mess which is Final Fantasy.
THE BAD
-Backtracking
This problem isn’t really apparent in Ys I as Ys I’s world is pretty small, and the story is considerably shorter than Ys II. However, in Ys II, there are a lot of times in the game where the main story requires you to backtrack. Of course, to makes things easier, you are given Warp Magic pretty early in the game which allows you to warp to any town you have visited. But the problem is that the map of Ys II is non-linear. A lot of areas are maze-like and it’s easy to get lost or struggle to find a door you stumbled upon previously but couldn’t unlock because you didn’t have the key yet. I get that backtracking is quite normal in RPGs and honestly I’m not really against it. What I am against though, is the maze-like areas which require backtracking. It gets annoying pretty quickly and at times feels like a lazy way to lengthen the game unnecessarily.
OVERALL
All in all, this is the first (and second) Ys game(s) I've played and I had a lot of fun. I'm a huge fan of this franchise now and can't wait to play another Ys game.

One of my favourite strategy games of all time. On the front it is an easy to understand, easy to get into and insanely enjoyable experience. The in-game information is incredibly detailed, and where the tutorial is lacking, the in game wiki of sorts will pick up the pieces for those with the mindset that suits someone who will enjoy Civ V. On face value the game offers a compelling experience with a number of options and player driven storytelling that will provide an engaging experience for those with a like for the genre. Furthermore, the diffirent Civs, while never really changing the whole gameplay experience in any serious way, will change the way you approach certain situations, and combined with the great world generation, makes every game just a little bit different from the last. Speaking of map types, playing with all the DLC and updates, there are a decent selection of maps, I think it could be a little more interesting, but I'm never seeking out a map type that is unavailable. Gods & Kings adds a deep mechanic or two that effect the game in a major way without changing the way Civ V works at it's core, while Brave New World is one of the best add-on pieces of content in video game history for me. The way it refines diplomacy and enriches many aspect of the game is truely top notch, and I love the changes to the combat system and tech tree which really helped the game become a much more complete experience. Once you dive deeper into the science and growth systems, and see how powerful they can be, messing with more detailed mechanics such as comboing buildings and hitting techs at the right time, or managing what tiles your cities are working, the game opens up a whole new world for you. It's a simple game on its face, and amazing complex when you dive deeper, and that's not even mentioning mods and the Multiplayer scene, which I have yet to dive into. Civ V is a great experience.

These are my first Ys games.
The combat system is a unique bump system where you don't have button to attack. You need to bump the enemies to deal damage but avoid bumping them at center of the sprite because you will get damaged too.
On Ys I bosses, you can bump them anywhere on their body, because their source of damage are different from the normal mobs. While Ys II bosses will be damaged by using your magic.
Played them on nightmare on first playthrough and I truly had nightmares on Ys I. The difficulties are so good, I love it.
Why Ys I so hard? Because the level cap is 10, and I already reached level 10 at 3rd boss fight, so you can't just beat the bosses by being overleveled, you need to get better at the game.
Lovely, isn't it?
Unlike the Ys I, the Ys II's difficulty isn't as hard as Ys I because it has much higher level cap (I was level 50 when I ended Ys II) and there is magic introduced in there so you can do ranged attacks.
The only thing that I don't really like about Ys II is that cancel button are the same with walk button and the magic button are the same with OK button (Ys I doesn't have magic). Sometimes I want to charge my magic while walking so I need to press A and B together, on Ys Origin, my magic button is on LB and walk is on RB, it's much more comfortable that way.
You can rebind the button but OK and cancel button should be separated from magic and walk.
The story are okayish but the OSTs are so beautiful and the boss' fights are so enjoyable, I love'em all, I ended buying the other Ys on steam.
I recommend that you play Ys I & II first then play Ys Origin.

XCOM: Enemy Within. (Minor Spoilers)
So began March 1st, with aliens invading for little to no apparent reason. After the 1st mission where 3/4th of Delta squad died, I guess 2K wanted you to know the brutality that would encounter on your journey. So, quickly picking up the tactics and general gameplay. I thought I was doing okay, and getting the hang of things. Until 1 difficulty spike forced me to rage, and restart the entire game halfway through.
The strategy game of shooting aliens and taking cover is executed fairly well. Additionally, building up the XCOM facility and choosing what research you think will be best for the survival of your unit makes the game exciting and fun. It does give the game strategy and replayability. The game also relies on luck to decide which shots hit you or the enemy, so minimizing risk by taking cover in safe areas also adds to the strategy. But, as you progress further on, you'll have more items and tools to ultilize making it fun to progress.
The progression of the game feels right, for the most part. Getting further, you encounter more enemies, strategies, and techniques that you'll want to implement to best the invaders. The game doesn't throw you way too many new enemies or weapons at once, making it managable and enjoyable to fight the unknown with your continually growing crew.
However, 1 major flaw I feel is the lack of tutorials about how to build up the XCOM facility and the new tools and abilities you'll acquire. After you complete the turtorial, the game gives little guidance about why you'll require science or engineering fields. Additionally, there is barely any mention about new armor, weapons, upgrades until you bother to research and try it out. So, if you don't experiment with them, and try continuing on with the objectives, then you'll run into a massive difficulty spike (and without warning).
The last gripe would be that a few story missions take a long time to beat, which can make them drawn out, difficult, and boring due to the slow rate at which the aliens will approach you. Additionally, it makes having a support class on your strike team crucial.
Overall though, I would recommend this game for anyone who likes strategy in a turn based combat.

In this choose your own adventure style action RPG, you lead the dashing rogue Reynaldo the fox through dozens of different stories and locations as he tries to recall his past. You have to make choices as to your next step, and every choice leads to a (usually disastrous) different ending. As a story ends, you start over (usually on different locations as to keep it interesting) and make different choices to unlock more secrets (which presumably lead to the real story, as you unlock them all).
Each story lasts about an hour, so they're nicely sized to do one per sitting. The narrator usually employs dry humor, lots of media references and puns, and usually messes with you for the choices you made. There's a decently sized skill-tree in which you unlock more and more as you progress through different stories. You can also craft and upgrade different swords for different combat effects and unlocking more paths (they also act as keys). The movement and combat itself is a bit clunky (m/kb) but works well enough to be enjoyable. You move and fight mostly with your mouse, but use a couple of keyboard buttons as you unlock more skills. You can't seem to rebind the buttons, which is a bit annoying as they're not very conveniently placed imo.
Overall i'm enjoying this game enough to recommend it.
Tl,dr: Fun narration and story, lots of replayability (the game is designed around it), combat is a bit clunky on m/kb but still enjoyable.

I really enjoyed this game. The storytelling is very good: you get dropped right into it and then it really builds up the world for you. Mostly through dialogues, but there is a huge amount of detail hidden in the map. All in all the world building is top-notch and the presentation doesn't rely on exposition. But the point that really sets this game apart, is the way it handles decisions. No red/blue points to hint what is what, no easy predictions what the right decision is, not even certainty, what each decision will actually result in. You decide and you have to live with the results.
I consider storytelling to be what makes or breaks RPGs. I can sit through mediocre combat, if the story is good enough, but not the other way round. Fortunately, The Banner Saga also has very solid mechanics. The principle is both easy to get and still gives you options during the fights.
You get to level your characters, although the paths you can take a given one are a bit limited. However, leveling consumes the same resources that is required for items and provisions. The last even ties your resource management into the story, since you're not going to starve your fellow refugees to buy shiny weapons. Or are you?
All in all, I can fully recommend this game. The only thing that's missing is a hole in the earth that swallows

I don't play that often and when I do I simply want to enjoy. Enjoy the world, the challenge, the story and all the other stuff. This game, even in its early access form, gives me exactly what  I want. The world seems interesting, the item embuing thing seems fun and the 2-way character build is something new. It is a bit of a Diablo, but in a good way. What I especially love is the difficulty level of battles already from the beginning. Unlike in many other games where you can simply run into any foe and click your way through, especially early game, Grim Dawn gives just enough for you to think when to rush in and when to actually kite around for a while. The game is by no means hard, but the difficulty level is just enough for me to feel engaged in battles. Especially against enemy heroes. This means I can actualyl enjoy the game casually all the way from the beginning - I don't have to rush and push my way through to end-game to have all the fun. I can have casual fun when getting to the end-game.
Of course the game is not perfect. It is sometimes hard to target in battles due to environment and sometimes your surroundings might block your ranged attacks even when you don't see an obstacle between you and your target. But I am sure these are more of early access "features" rather than real problems.
Either way I strongly recommend the game for ARPG guys around. Even for the more casual ones.

Probably the best pc game made in 21st century. It doesn't rely on  superficial stuff like great graphics(I don't mean it has bad graphics, it's just irrelevant). This game is almost perfect and you can't really expect any more from this game. The only problem is that it takes too long to finish a game(especially multiplayer).

First note of business, I implore you to spend a lot of time in the character creation screen. You can go in and "Customise" individual stats. For instance, you could have an ability right off the bat to talk to pets or to identify items or better yourself in crafting, etc. It's like a Pen and Paper RPG. I found it fun to start off with two ranged characters, and equally fun to have one of them a Wizard. Up to you though.
Second, you are going to die a lot. There is a Quick-Save/Quick-Load mechanic. Study your environment, break apart from the group and sneak, use every tactic available to take out a group. After the tutorial dungeon, and initial town (where you'll spend the first few hours), when you start off into the wilds...you will die.
Overall, I'm having a great time with this game. The action point mechanic is fun as you don't need to worry about mana or stamina (although abilities do have cooldowns). The battles are fun, the quests make you think and everything looks gorgeous. If you ever had fun with Bioware RPG in the past (pre-2006), you will highly enjoy this.

I had heard nothing about this game before buying it in the sale.  So far it's been really good.  I like the story and the branching paths are compelling.  I am a little tired of being ripped out of the game to be read a story by the narrator, it would be a lot better if the branching paths were integrated into the game itself, but it still works.
I have to say that the combat does get EXTREMELY frustrating at times.  You'll go to grapple the shield from one enemy, only to have it smart target the exploding guy next to him instead, instantly killing you.  Or you'll get bored of the constant clicking and try to grab an enemy to throw him off a cliff, only to have every enemy on screen attack at the same time while you're defenseless.  It seems like whenever I try to play by the game's rules and do something fancy, it pulls some cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and punishes me for it.  Aside from a few too many cheap deaths, fighting is fun in the game overall.  In fact I find myself wishing there were more enemies most of the time.
Probably my biggest gripe with the game is that they put the most important resource in breakable barrels, and then patronize you when you break a lot of barrels.  I'm kind of sick of the quips about how many barrels I've broken trying to get ore when it's something that I NEED to progress.  It was cute when Bastion did it that one time, but it's kind of lame when you hear about it every 15 minutes.
EDIT AFTER COMPLETION:  So I got the final 'true' ending, pretty unexpectedly.  I was hoping that the branching paths would coincide a little bit more and I'm disappointed that out of the 25ish endings, you only need to complete 4 before you can beat the game.  This is probably a good thing though, because I was starting to get tired of the same 6-7 stages that never seemed to change.  Overall I still think it's worth the purchase, but I feel a bit let down by the end of it.

The artwork and style are wonderful, but you already know that from any screenshot you've seen.  I bought it based on the style, and I'll play it again because it's such a treat to look at.
The gameplay is good, the strategic tempo of a game of chess, but there's not enough of it, and the AI is not smart, often deliberately choosing an area attack on its own pieces.  The user interface was obviously created with tablets in mind, but it's not too bad on a PC and the battle system feels unique and fresh giving you a fair about of strategic choices and gambles to make.
It's turn based combat, but much of your time with this game will be reading dialogue in cutscenes and watching your caravan slowly and automatically walk across 2D landscape scenes and making choices ala Oregon Trail, without even being able to alter your path whatsoever.
The story is alright but the presentation is terribly boring, done through landscape establishing shots,  it's usually shown from a mile away as your caravan slowly marches along (you couldn't be further removed).  I like to read, but I never liked choose your own adventure books, and I don't like it in video games, there are much more engaging and effective storytelling methods than the endless cutscenes.  It's like an interactive book with a strategy game thrown in as a bonus, I would have preferred the opposite or a better blend of the two.
If this were $10 or contained more gameplay I would recommend it.  Try the free multiplayer version called Factions until this comes down in price.

I was excited to play a new X-Com game. The free UFO: Alien Invasion X-Com clone was a neat revamping of the old games and true to the original spirit of the them. Unfortunately, it was never completed and left me wanting more. Even so, it is still better than this one.
Enemy Unknown is not true to the spirit of the original games. The tutorial/start mission was already disappointing. I don't like scripted games - you play through once and now you know what's supposed to happen. The way the enemies get to jump out when your troops get into a certain zone is also infuriating. The cat-and-mouse game of the originals is thus lost on this new version. I enjoyed the hunt and being hunted. It made my heart race, even though combat was turn-based. When I play this game, I feel like I'm just going through the motions.
It's clear this game was made for consoles. It's also clear it does not contain the polish of the original games, or even the free inspired-by. If I had never played the other versions, I might have liked this for what it is. Knowing how much better it could have been makes me not like it though. I'm glad it was a gift, because I would have been disappointed if I had purchased it myself.

Beautiful game, great mechanics, quality soundtrack but in terms of the journey I'd say it reminds me a bit of FTL in that you need to learn the ropes a bit before it all clicks (though the randomness is thankfully confined to the combat maps).
Much like Dark Souls the game has a singular currency (in this case renown) which you acquire as the result of combat victories as well as the occasionally canny judgement call during the games story line. You can spend renown in one of two ways. Firstly to buy levels for your individual heroes once they have hit a certain number of kills, and secondly you can spend it in the occasional town market you stumble across to buy both food supplies for you caravans as well the odd trinket that a hero can wear to boost their stats/enhance their abilities (though you do find these/can win them in exceptional combat victories).
All well and good, but for the fact that renown is not easily earned until you know what you're doing (and even then it's a finite amount) and all too often you'll find yourself ploughing points into characters who aren't necessarily going to stick the course and will invariably end up buggering off at some point which can be a tad frustrating to say the least in terms of investment. My advice would be to play the game on easy initially to get a feel for the mechanics and the way the story-line unfolds and then once you're happy with that then try normal. Much like FTL the conclusion favours you better if you're coming loaded for bear rather than happy go lucky.
Highly recommended regardless. Very much looking forward to the the next title in the series.

Stories: TPOD is a Narrative Adventure action RPG, with a lot of similarities to bastion. The game features amazing backgrounds which just ooze style and you’ll love the storybook like narration as the narrators voices all the characters and even uses terms such as ‘she said’ and ‘he turned around’. The game allows for several playthroughs as every time you ‘finish’ the game you learn more ‘truths’. These truths give you new options as you now have more information.
Full video review:
There’ll be a lot of fighting; luckily the combat system isn’t too bad. It’s similar to the Batman Arkham Knights gameplay, you have counters, evades, some basic special moves and throws. It works pretty well to be honest, though there were times were I felt a bit unresponsive. The gameplay doesn’t really evolve and isn’t that difficult, a little lacking in my opinion for an ‘action RPG’. Luckily the interesting story technique carries the game and the combat can be kind of seen as filler between different areas and zones.
The world is beautiful; it has an amazing setting and intriguing story replay system. People have been calling this game short, but I’ve put in nearly 6-7 hours and I’m only halfway through the core story with only doing a little bit of backtracking. The value is what you make of it, personally I loved going back, seeing areas I couldn’t reach before and learning more about the world as I unlock more truths.
It is a great game overall, with storyline and gameplay, however it is way too short. You can finish the whole game in day.

One of my favourite strategy games of all time. On the front it is an easy to understand, easy to get into and insanely enjoyable experience. The in-game information is incredibly detailed, and where the tutorial is lacking, the in game wiki of sorts will pick up the pieces for those with the mindset that suits someone who will enjoy Civ V. On face value the game offers a compelling experience with a number of options and player driven storytelling that will provide an engaging experience for those with a like for the genre. Furthermore, the diffirent Civs, while never really changing the whole gameplay experience in any serious way, will change the way you approach certain situations, and combined with the great world generation, makes every game just a little bit different from the last. Speaking of map types, playing with all the DLC and updates, there are a decent selection of maps, I think it could be a little more interesting, but I'm never seeking out a map type that is unavailable. Gods & Kings adds a deep mechanic or two that effect the game in a major way without changing the way Civ V works at it's core, while Brave New World is one of the best add-on pieces of content in video game history for me. The way it refines diplomacy and enriches many aspect of the game is truely top notch, and I love the changes to the combat system and tech tree which really helped the game become a much more complete experience. Once you dive deeper into the science and growth systems, and see how powerful they can be, messing with more detailed mechanics such as comboing buildings and hitting techs at the right time, or managing what tiles your cities are working, the game opens up a whole new world for you. It's a simple game on its face, and amazing complex when you dive deeper, and that's not even mentioning mods and the Multiplayer scene, which I have yet to dive into. Civ V is a great experience.

After nearly 500 hours of early access playtime I feel i should weigh in on Grim Dawn. Also at 491 hours and rising it should tell you i've enjoyed this game greatly, and have paid for two other copies that i gave to my brother and a friend. Now lets get to the actual Review.
Grim Dawn as a game does not hold your hand, in quests you are told to seek out something or someone at a location, after that you are left on your own to search for your objective, only once you get near your objective(about near the edge of your screen) does a marker show up. This encourages exploration of areas in full and i also reccomend that you fully explore an area there are many secrets in the game to be found, from loot, to quests, to bosses that may or may not kill your character when you first meet them.
The world is also not sectioned off like say as it was in Titan Quest or Diablo, it is instead one continous worldspace, akin to Sacred, some complain about this giving the games world areas too similar to one another, i personally enjoy this as it creates a more cohesive world.
As for the games story, i find it enjoyable enough, when you start the game your character was to be hung at the gallows for being possessed by an Aetherial spirit, said spirit abandons ship before it dies with you, you're cut down, then asked if you want to stay you need to earn your keep by assisting the settlement of Devils Crossing, i wont spoil much more, but another thing i would like to address about the games story is that some NPC's you meet arent helpless sods needing rescue, bar some casses. theres quite a few times in the game where you find the odd NPC camped out somewhere surrounded by slain monsters, I find this a refreshing change of pace compaired to other ARPGs. Lastly much of Grim Dawn's history, backstory, and lore are found via notes scattered throughout the world, some are journals from before the game, others history of the world, or just the odd bit of why a particular foe is with a faction. Again encouraing more exploration of the world.
Now to the meat and bones of any ARPG, Character customiztion, progression and loot. Lets start with the Masteries, in Grim Dawn there are 5(and a 6th coming in the next build, Build 27) Masteries, Soldier, Demolitionist, Occultist, Nightblade, and Arcanist, and soon to be the Shaman.
the Soldier is your melee specialist,  hearty and strong, a robust choice for someone new to grim dawn.
The Demolitionist is all about explosions and fire. Like seeing the world burn? then this is the mastery for you.
The Occultist Focuses on debuffs, pets, and debilitating attack spells. command minions to maul your foes or debilitate them with vile curses.
The Nightblade is your melee dual wielder, focusing on speed, and very fast attacks, want to shred your enemies into ribbons? chose the nightblade
The Arcanist is a pure spellcaster  that rains down destruction and devastation. the glass cannon of the game
Each of these masteries can be combined with another to create a dual class, covering one masteries weakness or bolstering anothers strengths. in my opinion this lends the game a great deal of replay value because i am the kind of person who will explore all avenues of play. with the varied skill pool of a single mastery there are quite a few dual class combinations you can take advantage of and explore different playstyles.
The loot in Grim Dawn is quite good, the qualities ranging from White(basic), Yellow(magic), Green(rare or rare monster infrequent), Blue(epic) and Purple(Legendary, not yet in the game). Curiously magic rare and epic are competative, in some character builds a good yellow might be all you need to properly outfit an equipment slot,  while another can get by with some basic epic items, or builds looking to gear in all rare equipment. there are a number of affixes to suit any and all builds, as well as epics.
There is also a Faction system in Grim Dawn, there are many groups you can aid, and many you can anger. Increasing your standing with friendly factions allows you access to their equipment and augments. these augments offer additional bonuses to your items and can be worth the effort to obtain access to them. Conversely further angering hostile factions makes them send more dangerous enemies at each threshold, culminating in the chance to encounter a Nemesis, a random boss linked to the faction you angered. these nemesis bosses while rare drop incredible loot, and assure an epic from their defeat, and once they are in the game, an increased chance of legendary drops.
this last section I am going to adress some deal breakers: Many ask "will there be secure servers?" at this time there are no plans for such, it is however under consideration if Grim Dawn sells enough to pay for the required infrastructure and personel to maintain them. Tying into that, Grim Dawns files are all stored locally, every game file and every save file is on your hard drive, to those with the ability to edit and modify them, they can. this leads to seeing some oddities in multiplayer games, like players exceeding the current set level cap, items that are unobtainable legitamately, and stats that are likewise impossible. Grim Dawn is going to be moddable, this is why the games files are on our hard drives, so that once we have the mod tools we can edit the files as we please. Lastly while there is PvP, it is not the focus of the game and is not balanced accordingly, in fact most pvp matches tend to be whoever gets hit first dies. Grim dawn is primarily PvE and will remain as such.
To close this out, if you want an ARPG that offers very deep character customization and itemization and great gameplay and atmosphere then this game is for you. If you want a secure multiplayer experience away from what you would consider cheaters this might not be your cup of tea.

One of my first online RPG experiences was with the original Diablo 1 - the game was brilliant back then. It had so much going for it and was way ahead of time.
Grim Dawn is essentially the recreation of that old formula with the addition of many new features.
In a nutshell, it's an excellent ARPG - a game similar to Diablo series, Torchlight, Van Helsing, Sacred and more specifically Titan Quest.
If you had played Titan Quest you will recognize many of the features in Grim Dawn as well.
What makes it stand out though is the absolutely brilliant atmosphere that is reinforced by really well made 3d graphics and incredible music. It also features well created character progression very similar to Titan Quest where you can essentially make a character that you want to play and choose the style that suits you best and most importantly, a variety of excellent and well thought-out items that will make you want to pursue various difficult assignments or dungeons just to get that special sword that may occasionaly drop.
At first, I wasn't sure how I felt about the steampunk approach to this fantasy genre, but it turned out to be great as the only steam punk thing you'll really appreciate is the addition of excellent gunpowder based weaponry (rifles, pistols, handcannons etc...) but other than that this is as fantasy as it gets.
Most importantly, this game combines all of these features absolutely brilliantly and is actually very challenging which was very important for me. Even on normal, finishing a very specific dungeon called Torment was ridiculously hard, I can't wait to try it again on Veteran mode and then again on Hardcore.
What was really surprising on top of that is that the game actually scared me a few times, and this is after playing games like Alien Isolation and such. There are a few areas where the darkness and the ambience does such a good job at ticklingg your nerves that when things jump out at you, expect urine in pants.
All in all, this was probably THE BEST Early Access purchase ever. I regret nothing and I will definitely support this game fully when it comes out.
This is GOTY material when it's finished and will very likely become a classic, beating Diablo 3 and even Torchlight 2 under the rug.
tl;dr:
+excellent atmosphere
+challenging, but fair
+great music
+lots of powerful items that matter
+great graphics for the genre
+best early access purchase (personal opinion)
-still not finished - only 3/4 acts done

Antichamber is puzzle game set apart from many other puzzle games. It takes advantage of being a 3D exploration game by having puzzles that take advantage of camera angles and occasionally non-sensical map layouts that just are not possible from a 2H puzzle game. Although the controls can be a bit cumbersome in 3D it generally does not interfere except for a few puzzles (which I may have over complicated for myself...).
The game does not explain how to play so you are expected to figure things out on your own. My advice is to look for a new tool if you ever feel like a puzzle is impossibly hard or tedious to solve with what you currently have. The map is rather large and wraps upon itself a lot so a good part of the entertainment involves exploration. Definitely worth a play through if you enjoy puzzle and exploration games beyond block puzzles.

is an amazing take on a tower defense/3rd-person action combo.  Attributes of both genres are blended together perfectly to form an addictive and entertaining little game. This is a game that is very easy to enjoy.
does a great job taking 3rd-person action elements and blending them with some tower defense to establish a good basis. Then they sprinkle in the lighthearted atmosphere and charming characters with the simplistic-yet-captivating mechanics of the game… and it shapes up to be a really fun, delightful experience. It’s definitely the kind of game you can dive right into and get hooked for hours.
There is a relatively large amount of different towers and abilities in the game when compared to many other games in the tower defense genre. You have plenty of options and can have fun experimenting with different strategies. The level designs also vary enough that they call for different approaches to beat them, so you will have to try out different tactics in order to succeed. And there is a fair amount of different enemies which keeps things fresh as you progress through the game.
There is also a scoring system and leaderboards to add replay value.
This game is just downright fun.

This is a game about killing orcs. The concept is simple enough, but the execution is high quality.
The game is basically a 3rd person shooter in which you have to defend a magical rift in a castle from a horde of orcs and other monsters that are trying to get through it. If too many monsters make it to the rift you lose.
One man against a relentless horde of monsters may not seem fair, but you have a lot of advantages. In addition to your trusty crossbow, you'll have a large arsenal of spells, traps, and guardians to help out. Furthermore you earn skulls for completing levels, and you can then spend these skulls on further upgrading your arsenal.
At the start of each level you'll have time to plan and set up your defenses and get a feel for the layout of the area. You'll be told where the orcs are coming from, what route they are likely to take, how many waves there are, and even what monsters you can expect to come knocking down your door.
This is important because, despite the simple premise of "orcs must die," this is really a tactician's game. The first few levels you may be able to survive using just your crossbow, but as the difficulty level increases you will have to diversify your tactics or perish. You'll start facing more orcs, tougher monsters, monsters that come from multiple entrances, and even multiple rifts that must be defended simultaneously.
I will give one bit of warning that is not mentioned in the game-- if you intend to play on the default (war mage) difficulty level as I did, in order to earn the maximum of 5 skulls per level you not only need to prevent any orcs from reaching the rift, you've also got to do it within the par time. Once you start the initial wave the timer starts, and it doesn't stop even during the "break" periods you sometimes get between waves.
The game is single player only. The graphics and music are adequate, but not AAA quality (this is an indie game, after all, and I don't expect AAA quality here).
There is a storyline which is short, simple, and entertaining. Borderlands fans will recognize the voice of Axton the Commando as the War Mage.
If you like third person shooters or defense-centered gameplay you'll like Orcs Must Die!

If you're looking for that new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-hard game to get hopelessly addicted to, look no further than Super Hexagon.  It's a simple game with 3 initial levels which, as you individually complete them, unlock an even harder version of themselves called Hyper Mode.  Your goal in the game is to guide a small arrow through a series of visually perplexing walls and mazes that spin and pulse to the tune of techno music, until you reach the 60-second mark where a level is considered complete.  Even the most basic level is called "Hard", with subsequent levels being "Harder", "Hardest", and even "Hardester" once you unlock the Hyper levels.
If this is any indication, this game is not for the faint of heart as the challenge can get mind-meltingly difficult.  Yet, when you first boot up the game and undoubtedly get put to shame a few times, sleep on it and you'll find that the game is indeed possible to beat.  It takes some mental training and twitchy fingers, but the fun of it all will carry you until you're able to rise to the occasion.  It's a blast to play and the kind of game you can quickly load, try your skills at for a few minutes, then leave for another time.  Eventually you'll find that the easiest level you once thought unbeatable has become a cake walk compared to where you ended up.  No doubt then, that Super Hexagon gives you an adrenaline rush like few things do, and for $3, it's much cheaper than skydiving.

It's been a long time since I've played an old school RPG of this quality. I highly recommend it to RPG fans! Here is my breakdown:
THINGS THIS GAME DOES RIGHT
Customization - Instead of setting the length and thickness of your character's nose, you get options that matter, like choosing skills, talents, and stats which add up to make your own custom class. Of course, you can pick from a default list and build it however you want if you prefer. This is customization done right.
Difficulty - This game will kill you. It's not Dark Souls hard, but it's hard enough to give you a sense of satisfcation when overcomingits challenges.
Non-linearity - Aspects of this game are non-linear. Ultimately it does have a linear narrative, but you can almost completely freely explore the world. You're limited mostly by your level, which is the main barrier limiting progression.
Grinding - Most RPGs allow you (or force you) to gain excessive amounts of experience to out-level the game's content. That is the fundamental principle of the JRPG. This game only gives you enough experience to survive the next challenge which ensures that the difficulty of the game is more fine tuned and harder to trivialize.
Puzzles - Not everything is explicitly a puzzle. Sometimes advancing the story is a puzzle in itself (like the old adventure games). Sometimes a combat has puzzle elements. Sometimes it's just a room full of traps. Either way, there's almost always a problem to figure out.
THINGS YOU MAY OR MAY NOT LIKE
Speed of Play - This is a slow methodical game best spent enjoyed at a leisurely pace. The turn based combat, sprawling maps, and slower paced movement speed means that it'll take hours to progress through what some may consider a small amount of content. For the perceptive and the patient, though, that content has a lot to offer.
Tone - It's a fairly straight forward fantasy setting. It's fun, whimsical, and self aware at times. It doesn't get overly dark nor overly comical. It's not too geneteric or creative. It serves primarily as a backdrop for the gameplay.
Co-op Dialogue - You can do rock-paper-scissors to overcome disagreements. What you choose impacts your stats in small ways. Min-maxers beware. Everyone else; have fun.
Random Loot - This has pros and cons. On the one hand, each playthrough is different. On the otherhand, a lot of loot sucks. It's debatable whether or not random loot works in a game with a limited pool of enemies.
Nietzsche - He can join your party. It's pretty neat if you're in to that sort of thing. The devs didn't actually name him Nietzsche, but you'll figure it out if you went through that phase in your teen years.
THINGS YOU PROBABLY WONT LIKE
Oops - It can be easy to make it hard or impossible to progress in the game by killing an NPC, letting them get killed, or just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off enough. Same goes for accidently clicking on an object or walking into a room that causes the entire town to aggro on you. Save often.
Bugs - There's still quite a number of bugs, but they are very quickly being addressed. Still, be warned. Save often.
