This is a decision-branch adventure game with short play-sessions and a really fun narrator (think Bastion, but with charm over grit and a slight British touch). The level variety is fairly small, and due to the decision-branch nature of how the campaigns progress, each level is played through multiple times (especially for a completionist).
I binge-played, but I don't personally mind going through the same decision paths over-and-over. A campaign takes anywhere from half an hour to an hour, depending on your decisions.
For those that want to complete the game, but would rather bounce around the branch-paths, drawing what choices you've already made may help keep you from accidentally repeating a path you've already been down. There hints in-game that indicate paths that were already taken and ones still yet to take, and there is a way to review the full path of a compaign, but when you're in the middle thinking if the choice you make now leads to choices you haven't made in the next chapter, it will be easier to keep track separately.
The puzzle-solving is minimal, and honestly after a while I just took the trade-off damage to avoid having to repeat them over and over. Combat is counter-based, ala Arkham Asylum, and pretty well implemented. It took me maybe 3 or 4 campaigns to figure out what worked best for me, and I have watched players / streamers have some trouble with it, so it could be challenging depending on your skill-level.
There are some combat-related glitches (freezing in-place until hit or for a few frantic seconds, throwing enemies at everything but where you feel like you're aiming), and the camera can lead to some cheap-shots by mobs or "blind-faith" attacks against certain enemies that you really don't actually want to attack, which can get frustrating. But, when you pull off a seamless fight with lots of flare, it feels really awesome.
The levels have some branching, but this is either optional or under certain conditions. Some levels have a set path that is taken every time, some have a path depending on the choice you make. However, there isn't enough level-path variety to make more than 3 or 4 passes unique. Fair warning, while it may be tempting (and mechanically convenient) to dash through breakable objects, there is a chance that the debris will get you stuck in the floor, and I was only lucky enough to save from having to reset the level once.
The loading times are longer than I expected, but I think they improve a bit if you've already loaded the level previously in the same play session. When I first started playing the game crashed, but that was the only time, and I was messing around with the options quite a bit.
The music is wonderful. I caught myself humming the tunes several times, and I did get the soundtrack. The artwork is fairly good, too, although the in-game models don't quite have the same color or look that the avatars do. I have seen gameplay where the story-bits between gameplay were skipped, but I don't know how that was done, as I tried to skip it and whatever buttons I pressed (controller) didn't work, so that would have probably cut down on time and some monotony if I could have figured that out or if it was made obvious by a "skip" prompt.
All-in-all, I enjoyed it. Will probably come back to it in a year or so when I've forgotten the story, to play it again.

This game was genuinely awful, and I don't understand how the reviews argue otherwise. Don't take my time played and dismiss why I'm leaving a negative review, the gameplay and easiness was all fine, but a lot of problems exist.
Pros +
+ Multiple paths
+Very nice visuals
+ Movement looks nice
+ Dialog has funny and quirky moments
+ Enjoyable progression system
+ Relaxing, easy game
+ Hack n' slashing is always fun
+ Apparent 60 FPS
+ Controller controls are fine
Cons - And there are a LOT
First this game does not run well at all. The game by default reccomended all minimum settings on my computer with these specs:
Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-4690K CPU @ 3.50GHz
NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970
Microsoft Windows 10 (build 10586), 64-bit
8 GB RAM
Cranking the game up to its fullest settings didn't slow it down at all, but the graphics were horridly buggy, especially shadows.
LOOK AND FEEL ISSUES (Graphics and controls)
- Visual shortcuts everywhere
- Lots of clipping textures
- Pop-in Textures are very distracting and un-immersive
- Shadows took several restarts before loading correctly (Mostly character shadows, enviornment shadows were fine)
- Load times range from instant to several minutes, and are VERY frequent.
- Several issues occured with controls
- Keyboard/Mouse is non-rebindable and native controls are awful (Left MB, Right MB, Shift, Ctrl, Alt) Don't you love when games have you float all around that Windows key.
- Frequently lost control of character on keyboard/mouse (character would begin moving on its own until the game was paused and unpaused)
- Several Xbox One controllers had movement lock issues, until the control was removed and reinserted. This occured about every 3 minutes, rending the game unplayable for me with the controller..
GAMEPLAY ISSUES
- Boring gameplay
- Grappling is pointless, and only serves as forced movement sections
- Puzzles all trivial, which isn't technically a con, but at a certain point it goes from easy to unintresting
- Dash mechanic is flashy but useless
- Sword "toggles" are relatively pointless.
- Enemy variety is awful
- No Bosses (again, not necessarily a con, but it does work toward a bigger issue the game has, which is it gets boring quickly due to no difficulty or variety.
- Few mechanics
- No backtracking, game promotes collecting, but then punishes the player for making any wrong turns, by blocking the way back very very frequently (Every 60-120 seconds)
- Checking destructables for loot is time consuming, rarely fruitful, and boring
STORY ISSUES
This is where this game lost me VERY quickly
- Story is very rushed
- "The ship crashed and your now here" used over and over and over and over.
- Characters have 0 development, I would easily argue some characters have NEGATIVE development. (This means characters go from having some interesting lore and are just turned in to meat sacks or love objects)
- Dialog is very hit and miss, but mostly miss.
- Story is pictured through comic book style panes between levels, but these panes are very boring and are reused
- I got a hour in to the game, and noticed a pane had been reused twice already.
- This game does not understand repition in excess is always bad
I have never left a negative review, but this game was just not finished, and if this is what developers think is a finished game, then this is a joke.

This game is basically a dungeon crawler, you have to make choices, and a RTS/Turn based strategy. What I mean by that is you're constantly fighting the enemy ship do he won't stop firing to give you a chance to blow him up, but you also have to use the pause button every few seconds to not be overwhelmed by the fast pace. This gives the player control over what speed they play the game. A newer player can take it slow and see what their enemy has, any problems with the ship, and how to defeat them. A very good player can play without the pause button, relying on quick reactions and instinct, which makes the game a lot harder, even when this game is already challenging. The best part of this game I would say is the replay value. This game won't be beat on your first try, not even your fifth, even on easy mode. When you do complete it, there's still more you can do. You can play on the harder difficulty ("Normal" Mode), you can use different ships (which you have to unlock), you can try different strategies, you can download mods. You can even make your own challenges, like playing without oxygen. The only thing bad I would say is that the weapons don't "feel" powerful. I would like to see updates, like visual damage to the ship (burn marks), more exploration, and multi-ship combat.
Overall, this game is definitely worth the $10, (I got it on sale for five). It's simple, but so complex.

TLDR; Great ARPG in the style of Diablo 2 and Titan Quest with dreary atmosphere, great music and hordes of enemies to kill and loot. 10/10 would mercilessly annihilate hordes of enemies again.
If you love ARPG's like Diablo 3 and Torchlight but miss the gritty and brutal atmosphere of Diablo 2 then this game is something that should be on your radar. Fantastic atmosphere with unique classes and an interesting dual class leveling system. Combat feels responsive and solid. The character animations leave a bit to be desired but it is very easy to overlook this gripe with the shear amount of fun you are gonna have clicking on things to make them explode. It's not a bad looker either with strangely vibrant colors for such a dreary world. The story is what you'd expect from an ARPG like this. Wonderful post-apocalyptic Action RPG. Spiritual successor to titan quest made by the team reponsible for Titan Quest. Even though it's in early access, the game does a wonderful job of holding my interest via massive skill trees and a multitude of wonderful combinations therein. The difficulty can be quite brutal, and at least for me that is some of the games' charm.
It's about time I updated this reviw in light of all the new elements Crate has added to this wonderful title.
Let's talk about Devotion system first. You run around the world purifying and repairing sanctuaries that have been damaged or defiled by an evil presence. As you do this you gain Devotion Points, you assign them to various constellations to unlock bonuses that range from passive stat boosts, to skills that proc on hit/certain damage type/etc. to active skills. It adds an extra layer of customization to your character that is separate from, and can be extremely complementary to, your mastery build. The number of constellations is staggering. There are 45+, each ranging from 5-8 nodes. With Devotion Points capping at 50, you have to pick and choose very carefully, as each constellation awards you with certain attunement bonuses. Other constellations require one or more (depending on how potent they are)attunement bonuses in order for you to be able to invest in them.
The only downside to the Devotion system appears to be how long it can take to acquire your points to really delve into the system.
On to the new mastery types! During 2015 Crate added two new masteries to the game: Shaman and Arcanist. Shaman is a full-time two-handed weapon wielder, with a solid repoitoire of utility skills, and even a few pet summons.
Arcanist on the other hand is essentially your typical mage build. Defensive skills that can prevent or reduce damage, utility skills that can remove negative effects from yourself/party members and beneficial effects from enemies.
Both masteries pair quite well with a number of the original 4.

This is a pretty fun old-school adventure RPG.

One possible complaint (depending on how much of stick up the♥♥♥♥♥♥you have about faithful translation) is that the localizers clearly took some liberties and added jokes and references that prooobably weren't there in the original, though I found it more charming than annoying.
The combat is a lot of fun. It's quite simple, but very satisfying in a primal, "popping bubble-wrap" kind of way, with a lot of surprisingly subtle ways for the player to determine the difficulty themselves. Same goes for exploration.
Overall, the gameplay is rock solid here.
The solutions to problems can sometimes be a bit obtuse, it's quite easy to get lost and some of the bosses are some cheap BS, but the charm of the game makes up for these flaws. It's a satisfying, fun adventure from a simpler time. Definitely pick it up if it's on sale!

I wasn't expecting to like this game as much as I have been. In all honesty, this is a fun little game! There's several different kinds of combinations you can make with your characters, and there's also new classes to unlock along the way, which just adds to the replayability to see all the different kinds of combinations. The gameplay is incredibly simple, but it's fun to kind of 'multitask' as you're doing something in the background while also playing this game in windowed mode.
The game also kind of lets you 'choose' how the game progresses, as you're essentially the Dungeon Master. You can choose what kind of enemy to fight, and also how many of them. This allows for you to play at your own pace!
You can also add on more characters as you go along (up to five in total), but you'd have to level them up all the way from level one, which can be kind of a pain, but, ya know, comes with the territory. The same applies for whenever you unlock a class and want to use them. You'd have to level them up from level one. Kind of sucks, but once again, this is supposed to be reminiscent of old-school RPG's. You want to play that new class you just unlocked? Gotta start 'em from the beginning.
Overall, even though I'm only a few hours into the game, I still want to play it and progress even further. This game could definitely keep you occupied for a while, especially if you're looking for a more traditional, old-school RPG. Check it out!

When I first played the legend UFO: Enemy unknown, I was only maybe 12 years old. I was able to say maybe three words in english (pretty nice progress since then), so I really can not enjoy the full extend of that remarkable game. I was literally frustrated all over my head - aliens kicked my♥♥♥♥♥every time, and I can't really do anything to stop them, because I didn't understadn what are my own scientists telling to me.
This game is trying to be a remake. Well, in my opinion this should not be revealed as a remake of UFO in the first place. This is a game on its own. It has its own infuence, story is rather different, and also mechanics ale incredibly advanced and - also modified to become easier. I remember taking magazines with me in classic UFO, for example. Here, your pistol has infinite amunnition. If I will start with a compare between these titles, I would already be complainng about this modifications, which makes game a lot easier. And I would continue with whiming and complaining... But for what purpose?
Let's just take a fresh look on this game instead. A unique combination of styles, mixing strategy, simulation, RPG and action styles together. That is what I like most - this unique, yet still well working set of styles. You have a large base, which you must plan carefully, because there is never enought money for everything. You have an army of best soldiers on Earth at your command - and you will command them on every step they made. You are going to guide every single human on this complex through the war between you and aliens - or between you and someone else... I guess you will have to find out.
Game itself was built on a nice physique engine - but I am going to give it only 6/10. Well, basic functionality is pretty good, but this engine just lacks a lot of power - for example, try to hide with a heavy in a corner and shoot a rocket downstairs - and your heavy will leave the corner, he will make a step into open space right next to him and shoot. Exactly - your heavy can fly. In a game like this, you simply can not afford to make such bugs. There is of course more.
Fortunately, engine is not the only one component of this game. Let's continue with the best part - music. Soundtracks are simply amazing, and they are one of the best I ever heard. 11/10 for those. Sounds are also amazing and realistic, with great time work, so I will give them 10/10. On my new computer, I am able to play this game on medium setting or so, and I am pretty amazed by the animations. Just try to fire from a plasma sniper or plasma rocket blaster and enjoy. Explosions are simply amazing - I love them. Aliens looks also great. So animations 9/10 and textures also 9/10. Altogether with other graphics elements - I can give the graphics 9/10, I am really impressed byt artworks, but I miss more different enviroments, or cities.
What else can I saz about this gem? It is a beautifull game with enormous possibilities and options (just to mention research and soldier training), with amazing sounds and astonishing soundtrack. Althoug the physics engine lacks nessesary power, game its still amazing. So, what do you say? Do you have guts to take on creatures from the entire galaxy? Can you protect Earth, or maybe defeat your enemies and win this war? Go, and find out, Commander. Because after all - you are our last hope.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

I've seen some mixed opinions about this game so I thought I'd give you mine.
I'm at what I think is the last or one of the last battles in this game so I'm pretty far in.
I noticed this game on the "coming soon" list some time ago and without hesitation I pre-ordered it. Why? Simply based on the artwork, turnbased combat and the setting of the game. And mostly, your decisions affect your journey! I played The Walking Dead and The Wolf Among us and I like to have some choice in the direction a story is heading.
Basically it's Vikings on the Run (would have been a good title as well, but not nearly as cool as The Banner Saga). You're fleeing from a "robotic" army called the Dredge. On your journey you meet people, villages and enemies. You meet a lot of those so you have to make a lot of decisions on how to approach each situation.
For example: A Village you pass is under attack by Dredge. Will you help the villagers (chance of casualties or other surprises and possibly a cool reward), wil you sneak past (no casualties if you aren't discovered) or will you watch the fight (and later check out the village and maybe kill the remaining Dredge)?
All
lead to a different situation, and they can not be taken back. Luckily there is no time limit on your decision so you can take your time to think it through. Whatever you choose, you never know what's going to happen. You might even lose main characters by "bad" decisions, and believe me, you WILL make bad decisions ;)
So you're on the run with a rather large crew of Vikings: Warriors, women, old people, giants, kids... a whole community.
Lot of people means a lot of problems. You're not only fighting the Dredge, there's a lot more happening. Intrigue, jealousy, betrayel, you name it. And they need food too, so you have to keep that in mind as well.
Now the
part. You fight a lot in this game so don't underestimate it.
It's turnbased and actually imo it's the worst part of the game. Once you find a tactic that works you can stick to that most of the game. There isnt much variation in fighters: you have your tanks, archers, warriors and a rare magician. All characters have different special skills, but you can finish most battles without thinking too hard which characters to use (simply those who have the highest skills). Oh, and each character can equip 1 special item to boost some stats. These special items can be found on your journey or bought at a town market.

First it should be said that I am a huge telltale game fan. I loved the entire Walking Dead series (both seasons), Tales of Borderlands, The Wolf Among us, everything. I've always loved the fascinating characters, story arcs, emotional scenes, humor (particularly in Borderlands), and everything else talltale has always had to offer. They really are a genre of thier own.
Not so much this time.
The Walking Dead: Michonne was probably the most disapointing telltale game I've played. While the characters were vaguely interesting and the plot wasn't bad, it was the actual amount of content that was dissapointing. The entire game took me maybe three hours to complete, with each episode barely being an hour. Keep in mind that each Borderlands episode took me two hours and sometimes more (and there was five episodes, making it a really solid game). I recgonize that this is a mini series but then the price should be cut drastically to match the gametime.
Additionally, actual gameplay, although pretty decent wasn't the same compared to the other Walking Dead games and for me, it was because of emotional investment. At the end of Walking Dead Season 1, I was crying hysterically. I was so invested in Lee and Clem that the ending literally had me emotionally striken, and I left with tons of feelings even days after completing the game. After I finished Michonne, I kind of just stared at my screen and shrugged like, "Alright." I couldn't get very emotionally invested in the characters and it seemed as if the game was simply telling you who to get invested in and what to think. "These are the bad guys, you are the good guys, they're gonna chase you, you gotta do things to save yourself but some will die, the end." Whereas with Walking Dead Season 1 was more like, "Hey, here is this kid named Benny, he is going to really suck sometimes so you can either take sympathy on the poor kid or you can completely screw him over, or do a combination of both or neither." It was the same way with Kenny, Clem, and everyone else you made moral decisions about. The game didn't tell you to care about certain characters or view certain characters as strictly bad guys. It was up to you to make that decision for yourself.
Overall, if this game was on sale (5~10) and you are a fan of talltale I'd still probably suggest you get it, but just keep in mind that it's not a very long game at all and you may not get as emotionally invested as you would playing Season 1 or Season 2.

If you're looking for that new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-hard game to get hopelessly addicted to, look no further than Super Hexagon.  It's a simple game with 3 initial levels which, as you individually complete them, unlock an even harder version of themselves called Hyper Mode.  Your goal in the game is to guide a small arrow through a series of visually perplexing walls and mazes that spin and pulse to the tune of techno music, until you reach the 60-second mark where a level is considered complete.  Even the most basic level is called "Hard", with subsequent levels being "Harder", "Hardest", and even "Hardester" once you unlock the Hyper levels.
If this is any indication, this game is not for the faint of heart as the challenge can get mind-meltingly difficult.  Yet, when you first boot up the game and undoubtedly get put to shame a few times, sleep on it and you'll find that the game is indeed possible to beat.  It takes some mental training and twitchy fingers, but the fun of it all will carry you until you're able to rise to the occasion.  It's a blast to play and the kind of game you can quickly load, try your skills at for a few minutes, then leave for another time.  Eventually you'll find that the easiest level you once thought unbeatable has become a cake walk compared to where you ended up.  No doubt then, that Super Hexagon gives you an adrenaline rush like few things do, and for $3, it's much cheaper than skydiving.

I'm hoping that with community-driven content - as mods and new modules are pushed out, we'll see some very well-designed quests and narratives ahead.

This game is basically a dungeon crawler, you have to make choices, and a RTS/Turn based strategy. What I mean by that is you're constantly fighting the enemy ship do he won't stop firing to give you a chance to blow him up, but you also have to use the pause button every few seconds to not be overwhelmed by the fast pace. This gives the player control over what speed they play the game. A newer player can take it slow and see what their enemy has, any problems with the ship, and how to defeat them. A very good player can play without the pause button, relying on quick reactions and instinct, which makes the game a lot harder, even when this game is already challenging. The best part of this game I would say is the replay value. This game won't be beat on your first try, not even your fifth, even on easy mode. When you do complete it, there's still more you can do. You can play on the harder difficulty ("Normal" Mode), you can use different ships (which you have to unlock), you can try different strategies, you can download mods. You can even make your own challenges, like playing without oxygen. The only thing bad I would say is that the weapons don't "feel" powerful. I would like to see updates, like visual damage to the ship (burn marks), more exploration, and multi-ship combat.
Overall, this game is definitely worth the $10, (I got it on sale for five). It's simple, but so complex.

Stories is an action-adventure game with a nicely sarcastic narrator, unique characters, a fast-paced combat system, and enough ways to get through the game to keep you coming back for more. The game is set up as if you are reading an adventure story about a swashbuckling fox name Reynardo – specifically, your own story.
If you play your cards right, you will also learn a number of significant "Truths" along the way, and these stay with you in future playthroughs – the narration, dialogue, and possible decisions you are offered will vary based on your character's memory of what has gone before. For example, if you learn that a special item you collected in one run has a rather nasty downside, the narration will remind you to be more careful with it in the future, and you will even get extra bits of narration reminding you of the consequences of using it. In the end, you must unlock four different "Truths" in order to unlock the path to the final, true ending; thus, the game is beatable in under six hours, though experiencing all of the potential storylines can easily take you upwards of thirty hours.
Some stories might end up with you coming ever so close to your goal, only to take an arrow to the knee. Some mean the end of the world. Some find you all alone and mortally wounded as a dozen enemies slowly crowd in around you...and then the story begins again, until you get it right. There are even a small number of mid-mission choices that will result in an instant death, but these simply kick you back a bit in the level so that you can change your mind the next time.
Movement and attacking are controlled with the mouse; your character will always look towards the cursor, even without a button held. Get used to parrying an incoming attacks – You'll want to get this down ASAP, as you won't live long without this and the occasional dash. The movement method takes a little getting used to, but it quickly becomes second nature. Later upgrades will grant you abilities such as slowing down time when you parry at just the right time, or follow-up a melee strike just as your first hit strikes the target.
Combat is fast-paced, with an emphasis on getting high combo numbers, and timing is very important. Fortunately, the game facilitates moving from one foe to another – just click on your new target and your character will zip over to them (the current enemy doesn't have to be dead yet). If there are no enemies on screen, click in the direction where you think they are hiding, and he'll haul tail over to them anyway. Clicking a downed enemy will result in a coup de grace, via a leaping stab, for an instant kill. All fights are handled in small, clearly-defined areas, with EXP awarded for kills, combo chains, style/variety, and whether you escaped unharmed once the current batch of enemies are all dead.
Graphics are of the Cel-shaded variety, minus the thick black lines sometimes associated with the technique. Camera view is often rather zoomed out when not in combat, but it pulls in closer when you are going toe-to-toe with a hulking black raven. It's not as fancy or as flashy as a Triple-A game (but it still looks quite nice for the price), but the visuals suit the method of storytelling, and the adventure mode graphics mesh up with the stylized look of the still images in the framing storybook quite well. Plenty of places where you can see paths that you missed on the current run, as the entire playable world is made up of small, floating islands. As you are riding a floating platform up to a new ledge, you may see paths unexplored, doors and chests unopened, and more, fading out into the distance far below.

Like a love child of Prince of Persia and Portal.
Freedom of action and parkour are the keywords here.
The mechanics feels like the ones shown in PoP and AC, but way more advanced and fascinating.
(rant: This should be what AC becomes after a dozen of iterations, not more sidequests and lootings.)
The Portal vibe comes from the freedom of Mirror Edge, and cluelessness. And the streamlined campaign.
You just move through checkpoints with Faith's parkour and a bit of puzzle solving, which is hard at times when you need to combine the best of two to call it a day.
Plot wise it's kind of blank, and shouldn't be what you aiming for in this parkour classic.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Biggest weakpoint other than the plot is the gameplay.
It's a gem of parkour, but is released at 2008, thus the mechanics are unpolished at some points.
Compare to modern parkour sandboxes like Dying Light, it feels broken.
As a semi-sandbox game with an astonishing parkour dynamics,A lot of trials and errors are needed to grasp what Faith is capable of, AND WHAT SHE'S NOT CAPABLE.
The tech at 2008 simply can't pinpoint Faith's actions accurately and you will kill her easily by missing ledges and checkpoints. This game feels like Dark Souls especially at the front part of the game where you learn to master Faith's actions.
Combat wise the fun lies at evading and disarming foes rather than shooting at them, 1-hit-KO is guaranteed most of the time, makes fighting them with weapons absurdly boring, which is not intended by the game and is not rewarding.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Mirror's Edge is a fun game that feels futuristic since 7 years ago.
There should be sequel for this long ago, it's coming, but under EAvil Corp it's a waste to this gem's potential.
The brilliant mechanics are only mimicked by a few games which is a shame considering it's gamechanging dynamics.
Thou shall screw EA but do not skip this gem.

Oddly for only this game out of the hundreds I've tested, Adaptive V-sync causes a 100FPS cap, while Standard V-sync on or off behaves as normal. Cutscenes, both in-engine and pre-rendered are locked to 30FPS. While performance is good, it frequently drops making a solid 120 extremely hard to maintain. For some reason though even with the drops, it remains relatively smooth without the stuttering you might expect from fluctuation between 85-120 on a 120hz display. FOV is only adjustable via an external tool (has slider, you hit apply and it edits for you, works with SR3/4+GatOuttaHell). A mod that adds extra cheats can be used to disable some extra effects and disable the HUD. With 120Hz+, you might need to apply the graphics options with each launch. There's no refreshrate option in the settings, but it somehow triggers proper display detection that doesn't occur otherwise.
It's definitely not exactly like Saints Row The Third as tons of people would seem to claim. The mobility, types of activities, mission structures are very different from the older games. It's very fun, but I definitely don't think they can pull this gimmick again for the 5th game. If they do, they'll need to go all out with the superpowers, but then it would be a open world super hero game, and not really Saints Row anymore.
The ground gameplay is just as you remember, but now you can run extremely fast, jump like the hulk, and use various powers tweakable with different elements. There are tons of different vehicles and customization options, and many of them are one of a kind special vehicles that you can get from these missions. The problem is, you won't even use them until the end of the game when you have nothing left to do, and just want to role-play or mess around. There are boatloads of collectibles around the world, mainly on rooftops, and you'll be seriously behind on upgrades if you decide to drive instead of hopping between buildings.
On the normal difficulty most of the gameplay isn't necessarily hard, but it does require a decent amount of skill to do well. The aiming on a controller feels bad, and everything is less responsive, with the only upside being driving, which as I said, you won't ever be doing. Definitely play with a keyboard and mouse at a relatively high sensitivity. Very often do enemies come from all sides including above and beneath, so turning the camera slowly is going to give you trouble.
The game consists of doing a lot of the same things over and over again in different places on the map, with most of the main story missions taking place out of the city entirely. But for some reason, probably because of how much stuff it throws at you every damn second with all the events and collectibles, it doesn't really get boring as soon as you'd think even in a 10 hour sitting. In GTAs and SR3, you'd drive for a huge amount of time between missions. With this, you are running and flying, and you can easily stop for a second to clear a area of enemies or hop along buildings to gather collectibles. On PC, there is basically zero loading, so doing a quick mini game along the way is way less of a chore than it could be.
Visually, it definitely looks loads better than SR3 and more colorful and diverse, but there is one thing I hate. It had film grain which can thankfully be turned off, but most of the buildings in the game do this weird moving texture glitch thing that signifies that the whole city is a simulation, but I find it annoying. Most of the time you are moving too fast to even care, but when I just walked along the street it really annoyed me. This can be turned off, but only via a mod that adds extra cheats and stops the cheats from disabling achievements, and you'll have to enable the cheat each time you start the game via the in-game phone menu.
Almost all of the weapons can be upgraded with better stats, a unique modification that changes the way it works, and the visual style of it, which can also change the color of projectiles for laser weapons. Its nice because it lets you have the mechanics of a gun you like, and also a gun that you like the looks of as well. Most of the guns have 2-4 different shapes, and then a few different color options for each. The more unique weapons have less customization, usually just colors. There is a lightsaber katana that you unlock later in the game, and it only has 3 color options. Then missions pop up here and there that add upgrades to it, and more color options. Most of the upgrades can just be bought with the currencies, but the really top tier weapons and abilities seem to come from completing challenges or dedicated missions.
Many people have claimed that Saints Row 4 is simply a big DLC pack, and I would seriously beg to differ. It honestly doesn't feel the same, aside from the explosions, familiar faces and voices, and the really tight gunplay of Saints Row 3. You could probably play both games back to back and not get bored, because they really are that different. The mobility super powers completely replace the vehicles (although there are still tons available, easier than ever to find, collect, and summon), and the combat powers are used constantly in fights.
The port has a few issues and could do with more effect toggle options, but it's a gigantic step up from the SR3 which was painful to configure on >60hz setups and performed terribly while looking far worse.
If you want the game, only buy the complete "Game of the Century" version on sale (usually $6 or less). The DLC adds quite a bit of new stuff to play with and a few missions, and buying it after already owning the base game would cost FAR more than the $2 extra of the complete version.

First off, I like others had high hopes for this game. I adore turn-based tactical RPGs. Ogre Tactics, Final Fantasy Tactics, I eat 'em up. This game looked interesting so I gave it a go.
First part it was great. Beautiful gameplay, detailed world, interesting plot, etc. The real issue however? The combat. Oh, the combat.
First off, the tutorial is very lacking and sporadic. For example, I didn't realize I could change initiative order into much further in the game which can really make or break combat.
The lack of stats and distinct "classes" made the game really cringe worthy too. Both health and attack power are the same stat. So, as you lose health you start hitting like a wet noodle. I disliked this from the get-go but worked with it as best as I could. It made combat so tedious.
It feels like they tried to streamline the gameplay as much as possible but it just made the combat terrible.
Another big decision flaw: the fact that your only resource (Renown) was used to level characters, buy supplies, and buy items. And let me tell you, there's not enough to go around. It's basically a "you're screwed" kind of scenario no matter what.
The fact that you could lose your max geared characters on a random decision outside of combat hurt too. Oh no! I choose the random option B and lost my awesome hero! Let me just reload my last save and-wait, why's my last save from three combats ago? What...
Yup. The game auto-saves for you and doesn't let you have any say in the matter. This really, REALLY bugged me. Part of being a single-player game is the ability to save whenever you could (with limitations of course). Not having this ability really sucked since you pretty much got stuck with whatever bad decision you may have inadvertantly made.
All in all, this game felt like it was doing nothing but screwing over the player which is apparently part of its goal but there comes a point too when the game needs to be fun and engaging. It's not engaging when I lose my best heroes because I chose to eat turnips instead of carrots. It's not fun when the last boss gets to act 6 times a round simply because he's the last one standing (and regenerate each time he gets a turn!).
So if the equivalent of getting smacked in the face with a fish for 9 hours doesn't appeal to you, I'd recommend not getting this game or waiting until it's much cheaper. As is, it's not worth it's current price.

This game is trying to be a remake. Well, in my opinion this should not be revealed as a remake of UFO in the first place. This is a game on its own. It has its own infuence, story is rather different, and also mechanics ale incredibly advanced and - also modified to become easier. I remember taking magazines with me in classic UFO, for example. Let's just take a fresh look on this game instead. A unique combination of styles, mixing strategy, simulation, RPG and action styles together. Fortunately, engine is not the only one component of this game. Let's continue with the best part - music. Soundtracks are simply amazing, and they are one of the best I ever heard. 11/10 for those. Sounds are also amazing and realistic, with great time work, so I will give them 10/10. On my new computer, I am able to play this game on medium setting or so, and I am pretty amazed by the animations. Just try to fire from a plasma sniper or plasma rocket blaster and enjoy. Explosions are simply amazing - I love them. Aliens looks also great. So animations 9/10 and textures also 9/10. Altogether with other graphics elements - I can give the graphics 9/10, I am really impressed byt artworks, but I miss more different enviroments, or cities.
What else can I saz about this gem? It is a beautifull game with enormous possibilities and options (just to mention research and soldier training), with amazing sounds and astonishing soundtrack. Althoug the physics engine lacks nessesary power, game its still amazing. So, what do you say? Do you have guts to take on creatures from the entire galaxy? Can you protect Earth, or maybe defeat your enemies and win this war? Go, and find out, Commander. Because after all - you are our last hope.

First, I'll start by stating the obvious.  The graphical design, battle animations, and music are absolutley amazing!  I felt like I was engaged in a movie (in a good way) as well as playing a game.  I only crashed once while playing this game, so I'd say it's stable.
If you are looking for an action packed game, then this is NOT for you.  I would say this is a casual, relaxing game at best.  All you need is a mouse to point and click.  TBS is as linear as a game can be.
There is a very detailed map in the game that feels wasted.   Every nook and cranny has detailed lore about it, but you're not going to explore over half of it, which is a shame.
There are 3 races in the game.  Humans, Varl and Dredge.  I feel like they could have done more with the Dredge.  There are about 4 or 5 different looking dedge sculpts, then each of those has a couple colour variations of the same sculpt.  So after a few battles with them, it can get a bit tedious fighting the same enemies over and over again.
The reknown system is both your XP and currency.  You gain it from killing enemies, or through the decisions you make throughout your travels.  It can get very frustrating when you have to make a choice of starving your army or promoting or buying items.  I really wish they would have put gold or silver in the game to buy items and supplies.
You get 1 reknown for killing an enemy, no matter how big or how small.  It would be nice to be rewarded a bit more for killing larger enemies.
Also, your characters only get a reknown towards their promotion if they get the killing blow on an enemy.  I'm still trying to figure out if I like this or not, because it definitely adds strategy to the game, if you are trying to level up a certain character.  The downside is you could have a character make some really critical strikes that help your teamates, but if they don't get that last shot to kill the enemy they will stay a low rank and die easily as you progress.
Combat is simplistic.  Hit their strength or armor.  There are no tactics such as flanking or backstabbing, which really makes the battles feel tedious as you progess through.  I think they can do a lot more with this system to spice it up rather than just rushing forward and hoping you kill them before they kill you.
On to the caravan sequences.  As you travel town to town you will get dialog options that will help, harm, or do nothing based on your dialog choices.  You will lose caravan followers, supplies, and even playable characters (used in battles).   A lot of people feel like this is just a pointless guessing game, as some logical choices harm you and some bad choices help you, but not always.... so in a way they are right, it is a guessing game, but there were a lot of times when I was really surpised by the outcome, good or bad, it gave the game some depth for me and really brought me into some dark times (people starving, poor morale, people unhappy with my choices and leaving), but Iwas fine with that.  It really playied into the dark depressing atmosphere of the game, and because my main characters were not natural leaders, the guessing part really made sense to me.  It made me appreciate those choices that worked out in my favor that much more!
All in all, I recommend this game!  I really enjoyed it and felt like I got my moneys worth.   It was a breath of fresh air from the games I usually play. Yes, there are some things they can improve on and I'm sure they will if they make another installment.

The Walking Dead: Michonne is a mini-series from the prominent point and click developers, Telltale Games. Releasing in February 2016, we follow the story of a sword-wielding woman called Michonne. The story is based on the comic books from the franchise. The game only includes three episodes which is much shorter than the other games in the Telltale catalogue.
Gameplay wise, it is what you should come to expect from any Telltale game now, a gripping story where you have to make quick fire decisions when it comes to dialog and what actions to carry out. Throughout a couple of chapters you get multiple options which will really shape the way the rest of the game. Of course the quick time events make a return here, but they only appear in moments where you would expect and don’t make an appearance too often compared to the rest of the series.
Most people will be playing this game for the story, and as someone who hasn’t read the comics or even watch much of the TV show, I have to say I really enjoyed following the story from beginning until conclusion. You are shown glimpse of memories of Michonne’s past throughout and it will leave you guessing until the end as to what will happen. You will encounter plenty of other characters along the way with whom you can develop relationships with depending on dialogue choices. Each of the three episodes are split into five or six easy to distinguish chapters as there is a clear cut off in scenes and when the story is about to take a different turn.
The art style from Michonne is again, as you would expect from a Telltale game, the comic book look does the game complete justice, there is nothing fancy about them, and it just looks really good. From the animations of all of the characters movement, facial expressions and textures, this game looks brilliant. The voice acting is again top notch; I would expect nothing less from a Telltale game now. There were times when interacting with objects didn’t make a sound, but you anticipate it happening which did kind of knock me out of the immersion at points, but I was able to overlook that given the quality of the story being told.
The Walking Dead Michonne took me just under five hours to complete. This is easily a game you can complete in an afternoon’s worth of time. I wouldn’t say there is any real difficulty to this game though; you are in it more for the ride rather than a game play experience. The lack of any “puzzles” or tricky action scenes may put a handful of people off unfortunately. You could always make the game a little more challenging by turning off any of the hints at the start if you did want that added layer of difficulty.  I’d say this title does have at least some replay ability in place – the key decisions you make throughout the story will reward you with different plot points and different endings.
Sadly the game does come with a couple of technical issues. Firstly the loading times, every scene change requires a black screen of at least 10-15 seconds worth of loading, even on my SSD.  Secondly, the game will sometimes completely lock up and you just have to sit and wait for a good minute for it to actually sort itself out. This at times will give you a heart attack as you don’t really know when the last time you hit a checkpoint – just bit a little patient and any lock ups will usually sort them self out. Thankfully I didn’t actually get any hard crashes which sent me to desktop which I guess could be a saving grace in this day and age.
I completely enjoyed my time playing through Michonne, no it doesn’t have the long story that the rest of the seasons have, but it’s not meant to.  This an evening’s worth of entertainment that is well worth the low price of £10.99. You’d spend that on 2 hours at a movie and to be honest you are going to get a more enthralling story from this game, along with the added replay ability. Telltale fans will have already played this game through by now, but even if you have a passing interest in point and click adventures or The Walking Dead franchise, this is worth both your time and money.

Ys I is great. It's a tight, short game with simple mechanics. You just 'bump' into enemeis to attack, but never straight on, so there is finesse to it. Running across the fields, mowing enemies and running into them as they all blow up into bits of bones flesh and gore is so satisfying. Bosses are a really good challenge, and torwards the end they all become consistently high quality and are rewarding to defeat. The music is fantastic as well.
Ys II is almost good. It brings the same gameplay to the table, adding in magic and mapping items to a key to heal on the fly. The magic is good- light to brighten up surroundings and reveal hidden enemies, fire as a standard chargeable projectile, and my favorite- turning into a creature to converse with enemies, with each you encounter having specific and unique dialogues. They talk a lot about shifts and something of urban legends about the protagonist, or just funny things. It's great.
However, Ys II falters in a few ways. The game is just SO labrynthine. This wasn't a problem in I- there was one cave area which was annoying but it doesn't really even touch how bad it gets in II. Places are just so large and complex, which would be okay, but often times paths look very similiar and there aren't enough landmarks or distinctive areas to really know where the hell you are a lot of the time. And lots of dead ends too. Being an ARPG this isn't as bad as it could be, but enemies will still respawn and there's just no map function. Worse yet, combined with this you can miss important items and will have to backtrack again on top of already required backtracking. It's annoying, especially when you've finally reached a boss but it turns out there's a sword that will let you do more than mere chip damage to them. I couldn't finish the game, I reached about 3/4ths through it when I decided I had enough. It's a shame because there's a lot of good qualities but the map design makes it a tedious game.
The end result is that I is fantastic and II is worth a shot but not as good. Regardless, they both have good qualities. Not enough can be said of the good music, and the core gameplay is still good in both- just bogged down in II by other things.

Classic, old school, and a challenge.
Ys I & II Chronicles is a good remake spin on a old school way of gaming. This is a fun RPG set that's fast paced, fun, and has outstanding music!  At the time of this review i've finished Ys I, and am currently working on Ys 2, but i've seen enough to work this review.   The games are well developed and actually well balanced in several aspects. Game makes you feel powerful and gives you lots of levels for grinding, but does a good job keeping you down until you get your next set of equipment. The challenges of this game are actually very reminiscent of Zelda 1 in the aspect of exploration and  discovery. The game will give you clues, but will not hold your hand. If you don't pay attention, you can get lost on what to do. Details are in the text, and the rest is up to you to discover how to bridge the next piece of the story. This is a good reminder of a time before the internet and walkthroughs, and how you needed to be in charge of the game and make your way through on your own.  I won't spoil any story points, but I can say that it can be REALLY challenging at times.
Music is outstanding, as I mentioned with a lot of great multi-instrumental sounds based on where you are, and it never gets old. These are the kind of tunes for your gaming music playlist.
Sound is pretty typical, no voice acting, and without music, it's just a bunch of floor tapping and sword swiping, so nothing too great there.
Controls are okay.  The combat is a bumper system, which is another old school RPG method. Kind of interesting to play it in a modern time, but it's simple. In Ys II you get magic, and casting is just A, so that's about the only innovative thing. To talk to people, you just bump into them as well.
Overall, Ys Chronicles is a great game. It's not perfect, and can be frustrating at times too, but a great game because it's classic, and not catering to the player. It welcomes the player to think and figure out the story. They give you the string, and you follow it.  This is a perfect game for those who loved Zelda 1, and other old school style RPG's!
EDIT : I want to add, that the ability to change from modern to classic graphics was a nice touch too. Art work differences is something interesting to look at.

Review:
I personally knew nothing of this game prior to one or two days before its release date. I read up a bit about the game and liked the idea of it, reminded me of infamous, one of my personal top five favourite games. Choice your path sort of deals; will you be good or evil? After playing through the game and completing my first path, I thought to myself, "Holy crap, this game has a shi t-ton of replay value" If I wanted too, I could re-pick my previous choices and just change the last one if I wanted too and get a completely different ending or maybe even more levels to explore. Each level has multiple paths, each one requires different abilities or weapons to proceed. So, not only does this game allow the discovery of new levels but new paths in the same levels you've already "beaten". I say beaten in quotations because as I said, each level having different routes to take allows you to beat the level in different ways. Not to mention every play-though throws in something new to the mix from the looks of it, opening up more choices and more levels to choice and explore! Sadly, with each indie game comes problems and bugs. Clipping is an issue in this game but can be over looked due to the fact that you only notice it when in-game cut-scenes are playing. Not to mention clipping is a pretty hard bug to fix when you've got flowing capes and cloths. Another issue is the fact that the game doesn't run very well on high settings even with a beefy PC. I wish there was a way to set specific settings high - low - off. I don't mind running the game on medium, the only problem is you get a blur overlay which can be straining on one’s eyes. Surely there must be another way. I also notice less foliage and stuff like that when turning down the settings from high so the blur overlay should be an option rather then forced if not on high settings. Going back to the game itself, as I was completing my first path, I was awarded an achievement as/before the cut-scene was being played out? It spoiled what was going to happen, granted it was just in the next few seconds but it does still take away from the story telling aspect. Maybe award the player the achievement when you return to the menu so this does not happen? It was a real shame but it was overlooked as soon as I saw how many paths there were.
Overall, this is a pretty good game but I need to play more of it before I can speak anymore for this game or recommend buying it. This review can be changed as I progress with the game.

I have now completed the game twice and feel like I can properly review the experience. Starting off, this is a very nice change of pace from the regular game, mixing a blend of choose-your-own-adventure with some turn-based combat. Add to that a beautiful artstyle and a superb soundtrack and you get a thoroughly enjoyable experience from beginning to end.
The first playthrough was definitely the most memorable as each choice you are presented provides a provocative and ethical dilemma that needs to be solved, often pitting you against a range of really bad choices where there's no real "good" outcome to any of them. The feeling of hopelessness and desperation oozes from every minute you play it, and it truly feels like you are the last hope and salvation of your entire caravan of people and fighters. On the second playthrough, things are a little less engaging, as you start to realise that some of the choices you can make through the journey are somewhat arbitrary and you end up running into most encounters and situations no matter what choice you make along the road. You are also aware of some of the more important events and can easily avoid them by, for instance, refusing to allow certain characters to join your party along the way.
The combat is fairly well balanced throughout the game and often provides a nice challenge even on Normal difficulty. There are portions of the game where you are part of a smaller battle sequence where a regular turn-based fight can be extended into a second round, but you are almost always at such a severe disadvantage when you launch a second round that I ended up only attempting it a single time, getting my♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to me, and then staying away from them for the rest of the experience.
Here I can take the time to address one of the problems with the game, being the isometric perspective of the battles. At times it can become very cluttered when a lot of allies and enemies are placed in squares next to each other, making targeting of enemies and using abilities somewhat annoying at times. The option to turn the camera, so to say, would have helped here, allowing for easier battle management. However, this could be seen as part of the design, making the heat of battle seem more confusing for the commander.
This following paragraph is somewhat of a spoiler, but not a massive one, so skip to the next one if you want to experience everything for yourself: The very final battle (and the preparation leading up to it as well) is a very stiff challenge, and if you have been unlucky or have been spreading out your experience points and currency too much, you might not even be able to finish the game. On both my playthroughs, the final fight took a number of attempts to finish, and me winning mostly just comes down to being lucky in the rounds that I won on. The fight itself is very unfair at times and can leave you very frustrated. However, as it is the last fight in the game, the stiff challenge is somewhat appropriate, but it could be more fairly balanced. Seeing as you could possibly end up in a situation where the entire sequence becomes impossible, ruining a perhaps 12-hour game for a player and forcing them to restart or jump back to a previous point, I can understand that a lot of players are really frustrated at this part.
The game also ends rather abruptly, but with a nice climax in the story. I can only imagine that this is because the developers are working in an episodic format and I have heard people mentioning that this is supposed to be the first part in a three part story, which would make perfect sense with the way the story is formatted. Overall, the story is engaging and you truly want to see the characters come through it.
All in all, I strongly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys a good story-driven game with an emphasis on turn-based combat. If you're a fan of the old choose-your-own-adventure type games and books, this is also very appropriate for you. The beautiful artwork and soundtrack should also peak your interest, and if you're more interested in the story, the visuals, and the sound, you could turn down the difficulty to Easy and just enjoy the ride. You won't regret it. :)

What You are about to delve into is a game that is highly simular to MECC's 1974 classic "The Oregon trail" It is about the Journey you take with your warriors and clansmen through the harsh Nordic landscape while you manage things like food, Morale, and rank. Fights earn you renown whitch is the currency you use in town to purchase items, and food to make shure your party doesnt starve. You have to strike a balance though, if your party is too weak in combat, you may never make it to the end. Half the fun in a way, is the fact that this game doesnt let you save. It forces you to make your decisions and live with them, so you can think of all the coulda/shoulda/whoulda's after the chapters end.

To be totaly fair before ripping into the game, it has a bunch of good things that make it fun.  There's a whole host of lovely powerups (if you can find/afford them), the levels are large enough to satisfy your explorer's heart (although if you spend time exploring you run the risk of not surviving the ramping difficulty), the controls work really well (as long as you take the time after your first game to reset them to something more workable), and I love the Video Zoom option to make the itty bitty guy easier to see amongst all the other stuff going on, BUT...
I simply CANNOT "enjoy" the game. I like to Play in my spare time away from work, not Work after working.  Besides the utterly ridiculously random spread of viable powerups (I had a complete level of nothing but itty bitty gold chests and NO powerups to beat the boss with), the chief complaint about it is that the difficulty ramps up WAY too fast (over time), and it does not reset per world.  I could see if the difficulty were to ramp up faster by world then it might be enjoyable.  By the time you've collected enough gear to make it enjoyably playable, the creatures are spawning so bloody fast that you cannot even travel across the screen without being swamped. One feature that stands The Walking Dead: Michonne (
) out from its predecessors was the fantastic blending of the flashbacks, visions & main story arcs. I really like how this was done, often occurring at unexpected moments seamlessly merging the stories together, where actions in both worlds are linked. The visions Michonne experiences are rather creepy with a strong horror movie feel, & with some nice post effects to help you distinguish when the focus changes.
The flashbacks & vision sequences were the highlight of what was a rather dull main story. For me, there just weren’t a lot of memorable characters or events. Most of the personalities felt standardised, one dimensional & a bit predictable. This may also be in part due to the shorter three episode length which doesn’t really lend itself to develop the characters too deeply or allow much in the way of twists in the story.
It’s certainly not all bad though, & as expected there was plenty of zombie killing action throughout to keep things moving swiftly along. Some of these fights were very impressive, with creative use of the 3D rotating camera & bullet time for many of the larger scenes, & the occasional rare button combo spots that can throw you off balance. I do wish there were more combos sections to show off Michonne’s
& to help increase the difficulty … keeping the player on their toes.
Soundtrack was a fitting & enjoyable addition to the experience with other sound effects & voice acting also top quality.


didn’t do the voice, but I was pleasantly surprised to find voice acting was pretty spot on! Likewise, capturing the personality in the character’s look & animations often reminded me of how Danai may have acted it out on the show.  Animations overall are very good in
, I didn’t notice any buggy animations, jumpy textures or strange camera work which I have seen in most of the earlier TTG games.  I did however have a few .exe crashes
using Steam In-Home Streaming during my play through.
is a decent outing, that I would summarise as good but not great. Little short at 3 streamlined chapters, totalling around 3-4hrs of gameplay. It could quite easily have been fleshed out to 5
as the shorter length, I feel, ultimately works against the story telling & character development. It really needed some more space to give the characters time to show some depth, personality & explore their stories, not to mention the main story arcs further. There was a good balance between action & dialog in what was there, but it was let down a degree by a mediocre story & script.
Certainly still good enough that it’s worth a play
, & especially if you are a fan of the Walking Dead.

A brilliant pair of games.  Everything from the lore to the characters is top-notch, and the combat is simple and addictive, combined with a classic dungeoncrawling experience, as well as some shmup elements for bosses.  This honestly may be one of the best RPGs of all time, simply by virtue of it's excellent storytelling.  Your attachments and relationships with the characters feel genuine and organic.  Every single NPC has a fleshed out backstory and their position in the world makes sense.  Even though the story is linear, it doesn't feel like the game is just railroading you from point A to point B.  Instead, your objectives unfold naturally from talking to NPCs and you feel immersed in a living, breathing world.  The attention to detail is surprisingly high, particularly in regards to how dialogue changes depending on the circumstances.  Some players may find themselves at odds with the game's cryptic progression, but if you're the type that doesn't like their hand held, and a fan of classic RPGs, this is a solid recommendation.

If you like RPGs or in general you’re looking for something easy to pick up and play, this one’s for you.

Back in the day I was a big fan of the Tony Hawk Series up until THUG2, and a played many snowboarding games mainly the SSX series. What Steep does is roughly the same idea but on a grander scale. Many will find this game to be reptitive, and that could be a similar thing said about Dynasty Warriors, but in saying this that describes the kinds of fanbases and what the game is offering. Steep offers a sandbox experience in which you can travel across an entire peak without load zones and compete in time trials, challenges or play amongst the various story missions. You have the options of Snowboarding, Skiing, Paragliding and Wingsuit/Sky Diving. The charm of the game comes from it's gameplay, IF YOU DO NOT LIKE THIS KIND OF GAMEPLAY, then I 110% recommend you do not buy this game, it will get boring quick. Although if you are a fan of the aforementioned sports games then I fully recommend this game.
Performance wise, since the engine is rendering mostly snow and terrain LOD the game does run fairly well, I still would recommend having a decent setup as any thing below 60fps will turn anyone off on a fast paced xtreme sports game such as this.
Graphically I would assume its a similar engine to other Ubisoft games but I have not done extensive research in this.
Base game content isn't sparse although since it is a sandbox some of that comes down to the player also. With upcoming season pass content but also free content updates with an free Alaska peak DLC, I would say you are looking at a minimum 50 hours of content to muck around with until the DLC drops. Leveling up your main skill level will liekly be a quick experience [depends on your apptitude] but levelling up the various sub categories to the game will take some time.
Live events are included also.
8/10

Be warned: this part is lengthy, in-depth, unprofessional (in my opinion), and may contain too many spoilers to sensor.  You can skip to the bottom summary if you want.  Otherwise, continue reading.
In this sci-fi, rogue-like game, you are a ragtag crew of beings aboard a reconditioned ship of your choosing, attempting to relay critical intel to the Federation while the Rebels chase you across a randomly generated galaxy.  On the way to Federation HQ, you will encounter strange and somewhat disturbing phenomenon that could mean the prosperity or end of you and your fellow shipmates.  It is up to you to decide what is the best course of action as you navigate through this skeptical society torn by war, but you will insure a bright future for all who inhabit the galaxy if you manage to succeed in your mission.
Right off the bat, the first things I noticed about the game were the impressive art involved and the superb background music.  It is apparent that the developers spent much effort into creating the setting and its characters while keeping simplicity in mind, and the music could not be better matched for the scenarios incorporated.  Very space-esque, very attractive.
Let's jump right into it.  With almost every game started fresh, there is usually some kind of starting equipment to get you ready for the rest of the game.  Now I don't expect to be pampered with the best ship in the fleet, but I didn't expect to get a junker with pee shooters either.  The game even tells you so in the description of the ship, and is enforced when the game explicitly recommends playing on easy before being adventurous and trying normal.  You do NOT want to go guns blazing on normal until you've got more of a feel for the game, but I'm not here to stop you from that and that's fine.  Once you get a hang of things, you'll realize that the first ship is not a junker at all, but that the game is unforgiving for making mistakes.  Additionally, other ships can be unlocked by completing certain achievements or by successfully completing special events, with each ship having their own unique attributes.
When you're done picking a ship and customizing your crew, you find yourself in the middle of nowhere with a message box updating you on the situation.  After some fiddling with the controls, you discover how to jump to the next nearby beacon in the sector, expending some of your fuel in the process. However, you've neglected to properly allocate the energy supply of your ship and the work of your crew in balance, and find yourself toe to toe with a pirate ship charging its guns up for a first strike.  Not the best way to spearhead the mission, but you'll be up to speed in no time with the handy tutorial at the main menu screen... which you're not at right now.  Well, somehow you manage to persuade the pirate into sparing both your lives and receive a hefty supply of scrap, missiles, and whatnot.
Which brings me to the save mechanic... not the best way to save a game, but it does prevent cheating your way back from an unfavorable situation, something the game is somewhat dependent on since you will find out later on most beacon encounters are random.  You figure that out quickly and wonder why the game doesn't pick up at the last checkpoint (hint: there are no checkpoints).  At least this will give you time to check out the tutorial.
The tutorial is pretty simple and gives the basics on how to keep your ship from falling to pieces... not much else to say about that.  Afterwards, you jump right back into the frey prepared and confront another enemy at the next beacon.
Combat takes place in RTS style as you attempt to capture or destroy the enemy ship, all while defending your ship from hostile fire and boarding parties.  Strategic advantage can be gained by disrupting specific functions of hostile ships, with the same  vulnerabilites applying to your ship, so keeping everything in working condition is generally a good habit to adopt lest you like being a sitting duck.  With this in mind, you quickly dispatch your newfound foe and profit from what can be salvaged of the remains.
Weapon variety and distribution is rather random.  Sometimes you'll get the best weapon of the game early on but never actually use it; other times you'll find yourself with an over abundance of pee shooters (which, in retrospect, is probably good to start with, but should be traded in later on).  Some weapons have similar names but require different resources as well, which can be somewhat confusing. Luckily, whatever you don't need can be traded in at a shop for extra scrap, which can be used to upgrade the performance of your ship to be better suited in combat, used as currency to purchase resources and equipment, or commited to repairs of your ship after a rather dangerous encounter.
Don't get me wrong, though.  Not everything in the game is completely combat.  Oftentimes you'll encounter other travelers in need of assistance, come across stray wreckages holding caches of equipment, or accidently stray too close to the stars.  It's up to you whether or not you want to participate in these events, but keep in mind that, under normal circumstances, the odds are always stacked against you.  That's why Bill didn't make it back to the ship in time.
In short, FTL provides a plethora of addicting and exciting, new content for players to enjoy, with each playthrough uniquely different from the last.  While there are a few disagreeable methods implemented, some are there to prevent the experience from being shattered so the player's attention and enjoyment can truely be fulfilled without interruption.
- Great Artwork and Sound / Simple story and background
- Permadeath feature / Temporary Save
- Strategic / Semi-linear gameplay
- Randomly generated encounters / galaxies
- Player choice heavily emphasized
- High replay value
-
- Somewhat misleading difficulty settings
- The occasional no-chance-in-hell playthrough
9/10

Oddly for only this game out of the hundreds I've tested, Adaptive V-sync causes a 100FPS cap, while Standard V-sync on or off behaves as normal. Cutscenes, both in-engine and pre-rendered are locked to 30FPS. While performance is good, it frequently drops making a solid 120 extremely hard to maintain. For some reason though even with the drops, it remains relatively smooth without the stuttering you might expect from fluctuation between 85-120 on a 120hz display. FOV is only adjustable via an external tool (has slider, you hit apply and it edits for you, works with SR3/4+GatOuttaHell). A mod that adds extra cheats can be used to disable some extra effects and disable the HUD. With 120Hz+, you might need to apply the graphics options with each launch. There's no refreshrate option in the settings, but it somehow triggers proper display detection that doesn't occur otherwise.
It's definitely not exactly like Saints Row The Third as tons of people would seem to claim. The mobility, types of activities, mission structures are very different from the older games. It's very fun, but I definitely don't think they can pull this gimmick again for the 5th game. If they do, they'll need to go all out with the superpowers, but then it would be a open world super hero game, and not really Saints Row anymore.
The ground gameplay is just as you remember, but now you can run extremely fast, jump like the hulk, and use various powers tweakable with different elements. There are tons of different vehicles and customization options, and many of them are one of a kind special vehicles that you can get from these missions. The problem is, you won't even use them until the end of the game when you have nothing left to do, and just want to role-play or mess around. There are boatloads of collectibles around the world, mainly on rooftops, and you'll be seriously behind on upgrades if you decide to drive instead of hopping between buildings.
On the normal difficulty most of the gameplay isn't necessarily hard, but it does require a decent amount of skill to do well. The aiming on a controller feels bad, and everything is less responsive, with the only upside being driving, which as I said, you won't ever be doing. Definitely play with a keyboard and mouse at a relatively high sensitivity. Very often do enemies come from all sides including above and beneath, so turning the camera slowly is going to give you trouble.
The game consists of doing a lot of the same things over and over again in different places on the map, with most of the main story missions taking place out of the city entirely. But for some reason, probably because of how much stuff it throws at you every damn second with all the events and collectibles, it doesn't really get boring as soon as you'd think even in a 10 hour sitting. In GTAs and SR3, you'd drive for a huge amount of time between missions. With this, you are running and flying, and you can easily stop for a second to clear a area of enemies or hop along buildings to gather collectibles. On PC, there is basically zero loading, so doing a quick mini game along the way is way less of a chore than it could be.
Visually, it definitely looks loads better than SR3 and more colorful and diverse, but there is one thing I hate. It had film grain which can thankfully be turned off, but most of the buildings in the game do this weird moving texture glitch thing that signifies that the whole city is a simulation, but I find it annoying. Most of the time you are moving too fast to even care, but when I just walked along the street it really annoyed me. This can be turned off, but only via a mod that adds extra cheats and stops the cheats from disabling achievements, and you'll have to enable the cheat each time you start the game via the in-game phone menu.
Almost all of the weapons can be upgraded with better stats, a unique modification that changes the way it works, and the visual style of it, which can also change the color of projectiles for laser weapons. Its nice because it lets you have the mechanics of a gun you like, and also a gun that you like the looks of as well. Most of the guns have 2-4 different shapes, and then a few different color options for each. The more unique weapons have less customization, usually just colors. There is a lightsaber katana that you unlock later in the game, and it only has 3 color options. Then missions pop up here and there that add upgrades to it, and more color options. Most of the upgrades can just be bought with the currencies, but the really top tier weapons and abilities seem to come from completing challenges or dedicated missions.
Many people have claimed that Saints Row 4 is simply a big DLC pack, and I would seriously beg to differ. It honestly doesn't feel the same, aside from the explosions, familiar faces and voices, and the really tight gunplay of Saints Row 3. You could probably play both games back to back and not get bored, because they really are that different. The mobility super powers completely replace the vehicles (although there are still tons available, easier than ever to find, collect, and summon), and the combat powers are used constantly in fights.
The port has a few issues and could do with more effect toggle options, but it's a gigantic step up from the SR3 which was painful to configure on >60hz setups and performed terribly while looking far worse.
If you want the game, only buy the complete "Game of the Century" version on sale (usually $6 or less). The DLC adds quite a bit of new stuff to play with and a few missions, and buying it after already owning the base game would cost FAR more than the $2 extra of the complete version.
