As an huge fan of the comics and the telltale game series, this was in fact another smash hit in there emotional joy rides we call videogames.
I was real quick to play through, only a few hours, but the action was certaintly there. Some of the cut scenes from the previous games were very slow and only story driven. Knowing how bad *** Michonne is, This game changes that habit. With Michonnes intense swordsmanship, you have to string plenty of keys together to kill your enemies. There is a lot of dodging, attacking, and you aren't always sure when its going to happen so you have to stay on guard for them.
I noticed though I played this differently than the other two. Where Lee and Clementine were blank slate characters with no back story except what you give them, they are you essentially. Michonne has a back story, she's been in 150+ issues of a comic series where so much has happened. As a fan of the comics, I noticed i was picking choices she would pick, even though my moral compass is higher, hers wasn't. This trend might also be seen through other fans (of the show or comic series). This is not neccessarily a good or bad thing, just an interesting feeling. I do, however, recommend you watch the show or read the comics to get a feel for the character before playing because, like i said, she is not blank slate and is a very dynamic character.
Also I felt the story was pretty rushed. It was like Telltale had a schedule, and extending it from a miniseries to a full series would have made it more worth while, but they wanted to just be done with it. I vividly recall a part in the second episode, not spoiling anything, but you think this is going to be a real character defining moment, like one of those major choices you see at the end, but there is a huge left turn, just out of nowhere and its not story anymore its action.
that happened i guess..."
It was definitley a noticeably rushed story, but this one wasn't about the overall story. I'd like to emphasise that this game isn't centered around the people she meets and what she does in this game. Its about her coping with the loss of her kids. Even from the first episode, although its underlying, its the whole focus of coping with extreme guilt that she has put off for so long. This is the charcter defining moment she needed explained in the comics, but kirkman never went back and told. (Rick tries and ask her where she went when she left and she dodges it. Basically the end of that in the comics.)
Overall I did enjoy the story, but it was more satisfying knowing that this game filled the void a story I have enjoyed left out. The up front story was rushed but the underlying story was more powerful and neccessary in the end. It played well, got stuck at a few loading screens every now and again, but not a big deal. Another successful walking dead game for telltale. But I do still suggest looking into Michonnne's character if you have not, you'll enjoy this game more.

The story in this game is a nice addition to the Telltale Walking Dead series but I have few issues with the game.
First the good:
-Love the story and the background on Michonne. I have not read the comics and do not know how much they give on Michonne's history but after playing this game, I connect with Michonne's character from the TV show a lot more.
-Killing zombies is amazing. It's just button mashing, sure, but they did a good job with the animation and mini-cutscenes that make the expeirence ssooooo satisfying. Michonne is very clearly portrayed as a capable woman and a zombie death machine.
Then the bad:
-I hated some of the mechanics of this game. One wrong button push will get you killed in a really dumb way. One minute you are murdering a bunch of zombies and the next you are being killed by a zombie who's jaw has been removed because of one bad button push. The other games had some forgiveness on this but not in this game... and that led to some really ridiculous and frustrating deaths.
-Some of the scenes in this game make no sense. One minute, bad guys are shooting at you and almost hitting you everytime and the next, you are walking away from them and the bullets don't even come close. There were a few scenes like this that just made my jaw drop in disbelief at how badly they were thought through.
-The game is just too short for $15 (in my opinion). I completed the game in less than 4 hours and have no intrest in replaying it. I would suggest picking it up for anything between $5 and $10.
**** Overall this is a good game and I would recommend it. Just be aware that this is not as good as any of the other Walking Dead titles by Telltale.

Steep is an open world Ski/Extreme Sports game with a lot of potential.
I really love this game!
The map is huge allowing you to explore for hours, a variety of different challenges and no serious competetive elements at all. The soundtrack to the game is great and the sound design is top notch. The graphics are beautiful and surpise me with how well they run on my computer and with (most of the time) steady frames. Customisation is lacking though, don't get me wrong there is quite a variety of what you can customise but in each section there isn't too much to customise, e.g there are quite a lot of helmets but barely any variety in gloves. The game is a bit buggy and if i'm honest, sometimes you lose momentum for no reason and i've managed to glitch through a few walls. However, for what it's priced at (40 pounds in the UK) I don't feel the game is worth it, I personally waited until the game went on sale and got it for about 26. Although this idea isn't fresh in the industry, Steep does differ from other similair games like SSX with it's atmosphere and vibes the game gives you, I feel really mellowed out when playing which I don't really get from many games. To be clear, I haven't played with friends yet but I HAVE played with randoms and trying to get the high score on certain challenges is really fun without having to take it seriously. In my opinion though, one of the things that let this game down is that it really feels like something is missing. Although you can Walk/Snowboard/Ski and Fly, it doesn't feel like it's enough, I think snowmobiles would be a cool feature further down the line as the game is still kind of in its early days, but for now I'm happy to keep things like this. My final thing that I would like to nag about is the fact that some challenges in particular are boring as ♥♥♥♥, for instance one of them consisted of literally following an AI whilst some voice over went on about its fetish for the mountains (sounds funny but at the time I would rather have fallen down the slopes and cracked my neck).
The biggest complaint I see from OTHER people is that the game gets repetetive and boring, so if you're extremely in-patient then I suppose this isn't for you. I can understand the idea of using the same mechanics over and over again can get boring after a while, but really what do you expect from a sports game? It's like buying handball 2017 and then saying "this is boring, how come I can't kick the ♥♥♥♥ing ball?"
TL;DR
I recommend this game (WHEN IT'S ON SALE)
Pros:
-Great graphics
-Huge map
-Something fresh
-Music fits well
-Online
-A decent amount of customisation
-Basically what it says on the tin
Cons:
-Buggy at times
-A few challenges are pointless
-Frames can stutter MASSIVELY now and then
-Tutorial is a bit long and I don't think it's skippable
Rating: 8.5/10

This is my story:
I beat diety difficulty with on a huge with continents as the Celts and a full load of civilizations and city states. Venice became excessively wealthy and I was their closest ally and adopted my religion early in the game - being the closest civilization on my continent and celts having fast religion. I wiped out the Egyptians (in the middle of the continent) with the French at the farther end (and France wiped out another civilization over there earliery apparently.) Another civilization had gotten stuck between the Egyptians and the French expansion, and failed to really get going but lasted a few more centuries with 2-3 cities, I took one of them when France declared war, I sold it to venice for an excessive amount of gold, which funded international colonization (giving them each a solid beginning with basic buildings.) I further funded this by greatly reducing the standing population among the main part of my civilization. My continent was incredibly peaceful, whereas the other continents were filled with internal war (with Japan and England pushing themselves ahead on their respective continents. At around 1700-50 A.D. I managed to make my religion the world religion. All civs except for Venice and Japan suddenly hate me (obvious reason.)

I'm honestly not sure if recommended is the right term for this game. This game feels like a testbed for an entire sub-genre, the First Person Platformer, its so far is the only unique example of it and it shows. When the game is in its stride it feels exhilarating to play with an amazing sense of direction and unique style in graphics that really has stopped it looking dated several years later.
Unfortunately the combat sequences can feel really out of place and can get frustrating very quickly and the game can quickly confuse the player about where exactly they need to be to the point where you have to look up videos on Youtube just to get an idea of where you are supposed to be. These two negatives can also get happen all at once which only serves to unduly stress the player. The story itself is also a letdown with no real talking points or standout characters excluding that of the protagonist Faith.
So with two glaring flaws why do I give this the thumbs up? I feel simply the concept that this game shows is full of potential, if DICE can iron out these flaws in the upcoming sequel it could really fly. Knights of Pen and Paper +1 Edition is an example of what is wrong with the gaming industry, publishers and developers working together to make a game that is less than a full and proper experience without first investing heavily in it.  In most cases, that means you must use real world money to make your game run the way it should in the first place.  Luckily the game gives players a choice, you have the choice to play the game a great deal, or to buy shortcuts to make the game better.  Everywhere you turn there is a price attached to everything, you can gain the currency with playing or with plastic, and playing takes way too long.
I would say that the game itself, when you ignore this horrible choice of microtransactions, is mediocre, not exceptional.  It has several novel ideas, but it lacks any real pay off, there is nothing revolutionary or deeply engaging about it.  Even the flavour text, the stuff you would hope would be most entertaining in a dungeons and dragons type of game feels weak and boring, as though the developers were not into it.
Overall, I was quite disappointed with this title and I don't think many people will be able to enjoy it.

Firstly I will tell you this game is a mobile port.Second it has a microtransaction of buying ingame gold for cash,but you never  and I mean never need to use it.There are plenty of items ingame that increase the amount of gold you get dropped that have other stats to them.Now to the review.
Game has classes you can swap in and out,skills that you can level individually,upgradeable class locked weapons/armor and plenty of item accessories and consumables.The game has pop culture reference comedy all throughout it,hardly any variation in quest types and is grindy since you only turn-base fight your way through each situation for the most part.Plenty of boss fights in the game,no puzzles, and a small learning curve on how to handle things. Uses dice roll to determine things such as crafting chance,battles,etc.
If you like games you can play 5min-1hr + at a time,do not mind grind , a pop culture heavy comedic story, and little varation in gameplay then pick it up on sale, or in a bundle. I would not pay full price,just does not feel like a $10 game , more like a $2.50-$5 one.
The game itself is a comedic sort of table top dice roll turned into a video game.The dialog trees,characters, and the story have comedy all throughout them. The game has tons of pop culture references from 1970s- onward in both enemies,outfits and dialog.
Gameplay mechanic wise you pretty much fight turn based fight your way through all the quests you do.There is hardly any variation in the quests escort,item fetch/deliever,rescue, and fight/slay. They incorporate you grind fighting your way through.There are no puzzles or anything so do not expect much outsite of witty dialog and fights.
Items in the game are what you would expect, consumables with stat buffs that last for a certain time.Weapons/armor are not sold but are upgraded by blacksmiths.They are only found in towns as well as item purchases.There are different character classes each with 4 skills that you can level up individually.When you decide what character classes you want you have to pick a person whom hs their on special stat they add to be that class.You can swap in and out character classes that you level up when you are at towns with taverns.
The game can be played for 5min- 1hr+ depending on how much grinding and story you are willing to play through. There is a NG+ when you beat the game to continue on your adventures which resets all the quests making the mobs tougher at the beginning onward.
My final verdict on this game is if you do not mind the grind,it is a enjoyable title.Its simple yet to the point.I played it in spurts and had fun playing it.Its deffinately not for everyone but no game out there is.Get it on sale or in a bundle, not worth $10 to me more like $2.50-$5 game.Not for lack of content,more for lack of variations in quests and gameplay mechanics.

Also, I absolutely hated the storyline (If there even is one....). Sure it was just average through 75% of the campaign, but from that point onwards it seems that the script writers ran out of ideas and just started throwing random stuff at you.
Regardless, the gameplay of this game makes up for most of it's flaws and I would really recommend this.

- Has co op(co op is always fun =) )
CONS

Shadowgrounds from Frozenbyte is a top-down sci-fi alien murderfest.  Shoot thousands of giant bugs and cyborg spiders with a multitude of different weapons.
Humanity has successfully terraformed Ganymede, and there is a burgeoning scientific and military presence establishing a foothold here.  But when the power generator is mysteriously sent offline, the mechanic Tyler has to go investigate.  Turns out there is blood smeared everywhere and bodies lying all over.  What he finds after that will change the course of history.  The story tries to take itself seriously, but in all honesty, it isn’t very original or all that engaging.  But it’s a good enough excuse for indiscriminately blowing up aliens.
Shadowgrounds is a top-down shooter, which takes a few minutes to get used to, as atmospheric games like this usually are in first person.  The game is focused on exploring the different alien-infested buildings in each level, finding keycards to unlock the next section, and shooting anything that moves.  You’ll constantly be concerned with your ammo reserves (especially on boss levels, as bosses can take A LOT of damage) but for most of the game ammo is plentiful.  Enemies have an annoying tendency to be bullet sponges, requiring you to empty a clip or more into some of them in order to kill them.  You’ll never be completely helpless, as your pistol has infinite shots.  The other weapons are all unique and satisfying to use, each giving you different strategies to employ and allowing you an easier time of taking out certain enemies.  Dead aliens will sometimes drop upgrade parts, which you can spend to give your weapons new abilities like higher damage, rapid fire, or extended magazines.  You can read documents that have been left lying around on PDAs or on computers in order to figure out what is really going on, but it is completely optional, and frankly not all that interesting.
The visuals are pretty simplistic, and the textures of the different buildings do little to set themselves apart from one another.  But the way the game handles lighting is superb.  The smaller alien bugs will actually run away from you if your flashlight is on.  This is useful knowledge, but know that objects like crates or doors will block your flashlight just like in real life.  The way light bends (or more accurately, doesn’t) around corners is a surprisingly nice touch.  In later levels, you’ll come across invisible enemies that will flicker in the beam of your flashlight, giving an eerie screech as they try to dismember you.
The audio quality is passable, overall.  The voice acting is definitely the low point, as lines are delivered with over-the-top and unconvincing cheesiness.  The soundtrack is this cool hard rock techno you might find in a summer action movie, which fits the theme very well.  Enemy screeches and clanging objects will let you know what is coming once you learn how each enemy behaves.
The biggest issue with this game is that it really wants me to care about the story it is trying to tell, and while I enjoyed it near the end, it was quite diffult to get into.  The subpar voice acting doesn’t really help in that regard, but I enjoyed my time in Shadowgrounds.  The developers did a great job making levels seem just a little different from each other, which gives some uniqueness to each encounter.  In one, you’ll be defending a base full of survivors from waves of attackers, and in another you’ll be negotiating a twisting canyon as aliens climb down and surprise you.
Having said all that, do I recommend Shadowgrounds?  The easiest way I can describe it is that it feels like a poor man’s Halo.  Fun, frentic combat makes up for a lot of the game’s other faults, and playing it on Easy is a decent waste of a Saturday afternoon, but I wouldn’t say you’ll be missing out on much if you skip this game.

I had a lot of fun with it in spite of some weird bugs and the limited level varieties. The story itself is filled with your usual hero tropes, but screws with them in enough ways to be entertaining and charming, and the combat (when it's not giving me unlimited health or some weird thing, from a bug I'd guess) was fun enough to carry me through the experience the 8 or 9 times I needed to get the ideal ending. There's some interface fixes absent that would have made things much smoother, like mapping the sword select to each direction on the dpad for immediate access to your weapon of choice, and leaving the cycling method of sword selection to bumpers. I'm not so fond of when buttons go unused when they could streamline the gameplay, but here's hoping that's something Spearhead will add later. There are also some things I'd love to be able to skip (the "Game changer" paragraph that repeats each time you want to do a new playthrough is unskippable, for example).
I'm actually happy with my time with this game, despite the above complaints. It's goofy and fun, looks nice, and sometimes plays nice too! The upgrade system gave interesting bonuses that had me looking forward to new encounters, and I have to say my favorite part of this game was watching how Reynardo's paths fall apart each time. If the game had a greater enemy variety and more levels to cycle through, I'd probably adore it. As it is, I only greatly enjoyed it, which is awesome because I love greatly enjoying things. Here's hoping Spearhead's next endeavor is more polished, but still unabashedly gleeful.

When I saw this game on the featured list I was like "Eh, it seems to have a nice design, might as well try it out". Turns out nice design is only the beginning of the story.
First of all, of course, what drew me into this game: It's design. It is not groundbreaking by any means, but it is very well executed. You can see that the developers had put a lot of effort to try and make this game pop out, and it does! This makes exploration a necessary part of the game. Sure sometimes it may get grindy and repetitive a bit but if you are like me, you will definitely want to explore and find out as much as you possibly can, if not for the sake of completing the game 100% but for the sake of finding out what kind of interesting ending you may come across next. Sometimes the game even throws curve balls at you that made me just sit there for a minute and then bursting out laughing and calling out the narrator a cheeky git.
As for the combat, this was my first ever hack and slash type game. For me, even if I played with a keyboard the combat seemed to border somewhere between repetitive and oddly satisfying. Sometimes I'd go through a hoard of enemies with the feeling of "I am tired of this" and the next time I'd feel like it is the most satisfying thing in the world. So while not the most amazing part of the game, it is definitely well done.
As an overall game, I can definitely recommend it. A bit of polish here and there and it will be a truely wonderful experience. 8/10

Charts showing times for public transport such as trains, planes or buses are fascinating things wouldn't you say? I mean the sheer complexity of them and the amount of effort and work that goes into their creation is immense. Sure people say that buses never run on time but consider that they have to work out the typical speed of a bus through certain sections of a city, taking into account the usual traffic and roughly how long is needed to load and unload passengers at each stop. They really are a huge technical achievement. So why aren't people more interested in them when they claim that Antichamber is one of the most amazing puzzle games ever despite it being nothing more than an incredibly boring yet technically masterful piece of game design?
This may seem harsh but the fact is that the developer(s) behind Antichamber clearly know their stuff when it comes to the technical side of using the more advanced trickery in level design. And yet while performing all of this wizardry they completely forgot that it was meant to be fun.
Visually it is destinctive only because the frequent use of portals required flat colours or else you could easily notice them. Fair enough. Make technical limitations work for you by building around them. Fine. I can accept that. But then why was it nessersary to makes puzzles such as 'stare at this wall', 'keep running in circles for a minute' and lets not forget those oh so frequently used 'run backwards' puzzles. Antichambers starts off with these being novel ideas but eventually you end up literally in a plain box room with no indications which of these novel ideas are supposed to be used. So you start doing things like running around the walls to see if there is a hidden path that only appears when you're next to it, running backwards towards the door you just came in, walking to see if that triggers something. The list goes on and on.  Puzzle solving isn't about methodically running through every possible trick you know one by one until you get it right, it's supposed to be about being thoughtful or logical.
The fact is that there are some very clever puzzles in there but they are far outnumbered by stupidly vague or frustratingly tedious ones that seem more like the developers showing off their technical skills than trying to create an entertaining experience. There is a multitude of better games than this such as The Room or dare I say Riven or Myst if you want a real test of your memory and logic.

Well.
First things first: it's short, it's part of a trilogy so this is merely chapter one. Kind of irks me that the price for a single chapter is the better part of $25 but I also hope they're going to offer the following chapters as DLC. Otherwise this is a massive cash-grab.
That being said - wow. An amazingly well-constructed world and lore out the wazoo. Grammatical errors and switching from second- and third-person narratives willy-nilly aside, the story was also very well written. My skin crawled and shivered several times during the playthrough.
I had moments where I wanted to throw my keyboard at the game. I wanted to quit, to uninstall it and leave it to rot in my basement where I would keep it until such a time where I had forgotten the injustice it had done to me and I would allow it a glimmer of sunlight once more. But I didn't. I decided it wasn't the game, it was me. I felt like a victim of household abuse. If the companions I had fought so hard to keep alive suddenly died because of a wrong decision by me, then it's my fault. Mine and mine alone. I learned to live with my regrets, learned to cope with them and keep going; by far, the best thing the creators of the game could have done was not have a savegame feature. You live with the consequences of your choices - and more often than not, there's always a second side to the story.
The story ended just as it had begun to make a small portion of sense, though by asking more questions than answering them. I went back to the title screen and was about to hit "Restart" when a message popped up - "If you restart the game, all your previous decisions will be overwritten". I stopped. Yes, I can go back and play the game and know what to expect now, and probably make a lot less of a fool of myself by making better decisions. But then, it wouldn't be the experience it was meant to be. The experience of putting you in a world that is dying, possibly already dead, where your only hope is to survive; to save a few lives on the way is a bonus, but hard decisions will need to be made. Hard decisions that will stick with you, long after you've finished playing the game.
So I didn't restart it, and my ill-conceived decisions are going to sit there until Chapter 2, where I can relive them again. And I will miss some characters dearly, while others I will not bat an eyelid to. This is what a great game is meant to encourage. In a bleak world where the hopelesness and fear seem to be the only constant, where even mountains can be torn asunder, you cling on to the fact that though you may have sacrificed a few men, you survived. And that's all that matters.
Because don't you know, the Gods are dead?

The game is very enjoyable. There is no thinking involved. You simply shoot to kill - with various zombies running around and bosses, once you get to the last round of the game.
The main problem is the microtransactions. The game features 100's of different skins and so forth. Some of these can be unlocked in game, if you can do impossible tasks. The developers say the microtransactions help support future updates - but even the updates are worse than some of the community mods.
I have an extremely fast rig and the game takes 1 - 2 minutes to load up since the recent updates.
The latest summer 2017 update removes the previous skins and adds clowns and pin-heads into the game. This is a total train wreck as the new skins appear in every single level. You can't pick which zombie skins to fight against. Simply seeing 100 of the same skin CLOWN seriously puts me off the game. There should be 10 different skins of the same clown or pin-head. This would help keep the game interesting, rather than extremely dull.
There should be a difficulty that includes at least 300 to 500 zombies - rather than the current cap, that the game features.
If you buy this game then beware of the skins issue. You will get extremely bored of seeing the same NOT SCARY clown 1000 times over. There is not enough different levels and half the community mods will crash or slow the game down to a slug.
The developers need to seriously release an emergency update and allow zombie skins to be selected and add a few more levels into the game or this will be the death knell for Killing Floor 2 in a matter of weeks or months.

Clicking on Quit without saving will *also erase* the save point, so you end up starting over next time you start playing.  This I found when I made a bad purchasing decision and wanted to redo it.
Be *very* careful what you do in this game.  the save point is a useless one-off, and you're either stuck with whatever decision you make, or you're starting over from scratch.  There's no real way to save a game.

In light of the Steam Awards nominations, I felt that it was deserved to redo my ancient review of this game. (and plus I wanted the full level of the badge so deal with it.) Looking back on the nearly 4 years since this game's release and my purchase of it, I can say that this game was well deserved of my nomination in the "Test of Time" category. There are few games that manage to linger in my mind months or even years after I've finished them, and FTL stands as one of those proud few. I can still remember some of my first runs in this game, some of my worst failures, and some of my cluchest victories in rather great detail. Even 4 years later, this game is still used as a benchmark for me in terms of how well I've enjoyed it, no other game has truly surpassed this in terms of, well, anything. Sure there are other games that look better, some games that sound better, that play better, or that have a better story or better etc, etc. However I have failed to find a game that surpasses this one in all those terms. The story may be simplistic but it so easy to get lost in, thinking about what happens on what happens beyond the bulkheads of your ship. The gameplay is simple to learn and  difficult to master, extremly punishing and forcing you to restart again and again to progress past the first few sectors but once you do it feels so rewarding. The RNG in this game is prevelant yet still a great deal of skill is required, and in most cases RNG can be defeated by skill. The art style is clean and has aged well over its life span, and the soundtrack is probably one of my favorite soundtracks from any game. Turning towards the community, FTL is still going strong. Many talented people have come together to make art, music, and mods for this game that make me say that FTL has one of the best fanbases of any game I have ever seen. The modding community alone is probably one of the best in the entire community of games, in my mind it is only surpassed by KSP and X-Com's modding communities.
Sorry for that wall of text, here's the TLDR:
This game is well worthy for the Test of Time reward because it is one of the few games that you can go back and play years (in this case 4) after release and still get that same feeling of joy, of sadness, of frustration, of tension, of accomplishment that you got on day 1 of release. And with the ammount of time I have spent, the ammount of time it has been, the $10 for the game is completly worth what this game is.

TLDR: if you're a fan of these diablo-esque games, than you'll love this one to bits. If you've loved Titan Quest Immortal Throne, then you'll love it even more. If you loved the latter game because of the ancient mythology, well that's too bad.
Grim Dawn, like its predecessor TQ, gives you more freedom in creating toons than in most other ARPG's. 'Building a Character' seems a much more appropriate description for its skill system than normal. For instance, there are no class specific items and gear. All loot has requirements based on attribute points and level instead of class. You can quite literally build stupid characters; soldiers wielding crossbows that have mostly debuff skills etc. The enemies you encounter will let you know if it's a viable strategy (i.e. if you get r4ped or not).
Some novel ideas that are being implemented are factions and (in relationship to TQ) an expanded crafting system. Factions allow for a more convincing interaction with the many npc's and enemies in the world of Cairn. And on top of building relics (powerful buffing gear that create a challenge to come by and craft) you can find blueprints for all kinds of cool gear. Furthermore you have too find these characters, like more merchants and a blacksmith in the world and transport them back to your starting town Devil's Crossing.
The world itself is dark and gloomy (grim) and feature the usual zombie-like enemies one comes to expect from games these days. But over time in early access all kinds of neat villains and monsters have been added, like orcish hordes, insects, enemy humans and so on and so on... you get the picture: loads of fresh meat to slaughter :)
And slaughtering comes in busloads of weapons and skills with cool shiny effects and lights :D YEEEEE!
I strongly recommend playing veteran if you're experienced in other such games, as it might be too easy on normal, veteran mode for me seems to work quite well however.

Started out playing Ys Origin when it came out on steam. I loved it's combat and music. Amazing game. Instantly bought Oath in Felghana (also a great Ys game) and Chronicles+ the moment they hit steam.
Althought the combat is different with its bumper cars, it's still great. It's not a combat system that you would find in modern games today, which is kinda sad, since it works extremely well in a 2D, top-down view game.
It's a fairly simple system. If you hit an enemy, you damage the enemy. If you hit it face-on, you'll take damage, but hit it in the side or from an angle and you can easily melt every normal enemy in the game without ever taking damage.
It's fast, fun and fluid. The controls are responsive and the hit detection is very good.

I'm not the world's biggest South Park fan. I've seen a few shows and quite like them, but I have never bothered to watch a complete season. When the Stick of Truth (tSoT) was released, I was amused by the trailers and the decent reviews made me interested in the game. Paying full price for it did not seem an option to me; I expected this to be fun but short-lived. 26 hours of amusing gameplay later, I am finally looking at the end-game credits. Not bad at all!
Obviously, an appreciation of the typical South Park humour is a prerequisite for playing this game; that just cannot be stressed enough. But hey, you weren't looking at these reviews if you disliked the show.
Visually, this game is true to the cartoon. Do not expect fancy 3d FPS-like graphics. This has it's advantages, since the game runs smoothly on any current Intell laptop CPU on a full HD resolution, without the need for extra GPU power.
The audio is wonderful. All original voices are being used for the characters and the music ads to the atmosphere and the storyline. It's perhaps just a little repetitive.
For an RPG, the actual gameplay is a bit simplistic. A lot of puzzles can be solved by using specific abilities on items in the environment, but they never get very complicated. The combat system is easy to learn and on the 'normal' difficulty setting, enemies wont often be a real challenge.
A small sidenote: the Steam Controller generally works well in this game, but it has one big flaw. The game is more or less mapped tot Xbox controllers, and it expects a R-stick to be present during some sequences (especially late-game farting. Yeah, don't ask... :P). Without the R-stick, these sequences are nigh impossible, and I used a workaround (unplugging the controller and using keyboard commands) to circumvent this. Not a really big problem, but annoying enough.
All in all, I really enjoyed this game and it makes me curious for the next installment (although I'm sure I like the D&D story better than the Super Hero one). Since tSoT is on sale (permanently?), now would be a great time to add it to your collection!

I was addicted to Divinity II, so after I heard they're making Divinity: Original Sin I started to obserwe how work on that game is progressing. When I heard about relase date- bought it ASAP ! I'm really picky about games, most of them lay on my shelf or in Steam library unplayed- but Divinity Original Sin took my hearth and social life away. About 60 hours of gameplay (played some time offline) full of great combat, funny dialogues and thinking about my next move- that was game I - and most of oldschool gamers- needed to revive from mindless smashing Left Mouse Button.
Game offers you at last 40 hours of gameplay (up to 100 hours if you're in mood to do all side quests and explore every corner of that big world), a lot of ways to customize your own heroes (Wanna be mage? Sure, make one. Warrior? Ok. Rogue with great sneaking skills and 2h sword that can cast fireballs and summon skeletons? Go for it!) and great visuals linked with big explorable world. Tons of skills that can make powerful combos (like freezing water, burning up oil or electryfing blood around enemy) and fights that will make you stop for a moment and think "What's best way to kill that Zombies without getting my tank killed?". You can hire 2 companions (will be more in upcoming major patch) that have their own personality, goals in life and history behind them. And if you prefer silent killing machine- you can always hire some Henchmans ;)
Would I recommend that game for someone? Certainly YES! Worth every cent you spend on it.

I remember when in 2008 was talk in gaming magazines speak about a game that is revolutionary. It was called Mirror's Edge. The parkour subculture was on it's peak around that time, and I was interested of that so called revolution of games, and never had time to get it and play. 6 years affter it's release my friend got it in a bundle,and since we shared games, I got it too. I wanted to give it a try, so I instaled it. To be honest I'm preaty disapointed in it. All the game offered was the same thing that Avalanche Software and Ubisoft offered 2003 with the game called  Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. It's basicly same game as M. Edge only without epic enemies, but enemies wearing blue and a badge.
First off, The story is simple: "some dude killed other dude and framed it on your sister and you have to prove her inocens." (by beating and ocasionally killing police officers). The game didn't offer anything special with story. You are an underdog who take on whole world.
The game is liniar. Your objective is to go from one place to another jumping,climbing or sliding across rooftops (mostly) with ocasional brawl. You are not given an open world to get to you objective, but you have to follow the set path made by developers.
Graphics. Well you can't rate it. The whole game consist of buildings which are all white-greyish with windows. NPC's are done so-so (low for 2009 but still). There are ocasional cut scenes who looks like an amateur hobbies made in god knows what softwear. The AI looks broken too. Police officers can't shoot you if you stand in front of them about a meter. It's just pure luck for them to actually hit you.  There are autosave checkpoints which are set on most random places (not counting the half map checkpoint e.g.: elevators and stuff like that).
All in all the hype the PR from the firms who made the game is not justifed, and the price 9.99 might be overpriced. I would give no more than 4-5$ for it.

After all those years this game is still perfect. Gameplay is over the top. Clever physics puzzles are really good for showing off the Source engine. Atmosphere is unreal and the fact that there are no cutscenes makes the game more immersive. Story is also a strong point for Sci-Fi fans like me. I played the game for the first time in 2015 and I was amazed how good it was. I usually can't stand games older than around 7 years, because of advancements in the game design and technology today. But for Half-Life 2, I haven't felt the "oldness" in the slightest. Sure, the graphics are nothing like the newest games but it doesn't look ugly either especially for a game that is not demanding at all. Because of that you can crank up the graphics options all the way and the free Half-Life 2: Update mod is definitely a welcome advancement in the graphics side. I was shocked to see the textures holding up just fine with even 4K resolutions. This game is definitely a PC gaming masterpiece and for any person who loves FPS games, puzzles and Sci-Fi, Half-Life 2 is a must play.

I played unconventionally nonchalantly until things finally clicked for me. Then the game becomes as expected, more intense, more in tune with what made the other two seasons work so well.
Michonne is decidedly the strongest Telltale lead from the Walking Dead miniseries so far, with a much more action-oriented nature than Lee or Clementine. Perhaps not so surprisingly, the game consequently contains many more QTE sequences, which while beautifully integrated here again were never really the series' main strengths. You will slice, stab and decapitate walkers with your machete, and spend less time exploring portions of the world discreetly.
This shorter three-episode story offers a refreshingly different style. The intro sequence is particularly polished. Hallucinations and flashbacks add a nice surreal touch to the formula, though they were somewhat infrequent.
I am not a fan of the comics or TV series, or zombies in general, but I absolutely love the first two Telltale seasons, and have great respect for their overall body of work. The good thing about TWD's stories is they've never been about the walkers. They're all about human relationships when facing extreme adversity, loss and tragedy, hardships endured and inflicted upon each other, what it means to be alive... and this is why the writing in TWD shines.
Your choices ultimately may not completely alter the story but they give it enough personality and substance to make it gratifying and vivid. The only minor downside is that episodes surprisingly don't end in gut-wrenching cliffhangers, unlike most Telltale episodes. There are also recurring themes with many situations almost too similar to some events of Season 2.
Technically, the game runs so much better on PC and in much higher resolution than on the X360, which almost made me regret not playing all my other Telltale games here instead. Be aware it is relatively short if that bothers you, though to me it was just perfect (just under 4 hours).
Telltale has got me hooked to their version of The Walking Dead. I'm definitely looking forward to the next chapter! Though since I like to play all episodes in binge sessions once they've all been released, usually one per evening, it'll be a while before I get my hand at this excellent series again.

This is definitely the best RPG I've played in years. The game has very little hand-holding and it makes you have to figure out stuff on your own. Quests aren't simply little exclamation points over character's heads, you don't have to necessarily run back to town to "turn in" a quest, you're not given a little point on a map for you to follow. This game wants you to become invested in its world, and invested I have definitely become. In most RPG's I've played recently I know the names of like, maybe 2 NPCs, because if I need to go to them for some reason the game will say, in capital letters, "GO HERE AND TURN IN THIS SPECIFIC QUEST TO PROCEED." This game doesn't do that, it's not its style.
The first main quest in the game is essentially a murder mystery, which might not sound too amazing on paper, but it's a fantastic starting point in the game because it forces you to become invested in the world by talking to all of the NPC's, learning their relationships, collecting clues, etc... Your journal in the game recounts what you've learned, but it doesn't make any of the deductions for your, it's up to you, the player, to deduce who you think is the murderer.
This type of quest design pervades throughout the game. If you play this game you may become a little frustrated at first because of how used current gamers are to having their hands held, but if you persevere (and please don't use a wiki) then you will find one of the most immersive and enjoyable games you'll ever play.

I think the issue with most people that bought this game is that they expected something similar to TWD 1 or TWD 2 and they didn’t take into consideration that we are talking about Michonne here. The cinematic feel the game has goes toe to toe with the main character, after all, as seen in the comics and series, Michonne is a killer, lighting fast that has become a new age samurai if you want to put it like that. Her life is full of death and tragedy, having lost countless people during her travels and I think this mini-series was focused on that. I enjoyed the game, though it did feel too quick, they could have added perhaps one or two more episodes, I wouldn’t have minded. Now, while I understand some people might complain that most of their choices don’t matter, I’ll add that the important ones do matter and the minor ones, as seen with previous TWD make little impact, perhaps change the way some conversations go, additionally, people are forgetting that the length of those games was at least double and hence, it made more sense for some things. All in all, I do recommend to buy and play the game and for those still not sure, then just wait for a discount.

Very very fun if you enjoy mostly linear turn based CRPGs with quirky takes on humour.
This game makes no apologies for what it is, if you are hoping it'd be like Diablo or something more action oriented then prepare to be disappointed since you can go for several hours at a time with no combat at all. There are no quest markers, the game expects you to pay attention to text and your surroundings and the freedom to build your character how you want means the freedom to ♥♥♥♥ it up as well.
The game is pretty damn long at around 50 hours for the main campaign, the map while not especially large in any one zone is none the less very detailed and well made. There is also a fully featured editor to allow you to create custom campaigns.
Combat I think benefits from being turn based and allows much more structure and to better allow you to take advantage of environmental effects and the game's surprisingly deep magic system. Most spells will leave effects on the battlefield and can thus combo with other spells and effects to turn the tide in your favour. Oil and poison ignites, water and blood can be electrified, ice will slip people up etc.
The game is not without it's flaws of course, loading times between zones is incredibly slow and the out of combat movement speed and lack of a rest feature in the field can make the pacing slow to a crawl when you need to backtrack. The balance is also all over the place with some skills being amazing and others worthless plus some spells are bugged and lack some of their functionality.
Difficulty wise the game starts off quite hard but soon tapers to being incredibly easy even on the hardest setting due to how overpowered you can become. Difficulty too only affects relative health and damage value and the AI never gets any smarter, this becomes incredibly apparent if you start abusing summons.
Plus a majority of spells you learn in the game are sold from vendors who sadly have a mostly randomized inventory. This can mean basic low level spells can be absent from your game for an incredibly long time because NPCs in the starting area have filled their inventories with stuff several levels above you.
These are minor gripes however and overall this game is a shining example that not all kickstarter/Early access games are unfinished scams.

It's quite difficult to properly rate this game. As someone who hasn't read the comics but rather watched the TV series, I probably didn't appreciate it as much.
First off, each episode is roughly an hour long. While I get that it's a miniseries, it still feels like it's way too short for the price you're paying. Telltale does however deliver with stunning graphics and an amazing soundtrack and VA.
Honestly I think I felt annoyed more than anything while I was playing. Half of the time you ended up with Michonne having hallucinations/flashbacks and seeing her daughters right in the middle of what should be important events. It took away from the events that were happening in real time. Maybe if I read the comics I would understand more but for someone who didn't, everything felt so vague in this series. It's like they put more time into the action scenes than the story itself. Seeing Michonne in action is cool and all but I'd prefer learning more about her. The story was decent but it wasn't engaging in any sort of way. When I started playing it seemed interesting but soon after I found myself wondering when it would be over.
The characters introduced have no real character development for you to get invested in them. Any interaction you have with 90% of the characters lasts only for a moment and then it's over. At no point would you feel any kind of attachment to them so whether or not they die doesn't really matter to you. Overall the characters felt bland.
Also, the whole 'choice's matter' really doesn't apply to this game. At least with the other two series your actions and dialog affect your gameplay to a degree. In this series it doesn't matter if Pete or Sam will remember what you said. Literally nothing will happen anyway. It also irked me to know that sometimes when you decide not to make a choice, the game will make it for you. Felt like a repeat of Beyond: Two Souls. Your only real big choice is during the finale. Live or stay with your daughters in your hallucination and I'm assuming die. Let's be real, for a big choice, it's practically already made for you. The dialog choices you get are questionable. As I said I never read the comics so I don't know what she was like before but it doesn't feel like anything Michonne would say.
In terms of recommending the game, I'd say no. It's an okay game but not for $15. You're better off saving that money for something else.  It's a short game so if you get the chance to play it then by all means go for it but just be ready for a bit of disappointment.

So you probably were like me and keep coming back to this games store page thinking, "Man I would like a really good snowboarding/skiing/wingsuit game for PC! But this game is only "Mostly Positive"..."
Fear not child, for I have good news.  Steep is a very good game.
I LOVED the SSX games.  Have probably a collective 400+hrs in that series. If you are looking for a game like SSX, you will get some of the things you want and some things you don't want out of Steep.  Before I say what these are I just want to say that I realize as I played Steep, that even though I wanted a game like SSX at first, I realized what I really just wanted was a snowboarding game that feels good in it's controls and is confident in what it's trying to be.  Steep is both of those things.
You will like:
+ The CONTROLS feel good.  They are tight and responsive.  You feel in control of what you are trying to do.
+ The GRAPHICS are very nice.  Very big and varied enviriontments lush with detail. Lighting is awesome.  Animations are great.  Snow looks better than any other game i've played. Overall awesome atmosphere.
+  The SOUNDS are very good. Great soundtrack.  Nothing too specific to mention.  The sounds just do their job well.
+ The REPLAYABILITY.  Some people may not be able to sit and play hours worth of this game in a single session (I can because I like exploring).  But regardless, this game has A LOT of challenges to complete.  You wont be done anytime soon.
You may not like:
-+ The CHARACTERS.  I feel some of the characters and their voices can be a bit dramatic and cringy.  Others are much better at not sounding so ridiculous.  However, some people may like this.  I'm indifferent about it.
-+ The PHYSICS.  On the whole, I like them.  However I think that everyone who has played this game can agree that sometime your skiis or snowboard just act kinda "funny" when going over a slope or bumping into something. sometimes you remain connected on the ground when it feels like you should've left the ground for a second or two.  Sometimes you just turn to tight or lose momentum when it feels like you shouldnt have.  The thing to remember here is that these instances are rare on the whole and the positive physics experiences outweigh the bad by a considerable amount.
-+ The PRICE.  A lot of people keep mentioning the price of this game being too expensive.  I do not agree.  I bought this at $60 and I definitely feel like i've gotten my moneys worth.  However, I seem to be in the minority on that one.  Keep in mind though that if you love snowboarding and skiing games, and love to explore, I dont think the price will bother you.
Overall, If you are looking for a great extreme snow sports title I just dont think you can go wrong with Steep.

The fact that I've amassed 30 hours on this since its most recent sale a week ago should suggest just how much I'm enjoying this game. While at times it has seemed to drag on (particularly with some of the fetch quests, but what game with fetch quests DOESN'T drag at those points really), I have thoroughly enjoyed the experience of what is effectively D'n'D in video game form.
I think the one thing I've enjoyed the most about this experience though is that you control exactly how easy/hard the game is for more or less the duration of the game. For about 90% of the battles,
decide just how many monsters you face, whether you make it easy on yourself and just take on one small bat for minimal but easy exp, or whether you take on a horde of Invaders for major risk/reward exp/gold - a concept which I thought is pretty damn neat. Along with being able to change your party at any point in the game (with more classes to unlock as you playthrough), you can really make the experience your own every time and try all sorts of weird and wonderful combinations.
Fun addicting title with neat graphics and a good soundtrack that I'm sure I'll be playing for many many moons to come.

You really have to think of Stories like a hack-and-slash Dyscourse instead of a choose-your-own-adventure Bastion.
The concept behind the game is that you play through it multiple times, making different choices and taking different paths each time to see how the story unfolds differently. Each playthrough lasts about 30 minutes to an hour, visiting the same handful of locations each time. Getting to the best ending takes about 5 hours, and getting all the endings would probably take about 20+ hours. (Edit: 19.1 hours!)
The hack-and-slash and RPG gameplay elements are simple, which with any other game would probably be a mark against it. However, with Stories, I'm really interested in finding out what happens next rather than getting bogged down in combat. So being able to quickly max everything out and blow through combat easily is actually a plus. Once you get the best ending, you're pretty much able to walk through the levels without too much distraction.
I'm really enjoying Stories a lot, but for its narrative, characters, and art style more than its gameplay. If you like games like Dyscourse or The Stanley Parable, then I think you'll enjoy it. If you're looking for something like Bastion or Hyper Light Drifter, then you're going to be disappointed.
Oh, and its cast is entirely talking animal people, so bonus points from me for that! >^_^<

The Banner Saga is a compelling tale following close knit to Norse Mythology. The Viking-esque feel is excellent for the type of story. The cause and effect style to the story really makes the player (myself) think long and hard about choices before rapidly doing things. The game is quite... real, it doesn't beat around the bush with the story. It really feels like the end of the world. When you have maybe 350 clansmen, 140 warriors and 60 varl in your caravan, with limited supplies running, you're forced to be conservative at most times and on occasion, be the polar opposite, offensive and assertive, to gain supplies from meek farmers. The characters really interact with your decisions too and tug on how you want to convey yourself as a character to those close to you. All in all an excellent game. 10/10 Gameplay, 11/10 story and I absolutely love the 'cause and effect'-esque mechanics. Nothing like having to really think before performing actions. The replay value is excellent as well, to see how you could play differently to get different reactions from characters, the caravans, or to earn new heroes from placing yourself in more "immediate" danger.

It’s not often that Kickstarted games bear fruit. Up to now, anyway. The Banner Saga is an underdog Kickstarter story that has finally come to fruition. So was it worth the long wait and does it make good on its promises? Or does it instead fall flat on its metaphorical face? Well, luckily for you it’s sort of my job to find out. Or does that actually make me the lucky one? Either way, I’m going to review this thing and see what kind of game we’ve ended up with.
For starters, the multiplayer component of the game was released as a standalone free-to-play title some months back, while the single player campaign was kept under development until now. So we’ll be doing this in a couple of sections. We’ll start by briefly covering the multiplayer aspect. It’s titled The Banner Saga: Factions, and is free-to-play for anyone who might wish to try it. Like any other game in the free-to-play field, it contains micro-transactions for in-game perks and advantages. These include, but are not limited to, experience bonuses, additional space for units, and increases to battle rewards. They aren’t exactly pay to win, but they do stack the cards just a little bit in favor of the players who spend money. The gameplay here is all battles; there is no story of any kind, no management, and no depth outside of the battles themselves. The combat, however, is identical to the single player portion of the game. Each unit acts in turn on an isometric grid-based battlefield. Units take turns whacking at each other to lower health and armor values until one team remains standing. It’s fairly bare-bones, but it’s free so who can complain?

Now on to the meat of things! The Banner Saga! The game is a story-driven experience that changes based on your choices and your actions. There are consequences to every decision, and the frequent auto-saving means there is no going back and trying to get a better outcome. Characters will die. You will do horrible things, perhaps unwillingly, but sometimes it’s what must be done. The Banner Saga may have the art style of a Disney film, but it has the atmosphere and story of Game of Thrones. Death is a part of life in The Banner Saga, and you can’t easily rewind and try again.

Think of it as a kind of reimagining of the fantastic classic game, The Oregon Trail. It is up to you to manage a caravan of villagers, warriors and refugees as they automatically make their way across a vast frozen landscape. The journey takes place automatically, whether you like it or not. Along the way, random events, problems, conflicts and what have you pop up and you are required to deal with them. This can involve a choice as seemingly simple as allowing a new group of warriors join your band, or it can be as brutal as deciding whether or not to leave a wounded man behind to die, or use extra rations, slow down your travel, and put your entire caravan at risk. Either way, there will be consequences. Some are good, some not so much. For example, if you allow the band of warriors to join you and beef up your security, it may very well backfire when they rob you blind in the night, slaughtering some villagers and making off with a good deal of your supplies. On the flipside, if you choose to leave them behind you may find your caravan under attack by a band of brigands containing those warriors. It is a brutal landscape, and it will not apologize for it.
Battles play out in the same way as the multiplayer component. There are a couple of new classes, but the review stands above. The notable difference comes in how the game handles defeat. Losing a battle does not mean a game over. In fact the game picks you up and continues along the way, with a few changes in place. Beloved characters may die, a detour may be forced, or cities may be destroyed. There will be a consequence you must suffer for the loss but it won’t be game ending. It’s an interesting take on defeat, and one more games can take an example from. It fits into the overall motif of all choices and actions having consequences. I keep bringing it up because the game will not let you forget this feature, and you should really be ready for it. Drill that fact into your consciousness and be prepared for it to slap you on the forehead with a big floppy piece of raw, gooey sadness.

On top of the solid gameplay and story, the art style and music of the game are a fantastic achievement of their own. The soundtrack evokes all the right emotions at the right ties, from sweeping orchestral pieces on the gorgeous mountain heavy world map down to slow heart-wrenching keys when a difficult decision has been made. The battle music is the exception, being just a little bothersome in how often it repeats itself. This shouldn’t detract from the overall enjoyment of the musical package, however. The art style is simply gorgeous. It’s entirely hand-drawn and plays a stark, blinding contrast to the tone of the story. It’s light and smooth, very much in the vein of a Disney style. Each and every character and location is painstakingly hand-drawn piece by piece, and that devotion shows in every face, every new town. It also makes a fantastic backdrop for the amount of heartbreak and violence that actually takes place over the course of the game. It’s as though Disney animated a season of Game of Thrones.
The Banner Saga is easily worth your time if you’re even moderately interested. If you enjoy it, a second play-through is recommended to see just how vastly different things can turn out. For the $15 price tag, it’s pretty hard to go wrong.

I spent a lot of time playing Diablo 2 when I was younger, and spent even more time playing Diablo 3. I was a fan of the game, even before it got fixed with ROS. I ran every class in Torchlight and Torchlight 2. Point being; I ♥♥♥♥ing love my dungeon crawling, and I love my loot fests.
I've followed Grim Dawn's progress since the Kickstarter. I didn't have a job at the time, so I never invested and I've held off on purchasing in Early Access because I didn't want to get a bad impression of the game. I finally cracked and bought into it.
The game starts in a basic hub city, and with a basic "go kill this weak boss" quest. After that, the world opens up. You are indroduced to factions that you may work for and gain reputation that gives you access to faction stores (not unlike WoW). Some areas you'll never see in the main quest line, and the game really rewards exploration with lore and loot.
And the class system is divine. It can be a little overwhelming at first (don't expect to keep your first character). The game has a wide selection of classes that all play differently. They all fit a stereotype (Soldier = Warrior, Nightblade = Rouge, etc.) but at level 10 you get to select a second class. Some of the classes don't blend very well, such as a Soldier/Nightblade build. Many skills require certain weapons in each class, and they can conflict with each other. There's so much good to say about Ys I and II Chronicles. First of all, it's two games in one, and both games are of stellar quality. Excellent sprite and artwork, an absolutely stunning soundtrack, endearing characters, especially that of the main character, Adol, and a surprisingly efficient and fast-paced combat system.
When a game features combat but 'not' an attack button, that would give any gamer pause. On paper, that would seem clunky at best and unintuitive at worst. However, the "bump system" implimented renders the need for an attack button practically obsolete, to the point where I actually question the very existence of what is otherwise an unquestionably essential feature in an action game.
What the bump system does is automatically calculate your attack, your defence, and your receiving of damage upon colliding with any enemy, and the chances of how that collision will play out change depending on which angle you bump into the enemy. If you hit them from behind or from an angle, typically your mow through them like a lawn mower. If you get bumped into yourself, you'll take damage, and if you collide face first with an enemy, you and the enemy will either take damage or block, and both will be knocked away.
Once you master the bump system, you'll literally mow down enemies at a much faster pace than you would a Zelda title, which this game resembles aesthetically. In fact, the Ys series is, in many ways, the Sonic to Zelda's Mario. Where Zelda is a more balanced and safe experience, where you can always expect a blend of puzzles and combat, Ys games, typically, are faster, flashier, and more experimental than any Zelda title. While this has had mixed to poor resulte for Sonic, I've yet to play an Ys game I didn't like.
If you're looking to get into the Ys series, this is definitely the game(s) to do it with.

Recently, after having decided to replay Mirror's Edge I remembered why it was that the experience was so underwhelming. And it's not because of the three dimensional parkour, that's exactly what made me want to replay Mirror's Edge. The parkour mechanic is simple and well developed. You use one button to move up and another button to move down and overall controlling your character is very enjoyable.
The problem is that Mirror's Edge doesn't seem to understand that very well.
A platformer at its core is a game about execution. You want to go fast. You want to press all the right buttons in the right order and get to the end of the level. It's comparable to a rhythm game like Rock Band or Osu, where the main engagement is tied to a sense of performance. And it doesn't matter if you are literally given the instructions on a scrolling track because it's your execution that is fun. And the execution really is fun, but a lot hangs on the level designs and the levels in Mirror's Edge are continuously ambiguous.
In a platformer it must be easy to understand the flow of space. Just moving from two dimensional space to three dimensions already makes this a daunting task. In a three dimensional space we cannot usually see all the sides of an object at once, thus simply viewing a level from a different position or angle can change the 'problem' the player is presented with, and it is very important to either give the player visual cues or have atrociously good level design to compensate for this.
But time and time again Mirror’s Edge will throw you into a claustrophobic corridor where the exit is a door you can't see unless you stop and turn around, or a construction site the game itself labels labyrinthic. You will be faced with an environment where the path to the end goal is unclear and you have to keep moving or be shot and have to reload, breaking the tension and essentially making you feel stupid.
And that is the second challenge that faces Mirror’s Edge. It is imperative to have very low repetition times for failures. And not just death from a fall or a gunshot, but also from something as simple as not seeing a jump, or running into a dead end. When you miss a note in Guitar Hero you do not have to stop the song, track back five seconds and play it over again. It would feel strange and completely break the immersion. But  that is exactly what happens in a platformer if you smack into a wall and have to walk back to the right distance to try the jump again. Again, this depends a lot on the level design. The advantage of a more open world might be that you can have the player take any path and eventually reach the goal, but building a truly open world is very expensive, hard to mesh with a linear story, and ultimately much more difficult to avoid the problems of three dimensional platforming than having a more linear level design.
These problems are only even more compounded in the combat mechanics of the game. It is indicated to you from the start that you should always run from a fight if you can, and also very clearly established that it takes Faith three to four hits to disable a guard. It also requires you to stand still, which again, goes against one of the main strengths of the game’s mechanics, and the core feature of a platformer. But there are multiple occasions where you are forced into a fight. Others where you have to navigate a very unclear space to evade the attackers. And still another place where your entire continuation of the game rests on what is basically a quick time event.
It is not that I think the combat shouldn’t have been a part of the game, it too feels fun in small doses, but the game’s mechanics certainly make it feel like a last resort, and yet more often than not you are fighting and not running.
Overall Mirror’s Edge isn’t a bad game. It has lots of good mechanics and a beautiful minimalistic aesthetic that creates an interesting feel for the space you have to run around in, but it’s a game that feels frustrating and could have been vastly improved with some more linear level design choices.

TellTales The Walking Dead Michonne is another decent interactive story from TellTales that offers a look into an unkown period of time in Michonne's story from the comics. In the comics Michonne is torn between finally being happy in life and the memories of her pre-apocolyptic life that she lost so much including her child. Not feeling right about living happily ever after when she couldn't protect those who she loved at the start of the outbreak she sheds all that is making her happy and leaves the comforts of Rick and his group. The next time we see Michonne in the comics is when she returns on a boat after a voyage with some new friends and this story shows what happened during her trip and why she than feels returning to the group and happy life is something that she can do.
Pros
-Yet another great plot from TellTales and it even fits fairly well with the story that the comics told
-Zombies and one of the most beloved Walking Dead characters
-Simple controls make it easy for anyone to pick up and play
Cons
-Short, each episode can be beat in an hour or two
-The ending could have been better and I think that it may have been better if it showed the moment she left the group in the comics and ended with showing her return to the group as seen in the comics. This could have provided an oppertunity to include more montages and also made the game fit perfectly with the comic
Overall
If you read The Walking Dead comics you'll probably love this as it fills in a blank of the comics, if you enjoy the show you'll likely enjoy this because it's basiclly an interactive cartoon, if you don't follow the franchise but enjoy decent stories you may like this, but if you're looking a button mashing styled fighting game you may not like this since it isn't overly interactive. Me personally, outside of the length of the game and the ending enjoyed it though.

A classic that retains much of its charm, but also is bogged down with antiquated mechanics.
The + edition is far superior to the original graphically and really helps the game get over some of its hurdles.
This game is not for everyone.
The Ys series are ARPGs with very minimal progression elements.  You wont be sifting through tons of loot, and you wont be spending stats or making builds.  You will instead be engaging in lots and lots of combat, which is the games biggest flaw. The fights in this game are very rudimentary, and they happen to the point of ad nasuem.  Sadly the progression elements render any kind of strategy null, as you'll either be far beyond any enemy in power, or unable to take two hits from them.
I may be ragging on the game a bit here, but Ys 1 & 2 are actually good games. The music is pretty decent, the visuals, especially the updated ones, are pleasant and harken back to high fantasy from the 80s/90s.  The world and environment really hammer the fantasy atmosphere home.
The story and characters arent all that intriguing, but that is owning, again, to the games dated nature.  The narrative here is nothing new, but it isnt annoying.  Faint praise, I know
Honestly, I do recommend this game, but cautiously.  If you enjoyed a lot of old high fantasy material, or you played some of the more recent games, give the game a go.  It may surprise you. If you instead play many RPGs or ARPGs of today's modern game designs you may find the barebones systems and story a bit too lackluster to get into.

A package of both the original Ys games in one remastered edition. It actually contains both the Chronicles (2001) and Complete (2009) editions, including updated visuals and soundtracks.
The Ys games are known for not dilly-dallying around and is a fast paced action game with light RPG elements. You run around bumping into enemies, leveling up, earning gold and buying better equipment.
The first game is not as good as the sequel, but is a solid introduction to the series nontheless. The story is that some ancient evil power thing is causing monsters to roam havoc in Ys and Esteria. One day Adol falls out of the sky and lands in this very land, becoming the protagonist and saviour of the land.
Both games features a bump system where you basically walk into enemies to take them out. The first game requires you to hit enemies off center to take them out without taking damage and this is further expanded upon in the sequel where you also can bump successfully diagonally. This makes the battles way easier, ensuring you're staying alive longer.
While the first Ys I is a bit easing on the mechanics, it does feature harder bosses than the sequel. It's around 6-7 hours in length, while Ys II Vanished the Final Chapter is around double the length, at around 12-14 hours. It is by far the superior of the two, featuring a much bigger world and alot more items to procure.
Speaking of items, both games requires you to do A-LOT of backtracking and won't hold your hand in telling you where all of them are. These are the type of games that enforces you to explore, run around and figuring it all out for yourself. If you're not using a guide, expect to get stuck some times as it is not always clear what to do next. Both games also features some highly missable (and some VERY doubious) achievements as well, like shoving a girl and a boy up in a corner to "measure" them. The game does feature plenty of humor too, though and like its tongue-in-cheek moments from time to time.
For the price you're getting a decent pack of entertainment here. Even better if you get it on sale (which happens pretty often). The story may not be very inspiring, but the soundtrack is stellar. Falcom is known for always composing great soundtrack for their games and this is no exception.
Rating:
Ys I: 5.5/10
Ys II Vanished The Final Chapter: 9/10

I've given myself pretty ample time to mess around with Steep. If you like the nostalgia of games like SSX or the Amped series, mixed in with the heavy, realistic-focused feel of the Skate series, this is a highly recommended title.
In 9 hours of playtime, I feel like I've only scratched the surface of the gameplay even though I've been playing challenges and mountain stories non-stop. The mechanics are smooth, doing tricks is fun, the scenery and snow deformation are beautiful, and the microtransactions, while present, are pointless because of how easy it is to get in-game currency through challenges to buy cosmetics (which is all the currency is for).
I only have a few gripes, which are the following:
-Pressing the button to try a challenge again will sometimes put you back in the same place but about a foot backward, causing you to go down the OTHER side of a hill if it's angled on the backside.
-While I have pretty great internet, the always-on DRM is worrying just because it's there. There is also no way to turn off multiplayer, and as such, performance hits can sometimes occur when encountering players because it has to track their playermodel among an already taxing scenery engine.
-The G-Force system, while providing a more realistic experience, can sometimes be a nuisance; even if you land a trick at the exact angle of the mountain facing the perfect angle, you can lose a substantial chunk of health even off a small jump. Overall, I think that mechanic needs some tweaking.
-The only things to do are free-roam around and do challenges. They are plentiful and there are tens of hours of content to be enjoyed, however, I would have liked to see a career mode or something similar with even a light storyline or something else to do that gave the game a more complete feel.

TL;DR: A fun game that missed out on the potential for greatness, buy it on sale for $10 or less.
Full Review:
Stories: The Paths of Destiny puts you in control of a daring mercenary/rebel/pirate? fox as he tries to defeat an empire and save the rebellion. You fail. Then you try again, branching choose your own adventure style, til you find the 'True Ending' save the empire, get the girl, et al.

Basic gameplay works well, you wander through levels fighting enemies, there are multiple paths through most levels unlocked by different swords you can craft, but more on that later.
Combat is fun and fluid though with certain upgrades (Shieldripper gem I'm looking at you) becomes too simple. When you come to enemies on your path you get locked in arena style until you defeat them, after defeating them you're given a score (and associated xp) based on style and whether you got hit or not. The combat is rythmic attack-attack-counter-attack-throw-etc. The timing is not so exacting to make it impossible though getting perfect rounds with great style or more is appropriately difficult.
Skill Tree: As you gain xp you gain levels and skill points to spend on a wide array of useful upgrades, relatively standard but the upgrades seem well thought out and work quite well.
Crafting: This is the place where I feel the most potential was missed. There are four swords and several gems to be crafted , found and upgraded. Early in the game I found the desire to upgrade driving my exploration within each level unfortunately before I finished my third 'story' (it takes a minimum of five to get the 'True Ending') I had found and upgraded everything possible. A more in depth crafting system would have significantly driven up replay value.
Narration: This one will probably depend on the person. I found it to be generally humorous, though the inability to skip certain cutscenes (especially the n-th time youve seen it) is a real flaw.
Puzzles: There in name only, the puzzles are so simple that they shouldn't really count as puzzles.
Underused concepts:
The hookshot, used for navigation. I would have loved to see some challenge maps or sections of the real game where you're not just hooking between stationary platforms.
The floating eyeballs, again they're interesting but when you run into them it's too easy to get by. Challenge maps or just more difficult encounters would be grand.
Crafting as discussed above.
In short this game would benefit greatly from some reasons to keep playing after finding the 'True Ending.' Specifically challenge maps and a deeper crafting system, and making the overall game more difficult
