Like many long-time RPG fans I've been waiting for a game like this since I first discovered the genre.
The game is beautiful. The graphics are gorgeous even when fully zoomed in. It's like Warcraft 3 in that there's a cartoon stylized aesthetic. The maps aren't vast; everything is condensed but even with fast travel (in the form of items and unlocks later in the game) it FEELS big. From camera effects like motion blur on height zoom to areas jam packed with content and secrets, it more than makes up for what may initially appear to be a lack of scale.
I probably spent the first 8-10 hours of the game in the main town, listening to the music, enjoying the scenery and talking to NPC's uncovering the secrets and lore behind the world of Divinity. You can play the game fast if you want, breeze through on easy if that's your thing, or you can read every book, every parchment and note you find hidden under barrels and behind trees and learn information that will help you in your quest. There are no map markers either, other than those you set for yourself. I found myself searching, scouring, travelling back and forth and enjoying it! The very mechanics that would have had me sighing and tapping my foot impatiently in Skyrim or Oblivion.
Character customization is sweet! You can create a battlemage that uses poisons and daggers or a silver-tongued archer that specialises in pyrotechnics.
I recommend this game. I also recommend that you commit to it. Give it a few hours of your undivided attention and you'll cream your-....I mean, you'll only want more.

Divinity : Original Sin redefines what we all know and love about classic fantasy roleplaying. Competing with its predecessors as well as games like, Baldurs Gate, Planescape Torment, Icewind Dale and Fallout. This game has an enormous pair of shoes to fill and few short comings aside I feel as though it fits them perfectly.
Here are a few things both GOOD and BAD that Divinity : Original Sin brings to the table.
THE GOOD:
-2 player Co-op both local and online (4 player with slight modification). Potential for 6 players in custom content made with the editor.
-Deep character customization
-Beautiful high resolution graphics that keep the game feeling like a classic of old but with a complete makeover for the modern day audience.
-Completely interactive environments to a degree of which has never been seen in a CRPG before.
-Thought provoking turn based combat where each move you make actually has consequences (even on EASY things can be tough).
-The two main characters develop traits based on your choices and every character you make has a genuine chance of being unique.
-A long and slow burning story that if given the chance will hold you attention for hours.
-Fantastic dialogue and a good sense of humour make the game almost seem self aware.
-The soundtrack fits in perfectly with the environments and rarely feels out of place.
-A persistent world that stays the way you left it. This means the choices you make actually matter.
THE BAD:
-Occasional bugs that cause equipment or traits to disappear (This can almost always be fixed by simply reloading your last save.) but will most likely be fixed in the future.
-The camera can sometimes get in the way but this happens very rarely.
-No customer character portraits.
-No EXPORT/IMPORT of characters. This may be for good reason as all companion characters newly hired or otherwise will auto level to match your party each time you have them join you.
-The turn based combat may feel slow to fans who prefer the SPACE TO PAUSE active battle system in older games.

I first discovered Antichamber via numerous Let's Plays of the game on YouTube, which I'm somewhat ashamed to say I watched all the way through before purchasing the game. Still, I wanted to try it for myself, and a ridiculous 91.6 hours later, I want to say why I like this game.
Antichamber can be considered a puzzle game, but I would argue that much of the game's purpose isn't solving the puzzles that it presents. In fact, nearly the entirety of the beginning of the game is just introducing the player to how the game messes with the player's perception of the game's reality and showing off core locations which are vital to later progression. However, after you reach a certain point, the game begins to show the actual puzzles, with visual hints to show what you can or can't do at that point in the game. Much like the test chambers in the original Portal, this game includes a tutorial subtle enough that many players likely won't realize that they're being taught anything.
I don't think I'd really call this much of a game. I'd call it a work of art. I would claim that there's not really too much that's left completely to the player, what with the map changing behind your back and the nearly constant hints pushing the player in the right direction, but somehow manages to convince the player through most of the game that they are in nearly full control of their actions.
Overall, it's a great game, and I'd definitely recommend it.

Single player Hack and Slash (magic warrior) choice-based action game with time travel (or prescience), lots of humor, several good RPG elements, and a somewhat convoluted  storyline.
Pros:
-Excellent combat system, easily the best I can remember seeing in a hack and slash/magic game.
-Great enemy strength to get into the game.  You'll probably die a few times, but not a slaughterfest.
-Good progress of enemies getting tougher, more numerous, and more diverse and dangerous as you get Truths.
-Excellent storyline, so many twists and turns!  Unlike other choice based games, all of your choices actually matter.
-Humor, it's a hurricane of puns, cultural references, fantasy references, sci fi references, etc.
-Very fun to play, I played through it in a day, because I couldn't set it down for long.
-Replayability is very high, there are many, many different endings, and even after you've gotten the true(best) one, you can still go back and find out what happens in all the others.
Cons:
-Length.  It's not short by any means, especially with the replayability, but you only really have to play through 5 times (The first 4 to collect secret "truths").

Playing alongside my GF's pyro mage, the knight and air mage companions the role of the dex char is not to dish out immense damage, it's to ensure that the tide turns in your favour early rather than fighting an uphill battle from the start. With excellent crowd control beginning at level 1 and giving you over 8 different CC options by level 10 (not including a further dozen from special arrows you can craft/find) the dex character always has the answer to take down even the most stubborn foe. Immune to stun? Blind them! Immune to that too, Knockdown! Still Immune? Use invisibility and let someone else worry about it!
The game's excellent turn-based combat system, well designed action point (AP) system and the ability to integrate environmental damage (oil barrels, water puddles) in your moves, the dex character will have an easy time finding the right way to go about controlling the board from turn 1.  While your damage might be the lowest of the 3 primary attributes, you more than make up for this in inventive opportunities to take out the enemies so you have more time to down them.
Playing Co-Op is also excellent because while you sneak about stealing everything but the kitchen sink your partner is free to run about, talk to animals, or just demand you steal the kitchen sink too so they can combine it using the game's crafting system to create a campfire (please note, game does not include removeable kitchen sinks).
With many puzzles requiring teamwork, the game is definitely made for 2 people to share and enjoy, and sometimes partake in a bit of rock/paper/scissors to decide who's right in an argument using the Dual dialogue options found all over the place.
If you're a couple of friends, colleagues or married and love the older style RPG games this game is definitely worth your time.
Please note I originally wouldn't recommend this game during early access because of the lack of damage for dex-based characters, but with release my opinion has changed thanks to the board control they've been given to ensure a fairness across the board.

A great game that only has a few minor faults. I just finished watching the end credits after about 5 hours of gameplay. I consider that an acceptable amount of time in game for the price that the devs are asking here... and I still have more things I can go do and see which should add on a few more hours as well. I've enjoyed my time playing this game and do have a few things I think could have been improved on, but thanks to the great writing, narration, gameplay, and overall experience the few things I take issue with feel kind of minor.
The main thing I feel that some people will have a problem with is the amount of re-visiting of old levels. You'll often find yourself experiencing an area that you've already been through. You may be on a different path through the level, and the reasons for being there might change; but the different levels become very familiar. Later visits will have you being able to unlock new areas, these often give nice bonuses but do not fundamentally change the story or experience. That said when you finally unlock a void door that you walked buy ages ago to see the other side… nice feeling. I also lost a bit of the previously mentioned nice feeling when I realized I could farm these areas for the bonuses they provide.
This game is very much designed for console players and it plays significantly better with controllers. There are a few cases where the game showed me the wrong controller prompts for particular buttons (I use an Xbox controller and would in some rare cases see PlayStation button prompts). These instances were rare and only happened in the menu system for me though so not too big a deal and something they can likely fix.
Gameplay wise this is game uses a counter system much like many third person action games these days. Happily you can’t just get away with hitting the counter/attack button a million times a second. Early unlocks reward better timed play, and counters require you to give a direction to counter. It’s a simple system, but at the very least it’s not like more recent examples from other games where spamming a button allowed you to win.
Difficulty wise I felt like I didn’t have much of a challenge. The game is definitely on the easy side. It is still a ton of fun, and I don’t regret my play time, however a hard mode or new game plus would make me happy. The lack of difficulty comes from a few things: enemies die fairly quickly and there aren’t very many of them in most groups, I found the AI a bit overly predictable, and often even if you do die the punishment is a respawn right before the encounter with 50% health. Things get even easier in late game when you can get a skill that lets you one shot most enemies. Again as I said, I still enjoyed the hell out of this and will be playing more but most players aren’t going to have a problem.
My last issue is that the game builds up the emperor or other characters at times as major enemies, then handles them in cut scenes. There’s no boss fights for a game that feels like it should have them. I believe that when it comes to a game I’d much rather do something than see or be told about something my character is supposed to have done. They player does get some agency in things though through making choices at the end of several cut scenes that direct you through the story, which helps some. But it does leave all the enemies just feeling very standard.
All in all I do look forward to playing more, and plan to finish the other paths I didn’t bother with initially.  I’m also planning on keeping an eye on the devs for whatever their next project is as this game was great fun and gave me a lot of what I’m looking for even if there were a few things I see as space for improvement.

FTL is quite an amazing strategy game. It has never gotten old because each of the 28 ship layouts requires that I use different tactics to succeed. A couple of ships don't have any weapons when you start out. One has no Medical Bay, so you have to use a Healing Burst bomb to heal your crew when they get hurt. Other ships have a cloaking system but no shields. Weaknesses in these ships need to be resolved quickly or you won't get far. Some of the ships are equipped so poorly that the odds against you are nearly insurmountable. There's one that I've never been able to win with and several others that I play very seldom, though I occasionally give them a go just to see how far I can get. Actually winning with one of them is a real treat that is incredibly satisfying. On the flip side, there are a few ships that are quite strong and the odds of winning with them are much higher.
The random combination of crew, weapons, systems, and augmentations you find (or don't find) along your run tends to keep the games interesting and fresh. Since they have such a dramatic affect on how your ship functions, managing the combination so it is effective can be challenging. Playing with a ship that has ion weapons and beams is very different from playing with one that has a battery of lasers. Even your crew makeup will affect your play. Got some Mantis, Lanius, or Chrystal Men in your crew? Get a teleporter and use them to board enemy ships to kill their crew and disable their systems.
Of course, all this randomness has its downside. There's quite a bit of equipment in the game that isn't very good and it can be frustrating when none of the stores you visit offer anything that will improve the effectiveness of your ship. This is the single biggest impediment to success. If your equipment can't keep up with that of the enemy as they progressively get better shields and weapons, then you'll eventually hit a point where it's impossible to beat them. The fact that your success is so dependent on this random factor rather than on your skill as a player is the only criticism I have of the game.
The randomness is also really the only thing that is responsible for the game's difficulty. I've completed every in-game achievement and unlocked every ship, and I think I'd classify as a very good player, yet my total win percentage, beginning from when I first installed the game and was just learning to play, is less then 9%. My win percentage is probably much higher these days but the point is that you should be prepared to fail... a lot.
One major reason FTL keeps drawing me back is that I can play a game in a relatively short period of time. A full game that includes defeating the boss ship takes me about three hours. Obviously, an unsuccessful run will take far less time, but the point is that you can play a game of FTL in a fraction of the time it takes to play most strategy games, making it a perfect choice for those times when you just don't feel like getting into something BIG.
One thing that needs mentioning is the music... it's absolutely fantastic. The tunes are incredibly catchy and they have a unique funkiness that sounds almost futuristic.
FTL has also turned into into one of the best entertainment values I've ever encountered. I purchased it on sale for $4.99 and have played nearly 1000 hours. Entertainment doesn't get much cheaper than that.

This 3rd person action/shooter game is why I love the genre now, but none have lived up to this. This sequel surpassed it's predecessor, and makes itself clear why it was the best selling Star Wars game of all time.
Let's just get the cons out of the way, because there's not that many.
1). The AI may have vastly improved from the first one, but still can be a bit shaky. This is a very minor problem.
2). Space battles are a great addition to the game, but aren't as fun as they were made out to be, and a slight disappointment
3). A couple of the best maps from the first, such as the Rhen Var and Bespin maps, were excluded from the second game, which was a bit of a let down.
Now that we have that out of the way, let's get to all the pros of this title.
1). Fast-paced action/combat that will always be fun, and never get old.
2). Tired of using blasters all the time? Well Jedi are now playable in this game, as well as Sith, Bounty Hunters, Rebel leaders, and smugglers. This also includes an assault mode that let's you play as only hero's, which was amazing.
3). Graphics from the first are greatly improved, and much nicer to look at. The environments are something to look at. The effects was great for it's time.
4). Soundtrack could never be better. Whether it's explosions, people yelling and screaming on the battlefront, or the sound of a blaster bolt whistling past you, it all sounds great. The music in the game is also something of a classic Star Wars feel, and it's something that goes great with the battles that you will fight.
5). The maps are phenomenal. Well made, have variety, big, detailed, and just all around fun to cause chaos in. You could be on Mustafar, and the enemies are crossing the bridge to the control room. Doesn't matter, shoot out the bridge control panel, and the sink into the lava and their own demise. Then just fix the panel, the bridge will rise again, and then cross over to the other side. There is literally endless ways of bring down your foes in this game, and it will always be fun on each map to discover strategies on how to win.
6). While Battlefront isn't known for story, this one at least tries better than the first to establish one. It's fun to play through, and has actual objectives. This makes it feel more like a real story, while it's not really focused on any main characters, but more like going through Episodes II & III as the soldiers.
7). In my opinion, best for last.... Galactic Conquest. I can't even explain how much I love this game mode, and it is much better than it was in the first. If your into shooting, but also want to put some strategy in as well, this is the right game mode. The idea is, you pick a time era, and then a faction, then try to either free the galaxy, or take it over, depending on what faction you are. This involves both teams starting off with the control of a certain amount of planets, and each traveling with their fleet, or multiple fleets in which you can buy, to try to take over the other faction's planets. Whether you win or lose, your faction will earn credits after a battle, but obviously more if you win. You can use these credits to build more fleets, get power-ups for battles, or recruit new classes such as, Wookies, Manguards, Dark Troopers, or Clone Commanders. This game mode provides a fun way to gain control of the galaxy, and I love it. You can also do a versus mode with it, where you can play with a friend, (locally), and you can both face of to see who can gain control of the galaxy first.
Basically, this game is a incredibly well-made 3rd person shooter. This game is well known for it's multiplayer, and is amazing to play with a friend, so I 100% recommend this title. I never regretted playing it, and neither will you.

I really enjoyed this game! This being Techland's new entry as another zombie game made me think that this was gonna be another game like dead island but it offers so much more. While this does borrow some elements from Dead Island, it added in parkour elements making it really fun to evade the zombie by climbing rooftops and sliding through holes.
It makes you feel like you are desperately trying to survive (especially at night when the night hunters come out!) as you start off the game really weak and killing even one zombie would take you a whole lot of effort. Making it much wiser to evade most fights if possible. Through the game, you will get stronger by doing the related actions and levelling up your skills so you will have an easier time taking down multiple zombies.
You can even get to play as a night hunter by invading another player's game instance. Would like to say more but I haven't played this enough to talk too much about it.
If I were to have any complaints, it would be that there are some abilities that after acquiring them makes the game too easy (namely camouflage) and that the difficulty of the game stops scaling after a certain point. Basically after the halfway point of the game, you will get stronger while your enemies will just stay the same.
Also, I absolutely hated the storyline (If there even is one....). Sure it was just average through 75% of the campaign, but from that point onwards it seems that the script writers ran out of ideas and just started throwing random stuff at you.
Regardless, the gameplay of this game makes up for most of it's flaws and I would really recommend this.
PROS
- Probably the only zombie game with parkour
- Decent graphics
- Has co op(co op is always fun =) )
CONS
- rather pointless storyline.
- Game difficulty does not scale with your character.

This is a full version of Ys I & II as it was released on early machines, with a visual and audible modernisation "glaze", both which can be reverted to the original format if you so wish.
This game chronicles the beginnings of Adol, a recurring protagonist of the Ys series that starts 700 years after Ys Origin. Most of the two games surround one of the main 'evils' encountered, which manifest in two forms -- one at the end of each game.
Combat in Ys I & II is awkward at the beginning, as it involves Adol bumping into enemies to attack them. To prevent return damage, he has to bump off-center or at the side. This eliminates the need of button-mashing and simplifies grinding -- even more so in Ys II. The audio is perfect for the two games.
Overall, what you are getting is the original experience, not some rework treatment like Ys: Oath in Felghana -- but these two games stand alone for its simplicity and engaging storyline.

What it does essentially, is improve cpu performance by constraining your o/s to a single core;

This is by far one of the most overrated games I've ever played.
Controls:
The controls wind up being difficult and clunky at first. Eventually you dial it in, but it's not quite right. Shooting guns in this game is difficult, but it's kind of a nice touch by the developers since your PC isn't a warrior. hand-to-hand handles better.
Combat:
As I said, I really like gun combat in this game. It's difficult, you don't get any reloads (just pick up guns) and it's hard to aim. It's a nice balance. Hand-to-hand has some interesting elements, and overall combat is good.
Free-Running:
I personally really didn't like the controls. There's often multiple ways to traverse an environment, which is nice because lots of these kinds of games are pretty linear. However, there are some areas where you're just following where the game wants you to go. This gets really frustrating when you can't figure out a puzzle, because the whole thing is utterly pointless.
The Story:
The good: The cutscenes were comic-like, and it added a nice stylistic touch. Somewhat intriguing characters.
The bad: Most of the characters were shallow. There are some "twists" in the story, except they aren't really twists. They were supposed to be twists, I think, because the protagonist (Faith) was surprised. But the twists were never set up, so it's not really surprising. This isn't helped by the short length of the game, because there wasn't much development for most of the characters. The ending is, IMO, incredibly anti-climactic. It leaves tons of loose ends, almost like they're setting up for a sequel. The stupid thing is, the universe of the game would be really open to a good sequel even if they tied up all the loose ends. On the other hand, the short length of the game meant it was over pretty fast.
Overall, I would not recommend this game. If it was $5 and you were really curious about the game, then maybe.

This game is difficult to recommend or not recommend. It simply boils down to this:
Recommended for the comic readers who want to know what happened to Michonne when she was noticably absent from the comics in issues 127 through 138, a big chunk of the story.
Not recommended for fans of
the game and/or the show.
For fans of just The Walking Dead Telltale game series, this will be a pretty big disappointment. The game is short, as to be expected with a mere 3 episodes, but even at that I personally was able to finish each episode in about an hour. Multiple characters within the game come and go and you are left with no real attachment to any of them, except for Michonne. A small handful of choices, and I mean really small handful, have only a slight effect on the game. Anything else you choose does not really matter in the end. When the action and fighting starts to happen, they don't really give you much of a choice there either. The graphics look cool and all, but all that happens is you are forced to choose a specific target or press a button. They don't really give you much freedom to make the wrong choices in this game and that kinda takes the fun out of it.
---
---
However, I recommended it because I am a reader of The Walking Dead comics. It was a fun way to show the readers what Michonne was up to during the time she wasn't part of the comic's storyline. It was also a very interesting and informative use of the game to show us the struggles Michonne has been having in dealing with the loss of her daughters and how she is "coping" with it, in terms of her suidicidal struggles. If I could change the game, I would incorporate more of the actual characters from The Walking Dead comics/show. Even though it would really be just having Michonne talk about Rick or Ezekiel, but it would still be nice to see that much more of a connection to the comic world.

After all those years this game is still perfect. Gameplay is over the top. Clever physics puzzles are really good for showing off the Source engine. Atmosphere is unreal and the fact that there are no cutscenes makes the game more immersive. Story is also a strong point for Sci-Fi fans like me. I played the game for the first time in 2015 and I was amazed how good it was. I usually can't stand games older than around 7 years, because of advancements in the game design and technology today. But for Half-Life 2, I haven't felt the "oldness" in the slightest. Sure, the graphics are nothing like the newest games but it doesn't look ugly either especially for a game that is not demanding at all. Because of that you can crank up the graphics options all the way and the free Half-Life 2: Update mod is definitely a welcome advancement in the graphics side. I was shocked to see the textures holding up just fine with even 4K resolutions. This game is definitely a PC gaming masterpiece and for any person who loves FPS games, puzzles and Sci-Fi, Half-Life 2 is a must play.

Good fun if you like a story where each run can reveal a bit more of how to get the true ending. The narration of the story changes as you uncover the four "Truths" of the game, and there are over 30 endings. It is surpringly satisfying to watch the narrator change his tune and mock those who previously screwed you over when the player unlocks new information.
Each run takes between 35-40 minutes once you get the hang of things, so there is a good amount of content for completionists.
Combat is servicable and the pacing between exploration and combat works. There is a very lite crafting/accessory system, which you can easily complete in 5 or so runs. There is an ability unlock system that requires more time, as the XP needed to level you up takes longer with higher levels. For comparison, I'm about 9 hours in and still have about 25% of the ability nodes to get, and the pace has slowed down a fair bit compared to the beginning.
So.... is it worth a buy? If the narrative structure of the game sound interesting to you, I'd say yes. If you are mainly looking for a combat or RPG game, then maybe check a LP first- to make sure its something you'd enjoy.
Bugs Status: I've enocountered a fair number of "mini-bugs" while playing. Nothing showstopping- the worst bug caused me to reload from a checkpoint and cost me 5 min of gameplay- but they exist for sure. If minor bugs are a dealbreaker, then pass on the game until/if more patches come out.

Update:
I have given Steep a second chance after several months. I'm still not a fan of the linearity of many of the missions, and the controls can be sluggish for the wingsuit missions. However, given time to reflect, I think I was too harsh in my first review. Now that I have completed nearly everything in the game, I'm finding the game a lot more fun. Starting at a summit and riding whereever you please for minutes feels great. I stil think there is room to improve, but Steep does enough right to be worth the purchase if you love snow-sports.
My initial review:
Steep is a difficult game to assess. Despite putting 40+ hours into the game I would say that I've enjoyed less than 4 of those hours. For me, the biggest failing of the game is that despite being open-world, most challenges lock you into a fixed route where you must pass through a bunch of checkpoints. These challenges are tedious and repetative, unless you enjoy memorizing lines and repeating/refining them.
However, Steep excels when it gets out of its own way and lets you be creative about the line you take. Unfortunately, maybe 10% of the missions give you just a start and end point, and leave what is inbetween up to you. One of the best ones is a multi-minute epic ride across multiple faces and ridges, but I have yet to encounter another challenge like it.
Overall I would say that Steep is far less enjoyable than Amped 2 was; which the last snowboarding game I played.
Pros:
It has some impressive graphics, particularly the lighting effects.
The wingsuit and hang-glider are interesting additions to an extreme sports game.
Some of the challenges are really fun; or very rewarding to pull off.
Large area to ride through.
Almost no loading time when teleporting around the mountains.
Cons:
Most of the challenges are boring/repetative.
Controls were very sluggish/unresponsive.
- Note: I was using an XBOX 360 controller, which I've used for a fair number of Steam games, but Steep seemed to ignore diagonal input entirely.
Using both sticks to control turning is an interesting concept, but was not a good design decision.
I was unable to use the character customization screen for more than a minute due to lag (eventually crashing the program).
Edit: I forgot to mention that the soundtrack is very limited, particularly compared to the Amped franchise.

Innovative, with a look to the past!
This game is brilliant, let me start off by saying that. Every aspect of this game shines, like few have recently in this genre. The game is full of nods to the old school era of isometric RPGs (Fallout 1 & 2, Baldur's Gate, Arcanum, Icewind Dale and so on), both in style of gameplay, dialogue and setting, while yet bringing lots of new things by making brave decisions.
Let me just say that I have played roughly fifteen hours, and just wandered around doing side-quests, trying to solve a ridiculously intriguing detective-story (so far I've got help from a dog sniffing the suspects pants and snuck into one of the suspects house to read her diary) amongst other things. It is a game full of content and stuff to do everywhere. The story holds up really well so far, but gives plenty of room for going off on other adventures.
The UI is great. Slick menus, nice inventory management, lovely character creation. Everything is easy on the eye. Details like these are really important.
The combat is great. Turn-based without using grids, the main feature of the combat is the brilliant way it uses elements. My aerothurge-mage conjures a pool of water around my enemies and my archer let's a lightning arrow hit it, ZAP, and they are stunned. Burn water and you get a steamy cloud. Zap it with electricity and you got a static cloud. Put acid on the ground and blow it up with a fireball. I've still not mastered it. You think you are safe but haven't noticed that your characters are all standing in a pool of water, or you think that barrel is just an ordinary one.
Lots of classes, easy customizations, nice leveling system with perks and abilities that you can use in different ways. Flare can either be a small fireball on your opponent, or use it on the ground and create a fiery surface that your opponents either will have to walk through and suffer burning damage, or walk around it. The system works great.
There is a very good crafting system in place in the game as well. It makes you think logically. In this game you have to pick up and read books with real words (not a fixed schematic) and then drag the items onto each other. Arrowhead and woodshaft, an arrow. A knife and a wood stake? A makeshift spear. There is also alchemy, and lots of reagents to find and pick up everywhere you go. I haven't delved into this part of the game yet, but I intend to.
Last but not least, the soundtrack is really great. I've found myself humming the tunes walking around in my apartment, and they complement the game in a great way.
It's been a long time since I enjoyed a game (in this genre) as much as this (probably BG2 now that I think of it), and I got lots of it left, thankfully.

I first discovered Antichamber via numerous Let's Plays of the game on YouTube, which I'm somewhat ashamed to say I watched all the way through before purchasing the game. Still, I wanted to try it for myself, and a ridiculous 91.6 hours later, I want to say why I like this game.
Antichamber can be considered a puzzle game, but I would argue that much of the game's purpose isn't solving the puzzles that it presents. In fact, nearly the entirety of the beginning of the game is just introducing the player to how the game messes with the player's perception of the game's reality and showing off core locations which are vital to later progression. However, after you reach a certain point, the game begins to show the actual puzzles, with visual hints to show what you can or can't do at that point in the game. Much like the test chambers in the original Portal, this game includes a tutorial subtle enough that many players likely won't realize that they're being taught anything.
I don't think I'd really call this much of a game. I'd call it a work of art. I would claim that there's not really too much that's left completely to the player, what with the map changing behind your back and the nearly constant hints pushing the player in the right direction, but somehow manages to convince the player through most of the game that they are in nearly full control of their actions.
Overall, it's a great game, and I'd definitely recommend it.

Stories is quite different from most of the games out there.
It takes familiar elements and mixes them up into something refreshingly new (in my personal opinion).
First of all, you have an amazing Bastion-like narrator with tons of really cool lines. I did hear a couple of repeated lines over my playtime but most was new every time. Oh, and by amazing I really do mean amazing - he voiced all game and it sounds insanely good.
Then there's action combat very similar to a (somewhat simplified) version of Arkham combat. It starts very easy, but the longer you play, the tougher it gets to kill all the enemies.
And, of course, there's an RPG-like progression - you got skills you can acquire, you got the gear you can upgrade. New gear will unlock new paths you can take in old levels.
Finally, there's choose your own adventure style storytelling. Essentially you are tasked with picking the "winning" story. It won't be easy, though, since you won't get all the paths from the start - you'll have to fail a couple of times to figure out new ways to change the story.
One of the great things about Stories is the way levels are designed. There are not that many of them (5 or so?), but every time you'll go through one, your objective will be different. That'll mean you'll need to take a different path. And the cool thing is - there's no such thing as wrong path here. Almost all of them lead to your goal but through a slightly different area.
Speaking of downsides - I haven't actually found that many. I had zero game breaking bugs, but I did encounter two minor ones.
First was getting stuck after dodge animation - dodging again fixed it. Second was falling through one of the elevators - I got teleported back to it instantly. Those'll probably get ironed out really quick.
Repeating the same story might sound boring, but the thing is - you will get a slightly different story every time. It'll be different enough to keep you interested in figuring out what do you need to do to get a happy end. The only question is basically - do you like good stories?

INTRODUCTION:
XCOM Enemy Unknown is a remake of the classic UFO and X-COM games from 1994 - 2004, the 2012 version aims to bring back the turn-based genre into mainstream market. It does so by introducing the series to modern day graphics, technologies , and a streamlined and revamped gameplay.
The player assumes the role of the XCOM Commander who is tasked to lead an elite team of soldiers, scientists and engineers from all across the globe in an effort to thwart a massive alien invasion. You are Earth's first, and last line of defense.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is incredibly fun. I love turn based games and this takes strategy to the fullest. In this game it is man vs. alien and we are fighting back to remove the aliens. You control a squad of soldiers that you move and tell them who to attack, defend, or to do overwatch to attack moving enemies. There are four types of soldiers you can get randomly when they level up and each will gain rank and you choose from 1 or 2 abilities when they do. If your soldiers die you have a chance to save them by healing them before they die but if they die they are gone forever. You also have the build up your forces by researching technology and spending resources to buy new technologies, weapons, and buildings.
This is a highly addictive game which can be pretty difficult if you don't cheat (save often and reload over and over again to get the best results). An interesting thing about XCom is it saves its random number generator so that means if you load a game and do the same actions over again you will get the same results but if you do things in a different order you can get different results (the chances to hit will be the same but if one soldier is more likely to hit, he might hit an enemy when another would miss).
That pretty much sums it up for me 10/10 best turn based strategy, and tactical game I've ever played.

You can even get to play as a night hunter by invading another player's game instance. Would like to say more but I haven't played this enough to talk too much about it.
If I were to have any complaints, it would be that there are some abilities that after acquiring them makes the game too easy (namely camouflage) and that the difficulty of the game stops scaling after a certain point. Basically after the halfway point of the game, you will get stronger while your enemies will just stay the same.
Also, I absolutely hated the storyline (If there even is one....). Sure it was just average through 75% of the campaign, but from that point onwards it seems that the script writers ran out of ideas and just started throwing random stuff at you.
Regardless, the gameplay of this game makes up for most of it's flaws and I would really recommend this.

The Banner Saga is a breathlessly attractive tactical game with survival elements that have no failure states, other than making you feel like the worst caravaneer in the universe. It's an RPG about priorities, at least on the human side. You can build up your fighters or buy relics or feed your people. You can't do all three. I'm not entirely sure you can do two.
The strength of the game is atmosphere and uncertainty. At least the first time you play, the text adventures convey an actual sense of dread. These are the only way you can lose fighters without outright losing the game; there's no permadeath in battle, only in the journey itself. If that's a bit jarring, the game balance would be extremely rough otherwise. Every time you lose health, you lose strength; wounded units are increasingly ineffective, unlike many tactical RPGs. Each battle is a war of attrition, and you will get damaged. You can get through without being an expert at the fighting (I played on normal), but knowing the ins and outs of positioning and special skills can only be helpful.
It's not terribly long and quite linear, but I'd still crack it open again to look over all the banners and that beautiful map, make a few more choices and see what happens, see if I can't get better at keeping people alive.

Ys I & II Chronicles is a much improved remake of the 1987/1988 Falcom games for the NEC PC88 and PC98 computers.  The two games are essentially one, with II being a direct sequel to I.  Unlike most Ys games, where the events are loosely connected and don't need to be played in any particular order, Ys I and II should be played together, in order.  I also personally recommend these games as an introduction to the series, as they introduce some of the main recurring characters of the series.  Both games come with 3 soundtracks - the original PC88 version, the Ys I & II Complete version, and the Ys I & II Chronicles version.  While I personally have a love for the FM synth of the original (PC98 VGM is amazing), all 3 soundtracks are fantastic and there's really no "best" version.  Having multiple choices was a very nice touch from Falcom.  With introductions out of the way though, let's get into the individual games.
- Ys I -
Ys I is a mediocre game with an odd charm.  While not nearly as good as its sequel, it's still a nice game.  Much of the time there's little clue where to go or what to do, but something about freely roaming the world talking to NPCs to find a clue as to what to do next reminds me of a simpler time and just has a nice feeling to it.  Also, unlike many RPGs, every NPC has a name and a small sense of uniqueness that makes the interactions with them more enjoyable.  This is honestly one of my favorite parts of this game, and of Falcom games in general.
The combat is pretty simplistic in Ys - bumping into enemies will damage them, but hitting them head-on will hurt you a lot as well, so you must hit them from off-center to avoid taking damage.  It's a nice system, and I like it, but it wasn't executed as well as it could have been in this game.  You reach the maximum level about halfway through the game, which makes fighting enemies feel unrewarding for the remainder.  The boss design also a bit poor, which is sad.  They're functional and not really "bad", but they're still some of the poorer-quality bosses of the series.  That said, while the gameplay is a touch mediocre, the characters, story, and music still work well to make the game feel nice despite its flaws.
- Ys II -
Ys II is the direct sequel to Ys I, taking place immediately after the events of its prequel.  This game takes everything that made Ys I good, and makes it better.  Then it takes everything that was bad about Ys I, and makes it good.  The game's progression feels so much smoother and more straight-forward than the first, and the combat system has been improved by adding magic to the mix.  Early in the game, Adol will gain access to his first spell, a chargable fireball spell, giving more choice in combat alongside the traditional bump-combat.  The boss design has also stepped up from mediocre to magnificent.  Ys II's bosses are very much up to par with the later installments of the series, and are by far the best of the 2d games.  Most bosses can only be damaged by the fireballs, giving them a shoot-em-up type feel, where you must dodge their attacks while shooting them with your charged up fireballs.  Also, unlike the first game, Adol will level up continually throughout the entire game, and experience gains are now adjusted relative to the difference in levels from enemies, helping to keep the player from being over or under leveled.  There's also lots of small touches to the game that add so much to it, such as being able to give gifts to NPCs for additional dialogues or other small secrets.  Ys II is a fantastic game and one of the best in the series, definitely standing up well alongside its 3d successors.  I highly recommend it.

I paid about $10 for The Walking Dead: Michonne and I'm not entirely disappointed, although I probably should have waited for a better sale. I'm a huge fan of Telltale generally, and think Season 1 of The Walking Dead is one of the best games of the last decade. This is definitely one of Telltale Games' weaker offerings. Significantly weaker than either Season 1 or Season 2 of The Walking Dead, although also much better than the underwhelming "400 Days" DLC. I find it unlikely that I will replay any part of this one, unlike Season 1 of The Walking Dead which I've replayed several times. For $10, at most 4 hours of gameplay (each episode is almost exactly 1 hour, with the first one maybe running 75 minutes) is on the high end of what I usually like to pay for a video game, especially considering one of the reasons this mini-series didn't do it for me is because the characters are so weak. The main villain (Norma is almost OK) are so unambiguously and obnoxiously evil that there's really no moral dilemma in your dealings with him. There was no moment of reflection in this season.

So, on the whole, this is a pretty weak offering from Telltale Games. That being said, even a mediocre offering from Telltale Games is still a bit better than a lot of other games out there. As mediocre as these episodes were, they still were much more compelling than the actively bad writing of the "Mad Max" game, and there's also something to be said for not just presenting a sandbox without characters or attempt at representation. So Telltale here gets a pass from me, although there are definitely other games from this developer that you should check out before this rather bland offering.
Final Rating: 3/5 Katanas

Having followed this game since I saw it unveiled on an E3 stream, I was eager to try it out. I tested it when the open beta was released on Steam and I wasn't disappointed in the slightest, the game hadn't visually changed much at all since it's unveiling, yet the actual experience of playing it myself was very different to watching someone else doing so, and I spent a good few days grinding out the available challenges alongside my friends and generally enjoying the free roam aspect of the game. Of course, as a beta it wasn't without it's strange behaviour and minor bugs but I had expected that, despite the inconvenience at times.  I had a good while to decide on whether the experience was worth spending money on for the full game and later, after christmas day, I decided I'd indulge myself and buy the game proper.
Getting down to brass tacks about the finished product I can tell you that the game, once again, still hasn't made much of a change since the beta. In fact, I was kind of disappointed in how little had been done since then on account of a fresh new set of bugs and what seemed to be barely, if any tweaking to the games mechanics, thankfully the biggest change I could see was a tweaking of the G-Force system which I'll explain a little bit later on.
Overall, Steep is a fun, open world experience with a charm that other snowy, mountainous sports games from memory seem to not manage to pull off in quite the same way. Initially, the game is set up to treat you like some kind of extreme sports rising superstar in generic fashion and, to be honest, I found it to be a lot more distracting from the overall experience of the game, since when you're out and about freeroaming and not partaking of the countless public challenges that dot interesting routes across the map, you can really take in the beauty of the sun shining on fresh snow, with a good ambient track to fill the silence, much like you probably would if you went skiing in the alps on holiday in real life. However, if you're not like me, the game is not without it's own soundtrack, comprised of a small selection of premade, dynamic playlists of a few genres that suit the game's setting and theme, in particular, I found it amusing to be cruising down a mountainside, weaving in and out of some blue glacier outcroppings glistening in the late afternoon sunlight to some almost zen like music only to hit a bump and smash my pretty face against one, the track throwing itself off and fading out while dusted myself off and shook myself back into reality, only to fade back in once I'd sorted myself out and got back underway, quickly dropping me back into the game before I could think of booking a much needed appointment at the nearest alpine dental practice.
The free roam aspect really is the meat and potatoes of the game, it's clear to anyone that the developers spent most of their time building the game around this, as you can waste a few hours simply travelling from one range to the next, finding new routes to experiment with or simply to enjoy the view, both of which can be customised by the option of changing the position of the sun or the ambience of the weather. Riding down the same mountainside in dark fog is a very different experience to doing the same in clear, cold sunlight! This is not to say that travelling around the map is a slow and laborious process, as you're given the ability to teleport between preset locations at will with the option of discovering many more along the way and, once you've unlocked the ability to do so, you can choose to teleport via helicopter to any part of the map you choose. For those hardcore masochists, if instant and near seamless travel is not your thing, you could spent a whole heck of a lot more time trying to walk back up the mountain if you're willing. Another aspect to the game is the flighty side - wingsuiting and paragliding. Of the four sports in the game, wingsuiting appeals to me the most, it is by far the fastest and most intense way to travel in the game, requiring fast reflexes and precognition if you don't want to turn into alpine pâté. Paragliding is the opposite: a much slower, more relaxed method of travel best for taking in the views while you sail along the mountainside.
For those that like to spend a little time tailoring their online image, Steep offers a few preset, voiced riders, all of which play in the same manner, but a LOT of clothing combinations for you to spend time deciding on. Some of the costumes you can get are incredibly amusing the first time you fly off a mountain or sail past someone, taunting them like a squeaky toy or a Yeti as they faceplant repeatedly.
Now, this game isn't perfect. In fact, in friendly competition, I've had more than a couple of colourful words to say about some of the mechanics of this game, most namely the G-Force system, which for a game that has a fairly comprehensive tutorial at the beginning, does absolutely nothing to explain, leaving it up to mere speculation as to the finer details of how it works. This mechanic can be downright infuriating if you're a completionist like I am as it makes your job of nailing a perfect jump or getting a race time down to an extremely fine margin a living nightmare. You WILL notice what I'm talking about simply through the course of the game. Heading down a steep slope before mounting a ramp for a jump, if you so much as tap your board or skis on the tiniest bump before reaching that ramp, you can say goodbye to your legs and spine, and enjoy your new diet of your own teeth and liquid hospital food, and a lot of the challenges are purposefully set in locations that have these hazards, adding a level of difficulty that sometimes isn't even related to the challenge you're trying to do. Trust me on this one, it sounds part and parcel for a mountain game but you'll see what I mean when you have to retry the same challenge over and over and over again. It really does test your patience in certain places.
Aside from this intentional yet seemingly unreasonable mechanic, the few other cons I have with this game are rather unintentional. This game is, for some reason, an online-only game, meaning you CANNOT play offline or, that if you have sub-par internet like I do, you can run into a few annoying issues such as lack of other players that are supposed to dynamically appear and disappear around you when in range. (A feature of the game, but a sort of psuedo matchmaking or instancing system), making the game rather lonely and desolate at times, with only the annoying narrator shouting generic motivation to their supposedly biggest bread winner over the radio every now and then.
This is tied with the games current instability, for example, occasional but random freezing that happens in game, usually at critical moments where you're at high speed, mid air pulling off a trick, or in the middle of winning a difficult challenge. It doesn't last for long, but it seems to be reported as happening to a lot of the playerbase, as well as all the friends I know that have played it.
All of that said, I don't regret buying Steep, I can sit and play it for a few minutes to pass the time or a few hours and still come away feeling like it was a worthwhile use of my spare cash.
My advice to those reading this far into this review is thus: Do NOT buy this at full price. I got it on the christmas sales and it was an adequate price for what I consider to be a better than average game.
I think of Steep as a relaxing, elaborate time waster, a calm immersive experience set aside from my usual library of carnage and mentally engaging games. Sure, there is an element of challenge to this game, it can be brutally unfair to you a lot of the time but if you keep your cool on those icy slopes, you'll find yourself enjoying the stunning vistas, fantastic sound effects and a surprisingly long lasting (yet not quite fully polished) ride down some impressive mountain ranges.

This is a distressingly accurate tabletop simulator.
It sort of feels like "Dungeons of Dredmore Does Tabletop" to me.  The sense of humor is mildly more down-to-earth, the battles are turn-based RPG style (with no tile-based / movement aspect), but the character progression is similar and the visual style reminds me of it in a good way.  The actual game mechanics are heavily simplified, and seem to be based as much off of japanese computer RPGs as they are off of any particular tabletop game.  The players for your party bicker and banter at eachother with one-liners now and again, I've found at least one quest that seems specifically designed to encourage lateral thinking ("why go to the area ten levels higher than you, when you can /buy/ the quest drop at a store?"), and there seems to be some kind of over-arching storyline that I haven't really gotten far with.
DoD is on my computer as sort of an equivalent / replacement for solitaire -- Knights of Pen and Paper is happily getting added into the same category.
[Edit]  On later reflection, it also reminds me of MMO's with the get quest / kill X things / get next quest / move to new area dynamic.  Unfortunately, they roam all over the world map and you can only hold one of them at a time -- meaning it's impossible to prioritize what order you want to do them in, particularly when many of them are multi-stage with each step in a different place.  There is very little strategy.  That said, it's still a good mindless game if you like the combat style.
Starts out slow - boring, even. But the more new abilities, traps, enemies and levels you unlock, the more addictive it gets!

While playing the game for the second time I had much more fun then on my first run. The game has a pretty good atmosphere, especially at the beginning when you still don't know what is going on and your arsenal is very limited. The dynamic shadows keep the tension up, since sometimes you are not sure if that was the enemy that moved or just the shadow. You can read personal logs on PDAs and computers and learn abut tragic deaths, fun jokes on the workplace while things were peaceful, and learn about what was happening before the events in the game. This is all just like in Doom 3, but it's still fun.
The soundtrack is pretty good and sets the mood just right, and when a large battle starts the music gets more energetic and makes you ready for the battle.
The maps are HUGE, some can take more than half an hour to finish, and first few levels are more open, so you can enter a building from various points. All the weapons are very fun to use and you can upgrade them. The upgrade system makes you explore the maps more, so you can kill more enemies and get the upgrade parts sooner.
There are not many enemies in the game, but they are all very different, and require slightly different tactics and weapons. Some run at you and jump, some get invisible and you need to use the flashlight to see them, some have shields on front, so you need to sneek from the back, some throw goo at you and slow you down... Unfortunatelly the AI is very limited, and sometimes they get stuck.
I enjoyed the story too, it is nothing groundbreaking, enough to give you some context and keep you going, but the ending was a surprise. I'm glad I replayed this game and now I think it is a much better game than I first thought.

As much as I wanted to be able to recommend this game as at least a casual mindless fun type of title, it turns out that the game is not even successful at that. The game's premise of telling a story from the point of view of people playing a Tabletop RPG is played painfully straight without any humor involved other than the premise itself. The game also provides no attempts at being an authentic Tabletop RPG experience by being restrictively linear and having a fixed storyline. Speaking of which, the game's story has no sense of atmospheric or emotional depth and is paper thin, no pun intended, and is literally the most generic and bare bones story you can think of for a fantasy game. Again no attempts are made to actually make this interesting or relate it to the game's premise.
The gameplay is made up entirely of fetch quests that are normally reserved for sidequests, and there is no exploration included at all. The game will stop being fun after about an hour. Also the game features micro-transactions in the form of buying in game money with real world money, and the game's design seems to be based around making you use up as much in game money as possible. Traveling to new locations, reviving dead partners both cost in game money despite making no logical sense why this should be the case. Up grading weapons is something that costs an absurd amount of money to attempt, but it starts out with only a 35% chance of working, and the only way to increase that percentage is to successfully upgrade weapons. Because of this, you will likely go through all your in game money really quickly, and seeing as how money takes a ridiculously long time to farm in this game, it seems entirely likely that the idea was to get you to use the micro-transactions.
This game is not recommended.

Michonne is a mediocre entry into The Walking Dead body of work. It requires little to no thinking compared to the other games in the series, and the emotional impact is largely missing. The game basically plays itself.
The biggest problem is really by comparison. Looking at a single episode of The Walking Dead Season 1 or 2, or another high quality Telltale game like The Wolf Among Us, Michonne is really lacking in meaningful choices. While there might be mini, immediate consequences to your actions, they don't last. The branching paths of the story seem to be glued together, coming apart for only for brief moments to give you the barest illusion of control. For a company that prides itself on making these sorts of games, Telltale seems to have forgotten the single most important aspect: agency.
Lacking that, the game should have at least told a good story. Sadly there were only a few lazy attempts at evoking feelings for Michonne's backstory. The primary driving action happening in the current timeline was a rote recitation of any equally forgettable story set in the The Walking Dead universe.
The graphics and sound are standard fare if you've played anything by Telltale before. No surprises there. Although I will say that the update with third episode improved the visuals slightly compared to the first and second parts. The controls are equally similar and unnoteworthy.
If you are a huge fan of The Walking Dead and/or Telltale and you've already played everything else then it's probably worth a quick playthrough. But for the average gamer it's not worth a second glance.

The game starts you off on a beach away from the main town you will be starting in. You will hit combat pretty early and find that it is indeed turn based. Anything outside of combat however is in real time. Most skills can be used in and out of combat for various effects. Mastering these skills and when to use them will be critical for your success when exploring the world and fighting off the baddies.
A common complaint is the difficulty of combat. The combat is hard at first. Since it is turnbased many people approach it like they would Final Fantasy Tactics. Rush your melee in close while sniping with ranged. While this MAY work in some cases here, it is best to understand your skills and use them in the best way possible. For example, running in with a melee character will allow him/her to take aggro nine times out of ten, but with overwhelming numbers, his HP will be hard to restore, even with health potions and spells. Crowd control will often times set this plan on the path for failure; knocked down units (Ally or Hostile) will automatically get hit 100% of the time. Meaning that tank of yours just got hit twice by every enemy on the map.
Think about your moves:
-What would happen if you backed up around this giant rock and let the melee come to you?
-Is there any special barrels around to set off at the right moments?
-What spells do I have? Should I skip my turn to combo them next turn?
-My tank is in danger, should I teleport him out and inflict friendly fire damage?
-There is just too many! Should I escape and try again later?
If you can get past the difficulty of combat, I can guarentee that many RPG fans will enjoy this game. BUYER BEWARE: This game is kind of like The Elder Scrolls: Morrowind in regards to no quest marker. The developers have done a fantastic job in not holding your hand while playing. You have to think, read, remember, keep track of everything. You never know what you'll need to solve the various mysteries and quests. There are bugs, and the developers have already been working their butts off to patch them and make this game even better.
The game supports Steam Workshop and the fourms are flooded with amazing ideas that I cannot wait to come to life to bring infinite replayability to the game.

"Choose your own adventure" the best way to do it?
"Stories: The Path of Destinies" is a very charming and beautiful designed action rpg / choose your own adventure type of game. A narration full of pop culture references leads you on multiple paths towards one of the many endings.
Time until I found the one, true ending: 7.3 hours according to steam.
This might seem short for a lot of players but keep in mind that I'm not even close to having all endings. So there is still plenty to do for completionists. Even though at this point I have all four swords and every gem maxed out, the skill tree still offers a lot to improve the character. I have so much fun with the combat system, that apparently somehow uses some sort of stacking bullet time, that I'll certainly keep playing it. The overall storytelling is awesome with a lot of unexpected twists. The levels may get a bit repetative, though. From my perspective this game is worth the money.
Pros:
+ Interesting, non-linear storytelling, charming narrated with funny pop-culture references and lovable characters
+ good combat system full of action and a good variety of possibilities with an interesting approach of the bullet time
+ moderate difficulty that rises accordingly to your own progress
+ Levels are beautiful and adjust slighty, depending on the current path and your progress on items and skills.
+ The soundtrack is absolute gold. Love it!
Cons:
- I'll add the unlockable "Truth Finder" to the cons since it is not an optional feature and makes it way too easy to find the true ending pretty early on.
- The combat sometimes feels a bit sluggish. Could be due to the slow motion. Still enjoyable though. Might get aswell polished with future patches.
- Since you visit the locations multiple times they get very familiar after a while.
- There are currently some narrations that don't fit to the subtitles. Due to the amount of narration that's a pretty common problem and could be polished too.

This is a rather frustrating game. Here are my gripes:
- Not an RPG, a visual novel. Narrator is blaberring non-stop, there is no way to skip and instead of playing you are listening. For a visual novel - good - for an RPG - bad.
- There are scrolls in the world with a wall-o-text. So feeding you generous helpings of story aurally is not enough, you are also supposed to spend another 5 minutes reading a god damn scroll. Well at least you can skip *that*.
- The loading screens are black. I'm not kidding you. You do not know that it's an area end, and suddenly your screen turns black. Out of nowhere. Did my PC just hang? No, that's a loading screen. It just happens to be tastfully pitch-black, no embelishments, no boring tips, no nonsense!
- The game is "optimized for controller" but it loses controller all the time. I mean I can move the mouse with steam controller, I can get to steam menu, by pressing the steam button while in game, so obviously controller itself works, and steam can talk to it, it's just the game itself suddenly stops reacting on controller button presses and stick movements. Not a kind of optimization I like.
- You cannot alt-tab from the game. The initial loading screen was taking too long and I made a mistake of alt-tabbing. That locked my machine well and good and I had to reboot. Switched to windowed mode for the next attempt to avoid that
- By the way, in the window mode they lock your cursor to the window, so although you are in windowed mode you cannot move your cursor out of the game window! Even if you want to click that little cross in top-right coner to shut it down. May be that's what they meant by "controller optimized"?
- There are altars and "crafting stations" in the game. At altars you improve your skills when you gain a level and at "crafting stations" you improve your weapon when you collected enough "ore". This makes sense. What does not, is that as you move forward, the areas behind you get closed off by something looking like an energy field. God knows why. Probably because developers did not want to deal with the possible bugs causing by player back tracking, so they just desided to close it off for a heck of it. This feels unrealistic, but on the top of it it's also annoying. Say you are one ore short to upgrade your weapon, while next to a "Crafting station". You go around the corner and find the missing ore. Now you want to go back to the crafting station, but no you can't it's now closed off. Wait for the next one.
- Finally, there are check points right before a battle. If you happen to be low health on the checkpoint, you are screwed. You get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you, but your only save is to right before the battle with your miniscule health. You can't win and you can't do anything, because you cannot go back and heal. So game over, start from the beginning.
I think I'm done.

Divinity: original sin is very similar in style to the old RPGs in the forgotten realms series (Baldur's gate etc). But unlike those games the combat in this game is all turn-based. I found the story interesting and there is a lot of areas to explore in the game. There is a lot of dialogue in the game and you can speak to most if not every npc in the game (including animals if you have the skill for it), although most non-quest related npc's have the same dialogue options. Divinity:OS also has a lot of humor in it and it has a certain sillyness to it in some places, which i love about this game. Quest wise there is a good assortment of quests in the game, many of them linked to eachother in some ways. It didn't feel very linear to me, there are pure sidequests in the game just for extra loot, xp or extra story. Oh and there is no such thing as a waypoint marker on your map telling you exactly where to go and what to do which i found very refreshing. You have to rely mostly on reading notes and diarys and using your brain to progress further. At the same time, in some cases it can be a bit too much. One thing that stands out is the need to solve puzzles in a few areas that involves really tiny buttons hidden in the environment, sometimes requiring your character(s) to have points in perception to even make them appear. It's not a huge deal but it can be annoying when you get stuck for hours on one puzzle during the main story (one in particular made me stay up until 6AM pulling my hair out until i finally got through)
Combat in Divinity:OS is fairly standard turn-based combat and i must say, very challenging at times even on normal difficulty, i found it easier a bit into the game though as the characters grew in power.  One nice addition that i really like is the ability to use the environment and the combination of elements (fire, water, air, earth) to create effects on the battlefield. Like for example electrifying a puddle of water with a lightning spell, stunning everyone standing in it (including any of your own characters standing in it) or setting of an explosion by throwing a fireball into a poisonus cloud.
This game also has a crafting system as well which i didn't use that much on my first run. It seems a bit hard to figure out what items you need to combine to make stuff in some cases unless you search the steam community or google. The system itself is fairly simple, just combine ingredients by dragging and dropping them onto eachother or to some tool in the environment (like a forge or an anvil), but you need to find books or papers describing what items to combine and even then, there are ingredients that can be added onto the end result of the craft to create new items that i didn't find a description for anywhere. I guess i'll have to dive deeper into this aspect of the game on my next playthrough.
Well, what more can i say? I loved the music, there is a great mix of moods, happy, sad, action and humor (a certain song played in taverns, a favorite). Graphics i won't go into that much, i enjoyed the level of detail in the game but it isn't next gen graphics, very minor issue imo. The other aspects of the game like story and gameplay is so much more important. Bugs then? I encountered one problem throughout the whole 50 or so hours of gameplay that seemed like a bug, getting stuck in a dialogue at one point. It was solved by restarting/reloading so nothing big. Other than that i had two crashes at the end of the game, after playing for about 18 hours straight!
All in all, i am very satisfied with this game, it was so much better than i expected it to be and it brought back that good feeling i had when i used to stay up for hours, immersed in games like Baldurs gate or Planescape:Torment. I really hope to see more Divinity games in the future or at least an expansion to this game. Thanks for making this wonderful game!

Before I launch into my review, I highly recommend looking at a gameplay video to decide if you're really interested as this game is not going to be for everyone.
This game is heavily story driven with a nice smattering of choice & consequence and turn based combat. While the story is fairly linear, you will end up in the same place no matter what, who is still alive when you get there will vary wildly from person to person. The game is built on the concept of an apocolypse and the developers had no problems bringing the harsh choices such an event would bring. The game gives a good frame work of the events and then allows the player to tailor how their individual journey plays out. Major plot points will be the same but the pieces that will in the blanks will be customized, and are often memoriable.
Cons: Some people don't like cartoony art (I think it's beautiful in this game). There is no save system, it autosaves but it saves multiple copies so it's easy to backtrack. The combat is far inferior to the Banner Saga Factions and not just because it's next to impossible to create an AI on the level of a human. In Factions, every unit has a special ability making positioning and targeting key to success. In Banner Saga, a fair amount of enemies have no special moves, even into late game, erroding some of the tactical depth. This is further compounded by the lack of enemy types. The game is also very short (took me 8 hours), if you don't replay games often this might be a big deal to you. There's also a lack of exploration due to the onrails nature of the story. And finally, RPS has said they found the story hard to follow early on. They don't give you all the details about why what's happening is happening until later but, I never understood where this confusion comes from but feel it's probably worth mentioning.

Pros: Very polished, great graphics (both tactical and immersive), addictive, high replay value... top example of the genre.
Cons: Limited RPG element, weak main storyline.  Requires the "Within" DLC to add depth in both these departments.
Recommendation: Yes, buy it. And on sale @75% off or more, a no-brainer.
As more of an FPS/RTS player, I was open but skeptical when i bought XCOM, even on sale.  Having now put a damnable number of hours into it, I can safely say that XCOM strikes me as one of those shining examples that are included in anyone's top picks of a genre.
While the turn-based tactical squad combat is the substance, it's woven around managing your base expansion, economy, research agenda, soldier roster (RPG element), and squadron of planes/ships, not to mention maintaining the happiness of individual countries on a global level via satellite placement and interventions.  Because there are so many ways to come at your overall approach, and because you get a new roster of soldiers to customize each time, the replay value is immense.
One note on that. As (also) an RPG player, I found myself getting invested in individual soldiers, since you can customize appearance and voice, not to mention skills and equipment (I still get wistful thinking about how badass my squad was, e.g. Ukrainian sniper Natalya "Vodka" Stolichnaya).  Much of the addictive and replay appeal is in evolving these characters, although many RPG fans may find these options painfully constrained.
And that brings me to one of my only critiques, something that was a thorn in my side even as I greatly enjoyed the game - limited customization and depth, which detracts from an already weak storyline (one grating example was that while you get a range of voices to choose from, they are all distinctively American English, which really clashed with the idea of an international team).   The expansion "Within" actually goes a long way to address this, by adding depth across the board (deeper story, more soldier skills and customization, even several languages) and while definitely worth getting for that and a host of other reasons, it's not a part of this game or review.
Overall, a solid game, worth getting.

How on earth Obsidian entertainment managed to make a good RPG out of South Park is beyond me. I knew they were capable game creators but they ended up crafting not just a good game but a great South park episode. You see and visit the whole town with enough interesting set pieces to stop the game becoming stale. Sewers, homes, streets, very small government facilities, very large bedrooms and...well lets just say something that will fly over peoples heads. The really ingenious aspect is having the whole game set whilst all the children in the town are fully engaged in a live action roleplay game pretending to be in a fantasy world of wizards and elves.
What would have been perfectly acceptable as a storyline takes repeated twists and turns, upping the ante until you would need someone like Morgan Freeman to come out and calmly narrate what the hell is going on. Yet at this point it's too late. You're smile is fixed and it's not going away until the credits roll.
The classes seem to end up having less of an effect on how you play but the animations that occur once you perform certain class specific moves. Weapons and armour have noticable differences in abilities and customization allows a suprisingly deep level of item managment. Much like in other games you will feel the pain of loss for replacing your favourite weapon for a statistical upgrade despite the fact you think it looks worse. Only in this game your favourite weapon will, coincidentally, probably end up being your mothers favourite as well.
Gameplay wise Obsidian have crafted a game that absolutely nails the basics but feels to abandon any attempt at advanced tactics or strategies. Whilst you can certainly use items and afflictions to your advantage there doesn't appear to be further challaenges aside from rushing down the apponenet and instead a greater impact is placed or interacting directly in combat in the form of quick time events. Quick time events are usually the bane of any game but here they are used in combat for boosts to attacking and defedning, spicing up what would otherwise be an animated menu selection into almost a rythm combat game. Somehow it all just
.
Possibly the most underrated and least talked about part of this game is how it won't take your life away. Everyone is familiar with the Bethesda epics like Skyrim, or the Witcher series by CD Projekt RED but so often these games feel like the save file is something you keep as part of your lineage. Handing down to your son when he comes of age and he too will pass it on to his son. That's great for a lot of people for a lot of reasons, but I'd also like games I can completely experience without needing to take half a year off work. South Park can be comfortably completed in under 25 hours and that includes all sidequests and collectibles. If this feels like bad value for money then we will have to fight, just remember to wait your turn.
