Ys is one of the grand-daddies of the modern JRPG with more remakes than Blade Runner. This version is based on the excellent PSP compilation that came out in 2009. It's basically Zelda with more anime and less attack button, but it's awesome nonetheless. You run into enemies to kill them, which sounds boring, but it makes backtracking and grinding far less tedious than in other RPGs, and the length of the game is fairly brief, which feels like a breath of fresh air in an RPG industry full of sprawling, 80+ hour, open-world epics. The localization work by XSeed is fantastic, and they actually licensed a really well-made fan translation of the original Japanese PC game for this release. The art design and soundtrack are godly. Especially the soundtrack, which is composed by the legendary Yuzo Koshiro, of ActRaiser and Streets of Rage fame. The story is fairly generic (this is a game from 1987, after all), but it doesn't outstay its welcome and it gets the job done. The gameplay is where Ys truly shines, though. I didn't think I'd be able to buy the idea of killing enemies by bumping into them, but it actually works and it's insanely fun. It's an arcade-y sort of RPG, and it holds up remarkably well.
This compilation contains the first two games in the series. The first one is fairly short and mainly exists to set up the story for the second game, which is more of the same, but with magic spells and bigger, more annoying mazes. If you're new to this series and don't mind the simplistic nature of the gameplay, dig this one up.

You're in for a story with many "What if?...". Each choice you make has its outcome. Each path will teach you something new, something you will take into account for the next time you come across that choice.
The game is often compared to Bastion (and rightly so) as it is indeed a top-down action RPG, colorful and wonderfully narrated. Stories also offers 3D graphics that are absolutely impressive for a small studio like Spearhead Games. As you venture around, you can contemplate the majestic backgrounds of what's to come. You can see the many floating pieces of land that seem impossible to reach at first but that you will visit soon enough. And fear not if you missed a platform or two, for you will come back... a lot. You will retry, and you will eventually succeed depending of what you have learned.
The key feature of Stories is that you play through a short adventure that could as well be told in 30-60 minutes, but it doesn't end well for Reynardo, our roguish fox-like character. You will then re-live the adventure from the beginning with what you already know so far from your previous experience. You will discover truths about your friends and foes, you will try to deal with everything differently... until you find the destiny that was meant to be!
The story is brilliantly narrated by Julian Casey who impersonates each characters as you would do using different voices while telling a story to a child, and it works very well! It contains lots of clever humor, subtle winks to popular cultures (videogames, movies, music). I've had my sides blasting off to outer space a few time with some of them :)
My personal favorite goes to the music that dynamically plays along with your actions, a very rare feature in video games, especially of this quality. It will reminds you of John Milius's awesome "Conan The Barbarian" soundtrack, as well as most Ghibli animes. It makes it all epic, plays well with the situations and emotions.
The fights are really fun and harder as you progress into the game. You gain more XP when performing bigger combos. You spend them in skills that will unlock new way to handle tougher fights, and you craft new weapons that will unlock new doors on your path, revealing shortcuts and more secrets.
So many secrets to unveil in a single story with so many outcomes!

Steep is a great game.
At first I have to admit that I was blown away by the open-world and the mountains themselves (I worked on Mt.Blanc for many years) but quite disapointed with the maniability of the game. The controls felt clunky and it took a while to get used to the system.
Having 4 sports to choose from really puts the game on another level. I really enjoyed exploring the map by paragliding around and found the windsuit exhilirating. Skiing is quite fun but snowboarding definitly takes the medal and after a few hours of gameplay it becomes pretty obvious that Steep was directly inspired but the S.K.A.T.E. Series. It is much either though and I will be hoping that Steep 2 will be a bit harder.
Pros:
Open World
Real mountains
4 Sports to choose from
Multiplayer unexpectedly fun
Scoring system (freeride/freestyle/extreme)
Cons:
Trick system too assisted and too easy
No real career mode
Gear is only esthetic
Music tracks will change if you reset your character
IMPROVEMENT IDEAS
A better trick system: The actual controls are too permissive. Since there is a lot of S.K.A.T.E. In this game, well go full distance and emphasise more on the analog sticks. Make tricks harder, add a trick list, make landing more intuitive and less assisted.
Snowmobile: open flat areas would be perfect playgrounds for the snowmobile, that can have it's on trick system. In multiplayer mode you could pull other players behind you.
Kickers: Build your own jump. Define the size, angle and slope. You could gain speed by being pulled by another player on a snowmobile. Kickers can be used for taking off and landing.
Snowline: Area walls, really? The best wall in this game would be... no snow. The ground at the bottom of the mountains are bear of snow and grass is appearant. No frozen lakes but water. Rivers could come out of glaciers around this altitude.
Punitive bails: You fall off a cliff and only K.O? Respecting the mountain means understanding how dangerous it can be. Show the broken bones of the crashed player model, make them loose a bit of money or make heir gear show damage!
Snow conditions/Avalanches: Making people more responsible when they go up the mountain to ride in real life and not get carried away after playing too much Steep by adding a disclamer on the loading screen is not enough. That also has to be implemented in the gameplay. The snow conditions (it's thickness, the max speed it allows, how you can land on it) could change and dangerous areas could appear, creating the conditions for a player to create an avalanche. Other players caught in it would bail but the player that started it would have to take responsibily for other player's demise.
Proximity bonus: Having your avatar score points next to a player of your group should add a bonus of share some of the points.
Helicopters: Make them flyable! Instead of having am automatic sequence and tickets, why not make a great simulator where you can carry other players around? It would be an end-game unlock.You could have to pay for your fuel and be paid by other players. I know this might sound like I want an Arma version of Steep but having one player pull off a double flip above a helicopter controlled by another player is just too rad.
Replay/HUD: Replay mode should be deepened. Static cameras, keyframes, more speed variations, and the possibility to save the replay as a standalone video.
That's it for now! I'm going right back into it, if I have more ideas I will probably come and make an edit. Tell me what you think!

Clearly a harkening back to the days of top-down arcade shooters, while Shadowgrounds gets the shooting and enemies right enough, it fails almost everywhere else.
An extremely underwhelming story paired with wooden voice acting leads the charge, but thankfully they're little more than a vehicle for the action.  This should, in theory, make the action worth your while, and in a sense, it is, with a solid assortment of weapons and upgrades to reward you for the hordes of enemies you power through.
The environments, however, wear on you quite quickly, with the same grays and browns making up every copy-pasted hallway across all 11 levels.  The stages aren't something you can quickly blitz through, either, and even though I was avoiding enemies at every chance near the end of the game, it still felt as though it dragged on far too long.  The music too was mediocre to the point of irritating, and I eventually shut it off in favor of my own more atmospheric tracks.
Though it's far from the worst game that I've ever played, there's little here that makes it worth your time.

It's not often that after only an hour of gameplay I don't feel the need to press on. The graphics are cute and the game sounds nice, but the gameplay and story are just not where they need to be. Yeah, the idea of playing a computer RPG about Pen & Paper RPGs is a cute idea, but the game is so damn meta that it actually feels like an amateur effort. Prepare to fight rats, goblins and evil wizards. Yawn. The character creation system looks very detailed at first, but then you realize that of the six initial classes, most only have 3 active skills and one passive skill for the ENTIRE game, and one or two have - gasp - FOUR skills. Here's every encounter in the game: rogue/mage use stuns, paladin use taunt, cleric heal, then attack, attack, attack, attack... Leveling up consists of upgrading one of your four skills, and weapons/armor upgrades require extreme grinding to level up your blacksmith to get a CHANCE at getting a straight upgrade. Oh and what's this? MICROTRANSACTIONS? In a game I already paid for? Even as a casual RPG, I would avoid getting this game at any price point. On a tablet? Maybe. On PC there are just way too many better indie titles at the same price point.

I loved Portal and found myself wondering if I enjoyed this game more than Portal 2. It's hard because Portal 1 was ground breaking and Portal 2 has a story which is entertaining. This game has no story per se but the puzzles and illusions are near flawless. The game looks so simple and generic but it's not. No game to date has as many unique interactive elements as this game. Remember how Portal was trying to explore what else could be done with 3D world other then the same old first person shooters. It's just shoot shoot shoot and E interact. Portal made you take note of your environment and really start to interact with it. Well Antichamber takes it to the next level. So many puzzle games are gimmicky where they reuse the same concept in different ways. Antichamber is unique and has so many new concepts of what can be done with a 3D world. Loved all the easter eggs and how the game continued... don't want to say to much without giving anything away. I would buy games like this all day. I think all devs should play this game to understand the possibilities. I had a friend explain to me why he doesn't like puzzle games, then I realized he had never really played one. Please make a sequel to this game and reinvent 3D all over again, the possibilities are endless. Next time though upgrade the story like Portal did from 1 to 2 and it will go viral.

"You are an engineer on a remote planet of the solar system.
Everything goes well until some strange events occures and leads our hero to be the last hope for the humankind..."
Basic for a sci-fi action game: In the future, a hero fights against hostile alien forces with undetermined motivations. Helped by some soldiers and scientists who played with forbidden technologies.
The dialogues/texts/characters are basic. The overall doesn't bring anything to the genre. Only the end might surprise the player.
Gameplay mechanics are easy to pick up. You see your character from above, look around with the mouse and walk with keyboard, you can also dodge shots by pressing space.
You have 8 different weapons: from the pistol, energy rifle to the rocket launcher. Nothing really special except some funny upgrades like for the basic rifle: a tazer to stun enemies or the minigun that can be dropped to serve as an automated sentry.
You can find ammunitions, health... basic stuff in general except the canisters wich can be used to unlock the upgrades i mentioned above.
Contrary to other games, you can nearly have every upgrades of the game. Only 3 or 4 can be missed before the end.
Levels are filled with darkness and your flashlight is a necessary tool especially to spot some sneaky aliens.
In general the game is not very scary especially if you consider the amount of ammo and the power of weapons.
You are the hero and a potential prey but.... in fact you're not.
"So why do you recommend it ?"
First, the game is fun. Even if enemy A.I is close to 0 and eat lead without any problems.
Or the fact that stress in general  is not very present. Because you don't have "huge" hordes of enemies to deal with and the number of different enemies is low (consider that the overall violence of the game is low too).
The game is still cool and some boss fights are nice such as the one in the mine or the last boss (i died alot !).
Second, the music is really good and plays an important role in the quality of the game.
It greatly compensate the story wich is poor and the unremarkable characters.
Third, Shadowgrounds is cheap. For this price you can have around 8 hours of correct action without any stress or great punishement.
If you buy it during a sale, like me, it became a real bargain.
A correct top-down shooter at a correct price.
What else ? ^^
N.B: In the same kind of game you can find "Alien Shooter". Not every games of this franchise are good but they are a good challenge.

Okay, first off I'll try to write this review in assumption that half of you reading have played games like this (Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights) while the other half aren't really familiar with the DnD playstyle.
The Good:
1) Visually satisfying. The environment, character modles, and partical effects of spells are stunning. I could try to describe it with and do it little justice. So just look at some screenshots and some gameplay videos. I'll try to reveal things about the game that you don't usually get from watching other people play.
2) Soundtrack is quite stellar as well, again though i won't do it much justice by describing it, just watch someone stream it on Twitch.tv
3) Lore/Story. I wont give anything away about the actual story, so I'll just describe how the game handles quest and such. It's a non-linear style questing system, so you can just go about your business and do whatever you want. There is a main questline in which you can progress through the main/side quests without going through a set series of NPCs to talk to. You need to find a missing NPC? You dont need to have the quest before hand. Exampl: NPC needs you to find a missing item. You can stumble upon it and retrieve it without having the quest and when the NPC requests you to find the item, you can present it to them. That goes with almost all other kinds of quests.
4) Crafting. Quite fun. The crafting is like MInecraft's system in a sense that you can make anything just know YOU (the player) personally know the what do combine. The only contributes in which crafting skills add is to unlock higher tiered items to make and crafting time (from what I've noticed). There are books in-game that have a fun (fun for me) description on how to craft stuff. A crafitng book may have a flavor like. . . "I'm no lumberjack, but anytime I come across a log, I take my trusty axe to get some. I'll whittle it away with a knife to make a couple of stakes, and those blasted wizards always want some of the leftover woodchips for some reason." So that recipe pretty much tells you to get logs from in-game environmental logs on the ground. Combine a knife and a log to make a stake and woodchips. Other examples of how to craft is by combining Flour and Water to make Dough. Combine a hammer to a tomato to make tomato sauce. Combine the sauce and dough to make pizza dough. Toss that into an oven to make a pizza!
Oh, and this made me EXCEEDLING happy when I found out that you can combine a Fly Agaric Mushroom and an Empty Flask to make a Poison Potion. THEN! you can combine it with a weapon, and your weapon will have a permanent Poison x-y damage. I'm still trying out some of the other crafting stuff, so there's still a lot to find out.
5) Combat. The nitty gritty of the game. It's turned base combat. The order in turns is determined by how much Intiative you have and it is affected by your Speed attribute; there are a total of 5 attribute stats: Strengh, Dexterity, Constitution, Speed, Perception. EVERYTHING in combat is dicated by Action Points (AP), there is no mana to cast spells; they all run on AP and cooldown timers (in turns, ie: 3 turn cooldown). You want to walk over to that zombie and start unloading on him? You need to spend AP to move there AND then spend more AP to swing your weapon. Movement dictates how many meters you can walk in 1 AP. Movement is affected by type of armor (heavier gives you a movement penalty, but can be reduced or removed with ability points), and the Speed attribute also dictates your movement. Various attribute stats also affect your Maximum AP, Starting AP, and Per Turn AP. Maximum Ap is pretty self-explanitory. Your starting AP determines how much of your max AP you have at the very beginning of the battle. Your Per Turn AP helps you gain more AP per turn. You may also save or roll-over unused AP to unleash on a monster that you just tripped (tripped/stunned monsters have a 100% to be hit). Different types of weapons inherintly use more or less AP. Daggers use 2, one-handed Axes/Swords/Maces use 3. Two-handed weapons use 4(two-handed axes/swords/staves). Bows use 4, and Crossbows use 6. I believe.
Okay, phew. Now that AP is taken cared of. Actual combat is quite challenging. It is imperative when battle is initiated that you analyze the battlefield, since all encounters have been hand-placed by the devs, each of the have different playstyle flavors. Some encounters will be better utilized if you have a wizard throw a fireball at barrels of oil to it will light up and burn them all. Or some encounters may favor a sneaky rogue backstabbing (backstabs have a 100% to crit) those mages in the back before your party rushes in. Analyzing the battlefield is so important, not just because of the combination of the monsters and their positions but environmental factors also play a huge role.
Elemental Synergy has been worked in this game beautifully. You see enemies standing in a puddle of water? Throw a lightening bolt in it and it will stun anyone in the puddle. Don't have a lightening skill? Throw a fireball or have a ranger shoot a fire arrow in the water to turn it into vapor-- which will obscure vision from those pesky archers *Beware, though, your vision is also hindered behind the vapor*
One of the available abilities in the game is Loremaster, which also allows you to identify magical items to see their properties. It also allows you to view the stats of the enemies whening holding down CTRL. With higher levels of Loremaster you'll be able to see the enemies Hp/Max HP, AP/Max AP, Resistances, Armor. Also if you like lore or you just like to be immersed in your games and read a lot/everything you can stumble upon useful information like, this archeologists tells you that skeletons are more resistant to piercing damage but if you have a mace or any crushing damage, their bones will turn to dust. Later on, you can find out through other spells that skeletons have a 75% resistance to piercing damage and take extra damage from crushing.
6) Co-op. I had generally wanted to list this in "The Bad" section only because the game limits you to two players, but there are available mods to make it into 4. I personally exptec it to be a 4 player game because its predecessor (Baldur's Gate & Neverwinter Nights) had 4 players, odd decision to go to a 2 player cap. ALTHOUGH, how many people really have 4 friends to really dive into the lore and play for hours and hours and only be level 2 or 3. So there's the counter-argument. Otherwise, the co-op is superb. The host saves and loads but there are also drop-in and drop-out public gameplay.
One of the features in this game allows the two main characters (both single and co-op) to both react to environmental factors or decisions. Early on, you find Ishmashell and you have two opposing options. One essentially good, the other evil. If both of you decide two different options there will be a rock-paper-scissors minigame. You need to score 10 points to win and have your way. If you have charm/intimidate/reason points then every win you get awards you the respective points. Someone with 4 intimidate battles someone with 2 reason, the person with 4 intimidate only needs to win 3 games; whereas, the latter person needs to win 5 games. This applies to trying to intimidate/reason/charm NPCs.

This is an excellently crafted turn-based game that utilizes upgrades, research, combat, and resource management well. XCOM is a pretty worthwhile purchase for anyone looking for something a bit different.
That said, it's important to know that the enemy AI in this game will cheat, and it will do it ALL THE TIME. Enemy aliens can hit you with no problem half a zone away in full cover, while your units can barely hit them at point-blank while they're standing in the open. The enemies get a turn to move in to cover NO MATTER WHAT YOU DO. Try to sneak up on a group? Too bad. They saw you, now they get to move to cover so you can't ambush them. Got a pair of Seekers ahead? Nope. They get to stealth before you can do anything. Conversely, enemies can (and will) ambush you frequently and kill you, because you do NOT get a free move like they do.
I absolutely recommend this game, but you MUST go into it knowing that you WILL break a keyboard or two in pure frustration. I can only hope that, one day, they will tweak the AI a bit, or remove the aliens' free move altogether.

Hey, Vsauce. Michael here. Now, one of my favorite treats of the holiday season is Gabriel's cake. It's a super solid based on Gabriel's Horn that you can make right at home, as long as your home is infinitely large. Okay, all right. Now, the first thing you want to do is bake a cake. I prepared this cake earlier. It's a real beautiful cake. It's a little large, but I bet you I could eat that whole thing in a day if I tried. Am I right? Okay, now the second step is cut the cake in half. Notice that while I cut this cake in half you don't add or create any new cake but the surface area of the cake has increased. It used to be completely covered and now we've got two regions on the inside that aren't covered. The next step is to cut this half, one of the halves, in half. Here we go. Again, the volume of cake on the table is the same as it was in the beginning but the surface area is going up. As you may be able to guess, the next step is going to be to cut one of these quarters of the original cake in half. It's getting pretty thin, but all you have to do is keep this up - cutting halves in half and half and half and half forever and once you've done that, well, you're almost there. When you finish cutting, stack the halves on top of one another in order, like this, to create a beautiful tiered dessert. Because you have an infinite number of thinner and thinner slices when you're done stacking them the cake's vertical height will be endless.

It's an OK RPG, it's a very good South Park game. Why the distinction ?
Well, as a pure RPG game it's not a very compelling proposition for fans of the genre. Yes there's leveling up, loot, some customisation of you character (both cosmetic and in terms of stats), yo have a few choices here and there but it's all very bare bones and not very deep. So if you want a solid RPG, this isn't it, go elsewhere.
There's no dialog system (although you could say for this particular game it can be excused), the map is just 3 lanes going from left to right, and the combat system, though I really like turn based combat systems, is quite boring. You'll very quickly learn which attacks deal the most damage and use them over and over ignoring the rest of your abilities.
There's also no crafting system. I have acumulated sooo much junk throught the first few hours of gameplay expecting it to matter somehow but nope, you can safely sell anything in the junk category.
Now, while it's not a very good RPG game it's a very good South Park game. What I mean by this is that this game does it's license justice. If you are a SP fan, you'll like this game no matter how repetetive the gameplay is. All the characters are here, the wacky humor, the voice acting from the TV show. Playing this game it's like watching either a very long episode or a whole season of the show.
On one hand it's a plus for the game but on the other after a few hours of gameplay it made me want to just watch w complete playthrough just to skip all the average gameplay and just get to the cutscenes and WATCH the story.
All in all it's an OK game at it's core while being a great adaptation of a TV Show. If you like South Park, get it, if you don't stay away.

I like it a lot, but I'm also a sucker for snowsports games. Reaching the level cap of 25 can be done pretty quickly, but actually doing every challenge (especially up to gold medal standards) will take a while unless you've entirely mastered the physics system and memorized every mountain face.
Pros:
-Huge amount of mountain terrain to explore with lots of unmarked stuff to find
-Visually beautiful
-Skiing and snowboarding have subtle differences that make each of them worth trying
-Soundtrack is well-designed for snowsports with a good variety
-Challenges are usually easy enough to get in one try
-Replay editing makes you feel like an amateur Warren Miller
Cons:
-Always online means you better be sure your connection is steady at all times
-Multiplayer feels a bit tacked on, haven't really seen any sort of reason to play with others unless you really need a score multiplier boost
-Physics are occasionally inconsistent, but no more so than Skate or any other extreme sports game
-Not enough music in the soundtrack, you will hear repeats very often when you're restarting a challenge
-Controls take a bit to get used to, mostly due to automapping the jump/ollie function to controller triggers
-No grindable surfaces, which feels a bit glaring considering almost every extreme sports game has had this
-Season Pass is not worth the price, and it's arguable that the base game price is a bit steep *badump tish*
If you're looking for a game where you make your own fun setting up lines and editing your footage, then Steep is certainly going to give you a lot of playtime and material to work with. If you're looking for a next-generation SSX game, then you'd better keep looking.

OMD is an entertaining, furiously addictive mixture of 3rd person shooter and tower defense, with a splendid soundtrack that perfectly compliments the frantic action.   You play as the rather dense but ♥♥♥♥♥ure Warmage, who must defend the magical Rifts from untold numbers of marauding orcs, using an array of traps, guardians, spells and weapons.   The main game of achieving a 5-skull rating (no orcs escaping, within a par-time) on all maps is a good challenge - which further fuels your abilities at large-scale orc maiming, as skulls can then be spent to upgrade your equipment.   Slaying the hordes is plenty fun enough, however therein also lies a complex combo-system adding much further depth of play, where the more traps and their afflictions hit an orc, the higher the combo-points, thus making every map replayable to experiment and chase that higher score.   Crisp graphics, great voicing, music, humour and still packed with pure, fun gameplay that's as good on a pad as with a mouse.   Quality arcade action that's only surpassed by it's more content heavy sequel, yet still worth playing first.

I'm not going to say this is a bad game, but what I will say is that this is a bad port. As such an example, turning V-Sync off actually makes most of the game ridiculously harder as the game is very frame dependant on a few bosses. If your frames are low enough, you're guaranteed to get hit on one of the bosses, while if your frames are high enough another boss rarely allows you to hit him (and this is already a very RNG dependant boss). So why is this an option? Because more options are supposed to make it better, right?
Beyond that, there's many things that have no reason not to be updated, but weren't. This is pretty much a remake four times over, and they've still left it so you need a guide. Lets also mention that some of that guide used to be an instruction booklet, something you're not /really/ going to have in the same sense with a digital game. I can't even begin to account how much of my time was wandering around aimlessly before I just opened a guide.
Here's an example, to progress in the game, at one point you need to talk to an NPC who's outside, an NPC who's inside, leave the city, then talk to the outside NPC inside as well. No hint that you need to leave. A normal person would even think "Well, I've already checked on her, so there's nothing of use." Nope, you need to check on her twice, in two different area, to progress. No hint whatsoever. And lets not forget these things could be patched. Things like additional dialogue boxes to tell the player where to go, or what options break what difficulties don't take long to implement. There's more that could be complained about, but you should really get the gist.
There's no excuse to having money and not buying this..

I have super mixed feelings about this game and it's such a shame, I feel like it had so much potential but it just felt rushed.
I finished this game with every single achievement in about 4 hours - I wasn't expecting a full game like TWD and TWDS2 but it still felt a little... empty. Whilst it was still fun and the characters were cool, I didn't feel like any proper connections were made like you do in TWD. Also, the main premise is about Michonne losing her daughters and feeling guilt and we, as the player, are meant to feel that too... I didn't. I felt more of a connection to Sam's brothers who we speak to for about 5/10 minutes because you have a moment to bond, I guess? We don't get that with Michonne's daughters.
Story aside, the gameplay brought up a few issues for me as well - the choices you make can't be made using the 1 2 3 4 keys which I liked, you have to do it with a mouse. Not a game changer, but it took me a moment to get used to. The QTEs seem a little strange too - I missed a couple and still survived like nothing had happened. To begin with I thought, well great, got away with it... but 5 or 6 more times down the line it felt like I didn't matter as a player and I had bought a film, not a game.
I've complained a lot, but I still think this is a good game and I'm glad I bought it, but I don't think I can recommend it simply because it doesn't (in my opinion) hold up to many of the other Telltale game standards... I'd recommend just holding on until Season 3 is out.

I'm going to give this game an overall thumbs up, but the more I play it, the less I want to.  I'll explain why.
Let me start off be confirming to readers (at least those smart enough TO read the reviews) that while this game LOOKS like Diablo, IT IS NOTHING LIKE DIABLO.  Let me state that again more clearly for everyone to follow:
THIS GAME IS NOTHING LIKE DIABLO. STOP ASKING.
YOU CANNOT TRANSFER CHARACTERS BETWEEN GAMES.
YOU CANNOT GRIND ANYTHING.
THIS IS NOT THAT KIND OF GAME.
If I were to liken it to anything, it would be some of the older AD&D games like Icewind Dale, or Balder's Gate, or maybe games like Fallout 1 and 2 (no, not the spiffy 3D 3 or New Vegas) except much much less random.  This is both good and bad. The world is beautifully crafted, the vistas are atractive, and everything you encounter has some part in the game's lore.
The main issue this creates however is that everything in the game is finite.
There's only so much loot you can EVER recieve.  Though you usually find more than you can ever use, and the crafting sysytem allows you a limited ability to upgrade things a bit, you can get screwed now any then by getting a bad run of luck in finding things your party can use resulting in much harder fights.  If you have done everything you can up until you hit a boss fight, you may find yourself outmatched with no option other to keep retrying the fight til you get lucky.
The second part of the finite gameplay issue is that there is only so much experience your characters can ever gain, and opportunities to do so CAN BE FAILED.  This means if you mess up a quest, you will permanently lose the experience points it would have granted you resulting in a lot of quicksave->attempt quest->fail->quickload-try again gameplay which isn't a very good design.  Ontop of this, if you blunder one quest, you may find yourself unable to complete other quests attached to the characters and locations involved in it, making the issue snowball and leaving your party underleveled.
Now again, there is a lot of opportunities for experience and loot.  The side content is plentiful and generally fun which helps to offset these previous two issues, but without simply reloading after failed quests, progress can feel frustrating at times, and you quest log begins to fill with uncompleteable missed opportunities.
Beyond these issues, the previously minor points that may have been easily overlooked slowly form into a bed of spikes.  For starters, you are given complete control over your two main characters (character 2 strangely is used as your "main character" that dialog defaults to, something to keep in mind when deciding who to give social skills to) and this is amazing! Class, gender, appearance (though the options are limited) and starting skills are all yours to choose.
However when filling out your four character party, the options are painfully limited (a knight and a wizard. That's it.), meaning that if you didn't select the RIGHT classes for your main characters, you're going to have a hard time progressing.  Also, these characters on offer are rather annoyingly written, and will pretty much complain about everything you do  The devs attempted to mitigate this by placing an NPC in you dwelling area, who feels VERY randomly inserted, offering a selection of characters to hire for a considderable (and mostly unaffordable) price.  The problem is, even this selection of chracters is oddly limited. There are literally NO healers for instance. A bizarre choice to be sure.  The problem of filling out your party could have been more easily rectified by placing a greater selection of characters in the first town you encounter (one of each class perhaps) or simply allowing the player to CREATE the characters they wanted.  Neither of these options were selected by the devs, regretably, and the game suffers greatly for it.
Basically: Make one of your main characters a tank, of br prepaired to be without one.
All this was annoying enough, but becomes compounded by the reality that the main plot of the game is, honestly, a meandering mess.  What startes as a murder investigation that uncovers greater, ever more sinister underpinning, quickly goes off the rails.  Things mentioned in conversation become contradicted at the next plot point, characters' actions and ambitions are inexplicable and shift wildly, and what's meant to be a complex web of subterfuge, collapses into a tangled pile of frayed threads and loose ends.  It really feels like the plot kept being changed as the the game was in development, but no one bothered to go back and change the conversation text to reflect the changes, or at least they weren't thorough in doing so.
Now, I'd still generally recommend this game because it does some things very well!
For instance, the combat is excellent.  For those who love tactics and planning, it is a goldmine with veins running very, very deep.  Spells and abilities work synergistically with eachother producing amazing, and often cackle-worthy results.  The battlefeild can be as much as weapon as any other, with various substances and surface materials used to your advantage making the difference between victory and defeate.  When fighting a zombie who spews poisonous ooz finds the tides turned against him because said ooz is flamable and EXPLODES on contact with your character's fire spells, it's a true treat, and makes every victory a rewarding experience.  And the effort put towords leveling and outfitting your characters to fill their designated roles (tank, damage dealer, support, etc.) is doubly rewarding.
Also of note is that the world generally feels alive.  While the devs scrapped the day/night cycles, and NPC schedules, the towns still bussle with activity. Merchants call out in the tiown square, patrons drink in the taverns, and people generally go about their (admittedly limited and repetitious) routines.  While the plot quickly goes off the rails, the world it takes place in is engrossing and emmersive.
Over all, I'd declair this game good, and worthy of play.  It's a return to much older RPG values, when people remembered that the RP stands for ROLE PLAY, and as such, there is planty of roleplay to be had here.  Your actiona matter, and people react to you for the most part as one would expect.  It's only regrettable that devs' dreams seemed to be far beyond their reach and that the story just falls appart.  Here's hoping that the modding community can stitch up some of these rough spots.  At the least, it's worth the purchase.
Oh, and one final caveat. The females are all wearing high heels, even the heavily armored, sword and board types.  Haven't games moved past this kind of thing yet?  It's simply juvenile, and a sign that the devs may have some growing up to do.

Divinity: Original Sin hails from the golden days of classic-RPG gaming.  It takes portions of what were great about past CRPGs like the Baldur's Gate series, Fallout, Icewind Dale, and the like, and stirs it into one big pot and offers you Divinity: Original Sin.
While the Divinity series is not new to some of us, if you can recall their other RPGs like Divine Divinity, Larian Studios pays great attention to detail and it shows.  Almost everything you do in D:OS has a consequence.  All the careful planning by Larian went into every little detail in Divinity's world.
Original Sin is text-heavy, so do not dive in expecting complete voiceover work for every main character and NPCs.  There are the occasional voiceover work, but they are few compared to the text dialogue.  This does not spoil the great writing though, but it gives it a very "right at home" feeling for those that enjoy classic RPGs.  The dialogue is wonderful, well-written, and full of humor.  Even dark humor which is not easy to pull off.
Divinity: Original Sin is a challenging game, but it is fair.  Right from the start, it does not hold your hand, but it begs you to search every corner of its vast world.  Every battle, not just boss fights, requires careful planning, strategy, and good tactics.  Your party could be wiped by a small group of common mobs.  But do not be discouraged.  Original Sin is not unfair and cheap against the player.  It simply means, you cannot just lay back and push a few buttons to win a fight so easily.  Allow me to give you one example where I was fighting this one boss, and I was down to my last party member with low health and the boss was also at low health (one hit away from death), and I managed to get off one last shot with my bow, killing it.  At the same time, there was joy, and relief.  You should also know that you can sometimes take on enemies that are 2-3 levels higher than your characters, but it requires great strategy.
One of the gameplay mechanics that really stood out for me was the ability to create different effects by applying magic and ability effects to your surroundings. For instance, if an enemy is standing in a puddle of water, you can target the water with an electric-type spell and stun your enemy for a number of turns.  Strategically speaking, you can also place oil barrels in position before battle in your enemy's path and strike it with a fireball spell, or an explosive arrow.  This gameplay mechanic fosters dynamic gameplay on the battlefield, and it rewards players that plan out their strategy.
The presentation in Divinity: Original Sin has been well executed.  The menus are easy to navigate, without all the clutter and needless micro-management.  The user interface is slick, clean, and simple yet complex in good ways.  I did not notice input lag.
The controls felt very intuitive for the most part, but not without a small learning curve.  Those that have played CRPGs before will feel right at home.  Those that have not played CRPGs before will get used to the controls within an hour or less.  The controls are very responsive, smooth, and it does not have input lag.  Mouse and keyboard work great.  I have not tried it with a controller.  Moving your party members in the levels feel responsive and fluid.
While Divinity: Original Sin does many things right, the ending was very anti-climatic.  Without spoiling it for you, I will just say this:  Try not to think of the end and enjoy the journey.  D:OS is all about the journey, the gameplay, and the rich detail.
Divinity: Original Sin was one of those games that took me by surprise.  It was a refreshing new release in 2014 that blew me away by its shear depth and classic feel.  In a sea of videogames that tend to hold your hand, Original Sin was the complete opposite of that.  It required motivation in thinking; planning out your strategy and tactics to win battles.  The reward was satisfaction from battles where you did not always know going in if you will win.  The tide turns, and you do not know if you will be the victor.  It allows for dynamic gameplay, unlike static gameplay that just lets you hit the "win button."  Larian Studios designed a game that respects the player, with a high risk, reward system that works.

The game looks very good, but for many of us PC gamers, the texture pop-ins and the medium res textures can be of annoyance. However, this is one of those games where graphics are secondary to the gameplay. Not to say the graphics are bad at all, they aren't, but it leaves allot of Titan cards bored.

I am a huge audiophile, I only accept the very best sound, no distortion, no jaggy treble, and this game is definitely to my satisfaction. The sound is all there, the footsteps, the grass, the sound of your weapon swinging and the soft sound of the rain is all jaw dropping in how well recorded/generated it is. The gameplay is a huge strong point of the game. The combat flows extremely well, the parkour flows even better, and chaining them both together will give you a bloody amazing gameplay experience. The gameplay takes the very best parts from Dead Island, and Assassins Creed/Mirrors Edge and slams those games and shows them how it's done. This game does the tower climbing better than Far Cry 3, Combat better than Dead Island, and Parkour better than Assassins Creed. I can't even begin to explain how satisfying the combat is, but just imagine running up a wall, jumping off, and in mid-air, dropkicking a zombie into a pit of spikes, or throwing a gas tank next to a big zombie and watch it smash the tank and explode. Completed this game, and I am not done at all.

Are the devs still active? Yes, they seem to be very active and they engage with their fans very frequently.

Okay, so the game's pretty as ♥♥♥♥ and has an amazing musical score that's dynamically implemented.  That's great and all, but I care about how a game PLAYS.  And to put that into perspective, we're going to have to get some♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the way right off the bat.
This game is a step away from the ordinary.  Some people are going to be turned off by that.  In fact, some people will cry.
Me?  I praise the sun.
See, The Banner Saga isn't a game that holds you by the hand.  It informs you of things to a degree, drops a few hints in the narration and dialogue that you have to actively seek out, and then expects you to make an educated guess on how the world around you will react to your choices.  And trust me, it doesn't always react nicely.  You'll have party members smashed for doubting in your own abilities.  You'll have friends betray you because you stuck to your opinion just a little more than they'd like.  You'll get mad.
Deal with it.
One of the best things about this game is that it's about prediction and reaction.  You're always given enough to predict things well enough, if you see the subtle signs in front of you.  And whether you catch those signs properly or not, you'll be reacting to how things play out, so keep a cool head and salvage your situation the best way possible.  Ultimately, you can replay it again and try to not make the same mistakes you did the first time around.  See how it changes your story.  I can guarantee that there will still be surprises even your third time around.
Replay value is basically the name of the game.  It's long enough to be an adventure, but short enough to keep multiple plays from becoming tedious and grinding.  There's a lot of choice, big and small, and all of it will impact your story in a major way by the end.
The combat, in a similar vein, is largely randomized encounters.  You can affect the difficulty of each war encounter by how you choose to approach it as well.  Rush in and take on the harder enemies to spare your army?  Take a cautious approach and let your army take the brunt of the forces so your own battles are less stressful?  There's a handful of possibile approaches that further alter your experience.  And don't let the simplicity of the combat statistics fool you, there's a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥to think about for every battle.
For everyone who's had the opportunity to learn the battle system via multiplayer battles in Factions, it's second nature already, but for all newcomers...there's a lot of subtle things that matter in very major ways.  Positioning is key.  Killing vs crippling a target can vastly affect momentum swings.  Effective use of willpower can clutch out an entire battle.  Sometimes letting a few allies actually die is exactly what you need to do to win.  There's a lot of forethought that can be applied and number crunching is crucial.  Can it be brutal at times?  Absolutely.  But it's never unfair.
So, let's sum this all up.
-Do you value transparency in choices?
-Do you like to know exactly what's going to happen before you do anything?
-Do you usually follow a walkthrough when playing through a game for the first time?
-Do you reload whenever a character permanently dies?
-Do you get frustrated when you can't just kill everything in your way?
Sorry, game's probably not your cup of tea.
-Do you like thinking ahead to predict outcomes?
-Do you like learning how to manipulate a system to your advantage?
-Do you value strategy over action?
-Do you like role playing and value decision making?
-Are you capable of taking responsibility for poor choices?
If these are the case, be prepared for an amazing experience you'll never forget.
With that said, this game gets my full recommendation.  I also encourage anyone interested to give The Banner Saga: Factions a try first, since it's free and will let you experience the battle system to your heart's content.

Mirror's Edge is a somewhat experimental FPS/wallruning/punching dudes in the face/artsy/this is way too many ♥♥♥♥ing slashes game that, at the best of times (the first 2-3 hours) is a fun filled, action packed blast to play through, and at the worst of times (pretty much the rest of the game) a boring chore that you have to force yourself to play through. If you want a quick review, I'd say get it to play through the first 4 hours, then stop playing, uninstall, wait 4 or 5 months, re-install and finish.
But, for those who want a bit longer of a review:
Mirror's Edge, at it's core is about freerunning around on top of buildings while being chased by the police. However, there are elements of First Person Shooting, as well as some jumping puzzles (which I will talk about both later).
The Good:
The freerunning in this game, is downright the best I have ever experienced in a first person game. The controls, while really janky with key/button binding. Are suprisingly tight and responsive. There have been very few times where I felt like Faith (The game's protagonist) failed to respond to one of my actions. One of the great things about this game, especially early on is that it really gives you a feeling of choice and freedom in where you go even though, you are constantly stuck on a linear path. They do this by designing many of their levels like links of chain where you are opened up to a small area to have some area of freedom, and whichever direction you go ends up with you going through a small bottleneck to take you to the next area. While this sounds awful when explaining it, it really is good at fooling you that you have an element of choice.
When running around, this game gives you a fantastic sense of momentum as you hear the wind whipping across your ears as you jump from building to building, and the corners of your vision become slightly blurred. While the combat can get in the way of this at times, luckily you can do a slide kick which allows you to keep at least some of that momentum.
The graphics, while certainly dated by this point, have a nice artsy asthetic to them.
Also, the soundtrack, while often times very minimalist is pretty nice to listen to
The Bad:
The combat is one of my central complaints with the game, and later on it really ruins a lot of your fun. At first, the combat seems really fluid and interesting, but it quickly turns into a game of you running up to a guard, standing still, waiting for him to attack you, then parrying his attack. This really disrupts the flow of things in the game because the further you get into the game, the more you are forced into this combat where you have to stand almost completely still and wait for them to attack you. Now, they did try to counteract this by adding guns to the game. However, guns feel woefully unpolished to the point to where one has to wonder why they didn't drop them entirely and just focus on making the hand to hand combat better. Not only does aiming a gun feel horribly awkward, but they also slow you down immensly, once again, breaking the flow of the game.
And, the further into the game you get, the more restrictive the levels become. At first, you start out on rooftops climbing fences, and jumping from roof to roof, but later on you start seeing many more indoor areas with only one singular path to take. Not only this, but the ever increasingly rare outdoors sections are disrupted by snipers and electrified fences that only serve to waste your time as you look for a way around them. Not only this, but you start to see, long, boring jumping puzzles start to emerge. These are an exercise in frustration as the game doesn't really like pointing you in the direction you're supposed to be going. So you end up mindlessly running up every single surface in the room until you are lucky enough to grab onto the right object.
And lastly, the story is simply atrocious. By the end I genuinely stopped caring about what was happening. The only thing that they use to convey the story are short 1-2 minutes long cutscenes between 1-2 hour long levels. It is far too easy to just forget what you are doing in this game and just try to have fun jumping around from wall to wall.
The Conclusion:
Mirror's Edge is a good albeit flawed little gem that deserves your attention, but can't really hold it. Definitely worth playing, but I'd recommend doing it at a friend's house rather than buying it.

No-one needs this game. It is entirely unessential. It is, however, pretty fun.
This is a top-down third person shooter, and, most importantly, the mechanics work pretty well. It's fun to shoot the many different monster types, especially once you upgrade your weapons so you have a range of different strategies you can take. The game is fairly easy (and quite short, about 9 hours), and if one part feels too hard then it's time to work out another strategy, at which point it'll probably become quite easy again. I do like the variety this provides, though, with the stealthy bits being particularly fun but rather short.
The graphics in-game are not so awful that it takes you out of the game, and there's a nice use of light and shadow, which improves the atmosphere. The music is absolutely awful, the kind of dross that Eastern European rock kids toss out when they first get access to a synthesiser. You can turn it off but it'll come back on during cut-scenes. The cut-scenes are pretty painful as it is, with terrible voice acting by the bland characters advancing a forgettable, and ultimately, nonsensical story. I do quite like the back-story you pick up by reading computer terminals dotted around the map, although a lot of it is fairly poorly written.
I should say that I didn't come across any bugs, apart from one room where the cut-scene at the end showed I should have endured some bullet hell and in fact I got one measly alien I finished off straight away then wandered around aimlessly for a few minutes. Sometimes if you accidentally do things in the wrong order then you might miss part of the story, but I'm pretty sure it won't be too big a loss. The friendly AI is bearable, if a little annoying when they get in your way, but at least they can't die and will attract enemy fire - although you can argue this brings you out of the reality of things a bit.
In short, it's worth it if it's on sale for a quid or whatever, but you have to wonder if you want just another game clogging up your steam library. It is, however, a nice little game that is fun whilst it lasts.
I cannot understand just how lucky we are, to be living in times where games like this, Grim Dawn, and Divinity 2 exists at the same time! It really is the golden age of CRGPs!

If you buy the Deluxe Edition DLC, you get the Magika Wizard, a character with a better passive skill advantage than most other (see next point) characters. Around level 15, you unlock the Developer Player Characters, self-inserts that have even better passives, making whatever current party you're using seem feeble in comparison.
Also around this time, you'll notice your strength isn't getting you as far as it did in the beginning, so you go to buy gear. Only, the blacksmith, by default, has a 30-some percent chance at actually crafting the item you pay him for. So, either you toss bags of money at the him, praying that he succeeds (because of course he doesn't reimburse you), or you get grindstones, items that let you "level him up". It takes around 2000 grindstones at 25 gold apiece to have him reach 100%. That's 50,000 gold. At level 15, you might gain 200 per fight.
Oh, but what's this? You can buy gold in-game for real money! Of course you can. Sadly, this game really was designed as a cash-hungry iOS game first and foremost. 4/10, for the initial hour or two of fun before the grind.

Overall this is a pretty decent game. The story is massive (the dev clearly cares about this), and there is great attention to the details of the backstory, dialogue between characters, and lore that can be found around the game.
  For me the battling is the best part. While it is not without its problems (sometimes tricky to pick the correct enemy - units pass through each other), in EA status it is clearly already in good form. It is tense and have genuinely felt my heart race to survive the onslaught.  Took me a few battles to get used to the mechanics…you really do have to make use of slow time, and be tactical, which is satisfying. I understand there are more battle modes to come, so looking forward to that.
Graphics look great, particularly when you have loads of enemies in battle, and I only ran into a frame drop once while running through the first proper level of the tower. (I am running it on Ultra settings though at 3440x1440 on a fairly decent card so not a surprise). I love the use of light and shadows in exploring, and understand this is to improve further. Use of particles is great. Visually it pops very well.
Audio is decent. Sound design is clear enough and helpful in battle, though some things are missing (here’s a noisy waterfall, there’s a silent one) - and I turned all the levels up in the settings. Music is good  to keep you playing, though I wish there was more orchestra, and sometimes it needs to have more punch. Particularly going in or out of battles, so you actually feel impending danger or success!
I think there is a lot of detail to the leveling up of heroes, inventory, skills etc which I was left to discover for myself. The city ‘menu’ idea is good and clearly shows the dev cares about connecting it all together with the backstory - will be interesting to see where the story goes. It’s promising a lot.
From what I understand from the dev, this is going to be a huge game in terms of content, and it is already well on its way.  In over 4 hours playing I only got to end of the tower’s first floor, so still got 3 more to go just in this current EA build! The dev is clearly committed to the game based on the responses here, so looking forward to seeing how much more it grows.

By turns sweet and funny, the narration and characters are reminiscent the best kind of fairy tales.  Our hero is "Reynardo" the scoundrel (and a fox with a sword), who gets to live his entire adventure over and over until he gets it right.  He's wisecracking and flawed, and the choices you make definitely matter.  You keep what you learn and find on each playthrough, and even when you repeat the same map, you usually have a lot of new paths and changes to the plot based on what you've already learned.  For example, when you learn to use your grappling hook, you can use it to leap to new platforms, and you can craft several different colorful swords that double as keys, letting you into new places.  Sometimes the same map is completely changed by what you learn about the story on earlier playthroughs.
The arcade-game part is pretty simple, with some easy puzzles and neat combo moves.  Even though it warns you at the start that you need a twin-stick gamepad, I played it just fine with the mouse.  The combat is partly depending on your RPG stats and what swords you make, but mostly it's about timing and good gameplay.  You can win almost any fight without a scratch if you play well, but it's also easy to get massacred if you play poorly.  Combat moves include picking things up and throwing them, grappling hooks, zipping forward, blocking, and attacking, among other options.  It's fast-paced but being clever pays off:  you are a fox, after all.
There are some bugs, including random slowdowns and places where you get stuck in the landscape.  I found that swinging the sword helped me get out of those, because you step when you slice.  Likewise, I kept getting major slowdowns when a big dragon-head door opened, but shooting the grappling hook seemed to unfreeze the screen.  Despite that, I am having a wonderful time and I already feel I've gotten $15 of pleasure out of it after 5 hours of playing.  Yes it's pretty short, but for me at least it was an experience worth having.  It deserves to be discovered by a wider audience.

The idea of playing through separate stories with completely different branching paths sounds cool until you realize that some of them (Or, at least the ones I've played, and I played quite a few!) are just repeating the same levels (especially the last one) in the same way, just with a different narration. The voiceovers are honestly just a poor man's attempt at Bastions, not bad, but they lack the sexy voice and wit that made it especially enjoyable in Bastion. The combat is comparable to Batman's counter fest but to it's credit it does get more fun when they introduce more enemies and abilities the further you get, but once again it's nothing like Bastion in terms of enemy variety and expansive weaponry and it seems you're only sticking with one weapon (a sword) that has different effects the whole way. I've been told that there was supposed to be some kind of special mechanic about the music dynamically changing as the story went on, but I've never noticed because the music itself was not particularly memorable. The artwork was honestly pretty gorgeous at times although it did slow down in some situations, but I take what I can get with a GTX 750 ti. Still, the only graphical presets you get are: Low, Medium, and High. Very limited.
Take what I'm saying with a grain of salt though as I've only put in three hours so far, and I'm thankful that Valve accepted my refund request. If you think you can stomach redoing the same brown battleship level in almost the same exact way for the fourth time, then this game might be up your alley. Otherwise, just play Bastion.

This game has many terrific aspects about it but there is one thing that shines the most - its marvellously executed co-op play. We've been playing the game with my wife for quite some time and we are having a blast. First of all, the ability to create a character, customize both skills and appearance and meaningfully roleplay and interact not only in the game world but also between the characters themselves - well, this is something we don't see often if ever. And then there are moral choices that contribute to your character's personality (which in turn provides usefull bonuses to stats and skills), simple but cleverly constructed way to solve players decision conflicts and thoroughly enjoyable banter between your ingame avatars. Add a vivid world, original mythology, interesting setting and a storyline with enough mysteries and twists to keep you involved - and you have a game that's transcends the boundaries of the genre to become something that I might recommend everyone to try. Moreso if you have a willing friend or that special someone to share your experience with.

Should you buy Antichamber? Yes
Is Antichamber a cool game? ♥♥♥♥ yes
Can I recommend Antichamber to somebody looking for a video game? Ehhh
Now, Antichamber is a program you download with the intent of "playing" it. I guess by that definition, it is a video game. But if you look at video games as an art or media form, the definition falls apart. What you CAN call Antichamber is a cool showcase of programming tricks with cute little tidbits of wisdolosophy sprinkled in, in a complete package that lends itself to a flawless, fulfilling experience. However, there's no plot, no context, and the necessitation of having to go to the menu (even if you're actually playing when you're in the menu, it's still the menu scre- uh, room!) really breaks any feeling of continuation, of having gone through it as one, singular experience. Don't get me wrong, I liked filling up my map and turning big squares into little squares, but at the end of the day it really is just a bunch of novel puzzles tied together in one big map that is yet never intended to have been finished in one, continuous go. And that just kills some fundamental part of playing and enjoying a video game for me
Don't get me wrong, I loved playing this♥♥♥♥♥♥ But know what you're getting into, alright? It definitely leaves you wanting

Ys 1 and 2 are two great story lines patches around a unique and rashly designed, but altogether satisfying fighting system that allows you to auto-attack your opponents by hitting their "bubbles", hit spots. Essentially split up into two games, the two games actually rate differently from each other, with the second game likely to be your favorite.
First, Ys 1 is a good game with a great story, it just gets pulled down by the inconsistent boss fights that were more from a lack of game design. Essentially, at least two bosses require the kind of patience of a Jedi Master because the controls and the gameplay are so inconsistent. Still, there are plenty of laughs to here, and I liked the way Reena is built in the game.
And yet, Ys 2 is amazing comparatively. Not only are the fighting mechanics improved, but throughout the game they change accordingly to the story. Compared to Ys 1, Ys 2's battles feel more mature and feel more satisfying in victory. Furthermore, the story is fantastic in Ys 2, with amazing detail for everyone you meet. Even the monsters you fight have things to say, and I was really impressed.
Ys 2 is without a doubt a masterpiece and together the story fits perfectly in a book or movie (there are some shows, but it was early Anime and not much effort is given). I loved how the game pulled me into the story, made me feel nervous and desperate as Adol races towards the top of a tower in one of the focal points of the game.
Likely, you'll beat Ys 1 and call it conquered, but Ys 2 will be the game you will nostalgically remember and play again. A fantastic series that was waylaid by its own mechanics in the beginning, Ys 1 and 2 stand out as fine examples of superior JRPG story-telling, and really feel in many ways like your watching the events unfold in front of you.

I think FTL is probably my favorite new game I played this year, I absolutely loved this game. FTL is pretty much Star Trek: The videogame, but without the license. You manage the crew and systems of a starship while exploring the galaxy and fighting aliens. The gameplay sessions of FTL are typically short, you play until you die. So depending on your luck, skill, and familiarity with the game, a session can last between 15 minutes to maybe 2 hours.
What kept me playing this game again and again is that everything in a play session is randomized: The layout of the galaxy is different each time, the encounters you’ll experience are different each time, and the weapons and upgrades you’ll get are different each time. Each upgrade you get will likely change your battle strategy and tactics too, so it never feels like you’re doing the same thing over again. Plus completing certain achievements or sidequests in the game can unlock other starships you can use on your next playthrough that have totally different weapons and playstyles, so it kept me coming back for more. It really has some pretty brilliant game design.
FTL is also a fairly difficult game overall. There are currently only two difficulty settings: “easy” and “normal”. I probably would have labeled them “normal” and “hard”, but whatever. My only real knock on this game is that success in FTL can be dependent on which encounters you get, which is somewhat luck based. A few unlucky encounters in a row can be crippling, especially on normal(hard) difficulty. It’s also not that pretty of a game to look at either, but for an indie game made by a team of only two people, that’s to be expected. If you go and watch gameplay footage of FTL on YouTube, you’ll see what I mean.
But don’t let its looks scare you off, I found FTL to be an excellent game. I think most gamers can enjoy this game, but I’d highly recommend it to fans of challenging strategy games or fans of Star Trek who’d like to see an actual good Star Trek game. I also hear the creators are releasing a free expansion pack with new weapons, ships and scenarios in the near future, so I’m pumped to play more FTL when that comes out.

One of the first PC games I ever played as a kid, and loved immensely. A simple RPG with an equally simple combat mechanic: no button-mashing or commands, just run around and bump into enemies. Direction and angle are the only factors involved.
The updated version gives this game a whole new life and feel. What was once before a barebones plot akin to the games of the late 80s (here's a paragraph of exposition, now go be a hero) is now a storyline you can follow and become involved in. Cutscenes and NPC movement add to the narrative, and a few NPCs—and even some items—that were once inconsequential have purpose to the story. And all the NPC now have little stories of their own. The monsters have a 'bestiary' as well now, and you're encouraged to fight them more to learn all there is to know about each one.
The graphics and sounds are both greatly improved, giving it a feel of a later-generation game. Even the simple combat is improved with the addition of sword-slashing animations and SFX, and enemy death animations. Rings can be swapped with a press of a button, you can toggle the display of stats and equipment (or turn them off completely), and there's even an option to turn off the blood effect, if you want the game to be more kid-friendly. Also, the controls are now configurable with 'righty' and 'lefty' options, one giving you the classic NumPad/arrow key movement and the other the now-standard WASD movement.
The only downside, and I hesitate to call it that, is that like many other old 'remastered' games, it removes the inherent advantage of hardware lag and makes some gameplay elements harder than the original. For this remake, it's mostly in the boss fights. While a couple of them are actually *much* easier than the original, the rest are significantly harder and rely on luck a little more than is fun. This is especially true for the final boss, which is now a 99% luck-based bullet hell DPS race with an instant death factor. To be fair, it's the same exact fight as the original, but the original's hardware limitations at least gave you a fighting chance. However, the remake has introduced difficulty levels (though personally, I can't even begin to imagine beating the final boss on Nightmare), so you can make those tough boss fights a little easier.
All in all, a great older title that paid for itself many times over in every way, and a fun nostalgia trip to boot. If you're at all a fan of the old school JRPGs, Ys Chronicles is well worth picking up.

It may only be early access at this point, but the game deserves massive props. On first playthrough, there are scenarios that are placed that will try to deceive you and force you to use your better judgement. Using your judgement incorrectly can force you to kill otherwise 'mostly' innocent NPCs (Julius & Helen in Arkovia for example). Things are not always what they seem with the setups.
The class system is brilliant for an ARPG, two characters playing the same class-combo can end up entirely different depending on playstyle. It's a fairly new take on things that ARPGs have been building on for decades now; For example, two Blademasters (Soldier+Nightblade) can end up with one being a two-handed using tanky warrior type, while the other ends up more like a dual-wielding assassin with an arsenal of area effect abilities at their hand. All the skills are fairly decent and there isn't a wrong way to build your class --and if you feel you have built it 'wrong', you get a second chance with skill resets whenever you want.
The game is also very fluid. Other than the given glitches that will most likely be fixed in full release, I have no complaints about this game.

Mirror's Edge is a first person Parkour game developed by DICE in 2009. I don't know if this is “the first Parkour game ever developed”, but it is the first I've ever played, and I suspect it can earn its place as one
the first and one
the good ones.
You play as the Protagonist named “Faith”...
Faith is part of a rebel group that has risen up against the oppressive ruling government which monitors all communication within this city,
Faith is a “runner”, runners are individuals who act as couriers that carries messages around the city. Runners see the world in a different way; where one person might see a dead end, a runner see's opportunities to climb, jump, and vault to get to their objective.
Mirror's Edge has one extremely strong selling point: First person Parkour. Have you ever wanted to jump off a building
? Have you ever wanted to travel a zip line from a skyscaper? Mirror's Edge is for you!
There are various types of obstacles that you'll face throughout the game, the game teaches you how to deal with each one by going through a “training” session before you start the game. This training is skip-able but I suggest you get through it... but I'll be honest, I probably spent more time on the training then the first level. I could not master the “turn-around-wall-jump”, every time I missed the game would force-ably restart my attempt.
At this time there are no steam achievements for Mirror's Edge, however on the Xbox there are 50 Achievements, so it's possible sometime in the future Mirror's Edge might have achievements, but at this time (08/03/15) there are no achievements.
There might not be achievements for Mirror's Edge, but there are time trials that you can complete against your friends on, unfortunately they're not sync-ed with steam leaderboards, so you would need to add your friends in game via Origin account.
Mirror's Edge is priced at $19.99, I completed this game on Normal difficulty in 7 hours. I want my games to go an hour for every dollar spent... If you go by that standard you should wait for this game to go on sale.
However if you have the money, this is an excellent Parkour game that you definitely should give a try at some point, regardless of cost.
To recap... Story: Okay, Gameplay: Excellent + Parkour, Achievements: Not available at this time, Price: a bit high.

I loved the first 2 Seasons of TWD games and I've been a fan of the comic series for over 6 years.
I can't recommend this because it feels a bit like a badly optimized cash-in with nothing at stake emotionally and it seems to borrow very heavily from the 2 previous seasons.
The dialogue choices you are given don't result in what you're trying to do; if I was given some real choices in these situations I could have stopped a lot of the following unpleasantness quite easily.
So, things that TWD game fans liked:
-Engaging characters
-Time to wander around an environment a bit and chat with people aimlessly to know them better
-Episodes being a good length but not too long
-Choices feeling like they actually matter to some extent
-Characters ‘remembering that’ actually meaning something.
-Not feeling the game is completely on rails with some window dressing to give the illusion of free choice.
... Yeah this one has none of those things.
If you read the comic you'll know how tough Michonne is already (and if she comes back from this venture or not)... at times this game feels like it's going in a Metroid: Other M direction where a strong female character HAS to be weak on the inside due to maternal instincts... it can work but it doesn’t work at all here really.
In this case, Michonne has the same basic hallucination elements about fifteen times an episode (which feels like once every five minutes) and after a while seems to be for padding the time of the game rather than adding anything interesting, by episode 3 I was groaning every time it started.
It's not all bad; there was some effort obvious in the game and the voice acting is pretty good and there's some nice scenic camera work and shots ... which is nice when the game’s FPS is actually above 20 and it’s had its one-or-two-times-an-episode-twenty-second-hang over and done with.
TellTale can't just sit on their previous success and make half-arsed things that vaguely resemble that success and expect it to work forever, people will wise up eventually and then what?
Here's hoping they're going to be making Season 3 better optimized, with updated graphics, animations and with actual choices.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is essentially a choose your own adventure game, but with a heavy focus on the narrative story and fluid combat system. It was almost as if you were experiencing Groundhog Day until you get it right.
Based on the choices you make, different stories take place. Most of the choices will inevitably lead to death in one way or another, but the narrative does a good job at making you think that this time, you might be on the right path to destiny. The stories you experience will give you clues or ‘truths’ that help you make the appropriate decisions to succeed.
The narrative reminded me a little bit of Bastion, but I liked the narrative better in Path of Destinies than I did in Bastion. In Path of Destines, the narrator reacts to what you’re doing and makes snide remarks, references to other games, and other cheesy puns. I didn’t think they were spammy or overdone, and I found them humorous at times, and I got a kick out of some of the comments. However, some people might not enjoy the snide remarks or appreciate them.
The combat reminded me of a super simple and dumbed down Batman Arkham style combat. Your successful attacks and counters add up on your combo streak, but there wasn’t any cool finishing moves to activate as combo steak gets higher. If you wanted to add some variation to the combat, you could also dash around, throw, and grapple hook enemies.
There were 4 swords that could be crafted with unique activated abilities. Using the abilities costs energy, but I usually just saved my energy in case I needed to heal. These swords also unlock special doors for hidden chests that contain gems you can equip. As you defeat enemies, you also gain xp, and level up to unlock skill points. Between obtaining new skill points, and gems, the combat gets even easier. Still, I really enjoyed the combat, even though it wasn’t very difficult.
At first, I really liked the choose your own adventure format, but after discovering about 6 truths, and finishing the proper story line, I found it got much too repetitive. I really wanted to go back and play the rest of the story paths, but before you make each decision, you have to sit through the opening dialog, and you can’t skip it. I got really bored of listening to the same first few chapters, just to make a separate choice going into the later chapters. I would liked to have been able to just skip entire chapters that I already experienced all the decisions for, especially since I already beat the game.
Each playthrough took 45-60 minutes, and I really did like the game a lot for the first 6-7 hours I played. I continued to play for a couple hours after that, and I probably would have kept playing to discover all the truths, but not being able to skip all the things I had already fully experienced was much too tedious to sit through over and over again. It was still a decent purchase though, and I don’t regret it.
