Let me rule out the pros and cons of this episodic game, without specifying them (no spoilers):
Episode 1 gives you an introduction to your friends, and what your motive is. Pete is who seems to be the crew's leader, he wants to find his friends. Instead, you come across a duo, and stumble onto something bigger.
Episode 2 carries on what you stumbled onto in episode 1.
Episode 3 gives you the big finale.
One thing I dislike about this game is the constant "halucination" that Michonne faces, as it interrupts the main narrative of the game with a side-narrative that isn't as important until the end-game choice.
Another thing is that Pete's "friends" that he was looking for, are not even in the game. And that's no spoiler, they just.. weren't mentioned. No dialogue about it post-episode 1, nothing.
Hell, the crew isn't even mentioned after episode 1 until the end of episode 2, and even then; you don't see them until episode 3.
I feel like the game doesn't make the most out of the experience, gameplay and story along with character development simply because it's three episodes long. I was able to complete episode 1 in under 45 minutes, episode 2 and 3 I took my time on, however.
My playtime is based off of pausing, exploring, reading every piece of dialogue I could, and replaying episode 1 before episode 2 was released. So don't be fooled by the 3 episodes' length of playtime being long due to my hour count on this game.
I would recommend this game if you are a Telltales fan, as the dialogue is interesting, a new story is fun, and the introductions to each episode are fantastic! I also love one of the 'main' characters, Sam, and for one reason or another; she reminds me of Clementine, so you might want the game if you're looking for a favorite character you'd catch onto after EP 1.
It's easy to run, has a few freezes every so often though, I've witnessed a couple FPS drops, I feel like TWD Season 1 was a better playthrough in terms of how well it ran on my computer.
CPU: Intel i5 Core 4690k @ 3.5GHz.

As a Telltales TWD game fan, I will give this a thumbs up. But that's because I'm biased, though it is a shame as I would have expected more from this game.

Great old-school style RPG.  I'm really enjoying it, certainly more than Torment 2, even more than  Pillars of Eternity actually.  Come to think of it, I don't believe I have had this much fun playing an isometric RPG since the original Neverwinter Nights and that is high praise coming from me.
The combat system is fun, similar to RTwP you see in Pillars of Eternity, but instead of pausing the action completely, it slows down to a crawl when you activate the tactics mode.  I'd say the combat requires good tactics and reactions even on normal difficulty.  I've wiped a couple times on bosses, but  overall I'd say Normal is challenging, but not too difficult. There is a good variety of enemy types with varied abilities and your party members each have multiple skills that they can modify with different properties.   So far (about 1/2 through the first act) I found the story engaging and interesting, and I'm enjoying it more than PoE.  The story is mainly told through conversations between your party members and various books and notes scatered around the levels, but there are occasional cut-scenes during important moments.  As for the visuals, the level design is really great for an Infinity engine game IMO, vibrants colors, water effects, lighting effects and overall good variety in tilesets.  The characters models leave a bit to be desired though, they are somewhat blocky and have no visual customization besides weapons (update: while individual pieces of armor do not show, there will be 5 skins per character based on the quality/tier of armor they are wearing).
I would highly recommend this game if you are into old-school RPGs like Baldur's Gate, IWD, Arcanum and Neverwinter Nights.  I am certainly enjoying it far more than other recent efforts to bring this genre back such as PoE, Torment 2, and Divinity:OS.  It is still in Early Access, but the level of polish even now is pretty good, I've found a couple minor bugs, but they are getting squashed quickly with frequent updates.  Presently, only the first act is available (~25 hours), with 3 acts planned, the devs indicate that the final length will be around 50 hours, which at the current price is a steal for a game of this quality.

No quest markers is the best thing that this game has. Some people would probably put it among their cons list but I wouldn't. Even when I played Skyrim, I used a mod the simply switched off the compass. In these games, and in order to live the best experience possible, it is always better to indulge yourself in the lore as much as possible. Make yourself one with the game, live the game, make that world yours, only then can you get focused enough to enjoy every bit of it. If you see yourself in what I just said, Divinity: Original Sin is definitely for you.
I will say that this game is not for everyone, but I'm pretty sure that every Baldur's Gate fan or Ultima fan would enjoy it. The level of detail in the game is astonishing, you can almost interact with everything in the game. When I first entered Cyseal (the first City) I kinda felt depressed, compared to all the similar games I have played, it felt waaaaaaaaay toooo big, but spending more than 18 hours on the same map didn't feel as depressing, on contrary, I don't want to leave this place at all. The combat is pretty fun and not reptitive. Don't worry about the class you choose, don't waste too much in character creation. If you see my character, he'a a rogue, Assassin, warrior, geomancer, Witchcraft master, and a healer at the same time. There are no limits to the combos you can make in the game. Your infeluence in the game progression is also very impactive, depending on your decisions, conversation choices, alot changes.
I wouldn't say that the game is perfect though, I can note a few bugs that are still in the game. For instance, going through an open door can be a real pain sometimes, you would have to close the door first and then reopen it again. Entering building is also not very smooth, have to click very close to the walls or doors to reveal the interiors. Also it would be helpul to have a toggle item reveal control button instead of having to hold ALT to reveal the environment, but let's just add that to it being lore-friendly. last bug I want to note is that sometimes the camera would go very far away, like very zoomed out, and the only way to get it to normal view is to quicksave. That would get you zoomed in and zooming out after that brings it to normal view.
Nevertheless I'm very impressed with where we have come, great game, I highly recommend it.

Do you enjoy simple, yet slightly addictive gameplay? What about in-depth, branching story lines with multiple endings? Or endearing, relatable characters that really seem to grow on you? Well then, you're in luck, because this game is for you!
The game is structured in such a way that you play through five chapters, each containing a variation of exploration and combat encounters, and then receiving an ending. Once you've viewed the ending, you have two choices. You can say, "well, that was short and hardly worth the money," or you can do what the game intends and...play through it again.
Yep. You heard me. You play through another five chapters and that's it. Game Over. Now, this sounds boring and rather pointless, yeah? Here's the thing. At the end of every chapter, you get to make a choice. The choice you pick determins how the story branches. Save a character? Kill a character? Use an artifact? Every single choice leads you to a different path, and with each playthrough, more revelations are made regarding the story, and slowly things start to piece together. After several playthroughs, you can unlock the "true ending." That is, if you've made the right choices. And don't worry, the game will tell you upon a new playthrough which choices you've picked before. There seem to be over 20 different endings to the game, with each being unique.
The characters themselves are a hoot. You really get a sense of developement through the game as the game's narrator reads aloud all the dialog, like an audio book. Speaking of the dialog, I personally really enjoyed it. Random quips and whatnot from the narrator really add flair to the game.
The one downside is the actual gameplay. I'm sure some will find it repetive, boring, and tiresome. Mash X until things die. No, really. You do get some skills and abilities that spice things up, but in the end it's "walk into an encounter, kill enemies." Still, as you progress through the game and go through multiple play throughs, the combat does get a bit challenging. Despite the repetiveness, I really enjoyed the combat and found every encounter was fun. Oh, and speaking of abilities and skills, your level/skills DO carry over from every playthrough, so you're not starting from scratch every time. Also, there are some areas early on that are inaccessable unless you have a certain key item, which you can only get later in the game. It mixes up the levels just enough to keep you coming back for more.
In the end, Stories: TPoD is one of the better games I've played as of late, and I would highly suggest it. It's well worth the price tag.

Coming after Moon Hunters with ambitious narrative ideas, I feel like a broken record for saying I admire this game as a failed experiment. Only I don't know what they were trying to accomplish.
Upon first-impressions, the gamelay is Bastion with an Arkham style combat system, and yet the system is more shallow. The game boasts of its choice system in shaping future events--which is mostly true--however, the gameplay doesn't offer enough variation to keep you playing. And even when its novel concept shines, there are mistakes made that make the reward of the "good" ending feel cheap.
The best thing I can say is the game is functional and satisfying (for a while). Aside from the optomization issues on higher-end settings and some bugs that may impede your overall enjoyment, nothing about the gameplay is broken or bad. It's such a shame that it probably won't keep you playing to complete the whole journey.
The strangest complaint I have is that the game feels like it's in the wrong genre.
The trailer and description of STPD is one of learning from your mistakes in Reynold's quest to be a hero--and live to tell the tale. With roughly 45 mins to an hour and a half of a playthrough, the game is structured in a bite-sized format. The game encourages huge replaybability with 20+ hours of content. And the accumulation of your previous actions and newfound abilities will influence later playthroughs--storywise and gameplay.
Maybe I am alone but this game seems perfect to be a rouge-lite. It wouldn't have to be brutally hard, maybe a casual-friendly one that emphasizes replaying for the narrative, but the game's structure would better suit that type of genre. And this is said by someone who detests rogue-lites.
The reason why I mention this idea is because some of the better qualities of roguelites would be to STPD's benefit. Specfically, procedurally generated environments as well as a diverse progression system, which are the two biggest problems with the gameplay. STPD simply gets way too samey way too fast.
In total, there are seven environments that use the same level-layout across all playthroughs. Every playthrough involves tackling five of these areas in some player-driven order, which starts off with three choices that all lead to the final area of the game (which is always the same). Unlocking new swords can shape your paths through these levels, but only for small detours for loot. When you get all four swords, these environments offer nothing new for exploration.
Speaking of unlocking new weapons, it won't take you that long to get your full arsenal maxed up. It took me under four hours without grinding (including the Gems), and afterwards you'll avoid finding chests because Gems/Resources are all randomly given to you, not in specific locations. Like the environments, progression reaches a point of becoming a blur.  Only the skill-tree will offer you something to look forward to get, but it requires grinding.
Unfortunately, because of how the game is structured, you are expected to complete all 25 storylines with one character that carries over all your progression. There are no additional weapon types nor any difficulty modifiers to vary up either the gameplay or the difficulty. The result is that combat makes an otherwise novel approach to storytelling in games a chore to play.
Again, like with Moon Hunters, I find it hard to say a whole lot about the combat system because it's too simplified to stay interesting for what is a lengthy game (20+ hours). Unlike MH, STPD's combat is actually a good combat system.
Fighting boils down to being able to use your sword, grapple-hook and magical attack. You have a total of four swords which can either give you back health, boost your attack speed or do frost or fire damage. The grappling hook can be used to pull enemies in close, stun them or yank shields away. The sword can also do a parry manuever like Metal Gear Rising where you press the attack button in the direction of an oncoming attack, and the button can also be used to grab and throw enemies. Lastly, you have a dash manuever that can stun enemies.
Skill-points can be used that can provide additional benefits like being able to dash through shields or to do damage with counter-attacks or grabs. They offer enough of a visual change to your fighting that they are more than stat-changes, and with the excellent fighting animation they are a good incenitive to keep playing.
However, and what is the main problem, I have essentially listed the entire combat system there. For whatever reason the developers did not use all the buttons on a standard controller (no shoulder buttons or the left trigger). Not that I ever felt inequipped as I felt too powerful from the beginning to the end, even when I died. Death may even benefit you as you return with 50% health and energy.
It also doesn't help that for a simple fighting system there are only four mook varieties (one is only a stealthy enemy type) along with a super-form for them. Had the game kept adding additional enemy types like the first two runs, the replayabilty could have been tolerated with harder obstacles to make each playthrough more interesting.
Instead of fleshing out the combat system, however, the rest of the game's attention was focused on the narrative. Something I think is moderately a success of an idea.

As mentioned beforehand, this game's first impression is definitely one of Super Giant's style both of Bastion's art direction as well as narrator-voiced storytelling. I personally am happy to see other developers try their hands at the style, and STPD does the job adequately enough. If you can tolerate its sense of humor and expository writing.
STPD, like with Larian Studios, shares the same tongue-in-cheek writing quality that does its job to entertain you as you play as well as disarm you when things become grave. The trope-heavy, "so bad it's good" comedy is definitely not everyone's taste. However, it's hard to remember most lines as they are forgettable but I rarely ever heard a repeated phrase except at specific sections of the level.
The gist of STPD's storytelling idea is that you have to discover four hidden truths about related characters/items that will help Reynold figure out how he survives his adventure. Twenty-four out of the twenty-five stories are all "fail states", which isn't a spoiler as the trailer tells you this information.
Thankfully, you are not required to unlock them all. As soon as you have unlocked all four truths, you can then access the "Hero's Ending. It uses the information you learned to weave a story, pressumably of Reynold's invention, to make your own destiny. Had the game not explicty told you the solution the idea could've been something groundbreaking.
What confuses me is that each time the narrator butts in there is an icon that shows something relevant to a past truth. The game doesn't let you piece together the connections yourself. Instead, the correct series of choices are forced upon you. (Sometimes a choice can even result in a game-over that forces you to replace the previous level.)
I'm not sure why this was chosen but it ruins what could've been a reward to explore every scenario to solve the narrative like a puzzle from character studies and/or context clues. (Or at least more than four truths.)
You can't even make the correct series of options without finding all four truths first, so the "real ending" feels like a gimmick of an idea than an acheivable goal.
If that's too cryptic: I had fun in spite of the obvious flaws of its far-reaching goals (and I may have challenged the odds.)

It's hard to explain what XCOM: Enemy Unknown (XC:EU) is all about without playing it- it's a turn-based tactical shooter, but with strategic elements relating to base management, upgrades, research, unit loadouts, and preventing worldwide panic.
You take the roll of an international paramilitary organization called XCOM, tasked with repelling an alien invasion of Earth. While not in combat, you will build your base, weapons, armor, and manage your soldiers, research, and engineering. These tasks are punctuated by tactical missions where you fly your squad of soldiers out to stop abductions, raid UFO landing sites, quell 'terror' attacks on cities, and more.
If you start out on Normal difficulty (which you should), you may find that you get about halfway through the game and say to yourself "I think I've got the hang of this." Then you might start a game in Classic difficulty, and you will promptly get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you.
This is where the fun is, however. In Normal difficulty, you get some breathing room regarding the choices you make. Your soldiers will ascend to Colonel rank and become efficient alien killing machines. In Classic mode, your soldiers will die. Often. Each move must be carefully considered to balance keeping your soldiers behind cover, trying to flank the enemy while preventing them from flanking you, trying not to alert more aliens and become outnumbered, and using your soldiers' abilities wisely. Too many bad decisions will mean you simply don't have the manpower or resources to fight off the aliens, and you'll be forced to start over. I've had my entire squad wiped out on a mission. Part of the fun comes in learning from your mistakes and figuring out how to press on.
There are still WTF moments, though, like an alien one-shot-killing a soldier behind full cover from ridiculously far away, or one of your soldiers panics and blows another soldier's head off, or your soldier missing a shot that is 99% likely to hit (I've read posts about missing 100% shots). This makes it especially hard to play in Ironman mode, where you get one save slot and the game saves after every decision, keeping you from undoing any mistakes (or utter unfairness).
In short, this game is brutally challenging, stressful, and at times frustrating. It's still, however, one of my favorite games ever. The only thing keeping XC:EU from reaching true excellence is that it's buggy. You may decide to spare your soldiers a violent death and pull them back to the drop point to evacuate- except that the drop point is missing. I've also seen instances where cricially wounded soldiers fall off the map, or get pushed outside of the map's boundary so that your medics can't stabilize them. I've read that reloading the saved game can solve these issues, but these are still problems the developer is unlikely to address at this point. There's also some funny graphics hiccups, like shots through walls, or soldiers losing their hair during their death animation, and these do detract from the cinematic feel of the game. Another minor gripe is that there's maybe a dozen maps that get recycled as you play through, so the challenge of figuring out the best way to navigate a mission gets lost after a while.
All in all, I definitely recommend this game. It's brutal, addictive, and has amazing replay value.

KoPP is modeled after D&D gameplay. You play as a group of roleplayers sitting around a table, going on an adventure led by a dungeon master. No, really. The DM is actually there, narrating the quest. It’s a really unique RPG in its presentation, though not so much in its gameplay, which is a rather simple turn-based battle system.
The simplicity owes to the game's origins on mobile platforms, and this is why recommending KoPP is complicated for me: It still plays exactly like a mobile game, much better suited for playing in small intervals. Understandably, a lot of people don't expect that from a $10 PC game. If it was the same price as the mobile version ($3), maybe it could get away with its lack of depth. Not for this price.
It's also worth noting that there are microtransactions in the game. [Update: Not anymore. As of patch 2.09 (2014/02/14), they have been removed from the game.]. Also, some achievements are broken, and won't be fixed for a while. [Update: Also fixed in patch 2.09, I was able to obtain all of them.]
You may be wondering why I recommend the game after all. Very simple. I still enjoyed it. I'd play it while watching a stream or something, when I wanted to unwind and avoid ultra-complex games. In a way, I went through it with the mobile mindset, and this is the case in which I'd recommend KoPP, if you want a simple game.
Just don't get it for full price, even if you really want it. It's not worth it. Wait for a sale of at least 50% off.

Welcome to Ys,* a world filled with magic** and fun*** combat!
Serious time. This series started in 1989 on the PC-Engine, predeccesor to the TurboGraphX 16. Betcha haven't heard of either of those, have you? I grew up with a TGX, but i believe the PCE was Japan-only. *ahem* Now, these aren't the original games, obviously. This is Chronicles+. The steam version of Chronicles, which was originally released on the PSP, as a remake of the originals. there's also Ys I&II Eternal, Complete, and a (Terrible) DS version: Legacy of Ys.
If you've never heard of these games before, Ys is widely-known for it's balls-hard difficulty, bosses in particular. Unfortunately, the bosses in these two games aren't very fun. In Ys I, you get a
small window of attacking for all of them, save for two which you just have to tank all the damage for and hope you can out-damage them before they kill you.
Ys II is a bit better, though every boss
Can only take damage from
It's about as lengthy as you'd think.
Let's talk music, which is easily the best feature out of all of the Ys games. It kicks some serious♥♥♥♥♥ Give it a listen.
You also have diffrent options for the music, i might add. Heading into options, you can swap out your reorchestrated masterpieces for... er... the original PC-88 chiptunes? And the soundtrack from Complete, which is like a remix of the chiptunes, and actually sounds good! Like it came right out of a good SNES game.
But gameplay, oh boy...
If you're playing the series in chronological order and you just came here from Origins? Prepare for an♥♥♥♥♥whoopin', sonny. These games use a "Bump System". Which you will hate. It goes against all logic you'd expect of a gamer and it'll screw with your head by the end of this.
So what
this bump system? Well, you attack enemies by running into them. But if you don't do it off-center, you'll take damage. There is no attack button. You swing your sword automatically. This is PAINFULLY bad, especially in Ys I, as you have no other means of attacking. It's a big learning curve, but it's actually quite fun when you get used to it. When i moved to Oath in Felghana, i actually subconsciously started running into enemies.
Ys II handles this
For starters: You only take damage if the enemy is facing right at you when you hit them. this is a GODSEND. You can also attack diagonally, which is reaaaally helpful, and makes the system a lot more fun. There's also Magic, if you hate the bump system as much as i do. Fire magic, Light magic, Return magic, Alter magic, Time magic, and Shield magic.
The story is also great! Though there are a few plotholes if you've played Origin.
As well as others that i either can't recall or won't bring up here.
Overall, these are great games. I reccomend giving them a shot when they go on sale, but if you're in it for the story, play Origin first.

I'll say from the outset that this was a GOOD game but it fell short of being a GREAT game.
What it did right:
-Gorgeous design and presentation
-An Epic overall story and feeling
-Excellent and uniquely viking music
-Engaging turn based strategy combat system
-Not a game about getting 'uber' equipment and weapons but using combat tactics to win battles.
-Story-driven (linear but with enough sense of choice and consequence to feel you've made a difference)
-The feeling of randomness and adventure
-The feeling of survival and limited resources (part of the adventure feeling).
The combat:
Contrary to many other reviews, I quite enjoyed the turn based tactics, the randomness of each encounter, the strategy involved in choosing who goes first, the little reliance on items to make a substantial difference and all the other tactical dimensions including positioning and combining and configuring the strengths and weaknesses of each character's class.) This was a unique take on turn based strategy and i think the whole experience was very enjoyable without it being too complicated.
The 'adventureness':
This is clearly one of the strongest points of the game. Serendipitous events, challenging moral situations (ie do i help everyone along the way at the expense of food and clansmen? Do i shoot arrows into a crowd of rioters to control a city? :P), the feeling of uncertainty of any action (Do i eat these berries i found--they could be poisonous? :P)--these are all the things that create a feeling of adventure--a feeling of the unexpected. To those who are completionists or who enjoy more control and are annoyed at how you could not power up all your characters, have abundant resources, equipment or shag all the women to get picture cards--the game was likely intended that way. If you can't hack the adventureness of it all--then play some other game.
The story:
I agree the broad story is linear but i do not think this is a bad thing. You are pushed along across rolling new landscapes and there are 'landmark' events that are breath-taking and done very well. The small quests you do along the way, the choices you make-- personally inform how you imagine each character (is Hakon for example a blood-hungry barbarian who chases down his enemies or a quiet soldier or something entirely else?--this will determine how u lead his army.)
The only problem with the lack of pre-defining characteristics for each character is that there is no grounding as to what they're meant to be--how their character will impact upon the broad story, what their destiny is etc.  In essence, the game is story-driven, not character-driven and there is an imbalance in this regard.
What it needed to do to be a 'great' game:
-More cutscenes or mini-quests that establish character
This game clearly had the epic story arcs done very well--it is land rich in lore and history, at peril of invading enemy and deep in mystery and intrigue.

However i felt there could have been romance, betrayal, cowardice, heroic acts between the characters that give more depth to the gaming experience. More interaction was needed between the characters amongst all the 'adventureness' (see above).
-More character development:
It is clear that each arc had central characters who push the story forward and events transpire around them. However, it felt at times they were billboard characters with a written biography and all they were useful for was combat. Towards the end, it did feel rushed--characters were brought back together but with no true sense of how they might impact the story (ie Hakon and Ludin).
-Less linear story
The broad story being linear is fine. However, there could have been points in time, where not only one party was fighting one enemy. Multiple enemies in one battle could mean that you had to split your forces decisively to determine, for example, who was defending, who was attacking , who needed to split up to get supplies etc.
Possibly also more variety in gameplay was needed just to break up the 'moving caravan thing.' For example, rolling scenes within the towns with characters doing smaller quests.
OVERALL:
For an independent game (made by three developers?) this is an unexpectedly good game. It is a story-driven and linear game that is like reading a good book whilst imagining how each character will react to unfolding events (both epic and small) and tactically how each battle takes shape.
There is alot of potential to this game and that, i think, is a good thing. It is a short game so I'm giving this review with the expectation that this is an episodic game that will improve and diversify over each installment. For the first instalment, i think it sets the scene very well and i personally cannot wait for the next instalment. There are more lands to explore (Arberrang for example), no doubt more characters and interesting quests to be introduced. Highly recommended.

Saints Row started out as pretty much what we can call of "GTA Clone". If before we had a bunch of crazed fools trying to destroy a city, why not an entire game made just for that? Even though the game is made up of stupidty and ridiculousness, Saints Row is actually a good game.
I haven't played the previous releases, and as I don't really follow nor base my opinion on Gameplay videos and other people's reviews, I won't comment on what I do not know.
Either way, Deep Silver is known for releasing games filled with bugs and are only sorted months after released; And yes, the game sometimes bugs out and one does not know what is going on. - I went through it myself, even playing only several months after it's launch. However they weren't game-breaking bugs and never had to restart a mission, nor spend any time shouting and screaming annoyed at the game.
● Graphical wise, they are not really up-to-date nor can they really be compared to some of the previous generation's titles; but I actually like the game's graphical style! Granted I'm not usually one to care and totally base my opinion on a game's graphics. Graphics do NOT make a game good, okey? Okey!
● I enjoyed the Story, even thought I didn't understand it fully (and I still think Deep Silver could actually ship games with Portuguese Language possibility..). I really liked the humour part, really different from what I'm used to with games like GTA, which ended up becoming something quite serious, aiming for extreme reality.
●Regarding the Characters, I found them to be quite charismatic. I found them to be actual supports to a good narrative and not simply prop-adresses there just to be used - like in many other games.
There were times in which I wish I had played Saints Row: The Third (and I confess it's on my "To-Play List"..). I found the ending to be quite interesting and I am most certainly hoping for yet another Sequel to the story.
[SPOILER ALERT!!!! - SERIOUSLY!] I really LOVED that I ended up with the bad guy's head on my bare hands!
● The gameplay style of the game is also quite nice - plenty of features that are not really common on other games I've played - especially in certain Main Missions, such as Rescue, Text-Adventure, 2D Platforming and even Stealth!
Seriously.. there were times in which I thought to myself "Oh no they didn't!"; Because there are so many surreal things happening that we have to think to ourselves what goes in the mind of someone that thinks about this sort of things.
Being fully CO-OP capable is also one of the outstanding features I'd like to talk about. It's certainly way more amusing to play with a friend than alone
● Not to mention the Soundtrack - it gets to a point of having someone singing "Baby don't hurt me!", out loud at your ears and .. yeah - that's Saints Row for you! One gets to see the real side of the people you play with!
● And yes, before anyone steps forward and shouts that the game is "Too easy" and "Handhelds you" by giving you tons of power and bonuses in the first 20 minutes of the game - and the fact that you can pretty much wreck most enemies during the entire game's duration - some levels are actually tough to get through, especially if one isn't the best player around, or doesn't have help of a friend.
Honestly, I had to honor this game and distinguish it from all the other games I've played in the past. And even though I know plenty of people will disagree with me with the following Score I'll award it with - I'll only give you one advice: Play with a friend. Hopefully a goofy one! Then return to me and tell me what you thought about it now. - I have never laughed so hard at a game before, and I'll even go further and claim I prefer this "GTA Clone" to the actual GTA - but hey, I'll be the first one to admit they are two different games now.
Saints Row IV is certainly one of the best games I've played in my life.

Here's the TL;DR: Port of the PSP remake from the TG16 remake of the Sega release in 1987.
If you like the "Jousting" form of combat which made this "new" form of battle system new in the late 80's on Sega Master System, then you're in for a treat. The graphics and videos all transcribed from their original version perfectly, and the quests are in full-fledged happiness. The only problem I ran into was attempting to find out where all the keys went.
The first time I played Y's: The Vanished Omen, I was 10. I had hand-drawn maps for all the various caves and towers to help find my way around, and small hints to remember to grab the wings or mirror this boss... It was a time before people sent cat pictures to each other and spent days arguing over who obtained the greatest HP in SWAG.
Adol's questing also taught young me something else: that everyone in the village has a voice in the storyline, and even if people aren't the main character, sometimes the least important character offers the most information - and it's best to treat people equally.
Thankfully, the conversion process from Falcom kept 95% of the voices and music (oh man, the MUSIC...) in tact, and simply walking around the fields and various cities brought me back to a much simpler time in my own life, when rushing home off the bus and staring at a 13" color Quasar television on a rickety pile of Yellow Pages was the absolute highlight of the week.
Games like Y's, Phantasy Star, Warhammer, and Final Fantasy may still have influential portions in titles today, but nothing like the shape in the designing of those of us who played them until mom flicked the power breaker in the kitchen.

Civilization V is a game both loyal to the franchise, but also tweaks some certain elements to improvise something unique. Its amazing blend of beautiful presentation, addicting gameplay, crazy geography and historical paradox make it a title to be loved by both casuals and hardcore gamers.
will nuke you, giant mechas will raze your towns, your paratroopers will have to deal with 15th century pikemen and many, many more hilarious moments are sure to keep you busy for a good amount of time.
Starting off, you begin with a single settler in 4.000 BC and have to work your way up over the next 6.000 years or so. Watch and guide your humble and small nation to becoming a massive empire, building the world's greatest wonders and researching the greatest state-of-the-art technologies. There is no campaign, only an assortment of scenarios based on certain historical moments like the Crusades etc.
Visually, the game has aged beautifully since 2010. It's like a beautiful painting over google maps, with bright, flashy colors and an interesting amount of attention to detail. Zooming in to your resources reveals animals eating or running around, plus the animals are appropriate to each resource, like elephants for ivory, foxes for furs etc. For fans of
maps and battles, the game will be dissapointing (probably). Keep in mind though, that its turn-based nature eventually
the game to adapt.
As for the gameplay, that's the game's best moment. You have several ways to achieve victory like conquest, cultural supremacy, etc. Each nation is led by its greatest leader and has unique benefits that can aid you. For example, France has huge bonuses towards cultural victory while Germany has special units that aid to military victory.
, you can play in any way you want. But still, some things work better than others. If you seek a challenge, try a military victory with a cultural nation.
Civ merely borrows some elements and great personas from history and turns them into the bedrock you will step on to build your great nation and story. You can take the Aztecs and turn them to a fascist nation obsessed with world domination, or turn the Japanese to a peace-loving nation that only wants to build opera houses and other artistic buildings. You forge your own history in a world full of rivalry and each turn you take is another page in your book. And that's why Civ has such an endless replayability. You will never have enough of experimenting with the world's nations and the way you will conquer the world. The combinations, the paths, the strategies are endless and laid on your feet to choose what you want mostly.
On the downside, Civ V threw out of the window some things that made it, let's say,
. In Civ IV, you could force stuff on your nation as well as your enemies, like religion and politics. Instead, in Civ V, you got
as a resource, in order to spend it to
that give your civilization bonuses. For example, the
tree adds extra bonuses to your army, like extra experience from combat. It's an OK system, but I personally miss the sinister feeling of forcing my religion to my enemies because I was out to conquer their hearts and minds.
As for the
system, it's simply mediocre. You have far too few interactions with them, and while at first they may seem extremely helpful to be on your side, eventually they become nothing more but a state living with ancient technology and units. It's fun to become allies with a city-state behind your enemy's lines and watch them attack from their flanks, but that's the most useful thing they can do for you.
Eventually, this game is like a good old wine, worth every sip and it gets better as time goes by *cough*

I have minimal playtime with this program, so read my review with a pinch of salt.
As others have said, if your computer is already running games at 60 FPS with minimal/no lag then this program won't be much help. That's because it isn't a graphics enhancer, it diverts system resources towards the game instead of away from it. You can use said resources to higher your in-game graphics or texture qualities, but that's about it.
However, That doesn't mean the program is limited in functionality.
For those of us without beastly gaming PCs or lower-end laptops (and I'm part of the latter), the tiny FPS boost you gain from, say, marking your game as a higher-than-normal process mean a lot depending on what game you're playing ( I love fighting games, so FPS is especially important for me ).  Also, CPUCores is constantly recieving feedback and adjusting for bugs and glitches, fixing one of the most common problems for these types of software: stagnation.
With all these benefits, I'd recommend this software because it's able to improve a game's experience for minimal cost.
Tl;dr: Power diverter, not power giver. Good on small systems, useless on gaming rigs.

This game is awesome. If I had to apply a mathematical formula...
"Style" of Dust (anthromorph world) + Bastion + Shadows of Destiny + Shadows of Mordor = Stories.
Explanation:
Dust - Effectively an anthro world. Different anthros have appropriate personalities. Foxes are sly, perceptive, hares are mad, etc. This also means that there is a bit of the "simple, sickly sweet" aspect of that world as well. It's fine for me, but it might bother some people. In general, the game is very much like an anime, particularly when fighting the eye monsters.
Bastion: The Narrator describes what you're doing. On one playthrough, I didn't hear a single repeated phrase. I can't say the same for the rest of the game. Also, it's in the isometric fixed camera perspective. Also also, you keep character progression on each playthrough, including items.
Shadows of Destiny: For those of you who don't remember, Shadows of Destiny was a game about choices, and time travel. This isn't quite it, but in SoD, the main character uses knowledge of the future to affect the past and alter his future. Not quite the same thing here, but similar enough to the point where you can draw parallels between the two mechanics. Choices you make in the story are recorded and have obvious effects. It's very "Choose Your Own Adventure-y".
Shadows of Mordor - The game's combat mechanics are pretty similar to Shadows of Mordor, in terms of how a normal fight goes. Hitting things at the right time will increase combo count and damage; there's counters that stop enemies in their tracks, there's dodging, etc. One thing that this game does have that Shadows doesn't is a Hookshot. :D Hearing the character go "Get over here!" is pretty great.
Regarding the Narrator - The narration is a pretty large part of this game, so it feels fair to give a heads up about the Narrator. The guy is no Logan Cunningham, but he doesn't suck, either. In all honesty, the Narrator's voice occasionally reminds me of David Tennant or the Stanley Parable narrator, but that could just be the English talking. In any case, one of the things that I find interesting is that the Narrator tells the story "through" the characters. Basically, it's as if the Narrator is reading a storybook. Surprise. Meaning, he changes his voice depending on the character that's speaking. This works for some characters, but not for others. Of course, it could simply be said that it's as though he's a normal guy who's reading a book, so he might not get the voices exactly right every time.
Also, the Narrator does a pretty good job of actually voice acting. That is, he's not over the top, and he's not underwhelming, or hamming it up too much.
Pros:
Very interesting story mechanic / choices. - Ability to go back after playing through and making new choices is awesome.
Combat is decent. Sometimes it feels like it lacks impact, but at other times, it feels right on. Very cool mechanics - grab, throws, combos, style rewards.
Lovely world / aesthetic. Believeable characters, entertaining conversations, courtesy of the Narrator.
Multiple endings. Super cool.
Cons:
Graphical performance issues on mid-high end systems with High settings. Certain wind / particle effects / draw distance were causing me to drop frames.
Long-ish loading screens. Unsure if it has to do with graphics, but on starting the game for the first time, I believe I had to wait about a minute before the beginning of the game played after I hit "New Game." I didn't see much of a wait for anything after that, though.
In any case, it's a bit of a flawed gem. I'd recommend it if story-based adventuring is your deal, if you enjoy Choose Your Own Adventure books, liked the world / style of Dust or liked the game Brave Fencer Musashi.

This game is a tight 5 - 6 hours-ish "Choose Your Own Adventure" story experience with action combat similar to, but a fair bit more complex than, Hand of Fate.
As you make decisions about what story path to choose, you'll inevitably hit snags and the story will dead-end. In fact, the game requires this! As you make choices and complete story paths, you'll unlock clues as to what the correct path is. The storyline itself is interesting, and you learn more about the world you're in and the characters, and even why you're fighting as each path runs its course. Very few raw expository dumps! A few lines made me laugh out loud, even, partly because of the text, but also partly because of the delivery. The narrator does a pretty damn good job throughout.
As mentioned, combat isn't super complex, but you have a few actions to deal with your enemies, a few spells, and a lot of skills to level up. There's a rudimentary crafting system, which I maxed out by about 2/3rds of the way through the game, but even maxed out won't really make you overpowered. The final battle I died a couple times before nailing it.
6 hours doesn't sound like that long of a game, but personally I think it was about perfect. It gave a really good feel for the story and combat mechanics without overstaying its welcome. Much longer and I'd probably have gotten bored, but as a shorter game, it's definitely worth the price of admission.
Edit:
There a few places where the game chugs (usually when an above-view would have a lot of geometry below, or lots of particle effects overlaying the game), and half of my achievements didn't register correctly. Didn't really detract from the gameplay imho.

I am shocked by the quality for a 15$ game, as I have paid more for much less polished early access titles. I was not expecting an early access game to be this developed, honestly. To me, the music stuck out as being well above par of many full-fledged titles. I have just finished the first of four levels, and the story progress is such that I find myself trying to find every little note and journal because it provides an interesting sort of "cookie crumb trail" that makes you want to find the next hint as to what's happening. I rarely buy a game and play it for more than an hour or so in the first sitting, but Tower of Time had me hooked right off the bat.
The combat shines as well, especially the slow-down feature, which puts it somewhat in between baldur's gate, an RTS, and a MOBA. There are multiple tactical choices for each battle, and finding the right combination provides for some interesting effects. For example, getting overwhelmed? Form a wall around the ranged attackers to keep them at bay. Or hide around a corner and lead the monsters into an array of traps, summons, and AOE binds. No matter what the strategy, there are many tools to take advantage of.
I am playing on normal, and the difficulty seems just right. You can't just stand in one spot in a boss fight and take hits. You actually have to taunt, kite, snare, heal, and arrange your party in a tactical manner. I can definitely see that the higher difficulties would get hectic, but the battle challenge / arena fights available in the town can be repeated, allowing for a chance to farm up some gold and equipment when you get stuck.
All in all, an excellent experience so far.

This game is frustrating. Not because its easy, not because its hard, but because it has that annoying combination of brilliance and lazy shortcuts.
If you are looking for a snowboard/alpine sportsgame, then Steep will frustrate you endlessly. But at the same time, if you're (like me) not looking for a wingsuit/paraglider, then Steep will surprise you. Its remarkable how the core substance of snowboard and ski are so poorly developed as it is, while the two spicey alternatives both excell so well.
I bought Steep for the snowboard offpist sensation. And thats why ive stayed with it. The beauty of this game is remarkable, the snow-physics, the glare, the sound ... it gives me goosebumps regularly, thats how good it is!
Steep has genius aspects to it that they just got right. The mapdesign, the quick restartbutton (which had me always doing 20-30 attempts than I intended), the partially amazing voicecasting. These things are a big plus. Thats why its so frustrating that the negatives are just as big. Snowboard and ski has glue-physics to non-snow substance (a small rock can slingshot you 120 degrees around f.ex.), its impossible to swap or pick which direction you want to accelerate, some challenges have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pitches and voices, customization of riders are weak, jumps and tricks and score system all make equally little sense. Riding 20m on ice can score just as high as a 1080 tweak for example, whats up with that?? The design choice by devs to build the game up around a «carrier» is a good one, but alas a poorly executed one. In summary, most of these flaws to the game feels to me like they were caused by a lack of more time for developing.
All in all, I recommend. Pray that they patch and update the game further. Steep is a dirty, muddied gem. May it shine brighter one day soon.

This concept sounds good on paper; classic D&D how you remember playing classic D&D. Unfortunately, they left out the game part of D&D.
Essentially, this game is trying to be a humorous game. It's not one you play for a challenge or for fun, but to laugh at. Unfortunately, there are only so many jokes, and there's lots of battling that must be done to go forward. Typically, you'll spend at least ten minutes battling before the next joke or reference, and there's still no guarantee you'll even find it funny.
That might be acceptable if battling was any fun, but unfortunately, it isn't. Every enemy in the game (at least those that I saw) does the exact same thing: Attack on their turn. There is literally nothing to react to except damage. To make matters worse, once you reach level 5 and unlock each of your skills, you can kiss any sense of progression goodbye, since every subsequent level only grants more stat-ups and numerical upgrades to said skills. As for loot and gear, the fun is sucked out of that too; while loot often drops, you have access to a store that sells pretty much any gear you could ever need, so if you're halfway intelligent about visiting it, any loot that drops will always be inferior vendor trash.
Lastly, the game is OBSCENELY grindy. This is the level of grind I would expect from an poorly-made free MMO. Doing almost anything in the game costs coins; often a lot of them. And there are two ways to get coins: A) Win battles, or B) Buy them with real money.
I recommend this very much

One of my favorite games in the genre.
The soundtrack, the environment, the artstyle, everything about this game is dark and gritty. People are comparing it to Diablo 3, but this game doesn't take a page out of Blizzard's World of Warcraft artstyle that looks like it came straight out of a Disney cartoon. Instead it tries to show you a bleak world where there is little hope of a better tomorrow.
The story isn't spoon-fed on a silver platter, but instead small notes you read along the way really set the tone of the game. SLIGHT SPOILER: It starts with a sense of mistery. You WANT to know what happened to fallen kingdoms, forgotten cities, destroyed families. The notes you read at the start only give you clues to the events that befell the world around you. It really grabs you and immerses you into the world (if you actually try rather than just mindlessly killing things).
This isn't an "MMO" like Path of Exiles or Diablo 3 claim to be. Instead this is more of a single-player game WITH multiplayer elements (CO-OP). Even in its early state this game is worth the money since it already has a large amount of playable content that will keep you entertained.
The gear is great, the abilities are fun, and combat is good. I did experience some crashing when playing in CO-OP though. Overall, if you like this genre and like the dark setting Diablo 2 had and enjoy a decent story then this is definitely a purchase you can't pass up.

While I like the complexity this game seems to offer, so far it feels more like an old point and click adventure than an RPG, with all the randomness that entails.
This game is advertised as a spiritual succesor to games like Baldur's Gate and Neverwinter Nights, but lacks the sweeping narrative and successive events that propel the heroes forward.
After playing for 35 hours I have still not progresed much beyond the first quest hub, trying to solve the very first quest; a murder mystery.
Solving a murder mystery is a wonderful idea, something of the like has been done before, and done well. Unfortunately, after two days of carefull exploration (avoiding the suddenly impossible fights a little further away from the city) I've managed to advance neither the story or my characters. A mystery is fun, but after wandering around the town for (literally) days, it is no longer fun, but an exercise in rage-inducing bouts of clicking on every container, and speaking to every NPC in the hopes of obtaining some hint as to what I am supposed to do next. The worst part is that, although you are free to choose whatever build you like to start with, a thief seems to be impossible to do without since some key plotpoints are found behind locked doors with no key in sight.
I was hoping for a thinking-mans dungeon crawler, but while the pace of the game is indeed crawling, I've yet to see a single dungeon after 35 hours of gameplay.
Unless you enjoy hearing the same two lines from wandering villagers for days on end, or have a propensity for aimlesly wandering around in circles in a beleaguered city you have no power to defend (seriously, the first enemies will f*ck you up if you have not gained at least 2 levels from exploration experience) I must, with pain in my heart since this game has such promise, recommend you NOT buy this game.
Those 35 hours would have been better spent flogging myself to build my own character, instead of two wussy digital magic-hunters who fall to bits at the first sight of a skeleton.
This game is little more than a pixellated way of spending money for no good reason.

When it comes to video games based off of movies and tv-shows, there has been plenty. The countless Spider-Man movie games all the way down to The Simpsons Hit n' Run, has all been a fun goof off for an hour or two before you get bored with it due to the lack of actual substance. Now, when I tell you that South Park: The Stick of Truth is the GOD of all movie/tv-games, I need you to understand my full meaning.
South Park: The Stick of Truth drops you in the middle of an actual episode of South Park. You are right there, and part of the quiet little mountain town for several hours of gameplay that is simple in its ways, but great all the same. Fight alongside the boys as their innocent games turn into yet another nation-wide catastrophy, and revisit memories from all the past seasons.
The turnbased combat is, again, extremly simplistic but does the trick as all fights has a decent flow to them and makes room for tons of comedy.
The graphics are no more or less than what South Park has always been. Truth be told, the fact that the developers chose to keep the simple visuals from the series only makes it more true to its original.
The RPG-part is little more than an inventory, loot, and a somewhat sloppy skill tree, but as simple as the rest it, I'd say that it is not something that lowers the over all quality too much.
In the end, The Stick of Truth is a fantastic game. It truly is, IF you are a fan of South Park. If you are not familiar with it, or maybe one of those people that finds South Park distasteful, save your money.
If you, like me, adores South Park. Can you please get this game, RIGHT NOW?! *Cartman voice*

This absolutely beautiful and gripping game is worth a playthough for any gamer.  While your initial reaction may be to how graphically stunning of a game this is, the gameplay is also very solid.  It's primarily a turn based strategy game with an oregon trail-esqe overworld, FTL-like "random" events, and light Mass Effect style conversations.
This is a story of a realm caught off guard by a surprise invasion of an old enemy.  You and your allies are constantly caught off guard or seemingly making a last stand.  Just when it seems like things are getting better, the game deals another blow to your story.  Despite the crushing setbacks that are often out of your control, it's still hard to put this game down.  It's not a frustrating experience in any way.  Instead, you are driven to push on with the hopes that things can't possibly get worse.
The gameplay is solid.  Even on normal, the strategy parts are difficult to perfect and the oregon-trail style overworld is unforgiving.  As the game wore on, I went from an optimistic leader that gave everyone a chance to prove themselves to a leader skeptical of everyone we came across and quick to fight.
Overall, this is a truly great experience that many will probably be drawn to play a 2nd or 3rd time.  It will be interesting to see where this story goes in the second and third installments.

Sublime experience so far, great polish to it,  for an early access game, hell even a complete game. I used to feel like the world was so cluttered with things to find in Baldurs gate, and that it was filled with NPC's and items that had no significance, but this game feels like it's cut all that crap out, though it's more focussed on a dungeon of sorts, you're not really walking aroun NPC infested areas, full of items to click endlessly, everything you click is story related or important information.
Pros.
-Combat, combat takes place as encounters, and you're face with the waves of enemies listed at the start of the encounter, you have a choice to fight or withdraw.. well unless you're ambushed. feels fun and polished, each character contributes in their own way, how it should be.
-Level design, the lighting and atmosphere are great, everything seems so pretty and immersive.
-Excellent auto-save, been acouple of times I've ♥♥♥♥ed it and I've been like god no! where's my last save only to find it auto-saved seconds in advance as if it's knew every point I'd need it.
-Character progression is based on gold and training, so you can't level up through combat, you have to spend and pick wiseley, and keep an eye out for blueprints to upgrade said buildings.
-Story, the story is engaging and keeps you interested in the mystery of the Magus tower, keeps you wanting to progress for that next scrap of evidence of what has taken place.
-Challenge mode, little challenge fights you can do to make an extra buck.
Cons.

Oh one more thing that deserves a mention.. the price! the price is acceptable for once, these guys ain't greedy at all, this seems like a dev people can get behind, if they make an expansion later down the line after they've completed this, I'll be more than happy to give em another £10.99 it's like we've gone back a few years where decent PC games didn't cost the same as console prices.

Does the game respect my time?  Something RPGs must increasingly do the older I've gotten.  Does it want me to fight pointless battles, quests and grinding, earn a degree in loot charts and inventory management or does it give me it's best material and skip the rest?
Tower of Time is somewhere in-between.
Looting is simple (to loot something how many clicks does it take and do I have to make difficult decisions each time)?  I find in most RPGs you can spend a lot of time and energy looting hundreds of pieces of gear and you'll still end up about being at the average of where the game wants you to be, so why waste the time?  Why not just give the player 1 outfit and quit the pretense of loot?  That may be unpopular, but I want best from the developers, not an excel spreadsheet of stats that I must comb through every 20 minutes, because then it feels like work.
Battles: Do I look forward to them or dread them?
The unique-looking combat system is what interested me about this game.  I'm not involved in the secret war going on since the dawn of time between turn-based/rt with pause, a combat system should be what fits the game.  I find that the higher difficulties have been difficult (because I don't care to deal with the stats of armor-choosing often) and the easy settings seem a bit bland.  I haven't found the strategy beyond managing the basics of mana and cooldowns and moving units around to spread the damage out.  Perhaps it takes longer to find the strategy.  I would say thus far it's not that exciting as a Starcraft or not as fun or tactical as Grandia II, but there seems to be potential here.
The environment is nice.  The graphics are sufficient, but it's the music and polish that really set the tone.
I don't care to read all the text boxes or lore throughout it, the game must convince me the game is amazing before I'm ready to dedicate my time and energy to caring about those things.
The point-and-click adventure style seems to work well, because it's not labor-intensive or annoying.
Overall I don't hate the game, and that's enough to get a positive mark for now.  Clearly a lot of work put into it, I wonder if they plan on adding voice acting to supplement the text if it does well?

Tower of Time is a beautiful, story-driven fantasy RPG.  I highly recommend this game.
The most compelling aspect of the game for me is the cutscene artwork.  The still images are breathtaking.  They somehow manage to simultaneously show you how beautiful and developed Altara once was and the dire situation of the world today. The images manage to evoke strong emotions – a feat that few games have accomplished.
Each level is beautifully designed.  Heavy particle areas, such as waterfalls or long-distance renders, will tax your GPU.  It is easy to be immersed in each level and forget that everything you see is within a magic tower.
The story line is top notch and genuinely creative.  You, of course, are the main character, however, as the main character, you sit on your throne and do nothing.  Everything is accomplished by your heroes.  I won’t spoil the novelty of how this is done (from the context of the story).  The story quickly brings together the five races (humans, dwarves, elves, ice giants, and shadows) to give you plenty of options for creating your ideal party.
Each hero has a unique set of skills to give you an edge in combat.  You can easily customize the skills before each battle for a nominal fee.
The approach to combat is certainly unique.  The "slow time" gives you minute control over every detail.  In the early stages, I found this wasn't needed.  As the enemies became stronger with more abilities and combat lasted longer, events happen so quickly that my heroes would die before I realized what was happening.  Trying to micro-manage each hero without the slow-time would be near impossible due to the fast-paced nature of combat.
I would argue that gold is the most precious resource as it is the only resource that cannot be farmed.  You have the option of working through the main story or completing challenges.  Each challenge can be repeated, but you only get the gold and crystal reward once.  The item, however, can be farmed and deconstructed for crystals.  Need to make some new rare armor, but short on crystals?  No problem.  Do a couple challenges and you’re set.  The economy in general will need improvement.
Being an early access game, it has its own set of growing pains.  Improvements that are surely on the developer’s to-do list: no mini-map, can’t remap key assignments, moving around the city can be a little awkward, can’t make notes on the main map (can’t make notes of any kind, for that matter…not that the game is complex enough to require notes, but would be nice to know where certain things are that you think might be important), and can’t adjust the camera – to name a few.

TL;DR: Buy this game now, it's like nothing else you'll ever experience when you get in the zone.  When it sucks you in, it feels like there is nothing in the universe except you and Super Hexagon.  It's dirt cheap, so it wouldn't take much to make this game worth your money,  and it goes way above and beyond that standard.  Hard, fast, intense, mind-affecting, satisfying, and addictive - the videogaming meth.
In Super Hexagon, you control a tiny arrow, and your sole objective is to dodge increasingly-fast-and-complicated patterns of murderous walls.  Each stage lasts only 60 seconds.  'Survive for one minute?  Easy peasy,' you say.  Not so.  This is probably the hardest game I've ever played, at least as far as sheer difficulty of completion is concerned.
This game is crazy difficult, but not in an artificial 'I got you' way, like I Wanna Be the Guy or Dark Souls.  Every time you die, it was *your* fault, and then you mash the spacebar and try again.  And again.  And again.  Sometimes you will be frustrated, you will die 10 seconds in 12 times in a row.  But sometimes... sometimes you get into 'the zone,' that mythical feeling where all other sensations drop out and you become one with the Hexagon.  It's incredible - and I'm not exaggerating here, when you really get absorbed into this game it's like nothing else on planet Earth.  The feeling of finally beating a level you'd been working for ages is incomperable, like a...
(Sorry for stealing your joke, Bo Burnham c:)
The music is great - intense, upbeat chiptunes - and offers some rhythmic assistance for each level (although maybe that's just me and my musical mind).  There's not much to talk about regarding the graphics - simple, conveys the information it needs to.
There's not really anything I would change about this game - 10 hours of gameplay ago I would have asked to please get rid of the fast right-right-left-left-left pattern on the hardes♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ level - but having beaten that stage, I can say that it was I who was the problem, not the game itself.
I rate this game 10/10 - meaning that there is nothing I would change about it, it perfectly achieved what it set out to achieve (not necessarily that it is my favorite game of all time, though it's up there).

This game is an awful lot of fun. Initially I was weirded out by it's simple D&D style interface, but since I've picked it up, I've probably tried to play through it at least 30 times. It's a short space campaign, involving navigating to a fleet redevous. The battles are really strategic, and a lot of fun - at first they're usually a slogging match (aim for the shields, then attempt to blow everything else up), but they get more and more complicated as you buy unusual weapons, cloaking devices, teleporters. As you progress you'll have trade offs at frequent intervals - whether to stock up on missles and attack people, or fuel; whether to build up your shields or hire additional crew to man stations and fight fires.
All in all, its a really well thought out game that manages to be a ton of fun despite it's simplistic interface and graphics.

This game is frustrating. Not because its easy, not because its hard, but because it has that annoying combination of brilliance and lazy shortcuts.
If you are looking for a snowboard/alpine sportsgame, then Steep will frustrate you endlessly. But at the same time, if you're (like me) not looking for a wingsuit/paraglider, then Steep will surprise you. Its remarkable how the core substance of snowboard and ski are so poorly developed as it is, while the two spicey alternatives both excell so well.
I bought Steep for the snowboard offpist sensation. And thats why ive stayed with it. The beauty of this game is remarkable, the snow-physics, the glare, the sound ... it gives me goosebumps regularly, thats how good it is!
Steep has genius aspects to it that they just got right. The mapdesign, the quick restartbutton (which had me always doing 20-30 attempts than I intended), the partially amazing voicecasting. These things are a big plus. Thats why its so frustrating that the negatives are just as big. Snowboard and ski has glue-physics to non-snow substance (a small rock can slingshot you 120 degrees around f.ex.), its impossible to swap or pick which direction you want to accelerate, some challenges have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pitches and voices, customization of riders are weak, jumps and tricks and score system all make equally little sense. Riding 20m on ice can score just as high as a 1080 tweak for example, whats up with that?? The design choice by devs to build the game up around a «carrier» is a good one, but alas a poorly executed one. In summary, most of these flaws to the game feels to me like they were caused by a lack of more time for developing.
All in all, I recommend. Pray that they patch and update the game further. Steep is a dirty, muddied gem. May it shine brighter one day soon.

It's Oregon Trail + Final Fantasy Tactics lite. The combat seems pretty simple on the surface, but they way they use Armor and Strength is neat. A unit's Strength is effectively their HP, and the damage a unit can do is Strength - Armor.  If a unit's Strength < opponent's Armor, they have a (Armor - Strength)*10% chance to miss completely.  If you ignore armor and go for strength attacks, you run the risk of missing with your weaker characters, but if you only focus on armor, they can do more damage to you on their turn.
Between fights, you're on an oregon trail style adventure after the invasion of your village by Dredge, a race of heavily armored people from the north. They're the main antagonists of the game, forcing the main characters to flee from city to city looking for refuge. The number of supplies you have determine how many days you can travel before your clansmen and warriors begin to die. In addition, the longer you travel, the worse your clan's morale gets, meaning you have to balance supplies with camping and resting. Various dialog and story events play a part in the number of clansmen you lose or gain if they decide to join your caravan.
The story mainly revolves around a hunter named Rook, who falls into the leadership role in a caravan of refugees. You and the other characters are attempting to find refuge between two separate apocalyptic events and a horde of invading warriors. Similar to Game of Thrones, the story is barely ever not dark, but it fits the tone of the world. You're not on a quest to save the planet, you're just trying to get your people to safety.
Only downside is that it lacks closure on some of the bigger story elements. Looking forward to the sequel.

When it comes to video games based off of movies and tv-shows, there has been plenty. The countless Spider-Man movie games all the way down to The Simpsons Hit n' Run, has all been a fun goof off for an hour or two before you get bored with it due to the lack of actual substance. Now, when I tell you that South Park: The Stick of Truth is the GOD of all movie/tv-games, I need you to understand my full meaning.
South Park: The Stick of Truth drops you in the middle of an actual episode of South Park. You are right there, and part of the quiet little mountain town for several hours of gameplay that is simple in its ways, but great all the same. Fight alongside the boys as their innocent games turn into yet another nation-wide catastrophy, and revisit memories from all the past seasons.
The turnbased combat is, again, extremly simplistic but does the trick as all fights has a decent flow to them and makes room for tons of comedy.
The graphics are no more or less than what South Park has always been. Truth be told, the fact that the developers chose to keep the simple visuals from the series only makes it more true to its original.
The RPG-part is little more than an inventory, loot, and a somewhat sloppy skill tree, but as simple as the rest it, I'd say that it is not something that lowers the over all quality too much.
In the end, The Stick of Truth is a fantastic game. It truly is, IF you are a fan of South Park. If you are not familiar with it, or maybe one of those people that finds South Park distasteful, save your money.
If you, like me, adores South Park. Can you please get this game, RIGHT NOW?! *Cartman voice*

The bad:
Not alot of character customization and potraits. You have the hulky male and default woman.
I like how the battlesystem works (turnbased) but like alot in this game, you need to be patient. Don't expect a quest summary telling you what to do and where to do it. You can't skip by dialogues, book contents and events quickly without losing some vital information. The initial quest (solving the murder) took me hours to complete. Although I like this, sometimes you wish you had just a little bit more clues and sometimes a few short quests for quick exp.
The leveling is slow, and although guards tell you not to go to certain areas, you actually need to take a bit of risk to get further. At 10hrs in, I'm still at level 4.
There are a lot of hidden features. For instance, you can drag a bone onto a mortar to get dust. No one really tells you this, it's just something you figure out. And then you have a pile of dust, and now what? You hope you find a recipe, or you hope that by dragging the dust on every item in your inventory somehow magicly creates a recipe. This makes the game interesting but at some point you just give up trying to find the matching ingredient. This could just be me, I had the same with other games like Elderscrolls and Witcher. I rather saw some crafting menu with unlocked recipes and hints to unlock others (think of jrpgs like atelier iris).
Some stuff in the UI can be improved. Selling stuff to a vendor sometimes feels like a choir. So much loot divided over 4 characters and you need to finish selling with one party member before you can sell stuff with another party member.
The game is sometimes unforgiving. Traps that oneshot your whole party, while the guard says the area is good enough for your party to handle. Enemies that do 4 hits in 1 turn, instantly killing you. Be prepared to save often and have ressurect scrolls.
The coop game is alot of fun, but the person that joins can't bring his own character, and everything he does is in vain. He can't bring over exp, items or whatever to his own game. Try to find a friend that likes to invest x hours in your game and then return to his game and do it all over again.
Overall I really like this game, but I would understand if people were let down by it's pace and sometimes lack of information, while other love the freedom and I wouldnt say difficulty level but rather a high learning curve and time investment. I bet the second playthrough would be better.

Maybe... but for the time being, I'll rest easier knowing they've got their own room now and won't be slobbering all over my toys and video-game genres. Don't try to be a gangster sandbox game if 80% of what you spend your time on is dong-launching, gold plated, diamond powered, satellite guided cheat code DLC packages. So, here we go, the first two parts of critically acclaimed Japanese series Ys. As I already played Ys Origin (that I really liked) I expected having similar fun, though I knew from beginning that this games have different (unique) combat system.
All combat is done by bumping to your enemies - you bump his back/shoulder, you deal damage. If you bump your enemy directly in the front, he'll also deal some damage back to you. It's not complex at all, it's pretty much undemanding. But here comes the right question - Is it fun?
Well, it might be fun for the first time, but after you beat tenth NPC? What about hundredth NPC? If you are going to play Ys I & II, plan for grinding. There's a lot of grinding for experience and gold with obsolete formula - if NPCs around you are too hard to beat, return to previous zone and kill as many enemies as you can. Once you get stronger, get back to the following zone and beat everybody, thinking about how easy it is.
The game even encourages you so hardly to grind enemies that you'll clearly see that any NPC you kill is respawned in few seconds. Welcome to the game where running and bumping enemies with your sword is the meaning of life.
All this grinding actually ruins impression from the environment and story for me but if you can get over it, you can be happy for many seriously written fantasy dialogues, sweet pixelart graphics and good soundtrack.
Anyway, if this review make you lose interest on Ys, I'd still recommend you to try other Ys games as they have taken different (and more classic) take on combat. I'm still definitely going to play the other Ys games later.

Ys I
An ARPG classic.
The bump system may put some people off by it's simplicity, but it generally feels good and looks cool. Keep in mind that this is based on a game released in 1989, so some of the system's features are strictly bare-bones, but the remake has been upgraded in some aspects to make the game a much smoother experience than the '89 original. Boss encounters are a bit hit and miss, and usually rely on you being a certain level or having certain equipment to beat, but are enjoyable all in all. Not especially tough, but they can still be challenging enough for you to have to retry a few times before you understand the patterns. I played it on normal, but if you find the game too easy there is always the option to try a higher difficulty setting.
The music is great, also, as is usually the case with Falcom games. Also, there's an option available to switch to/from classic and remade tunes, which is always nice.
The minimalistic story is interesting and Adol Christin is a cool protagonist, but don't expect a convoluted epic; this is a standard tale of a dualistic nature, with good and evil, dark and light.
Progression through the game is generally uncomplicated, and the areas you are supposed to visit are few and easy to find, but the game can, however, be a bit cryptic when it comes to what you're supposed to do next, so if you're a newcomer you should expect to get stuck a few times before you are able to proceed. That said, the game is pretty short, short enough to be suited for speedrunning and such, for sure.
I mostly play it for nostalgic reasons nowadays, but, nostalgia aside, it is still a pretty good game and still holds up fairly well even today. Thoroughly recommended.
Ys I score
7.5 / 10
Ys II
Ys II continues the adventure of Adol Christin and concludes the story of Ys I & II Chronicles.
The bump system is back, and not much has changed. Included, however, is the ability to use magic, which have a variety of uses ranging from an attack spell to spells useful to progress the game. Basically, if you liked the first game's system, there should be no reason for you to disike the one in Ys II, as they are pretty similar. Boss encounters are a bit more challenging than the ones in Ys I, but sometimes it comes down to just finding out cerrtain gimmicks in order to beat them.
The music is at least as good as in Ys I and has some of my favorite Ys tunes of all time. Definitely one of the highlights of the game, and the abiity to switch between classic and remade tunes is a plus. Top notch.
The story in general has a bit more depth than Ys I, and is less melancholic, but all in all it's still pretty simple. There are some surprises down the road to make it interesting though, so it is fairly well conceived, although I don't feel like the villains are as intimidating as the ones in Ys I. I liked the first one better, but it's all a matter of taste.
Progression through the game is fairly linear, but there were a number of times where I got stuck and didn't know how to proceed. It usually boils down to not having the required items or paying close attention to your environments, though, so if you can't proceed there is probably something you've missed an area accessible to you at your current point in the adventure. The game is probably twice as long as Ys I, but can be completed fairly quickly if you know what to do and where to go.
Recommended.
