The graphical fidelity and mechanics found in this game might not be the best or most interesting by today's standards, though the lighting is still pretty good, but the atmosphere still holds and is what I found most compelling about this game.
I saw a couple instances where the enemies just kinda derped around and didn't attack me, one guy just kinda charged past me and faceplanted into a door, but most of the time they act fairly intelligently and they sometimes even try to flank you--had a couple manage to sneak up on me and take a bite or two. The first boss fight was pretty tough, if fairly repetitive (he has a pattern of attack you need to learn and dance around). They give you up to 4 respawns if you die and the boss' health does not regenerate, but those extra lives are imo more than balanced by the fact that you can't get any more ammo on a respawn (unless you backtrack trying to look for it, I guess). This was also on Medium difficulty, so I would expect Hard to give fewer attempts.
The game's supply of med kits and ammo has been fairly reasonable up to this point. It would likely have been more tense and thereby more thrilling on Medium difficulty if I'd had a couple fewer med kits and a bit less ammo, but I'm guessing playing on Hard would fix that. I do plan on finishing the game on Medium and if the rest of the game feels as good as the first hour I'll probably replay it on Hard. Btw at first it seems like you're getting way too much rifle ammo, stacking up over 500 at times, but you really do burn through it quick. And you might want to save as much ammo as possible for the boss fight.

So far rather loving it. Firstly I´m playing with K&M and it´s serviceable though very clearly Stories has been built around the controller. The bulk of the game from combat to characters, visuals, music ect are as advertised in the trailers and screenshots so all around very enjoyable and well made. In particular the visuals/writing/characters are very storybook-ish and I´d say very charming. It has its issues but I´m hooked to this style so it´s great IMO.
Length-wise(which was my biggest hesitation going in) Stories seems to pass with flying colors. This is a game built around multiple "playthroughs" with your upgrades intact, new areas unlocking and new truths about the world and characters being revealed depending on the choices you make. I have just gotten through my first playthrough(took about an hour) but the choices made very clearly change everything from story progression to levels visited. And as said upgrades stack. This cycle is also a part of the story with a definitive end in sight, and I see this game very much staying fresh up to that end and beyond(since the end clearly doesn´t require going through anywhere near every possible scenario).
So yeah it looks like Stories does the "choices matter" thing actually correctly, though it is very much built around those multiple playthroughs as well.  Can highly recommend as long as you don´t get a rash from a storybookish style.
EDIT: After 8 hours, 9 playthroughs and having "finished" the game(still plenty of scenarios to go through) my thoughts remain largely the same, except I have been running into a bunch of technical difficulties. Most importantly my final pathbugged out pretty bad both times I tried it. I´ve also had my movement speed set to either way lower or way faster than intended about 4-5 times total now for one level after a combat sequence. Plus some more general performance issues.
Still a worthy game especially if you roleplay a bit and try to make short 2-3 playthrough stories work out instead of just hammering through the variety of options. But the technical stuff does add up even though I usually don´t care much about it.
EDITEDIT: also I appreciate the "godmode" given after completion, but It´s not optional and it really should be given how badly it ends up clashing with the stories.

Stories: The Path of Destinies is a beautiful action RPG, where your choices matter.
The game is very reminiscent of Bastion in quite a few ways. The combat and the way the story is told are both quite similar.
The first thing you'll notice is the beautiful art style. Levels constantly vary the environment, with highly saturated and beautiful worlds. It really is a joy to explore. The character designs are also very cool to look at.
The story is told by a narrator, who will comment on everything your character Reynardo does. Even small things like swinging your sword wildly in the air. All of the characters are also voiced by the narrator, which gives the entire game a very cozy feeling of a grand adventure in a bed-time story.
After almost every single level, you will be given a choice where you can branch the story into completely unique places. The choices will even have you play an entirely new level, which is great for adding replay value to the game. I love that not all of the choices are black and white, in the sense that it isn't as simple as "Good or Bad". Things can have unforeseen consequences, while others can have surprisingly good outcomes.
The combat can be quite diverse. You can slash your sword and use spells depending on the weapon you have. Grappling hooks can pull your enemies towards you, and you may grab and throw enemies at others or off of cliffs. Countering, slow-motion and dodging all play roles in the combat as well.
The game rewards you for exploring through hidden chests and materials that you may use to create new weapons. It's all very satisfying.
Overall, I'm really in love with the game's world. Although the dialogue isn't the best it could be, for the most part it's quite charming, funny and nice to listen to. The world looks beautiful, and the characters are likable. The combat is also very satisfying and easy to use! Great game!

What is Stories: The Path of Destinies?  It's kind of an ambiguous title until you get into the game.  It's a choose your own adventure style action rpg that brings us back to the nostalgia of classic tales on PC and Playstation 4. Hacking and slashing our way through to the very end.  Fighting, Making Bad Choices, Dying, and Repeating.  It's like Edge of Tomorrow, but with a fox instead of Tom Cruise.  So is this game any good?  Let's find out.  Also this game was provided by the publisher for review.
Story
In Stories you play as Reynardo, a fox who is caught in the middle of a rebellion.  The game is a series of choices.  What's interesting about all these different choices is that they aren't predictable.  The setup makes you think with your emotions.  Do you choose to help your friend or save the rebels?  You think you know the right answer, but the consequences are sometimes completely different.
There's very few cutscenes in the game and the ones that are there come much later in the story.  Instead, the narrative is told by pages from a book with images described by the narrator.  It's kind of a creative way of avoiding cutscenes, but the voice acting is really good and the situations that Reynardo finds himself in are interesting.  You have to use your imagination which is something that we completely forget about in the age of digital games.
There's also a few interesting motifs in the game.  You play as a fox who is often known in stories for being a sly creature, but you'll notice that the negative consequences make you seem the opposite of a sly decision maker.  There's also heavy moral themes.  Betrayal, trust, leadership, heroism.  You'll have to play it yourself if you want to know how these themes are revealed.
There's also elements of fiction because you are an anthropormohic fox who is trained in sword fu.  What the hell is sword fu?  But it's handled with eloquence and the writers didn't create a caricature as you would expect.  The story and the characters are mature enough to be taken seriously.
Gameplay
On first impression stories can be bland.  You get into your first fight and immediately think “Batman Arkham Combat”.  Because it does have the unreal engine blow for blow counter and back to more pummeling type of gameplay.  Then you run around from point A to point B in a linear fashion.
The game is a slow starter, but after you pass the first few stories things get interesting.  Combat gains more depth through the upgrade system.  You get access to four different swords of fire, void, ice, and the basic hero sword.  Each one has a special powerup.  Then you get a few combo abilities, stamina boost, and other cool stuff.  They clearly took a page out of Shadow of Mordor which is a game that really perfected this type of combat with a new level of complexity.  In most games combat gets easier as powerups get more plentiful, however in stories it gets much tougher because the enemies scale faster than your upgrades which is a good thing because it gives you a progressive challenge.
However, enemy types are mostly the same throughout the game and there are no boss battles, so it becomes pretty routine going from fight to fight.
Each quote unquote story is like a level of the game and it gives you information on how to reach the final resolution.  There's fourth “truths” that help you reach the conclusion.  At the end of each section you are presented with a split of choices and the game tags the paths that you haven't crossed yet to guide you along the way.  The idea is that you keep repeating the story, making different educated choices based on what you learned from your last play through.
The middle of the game is probably the most interesting part because you get a sense of discovery.  Exploring new areas that open up thanks to your new swords and choosing new paths based on information.  This is where things get interesting.  You also start to learn that health is not plentiful.  You don't get a health refill after each fight or even after each section.  You need to conserve your health and energy otherwise you'll just run out.  You also start to open up those colorful doors and get a sense of loot hunting as you pick up these gems that give you different perks.  The RPG aspects start to reveal themselves.  Ironically the game crushes the loot aspect in some ways by providing you with vases to break that rarely have anything in them.  Maybe 20% of the time you can get some health pickups, but it kind of feels like a waste of time destroying property.
The story mode can be completed in about maybe 6 hours, but there are remaining scenarios to discover if you want to be a completionist.  Most of your character upgrades will be filled out by the time you get to the end.
Graphics
Stories has a really warm color tone that suits it's atmosphere.  Everything about the game strikes you as friendly, but fierce.  It's not a kiddie game, nor are the graphics cartoony, yet it's still approachable for gamers of all ages.
The game has a really attractive art style and this shines through more than any effects or textures.  Because the effects and textures are good, but not really a standout feature.
One issue with the graphics is that the special effects are used sparingly, but when they are used it's so bright it's blinding.  Even with the basic hero sword, every swing is so white and so bright that you can't actually focus on the hits.  You have to look around to your periphery rather than focus on who you are actually fighting.
And further more, an action rpg shouldn't be afraid to bring the camera in more often.  You don't exactly need cinematic dramatic cutscenes, but I'd like to get a closer detail in the graphics.  Sort of like how XCOM shows you the finishing blow or the introduction of a new enemy.  Many action RPGs are guilty not using enough close ups.  And running on Unreal Engine 4 there should be some level of fidelity so there's no excuse not to.
The game has nothing but low, medium, and high settings on the PC so there aren't many options for detail, anti aliasing, or vsync.  The game runs well, albeit locked at 60fps, so it's not too much of an issue, but those of us with powerful PCs always want to squeeze more visuals out of the game.
Sound
The highlight of the sound design and the overall game is really the narration.  This game wouldn't work without our humble narrator.  It puts you in the world of a classic tale.  The narrator sort of reads you the choices and consequences of your actions with enough emotion to light your imagination.  The narrator also has some charming one liners throughout your adventure.
The score is filled with orchestral music that's epic when you're fighting.  But it's soothing during the exposition of the story.  Right from the moment you enter the title screen, you know you are in for a journey.
These two aspects of the sound really come together to help give the game a good feel.  It's arguably the strongest part of the game overall.
Stories has a lot of likable and charming elements.  But it takes a little bit of time to build up to it.  The first hour or two has very linear gameplay, boring combat, and it's a little overwhelming to find out how the stories or repeating the narrative works.  But once the game clicks, it all makes sense and begins to become a lot more fun.  I wish they could have brought more of that into the introduction by ramping up the upgrades faster.
The endgame kind of has you chasing after the concluding story to find out the real resolution of our main protagonist.  In other words, pacing could be better.  It doesn't kill the game by any means, but it's something that may stop an ADD player from getting started.
Stories is an interesting game.  It's old school in some ways and makes you remember that a game's narrative can be told in more than one way.

No commentary quicklook, first impressions below.
Stories is an action rpg game that's definitely more focused on the story, hence the name! With the narrated gameplay it played somewhat like a blend of bastion and torchlight, just don't expect to be out grinding mobs for epic loot drops. Playthroughs last around 30-60min, each containing 5 levels that once completed offer alternate paths or choices. Consider it a choose your own adventure of sorts. Initially it may feel a little 'rinse repeat' though once you collect enough materials to forge weapons, can then open gates that were not accessible in earlier runs. Enemies scale along with the player level but I felt the game was a little was on the easy side once you master the combo/parry systems.
No problems with performance, though in-game graphic options are completely lacking, offering low/medium/high without custom toggles for anything. Stories is using the unreal4 engine so you should be able to tweak further via ini files if need be and it should still perform well on lower spec systems, just something to keep in mind. Also worth mentioning is the fact you can't remap controls. Gamepad and keyboard both had reasonable layouts but it may be a problem for some people. Soundwork is fantastic and as for the games narrator, wanted to smack him over the head at times but he did fit well with the game. Devs cover the logistics of how he works on the following forum post.
It's been hard for me not to turn another page of the story since I've started playing, completed 4 of 30 odd so far. Would have liked to some new paths open up but I suspect they might if I play a little further (will update once I find out!) Recommended for those who don't mind a more casual focused rpg adventure. Just please keep in mind you may be disappointed if expecting a real challenge or hack n slash experience as mentioned earlier. Cheers folks and happy gaming!

Groundfox Day. That's the best way to describe Stories: The Path of Destinies. And from a storytelling perspective: the game really works. The narrator is able to deliver accessible writing to all ages with good referential humor that works for adults, yet still is nice for kids to follow along with. The narrator is the start here, as he reacts to your gameplay (here's a hint: go in circles really fast for a fun easter egg) and yet delivers good solid writing through the different story arcs, with a wide arrange of great endings from depressing to down right hilarious. But the storytelling has to carry the gameplay, which while functional, becomes a button masher quickly, in particular with an overly spammable counter move that can get you through the game entirely. It needed more variety in the long haul, and the difficulty is the major factor here as it may work for those looking for simple gameplay, but there's no difficulty levels or any sort of complications. But regardless, it's the story that will bring you to Stories, as Fairy Tale lovers will feel at home here, and trying to find all the endings will bring a sense of joy, yet fun along with it. You may just rush through the fights while doing it.

This game, it is truely something special.
This is a simple yet hard game about navigating a triangle through a series of patterns that fly towards you, kinda like a bullet hell game except the bullets are walls moving towards the centre of the screen. This game, as other who've played the game will tell you is... very difficult. Among one of the hardest games on Steam though certainly not THE hardest.
Part of it's difficulty is due to it's visuals. The levels are simplistic in design but very colourful in the sense that the colours frequently change and "pulse" with other colours. Combined with the constant rotation of the levels it makes for what some would call a trippy experience that is only amplified by a gorgeous soundtrack.
What you actually get in quantifiable terms is 6 very hard levels with three availible from the start. The aim of the game is identical across all six levels and is a deceptively simple goal. Just survive for 60 seconds. Doing this in levels 1 through 3 will unlock levels 4 through 6. The game boasts no multiplayer options but can be rather competetive when you constantly compare your personal best times on each level with those of your friends to try and be the best hexagoner.
Beating level 6, Hyper Hexagonest is quite a feat and by the time you manage it you'll likely have clocked in up to 20 hours on the game. The trick to beating levels is to first keep at it and never give up and second to keep going for long enough that you begin to recognise the patterns as the game throws them at you so that you can react in time with them.
One thing is for certain though. Once you're through with this game when you thing of a hexagon, you won't remember your first maths lessons in primary school, you won't think of bees and honeycombs, you'll think of this game. I highly recommend it. It'll be the most you'll ever get out of a £2 coin.

I havnt done the online yet., but Ive played the game start to finish on Drizzle and there genuinely isnt anything wrong with the game.
There are a few gaps in the game. But those are there because of the mechanics of the game:
- Game can be exploited and cheesed: Stand in the buffing circle of multiple Banners and you can solo 90% of the map. The Sniper can oneshot bosses.
- Reaching certain areas can be a pain: Having to jump across floating platforms to get to chests and whatnot can be super annoying, especially when being chased by Golems ;_;
- Difficulty/time restrictions: Having to burst down bosses while approaching higher difficulties is super annoying.
So how is RoR anything like Dark Souls? Simple. Monsoon. Lemme be frank, Rain (the Normal difficulty) is NOT that easy either. In fact I barely got past the first level using the Bandit. Monsoon is just a nightmare. Could you imagine doing Monsoon on HAHAHAHAHA difficulty?!! Sheer suicide.
And Drizzle isnt all that easy either. It can get tedious and sometimes, things go south quickly. I once had a bunch of drones die on me while fighting Providence, started running out of money to repair them and I nearly got annihilated by him. This was after playing for quite a long time.
You're forced most of the time to build into one or two different strategies and exploit the crap out of the game's mechanics. Trust me, playing an even build with your perks is suicide, especially at higher levels.
Risk of Rain that is designed to make you feel powerless as you are the alien invading another world. You are the outcast, fighting for your life and your future. Because of this, only the true hardcore/masochist gamers can Risk the Rain (At least at the higher levels...)

Tower of Time is an exquisitely beautiful RPG with an intriguing storyline.
The game world is individually crafted, down to the smallest detail.  Many of the puzzles in the game involved noticing tiny details and clicking on them. For example there is a statue hidden in vines that I did not see even when I walk past that location 5 or 6 times. There are also hidden rooms that are behind thick vegetations and journal updates that are hidden in libraries.  The landscapes are also very beautiful, including ice-covered caves, mechanical gadgets and a mix of technology and magic.
The game mechanics might be a bit difficult for those people that are used to turn-based RPG games. In fact, the games happen in real time, but you are given the opportunity to slow down time. However, even so, the fighting will keep you busy and you need to micro-manage them if you are playing on hard or epic levels. There is also the option of playing the game in easy or "story" levels as well. The player is given the choice of playing the game at any levels that he is most comfortable with.
The game world is extremely huge and consists of dungeons of many levels. Each level is made up of multiple sectors and the map is interspersed with teleportals to enable easy travel. Currently the game is in Early Access and more than half the contents are still under development. However, the contents that are currently release has given me many days of pleasure and enjoyment.
This game is like an exquisite gem and I would highly recommend it.

Simple though not too simple mechanics which are mostly intuitive.
Dynamic real time tactical combat, that feels a lot like a mix of tower defense and more traditional turn-based tactics.
A unique(ish) plot and storyline, with a lot to stay interesting, but not so much to bog you down..
Good to excellent graphics (shows up in cons too).
For being so close to EA release it has few bugs, which are responded  to very quickly with 2 major patches already released.
Extremely responsive developers, already very active on forums.
NPC's seem rather dynamic, hopefully this continues and your "choices" have lasting significant impact of party members attitude/composition/build/stats.
It's obvious the devs care.
Cons-
Way too colorful, maybe this is a style preference but it's generally much brighter and colorful than even a game like WoW; don't get me wrong it looks great, but it's a bit too vibrant especially on high resolution setting on a nice monitor.
With only so much game the story is a bit muddled, I imagine this will get better though.
Will update this review with the games developement.

[Characters - good]: You play as Adol, a red-haired swordsman who habitually washes up on the shores of lands with towers to climb and sealed ancient bad guys to slay. You must also sniff every girl who needs rescuing and frolic in their beds when they aren't looking... Also one boy became the target this one time. >_>
[Difficulty - good]: I've heard myths of the higher difficulty levels of some bosses, you won't be disappointed if you want a challenge. For those with poor reflexes, easy is totally playable and you shouldn't have too much trouble even on the most difficult bosses.
[Story - good]: Ys I: Climb a tower and leave nothing alive as you climb to the top. Ys II: Climb a variety of places while leaving nothing alive
. It may be short and simplistic but it's still well-written and easy to understand...besides, this is an action rpg and you're really here to kill things. :)
[Combat - excellent]: It's really a pity that Ys I & II are the only games to ever use the "bump" mechanic because I ended up having a blast using it. Ys I did not have magic but Ys II fixes that and polishes the "bump" mechanics a little more to make it even better. You can't go wrong with combat that allows you to literally plow through enemies and thus never have to stop moving to make for a very fast progression through the lands and dungeons.
[Graphics - good]: Though everyone has preferences for graphics, I'm in the retro crowd and prefer older games. Besides that, there's a lot of animation and detail packed into these games and they even included the option of the original character art or a newer style AND it has some rather beautiful cutscenes.
[Music - head bangingly awesome]: Seriously, you will get at least one song in either of these games stuck in your head at some point. They offer 3 variations of the musical score including the original score. I ended using the most recent variation which is orchestral and rock which was really well done.
[Replay - average]:  It would actually be bad but given the challenges some like to do on higher difficulties, there's the option to make it last longer. It does have amusing achievements though.
[Overall - good]: Ys I & II's combined playtime is about 10 hours on easy, give or take idling time. I had a lot of fun with both and really hope more Ys games will make it to Steam one day... For more adventures with our troublemaker, Adol.

I want to like this game more than I actually do. Overall, it's fun, which is the point, and why I clicked the Recommend button, but there are some flaws that detract from the amount of fun I could be having.
First, the graphics. They may seem slightly dated, but that isn't the issue. The biggest problem is the lack of options. My screen is 16:9, but the screen seems to display in something like 2.33:1, so everything is squished. Another problem is the lack of antialiasing, and while this might not be as noticeable if I could set the graphics to my screen's native resolution, the two problems combined really take away from the immersion.
Second, the controls. I've tried both keyboard/mouse and a 360 controller, the latter of which seems like the better option for an isometric shooter. The default values are difficult to use at best. Why are the triggers used for rotating the camera instead of firing weapons? And why is the camera so overly touchy? When I switched to the KB/mouse combo, the WASD setup was fine for most things, but camera rotation became such an issue that I simply avoided it.
I could make the writing and voice acting the third issue, and for some it may be problematic. I am a lover of B flicks however, so I didn't buy this game expecting a deep, rich story, or Hollywood A-list acting. While the script is predictable and the acting wooden, I could easily look past this and enjoy the game if it wasn't for the other flaws. (I've seen and loved almost every episode of MST3K, and if you know what that means, you'll understand.)
The one thing I have yet to check out is the main reason I bought it: co-op. Alas, if I can't sort out the issues with the controls, I don't know if I will bother. What I wanted was a PC version of Dead Nation, the brilliant PSN co-op zombie shooter. What I got was something less polished, and ultimately, less fun.
So why recommend it? Overall, it is somewhat fun, so if you get it on sale, go for it. There is some atmostphere about it, and some nice mechanics, including the weapon upgrade system--though this too lacks depth. Kill a critter and get some magic "upgrades"? How does that work exactly? This aside, and if you can look past the other flaws, it might be a nice way to waste some time.
Stay tuned for my review of the spin-off/sequel, Shadowgrounds Survivors, where I'm hoping that some of the issues listed above have been fixed. First, I need to finish this game.

This game goes down as one of my favorite games of all time. It really does give the feeling of being a spaceship captain in the depths of space. There are a thousand options to make during your journey, and it makes every playthrough different and unique. You can also customize your ship to fit your playstyle. Like unleashing barrages of laser and missile fire? Enjoy shutting down their engines and letting your boarding crews clean up the enemy crew? Feel like commanding drones to cripple their ship and block missile fire for you? All three are viable options for you to focus on.
I admit that at this point, the dialogue options and random events do feel a bit scripted, but I've put in A LOT of time into this game to get to this point. It does add to the adventure and intensity though. Do you risk your own crew members to gain more crew? Do you risk hull damage to gain more scrap or a weapon? No matter how much you've played, the game will still feel fresh and new every playthrough.
Also, be sure to name your crew after friends and family members. It heightens the drama.

This game takes my love of a good defense game, with a wide array of traps and some varied terrain, and combines it with some goofy humor and a 3-D first-person perspective.  Watching orcs get hacked to bits is fun!
You can't entirely rely on your traps to do all the hacking, though: Some you will have to handle yourself, with crossbow, sword, or spells.  I'm ambivalent about that part, as it does keep you on your toes and give you a chance to catch what your traps missed, but trying to chase down a scurrying kobold with a crossbow detracts from the base-building gameplay if you have to do it too much.  All in all though I found it reasonably well balanced at normal difficulty.
In addition to your choice of traps and spells, in later levels you can choose for each level which of three "weavers" to work with, each with their own upgrade tree, which opens up more strategies.  How do you want your orcs to die today?

Fantastic game so far. Even though it's early access, there's still plenty to do and there will be more story added. The combat was a little difficult at first, but after a while I needed to raise the difficulty. Combat is a separate entity to exploration, you know when you're getting into a battle The skill system has a Dragon Age style of levelling up, an ability then a choice of A or B to add to that ability. The devs also answer questions on the forum section of Steam, which is nice to see. I even saw them offering to edit someone's save if they encountered an unsurpassable bug.
Pros:
-Loot based system has that familiar rpg feel to it.
-Teleporting is instant.
-Enemy analysis before battle, shows resistances/weaknesses.
-Beastiary shows every enemy you've faced, so you can learn how to take them down for next time.
-If you fail a battle, you can retry or load last save.
-Crafting system is simple and effortless.
-Soundtrack is enjoyable.
Cons:
-No controls option. Although they are simple, but it would be nice to have an option to check them.
-Low amount of save slots - 5 and an autosave (I prefer to have as many as I require but not a dealbreaker).
-Sometimes you may need to click more than once for an ability to activate, minor bug but it will be fixed.
Do I recommend this game? Absolutely, and it's only going to be improved upon. If you like Dragon Age style rpgs without as much dialogue, this is a game for you.

I'm probably going against the grain with this review. The game itself, matches the original. Unlike films, I tend to think sequels and later versions tend to end up better and with XCOM, this doesn't generally happen.
I watched the video and description of the development of XCOM, having been out of the gaming world for a while actually thought it wasn't out. When I realised it was, quickly purchased it (let me say now, its worth £4). I'm going to cover the main annoyances I had with this. To summarise, its better looking than the original, the resource management is more engaging but the gameplay is worse.
Glamcam
While developing, this was called the Glamcam, which is really just a slow motion events view change when action happens. Its not a particular innovative idea and due to the reasons listen below you can spend 3 minutes watching multiple misses. I've also seen it break windows that aren't there or even in the line of sight.
Probability.
So you think that there is a 50% chance of hitting the alien. Why? Well you're told that on the aiming screen. Due to the difficulty of some of the levels and the seeming inability for your soldiers to hit anything (despite their experience). You'll resort to save and reload. During this I once attempted a shot, which said 50% over 30 times, not hitting once.
Cover.
In the old XCOM, this existed, you could also crouch, lay prone and basically be hidden. If you knew something was behind it you could also blast it away and in reverse you could also hide (the AI would not see you, BUT would know the direction you were if you'd been seen). In this version, cover exists, but even if completely covered, you can be hit (and not always through the object). If you're also just around the corner, you can both be seen and hit. Also if you see something, it instantly sees you, as well as well as the group is near (and randomly other groups, but less so if they're further away). Basically if you watch the video, cover is almost described as something they thought of, yet, its more effectively used and understandable in the original.
Crysalids
Particularly annoying. The zombies have the same distance (they're quick) as the Crysalids, so staying at a distance is almost impossible, since if you have a group of them, they'll close, kill, then a turn or two later you've got basically another Crysalids, since the Zombies seem to have the same damage/hit as the Crysalids. They seem to ignore you when you've killed one of them and quickly kill as many civilians as possible to regenerate their numbers. Until you've killed one they seem focused on you or taking cover.
Time
Maybe its just me, but I like to enjoy a game and not feel like i'm waiting a while. After a bit I turned of the event cameras and everything to speed it up, but the frequent saves and reloads to ensure all the council don't leave due to Ufo's tending to turn up in the same areas all the time (despite having expanded the satellite network.
Inventory/Loadout
There is lots of opportunity to develop items. Previously you could even collect the alien fragments and use the weaponry once you had researched it. With this, its almost like the game plot has been changed to incorporate not being able to pick up or use more items. not being able to change weapons and also have a reduced `loadout`. This hasn't been added to enhance the game, its merely to cut out that element of the game. So, although you might think this game has more (it has less). Oh, some of the soldiers have the ability to carry 2 items. If they're Generals. This means you don't have to keep building/buying ammo. There isn't any (although soldiers need to reload). There is an almost arcade atmosphere to the game because of this.
I suppose these are a lot of gripes and maybe more effort is required, but even on easy mode there is no ignoring the difficulty and that the game has left more out than it has added in. It has a feeling like a lot of shortcuts were made on this game. Sure, its better than a lot of games, but I think I'd rather play the original.

The game is good, but I'm requesting a refund because Ubisoft are awful.

My first civilization was Russia. I rushed through the tutorial because there was so much reading and kinda quit halfway through. I ended up just starting a new game with the default settings and jumping right in. First off, there was so much to read and look at, I felt completely lost. I still do but not nearly as much, but as you get further into the game you feel accomplished as you begin to understand the mechanics and workings of this game. I first began by working with Japan and being friendly with them because they were the closest civilization. The next ruler I met was, of course, George Washington. He was a♥♥♥♥♥♥to me from the start. So I eliminated him with the help of Japan. I expanded and grew my city until it engulfed nearly half the continent, which helped me get ahead in nearly every way. Japan didn't like that, their leader said I was a bloodthirsty warmonger. That's when I first started to hate Japan. I soon discovered there were MORE continents to explore. I sent out ships and eventually met the Aztecs and the Iroquois on the next island. I decided to just stick with my own island rather than declaring war on them. As I expanded my colony to small islands hidden around the world, Japan seemed to follow, settling their people in the most ridiculous places just to assert dominance. They began to act like little kids calling "shotgun" on every little piece of unclaimed land they could find, utterly frustrating me. So you know what I did? I rushed the space age and dedicated all my resources to science in the year 1970. This gave me just enough time to finish my entire ship by 2012. But before I launched my ship into space and claimed victory, I had to settle the score with Japan. So I deployed every single one of my naval ships on Nagasaki and finished them off with an atomic bomb. I destroyed them not because I had to, but for the glory of Mother Russia. Anyways, that was my first game and it felt involving the entire time and I am excited to play another round soon.
Overall, this game doesn't have over 80,000 positive reviews for nothing. The only possible problem with this game is I occasionally get small lag spikes, nothing significant though. This is basically Dead Island with better graphics and parkour (free-running/climbing), and weapons will inevitably break, impossible to maintain forever. Okay, so that's not fair...there's also a day/night cycle, skill upgrades that make more of a difference per point than in Dead Island (but only one character, so there aren't several characters each with different skills), better (but not great) gunplay than Dead Island, no vehicles (until DLC), and more story. Overall, everything is better...except that last part.
The story in this game is pretty poor. It starts out interesting, though there are very few characters that come across as interesting or even likable. If you even do manage to somewhat like a character, with this being a zombie game, it's a safe bet that character's going to die. Honestly, more characters were memorable and likable for me in Dead Island, which is pretty sad. The worst thing in the entire game is a specific character: the villain.
I'm fairly certain that Dying Light's villain stumbled upon a copy of the game's script, read that he was a villain, and rewrote his own lines to sound like what he thought a villain should say, based off cartoons he watched as a kid, because Gargamel from The Smurfs had more compelling dialog. Captain Planet had better villains than this guy. He actually has lines where he says stuff about wanting to spread chaos. No, not an amazing Batman-quality memorable villain with a plan that uses chaos as a catalyst...the guy just seems to get off on threatening people and being evil for the sake of being evil. Heath Ledger's Joker totally pulled off the whole "I am an agent of chaos" thing. This game's villain? No. Hell no. I cannot stress how uninteresting and dull this game's villain is. The lines were groan-worthy, and not in a so-bad-it's-good way.
The next worst thing about this game is its forced singleplayer ending. At the beginning, you're forced to play singleplayer until the end of your first day, which is a little annoying if you're wanting to play with friends, as I did, but on the bright side, it shows the ropes to new players, thus preventing people who don't know how to even do parkour yet from joining your game. That's a plus, but the very final mission of the game can only be played solo. It's really awkward to play for 40 hours with your friends online, only to have to say goodbye to do the final mission. I know why it's single player, but they could've redesigned the final mission and done it in co-op with end story tweaks. While much of the game has an open world feel to it, the ending has an extremely on-rails feeling to it that really left me feeling a bit conflicted about the game. Oh...and the final "boss" is a pretty bland quick time event.
That said, this is a very fun game that I had a great co-op experience with. I highly recommend it, but simply advise that you brace yourself for just how cliche and annoying the villain is, how few characters you'll care about, and the poor ending mission's QTE and forced singleplayer for it. You grow in power from very weak and afraid of big groups of zombies to the point where you're eventually wading through swarms of them killing them en masse. It's wonderful.

I am completely enthralled with this game :)
And as I'm progressing in my age :O that does not happen all that often anymore...
First of all, I will admit that fans of the series, or simply people familiar with the previous installments, are surely more likely to get more out of this title :) But isn't that always true? And is it a "con?" That said, it being a prequel - it is absolutely unnecessary for anyone to play any of the previous games ;)
Meeting old pals, or in this case, "premet" pals (like preheated or precooked or something? :O), references to some special quests (the healing conundrum, anyone? :D), and other lore quirks that transcend all the titles - the game is brimming with those! And I absolutely adored the original Divinie Divinity - one of my first crpgs I have ever played to completion and with multiple playthroughs. Some of the other sequels to the original were... let's just say, they were trying different approaches. But finally, Larian Studios struck gold, by creating this masterpiece of a game :)
I have spent about 10 hours in this new version of the realm of Rivellon and I haven't even moved out of the starting hub xD Really! I have scouted every nook and cranny of this little town, discovering its secrets and easter eggs :D And if the remainder of the content is anything like the starting town, the game is just huge! But not as much in area as in detail, and I find that to be a much more valuable trait - one often ignored in times of vast, open-world games, which offer size, but not quality :/
The sneaking system - OMG, so funny! Metal Gear Solid references there I can see... is what Yoda would have said... :O Anyways, there is plenty of these innuendoes, references to other games, to life in general. At one point, the two main heroes, who are your avatars (yes, you lead two characters, but you command a larger party later on), comment on how ridiculous it is, that they can't jump over a simple rope to get to a loot chest. And in fact, nothing can be done to the rope, and there is no way to go around it with the chest being on a pier. But there is a way to get to the loot :)
And this is the next thing I want to talk about. These days, when developers say "multiple choices, multiple approaches, multiple endings," I usually cringe, because the word multiple often does not go beyond the number two... sometimes 3... but, I guess, technicially, 3 qualifies as multpile... -.- Anyway, in Divinity: Original Sin, if you can think it, you can probably do it :) Well obviously, I'm exaggerating, but what is not exaggerated, though, is the word multiple in this game ;) Sneaking, and stealing, using your characters as distractions to divert the line of sight of unsuspecting owners, suffering the consequences if caught and reaping the benefits, if not, could be a game on its own :) And I loved, when I looted yet another painting off a wall (I found them to be a great source of income!) and my partner congratulated me on yet another heist well done. Usually in those random conversations the options are only binary, however, they each have a consequence which often reflects in a trait in permanent stats of the characters.
And yes the stats! Talents, abilities, skills.... so many things to make each character unique, offering infinite replayability. And the number of classes has also increased, when compared to other Divinity RPGs. Most of your talents affect one another, not just spells, interacting with the environment, but other traits as well - charisma, speed, leadership, luck - there are so many factors to affect your gameplay, yet it is all seemlessly blended in, so that you always intuitively know which stat to boost and which to ignore (telekinesis FTW, though! It reminded me so much of the original Divinity :D).
Only, if the game was more graphically pleasing... Just kidding - it is truly gorgeous! The world is rich and detailed, as is the whole game. The depth of field does wonders at closer zoom, the characters are nicely outlined, so that it is never too confusing during the battles.... Oh, yes! The fighting system.
Now, turn-based is the way to go in classic crpgs, in my opinion. Trigger-happy button smashing is fun, but for action-adventure games. For RPGs, which aim at a longer gameplay, richer plot, multitude of side-quests, a turn-based system fits better into the general mechanic and is consistent with the source behind cRPGs - the actual role-playing games, which obviously are based on the dice ;) With the amount of interactivity between the various talents and the environment, this particular system makes each encounter a unique experience. And again, the game rewards clever thinking, choosing the path less traveled by, which may be less obvious, too, but offers a more visceral final scores :)
Scores... Have I talked about the music already? No, and I should have started with that - it is gorgeous, no wait, already used gorgeous... mesmerizing, yes! It is mesmerizingly beautiful. There are lovely new scores, as well as some tracks from the orignal Divine Divinity, whose soundtrack is often praised to this day! And some of the tracks are even variations on those original tracks! It's so nice when you hear the tavern music, or the Rivertown farmlands choiry march one more time and it actually has some twist to it :) The music in the Divnity titles has always been of high quality, and this legacy is well-kept still.
I have mentioned rewarding clever thinking. I think, coming to a close here, that the success of this game is the best kind of a reward for the clever thinking the developers have resorted to in creating this title :) It is a true spiritual successor to the highly acclaimed Divine Divinity - both in mechanics, interactivity of the environment, a unique twist on the classical fantasy paradigm, but - above all - in the range of options that is given to the player to progress in the game. There is a million other things I probably wanted to have said but did not... and remember, I only experienced the very beginning :) Larian Studios has long saught to find a formula to repeat their initial success - I strongly believe they have found one :)
Congratulations to them, and salutations to all of you - I hope you are, or will be, as satisfied with Divinity: Original Sin as I am.

As much of a puzzle game as it is "an experience". Might seem short, but it never becomes boring or outstays it's welcome. Just the right length, in my opinion. Also packed full of interesting wisdom and in general is very "zen" to play.
The puzzle elements are solid, with very well thought out mechanics (gun upgrades) with a little bit of backtracking (due to said gun upgrades). The basic gist of it - you can "store" and place blocks and make them do various things, depending on the upgrade. Like make them move to some place or place them in a circle (as circle as a voxel based circle can be).
It's extremely abstact at times, with me running around not knowing exactly what to do. But the map (the thing you see at "the main menu" alleviates the issue, once you understand how to interpret all the simbols it shows).
All in all, definitely recommended, one of the best puzzle games (especially FPS ones) I've played. It will be a rewarding experience, at least for me it was.

I didn't recommend this game so its a warning to MAC USERS. (That being said, PLEASE do not say my review was unhelpful unless you are, in fact, a Mac user as I simply wish to warn my fellow OS users.)
First, let me say I enjoyed what I was able to play of this game.  Its very simple, the voice acting is horrendous, but the gameplay is fairly fun, albeit simple.  I got it for very cheap off of humble bundle so no complaints.  For $0.69 it was totally worth it I'd say.
Now, if you have a mac, DO NOT BUY.  This game is broken on Macs.  Once I got to the 3rd or 4th (can't remember) chapter, the framerate dropped to maybe like 12 frames per minute.  Yes. Per MINUTE.  It was unplayable.  I thought, perhaps my laptop is just experiencing difficulties.  I restarted and retried.  I will now add that this game only autosaves once you complete a chapter and some of the chapters begin taking 1+ hours to beat.  I had to restart the chapter I was on, but it was ok at the time.  However, at roughly the same amount of time into said chapter, I encountered the same problem.
I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  I contacted the devs as well as searched forums.  Turns out this is a VERY common problem on macs.  Frozenbyte basically said, "oh yeah we know about it but we don't know what causes it but hopefully our new games won't have the same problem."  Great load of help, that.
Anyway, I'm sick of developers apparently not even hardly testing their product before releasing to Mac.  Currently, it is fraud that they are selling this game for mac, as it DOES NOT WORK.
TL;DR:  If you want a simple isometric shooter, with voice acting on par with an arcade game, go for it. UNLESS you have a Mac in which case beware that this game probably will be unplayable for you.  Thank you.

So after finishing up all 3 episodes, I can give this a proper review. Overall, I thought the game was fun but it had some flaws. Warning: I am biased because I absolutely love TWD comics and the Telltale games.
Pros:
-Story. As with a lot of TTG titles, this game had an overall great story. Bringing "backstory" to one of the most loved Walking Dead characters made me love the character even more. It also fills in the blank of her absence from the comics which I was curious about.
-Characters. Most of the characters are interesting. Without spoilers, the main antagonist of the mini series really made me question whether or not they were bad which I thought was good.
Cons:
-Short. 3 hours for 15 bucks? I took my time with this game and still only ended up with 3 hours in gametime. Kind of disappointing.
-Choices. I feel like half my choices don't even matter. Most of them felt bland and very cliche and most just end in the same result.
-Predictable. Considering I knew which characters were still alive thanks to the comics, there was no surprise on who lived and who died. Plus, there were a lot of parts in the game where you can pretty much guess what was gonna happen.
Overall, the game is good and I definitely recommend it for fans of TWD or TTG, but I'd recommend waiting for a sale. 15 bucks is just a little too much for 3 hours of gameplay. My final rating for this game is a 6.5/10

This recommendation is a bit on the hesitant side, though I'll get to why later.
Anyway, First off,
has a great soundtrack - and an interesting one at that. It tries to give a cinimatic feel without using orchestral instruments, and as a result it has a distinct sound. Bonus points are given for utilizing a leitmotief, and even more for making it subtle.
Graphically, there's not much to speak of.
has a very retro look, though kinda on the low-end of 16 bit or the high-end of 8 bit. The sprites are large and high-res, but there's no shading to speak of. The backgrounds feel a bit, well, stock, but look nice.
's gameplay is easy to learn but takes a long time to master. You can get the hang of the game very quickly, but the difficulty is notable. It's not the hardest game I've played, but it's definately a challenge.
Which brings me to why I'm hesitant to recommend this game. Saying the game "isn't the hardest game I've played" is not a very accurate way to judge difficulty, as I've played a few games that were so hard the average gamer would considder it torture (
comes to mind). This game is definately out to get you (like any Roguelike) and is VERY obvious about it.
Story-wise,
is pretty simple and a bit reminicent of one of the underlying plots of
, just in reverse. You've stolen the plans to the rebel flagship and are running from the rebel fleet. You must bring the plans to the federation HQ and then destroy the rebel flagship. There are a ton of side-quests and events that spice things up, and no playthrough is the same.
Overall, I can say that this game is fun and challenging, and has a great soundtrack. However, the difficulty is definately something to note, and the graphics are only half-decent even for a retro-styled game. I give it a 6.5/10, or a solid 8/10 if you like difficult games. I also give it a recommendation, though be warned - this game is quite a challenge.
Recommended for: Retro gamers who don't care about the quality of their pixels, fans of roguelikes, soundtrack junkies and anyone looking for a challenge.
Not recommended for: "ub3r 1337 gamzorz 111" type players, casuals, graphics junkies or people who hate losing.
The Bottom Line: Fun, challenging, and a great soundtrack, but half-decent graphics and the shear difficulty level mean that
is not for everyone.

I'm probably going against the grain with this review. The game itself, matches the original. Unlike films, I tend to think sequels and later versions tend to end up better and with XCOM, this doesn't generally happen.
I watched the video and description of the development of XCOM, having been out of the gaming world for a while actually thought it wasn't out. When I realised it was, quickly purchased it (let me say now, its worth £4). I'm going to cover the main annoyances I had with this. To summarise, its better looking than the original, the resource management is more engaging but the gameplay is worse.
Glamcam
While developing, this was called the Glamcam, which is really just a slow motion events view change when action happens. Its not a particular innovative idea and due to the reasons listen below you can spend 3 minutes watching multiple misses. I've also seen it break windows that aren't there or even in the line of sight.
Probability.
So you think that there is a 50% chance of hitting the alien. Why? Well you're told that on the aiming screen. Due to the difficulty of some of the levels and the seeming inability for your soldiers to hit anything (despite their experience). You'll resort to save and reload. During this I once attempted a shot, which said 50% over 30 times, not hitting once.
Cover.
In the old XCOM, this existed, you could also crouch, lay prone and basically be hidden. If you knew something was behind it you could also blast it away and in reverse you could also hide (the AI would not see you, BUT would know the direction you were if you'd been seen). In this version, cover exists, but even if completely covered, you can be hit (and not always through the object). If you're also just around the corner, you can both be seen and hit. Also if you see something, it instantly sees you, as well as well as the group is near (and randomly other groups, but less so if they're further away). Basically if you watch the video, cover is almost described as something they thought of, yet, its more effectively used and understandable in the original.
Crysalids
Particularly annoying. The zombies have the same distance (they're quick) as the Crysalids, so staying at a distance is almost impossible, since if you have a group of them, they'll close, kill, then a turn or two later you've got basically another Crysalids, since the Zombies seem to have the same damage/hit as the Crysalids. They seem to ignore you when you've killed one of them and quickly kill as many civilians as possible to regenerate their numbers. Until you've killed one they seem focused on you or taking cover.
Time
Maybe its just me, but I like to enjoy a game and not feel like i'm waiting a while. After a bit I turned of the event cameras and everything to speed it up, but the frequent saves and reloads to ensure all the council don't leave due to Ufo's tending to turn up in the same areas all the time (despite having expanded the satellite network.
Inventory/Loadout
There is lots of opportunity to develop items. Previously you could even collect the alien fragments and use the weaponry once you had researched it. With this, its almost like the game plot has been changed to incorporate not being able to pick up or use more items. not being able to change weapons and also have a reduced `loadout`. This hasn't been added to enhance the game, its merely to cut out that element of the game. So, although you might think this game has more (it has less). Oh, some of the soldiers have the ability to carry 2 items. If they're Generals. This means you don't have to keep building/buying ammo. There isn't any (although soldiers need to reload). There is an almost arcade atmosphere to the game because of this.
I suppose these are a lot of gripes and maybe more effort is required, but even on easy mode there is no ignoring the difficulty and that the game has left more out than it has added in. It has a feeling like a lot of shortcuts were made on this game. Sure, its better than a lot of games, but I think I'd rather play the original.

Orcs Must Die! is a tower defence game that uses a third person action oriented perspective instead of the traditional top down view of similar games.
Its a very fun and entertaining game that will last you around 11 hours depending on your playstyle. A constant progression of new weapons, traps and enemies drives you through the adventure, and ensure the same strategy won't work for every level.
Not only do you lay traps as in a typical tower defence game, your character can also move around and contribute to the kills to complement the traps you have set. The graphics are bright and colourful and animations are very fluid. Music and sound are crisp and clear and the game is a joy to play.
Downsides, this game is single-player only. Having a friend in multiplayer mode to help cover some of multiple enemy entrances would have made it an even more enjoyable experience.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10
Entertaining and fun game in a new twist on the tower defence genre. Don't miss it.

The game has a very large map and once it is loaded from the menu, you will not have any loading screens while you move about to different peaks.
[This part has the negative aspects] HOWEVER, there are some absolutely gamebreaking problems with this game. First of all, the physics engine is completely broken AND the game is unforgiving.  It would be one thing to have a bad physics system with forgiving gameplay, but Ubisoft says F%%% you, we don't care. The physics engine has no idea what friction is nor how gravity works. If your board TOUCHES anything other than snow, you are dead. The rocks will either have infinite friction, act like magnets and suck you into them, or launch you at infinite speed. This is a major problem in some challenges (BOBSLED CHALLENGE) because the physics make it impossible to even complete. In addition to this, jumping is cruel. You have to jump well before you leave the ramps, so many of the smaller jumps are practically impossible to time properly. You end up with a .05 second window to execute a jump or you fail.
NEUTRAL PIECES. The characters are either forgettable or obnoxious. They try to make a story or something out of the game, but nothing is coherent and you just cram challenges in so you get gear, XP, and credits. It would be cool (and really easy) if they made this something like a "career mode" and you created a character and progressed through challenges (kind of like Tony Hawk's Underground back in the day). You just get to Mont Blanc as quickly as possible and forget about any dialogue or any sort of narrative the game tries to feed you.
Overall, it is hard to recommend this game. If you can find it on sale, buy it. I paid $40 but still feel bad about the price. If you can get it for $30 or less, then buy it. The concept is excellent and the game is great fun when it is working properly. HOWEVER, when the game is NOT working properly (physics engine, I am looking at you), then it makes you want to punt puppies across the room.
tl;dr the game has its moments, but it is so broken in other aspects that it only makes it a 6.5 out of 10. Some challenges are great fun and others make your blood boil.
Fix the physics engine and it will easily be a solid 8.5/10. This game is AWESOME when it is working correctly.

Overall, a great game well worth the $40 I paid on sale.

Tower of Time is one these rare indie games that has amazing graphics, music and story that I feel is on par with some of the larger companies. Each floor of the tower has a theme to it, and that, mixed with the music makes the game feel very atmospheric. The story is one of the strongest aspects of this game and you will get most of it through the main play but will find little extra tidbits of story hidden throughout each floor of the tower. There are more than just story hidden around the tower though, there are also hidden treasure stashes and some secrets to uncover.
Combat in this game is much more than just using the best spells and blowing your oppenents away. There are tactics that should be considered on each group of enemies and different enemies have different weaknesses. It will take more than just the best gear to overcome each encounter. You have to plan out how to get the most out of each spell/skill you have at your disposal. I feel this kind of combat is rare in most RPGs and I like how challenging some of the fights can be. But even if you fail the game lets you restart that fight again without having to go back to the last time you saved.
There is also a crafting system in the game that is simple but effective for gearing out your champions. You will get gear drops from treasure chests and encounters. You will also get crafting crystals which can be used to craft more gear. Old gear you no longer want can be disassebled to gain more crafting crystals to make more gear.
Overall this game is really good and I am looking forward to seeing it through to completion.

Tower of Time is a journey through an exquisite landscape, which promises both a rich story, (over 80k words!), and also satisfying RPG gameplay & tactical real-time-with-slowdown combat.
From the very beginning of the game, the story draws you in with intrigue, and a powerful desire to find out the history of the main character!  The environments are hand-crafted, beautifully detailed -- the quality and care of the designers shows from the very first second of gameplay!
The tutorials on how to play -- explaining skills, the points system, equipment, combat, etc. -- are very easily understandable and make it easy to pick up the game without struggling in ignorance or needing to consult a wiki.
Controls are quite natural and fluid with Diablo-style movement.  I really like that you can view the entire battlefield in combat, without the camera being locked on your character.  This enables you to position your characters optimally, planning for enemy movements and attacks.
Points put into character skills, (special attacks), can be respecced at any time, which is nice if you come across a particularly difficult group of enemies and need to change your strategy on the fly.
The dialogue, story, and found bits of text are EXTRAORDINARILY well-written -- easy to read, yet interesting and entertaining.  Some games have repetitive dialogue or become boring within the first 5 minutes... not so with Tower of Time -- it reads like a lovingly-crafted novel -- a work of literature unto itself.
I am still at the beginning of my journey with the game, but it has already impressed me to no end!  (And remember, this is an indie title!  The work done by the team is well beyond any expectation!)
I'm anxious to continue my journey, and see what other secrets the game holds!  I'll be updating my review as I get further into the game :-)

Do you like great storytelling? What about Vikings? Do you like them? Do you enjoy making difficult choices and seeing consequences? If answer to all these questions is "yes", then this is the game for you. And don't let the screenshots fool you. Yes, it's 2D game, but a great one.
Of course, it's not as simple as that. In this game you will be playing the role of a caravan leader and you will be responsible not only for your life, but also for the lives of all the people who trusted you and have chosen to side with you in this journey. Be sure to think about every choice you will be making or suffer the consequences.
There is no single, "right", path. You can lose all your characters in a blink of an eye and yet the caravan will be moving forward. It's a bleak, tough life and you must be prepared to do what it's needed for survival. Just don't be to ambitious. There is no need to play this game on the "Hard" difficulty. I am not even sure, if the "Hard" difficulty is beatable at the moment. "Normal" is challenging enough. Enemies are still deadly and food is still scarse.
Don't rush, enjoy the story and I guarantee you that it will be worth it.

It's by no means a bad game, but I was actually disappointed with The Banner Saga, despite everything about it seeming like it would be a perfect fit for my tastes. An epic tale with branching paths, some tactical RPG combat, a hint of managerial simulation, and of course the breathtaking visuals and music.
For me there were two main issues: combat isn't deep enough, and the caravan management seems tokenistic.
Combat is a rare occurence in the game, which is rather short in comparison to most tactical RPGs. As a result, characters don't get much of an opportunity to grow. There's no way (that I know of) to go out and farm battles, so using newly-acquired characters that haven't had a chance to gain levels is often just asking for trouble. There are only five levels, however, so it's not a huge risk, but in most cases your characters won't get a chance to develop fully. Gaining xp is only achieved through kills, so this is also a problem for some of the more support-oriented characters.
The other "half" of the gameplay is managing your caravan, but this can almost be completely ignored, and is probably the most efficient route if you want your characters to get as strong as possible. There is a small penalty in it reduces your characters' willpower (extra moves you can make in combat), but compared with additional stat points it's a minor inconvenience.
In the end, I found myself just clicking to go through the motions of combat and reach the end as soon as possible, which was about 8 hours. It's a worthy game but it has its flaws, so while I recommend it, I suggest waiting for a price drop.

Shadowgrounds is an action over the head shooter from Frozenbyte that got a lot of mixed reviews so I got curious and had to review it myself as well.
Indeed the game is a bag that can give you mixed feelings. The intro starts off wich seems to be the setting for your basic military experiment/conspiracy, which even though it has written low budget all over it, it still kind of sets the games premises on pretty good.
The menu is looking ok as well and the background always keeps it a bit interesting and makes you hope something is going to happen . The first thing you will notice is that it DOES NOT have a save option.Yes, in this game you cannot save. You just have a couple of lives/respawns after wich it is game over. Like in the good old PlayStation Arcade games. This may put off a lot of people because the game can be surprisingly hard at some points, but for people like me it is a welcoming challenge.
For all the others, well at least there is a save progress at the start of each level at least.
The story starts off with the hero (Tyler) , a former military , current mechanic guy , beeng sent to fix some random generators with his buddies. The starting tone was very creepy and reminded me of a Dead Space atmosphere, which was great to notice, considering that this game is definetly not a triple A title. You fix the generators and notice that all the sudden there are bodies and blood everywhere,and surprisingly enough there is an alien invasion on your planet. You meet the army and start cleaning up. While not the most original type of story (has Doom 3) written all over it, the story holds up surprisingly well.
Moving on to the characters. All of them, including Tyler, seem very under developed. The game tries to tell you something at the start to make you care,but it just fails to deliver or generally fails at the character development section.
Graphic wise, everything seems decent, even though most of the graphics seem a bit washed up,even for a top down shooter. The details to the terrain/rooms are quite astonishing at some points. Overall the graphic,while not impressive in any way,does its job, just because of the attention to detail.The character models look just really low budget and plain dumb. The graphics type for the characters is really low quality compared to the overall graphics of the game.
Music and sound FX. These just do their job but nothing more. No memorable music here and the SFX just blend in with the atmosphere. Some sound FX reminded me of the first Unreal game for some reason.
The enemies, are your generic alien types and all are very annoying because they can just randomly appear in front of you and outnumber you directly. Their attack types get some time to get used to,and you do need some patience with each. You cannot just rush everything because you will die extremely fast.
Gameplay and atmosphere. The game tries a dark and gritty atmosphere that initially delivers very well but it is just lost along the way. The flashlight object shadowing mechanic is very cool to look at but it gets old too quick. Overall the atmosphere is fairly decent, the game does tempt you to go back and finish it.
Regarding gameplay only. It is quite satisfying to roll over large amounts of aliens but there are several points when it just feels unpolished. You need to do a lot of barrel rolling to avoid instant kill and you need to be aware of your environment all the time because if you hit a wall or an object,the character fails to respond quickly enough,and this causes a delay in movement,delay which will most of the time get you killed. This “stuck syndrome” is met in a large number of times,and really brings the game down as especially in the outdoor environments, you can get stuck a lot in the terrain because there are invisible walls in the middle of the map or the terrain was intended to be unpassable but on the map it looks just normal walking terrain. The gameplay overall feels initially good but gets repetitive and feels too hard at some points.
The weapons to me were very disappointing. While the game does have some sort of upgrade system to keep things interesting, I found myself way too many times using the standard pistol with unlimited ammo because everything else has very scarce ammo. Speaking of weapons, most of them seem very ineffective to the aliens. You waste an entire magazine on one enemy at times. Now this beeing good or bad,it is debateble. It does add a survival element to the game, but this element feels like it just happen to be in the game. Does not seem an intended behaivour. The ammo supplies are low, the weapons are largely ineffective and the only thing that keeps this aspect up is the upgrade system,which turns like a chore fast. It’s does not feel crucial on what type of upgrades you need to take.
Throughout the game you get upgrade parts to upgarde the weapons, which is a bit refreshing but again,gets old fast and also you find several computer terminals that fill in on the back story.
After managing to finish the game, I realized that the atmospheric music was much better than what it was initially and also what seemed to be a generic military/alien invasion had quite an interesting twist in the end. The story seemed stale throught the game but the ending was really weird to witness. Also with the right upgrades,the weapons DO seem to deliver some punch ,but for me it was still a bit of a disappointment.
I will recommend this game to fans of the genre and even to people that just want something new. Be advised, that the game is good but it is definetely not great, it does have the weight of a budget title all over it, but in the end it manages to deliver.

The amount of times these games have been redone is truly mindblowing, but then again Ys has been around since 1987. What we have here is an enhanced port of a PSP port of an enhanced edition of a windows remake of a combined turbografx-16/pc-engine remake of a pair of games on an ancient japanese pc. Rolls right off the tongue and I'm not even gonna get into how many ports the original games themselves got. I'm fairly certain this won't be the last remake either.
Now that I got that bit of nonsence out of the way let's move on to the review.
The island of Esteria which is known for its trade in silver has been cut off from mainland Europe by a phenomenon called the stormwall for the last six months. Enter Adol Christin, a 17 year old young man with a passion for adventure and measuring women
. He sails to Esteria from the port town of Promarock (or Promalock depending on the translation) but his boat gets caught in the stormwall and he shipwrecks off the coast of the island. He is found by villagers and taken to the nearby town's clinic. This is where the game starts. From here on cue battles with monsters, ancient civilizations, saving the world and the usual business when it comes to JRPGs.
Overall the story is not a groundbreaking epic that will shock you with amazing plot twists, but it is really well written and will suck you in if you take your time with it. Even the most trivial NPCs usually have something new and interesting to say as the story moves forward (this is something Nihon Falcom does a lot). Ys II takes place immediately after Ys I, so my recommendation is to play both games in one go. There's also a bit of humour added by XSEED which fits quite well since it's put in the right places and doesn't feel forced.
If you've read the nonsence at the top or looked at the screenshots you should already know what to expect in terms of graphics. Enhancements or not you're looking at slightly improved visuals from a 1997 Windows game. That said Chronicles does have a nifty feature where you can pick from the original PC interface or the PSP one as well as picking between the original late 90s anime artstyle or the more modern artstyle for the character portraits. That's all there is to be said about the graphics, wether you like them or not is up to you, but I wouldn't judge the game based on looks alone.
PS: There is no FPS lock, so stop whining, you babies.

As far as I'm concerned Falcom Sound Team JDK are musical gods and I'll fight anyone who says otherwise.
With that out of the way, you have the option to pick from three different renditions of the soundtrack in the options menu (or just mod in whatever the hell you want because PC). The original PC-88 soundtrack from 1987, the PC Complete soundtrack from 2001 or the new Chronicles soundtrack from 2009. All three are great, though which one you go with depends on you. My personal recommendation is to mod the turbografx-16 audio in and enjoy one of the best versions of the soundtrack (why they never bothered to use it again is beyond me), some dude posted a mod for both games on the forums, you can find it if you look around.
Long story short: Music is 11/10.

While the rest of the games in the series are more traditional in terms of combat, Ys I & II are more of an acquired taste. The reason for this is because unlike most action RPGs at the time here you don't press a button to attack enemies. Instead you ram into them (slightly off center), that's it. In Ys II you get some spells which allow you to attack at range but the meat of the combat is once again dryhumping things with your sword (hence why a lot of people call it the bumper cars system).
Personally I wouldn't call the lack of an attack button a bad thing since in this case it makes the combat LIGHTNING FAST. I'm not even joking, you'll be murdering masses of monsters with such rapid speed it'll make someone like Guts look like a pansy in comparison (you don't mess with Adol Christin, the guy's a walking apocalypse). It also makes the usual grinding in JRPGs almost nonexistant which for me is a plus. I don't hate it mind you, but it gets stale fast if the game relies on it too much. Anyway on normal difficulty you'll be swimming in cash and exp before you know it.
The boss battles are the highlight of the series. In Ys I they are mostly hit and miss. Some are really good and there are others like Vagullion aka THAT !@(*$^ BAT and Dark Fact known as Dalk Fukt in Japan (if you manage beat him on nightmare mode you have the full right to rub that in everyone's faces because you earned it).
