This game screams: Epic. Retro. Action RPG. While we're at it, Ys Chronicles+ kicks Major♥♥♥♥♥(this is an E rated review)! The game mechanics are so simple and so addictive that you can literally spend hours grinding monsters, just because! And then you look at the clock and think, “Holy Pants! It's tomorrow! ...But maybe just a little longer...” and then you turn into a zombie. Yea, this is a hyperbole, but it's not as much of an overstatement as you might think.
And did I mention that this is a package of two games? Quick history lesson. When Falcom was developing Ys, limitations forced them to split the epic into two, resulting in two games, Ys I and II, collectively called (in this case) The Ys Chronicles (Ys Complete, Ys Eternal, Ys Epic Remake VII, these two games have seen a plethora of remakes, and Ys Chronicles+ is the latest and arguably greatest).
Pros:
- Impossibly good soundtrack
- Addictively simple (or simply addictive) gameplay
- Epic, just epic
- Two games in one
- Too many subtle little things to list
Cons:
- Some bosses (Ys I only) can be frustrating
- A few very minor things
- Review doesn't do it justice (but hopefully comes close)
Ys soundtracks are... you know what, there is no word that can properly describe how phenomenally awesome the music in Ys games are. In fact, Ys soundtracks should have their own special term. No really. I'm going to make one up right now: Ystoundingtrack. ...Maybe a work in progress. If you think the music doesn't somehow contribute to the addictiveness of this game, think again. The gameplay is addictive on its own. Now throw in the energizing rock music from the Ystoundingtrack and suddenly you have such an unstoppable locomotive of energy that you just want to cheer every time an enemy explodes into the aether (what a mouthful). The track that stands out the most in this respect is the Ys I overworld music. It's perfect. The rest of the Ystoundingtrack in both games are kick♥♥♥♥♥(darn E rating), but it's that overworld theme that's going to awesome the hours away.
Speaking of gameplay, Ys Chronicles has one of the most unbelievably simple yet inhumanly addictive gameplay ideas to every grace the world of video games. You ready for this? You sure? Well here it is: you bump into enemies, and they die. That's basically it. The game is presented in the standard top down perspective of retro RPG fame, and all you have to do is bump into enemies off centre to damage them, and then they die (if you run into them dead centre from the front or they run into you, you take damage... it's a little hard to explain with words alone). Now you might be thinking, “but how can something so mind-numbingly simple be so mind-numbingly addictive?” This gameplay element has been described by it's creators as the game equivalent of popping bubble wrap - they're not wrong. The gameplay results in very tight, fast paced action, and that only helps contribute to the energy of the game.
Other than the basic gameplay element, this is also an RPG. In Ys I, the RPG element is very downplayed, and by the time you reach the big mid-boss of the game, you basically have to be at max level (level 10) in order to face him. In Ys II, the RPG element is more developed and balanced. You also get the additional gameplay mechanic of magic in Ys II through the use of magical rods (bologna! they're magic wands - for those who don't know, bologna is pronounced: boloney). Ys II has a lot added features compared to Ys I (I'll get into some of these as I go along). In Ys I, the only thing enemies do is run around at varying speeds. It gets repetitive. Fortunately, Ys I is a short game, and it makes up for it's repetitive nature with creative and interesting locations (extra points for the enemies looking cool). In Ys II, however, every enemy has its own unique attack in addition to the regular means of damaging you.
The bosses are where Ys I becomes fiendishly hard. Don't believe me? The big bad mid-boss is a monster! A superboss!! Add to the fact that you can only properly fight him with... well I won't give it away, but if you've talked to everybody, you should have an idea of what you need to fight this boss. And that's not even the hardest boss in the game. That trophy goes to Ys I final boss. Every other boss can be defeated on skill alone, once you know what to do. The final boss, however, has such a luck factor involved that it's... awesome! Unbelievably, they somehow managed to make a luck based boss that's, in addition to frustrating, so frakin fun to fight that it's awesome. Don't ask me how, I honestly don't know. The bosses in Ys II aren't as challenging. In fact, that's the one thing I though was a downgrade from Ys I. The challenging bosses in Ys I is one of the things that I found made the game so enjoyable and memorable. Don't get me wrong, there's plenty of enjoyable and memorable to be had in Ys II. And the bosses are challenging and fun, just not as challenging as I would have liked. Also, most of the bosses can only be killed with fire magic. It would have been nice to have some of the other magic come into play, but... oh well.
Ys II makes up for this by being a huge game compared to Ys I with a much grander story to go with it. The story in Ys I is more basic with fewer characters, and because it has fewer characters, it feels like they had more time to focus on and develope them. In Ys II, while the many characters do get time for developement, it's hard to focus on any one character because there's just so many of them. Heck, there's also a present system in Ys II, and if you give people presents they'll say something different than before. Heck+, with the right spell, you can TALK TO EVERY ENEMY IN THE GAME! Did I mention you can BURN VILLAGERS?! (They don't die, they just say something funny). Everyone and everything has something unique to say, and often more than one solitary thing. The most memorable characters of both games leave a lasting impression for one reason or another (in one case, literally because of a hole in the wall). The plot of both games is basically the same, and it's RPG generic, but the story weaves its way around the plot in such an interesting way that it transforms the simplicity of the plot into a foundational strength. That takes serious skill. While not what I would call a perfect story, the characters, the locations, the events, it all works together to make for a truly fun and enjoyable experience.
As a retro RPG, these games do have some minor annoyances. In Ys I, there is one point where you have to talk to a character about something pointless before being able to proceed to the final dungeon of the game. All the other stuff you have to do makes sense, but this short conversation... doesn't. Why was it necessary (maybe it's a bug)? Ys II doesn't have this problem. Instead, it has the hide important gameplay elements issue. There is a very minor gameplay element that is critical for dealing with one boss (you can technically fight the boss without it, but that's nearing the realm of impossible). So, what do they do with the explanation of this gameplay element? As far as I know, one of the characters tells you about it, but only if you give them enough presents, and there are a huge number of characters in this game. Personally, I don't think stumbling onto gameplay elements is good game design. It's always fun to have some puzzles in a game, but these puzzles should be a unique application of the gameplay elements you already know, not somehow stumbling onto the fact that if you press a certain control a certain way for a certain magic, something different will happen (as an Easter egg it would be OK though).
Ys Chronicles+ are two phenomenal games filled with great energy and fast paced fun. Recommended. Period.

It's a budget and overtly campy game, allright. But it still gets the job done.
Even though the engine behind it shows its age nowadays, Shadowgrounds offers passable visuals with slick lighting and shadow effects, a setting and a threat that's clearly inspired by the 80's sci-fi classic Aliens (which is always a good thing in my book) and most importantly, enjoyable (if mostly repetitive) top-down action that's backed up with responsive controls and relevant mechanics to keep it interesting (i.e., rolling and the weapon upgrades).
On the con side, the story is a cliched one and it is presented through uninspired cutscenes with half-hearted voice acting. It only serves as a backbone for introducing challenges and an excuse for killing stuff. Albeit mostly boring, it comes with a nice twist in the end that I enjoyed.
Even though not as polished as one might think by looking at the screenshots, Shadowgrounds is a justifiable purchase on a budget price. It's a fine little time-waster that evokes the nostalgia of the classic top-down shooters of the bygone days. Just don't get your hopes that high up and enjoy your relaxed six-hour ride.

I think I agree with the several hundred people in these reviews when I say that this is one of the finest games I've ever played. Let me just give you a quick overview:
+you fight your enemies by bumping into them at specific angles. Your weapons will auto-attack them, and if you attack at the right angles, they won't be able to counterattack. Takes time to master, but it's very rewarding. I think this is actually a viable replacement for traditional turn based combat, odd as that may seem. You just surge through the game's dungeons at a brisk pace. Difficulty can be adjusted, allowing you to breeze through if it's too hard, but giving you an alternative if it's too easy.
+I'm very surprised how much I liked the story. It wasn't in-your-face like most story-heavy RPGs, and it knew when it to ease you into something big. I give it a nice plus because of it.
+soundtrack is beautiful, and you get a nice choice between the chronicles version, complete version, and nostalgic version. I recommend all three
+graphically the game is beautiful. It has a top notch sprite team, and it was very revolutionary back when it first came out. Even today it still holds up.
-the only downside I would consider is that the game doesn't hold your hand, which is normally a good thing, but this game gets downright cryptic. You need to remember every single thing about your world, and remember all of your items and their various uses. You will be tested on how good your puzzle and memory skills are. Myst and Riven have nothing on this.
The bottom line? Get. This. Game. It put a tear in my eye, a smile on my mouth, and a very small dent in my wallet. I truly fell in love with Ys because of this. So get a move on and give this game your time. Once you master the combat, I guarantee you won't regret it. I didn't, and this is coming from a guy who had no hope for RPGs/action games on steam.

3rd person or 1st person?
RCF is unique. Players can switch between 1st POV and 3rd POV by simply scrolling the mouse wheel or by pressing 'v'.
It is common for players to use this mechanic to camp enemies behind walls. Some like it, some hate it, but it is certainly one unique feature of this game.
Game Quality?
RCF does not have the best physics, sound effect, character voice, animations and graphics. That's why this game can look cheap and unpolished for some people.
But on the other hand, these features is what makes the game silly and unrealistic, which can bring fun experience for those who doesn't take things seriously.
This game is also very friendly to computers, so even those that does not own any gaming PCs can play this game with good texture qualities with a decent FPS.
(I get FPS around 60~80 in small maps, 40~50 in big maps when texture quality is set to low, and I use Mac Book Pro).
P2W?
RCF do have p2w features, where premium equipments easily overwhelm free equipments stats wise and premium weapons do have more attachments, which can sometimes boost the player's performance in matches.
P2W disadvantages are especially felt in vehicle maps, since the power gap between a free vehicle and a premium vehicle is very large.
Theoretically, non paid user can purchase premium weapons, but the amount of grinding needed to buy 1 Gold weapon, which costs 1000 coins or 100,000 honor points, is unimaginable.
Should I install?
Afterall, this game is free to play, and hence it is expected that there will be noticable bugs and glitches.
And we all know that it has P2W features, so that's another important thing to consider.
If you already own a good quality FPS game, then this game may not meet your expectation.
If you want to troll and experience unrealistic FPS game play, then this game may be for you.
If you want to put tons of money and r@pe others, then this game may be for you.

I can't come up with any other term that fits better than "Gamer Blue Balls".  The artwork was beautiful and unique, greatly reminding me of the best of 70's and 80's era line-art epics like Lord of The Rings or The Hobbit. They did an amazing job of creating a deep and interesting universe, from history to cultue and artwork. They have well-developed characters with mostly believeable behavior. The gameplay is challenging, especially in evoking the grim feeling of scarce resources and harsh choices.  You can build your characters up for combat, or you can try to keep your people alive, or you can do both poorly. There will never be enough currency (Renoun) to manage both. They managed to keep me interested in the civilians and the story enough to actually care about the choices I made, and agonize over the risk of starving them all to death in the cold. They built up an epic plot with several layers that were just coming to maturity when, out of nowhere, and with no warning at all, the credits start rolling. You finish a boss fight, that one of the characters even comes out and says won't actually kill the big bad guy, just put him down for a while. Enemy army - still rampaging through the world. Big world crisis - still utterly untouched and in full swing. Personal story - also still in the middle of everything. They created this grim, georgous, hugely challenging world that I absolutely loved, and just suddenly shoved a "The End" in your face at one random chapter about 1/3rd of the way in.
If they had either finished the rest of the game, or made it clear from the beginning that this was only Part 1 of several, I would have been so happy with it. Instead, I'm left dissorientated, unfulfilled, and rather irritated. Maybe they were more upfront about it with their backers, but I missed this Kickstarter, and all I know of the game is what was listed in Steam. Sorry, but unless they patch this with the rest of the game that they left out, I can't recommend this to anyone. Such a shame to waste so very much potential.

I have been playing a lot of Action RPG's lately, Diablo 3, Van Helsing, Torchlight 2, Path of Exile so I would call myself a fan of this genre for sure. I got Grim Dawn yesterday (4/6/15) and at this time have played 6 hours and have reached level 20.
A lot of people like to use reviews of games of this type to trash talk other games (mainly Diablo 3) but my focus will be a little different because of all the games I listed above they all have something about them that I like so what do I like about Grim Dawn?
- the art style is similar to Path of Exile and Van Helsing in that it's realistic and in this game also incredibly enjoyable to look at, the monsters themselves have very interesting models and one I like a lot in particular is the insect swarms, this is the only game I have played in which I have actually been somewhat intimidated by a massive swarm of insects. The game also has a weather system and a day/night cycle which makes certain areas incredibly pretty one minute and then extremely spooky the next.
, even on normal if you aren't careful you can and will be destroyed especially by bosses which all seem to have unique and somewhat challenging mechanics which makes me pay attention and I find that incredibly enjoyable.
-being able to stick with one class or have a secondary class really opens the door for a number of unique combinations and the skill system is very unique in that you can choose to give an ability a different effect but it could also add a cooldown or make your enemies run faster so you have to experiment with different abilites and see which customizations fit your playstyle and if you put a point somewhere you don't like, you can easily refund it in town so it's no big deal.
- Fighting is fast paced and fairly intense, mobs can swarm you easily and because some have unique abilities to me it never feels dull.
Overall I think the game in it's current state is worth the purchase and I haven't even gone very far into it yet. So far I have already encounted quests that have choices that have changed the game somewhat and I enjoy that, there has been multiple occasions where I could choose to help someone or kill someone and because I only can choose one it makes me want to play a different character and see what would happen if I chose the opposite which gives it replayability for sure.
If you are a fan of Action RPG's I highly recommend this game.

This game is one of those ever increasingly rare games that prove video games can be more than just a few hours of entertainment, they can be interactive art. the art style is incredible and animations are pretty well done, and the decisions you make the whole way are gut wrenching and could either help save you, or cause you problems. Trust this person, or this person, and if you trust the wrong one, then you could get betrayed. Sacrifice your travelling companions for your combat party, or risk yourselves for the better good. It truly started making me start questioning every decision, and really makes you question yourself as a leader.
Rook, basically the main character (theres a bunch of little storylines in there, but you are mostly playing as Rook), was simply a hunter, seeking to live a safe quiet life while protecting his daughter, when suddenly you are attacked and the leader of your small village is killed, and suddenly, everyone looks to you as the new leader. Thrust into your sudden leadership role, you must make tough decisions, that only get tougher as you go from leading a mere couple of dozen people to leading over 300-400+, all while seeking to protect the group and your daughter, and seek salvation.
As for the combat, the strategy is a bit tough to get used to, but incredibly well done, and makes you start depending on your team, but that can go badly if you make a poor decision and get one of those main allies killed. Leveling up is well done, especially since your "Renown" which you have to spend each time you level up and buy stuff like supplies and items, is not gained in huge amounts, but not gained in small amounts, making more decisions on whether you want to level up now, or spend some renown to get some more food supplies, which you might need, or risk running out of food before the next opportunity to get more.
As for the length, I found the game pleasently long, but not too long as to feel boring. The interesting interactions going on between characters made me not even notice how long I'd be playing, and that is something I really like. The other thing is that due to the sheer amount of choices you have, I almost want to go back through and play again just to make different choices.
However, about the one issue i had with this game is whenever you are travelling, all you can do is simply watch, and the environment is not much to watch, and there are times where you will travel for like 2 game days without anything happening, which kind of kills the pace of the game at times.
Overall, I very highly recommend this game. It's more than just a game, its truly what makes gaming great, showing that games can be art and entertaining.

***ACHIEVEMENTS***
If you are after the achievements look up the list carefully (Including the secret ones). I would advise looking up where all the missable friends, Chinpokomon, and items are before playing.
Accept the name that Cartman gives you. You're going to be called D-bag anyways so you might as well just accept it and get the achievement.

After the nazi zombie outbreak occurs. Go to the police station and talk to Yates. Finish his quest ASAP.
Don't forget to fart on the Prime minister of Canada (In the cave) and the Giant baby fetus.
If you forgot to fart on a dog. You can do that by travelling in the woods, after the end, and fart on one there.
To get the woodland critters as your friend. Go in the woods. Follow the paths. Right, Up, Right, Down, Right. Accept Satan and you're good.
***WARNING FOR PARENTS***
Keep in mind this game is based on South Park. Which should tell you right away that it's not really going to be child friendly. If you are a parent do not take the rating of this game lightly.

I can describe Knights of Pen and Paper as a Dungeons & Dragons simulator instead of your typical RPG. There is no exploration or movement. It is all menu and dialog based. The map is pretty segmented like a Mario map and there are not maps so much as there are quests. These quests revolve around typical and simplified RPG turn based combat. The catch is you also play your own dungeon master, so you can select your enemies to fight and how many you will fight. Its as if you're making your own busy work. The classes feel balanced, but the battles begin feel too long for the never ending grind that this game becomes. Unless you want to spend real money to buy in game gold.
The game has a lot of personalization. You start the game selecting characters and their classes. Each character has its own passive ability and then you assign a class. You can only have one of a class per party. Each class has 4 upgradeable abilities, some are passives like regenerate HP per turn and most are combat abilities. When you level up through experience defeating enemies, you can level up a skill. Leveling up skills increases the MP they use, so its a double edged sword where eventually you can only use a skill once or twice before you need to rest or use potions. There are items that will regenerate MP and HP along with increase maximums.
The combat abilities feel useful. Paladins have a leader strike that is a powerful attack. The strike will increase their threat to enemies driving the majority of attacks to that character. To balance the attention, the paladin has a temporary shield power, a flash heal for themselves and devotion that increases the base HP. A cleric can heal the entire party or focus healing on one character. They can also use a smite skill that damages an enemy and heals themselves. To round things out there is a weakening spell to debuff enemy attack power for three enemies. Mages have a single enemy damaging fireball that will burn them, damaging HP each turn. They also have a deep freeze that damages and stuns an enemy. Mages also have a meteor that damages an entire enemy party and finally a passive stream that increases the base MP. I can't cover all the classes, but they feel well rounded.
The classes have to feel well rounded, because the game is nothing but combat. A chess game between you and enemies that you chose to fight. The game has plenty of quests to give you and you can tackle them one at a time. Nothing that will stump you, since all the 'quests' seem to be collect X amount of Y or defeat X amount of Y enemies. Escort X from point A to B and then fight a battle. It wouldn't seem like such a grind if your travel had more exploration instead of moving along a line from location to location. There is some banter along the way, but its just your party sitting at a table facing a dungeon master with different beautiful backgrounds. The battles get long, even with better equipment. It gets frustrating when you complete a quest to kill 7 plants only to get another quest to kill 9 plants. Then that quest followed by another quest to get 19 carrots. How? By killing the same plants you've just slaughtered. You can always pick your quests, but its useless when you'll end up doing them all anyway.
When you visit a town, you don't walk to a store, you just click on an icon that will open up the store. The items are nice. Upgrading weapons and armor involves a gambling system. Sure it costs 150 gold to have a blacksmith upgrade your gear, but there's only a 35% chance he'll succeed. Seems like a gamble and a waste of gold. The blacksmith will get better with every try . You can even increase the blacksmith's experience by using grindstones that you'll buy or find in caves.
That leads me to warn you of this. Microtransactions. Why grind for gold when you can just buy it with real life money? The microtransactions aren't in your face or annoying, but they are there and some people have problems with that. If you want gold, go kill some enemies, there's nothing else to do in the game.
If someone in your party dies, that costs gold. Since resurrection costs gold, when your party gets wiped out and you don't have enough gold to resurrect one of them, that's it. It was originally a gameover, because the game will save itself preventing you from going back to a previous point when your party was alive. So you'd have to buy gold with real life money. Luckily, there is now a free continue that will resurrect everyone, but reset their level experience. I'm thankful of that. If you don't want to grind to level up your characters, you can always buy experience with gold. There is always a need for gold. Whether its experience, resurrection, traveling, or gambling to upgrade your equipment. Oh and don't forget buying stuff.
At some point, this game is busy work and you know some people are ok with that. In all, I would say its a fun game, but other RPGs are better. Since this is trying to be a Dungeons & Dragons simulator without being a true RPG its just lacking in some areas.
This game is a very fun and adrenaline rushing game. I highly recommend it.

In short: Larians latest instalment of the Divinity series proofs many publishers and devs wrong that think the only way to sell games these days is by dumbing them down as far as possible. Original Sin proofs the we gamers still very much enjoy games that keep the hand-holding to a minimum and let us explore the world on our own. It proofs that turn-based combat systems still work, that modern technology hasn't made them obsolete and that not every RPG has to be a clone of Diablo (1 and 2, not the bad one).
I guess I should mention that I've only played the game for about 30 hours at the moment. I am almost done with the first of the four acts but I haven't seen the whole game yet. So, keep in mind, everything written here is based on that.
I will update this review every time I finish another act.
It's sad that I feel the need to start with this, but, given how the term 'oldschool' has been abused in the recent years, it's better to be safe than sorry. 'Oldshool' doesn't mean you just use the name of an old franchise. It's not about making people that remember great games from their youth believe that your game will be similar to their somewhat romantic memories of days long gone past.
And Larian gets that. What they made is a game that might not share the name of the great series of our childhood but it still feels like Ultima, Baldur's Gate or maybe even Neverwinter Nights. Divinity: Original Sin is the kind of CRPG you played back in the day.
Original Sin has some Open World elements but it also can be extremely linear. This might sound controversial at first, but it truly isn't. In fact, when you ask me, the game perfectly combines the best elements from both worlds.
The game is linear cos it is story-driven. There are certain things you have to do in a particular order to progress, you can't just roam through the world and explore what's going on. Well, technically you could but you probably would just end up being crushed by enemies that are way above your level.
This may sound discouraging at first, especially if you are used to games like Skyrim, but on the other hand it allows for better storytelling. Okay, the story itself is not that great (at least not so far), but it still benefits from the games linear nature.
The open world aspect of the game comes in form of character development and the way quests are handled. When building a character you can pretty much do what you want, your mage can wear heavy armour, your rouge can cast lightning spells to teleport across the battlefield and your warrior can summon spiders or fire elementals. Granted, not every combination is a good idea and if you want to create a jack-of-all-trades you will need to spread you skill points thin, but, if you want to, you can do it.
Quests, except for the main quest line, are also very open. You can not only approach them in different ways but, based on what you do, the outcome will also differ. I can't really give you examples cos that would include spoilers, but pretty much every side quest has multiple possible endings and at least two, sometimes even four or more ways how you could do it. However, not all ways may be available to you cos some require certain skills.
The game does almost no hand-holding, at least not in the traditional sense of the term. There are (almost) no quest markers, no arrows that tell you where to go. Heck, sometimes quests only give you a vague idea of what you might have to do and then the game let's you figure it out on your own. This is appealing to a lot of us, but certainly not to everybody.
Let's take the main story as an example. At the start of the game a note tells you that you have been ordered to go to Cyseal and investigate the murder of councillor Jake. That's it. You go through a short tutorial, enter Cyseal, are immediately given the opportunity to do some side quest and then you have to figure out what's going on. You have to talk to quite a few people, that are not highlighted with exclamation marks by the way, before you figure out what might have happened.
However, if you do what the game wants you to do, if you talk to people, listen to their conversations and read the books you find, the game pretty much tells you what you have to do and when you have to do it.
To some the pacing of Original Sin might seem too slow or off, but that's not entirely true. Granted, it takes you about 10 hours before fights start to become more interesting and you can spend a whole day running through Cyseal doing side quest that don't involve combat and just learn as much about the world as possible. So yes, if you are looking for combat the game might seem to start to slow for you, but then again, that's not what Original Sin is about.
The game is a CRPG in the spirit of pen & paper RPGs like Das Schwarze Auge (engl: The Dark Eye), it is more about atmosphere and story-telling than about combat. It involves combat, a lot of it, but that's not the core mechanic.
When you encounter enemies the combat is handled in turn-based mode. You get a nice "Fight!" displayed on the screen, your party takes position and then the combat starts. The order in which characters acts is determined by their initiative and once it's their turn they can't wait till later, so you have to ensure that your buff chars have a higher initiative than your damage dealers. How many actions a character can perform depends on his action points, the more he has the further he can walk, the more attacks he can make and so on. Unspent action points are not lost but carried over into the next round, up to a maximum of course.
How difficult the game is depends heavily on how you play it. If you understand its mechanics and use them to your advantage the game can be pretty easy even on hard. Having a well rounded party also helps, 4 glass cannons won't help you, neither will 4 tanks.
So far combat doesn't sound very interesting, it's your basic CRPG turn-based stuff. However, there is more. In Original Sin you can combine elemental effects to your advantage. E.g. if you create a puddle of water - or blood - and then electrocute it with e.g. a lightning bolt everything in it will be stunned. If you let it rain fire elementals will be weaker and your chances to freeze enemies are higher, if you ignite a poison cloud it will explode and if you freeze liquids characters might slip on them (happened to the end boss of the first act, I almost fell out of my chair laughing).
Okay, so far I only mentioned the good stuff, but not game is perfect, here is a short list of the stuff Original Sin doesn't do that well:
- there are only two companions that interact with you, the rest doesn't talk at all
- some of the writing is really bad
- pathfinding works differently in combat, your chars don't avoid deadly lava any more
Buy the game!

Great zombie game with extremely satisfying combat and parkour elements
Pros:
- The most satisfying feeling of killing zombies in a game yet. The force and physics of hitting a baseballbat to the head of a zombie is great. So is throwing one from a rooftop
- Probably the best parkour free-running first person controls to date, even though not perfect.
- Great graphics and sound
- Great music that really fits the setting. Some parts, like an ambient tune often played in Old Town are amazing and almost gives a surreal feeling to some parts of the game.
- A really good hard mode
- Everything is real-time, including inventory managment and map viewing making the player feel more immersed and having to always be on the alert unless in safe zones.
- Real first person view where you actually see your legs and interaction with the world and where you are not just an invisible floating ghost with a camera. To few first person games have this.
Cons:
- Ugly clutterded unnecessary HUD unless using external mods to get rid of it. Incredible immersive breaking and the game should have had ingame options to toggle HUD options off. Probably even worse if playing on normal setting.
- There are really no way to easy climb down a wall or building, except from jumping off it. This can lead to problems in some parts where you need to do only vertical climbing.
- The concept of having more dangerous types of fast running zombies that are attracted to loud noises are great, but the way they just spawn close to the player when a high sound is made is immersion breaking. So is the fact that they home in on the player and seem to always know where you are. It would be more interesting and dynamic if they roamed the world like other zombies with a chance to attract them if you made a noise. As they are now they feel mosly frustrating and very artifical in their homing and spawny behaviour.
- Lockpick minigame is very tedious and waaay to frequently used. It is basically a copy of the lockpicking minigame in Skyrim, but feels less responsive.
-While the decision to have everything happen in real-time, there is no way to abort some actions quick enough. For example to abort lockpicking or opening a container when a zombie is eating your neck. It can often take a full second or two to abort an action and then it can be to late.
- Some "filler" missions where you should just kill enough zombies with specific weapons with a time limit or do parkour challanges. These just feel like cheap filler content and does not fit with the rest of the game or its setting at all. They just feel silly and out of place and the game would be better without them.

Divinity: Original Sin is an isometric CRPG which shares characteristics from games such as Baldur's Gate, mixed with the freedom of modern open-world titles (Skyrim, Fallout etc). D:OS is brimming with quality, content, lore and interesting characters, whilst also offering hours upon hours of gameplay, fleshed out gameplay features, consequences based on actions, multiple solutions, replayability and a level/modification editor to create your own content and adventures.
I brought this game on a whim after seeing some gameplay, and I can honestly say it's quickly become one of my favorite games and that I'm glad I paid the price I did for it. This is a true example of Kickstarter and Early Access gone right, with Larian Studios putting an incredible amount of effort into making an extraordinary game. Fans of classic RPG's are very much in need of giving this title a try, and newcomers to the genre will find themselves pleasantly surprised as to how good this game really is.
One particular feature I enjoy about this game is the amount of customisation you have with your characters. The start of the game allows you to pick a starting class, determining your initial attribute, skill and talent point allocation; aside from a few level restrictions, you are free to level up your character any way you see fit, allowing you to mould your character into specialising in one particular skillset, or becoming a jack-of-all-trades. Another feature I love is the ability to use the environment to your advantage. Elemental barrels litter the landscape and battlefield, allowing you to turn the tide of battle in your favour or remove a hazard in your way. Your own skills can assist in manipulating the environment, allowing players to set fire to oil using their spells, or produce rain to clear out fire. It's actually quite amazing how useful and thought out this feature really is.
Sadly, I do have a few criticisms about the game, but these are mostly personal preferances. Firstly, some indication that a spell will effect the environment would be handy, as often times I've tried setting fire to something only for me to be a fraction off hitting the target, or I've tried to electrify water only for it not to work at all. Another thing I'm disappointed about is the lack of four-player co-op in the campaign; I completely understand the developers intentions with a two-player only co-op story, but there has been some confusion surrounding this, and I can't help but feel they could have simply added the additional two players as non-influential characters (IE. Those who don't take part in dialogue).
Overall, this game is truly a work of art and I encourage anyone interested to give this game a shot. With frequent updates and promises of more content, Larian Studios will continue to support this game for quite some time, and the modding community will be active for years to come, providing you with new content to sink your teeth into. You won't be disappointed.

I'm just going to go ahead and say it: This game will KICK. YOUR. A**.
But that's not to say it is a bad game, nonono. In fact, the fact that it is hard makes it rewarding when you defeat a bulky enemy ship, win the game (as of yet I have not. No spoilers, but the final boss is SCARY difficult), etc.
Gameplay wise, FTL is simple in concept, but is very intricate in practice. There is a lot going on during an enemy encounter, and even if you're not fending off a ship, the decisions you sometimes have to make are gut-wrenching. Every text box for a choice leaves you thinking "what if, what if, what if..."
The biggest challenge of this game is probably the fact that even though you have a choice of "easy" or "normal" difficulty, BOTH are hardcore mode - you cannot reload earlier saves to undo a bad decision, and once you die, BAM! Game Over. Sayonara. Back to the Beginning With You! That is a huge part of why every action choice decision item/upgrade purchase decision is CRUCIAL to your survival.
Luckily, though, this game is not a marathon. You can easily go through 2-3 playthroughs in a day, even with getting obliterated at the very end. So losing is not the most aggrivating thing in the world (but still annoying at times).
Overall, the game's simple feel but inner intricacy, sheer risk/reward factor, along with retro graphics and an arcade-style game progression, make for a very enjoyable experience. I cannot wait for the Advanced Edition DLC. ^_^

A first-person non-linear puzzle game set in a nearly non-Euclidian labyrinth, Antichamber is a game that toys with a player's mind: walls appear out of nowhere, doorways lead halfway across the map, and passages alter their physical geometry if they're looked at the wrong way (or the right one).  No clear instructions or objectives beyond cryptic motivational posters are ever given, and even when the player stumbles upon a block-manipulating gun, it's not immediately clear what the rules of it and its upgrades are.  This forces the player to explore, experiment, and think outside of the box, as the individual puzzle rooms are themselves just pieces in the giant puzzle that is the entire game.  While a minority may find the confusing non-direction of the game frustrating and deceptive, overall Antichamber is a unique and surreal game experience that keeps the player guessing right until the very end.

The Banner saga sits somewhere between Fire Emblem and Oregon Trail, Gameplay is simple yet interesting, meaningful punishing. The map is a beautiful addition, but has no real use beyond offering the player an overwhelming amount of lore and otherwise useless information.  While I admire the attention to detail, a few more random encounters on the road or hard to obtain characters would have been a better use of development time.
The Banner Saga is an enjoyable and unpretentious game that was obviously crafted with love.  As a fan of tactics style games I highly enjoy it.  This game is for you if you long for more Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, Disgaea and games of that nature.  Though there are times you will need to quickly accept and cope with disappointment as a result of a conversation tree, there will be many times additional supplies and new Varl friends will make you heave a sigh of relief.

It is very pretty, artwork is very nice, setting is interesting, with a lot of effort seemingly having gone into creating a fascinating backstory for the world. There are some moments in the story which will provoke an emotional reaction. Mostly "noooo!", it is a bleak tale of the apparent end of the world after all.
However, it is short, I felt, for the price asked for. It is also apparently part 1, and part 2 and 3 are as yet, unfunded, according to the developers - they are waiting to see how well it sells before they can commit to making any more.
The balance at the moment, is somewhat off, as relating to management of resources. This is supposed to be addressed soon in a patch though. I experienced a few game lockups, which were very, very frustrating due to how the game saves its state. Having to force-close the game and reload, meant having to redo an hour or more.
I'm conflicted as to whether or not to recommend this. On the one hand, if I recommend it, then it raises the chances of the story being continued, and finding out what happens next. On the other hand, the length of the game, for the price asked, and some of the problems I encountered, and the prospect that parts 2 and 3 may never exist, means that I can't honestly recommend it at this time.
Pros: Art is great, setting is interesting, story is involving.
Cons: Short length, price, a few glitches, cliffhanger with uncertain prospect of resolution.

If viking Oregon trail and a turn based tactics game had a baby it'd be a lot like banner saga.
First thing you will notice about the banner saga is the art, rotoscoping isn't something that you see everyday let alone in a video game and the bannar saga excels at making each person, place or thing you encounter on your journey really come to life with beauty.
Speaking of journey the music in this game is composed by Austin Wintory who did the music for the game Journey. The entire game sounds fantastic from the heavy beating of drums to the triumphant bellow of horns the entire sounds epic from start to finish.
As I said before the game really feels like a great mix of turn based tactics and Oregon trail. Combat takes place on a grid and you and the enemy take turns bashing each other. With each character having different strengths and weaknesses and a simple yet deeping twist on how your units health works the game really makes you feel accomplished for each and ever battle you win. That is a good thing because honestly this like to give you a bad hand a lot.
The other half of the game is the traveling part, as you and your viking caravan cross mountians and icy wastes you must deal with a number of issues such as "Do we have enough food?" "Can we trust these strangers we just met?" The game makes you choose and everything you do has an effect on the caravan as a whole. Letting some strangers join you might mean they steal a bunch of the food in the night and then suddenly you are in the middle of nowhere and people are starving to death right and left as you push forward. You must make tough choices often times sacrificing one resource or another while trying to keep the people and warriors you take on in good spirits.
In the end the Banner saga is a deep game with rich lore and a enduring characters and it's a adventure worth taking.

Civilization V is, to this date, still a great game. It is up there on steam with the most played game, every single day. It is a quality gem. However, there are some cracks in this shining gem of a game, I'll go over them now:
Positives:
-Brilliant scenarios.
-Quality core mechanic play in singleplayer
-Warring other Civilizations is challanging and rewarding (depending on difficulty)
-A fantastic community (No Quitters, civ subreddit, helpful players, loads of tutorials which got me better at the game and lots of canals.)
-Performance wise it can run on almost any machine
-Great mechanics with additions of DLC (BNW Trade Routes, G&Ks Espionage and Religion)
-A pheonominal modding community, supported by the pillars of the workshop (only in SP, grr Firaxis!)
Now the things that absolutely ruin the game.
-Multiplayer is atrocious, making it clear that Firaxis ignored the absolutely vital thing that the players wanted and have ignored on improving ever since. These bugs include, crashing when in resync screens, lobbies being bugged and abhorrant lag between turns.
-Modding support it limited in Multiplayer, making different civs and civ leaders inaccessible.
-The fact policy openers such as Honour or Piety are not viable makes an aspect of the game wrought.
Now if Firaxis didn't produce the absolutely terrible Beyond Earth, perhaps they could've focoused on Civ V and fixed these things, but no, However, the positives outweigh the negatives, you should grab the complete edition if you are new whenever a steam sale occours or whenever it is on sale. If you were looking for a return to the semi-serious roots of the earlier Saints Row games, back when Volition were prancing around under Rockstar's "videogame crime movie" shadow, then you're out of luck.
It seems that, with each five-year timeskip the Third Street Saints go through, their exploits get all the more outrageous. Saints Row 2 turned the seemingly fatal yacht explosion into something which put your character into a coma, allowing them to reuse the character customisation system they've stuck to ever since.
Saints Row The Third took Stilwater's finest gangsters and turned them into world-famous pop culture icons. Their faces were on billboards across the city and they were nigh-on untouchable when it came to that pesky thing called the "legal system".
As each game passed, Volition were - little by little - unshackling their band of psychopaths and criminals. The first two games had them entrenched within the gang lifestyle; dealing with their rivals in their quest to take over the city. The Third took Johnny Gat, Shaundi, Pierce and the rest and transplanted them into a wild action movie which, despite its inherent craziness, still seemed to fit the madness prevalent within the Saints themselves.
If you thought that the jump from gangsters to cultural icons was maddening, you ain't seen nothing yet. Following on from the "Good" ending of Saints Row The Third, The Boss (the nickname for your character) has used their deeds as a springboard to run for the biggest political office in the land. Yup, that's right. You were a mere celebrity in #3. In #4, you're the damn President.
Kinzie's your press secretary, Benjamin King is your chief of staff, Anderson from Mass Effect is your VP, there are pole dancers in every hallway and there's a tiger in the living room. The Saints have well and truly taken over.
And that's BEFORE the story's even started.
As if the difficulties of political office weren't arduous enough, the Saints find themselves gripped by an alien invasion. Enter the Zin Empire and their superpowered alien commander, Zinyak; complete with a stereotypical "Hollywood Villain" British accent and a penchant for classical music.
After laying waste to the White House, you're thrown into a Matrix-esque simulation of Steelport, the city from the third game and, from there, you mount your resistance.
Graphically, very little - if anything at all - has really changed from the third game. While it will disappoint those looking for innovation with each sequel, it does put those without cutting-edge PCs somewhat at ease. If you were able to run Saints Row The Third to a decent standard, then chances are the fourth game will pose no problem.
While there is still gunplay and automotive mayhem to be had, both take a variable backseat to the new attraction in town: super powers! Yes, because you're now in what's essentially a videogame version of a city contained within a videogame (let's see Leo DiCaprio unravel THAT one), you're able to bend or outright break most of the world's physical rules. With a little help from your resident hacker, of course.
Although you can hurl elemental energy blasts and throw objects around with telekinesis, gunplay still remains rather relevant in this game; both working in tandem to provide a deeper - if still simplistic - repertoire. However, with the ability to sprint and glide at speeds vastly in excess of any mundane vehicle including aircraft, the driving aspect of this particular sandbox has been rendered almost entirely irrelevant. Despite this, you still have access to the same vehicular customisation features as the previous game so, if you want to show off, the option's still there.
Some might say that the fourth game has utterly ruined Saints Row and all it ever stood for. But, then again, they would be forgetting that it's only in the latter half of the franchise that Saints Row has actually stood for something that was completely and totally its own.
Saints Row wasn't about such trivial things such as an indepth storyline or realism. It was about giving you a world filled with pop culture references, high-powered weapons, balls-to-the-wall action, hilarious characters and missions you wouldn't be forgetting in a hurry. If you've looked through that little list and said, "yes! I want these in my life" - and you enjoyed Saints Row The Third - then you'll more than likely have a blast with this one.
As with The Third, it's certainly more fun playing through the game with a friend (and the progress with collectibles is shared between the both of you, so those 1200+ ability-enhancing fragments won't seem as daunting) and, with it being on a free weekend and a half-off sale, this is as good a time as any to give it a bash for yourself.

In a word: Avoid. Read on for reasons.
A game that simulates pen and paper RPGs? Sounds great, doesn't it? This game will do just that, but the Dungeon Master is largely unamusing, which leads to a mundane story. The comments your party makes are usually cheesy one-liners or memes, or video game references. You roll a d20 for quests, upgrading gear, getting grindstones in caves, resting in non-towns, and travelling, and failing a dice roll only makes the game more tedious. The battle system is all turn-based, and order is loosely based on initiative, but it's mostly random.
A more minor point though are the microtransactions for in-game gold which are COMPLETELY UNNECESSARY but for some reason every day some guy will complain about "ermergerd microtransactions" in the community hub. The microtransactions are NOT REQUIRED at any point in the game; the microtransactions only help you by shaving off a few minutes of your time that would otherwise have been spent doing what you already have to do for the entire game. The microtransactions only give you gold. You get gold from fighting monsters.

While I have yet to finish even the FIRST of the two original Ys games included here in this "Chronicles+" package, I can already quite firmly say that I am thrilled with my purchase, and would highly recommend this!  Whether or not you played any of the earlier iterations of these games, all RPG fans should be well pleased.  Even for those who are familiar with the original games (and the, before this, most superior version on Turbo CD) will have a good deal of new features to interest them and keep them excited.
The game offers a high level of customization, to allow for the best possible play experience, also.  I personally prefer to use a gamepad for MOST of my gaming, and with my Logitek controller playing this feels just like the good ol' days of 8- and 16-bit RPGs.  However, if you want to use your keyboard and mouse, that is fully customizable as well.  Also, you can choose to play the game with the map taking up the entire screen area, OR in the classic bordered ("windowed") view from the originals.  You can also choose the graphics style -- classic or the new updated version.  For me, it seems an obvious choice to play it fullscreen (within the game and on the monitor!) with the updated graphics -- as everything is absolutely beautiful and really keeps the feeling and spirit of the original while updating it for a new era.  As much as I love the classic look and feel of the oldschool stuff, when an update is done this well it truly does come off even better than the original.
The first two installments of Nihon Falcom's classic series are brought to life in an excellent way, and I highly recommend this game (and the other Ys games on Steam)!

I have played the game for +20 hours now. I participated in the Beta and been supporting the game since I heard of it during the Kickstarter campaign.
So far Divinity: Original Sin ("DOS") has captured me with all its features and parts; the gameplay, story, world, graphics, difficulty, music, dialogue. It all comes together with good harmony.
The game is still quite fresh and there are some minor issues on some areas, but the people at Larian Studios are really showing the effort on fixing all the issues with constant updates and hotfixes.
What I like the most in this game is maybe the fact how DOS emphasises the RP element. These days if the game has a character who has and inventory and you can choose his/her name its an RPG. In a way yes, but I think that the definition of RPG has become quite vague, but DOS really gives player the harnesses of his/her characters. You can feel the immersion as you become one with the world and truly make the story feel like your own. The amount of choices and paths player can choose to approach the goals in the game is huge and it doesn't even feel like you have to choose between something, but rather that you do exactly what you want. I hope that other RPG developers will catch on the fact that players of the RPG genre want RP!
The other important feature is the Co-op. I haven't yet dived too deep into this feature as I first want to discover thing by myself, but so far what I have seen and heard its good. One more thing for game developers in general, people want Story/Campaign Co-ops for their games!
But about the more specific game features:
Difficulty:
The game is really challenging, even of normal difficulty. I was quite shocked when I had my first real combat, but it was a positive surprise. The game is challenging yes, but you always have a feeling that you can do it, but something just went wrong this time.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is in general really nice. The turn-based combat works and is really fun. Sometimes in non-combat movement linked characters move a bit stupidly and sometimes seem to arrange themselves wrong in short distance placement. Also I find the party linking system still a bit clunky at times, but I'm confident the developers will keep polishing features like this.
World:
The world is truly immersive and it feels alive. The Larian humor can be seen in various places and forms, but it fits and it doesn't distract you from the atmosphere at all. Sometimes the city NPCs yelling the same old line comes as a bit of a nuisance, but its a minor thing.
Graphics:
The graphical look stays loyal to the Divinity saga and is really good in all its simpicity. There are few problems with the way shadows are made for example, but it mostly affects the higher resolution users and I see it also as quite minor issue for now. This also points that the game doesn't have to have top notch graphics with separately animated hair or super realistic 4k textures.
Music:
The nostalgy of hearing the tracks from Divinity 2, nice! The whole soundtrack is amazing and all the areas have quite nice variability on their sounds, it really fits the world. Only sometimes I have these somewhat intense parts in the music when I'm in the middle of a random dialogue or something and I'm like "Okay.. I guess this dialogue is quite intense." *Stares at the fish vendor* but it doesn't happen that often.
Story & Dialogue:
I really like the games non-linear story, from the very beginning the game doesn't force you to do anything for the story. You can go wherever you want and do what you want and skip all of the story if you so wish. Although I really recommend that you don't skip it :D but like previously stated you can approach the story from your own perspective. There are quests in the game but they have been cleverly hid as Journal entries that update when you do or discover something related to them. There are no handhelding quest markers or quest logs that tell you exactly what to do. I think this is great! Too many of the modern game underestimate the player and have all this cinematic slow motion "Press X" scenes and markers on the map to show you where stuff is so you can mindlessly roam from point A to point B. Of course those can of helpers are better with games that only offer one way of completing things in the game.
Dialogue is great, it fits the world, its fun with the little jokes every there and now and its believable. There could be more lines for the nameless NPCs because you can ask them quite a lot of stuff, so far they seem to have something like 3 lines per question, but once again quite minor stuff.
So as a conclusion; Divinity: Original Sin is a great piece of art to all people who love the RPG genre and great place to start for those who have not yet really dived into it. The game shows promise for the future of modern games and acts as an example for other developers that if you truly believe in it and want to make something great, you can. I'm eagerly following how the game develops even after the release and what's yet coming. I believe this game will be one to speak about in the future.
That's all for now, I will update this review if necessary and hoped you find it useful! :)

WTF is this??? A game for ants??? You fight monsters by bumping into them. You interact with townspeople by bumping into them.  You pick up items by bumping into them. A first-person non-linear puzzle game set in a nearly non-Euclidian labyrinth, Antichamber is a game that toys with a player's mind: walls appear out of nowhere, doorways lead halfway across the map, and passages alter their physical geometry if they're looked at the wrong way (or the right one).  No clear instructions or objectives beyond cryptic motivational posters are ever given, and even when the player stumbles upon a block-manipulating gun, it's not immediately clear what the rules of it and its upgrades are.  This forces the player to explore, experiment, and think outside of the box, as the individual puzzle rooms are themselves just pieces in the giant puzzle that is the entire game.  While a minority may find the confusing non-direction of the game frustrating and deceptive, overall Antichamber is a unique and surreal game experience that keeps the player guessing right until the very end.

I run most of my games on a terrible laptop with an Intel Celeron J1800 CPU w/ Intel integrated graphics because I am too lazy to get my laptop an upgrade. You are allowed to whitelist programs from being tampered with but when whitelisting programs, the prompt asks you for the process name and you have to type it in manually. Personally this was more of a nuisance than an actual problem as I am more used to a pop-up which allows you to select the process currently running. You will pretty much only use this to keep your web browsers or communication software (discord, skype, etc) functional.
The biggest question I had when utilizing the program was in the option to launch games outside of the steam client. For example, launching games such as League of Legends will enable the launch of the League of Legends Client, I personally have no clue if CPUcores will put all resources towards the launcher and ignore the actual game itself or if it will help provide resources towards all instances invoked by the client (In this case the game itself). While the manual does show that it can add League of Legends to its startup, It doesn't make it clear if it is the client which is considered the "game" or if it is the game that is considered the "game." Antichamber is a good puzzler that starts with simple mechanics and slowly builds them out to make complex challenges as it progresses to the end.
In Antichamber, you work your way through a convoluted collection of hallways, high jumps, and locked doors using relatively easy-to-grasp abilities in a deep variety of challenges. As you go along, you'll unlock a few new tools that are worked well (for the most part) into the later puzzles. You'll also find plaques that offer tiny philisophical quips that double as slightly veiled hints to solving each puzzle.
The levels have a good air of mystery and otherworldliness to them. They turn in on themselves with architecture based off of an M.C. Escher sketch. However, even though this fits the mind-bending theme of the game, I must admit that the complex nature of the hallways, elevators, and portals can sometimes lead to you not knowing where to go next for a new set of puzzles. After you clear a major portion of a level, there are arrows that indicate where you should go, but they are easy to lose in the strange geometry of the map.
Also, there was one point of the game where I was stuck thinking that I couldn't pass a puzzle without a new tool unlocked somewhere else. Turns out, I could solve it with what I had -- only, it was using an ability I didn't even know I had gained. It was the only point in the game that that happened, but it left a bad taste in my mouth.
All in all, I did enjoy the final set of puzzles, which were made up of a review of past puzzles with new approaches thrown in. While not a particularly long game, it was enjoyable for almost all of its run.

Antichamber is a rather unique puzzle game, where you go around a maze like area, exploring vague life lessons, and getting your mind blown by impossible objects and geometry. There's not much in ways of story, as the main theme is to complete a wide variety of puzzles in order to reach the end, but the game is fun regardless.
Gameplay and Visual wise: Everything about this game fits the tone of one word: unique. The game looks unique to say the least, as well as simplistic. If you're not a fan of bright colors, or bright colors hurt your head, you may want to tone down the brightness just a bit when playing through 85% of the game. The puzzles are quite unique, with some puzzles being rather challenging, while others can be easily accomplished with late game items (or item rather). There really was never a time I felt absolutely stumped on a puzzle, as the mechanics and the "cube ray" are demonstrated in a straightforward manner to the player.
Story and Completion wise: Really there is not much to say for either of these. There isn't much of a story in the game, other than life lessons that can be seen as collectibles, and completing the game is as simple as getting to the end and finding every life lesson. There are the purple blocks, yes, however you may easily find most of the blocks when exploring the various rooms. Keep a look out in every room you come across, and completing the game is easy.
Recommendation: For a puzzle game, this game does stand out with rather unique mechanics and looks, with life lessons being shown to the player along the way. If you want to have a relaxing time, solving puzzles and exploring, I would highly recommend this game.

For my review of this software, I decided to expirement with three games and three different settings.
Games:
1. Counter Strike Global Offensive
2. Dirt 4
3. Player Unknown's Battlegrounds
Settings:
1. CPU Cores turned off
2. CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading on
3, CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading off
I chose these three games as CSGO is popular to many people and almost every computer can run it, Dirt 4 as it's a more recent racing game, and PUGB as that games demands power based on graphics setting. Note: all games are running on ultra settings. Here were my results
CSGO:
1. CPU Cores Off
- 160 ~ 240 fps
2. CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading on
- 140 ~ 240 fps
3. CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading off
- 150 ~ 240 fps
Not much of a difference
Dirt 4:
1. CPU Cores off
- 50 ~ 60 fps
2. CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading on
- 40 ~ 60 fps
3. CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading off
- 50 ~ 70 fps
Noticable when taking sharp turns, the game felt a bit smoother with the 3rd setting as the fps was more stable
PUBG:
1. CPU Cores off
- 50 ~ 60 fps
2.CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading on
- 1 ~ 25 fps
3. CPU Cores turned on with hyper threading off
- 1 ~ 25 fps
With CPU Cores on, this game was unbearable, very choppy, and I was better off without it.
To generally sum it up, the effects were minor on certain games whether or not they were positive or negative, but on certain games like PUBG, and sometimes Insurgency, this would ruin the game. I wouldnt recomend unless your'e desperate for minor fps changes.

The first thing you'll notice is that Steep is visually stunning (like me). I was really excited to play this game, but the more I did so, the more obvious something became: I just wasn't enjoying it very much.
The RPG elements of the game aren't bad. They aren't great either, but they're not bad. Nothing to write home about either way.
The problem is with the turn-based tactical combat, which is bland and repetitive.  For starters, there is no terrain of any sort. You just get a blank grid with you and your enemies, with every square of the grid created equal. That means there's no choke points, no cover, no high ground, and so on.
This is made worse by the bizarre way that turn order is handled. First one of your units moves, then one of the enemies, then back to one of yours, and so on. This applies even when one side outnumbers the other, so if you have 6 people and there are only 2 enemies left, each enemy gets to move three times as often as each of your units. This disparity just further eliminates any possibilities for actual tactics, and turns combat into a mosh pit of repeatedly hitting each other until everyone on one side has fallen over.
Fortunately for the player, the enemy units and AI are sufficiently weak (at least on the default difficulty setting) that this is seldom a problem, especially as the game has no permadeath. You just keep on hitting the enemies until none of them are standing, and if a few of your side fall down in the process then it's no big deal.
Which brings me to another problem: there are no other mission types. Every single combat is a straight last team standing. There's no "control the point" or "survive for x turns" or "rescue the non-combat units" or anything else. Just your units, their units, and yet another identical fight to the death.

An RPG with turn-based tactical combat and lots of tough decisions and moral dilemmas, old-Bioware-style. Casual gamers who just want to play for the story will find an enjoyable, high-fantasy epic inspired by Norse mythology and culture.
Plenty of interesting characters, but many of them can die in the story based on your decisions. Perma-death can also occur if you lose certain scripted battles, which adds some XCOM-Ironman tension.
Hardcore gamers who want to master the combat will find that the mechanics are like a fusion between Devil Survivor + Dofus + Fire Emblem. Turns are always alternated between yourself and the opponent, and because damage and hitpoints both come from the same stat, you must always find a way to protect your damage dealers from harm -- otherwise the battle might become unwinnable because no one is able to deal damage. Basic, common-sensical turn-based tactics still apply here, but you must learn several new tricks (such as leaving near-dead enemies alive to obstruct stronger enemies from reaching you).
Overall, an enjoyable game for the combat, story, and tough in-game decisions. However, beware of the final boss battle: on Normal/Hard difficulty, it's an absolutely unfun and frustrating fight that will seriously test your patience.

I hesitated for quite some time before deciding to recommend this game. Here's why.
1) The game claims that every decision will be meaningful, and superficially, they are. The game provides you with nowhere near enough currency (renown) to upgrade every party member, purchase items, or maintain your supplies. Therefore, you must choose carefully where to spend your renown. However, there's no way to keep most characters from dying during a dialogue/decision. Even if they are fully upgraded, if a decisions outcome is that they will die, then there's nothing you can do except return to an earlier save. Also, the number of people in your caravan has little to no effect, except in a couple of decisions, so you may as well let them starve. Items can't be sold either, so there's little reason to invest in most of them. All this just left me feeling that there was no point to anything I was doing, as the game would arbitrarily take things from me regardless.
2) The combat definitely takes some getting used to. You are forced between choosing to attack your foes armour, to deal more damage later, or their health/strength, represented by a single number, which means you can get them closer to death as well as reduce your enemy's damage when they attack. As nuanced as this makes the battles, there is never any terrain to hide behind, put archers on, or bottleneck the enemy with, so it still becomes a matter of taking your highest strength party members and trying to get the first hit on any opponent strong enough to break through your armor. There's no perma-death from battles, as far as I could tell, only a few days of recovery from being felled, so you may as well bring the same six characters until the game cheapshots them in the unknowable outcome of a dialogue or decision.
3) It's very short, on the easiest difficulty it took me under 10 hours to reach the credits. It may take longer if you play on harder difficulties, but I feel the almost random nature of the consequences would make the experience futile. If you just masterfully won a battle with your last fit character at the hardest difficulty, what would you feel when a minute later when that character dies? Or half your party leaves because the plot said they would? Or because you picked the 'wrong' option, even though there was no indication what it might lead to? Better perhaps, to play on easier difficulties, where you at least feel like you can make a useful impact on the condition of your caravan.
So why then, would I recommend a game which blindsides you at every turn, makes you feel like you have no meaningful agency as a player, and seems clearly designed to depress you?
Because by doing those three things (and with it's incredibly beautiful rotoscoped graphic style and haunting music) it oozes the atmosphere it needs to provide an engaging story and world. If winning combat meant anything significant except less time injured, you'd have no reason to try and avoid it through your decisions. If you could keep everyone alive, you'd only pick the options which kept them so. If there was enough currency to upgrade everyone, you'd never have to worry about any single character being taken from you as you'd have a better replacement.
This may be a game you will find little to no joy in, but I feel like that's what it had to be to really capture the futility and helplessness so core to it's story. I cannot help but wonder if it might have been better as an animated film/mini-series, or whether that would only have reduced the thematic power of the story. Who knows?
What I can say, is that if you can approach the game as it wants to be approached (i.e. without imagining that you can 'win' or that your decisions can be 'right' instead of just 'yours'), there is definitely something worthwhile there.

If you were looking for a return to the semi-serious roots of the earlier Saints Row games, back when Volition were prancing around under Rockstar's "videogame crime movie" shadow, then you're out of luck.
It seems that, with each five-year timeskip the Third Street Saints go through, their exploits get all the more outrageous. Saints Row 2 turned the seemingly fatal yacht explosion into something which put your character into a coma, allowing them to reuse the character customisation system they've stuck to ever since.
Saints Row The Third took Stilwater's finest gangsters and turned them into world-famous pop culture icons. Their faces were on billboards across the city and they were nigh-on untouchable when it came to that pesky thing called the "legal system".
As each game passed, Volition were - little by little - unshackling their band of psychopaths and criminals. The first two games had them entrenched within the gang lifestyle; dealing with their rivals in their quest to take over the city. The Third took Johnny Gat, Shaundi, Pierce and the rest and transplanted them into a wild action movie which, despite its inherent craziness, still seemed to fit the madness prevalent within the Saints themselves.
If you thought that the jump from gangsters to cultural icons was maddening, you ain't seen nothing yet. Following on from the "Good" ending of Saints Row The Third, The Boss (the nickname for your character) has used their deeds as a springboard to run for the biggest political office in the land. Yup, that's right. You were a mere celebrity in #3. In #4, you're the damn President.
Kinzie's your press secretary, Benjamin King is your chief of staff, Anderson from Mass Effect is your VP, there are pole dancers in every hallway and there's a tiger in the living room. The Saints have well and truly taken over.
And that's BEFORE the story's even started.
As if the difficulties of political office weren't arduous enough, the Saints find themselves gripped by an alien invasion. Enter the Zin Empire and their superpowered alien commander, Zinyak; complete with a stereotypical "Hollywood Villain" British accent and a penchant for classical music.
After laying waste to the White House, you're thrown into a Matrix-esque simulation of Steelport, the city from the third game and, from there, you mount your resistance.
Graphically, very little - if anything at all - has really changed from the third game. While it will disappoint those looking for innovation with each sequel, it does put those without cutting-edge PCs somewhat at ease. If you were able to run Saints Row The Third to a decent standard, then chances are the fourth game will pose no problem.
While there is still gunplay and automotive mayhem to be had, both take a variable backseat to the new attraction in town: super powers! Yes, because you're now in what's essentially a videogame version of a city contained within a videogame (let's see Leo DiCaprio unravel THAT one), you're able to bend or outright break most of the world's physical rules. With a little help from your resident hacker, of course.
Although you can hurl elemental energy blasts and throw objects around with telekinesis, gunplay still remains rather relevant in this game; both working in tandem to provide a deeper - if still simplistic - repertoire. However, with the ability to sprint and glide at speeds vastly in excess of any mundane vehicle including aircraft, the driving aspect of this particular sandbox has been rendered almost entirely irrelevant. Despite this, you still have access to the same vehicular customisation features as the previous game so, if you want to show off, the option's still there.
Some might say that the fourth game has utterly ruined Saints Row and all it ever stood for. But, then again, they would be forgetting that it's only in the latter half of the franchise that Saints Row has actually stood for something that was completely and totally its own.
Saints Row wasn't about such trivial things such as an indepth storyline or realism. It was about giving you a world filled with pop culture references, high-powered weapons, balls-to-the-wall action, hilarious characters and missions you wouldn't be forgetting in a hurry. If you've looked through that little list and said, "yes! I want these in my life" - and you enjoyed Saints Row The Third - then you'll more than likely have a blast with this one.
As with The Third, it's certainly more fun playing through the game with a friend (and the progress with collectibles is shared between the both of you, so those 1200+ ability-enhancing fragments won't seem as daunting) and, with it being on a free weekend and a half-off sale, this is as good a time as any to give it a bash for yourself.
