I Kickstartered this game, and it certainly has all the extra-funded bells and whistles. What it doesn't have is a good story, power balance, or the promised open world.
The extras are plentiful; interactive spells, moveable furniture, talking animals, dual lead PCs who you can RP differently. But once that novelty wears off, you are trapped within interminable dialogues, a yawn-inducing adventure goal, tedious combat, and glacial leveling combined with overpowered mobs. The goofy, constantly joking tone feels like a taunt on top of all of this frustration. So does the turn-based combat when it becomes a 15-minute slow-motion death scene.
The first big, main quest involves solving a murder mystery. Whether you like murder mysteries in video games is a matter of taste; but unquestionably they slow the game way down, as they require constant searching of a vast area for minute clues, repeated dialogues with the same NPCs over and over, etc. In this case, you are solving the murder of someone you don't know and are given little reason to care about. While it is effective at prompting exploration of the town, and spawns at least one unexpectedly odd sidequest, it gave me no emotional investment or sense of urgency to continue on.
It also did not give me much experience points, which is quickly fatal. If you wander out into the "open" world, you are very quickly killed. Sometimes it by mobs who are two or more levels higher and outnumber you 2-to-1. Sometimes, incredibly, it is by invisible, instantly fatal traps. I did a bunch of side quests, I bought better armor, I filled out my party even though it meant employing a completely irritating NPC my own PCs would never want. I still got creamed quickly.
At this point, I have no idea how to proceed and no motivation to do so. Solving the murder mystery now means passing through part of the map where my party of four faces 8 higher-level mobs. Maybe I could somehow micro-tweak my characters, but good lord, I've done that for a couple hours already. Maybe I could level by doing more sidequests, but the remaining ones either provide no further direction, just a "keep your eyes open" type of thing, or direct me into still more instant-kill areas.
I enjoyed elements such as oil and water barrels that could be broken open, and that spells would react with them. But many game structures and devices simply feel unfinished or untested. Overall, magic seems overpowered, with extremely powerful cc's and dots, especially compared to melee characters. Some new tricks either don't work or lack explanation of how they do. For example, my Wayfarer was able to speak to animals, and one offered to help solve the murder mystery by smelling "any item" from the suspects. Yet I could not find any way to make it do that, no matter what items I brought (spending still more tedious minutes experimenting).
I have read that the gamemakers recently patched fixes for some other blatant oversights, such as NPC chatter being as loud as main conversation and distracting from reading the dialogues. While appreciated, it just underscores how much further playtesting and quality control this needed. I also doubt they will be changing the main storyline or overall world design.
I was a great fan of the classic isometric games, such as "Baldur's Gate" and "Icewind Dale," that this game claims to pay homage. Those games had compelling, urgent, emotionally involving stories. They had combat that was strategic but moved as quickly or slowly as the player desired. It is much more an homage to earlier Divinity games that similarly were goofy, difficult and more or less pointless.
The makers of this game simply forgot that you make bells and whistles, you need something solid to carry them.

In the Clem focused titles, we have no idea how it'll end, until we get there.
We don't know if Clem will survive the game at the end or not.
In this title, we do, so that aspect of 'survival' is gone, the characters in this game also aren't the same level as the Clem titles, where in those games, we care about the fates of many of the supporting cast, i personally don't really care too much about them in this title.
All said and done, it's still a strong title and a must purchase for all telltale fans or even just comic fans.
It may not match the level of the original Telltale games, but not many titles do.
EDIT.
After playing the whole game, i've changed my recommendation to a no.
The game overall is fine, if a little underwhelming compared to telltale's other walking dead ( 300 days included).
The story is average at best and doesn't really answer all the questions i had about Michonne's brief departure from Alexandria and the KIngdom.
It's still worth a play, but only of real value to fans of the comics and even then, it's not great.
If you're not desperate to play it, wait for it to be on sale.
If you're looking to get into Telltale's Walking Dead games, go for the original duo first.

The Ys games are small, short JRPGs. What really makes them stand out is the combat. Instead of turn based, selecting your move from a list, Ys instead adopts a mechanic wherein you “bump” into the enemies. This is done by walking into the enemies either off centre in the first game or at a diagonal in the second game.
The games overall are relatively simple. Bump into enemies, level up, continue on your quest. If you can no longer damage enemies you need an equipment upgrade or to level some more. The story is also pretty simple in both games as long as you pay attention to where you need to be heading, otherwise you can find yourself getting one hit killed by encountering certain enemies too early.
Both games have a great soundtrack, are bundled at a cheap price and are JRPGs that don’t take 60+ hours to complete. A warning though, the bosses in the second game are more bullet-hell so make sure you are prepared.

So far I've really enjoyed this, although it's a bit short.
I'll probably edit this when a new episode comes out or whatever, so anyways:
The opening was very good and also brutal, I really enjoyed the first decision that was put in the game as stuff like that kinda just helps to add to the experience, decisions that don't matter but add to the dramatism.
One thing I noticed was that none of the characters on the boat are really that memorable, like I understand they're very minor characters but I kinda feel the game would've been better had it been just Pete and Michonne on the ship as it felt the others kind of just got in the way when I realised how irrelevant they were.
A criticism I have of the first episode is the fact that the decision's matter even less than they would've in the main walking dead series, like, going up a ladder or through a window was given as a decision which doesn't really seem very relevant, as well as the decision to either chase Sam to get the bag back or to let her run, both of which still lead to you being held at a gun point. Often what you choose to say would be more important than what you choose to do.
Another let down is one that is seen in most telltale games, any character that is going to die barely talks at all, i.e. Greg who you are seperated from for most of the episode, it kinda leads to you only caring about certain characters.
I really enjoyed the entire last scene of episode 1 as there was a lot of tension although, when Greg died I found myself not even caring due to the aforementioned reasons. The decision at the end actually felt important which I liked.
Yeah the decision at the end of episode 1 really seemed important but no, because Zachary and Jonas just ♥♥♥♥ off anyways so I mean it was kind of a pointless decision as I doubt it's going to be important later on.
Onto the second decision on whether or not to stop Pete, which affects whether you'll see him again in the episode. If you stop him he will whine at you for the duration of the episode about why you shouldn't have stopped him and why you should listen, and if you let him go, you and Sam escape on the boat without him, and although the second option leads to you not wanting him to die it's also less morally defensible, oh well.
Also the whole thing about having walkers on leashes is done really shoddily as the ones she uses immediately stop attacking her as soon as they have no arms or jaw, I think it took the walkers in the comics a while to stop trying to eat her after they had no arms or jaw, but oh well.
Plus it doesn't really account for the walkers behind Sam and Michonne (and Pete if you stopped him) being able to smell them, I don't understand why they immediately walk away either as with the logic involved in that, herds of walkers shouldn't be a thing as they should all walk away from eachother. I've kinda digressed a bit but anyways, it would've been better if they'd just replaced the walkers on leashes with the group rubbing guts on themselves.
I'm not sure if the decisions you made while climbing mattered either, I don't see why they would but climbing felt very boring and would've been better if they'd just replaced it with holding W.
Helping Sam in the house felt familiar and boring, her dad felt predictable and typical I guess and I can't even remember the other woman's name.
I saw John's face getting blown off from a mile off, like as soon as we heard about him I knew he'd either kill Pete or die in this episode. As soon as he asked to talk to me in private then walked outside I knew it was the latter.
Having to fight Randall's goons was okayish, I guess it was funny when someone got shot in the face with a flare gun, probably. But I just don't understand why the ♥♥♥♥ they were wandering around outside, instead of storming the house, where we were most likely to be. Also why was Randall in the garage with what's her name and how did he get there like if he was in the garage he would have had to had walked past Michonne and Pete, unless he walked through the house, which also wouldn't make sense but who knows.
Fighting with Randall was fun, it felt quick and satisfying, I wish the series in general had more moments that flowed, where it didn't feel like you were waiting for the next fight sequence to load (Slamming his head down on the work bench was fun because of how well it flowed).
I enjoyed the entire last part of episode 2 as I actually had to think about what I was going to say and do and the right path for how I wanted to play wasn't entirely obvious. Overall it worked out for me but I don't see it having any consequences, judging by what Randall said about Norma going to be able to find us.
The final decision was hard to make, about whether to kill Randall or not, but again, didn't feel hard to make due to Sam saying that she'd kill Randall anyways, however I chose to kill him, despite Pete's whining, so I can't wait to see what Pete will have to say about it in the next episode when he'll probably die, due to his presence for the majority of the episode being determinant on a choice you make in the first 10 minutes of the episode.
This review seems so negative but I really enjoyed the two episodes I've played so far, it's just some of the characters are so stupid, but I would definitely recommend this especially to anyone who has played any telltale game before as the gameplay feels more refined especially the combat which flows a lot better than in the previous games.

CPUCores has 4 Main Functions:
Disabling Hyperthreading: This can be useful for some games disabling hyperthreading can increase fps and performance (not all the time mind you, but for some games like CSGO). This is pretty useful in of itself as disabling or enabling hyperthreading usually includes restarting the computer and going into your BIOS
Game on Dedicated Cores Only: Useful only if you want to spare cpu usage for something else other than the game(s) that you are playing, situational but useful.
Run Game with Higher Priority: Assigns a higher priority (meaning that the computer puts the game more important than other normal priority applications) to the game and increases fps.
Isolate and Constrain the Operating System: Putting your OS to a lower priority again puts your game in the foreground and other application suffer a little bit.
There are a few other things I would like to mention though, One is that CPUCores still has it functions running (The ones you chose to run of former 4 ones I mentioned) after you close out of the game and you have to click a button to stop it and I'm sure as I have forgot multiple times and hurt performance for example when running Google Chrome or the like.
CPUCores sees your games you have on steam and can add other non-steam games just like the normal steam library with the addition of being able to change the image of the games on CPUCores.
This type of software is used for people who really need increased CPU performance while waiting for an upgrade or those guys who want every competitive edge on fps you can get.
I would recommend using Razer Cortex which is another optimization software that can edit your windows registry to optimize your game, close non essiental programs to boost your RAM/memory and defrag your games.
EDIT: Developer comment mentioning a whole new overhaul for the program somewhat soon so you can look foward to that as well as the features I mentioned.

It has been a long time since I felt I played a really good RPG. This game encompases everything I love about RPGs and haven not been able to experience with the newer blend of RPGs. These days I feel most RPGs focus too much on action. I would say Dragon Age was the closest thing I had played before the Banner Saga to the style of RPG I prefer.
Banner Saga has an amaizingly good tactics combat system, composed of simple systems that put together make for a great experience. It doesn't hurt that most of the fights it feels like there is a good chance you might not make it out. The art direction was not something that drew me in at first but it grew on me very quicly and the music score was very good. Character development happens naturally and the story is a lot more interesting than what it looks at first glance. They also employ a more modern RPG approach to story with the use of constant player choices. Although they are never easy to figure out they always have interesting outcomes that shape your story.
Overall I would highly recommend this game to any RPG fan. Stoic did a marvelous job and I can't wait to see what they come up with in the future.

The Banner Saga, it was one of the few indie games of recent memory that I was truely pumped up and excited for... I guess I shouldnt have gone in with such lofty expectations.
This is no Final Fantasy Tactics or Agarest War if that's what your looking for, those games are way deeper in terms of combat and story. The Banner Saga is very bare bones when it comes to being a turn based strategy-RPG game.
Now I know that the Stoic team is mostly made up of a few ex-Bioware guys but the story similarities between The Banner Saga and Dragon Age are eerily similar, if you've played both games then you can probably see the parrallels.
The Banner Saga is supposedly going to be an episodic or trilogy style series, very lame considering nowhere on the steam store page does it say anything about this being an espisodic/trilogy half-baked half-made un-finished game... but this is an indie kickstarter game so why am I surprised. If you were like me and expected to have a full complete epic journey to sink into from start to finish then you are in for a very rude awakening, we got fleeced.
The first part which is available on Steam, is extremely short and when the credits roll there is literally no forward progress made in the story and your left with a giant TO BE CONTINUED....
I cannot reccommend this game in its current state unless your a hardcode turn based-RPG fan, and even then this will be a bit of a stretch because the campaign is so woefully short. This game is un-finished and not worth its current price of $25.00
Personal Pet Peeve: This game has nothing to do or in common with "true" viking/nordic mythology at all. I honestly dont even see how the developers can make such a claim on the store page, sure this game might be "inspired" by viking/nordic mythology but I would use that term extremely loosely in this case. There is nothing even remotely viking'esq about this game, only a perversion of what some developer who has probably never read an Edda thinks a viking might be like, for shame.

The boss battles are unspectacular, same-y grinds; and though you get plenty of weapons and superpowers, the most powerful attack by far is to simply run into enemies and punch them. Any other strategy ends in you getting killed- unless you spawn in a tank and blow the enemies away with it, and while I appreciate that the developers trust the player not to ruin his own fun by spawning overpowered vehicles too often, it tends to be the only way as to get through most combat sections.
While the game may or may not get better later on, I just can't grind through it any longer to find out.

Steep is an amazing exploration game disguised as an extreme winter sports game. There are, of course, snowboards, skis, wing suits, and parachutes. However, these can be used as tools to discover the massive open-world mountain range as much as they can be used for time challenges and stunts. The joy of this game is hiking the back country and creating your own line on a hidden slope. Steep, in many ways, is about creating your own fun. There is no official cross country skiiing in this game, but you can create your own cross country skiing event. There is no official ice skating in this game, but I once spent 15 minutes ice skating with another player on a frozen lake reachable only by wingsuit and parasail. I once spent 30 minutes climbing a mountain and found kristib112 just sitting at the summit, alone. We waved, stood a while longer, then both base jumped off the cliff, never to see each other again.
“You cannot stay on the summit forever; you have to come down again. So why bother in the first place? Just this: What is above knows what is below, but what is below does not know what is above. TLDR: If you're a fan of South Park, you'll like this game. Controller Recommended.
Despite a troubled development (THQ closing), Stick of Truth has shown how to make a liscenced game right. Every second of the game makes you feel like you're playing an episode of the show. You could even say this is the closest thing to a second South Park movie if you want to go that far. You're the new kid who's moved into town and your new friends (and Cartman) help you learn the basics of the game. Fans of the show will be treated to references across at least the first 14 seasons of the show, and there are points that even feel like fanservice. Combat follows a Paper Mario like set up, with your partners being one of six SP kids. However unlike Paper Mario the "action commands" in this case seem a bit more forced. The custom made graphical style means that game always runs in real time, even during cutscenes. Said cutscenes glitch occasionally with either you popping in and out between shots or lip sync being slow. Trey and Matt's involvement is clear from the start, with this being the best lampoon of the RPG genre this decade so far.
Length: 10 Hours
Should you buy this: If you're a fan of South Park, add this to your cart. If not it's a bit of a tougher sell. If you're a fan of RPGs though it's worth a look.
Worth: I would say $15, but most sales I end up seeing this game for less than $8 so wait for that.

Amazing game coming from the remnants of Iron Lore, developers of Titan Qest.  Incredible the amount of content for an early access game.  Pretty straightforward ARPG with already amazing graphics and performance (use Nvida inspector to add SSAO via Diablo 3 setting and make it even more amazing) and satisfying combat.  Love the world they created and the traditional feeling, takes me back to TQ days.  Skill system is pretty basic, same as TQ's 2 mastery system with some familiar moves, hoping they add in a little more in the finished product.
Story is a little on the weak side but what ARPG isn't?  That said, I like a little bit of story, not as much as Pillars of Eternity, but a little more in the lore department would be a welcome addition.  Music is actually really entertaining, creates great atmosphere and adds a dramtic edge.  Love the day/night cycle and the weather system, something missing from PoE and D3, not sure when ARPG developers gave up on pushing visuals but both those games were seriously lacking in different areas.  Physics are a little stiff but I know the dev is still actively working player mechanics and I'm not expecting D3 level physics from a Kickstarter anyway.
I'm not a fan of MMORPG's and online ARPG's primarily because they nerf any and every build that gains even the slightest advantage, I assume to prevent everybody from making the same builds. With the double-edged sword that is Early Access, it is great seeing that it does work when used right.
It took me about 14-15 months to pull the trigger on grabbing this game, as I was not sure which end of the spectrum Grim Dawn would fall on. I am happy to say that - after being patient - this game is to me everything Early Access was called into life for.
If you are an avid ARPG fan like myself, I find it hard to make a case against buying Grim Dawn, even though it is technically unfinished. The content available presently is quite fleshed out, considering how much more there is to come. I find myself collecting an insurmountable amount of items, just so I can prepare for the next character build I have in mind.  That is not to say the game makes you play alts in order to get the most out of it, rather it is a testament to how the build diversity makes you want to experiment and gets you excited to try other things. You are free to make a 'pure' build, using ony one class, or supplement it with one or more skills/passives of another class. Alter your skills' damage type to make it mesh better with your ideal build, or change the way it works entirely, making your big AoE skill a continuous basic attack. The Grim Dawn world is your oyster.
While Grim Dawn has its flaws, like any other ARPG, it absolutely nails that which it strives to be. It's grim, very much so. Many of the choices you get to make during quests have a sense of moral ambiguity. Some more or less than others, but a refreshing breeze in the genre, which often relies on simple "Kill X mob or boss" quests as you trot down the storyline. Not in Grim Dawn. Well, at least not in its entirety. Many of these quests certainy fall into the well-known standard we all experienced. Others have you decide on lives and allow you to shape the game to an extent. You can end up with more or less people in the game as you decide on whether or not to save them. You may or may not get access to a certain item if you decide to choose a particular path. It certainly allows for you to experience a slightly altered world next time around, adding to the replayability.
But what does all of this mean in the larger scope? We all look towards ARPG's for the same thing, I would think. Killing stuff, lots of it, in order to get stuff to kill more stuff faster and/or more efficiently. Grim Dawn certainly provides plenty of both. There are lots of armor sets to collect, some of which allow you to completely change your playstyle, sometimes in a way that seems counter-intuitive at first. It's in these details that the game shows its true self. The small mechanics that could change the way you think about some of the skills in the game, which you will likely only discover a good while into the game. Are you not concerned with these mechanics? That's ok, the game lends itself perfectly to those who simply want to barge through the game wreaking havoc. It's all up to you.
For those of you who are on the fence about the game, in regards to its similarities with Titan Quest, I can only say this: Grim Dawn is no less than a worthy spiritual successor to Titan Quest. It adds plenty, from a new narrative, new classes and areas, to new mechanics and playstyles. All in keeping with its roots, and building on that solid foundation that many of us look back on so fondly. This is not the same game, but it 'was' built with the same eye for detail and the same type of devotion to the genre we know from Titan Quest. It was made by people who love the game, for people who love the game. If you ask me, that's how you get a good game. Which leads to my verdict as the game stands at the time of writing this review:
A solid 8.5/10 Highly recommended for fans, certainly worthwhile still for those with a passing interest.
If they keep up the hard work, and after implementing the announced features and planned content, I might bump it up to a solid 9/10.
BUILD 28 UPDATE
We are now a good chunk further in development since my initial review. I let the game 'ripen' a bit and have not played much since build 24, giving me a wealth of new content to play around with.
I have to say, I was not prepared for what I'd find. Including the Factions (with the Bounty and Nemesis systems), Devotion System and new class on top of the remainder of Act 3 and first part of Act 4 and the additional 20 levels there is so much to do. The ability to diversify to this extent will make this game last as long as you want it to.
The prospect of almost unlimited replayability is exactly what I had hoped when I put down my money for an Early Access game.
With Build 28 also came a much needed boost in performance, and some polish in the graphics department, giving me a buttery smooth 60 FPS across the board.
Having seen this game grow from its infancy, where Act I was the entire game, to what it is now has been an experience that has made me truly appreciate the developers. I thank you, and all the other people who supported this game. Early Access is always a leap of faith on behalf of the consumer, with a trackrecord that is not without its blemishes. For a developer to follow through on their promises to this extent has been a breath of fresh air and spark of hope that this business model can produce wonderful products.
I was reserving judgment for my initial review score, as the game had so much to grow yet. We are nearing the full release at this point, and I have only become more hopeful for the end product, as it truly feels like a full game already.
It's easily a 9/10 for me at this point and a huge recommendation for anyone who wants to enjoy a new ARPG.
There is no better time to show your support for a developer who has earned my complete trust and support. I highly doubt you'd regret it.

Pros
- Melee weapons are incredibly fun.
- Enough varation of zombie types.
- Parkour system is fairly smooth
- Skill trees make sense and you skill up by using the skill (parkour increases agility, killing increases power, interacting with world increases survivor).

Neutral
- Looting. Even on hard it feels like there is too much loot but it kind of fits the games narrative if you intend to role play. The main story happens fairly quickly and is very time-sensitive but the game doesn't force a match between the day/night cycle and the story.
- Not much variety among guns and no scaling. I get that the point of the game is to go melee badass on zombies and also focus on stealth but the guns should at least scale a bit or have a way to upgrade. Basically the only time to use guns in this game is against the human factions/characters or mowing down weaker zombie types.
Cons
- Inventory. You get a globally accessible player stash but it has no panels to filter your items - it's just all one big list. It can get tiresome.
- No food/water gauge. I would love to see this implemented (even if only on hard mode or as an optional addon).

Well folks! It's Dying Light! An extremely hyped game that people had high hopes for! And for the most part, it succeeds. First, this may be a personal opinion, but the voice acting in this game seems to be iffy on certain characters, it's just a pet peev but still for a triple A game, you need to fix your voice actors microphones, that or make them put some emotion into their voice after hearing their hubby died, mmkay? But let's get down to brass tacks shall we?
(WARNING: This will be a LONG review, with as much information as I can muster into it, so if you're looking for the essentials, you may need to find another reviewer, or maybe I'll remember to get the big things down at the bottom.)
The Cons:
1) The Parkour system could use some work, there are certain situations that a nerdy kid who hasn't been outside in a week could climb, and your guy is just like "OH Iz D@t hou we Perker!? OopSIe!" But seriously, this dude is bi-polar about his effectiveness in this parkour system that is otherwise perfectly fine.
2) HUMAN ENEMIES! If you ever wanted enemies to hate, make it these guys, for some reason these people can hit a throwing knife outta the air because they are obviously Ninjas! Oh and whenever you swing they will block it, and there is no block for their attacks and the only way to really avoid them is to use their dodge system (We will get to THAT momentarily) or the grapple, which sometimes decides not to work, and I've tested it, I'm not just some scrub-lord! There are moments where your character refuses to throw this guy with a machete off the roof.
3) The Dodge mechanic, for whatever reason, this is honestly the most useless kind of dodge system ever, there are really only two situations you'll ever need it, and in both you'll be filled with dissapointment 65% of the time. So you can move back, left, and right, pretty simple, right? Well yeah it is, but the thing is if you base certain enemies on a dodge mechanic that doesn't work properly, then you'll just be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your consumers. One of the most annoying things in this game is when you try to dodge to the side to avoid that guy slashing at you, only to find that apparently he has the arc of a Warhammer, when he's using a Chef's knife, thus rendering only going back to effectively avoid the enemies and that gets boring and still at times, does not work.
4) The ending of the game, I'm not gonna give spoilers...But do you remember Button-mashing sequences? Yeah, I wasn't a fan of them either.
5) The story, to be fair, it's a zombie game so if you bought it for a story then you're already doing it wrong but seriously I guessed the entire plot as soon as I met the antagonist, but then again, my hindsight might just be a hinderence here. :P
Finally after sifting thru the bad, and occasionally the ugly! Let's move onto the good!
The Pros:
1) You can feel like the Ultimate zombie killing machine seriously, sometimes you just get these moments where you can jump down from a roof, stab that dude, throw a knife (granted if he didn't block it -_-) to stun that guy, slash his buddy and finish off the guy you threw a knife into. Seriously, there will be moments where you feel like you own the world and I like that, so hats off to ya ladies & gents!
2) The Parkour is pretty free-flowing, aside from the few situations as I said above, you can pretty much run, jump, and slide everywhere and it helps you move around the map FAR quicker than if you had to take all the backroads and dig a hole to China to get to objective A only to go to checkpoint B with even more frustration.
3) Guns, yes, yes, guns, I know there's a huge debacle wether or not a zombie game should be reliant on guns, but I feel this game has done a pretty swell job of getting it right. They don't give you super over-powered guns, nor do they give you much ammo, thus making the player conserve ammunition, and keep to your Melee weapon as your main source of damage until you REALLY need those bullets.
4) The side quests, these things actually give you some really cool stuff! Seriously, there's one in perticular that I did and I'm still using the tools the quest provided me with, just because it was an actually effective weapon that can last me quite a while.
5) The amount of weapons, seems to be pretty expansive, there's one-handed, and two-handed weapons that both obtain different points for as you level up, which yes there is a leveling up system, which will be addressed shortly. I can honestly say that I've only had to use the same looking weapon about twice, the rest of the time it seemed to have unique features that others did not, not to mention some of these weapons look awesome! And you'll feel awesome afer you slab a battery on it, and shock that zombies face off!
6) Multi-player, as always, butchering zombies with your friends is a blast, and you'll have funny stories reffering to "Your hammer, goes in, but doesn't always come out" plus, maybe you could work in a little imagination and make a role-playing thing out of it! I dunno, I'm just spitballing here.
7) The game at night, seriously, when you're wandering around this game at night you'll feel like there is something behind you, a LOT probably because there are several things behind you, two of which are seven feet tall and have an exceptional hankering for human flesh, although after a while it won't be as bad, you'll still have your fair share of jump-scares and creepy moments (Side note! There is one quest in particular that did it really well! I loved the sequence and I think that they should try doing it more in later games.)
To wrap this up we're gonna go over the Largest points of the game starting with the bad
Cons:
-Your character randomly forgetting how to climb that fence right there that you can most definetly climb.
-Human enemies are annoying and you will want to find and kill their families (if they're still alive.)
-Dodging feels really stupid and is very rarely actually useful.
-The end of the game, seriously you guys, if you are a true gamer you'll understand the sin committed here.
-The story, although this is relatively little because it's a zombie game, this one felt really cliche.
Pros:
-This game effectively makes you feel like you are indeed the Terminator himself
-Parkour is rather free-flowing and effective at getting around the maps.
-Guns aren't OP and they don't give you enough ammo to take over Africa single-handedly.
-Side quests are actually rewarding and can give you some pretty nifty equipment, especially later on in the game.
-The Sheer amount of melee weapons, gives you a big sense of "Oooh! Which one to pick! Decisions, decisions."
-Multi-player is fun, running around a map full of zombies is fun, although the PvP mode is a little iffy at first, with a little practice and patience, it can be extremely fun and heart-pounding
-This game has an amazing ability to become a horror game withing seconds, (specifically referring to night-time) and honestly, I like that a lot because it keeps the player on edge, and makes sure you don't run around like a dingus all the time.

The main bad thing about this game is the AI. Oh, the AI.
First, the AI is unpredictable. First, declaration of friendship. Next thing you know they denounce you for no reason. It's not backstabbing either, as that would involve attacking directly. They never appear to actually listen to demands either, regardless of how strong you are.
Also, the AI is very incompetent. They often fail to attack with ranged units properly, and frequently move their units back and forth WITHIN RANGE OF YOUR UNITS/CITIES for seemingly no reason.
Lastly, the AI is a cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They get more happiness, more production, faster growth, more science than you at pretty much every difficulty. They can found cities closer to each other, see future era resources and generally get a lot more things than you do.
Still, all in all the game is very good. The AI is just plain bad though.

I saw this game on sale and thought it looked similar to Alien Swarm (which has provided me with countless hours of entertainment) so I purchased this. At first I didn't like the feel of the controls and was starting to think it was a waste of money. I perservered and plowed on with the campaign. Before I knew it I was completely immersed into the story line and had come to terms with the controls. I think the initial dislike was the fact that the first Aliens you encounter are probably the hardest to shoot out of everything else in the game.
The story line was engaging enough for my liking but was somewhat predictable and recycled sci fi adventure themes resounded throughout. There were some extremely well made parts of the game that surprised me and brought a huge smile to my face. (The part where you fight loads of Aliens inside the Rave music room is EPIC. Loved the fact when outside of the main room you could hear the music muffled in the background. Very atmospheric.) The soundtrack was absolutely awesome. The dialogue in some sections between characters was a little forced and unnatural but they couldn't just stand in silence I guess.
It took me just a little over 8 hours to complete the entire campaign and I enjoyed every moment of it. Definitely worth a buy! I did however encounter a bug on 1 chapter which was literally right at the end of said chapter causing me to have to restart that particular chapter which irritated me somewhat. It was after prepping the space ship and the automated defense robots activate and come after you. I was on around 11hp after some poor combat vs the big ♥♥♥♥ers with forcefields and guns for hands. This caused me to die despite my best efforts vs the 2 automated defense robots and when I revived I was stuck behind the 2 blast doors you needed a key card for. This meant I could not get in to kill the robots and complete the chapter. Other than that it was a solid play and hugely enjoyable.

Well.. I wish I just could write a review sooner.. But I was really busy playing the game.
To me the game is made for chilling. I just go in and spend hours without noticing.
Here's what my thoughts are by the means on pros and cons;
Pros:
1-Game is fun, whatever you do paraglide/snowboard/skii/wingsuit, doesn't matter. Game will always stun you with it's beautiful views and somehow interesting story at times.
2-It doesn't force you to do missions at all, if you are bored; go around and explore, pull of stunts and share your great moments with players, dare them to a challenge!
3-Map is huuuuuuge. Yeah, it's not huge. It's what you call huuuuuuge. There are places I yet to explore, but so far all I can say is that the game haven't let me down yet.
4-Despite it's being only online, you can send party invites (i still haven't figured how to accept the invites though) and play with your friends, or make new friends by randomly sending invites. Don't hesitate, people always like to share good moments!
5-You are not obliged to follow mission's trails (well... except it's a checkpoint one). You can always pick up new routes to achieve what the mission says, do whatever you feel like, and just have fun out there!
Cons:
1-Game is a bit expensive, even in winter sale, but it just gives back what it takes from you so it's not a loss at all. For me at least.
2-Some stunts and tricks are really hard to pull off with keyboard, so in my opinion, it'd be better to play it with a controller.
3-As I stated above, I still couldn't figure how to accept the party invites I've got. I looked up for any leads, but people claim that G key works both when you are about to send a party invite or accept it. For me, if it's working, it's 10 seconds later or around. I hoped they would make it more clear so we could actually accept the invites.
So far that's all I've countered. Thanks for reading till the end.

The first thing one might notice is that this game seems extremely similar to two other first person puzzler games, at least that was what i though at first glance. But i figured that just because it clones other games doesn't make it automaticaly bad, so i went ahead and bought vitrum anyway.
I started up the game and was greeted by a really ugly, amateurish and lofi menu screen that just screamed college project. But i put my prejudices against its visuals aside and went ahead and started a level.
The framerate was terrible despite of running on a powerful machine so i had to search the forums for a fix. i found a couple of possible solutions, none of which worked. So i was just going to have to accept the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ framerate and play it anyway.
What i first noticed was that the sound effects were really tinny, But that the music was really great. (I would actually like to get my hands on the soundtrack) and then that the level design was pretty decent. with some relaxing puzzles with intresting powers involved.
then at about level 10-15 it started to go downhill, the levels became inconsistent and less clever, the game started to go for a more platformy approach. but this was fine with me however as i like platformers too. but let's just say that platforming design isn't vitrums strongest feature.
And at about level 20 (i think) the game started to slowly become a hellish precision platformer with power crystals less and less frequent. And it wasn't the good kind of precision platformer in my opinion. as the amount of precision (and sometimes even luck) required was at ridiculous levels. the checkpoints weren't generous either.
it kind of reminded me of counter strike's death run mod. in which victory is a sight rarely seen. i also found myself having no clue on where to go and what to do. but this may be my own fault however.
I came to a point were the platforming became too frustrating for me to endure, so i stopped playing there.
So all in all i do not recommend this game, if i would describe it in one phrase it would be "Student project"

Yeah you don't need me to tell you what every other bad review has told you over the years but so thought I when I got this in the sale. I should preface by saying I really wanted to enjoy it, I mean really really wanted too but by the end, I was mad enough having spend £3 on it I'd've probably been been spitting if I spent ten. The sheer number of times you'll imagine your environment is built for a certain action and instead it will end with you plummeting to the street below is unreal. Say what you will of Assassin's Creed, at least it only tends to throw you to your death if you take a flying leap. Mirror's Edge will fling you off a ledge like an infant sacrifice if you sneeze while pressing left. My only hope for people who play the sequel is that by then the dev team has fully worked up the environment and you can just fanny about in a giant playground should you so wish. My wishlist also follows; you have a circle of vision greater than the 45 degrees of wall you are facing when hanging from it; your only options when hitting a bloke isn't a one-two punch before getting rammed in the teeth with the butt of a rifle.
In fairness, the story's alright, bit short but not awful. Non-descript villains who haven't really done something awful  except be ordered to stop the murder suspect, but who I'm going to shoot in the face anayway etc. I'd imagine you get more story -and feel like less of an♥♥♥♥♥ if you bother finding the runner's cases, since over the whole 7 hours I was playing I only came across five (I eschewed actually looking for them in favour of ending the farce as quick a possible) and at number five got a random burst of history lesson/moral patter from Faith that gave me V for Vendetta flashbacks. But again I didn't walk that road. Faith herself? Bit of a cow. By that logic she and I should get on, but instead I felt slightly more justified about the numerous times I would purposely hurl her off buildings -usually after another Stupid Death(TM)- just to hear all her bones go crunch when she met the pavement. Its pretty too, I'll give it that. Although don't play in a dark room cos otherwise it ramps up from pretty to retina searing, say goodbye to a few colour receptors, because they will be inevitably BURNED AWAY.

I can also imagine a few years down the line, after turning the saturation down (like to a dog's level of colour appreciation) playing this on Oculus Rift, cos THAT would make FPP fun, even if it will leave me in a puddle of my own sick.

Mirror's Edge is a title that attempts to be a breath of fresh air, almost creating its own genre. However, while the game's concepts and themes are incredibly interesting, some problems in execution make the end product difficult to enjoy.
The first issue is in the way the player interacts with the world - it feels arbitrary. A crate, fence, pole, or any other object might be used as a part of a runner's path in one instance, but a similar-looking item might be useless later. Oftentimes, this leads to a severe loss of pace, as getting caught on an object not only leads to initial slowdown, but will often be a cause of death.
This brings up the crux of the issue I have with the game: the concept and the game itself are at war. Everything in this game wants to be about freedom and risk-taking. Even the main character's name, Faith, suggests this. The whole story is about how these runners desire to escape the structured lives of normal citizens and experience the thrill of life above the city, free from the invasive police and government. And initially, this concept seems like it would carry over to the gameplay excellently. After all, you get to run around and do parkour, taking leaps of faith and exploring the world of the city, right?
Wrong. The game may encourage you to look for alternate routes and multiple ways of getting to the same place, but ultimately it's very linear in design. Even more troublesome, the game actively punishes you for taking risks or going the wrong way, as even the smallest failure will lead to death, meaning you have to completely lose all sense of speed as you wait for the game to kill you and respawn you. And then you get to do it all again. There are no opportunities to explore the city at your own desired pace, and far too frequently, the game throws the cops on you, meaning any attempt to depart from the demanded path will likely result in a bullet through your skull. For a while, maybe you'll put up with the repeated deaths - "Oh, I just messed up that time. Now I know what to do, so I won't make the same mistake," you might say to yourself. But after still hearing Faith's body crumble into a lifeless heap a dozen times, this desire to keep playing begins to wane quite heavily.
There's no real sense of freedom here. You're just a tourist, taking the paths the game tells you to take, trying to run them as fast as you can, knowing that any deviation from the recommended path may very well kill you and take all the fun out of it. And even when you do exactly what the game suggests, you're still in danger, as if the Space Mountain ride at Disneyland might crumple underneath you.
While the game is remarkably interesting - in its story, visual style, and music especially - I cannot say that the gameplay lives up to its promise. It may be intriguing, but I can't say that a playthrough is really worthwhile, even for all the things it does right. Although Mirror's Edge may take a leap of faith, it ultimately falls flat on its face.

I have mixed feelings about Mirror's Edge. It's got an incredible aesthetic quality, it's new and refreshing, and sometimes you feel amazingly free.
However, it has an incredibly short story mode, very little to do afterwards, mediocre combat (which I tended to avoid) and oftentimes irritating parkour. While doing some precise parkour and jumping from wall to wall can be exhilarating, most of the time it was not. Why, you may ask? Far too clunky overall. Most of the parkour was done withing buildlings, slowly ascending areas or looking for routes to move through. When you're finally outdoors, unless you've played levels before and know the intended pathways, you're likely to lose your momentum and end up moving slowly as well. Overall, I think this game is worth a try, but it's hard to justify its pricetag for what feels like a short parkour simulator.
